stemHtml: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a growing lesion on his nose. Since infancy he has had severe sunburns after brief sun exposure, and he has extensive freckling over his face, neck and forearms. Examination shows a 1-cm ulcerated, crusted nodule on the nasal tip; biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma. Cultured skin fibroblasts from the patient show markedly reduced DNA repair after ultraviolet irradiation. Which of the following DNA repair activities is most likely defective?

options.label: A
options.html: Removal of uracil bases by a DNA glycosylase

options.label: B
options.html: Correction of mispaired nucleotides in newly synthesized DNA

options.label: C
options.html: Endonuclease excision of an oligonucleotide containing a pyrimidine dimer

options.label: D
options.html: Repair of double-strand breaks using the sister chromatid as template

options.label: E
options.html: Ligation of broken DNA ends without a homologous template

answerHtml: Answer: C. Endonuclease excision of an oligonucleotide containing a pyrimidine dimer
explanationHtml: UV light creates covalent thymine (pyrimidine) dimers that distort the helix. Nucleotide excision repair recognizes the distortion, cuts on both sides with specific endonucleases, removes the oligonucleotide, and fills the gap with DNA polymerase and ligase. Loss of NER = xeroderma pigmentosum (AR): childhood photosensitivity, freckling, and skin cancers (SCC, BCC, melanoma) decades earlier than usual.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — base excision repair handles single damaged bases (deaminated cytosine), not bulky dimers. B — mismatch repair defects cause Lynch syndrome (colon/endometrial cancer, microsatellite instability). D — homologous recombination (BRCA1/2) defects cause breast/ovarian cancer. E — nonhomologous end joining defects cause some forms of SCID and radiosensitivity, not UV sensitivity.

stemHtml: A 41-year-old man is evaluated for iron deficiency anemia. Colonoscopy shows an ulcerated mass in the cecum, and biopsy shows poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with prominent tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes. His mother was diagnosed with endometrial carcinoma at age 46, and a maternal uncle had colon cancer at age 50. Comparison of tumor DNA with DNA from normal tissue shows variation in the lengths of short tandem repeat sequences. Loss of which of the following normal functions most likely contributed to this tumor?

options.label: A
options.html: Recognition and excision of mismatched bases on the newly synthesized strand

options.label: B
options.html: Removal of bulky UV-induced thymine dimers

options.label: C
options.html: Targeting of cytoplasmic β-catenin for degradation

options.label: D
options.html: Homologous recombination repair of double-strand breaks

options.label: E
options.html: Addition of hexanucleotide repeats to chromosome ends

answerHtml: Answer: A. Recognition and excision of mismatched bases on the newly synthesized strand
explanationHtml: Early-onset right-sided colon cancer, endometrial cancer in a first-degree relative, and three affected relatives across two generations suggest Lynch syndrome (AD). Germline mutation in a mismatch repair gene (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) plus a somatic second hit leaves replication slippage errors uncorrected, so repeat lengths vary — microsatellite instability. MSI-high tumors are often poorly differentiated with abundant lymphocytes and respond to PD-1 inhibitors.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — NER defect (xeroderma pigmentosum) causes skin cancers. C — APC loss (familial adenomatous polyposis) causes hundreds of polyps and chromosomal instability, not MSI. D — HR defects (BRCA) mainly increase breast, ovarian, prostate and pancreatic cancer risk. E — telomerase is typically upregulated in cancer, not lost.

stemHtml: A 32-year-old man comes to the emergency department with severe vomiting, watery diarrhea and abdominal cramps that began 10 hours after he ate wild mushrooms he had picked. His symptoms improve with IV fluids, but 2 days later his serum AST is 4,200 U/L, ALT is 5,100 U/L and INR is 3.2. The toxin responsible inhibits an enzyme in hepatocyte nuclei. Synthesis of which of the following is most directly impaired?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Precursor messenger RNA
explanationHtml: Amanita phalloides contains α-amanitin, which binds and inhibits eukaryotic RNA polymerase II, the enzyme that transcribes pre-mRNA (hnRNA). Hepatocytes take up the toxin avidly (enterohepatic recirculation), stop making proteins and die — a delayed fulminant hepatitis after an initial GI phase.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — 28S, 18S and 5.8S rRNA are made by RNA pol I, which is resistant to α-amanitin. B and D — tRNA and 5S rRNA are made by RNA pol III, inhibited only at very high toxin concentrations. C — mitochondrial genes are transcribed by a separate single-subunit mitochondrial RNA polymerase that α-amanitin does not inhibit.

stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman has had a photosensitive facial rash, symmetric small-joint arthralgias and pleuritic chest pain for 3 months. Urinalysis shows 2+ protein. Her serum contains antibodies directed against core proteins of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (anti-Smith). In normal cells, the targets of these antibodies are required for which of the following processes?

options.label: A
options.html: Addition of a 7-methylguanosine cap to nascent transcripts

options.label: C
options.html: Addition of a poly-A tail to the 3' end of mRNA

options.label: D
options.html: Attachment of amino acids to tRNA

options.label: E
options.html: Peptide bond formation on the ribosome

answerHtml: Answer: B. Removal of introns from pre-mRNA
explanationHtml: snRNPs (U1, U2, U4/U6, U5) combine with pre-mRNA to form the spliceosome, which cuts at exon–intron junctions, forms a lariat and joins exons. Anti-Smith antibodies are highly specific for SLE; anti-U1 RNP antibodies define mixed connective tissue disease.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and C — capping and polyadenylation are performed by capping enzymes and poly-A polymerase, not snRNPs. D — aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charge tRNA. E — peptidyl transferase activity resides in the large-subunit rRNA (a ribozyme).

stemHtml: A 14-month-old girl is evaluated for developmental delay. She has coarse facial features, marked gingival hyperplasia, restricted movement of the shoulders and hips, and mild corneal clouding. Serum activities of multiple lysosomal hydrolases are 10 times the upper limit of normal, whereas her cultured fibroblasts have reduced intracellular hydrolase activity and contain numerous large inclusions. The underlying defect most likely impairs which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Initial N-linked glycosylation of nascent proteins in the rough endoplasmic reticulum

options.label: B
options.html: Binding of the signal recognition particle to newly synthesized polypeptides

options.label: C
options.html: Ubiquitin tagging of misfolded proteins for proteasomal degradation

options.label: D
options.html: Phosphorylation of mannose residues on lysosomal enzymes in the Golgi apparatus

options.label: E
options.html: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis of lipoproteins at the plasma membrane

answerHtml: Answer: D. Phosphorylation of mannose residues on lysosomal enzymes in the Golgi apparatus
explanationHtml: This is I-cell disease (mucolipidosis type II). N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase in the cis-Golgi normally starts the mannose-6-phosphate tag that targets acid hydrolases to lysosomes via M6P receptors. Without the tag, the enzymes follow the default secretory pathway into the blood (↑ serum activity), while lysosomes in cells lack them and fill with undegraded material ("inclusion cells"). Features resemble a severe mucopolysaccharidosis; death usually occurs in early childhood.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — N-linked glycosylation begins normally; the defect is the later Golgi modification. B — SRP failure would prevent ER entry, so enzymes would not be secreted into serum. C — ubiquitin–proteasome defects do not cause hydrolase secretion. E — impaired LDL endocytosis causes familial hypercholesterolemia.

stemHtml: A 72-year-old widower who lives alone is brought by his daughter because of fatigue and bleeding gums. For the past several months he has eaten mostly tea and toast. Examination shows swollen, friable gums; perifollicular hemorrhages on both legs; coiled, fragmented body hairs; and a poorly healing ulcer on his shin. Hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL. Which of the following steps in collagen synthesis is most likely impaired?

options.label: A
options.html: Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in the rough endoplasmic reticulum

options.label: B
options.html: Cleavage of terminal propeptides from procollagen

options.label: C
options.html: Cross-linking of tropocollagen by lysyl oxidase

options.label: E
options.html: Formation of disulfide bonds between C-terminal propeptides

answerHtml: Answer: A. Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in the rough endoplasmic reticulum
explanationHtml: Scurvy: vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases (keeps Fe²⁺ reduced). Hydroxyproline stabilizes the triple helix through hydrogen bonding; under-hydroxylated collagen is unstable and degraded, weakening vessel walls (perifollicular hemorrhage, gum bleeding), hair shafts (corkscrew hairs) and scars. Elderly people with "tea and toast" diets, alcoholism and restrictive eating are classic US vignettes.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — procollagen peptidase defects cause a rare EDS subtype. C — lysyl oxidase needs copper (Menkes), not vitamin C. D — γ-carboxylation is vitamin K–dependent; deficiency causes bleeding with ↑ PT but not corkscrew hairs or perifollicular hemorrhage. E — disulfide bonding does not require vitamin C.

stemHtml: A 4-month-old boy is evaluated for hypotonia, seizures and failure to thrive. His scalp hair is sparse, light-colored and brittle, and microscopy shows twisted hair shafts. Imaging shows tortuous intracranial arteries and bladder diverticula. Serum copper and ceruloplasmin concentrations are low. A maternal uncle died in infancy with a similar illness. Decreased activity of which of the following enzymes best explains the vascular and bladder abnormalities?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Lysyl oxidase
explanationHtml: Menkes disease is caused by mutation of ATP7A (X-linked recessive — note the affected maternal uncle), a copper-transporting ATPase needed for intestinal copper absorption and delivery of copper to enzymes. Lysyl oxidase is a copper-dependent enzyme that cross-links collagen and elastin; without it, connective tissue is weak, producing tortuous arteries, bladder diverticula and skin laxity. Other copper enzymes explain the rest: tyrosinase (hypopigmented hair), dopamine β-hydroxylase, cytochrome c oxidase (neurodegeneration).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — prolyl hydroxylase needs vitamin C and iron. B — procollagen peptidase is not copper-dependent. D — tyrosine hydroxylase uses iron and BH₄; the copper enzyme in catecholamine synthesis is dopamine β-hydroxylase. E — glucocerebrosidase deficiency is Gaucher disease.

stemHtml: A 30-year-old man and his wife come for preconception counseling. His sister has cystic fibrosis; he and both of his parents are healthy. His wife has no family history of cystic fibrosis and belongs to a population in which the disease prevalence is 1 in 2,500. Neither partner has had genetic testing. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, what is the probability that their first child will have cystic fibrosis?
answerHtml: Answer: E. 1/150
explanationHtml: His parents are obligate carriers (they had an affected child). Because he is unaffected, he must be one of three genotypes (AA, Aa, aA), two of which are carriers: probability 2/3. The wife's carrier risk: q² = 1/2,500 → q = 1/50 → 2pq ≈ 2q = 1/25. If both are carriers, the chance of an affected child is 1/4. Total: 2/3 × 1/25 × 1/4 = 2/300 = 1/150.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — population disease prevalence ignores the family history. B — 1/25 × 1/25 treats him as a random population member. C — 1/25 × 1/4 assumes he is a known carrier. D — 1/2 × 1/25 × 1/4 uses 1/2 instead of 2/3 for an unaffected sibling's carrier risk (the most common error — the affected genotype has already been excluded).

stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy is evaluated for obesity. As a newborn he had marked hypotonia and needed gavage feeding because of a weak suck. Over the past year he has developed an insatiable appetite and forages for food. He has small hands and feet, almond-shaped eyes, bilateral cryptorchidism and developmental delay. FISH shows two copies of the 15q11–q13 region, and DNA methylation analysis of this region shows only the maternal pattern. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's condition?

options.label: C
options.html: Deletion of 15q11–q13 on the maternally inherited chromosome

answerHtml: Answer: B. Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15
explanationHtml: Prader-Willi syndrome results from absent expression of paternally expressed genes in 15q11–q13 (maternal copies are normally silenced by imprinting). FISH showing two copies excludes a deletion; a purely maternal methylation pattern means both chromosomes 15 came from the mother — maternal UPD (~25% of cases, usually from maternal meiotic nondisjunction followed by trisomy rescue).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — paternal UPD causes Angelman syndrome (no maternal UBE3A expression). C — maternal deletion also causes Angelman, and FISH would show one copy. D — UBE3A mutation causes Angelman (seizures, ataxia, inappropriate laughter). E — fragile X causes ID with macroorchidism, not neonatal hypotonia followed by hyperphagia.

stemHtml: A 36-year-old man is brought by his wife because of 1 year of irritability, forgetfulness and involuntary, irregular jerking movements of his face and limbs. His father developed similar symptoms at age 52 and died in a nursing facility. MRI shows atrophy of the caudate nuclei. Which of the following best explains why this patient developed symptoms at an earlier age than his father?

options.label: A
options.html: Genomic imprinting of the maternally inherited allele

options.label: C
options.html: Incomplete penetrance of the mutant allele

options.label: D
options.html: Expansion of an unstable CAG repeat during spermatogenesis

answerHtml: Answer: D. Expansion of an unstable CAG repeat during spermatogenesis
explanationHtml: Huntington disease (AD; HTT on chromosome 4) is caused by an expanded CAG repeat encoding a polyglutamine tract. Repeats are unstable and tend to expand when transmitted through the male germline; longer repeats cause earlier onset and more severe disease — anticipation. Caudate atrophy causes chorea and behavioral change.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — HD is not imprinted, and the mutation came from the father. B — heteroplasmy explains variable mitochondrial disease. C — incomplete penetrance means some carriers never manifest; it does not explain earlier onset. E — somatic mosaicism would generally produce milder or patchy disease.

stemHtml: A 19-year-old man is hospitalized for his second stroke-like episode with right hemiparesis and aphasia; MRI lesions do not follow vascular territories. Serum lactate is 5.8 mmol/L. Muscle biopsy shows ragged-red fibers on modified Gomori trichrome stain. His mother has short stature, sensorineural hearing loss and diabetes mellitus; his maternal aunt has migraines only; his 16-year-old sister is asymptomatic. His father and paternal relatives are healthy. Which of the following best explains the variable severity among his affected relatives?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Heteroplasmy
explanationHtml: MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, stroke-like episodes; most often m.3243A>G in tRNA-Leu) is maternally inherited. Each cell contains hundreds of mtDNA copies; the proportion of mutant mtDNA varies among tissues and among siblings because of random segregation at oogenesis and cell division (heteroplasmy). Relatives with a low mutant load may have only diabetes and deafness or migraine; a high load produces encephalomyopathy.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — anticipation is due to repeat expansion. C — imprinting depends on parent of origin of nuclear genes. D — locus heterogeneity means different genes cause one phenotype; here the same maternal mutation is shared. E — skewed lyonization explains variable expression of X-linked disease in females, not in males or across a maternal mitochondrial lineage.

stemHtml: A 2-day-old boy has jitteriness and a generalized seizure. Serum calcium is 6.2 mg/dL and PTH is undetectable. Echocardiography shows truncus arteriosus. Chest x-ray shows absence of a thymic shadow, and examination shows a cleft palate and low-set ears. Abnormal development of which of the following embryologic structures best explains the endocrine and immune findings?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Third and fourth pharyngeal pouches
explanationHtml: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge): the third pouch gives rise to the thymus and inferior parathyroids, the fourth to the superior parathyroids. Failure → T-cell deficiency (absent thymic shadow, viral/fungal infections) and hypoparathyroid hypocalcemia (neonatal tetany/seizures). Neural crest migration defects cause conotruncal anomalies (truncus arteriosus, tetralogy, interrupted aortic arch) and facial features.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — first arch defects (Treacher Collins, Pierre Robin) affect the mandible, maxilla, ear ossicles. B — the second pouch forms palatine tonsil epithelium. C — persistent clefts produce branchial cleft cysts. D — 4th/6th arches form laryngeal cartilages and muscles, not the thymus/parathyroids.

stemHtml: In a diagnostic assay, wells of a microtiter plate are coated with a purified recombinant viral envelope protein. A patient's serum is added, and the wells are washed. An enzyme-conjugated goat antibody against human IgG is then added, followed by washing and a chromogenic substrate. A strong color change develops in the patient's well but not in control wells. This result indicates the presence of which of the following in the patient's serum?

options.label: A
options.html: IgG antibodies that bind the viral envelope protein

options.label: E
options.html: Goat antibodies that cross-react with human cells

answerHtml: Answer: A. IgG antibodies that bind the viral envelope protein
explanationHtml: This is an indirect ELISA: antigen is fixed to the plate; any patient antibody specific for that antigen binds and is then detected by an enzyme-labeled anti-human-IgG secondary antibody. Color means the patient has antigen-specific IgG (prior exposure/infection or vaccination). A sandwich (capture) ELISA, in contrast, uses a plate coated with antibody to detect antigen.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — detecting antigen would require an antibody-coated plate. C and D — nucleic acids are detected by PCR/RT-PCR or hybridization, not ELISA. E — the goat antibody is a reagent added by the lab, not a component of the patient's serum.

stemHtml: A 5-month-old boy is evaluated for hypotonia, poor head control and feeding difficulty. Serum lactate is 8.0 mmol/L (N <2.0), with elevated pyruvate and alanine and a normal lactate:pyruvate ratio; blood glucose is normal. Cultured fibroblasts show markedly decreased oxidation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. In addition to thiamine supplementation, which of the following dietary interventions is most appropriate?

options.label: C
options.html: High-fat diet enriched in lysine and leucine

answerHtml: Answer: C. High-fat diet enriched in lysine and leucine
explanationHtml: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency blocks entry of glucose-derived carbon into the TCA cycle; pyruvate backs up and is converted to lactate and alanine. A ketogenic diet supplies acetyl-CoA by a route that bypasses PDH (β-oxidation of fat; catabolism of the purely ketogenic amino acids lysine and leucine) and lowers the carbohydrate load that drives lactate production.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B — more carbohydrate (glucose or galactose) increases pyruvate and worsens lactic acidosis. D — fat restriction removes the alternative acetyl-CoA source. E — protein restriction is used for urea cycle and organic acid disorders, not PDH deficiency.

stemHtml: A 48-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is brought to the emergency department confused and hypoglycemic. He receives an IV infusion of dextrose. Several hours later he has horizontal nystagmus, bilateral lateral rectus weakness and a wide-based, unsteady gait. Measurement of which of the following is most useful to confirm the underlying vitamin deficiency?

options.label: C
options.html: Urinary xanthurenic acid after a tryptophan load

answerHtml: Answer: D. Erythrocyte transketolase activity
explanationHtml: Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia) results from thiamine deficiency and can be precipitated by glucose loading, which consumes remaining thiamine pyrophosphate in PDH and α-KG dehydrogenase. Thiamine status is assessed by RBC transketolase activity (an HMP shunt enzyme using TPP), with an increase after added TPP indicating deficiency (or by whole-blood thiamine level). Treat with IV thiamine before or with glucose.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — glutathione reductase activity assesses riboflavin (FAD). B — methylmalonic acid rises in B12 deficiency. C — xanthurenic acid excretion assesses B6. E — homocysteine rises in B12, folate or B6 deficiency, not thiamine.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old man who recently moved from India to the United States for graduate school is treated for Plasmodium vivax malaria with chloroquine followed by primaquine. Three days after starting primaquine he develops fatigue, dark urine and scleral icterus. Hemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL and reticulocyte count is 9%. The peripheral smear shows RBCs with semicircular "bites" removed, and supravital staining shows dark intracellular inclusions. Decreased generation of which of the following molecules most directly made his RBCs susceptible to this reaction?
answerHtml: Answer: A. NADPH
explanationHtml: G6PD deficiency (XLR; common in South Asia) reduces the oxidative HMP shunt, the RBC's only source of NADPH. NADPH is required by glutathione reductase to regenerate reduced glutathione, which detoxifies H₂O₂. Oxidant drugs such as primaquine overwhelm this defense, hemoglobin denatures into Heinz bodies, and splenic macrophages remove them, creating bite cells. US practice requires G6PD testing before primaquine or tafenoquine.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — ATP deficiency (pyruvate kinase deficiency) causes chronic hemolysis without Heinz bodies. C — 2,3-BPG affects O₂ affinity, not oxidant defense. D — NADH (via cytochrome b5 reductase) protects against methemoglobinemia, which causes cyanosis rather than Heinz-body hemolysis. E — ribose-5-P can still be made via the non-oxidative branch and is not the protective molecule.

stemHtml: A 6-year-old girl has had lifelong anemia with intermittent jaundice. Her parents are first cousins. Examination shows splenomegaly. Hemoglobin is 8.4 g/dL, reticulocyte count 12%, direct antiglobulin test negative. The smear shows echinocytes without spherocytes, and no Heinz bodies are seen on supravital staining. Osmotic fragility and G6PD activity are normal. Despite her anemia she plays soccer without dyspnea. Which of the following findings is most likely present in her erythrocytes?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Increased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate concentration
explanationHtml: Autosomal recessive chronic nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia without Heinz bodies and with normal G6PD suggests pyruvate kinase deficiency. Blocking the last glycolytic step lowers ATP (RBCs lose cation balance and deform → echinocytes, splenic destruction) and causes upstream intermediates, including 1,3-BPG, to accumulate; more is shunted through bisphosphoglycerate mutase to 2,3-BPG. This right-shifts the O₂ dissociation curve, improving tissue O₂ delivery and exercise tolerance.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — ATP is decreased. B — NADPH is generated normally by the HMP shunt. C and D — 2,3-BPG is increased, so O₂ affinity is decreased (right shift).

stemHtml: A 5-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department after a generalized seizure early in the morning, 5 hours after her last feed. Blood glucose is 28 mg/dL. She has chubby cheeks, thin extremities and a protuberant abdomen; the liver is palpable 6 cm below the costal margin. Serum lactate is 6.5 mmol/L, uric acid 9.8 mg/dL and triglycerides 640 mg/dL. Intramuscular glucagon does not raise her blood glucose. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Glucose-6-phosphatase
explanationHtml: Von Gierke disease (GSD Ia): the liver cannot release free glucose from either glycogenolysis or gluconeogenesis, so glucagon fails to raise glucose and fasting hypoglycemia is severe. Trapped G6P is shunted to glycolysis (↑ lactate), the HMP shunt and purine synthesis/degradation (↑ uric acid) and fatty acid/VLDL synthesis (↑ triglycerides); glycogen accumulates in liver and kidney. Treatment: frequent feeds, uncooked cornstarch, avoidance of fructose and galactose.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — Cori disease is milder, with normal lactate because gluconeogenesis is intact. B — Hers disease is mild with ketotic hypoglycemia and normal lactate/uric acid. C — Pompe disease causes cardiomegaly and hypotonia with normal glucose. E — McArdle disease affects muscle only (exercise cramps), with normal fasting glucose.

stemHtml: A 22-year-old man has had painful cramps and stiffness in his arms within minutes of starting weightlifting since adolescence. If he pauses briefly and resumes at a slower pace, he can continue with less discomfort. After an intense session last week, his urine turned dark brown. Serum creatine kinase is 2,400 U/L. During an ischemic forearm exercise test, venous ammonia rises normally but venous lactate does not rise. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Muscle glycogen phosphorylase
explanationHtml: McArdle disease (GSD V): muscle cannot break down glycogen for rapid anaerobic ATP generation, so brief intense exercise causes cramps, rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria, and lactate fails to rise (no glycolytic flux from glycogen). Ammonia rises normally because the purine nucleotide cycle is intact. The "second wind" occurs when increased blood flow delivers bloodstream glucose and free fatty acids.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — CPT II deficiency causes rhabdomyolysis after prolonged exercise or fasting; lactate rises normally and there is no second wind. B — Pompe disease causes progressive weakness/cardiomyopathy. D — myoadenylate deaminase deficiency gives a normal lactate rise but a flat ammonia response. E — G6Pase is not expressed in muscle; its deficiency causes hepatic disease.

stemHtml: A 7-month-old boy is evaluated for recurrent vomiting, sweating and lethargy after meals. His symptoms began 3 weeks ago, when his parents started him on pureed fruits and apple juice. He has hepatomegaly and mild jaundice. Blood glucose measured 30 minutes after a feed is 38 mg/dL. Urine tests positive for reducing substances but negative on a glucose oxidase dipstick. Which of the following best explains his hypoglycemia?

options.label: A
options.html: Absence of fructokinase, causing fructose loss in the urine

options.label: B
options.html: Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate, which inhibits phosphoglucomutase

options.label: D
options.html: Conversion of fructose to sorbitol, depleting NADPH

options.label: E
options.html: Sequestration of phosphate as fructose-1-phosphate, inhibiting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis

answerHtml: Answer: E. Sequestration of phosphate as fructose-1-phosphate, inhibiting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
explanationHtml: Hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency, AR) presents when fructose/sucrose enter the diet. Fructokinase keeps phosphorylating fructose, but fructose-1-P cannot be cleaved, trapping inorganic phosphate and depleting ATP. Low phosphate inhibits glycogen phosphorylase, and fructose-1-P inhibits gluconeogenesis, so glucose falls after a fructose meal. ATP depletion also raises uric acid and injures liver and proximal tubules. Treatment: eliminate fructose, sucrose and sorbitol.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — fructokinase deficiency (essential fructosuria) is benign. B — galactose-1-P accumulation is classic galactosemia, triggered by milk from birth, not by fruit. C — fructose is a weak insulin secretagogue; hypoglycemia here is not insulin-mediated. D — sorbitol accumulation relates to aldose reductase in diabetes and does not cause postprandial hypoglycemia.

stemHtml: A 9-month-old boy of Ashkenazi Jewish descent is evaluated because he can no longer sit unsupported, a skill he achieved at 6 months. He startles dramatically to ordinary sounds and is hypotonic. Fundoscopy shows a cherry-red spot in each macula. The liver and spleen are not enlarged. Accumulation of which of the following substances is most likely responsible?
answerHtml: Answer: B. GM2 ganglioside
explanationHtml: Tay-Sachs disease (hexosaminidase A deficiency, AR): GM2 ganglioside accumulates in neurons, producing developmental regression beginning at 3–6 months, an exaggerated startle response, and a cherry-red macula (ganglion cells around the fovea are pale with lipid; the fovea lacks ganglion cells). Lysosomes show concentric "onion-skin" whorls. Visceromegaly is absent.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — Niemann-Pick A (sphingomyelin) also has a cherry-red spot but prominent hepatosplenomegaly. C — Gaucher causes hepatosplenomegaly and bone disease. D — Krabbe (galactocerebroside) causes peripheral neuropathy, optic atrophy and globoid cells, without cherry-red spot. E — heparan sulfate accumulates in mucopolysaccharidoses with coarse facies and organomegaly.

stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman of Ashkenazi Jewish descent has fatigue, easy bruising and episodes of severe bone pain in her thighs. The spleen is palpable 10 cm below the left costal margin. Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL and platelet count 62,000/µL. Radiographs show flaring of the distal femoral metaphyses. Bone marrow biopsy shows large macrophages with fibrillary cytoplasm resembling crumpled paper. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term pharmacotherapy?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Imiglucerase
explanationHtml: Type 1 Gaucher disease (glucocerebrosidase deficiency) — the most common lysosomal storage disease — causes hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias (hypersplenism and marrow infiltration), bone crises, avascular necrosis and Erlenmeyer-flask deformity. Gaucher cells have "crumpled tissue paper" cytoplasm. Recombinant glucocerebrosidase (imiglucerase, velaglucerase alfa, taliglucerase alfa) is modified to expose mannose residues so it is taken up by macrophage mannose receptors. Oral substrate-reduction therapy (eliglustat) is an alternative.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — agalsidase treats Fabry disease (α-galactosidase A). B — alglucosidase alfa treats Pompe disease. C — laronidase treats Hurler syndrome (α-L-iduronidase). E — idursulfase treats Hunter syndrome.

stemHtml: A 16-month-old girl has had vomiting and poor oral intake for 24 hours because of viral gastroenteritis. She becomes progressively lethargic and has a seizure. Blood glucose is 32 mg/dL; urine is negative for ketones. Plasma ammonia and serum aminotransferases are mildly elevated. A plasma acylcarnitine profile shows a markedly elevated octanoylcarnitine (C8) level; free carnitine is mildly decreased. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase
explanationHtml: MCAD deficiency (AR; the most common fatty acid oxidation disorder; detected on US newborn screening) presents when fasting forces reliance on fatty acids. β-Oxidation stalls at medium-chain acyl-CoAs (C6–C10), which are exported as acylcarnitines (C8 characteristic) and ω-oxidized to dicarboxylic acids. Inadequate acetyl-CoA means little ketogenesis and no activation of pyruvate carboxylase for gluconeogenesis → hypoketotic hypoglycemia. Secondary carnitine depletion occurs. Management: avoid fasting; give IV dextrose during illness.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — OCTN2 defects cause very low free carnitine with low (not elevated) acylcarnitines, plus cardiomyopathy. C — HMG-CoA synthase deficiency causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia but a normal acylcarnitine profile. D — von Gierke causes lactic acidosis and massive hepatomegaly from infancy. E — OTC deficiency causes hyperammonemia without hypoglycemia.

stemHtml: Isolated rat hepatocytes are incubated in medium containing high glucose and insulin. Compared with cells incubated in low glucose and glucagon, these cells show a large increase in the activity of phosphofructokinase-1 and a decrease in the activity of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase. Which of the following changes most directly accounts for these effects?

options.label: A
options.html: Protein kinase A–mediated phosphorylation of the bifunctional PFK-2/FBPase-2 enzyme

answerHtml: Answer: C. Increased fructose-2,6-bisphosphate concentration
explanationHtml: In liver, insulin lowers cAMP and activates a phosphatase that dephosphorylates the bifunctional enzyme, switching on its PFK-2 activity. The product, fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, is the most potent allosteric activator of PFK-1 and simultaneously inhibits FBPase-1, so glycolysis increases and gluconeogenesis decreases reciprocally.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and D — glucagon raises cAMP, activating PKA, which phosphorylates the bifunctional enzyme to activate FBPase-2 and lower F2,6-BP (favoring gluconeogenesis). B — citrate inhibits PFK-1. E — ATP is an allosteric inhibitor of PFK-1 and does not explain reciprocal inhibition of FBPase-1.

stemHtml: A 32-year-old man comes for a routine examination. His father died of a myocardial infarction at age 41. Examination shows firm nodules along both Achilles tendons and a gray-white ring at the periphery of each cornea. Fasting lipid panel: total cholesterol 410 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol 330 mg/dL, HDL cholesterol 45 mg/dL, triglycerides 120 mg/dL. Which of the following proteins is most likely defective?
answerHtml: Answer: B. LDL receptor
explanationHtml: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (AD; ~1 in 250) most often results from LDL-receptor mutations (less often apo B-100 or gain-of-function PCSK9). Reduced hepatic LDL clearance raises LDL to roughly 190–400 mg/dL with normal triglycerides; cholesterol deposits in tendons (xanthomas) and corneas (premature arcus), and atherosclerosis is accelerated. Treat with a high-intensity statin, then add ezetimibe and/or a PCSK9 inhibitor; screen first-degree relatives (cascade screening).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and E — LPL or apo C-II deficiency causes type I hyperchylomicronemia with very high triglycerides and pancreatitis. C — apo E2 homozygosity causes dysbetalipoproteinemia with elevated cholesterol and triglycerides and palmar xanthomas. D — MTP deficiency (abetalipoproteinemia) causes very low cholesterol with fat malabsorption and acanthocytes.

stemHtml: A 3-day-old boy born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy becomes lethargic, feeds poorly and vomits. He is tachypneic. Plasma ammonia is 680 µmol/L (N <50). Arterial blood gas: pH 7.48, PCO₂ 30 mm Hg; anion gap is normal. BUN is 2 mg/dL and glucose is 85 mg/dL. Plasma citrulline is low, and urinary orotic acid is markedly elevated. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Ornithine transcarbamylase
explanationHtml: Neonatal hyperammonemia with respiratory alkalosis (ammonia stimulates the respiratory center), normal anion gap and low BUN indicates a urea cycle defect. Low citrulline localizes the block to the step that makes citrulline (CPS I or OTC). Elevated orotic acid distinguishes OTC deficiency: carbamoyl phosphate accumulates in mitochondria, leaks to the cytosol and enters pyrimidine synthesis via CPS II–independent conversion to orotate. OTC deficiency is X-linked — expect a boy.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — CPS I deficiency produces the same picture but normal or low orotic acid (no carbamoyl phosphate is made). B — argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency causes markedly elevated citrulline. C — arginase deficiency presents later with spastic diplegia and mild hyperammonemia. D — UMP synthase deficiency (orotic aciduria) causes megaloblastic anemia without hyperammonemia.

stemHtml: A 7-month-old girl had an elevated phenylalanine level on newborn screening and was started on a phenylalanine-restricted formula. Her phenylalanine concentrations have remained within the target range. Over the past 2 months she has developed progressive truncal hypotonia, limb dystonia, drooling, poor head control and seizures. Serum prolactin is elevated. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Dihydropteridine reductase
explanationHtml: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH₄) is the cofactor for phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan hydroxylases. DHPR regenerates BH₄ from dihydrobiopterin. Its deficiency raises phenylalanine (detected on newborn screening) but also blocks synthesis of dopamine (from tyrosine) and serotonin (from tryptophan). Dietary phenylalanine restriction corrects blood Phe but not the neurotransmitter deficiency, so neurologic deterioration continues; low dopamine removes tonic inhibition of prolactin. Treatment: BH₄, L-DOPA/carbidopa, 5-hydroxytryptophan, and folinic acid.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — classic PKU responds to Phe restriction; well-controlled patients develop normally. B — tyrosinase deficiency causes albinism. D — homogentisate oxidase deficiency (alkaptonuria) causes dark urine and adult arthropathy. E — FAH deficiency (tyrosinemia type I) causes liver failure and renal Fanconi syndrome with elevated tyrosine, not phenylalanine.

stemHtml: A 14-year-old boy is evaluated after a deep venous thrombosis of the left leg. He is tall and thin with long limbs, pectus excavatum and mild intellectual disability. Slit-lamp examination shows bilateral inferonasal displacement of the lenses. Plasma homocysteine and methionine concentrations are both markedly elevated. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Cystathionine β-synthase
explanationHtml: Classic homocystinuria (AR): CBS (pyridoxal phosphate–dependent) normally condenses homocysteine with serine to form cystathionine. A block causes homocysteine to accumulate and to be remethylated back to methionine, so both rise; cysteine becomes essential. Homocysteine damages fibrillin and endothelium → marfanoid habitus, downward lens dislocation, osteoporosis, intellectual disability and arterial/venous thrombosis. About half of patients respond to high-dose vitamin B6; others need methionine restriction, cysteine supplementation and betaine.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — fibrillin-1 is not an enzyme; Marfan syndrome causes upward lens dislocation with normal homocysteine and intelligence. C and D — remethylation defects (methionine synthase, MTHFR) raise homocysteine but lower methionine. E — lysyl hydroxylase deficiency causes kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos without hyperhomocysteinemia.

stemHtml: A 34-year-old man is treated with an ovine-derived antivenom after a rattlesnake bite. Nine days later he develops fever, a pruritic urticarial rash, polyarthralgia and generalized lymphadenopathy. Urinalysis shows mild proteinuria. Serum C3 and C4 concentrations are decreased. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: Cross-linking of preformed IgE on mast cells

options.label: B
options.html: Deposition of antigen–antibody complexes with complement activation

options.label: C
options.html: Antibodies directed against fixed basement membrane antigens

answerHtml: Answer: B. Deposition of antigen–antibody complexes with complement activation
explanationHtml: Serum sickness is a type III hypersensitivity reaction. Foreign proteins (animal-derived antivenom, antithymocyte globulin, chimeric monoclonal antibodies) persist in the circulation while the patient produces antibodies over 1–2 weeks. Circulating immune complexes form in slight antigen excess, deposit in vessel walls, joints and glomeruli, and activate complement (low C3/C4) and neutrophils, causing fever, rash, arthralgia and proteinuria. It resolves as antigen is cleared.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — type I reactions occur within minutes and do not lower complement. C — antibodies against fixed tissue antigens (type II, e.g., Goodpasture) do not explain the systemic, self-limited course timed to foreign protein. D — CD8-mediated keratinocyte death is SJS/TEN (type IV). E — GVHD requires engraftment of donor immune cells.

stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman develops intensely pruritic, erythematous papules and vesicles arranged in linear streaks on her forearms and shins 2 days after clearing brush from her backyard. She had a similar reaction last summer. Which of the following best describes the effector mechanism of this reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: Allergen-specific IgE bound to cutaneous mast cells

options.label: C
options.html: Immune complexes deposited in dermal vessels

options.label: D
options.html: Sensitized T lymphocytes that release cytokines on re-exposure

options.label: E
options.html: Alternative complement pathway activation by plant toxins

answerHtml: Answer: D. Sensitized T lymphocytes that release cytokines on re-exposure
explanationHtml: Allergic contact dermatitis from poison ivy (urushiol, a hapten that binds skin proteins) is type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity. Prior sensitization creates memory T cells; on re-exposure, Langerhans/dendritic cells present haptenated peptides, and CD4⁺ Th1 and CD8⁺ T cells release cytokines (IFN-γ) and kill keratinocytes, producing vesicles after 48–72 hours. Linear streaks reflect where the plant brushed the skin.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — IgE-mediated urticaria appears within minutes. B — anti-desmoglein IgG causes pemphigus vulgaris (flaccid bullae, mucosal erosions). C — immune complex vasculitis produces palpable purpura. E — urushiol does not act through direct complement activation.

stemHtml: A 2-year-old boy has had recurrent otitis media, two episodes of pneumococcal pneumonia and chronic diarrhea with Giardia since 8 months of age. Examination shows barely visible tonsils and no palpable cervical or inguinal lymph nodes. Serum IgG, IgA and IgM are all markedly decreased. Flow cytometry shows a normal number of CD3⁺ T cells and <1% CD19⁺ cells. A defect in which of the following proteins is most likely?

options.label: E
options.html: Common γ chain of cytokine receptors

answerHtml: Answer: A. Bruton tyrosine kinase
explanationHtml: X-linked agammaglobulinemia: BTK is required for pre-B-cell receptor signaling, so B cells arrest at the pre-B stage in marrow — circulating B cells are absent and all immunoglobulins are low. Lymphoid tissues lacking follicles are small (tiny tonsils, no nodes). Infections begin after maternal IgG wanes (~6 months): encapsulated bacteria, Giardia, enteroviruses. Treat with lifelong IVIG/SCIG; avoid live vaccines (notably oral polio).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — CD40L deficiency (hyper-IgM) has normal B-cell numbers and normal/high IgM. C and E — ADA deficiency and common γ-chain (IL2RG) deficiency cause SCID with absent T cells. D — NADPH oxidase defects (CGD) cause catalase-positive bacterial and fungal infections with normal immunoglobulins.

stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy is hospitalized with a liver abscess that grows Staphylococcus aureus. He has had recurrent skin abscesses, suppurative cervical lymphadenitis and, at age 2, pneumonia due to Aspergillus fumigatus. Neutrophil count is normal and neutrophils migrate normally into skin windows. On flow cytometry, his neutrophils fail to increase fluorescence when loaded with dihydrorhodamine and stimulated with phorbol ester. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely?
answerHtml: Answer: C. NADPH oxidase
explanationHtml: Chronic granulomatous disease (most often X-linked, CYBB/gp91phox): phagocytes cannot generate superoxide and downstream reactive oxygen species. In the DHR test, oxidants convert dihydrorhodamine to fluorescent rhodamine; absence of fluorescence = no respiratory burst. Catalase-positive organisms (S. aureus, Aspergillus, Burkholderia cepacia, Serratia, Nocardia) break down their own H₂O₂ and cannot be killed. Prophylaxis: TMP-SMX, itraconazole, IFN-γ; cure with HSCT.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — MPO deficiency is common and usually asymptomatic (occasional Candida); superoxide is produced, so DHR is near normal. B — SOD deficiency is not a recognized phagocyte immunodeficiency. D — Chédiak-Higashi causes partial albinism, neuropathy and giant granules. E — LAD-1 causes neutrophilia, absent pus and delayed cord separation, with impaired migration (migration is normal here).

stemHtml: A 10-month-old boy is hospitalized with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. He had recurrent otitis media beginning at 6 months. Serum IgM is 280 mg/dL (elevated); IgG, IgA and IgE are markedly decreased. B-cell and T-cell counts are normal. A lymph node biopsy shows no germinal centers. A defect in which of the following is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Bruton tyrosine kinase in B-cell precursors

options.label: E
options.html: CD40 ligand on activated CD4⁺ T cells

answerHtml: Answer: E. CD40 ligand on activated CD4⁺ T cells
explanationHtml: X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome: CD40L on helper T cells must engage CD40 on B cells to induce germinal centers, AID expression and class switching; without it B cells make only IgM. CD40L–CD40 signaling also activates macrophages and dendritic cells, so patients suffer opportunistic infections (PJP, Cryptosporidium, CMV) in addition to pyogenic sinopulmonary infections. Treatment: IVIG, PJP prophylaxis, HSCT.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — BTK defects produce absent B cells and low IgM. B — CD18 deficiency (LAD-1) affects neutrophil adhesion; immunoglobulins are normal. C — AIRE defects cause autoimmune polyendocrinopathy with mucocutaneous candidiasis. D — ADA deficiency causes SCID with lymphopenia.

stemHtml: A 19-year-old college student is hospitalized with meningococcal meningitis, his second episode; the first occurred at age 15. He has no other history of significant infections. Total hemolytic complement (CH50) and alternative pathway activity (AH50) are both undetectable; serum C3 and C4 concentrations are normal. Deficiency of which of the following is most likely?
answerHtml: Answer: D. C7
explanationHtml: Both CH50 (classical pathway through C9) and AH50 (alternative pathway through C9) require the shared terminal components, so a defect in C5, C6, C7, C8 or C9 abolishes both while C3 and C4 levels stay normal. Without the membrane attack complex, patients are uniquely susceptible to recurrent Neisseria infection, often with uncommon serogroups. Evaluate any second meningococcal episode with complement studies; vaccinate with MenACWY and MenB.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — C1-INH deficiency causes hereditary angioedema with low C4. B — C3 deficiency lowers serum C3 and causes severe pyogenic infections of many types. C — DAF/CD59 loss causes PNH (complement-mediated hemolysis), not low CH50. E — MBL deficiency leaves CH50 and AH50 normal (lectin pathway only).

stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman has had recurrent episodes of painless, nonpruritic swelling of her lips and eyelids lasting 2–3 days, as well as episodes of severe abdominal pain with vomiting. Her father had similar episodes. She has never had hives, and antihistamines and glucocorticoids have not helped. Serum C4 concentration and C1 esterase inhibitor level are low. She was recently found to have stage 1 hypertension. Which of the following antihypertensive drugs is most important to avoid?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Lisinopril
explanationHtml: Hereditary angioedema (AD, type I) is caused by deficient C1 esterase inhibitor, which normally inhibits kallikrein and factor XIIa as well as C1r/C1s. Unchecked kallikrein generates bradykinin, which increases vascular permeability (angioedema without urticaria; bowel wall edema → abdominal pain). Unregulated C1 consumes C4 (low C4 is the screening test). ACE (kininase II) degrades bradykinin, so ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin and can precipitate life-threatening laryngeal attacks. Estrogens also worsen attacks.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, C, D, E — calcium channel blockers, thiazides, β-blockers and mineralocorticoid antagonists do not affect bradykinin degradation and are acceptable choices.

stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has persistent synovitis despite methotrexate. She begins treatment with a recombinant fusion protein consisting of the extracellular domain of human CTLA-4 linked to a modified Fc portion of IgG1. Which of the following is the most direct mechanism of action of this drug?

options.label: B
options.html: Blocks the IL-6 receptor on hepatocytes and leukocytes

options.label: C
options.html: Binds CD80/CD86 on antigen-presenting cells, preventing CD28-mediated costimulation

options.label: D
options.html: Depletes CD20⁺ B cells by complement and ADCC

options.label: E
options.html: Inhibits JAK-mediated phosphorylation of STAT proteins

answerHtml: Answer: C. Binds CD80/CD86 on antigen-presenting cells, preventing CD28-mediated costimulation
explanationHtml: Abatacept is CTLA-4-Ig. Naive T cells need signal 1 (TCR–peptide/MHC) plus signal 2 (CD28 binding B7 = CD80/CD86). CTLA-4 binds B7 with higher affinity than CD28; the fusion protein occupies B7 so T cells receive signal 1 alone and become anergic. Belatacept, a higher-affinity variant, is used for kidney transplant maintenance. Opposite strategy: ipilimumab blocks CTLA-4 to unleash anti-tumor T cells.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — TNF inhibitors (etanercept is a TNF receptor–Fc fusion, not CTLA-4). B — tocilizumab/sarilumab block IL-6R. D — rituximab depletes CD20⁺ B cells. E — tofacitinib/baricitinib/upadacitinib inhibit JAKs.

stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman with end-stage kidney disease due to lupus nephritis, who has had three pregnancies and multiple blood transfusions, receives a deceased-donor kidney transplant. Within minutes of restoring blood flow to the graft, the kidney becomes mottled, cyanotic and flaccid and produces no urine. Biopsy shows neutrophils and fibrin thrombi within glomerular capillaries and arterioles. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism?

options.label: A
options.html: Donor T cells recognizing recipient MHC antigens

options.label: B
options.html: Recipient CD8⁺ T cells recognizing donor MHC class I molecules

options.label: C
options.html: Proliferation of intimal smooth muscle cells in graft arteries

options.label: D
options.html: New recipient antibodies to donor HLA developing over several weeks

options.label: E
options.html: Preformed recipient antibodies binding donor endothelial antigens

answerHtml: Answer: E. Preformed recipient antibodies binding donor endothelial antigens
explanationHtml: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes because antibodies already present in the recipient (anti-ABO or anti-HLA, from prior pregnancies, transfusions or transplants) bind graft endothelium, activate complement and trigger thrombosis and ischemic necrosis — a type II hypersensitivity reaction. It is prevented by ABO matching and a pretransplant crossmatch; the graft must be removed.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — donor T cells attacking the host is GVHD. B — T-cell–mediated acute cellular rejection takes days to weeks. C — intimal proliferation (graft arteriosclerosis) is chronic rejection over months to years. D — de novo donor-specific antibodies cause acute antibody-mediated rejection (C4d⁺) after weeks, not minutes.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old man who received a liver transplant 6 months ago takes tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil. He has a fine tremor of both hands and headaches. Fasting glucose is 168 mg/dL (previously normal), creatinine has increased from 1.0 to 1.8 mg/dL, and potassium is 5.6 mEq/L. Which of the following describes the mechanism of the drug most likely causing these findings?

options.label: A
options.html: Binds FKBP12; the complex inhibits calcineurin, preventing NFAT-dependent IL-2 transcription

options.label: B
options.html: Binds FKBP12; the complex inhibits mTOR, blocking IL-2–driven proliferation

options.label: C
options.html: Inhibits IMP dehydrogenase, depleting guanine nucleotides in lymphocytes

options.label: D
options.html: Binds cyclophilin; the complex inhibits calcineurin

options.label: E
options.html: Binds the α chain of the IL-2 receptor

answerHtml: Answer: A. Binds FKBP12; the complex inhibits calcineurin, preventing NFAT-dependent IL-2 transcription
explanationHtml: Tacrolimus causes nephrotoxicity (afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction), neurotoxicity (tremor, headache, seizures), post-transplant diabetes (β-cell toxicity) and hyperkalemia/hypomagnesemia. It binds FK506-binding protein 12, and the complex inhibits calcineurin, a phosphatase that dephosphorylates NFAT so it can enter the nucleus and drive IL-2 transcription. Check trough levels and drug interactions (CYP3A4 inhibitors).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — sirolimus/everolimus also bind FKBP12 but inhibit mTOR; they are relatively kidney-sparing and cause cytopenias, hyperlipidemia and poor wound healing. C — mycophenolate (his other drug) causes GI upset and cytopenias, not tremor or nephrotoxicity. D — this describes cyclosporine, which he is not taking. E — basiliximab is an induction agent.

stemHtml: A 30-year-old man with HIV infection comes for a pre-travel visit. He takes antiretroviral therapy but was recently diagnosed; his CD4⁺ count is 110/µL. Serologic testing shows that he is not immune to measles. Administration of which of the following vaccines is contraindicated at this time?

options.label: E
options.html: Tetanus, diphtheria and acellular pertussis vaccine

answerHtml: Answer: B. Measles, mumps and rubella vaccine
explanationHtml: MMR is a live attenuated vaccine. With severe immunosuppression (HIV with CD4⁺ count <200/µL), vaccine virus can replicate uncontrolled (e.g., fatal measles pneumonitis). MMR and varicella vaccines may be given to people with HIV once CD4⁺ counts are ≥200/µL. If exposed to measles meanwhile, he should receive immune globulin (passive immunity).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, C, D, E — inactivated, conjugate, recombinant subunit and toxoid vaccines cannot replicate and are safe (indeed recommended) in HIV, although responses may be weaker at low CD4⁺ counts.

stemHtml: A 3-year-old girl born in India received BCG vaccine at birth. At 6 months she developed suppurative axillary lymphadenitis that progressed to disseminated BCG infection requiring prolonged antimycobacterial therapy, and she is now hospitalized with Salmonella bacteremia. CD3⁺, CD4⁺, CD8⁺, CD19⁺ and NK cell counts and serum immunoglobulins are normal. The dihydrorhodamine test is normal. When her peripheral blood mononuclear cells are stimulated with mycobacterial antigens, monocytes secrete normal amounts of IL-12, but T cells and NK cells produce very little IFN-γ. Which of the following is the most likely defect?

options.label: B
options.html: Common γ chain of the IL-2 receptor

answerHtml: Answer: D. IL-12 receptor β1 subunit
explanationHtml: Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease: in the IL-12/IFN-γ axis, infected macrophages secrete IL-12, which acts through the IL-12 receptor on T and NK cells to induce IFN-γ; IFN-γ then activates macrophages to kill intracellular mycobacteria and Salmonella. Normal IL-12 production with low IFN-γ localizes the defect to the IL-12 receptor (IL12RB1 deficiency is the most common form). An IFN-γ receptor defect would instead show normal or high IFN-γ levels. Lymphocyte numbers and immunoglobulins are normal.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — CGD also causes BCG infection but the DHR test would be abnormal. B — common γ-chain deficiency is X-linked SCID with absent T and NK cells (and low TRECs). C — CD40L deficiency causes high IgM with low IgG/IgA. E — STAT3 (AD hyper-IgE) causes eczema, cold staphylococcal abscesses and very high IgE.

stemHtml: A 22-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 3 days after septoplasty with bilateral nasal packing. She has vomiting, watery diarrhea and a diffuse "sunburn-like" rash. Temperature is 39.8 °C (103.6 °F), pulse 128/min, and blood pressure 78/44 mm Hg. Creatinine is 2.1 mg/dL and platelets are 88,000/mm<sup>3</sup>. Blood cultures are negative; culture of the packing grows gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase-positive and coagulase-positive. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of the toxin responsible for her condition?

options.label: A
options.html: Binds MHC class II molecules and the T-cell receptor Vβ region outside the antigen-binding groove

options.label: C
options.html: Cleaves desmoglein-1 in the superficial epidermis

options.label: E
options.html: Activates Toll-like receptor 4 through lipid A

answerHtml: Answer: A. Superantigen (TSST-1) cross-linking MHC II and TCR Vβ
explanationHtml: Nasal packing (or tampons) + fever, hypotension, erythroderma and multiorgan involvement = staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome. TSST-1 is a superantigen: it bypasses normal antigen processing and binds the outside of MHC II and the Vβ chain of the TCR, activating up to 20% of all T cells at once. The result is a massive release of IL-2, IFN-γ and TNF-α → capillary leak and shock. Blood cultures are typically negative in staphylococcal TSS because the disease is toxin-mediated from a local focus; desquamation of palms and soles follows in 1–2 weeks. Management: remove the packing, fluids, an anti-staphylococcal agent plus clindamycin (to stop toxin synthesis).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B is diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A. C is exfoliative toxin (scalded skin syndrome — no hypotension, mucosa spared). D is Panton–Valentine leukocidin (necrotic skin and lung infection). E describes endotoxin of gram-negative bacteria; S. aureus has no LPS.

stemHtml: A 45-year-old man with known mitral valve prolapse and regurgitation has had low-grade fevers, night sweats and fatigue for 6 weeks. He had a molar extracted 2 months ago without antibiotic prophylaxis. Examination shows splinter hemorrhages and a louder holosystolic murmur. Three sets of blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in chains that are catalase-negative, α-hemolytic, optochin-resistant, insoluble in bile and do not grow in 6.5% NaCl. Which of the following properties of this organism most directly allowed it to colonize the valve?

options.label: A
options.html: M protein that binds complement factor H

options.label: B
options.html: A polysaccharide capsule that is lysed by bile salts

options.label: C
options.html: Production of dextrans that bind fibrin–platelet aggregates on damaged endothelium

options.label: D
options.html: Protein A that binds the Fc region of IgG

options.label: E
options.html: IgA protease that cleaves secretory antibody

answerHtml: Answer: C. Dextran production
explanationHtml: Catalase-negative, α-hemolytic, optochin-resistant, bile-insoluble cocci = viridans group streptococci, the classic cause of subacute endocarditis on an abnormal valve after dental work. Damaged endothelium exposes collagen and tissue factor → sterile fibrin–platelet vegetation (nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis). Transient bacteremia seeds it, and viridans streptococci synthesize extracellular dextrans from sucrose that bind fibrin and platelets. Note that current AHA guidance does not recommend dental prophylaxis for isolated mitral valve prolapse.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A is the GAS virulence factor (bacitracin-sensitive, β-hemolytic). B describes S. pneumoniae (optochin-sensitive, bile-soluble). D is S. aureus (catalase-positive). E belongs to S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae and Neisseria and helps mucosal colonization, not valve adherence.

stemHtml: A 2-day-old boy born at 39 weeks' gestation becomes lethargic with grunting respirations. Temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F). The mother had no prenatal care, and membranes were ruptured for 22 hours before delivery. Blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in chains that produce a narrow zone of β-hemolysis, are bacitracin-resistant and give a positive CAMP test. Which of the following would most likely have prevented this infection?

options.label: A
options.html: Oral amoxicillin to the mother at 28 weeks' gestation

options.label: C
options.html: Hepatitis B vaccine within 12 hours of birth

options.label: D
options.html: Maternal Tdap vaccination at 27–36 weeks' gestation

options.label: E
options.html: Rectovaginal culture at 36–37 weeks with intrapartum IV penicillin if positive

answerHtml: Answer: E. Universal GBS screening with intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis
explanationHtml: β-hemolytic, bacitracin-resistant, CAMP-positive cocci = Streptococcus agalactiae (GBS), the leading cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis. ACOG recommends rectovaginal culture at 36 0/7–37 6/7 weeks and intrapartum IV penicillin G (or ampicillin) for colonized women — and, without a screening result, for risk factors such as rupture of membranes ≥18 hours, intrapartum fever or preterm labor. Penicillin must be given ≥4 hours before delivery to be considered adequate.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — antenatal oral antibiotics do not eradicate colonization; recolonization is common, which is why prophylaxis is given in labor. B prevents gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum. C prevents perinatal HBV. D prevents infant pertussis.

stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman has 8 watery stools per day with crampy lower abdominal pain, starting 5 days after she completed a course of clindamycin for a dental abscess. Temperature is 38.1 °C (100.6 °F). Leukocyte count is 13,800/mm3, and creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL (baseline). A stool nucleic acid amplification test is positive for toxigenic Clostridioides difficile. This is her first episode. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Oral fidaxomicin
explanationHtml: This is a nonsevere initial episode (WBC <15,000, creatinine <1.5 mg/dL). The 2021 IDSA/SHEA update prefers oral fidaxomicin (a macrocyclic antibiotic that inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase, with minimal disruption of the normal flora and lower recurrence), with oral vancomycin 125 mg QID × 10 days as an acceptable alternative. The drug must reach the colonic lumen.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — IV metronidazole is used only as an adjunct in fulminant disease (with oral/rectal vancomycin); metronidazole is no longer first-line. C — IV vancomycin is not secreted into the colon and is ineffective for C. difficile. D — antimotility agents are avoided in active untreated colitis (risk of toxic megacolon). E — FMT is reserved for multiple (second or later) recurrences.

stemHtml: A 4-month-old boy is brought in because of 3 days of constipation, poor feeding and a weak cry. His father keeps bees, and the infant's pacifier has been dipped in raw honey. Examination shows bilateral ptosis, sluggish pupillary responses, poor head control and generalized hypotonia. Which of the following is the mechanism of the toxin responsible for this condition?

options.label: A
options.html: Blocks release of glycine and GABA from spinal inhibitory interneurons

options.label: B
options.html: Antibodies directed against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors

options.label: C
options.html: Antibodies directed against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels

options.label: D
options.html: Proteolytic cleavage of SNARE proteins required for acetylcholine exocytosis

answerHtml: Answer: D. SNARE cleavage by botulinum toxin
explanationHtml: Infant botulism: spores of C. botulinum in honey germinate in the immature infant gut and produce toxin in vivo. Botulinum toxin is a zinc protease that cleaves SNAP-25, syntaxin or synaptobrevin at peripheral cholinergic terminals → no ACh release → descending flaccid paralysis, ptosis, constipation (autonomic), weak suck and cry. Treatment is human-derived botulism immune globulin (BabyBIG); antibiotics are not given (lysis may release more toxin).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A is tetanus toxin (spastic paralysis). B is myasthenia gravis (no autonomic signs, not in infants except transient neonatal). C is Lambert–Eaton syndrome (paraneoplastic, improves with repetition). E is organophosphate poisoning (cholinergic excess: miosis, secretions, bradycardia) — the opposite picture.

stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation has fever, myalgias and back pain for 2 days. She regularly eats fresh unpasteurized soft cheese bought at a local market. Temperature is 38.9 °C (102 °F). Blood cultures grow short gram-positive rods that are β-hemolytic, catalase-positive and show end-over-end tumbling motility at room temperature. Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Ampicillin
explanationHtml: Tumbling motility, β-hemolysis and soft cheese exposure in a pregnant woman = Listeria monocytogenes. Pregnancy reduces cell-mediated immunity, and Listeria crosses the placenta (chorioamnionitis, preterm labor, stillbirth, granulomatosis infantiseptica). High-dose IV ampicillin (often with gentamicin for synergy in severe infection) is the drug of choice; TMP-SMX is the alternative for penicillin allergy outside late pregnancy.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — Listeria is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins (PBPs with low affinity), which is why ampicillin is added to empiric meningitis regimens in neonates and adults >50. B — vancomycin has unreliable clinical activity and is not recommended. D — macrolides are not effective therapy. E — tetracyclines are avoided in pregnancy and are not first-line.

stemHtml: A 6-year-old unimmunized boy has sore throat, low-grade fever and marked neck swelling for 3 days. A gray, adherent membrane covers both tonsils and bleeds when scraped. Culture on tellurite agar grows black colonies of club-shaped gram-positive rods. An isolate of the same species from an asymptomatic classmate is nontoxigenic and causes no disease. The gene encoding the major virulence factor of the patient's strain was most likely acquired by which of the following processes?

options.label: A
options.html: Lysogenic conversion by a temperate bacteriophage

options.label: B
options.html: Transformation with free DNA from lysed bacteria

options.label: C
options.html: Conjugation through an F plasmid sex pilus

options.label: D
options.html: Transposition from the bacterial chromosome to a plasmid

options.label: E
options.html: Generalized transduction by a lytic bacteriophage

answerHtml: Answer: A. Lysogenic conversion
explanationHtml: Diphtheria toxin (which ADP-ribosylates EF-2) is encoded by the tox gene of corynephage β. When the temperate phage integrates as a prophage, the bacterium gains the new phenotype — lysogenic conversion. Only lysogenized strains are toxigenic, which explains why the classmate's strain is harmless. Other phage-encoded toxins: Shiga-like toxin, cholera toxin, botulinum toxin (some types), erythrogenic toxin of GAS. Treatment is equine antitoxin (neutralizes only unbound toxin, so give early) plus erythromycin or penicillin; give the DTaP series after recovery because disease does not reliably confer immunity.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B (transformation) is classic for S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Neisseria. C transfers plasmids (resistance genes) between bacteria. D moves genes between DNA sites within a cell (e.g., vanA). E — in generalized transduction a lytic phage randomly packages host DNA by mistake; it is not how the tox gene is carried.

stemHtml: A 19-year-old college student is hospitalized with meningococcal meningitis. He had a similar episode caused by Neisseria meningitidis at age 15. He has no history of recurrent sinusitis, pneumonia or skin abscesses. Total hemolytic complement (CH50) activity is markedly reduced. A deficiency of which of the following is most likely?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Terminal complement (membrane attack complex) deficiency
explanationHtml: Neisseria species are uniquely dependent on MAC-mediated lysis for host clearance. Deficiency of C5, C6, C7, C8 or C9 → recurrent, often milder disseminated Neisseria infections, frequently with uncommon serogroups. Low CH50 confirms a classical-pathway component defect. Patients should receive MenACWY and MenB vaccines. Eculizumab (anti-C5) produces the same susceptibility.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — C1-INH deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, not infections. B — C3 deficiency causes severe recurrent pyogenic infections (sinopulmonary, encapsulated organisms) and immune-complex disease. C — myeloperoxidase deficiency is usually asymptomatic (occasional Candida). D — leukocyte adhesion deficiency causes delayed umbilical cord separation, skin infections without pus, and neutrophilia; CH50 is normal.

stemHtml: A 55-year-old man receiving chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukemia (absolute neutrophil count 200/mm<sup>3</sup>) develops fever and a painless red nodule on his thigh that rapidly becomes a necrotic ulcer with a black eschar. Blood cultures grow oxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative rods that produce a blue-green pigment and a grape-like odor. This organism's major exotoxin shares its mechanism of action with a toxin produced by which of the following organisms?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Corynebacterium diphtheriae
explanationHtml: Ecthyma gangrenosum in a neutropenic patient with an oxidase-positive, pigmented non-fermenter = Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Its exotoxin A ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2 (at a diphthamide residue), halting host protein synthesis — exactly like diphtheria toxin, although the two toxins use different receptors. Empiric therapy for febrile neutropenia covers Pseudomonas (cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or meropenem).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates G<sub>s</sub> (↑cAMP). B — pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates G<sub>i</sub>. C — Shiga toxin cleaves 28S rRNA of the 60S subunit (it also stops protein synthesis, but by a different mechanism — the trap). E — the black eschar mimics anthrax, but anthrax edema factor is an adenylate cyclase and lethal factor is a protease that cleaves MAPKK; the laboratory features here are of a gram-negative rod.

stemHtml: A 6-year-old girl has had abdominal cramps and bloody diarrhea for 3 days, beginning 2 days after eating an undercooked hamburger at a barbecue. She is afebrile and mildly dehydrated. Stool culture on sorbitol-MacConkey agar shows colorless colonies, and a stool Shiga toxin assay is positive. Hemoglobin is 12.1 g/dL, platelets 210,000/mm<sup>3</sup>, and creatinine 0.4 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.html: Intravenous isotonic fluids and serial monitoring of blood counts and creatinine, without antibiotics

answerHtml: Answer: B. Supportive care with fluids and monitoring; avoid antibiotics
explanationHtml: Sorbitol-nonfermenting, Shiga toxin–producing E. coli O157:H7 (STEC). Antibiotics (especially TMP-SMX, β-lactams and fluoroquinolones) can induce phage-mediated toxin release and are associated with a higher risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome, which develops in ~15% of young children 5–10 days after diarrhea begins. Early isotonic volume expansion reduces the risk and severity of HUS-related renal injury. Monitor CBC (hemolysis with schistocytes, thrombocytopenia) and creatinine.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, C, E — antibiotics do not shorten STEC illness and increase HUS risk. D — antimotility agents prolong toxin exposure and increase HUS and neurologic complications.

stemHtml: Public health officials investigate a cluster of febrile illness among patrons of a small restaurant. The cook, a 38-year-old woman, had a prolonged fever with abdominal pain 2 years ago while visiting relatives in India. She is now asymptomatic, but repeated stool cultures grow motile, lactose-nonfermenting, H<sub>2</sub>S-producing gram-negative rods that express a Vi capsular antigen. Ultrasonography shows multiple gallstones. In which of the following sites does the organism most likely persist?

options.label: A
options.html: Peyer patches of the terminal ileum

answerHtml: Answer: B. Gallbladder
explanationHtml: Salmonella Typhi (Vi antigen, H2S+, motile) has humans as its only reservoir. About 1–5% of patients become chronic carriers (excretion >1 year), mostly women with gallstones; bacteria form biofilms on gallstones and are shed in bile — the "Typhoid Mary" scenario. Management is prolonged fluoroquinolone (if susceptible) or other agent; cholecystectomy may be needed. Chronic carriage is also linked to gallbladder carcinoma.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — Peyer patches are invaded during acute infection (ulceration, perforation in week 3) but are not the carrier site. C — bone marrow culture is the most sensitive diagnostic specimen in acute typhoid, not the carriage site. D — mesenteric nodes are involved acutely. E — urinary carriage occurs mainly with schistosomiasis (S. haematobium) of the bladder, not with gallstones.

stemHtml: A 64-year-old man who smokes returns from a 10-day cruise with fever, nonproductive cough, watery diarrhea and confusion. Temperature is 39.6 °C (103.3 °F), and pulse is 88/min. Serum sodium is 127 mEq/L and AST is 96 U/L. Chest radiography shows right lower lobe consolidation. A sputum Gram stain shows many neutrophils but few organisms. Isolation of the most likely pathogen requires a medium supplemented with which of the following?

options.label: E
options.html: Charcoal, yeast extract, L-cysteine and iron

answerHtml: Answer: E. Buffered charcoal yeast extract with cysteine and iron
explanationHtml: Legionnaires disease: aerosolized water (cruise ship, hotel, cooling tower), older smoker, pneumonia with high fever, relative bradycardia, GI symptoms, hyponatremia, elevated transaminases and confusion. Legionella stains poorly with Gram stain (silver stain) and requires cysteine and iron to grow. The urinary antigen test (serogroup 1) is the fastest diagnostic test. Treatment: azithromycin or levofloxacin (intracellular penetration); β-lactams are ineffective.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — chocolate agar for H. influenzae. B — Thayer–Martin for Neisseria. C — tellurite for C. diphtheriae. D — Löwenstein–Jensen for mycobacteria.

stemHtml: A 40-year-old man has epigastric pain that improves with meals and worsens 2–3 hours afterward. Endoscopy shows a duodenal ulcer. Antral biopsy shows curved gram-negative rods in the mucus layer, and a rapid urease test on the specimen is positive. The enzyme detected by this test helps the organism survive in the stomach primarily by which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Generating ammonia that neutralizes acid in its microenvironment

options.label: B
options.html: Degrading hydrogen peroxide released by neutrophils

options.label: C
options.html: Cleaving secretory IgA on the mucosal surface

options.label: D
options.html: Converting fibrinogen to fibrin around the bacteria

options.label: E
options.html: Polymerizing host actin to spread between cells

answerHtml: Answer: A. Urease → ammonia buffers gastric acid
explanationHtml: H. pylori urease hydrolyzes urea to ammonia and CO2; ammonia buffers the local pH, allowing the organism to reach the mucus layer with its flagella and to adhere to epithelium. Ammonia is also directly toxic to epithelial cells. Breath test: ingested labeled urea → labeled CO2 exhaled. Antral-predominant gastritis ↑gastrin and acid → duodenal ulcer. First-line therapy in the US is bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days (ACG 2024).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B is catalase (H. pylori is catalase-positive, but that is not the urease test). C is IgA protease (Neisseria, H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae). D is coagulase (S. aureus). E is actin-based cell-to-cell spread (ActA in Listeria; IcsA in Shigella).

stemHtml: A 52-year-old man with alcohol use disorder and poor dentition has had fever, weight loss and foul-smelling sputum for 3 weeks. Chest radiography shows a thick-walled cavity with an air-fluid level in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe. Sputum Gram stain shows mixed flora. A medical student suggests adding gentamicin. Which of the following best explains why gentamicin would be ineffective against the most likely pathogens?

options.label: B
options.html: The organisms lack a 30S ribosomal subunit

options.label: C
options.html: β-lactamases in abscess fluid hydrolyze aminoglycosides

options.label: D
options.html: Aminoglycoside entry into bacteria requires oxygen-dependent active transport

options.label: E
options.html: The organisms constitutively methylate the 16S rRNA binding site

answerHtml: Answer: D. Oxygen-dependent uptake
explanationHtml: Aspiration while intoxicated + poor dentition + putrid sputum + cavity in a dependent segment = anaerobic lung abscess (Peptostreptococcus, Prevotella, Fusobacterium, Bacteroides). Aminoglycosides are cations that cross the cytoplasmic membrane by a process driven by the proton-motive force of aerobic respiration; obligate anaerobes lack it, so they are intrinsically resistant. The acidic, hypoxic environment of abscesses further reduces aminoglycoside activity. Treat with ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin (or amoxicillin-clavulanate orally) for weeks.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — all bacteria except Mycoplasma (and Chlamydia, which lacks classic muramic acid) have peptidoglycan; and aminoglycosides do not target it anyway. B — all bacteria have 70S ribosomes (30S + 50S). C — β-lactamases do not hydrolyze aminoglycosides; aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes are acetyl-, adenyl- and phosphotransferases. E — 16S rRNA methyltransferases are acquired resistance genes in some gram-negative rods, not the intrinsic mechanism in anaerobes.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old man who has sex with men had a painless penile ulcer 6 weeks ago that healed. He now has a diffuse nonpruritic maculopapular rash involving his palms and soles. RPR titer is 1:64 and a treponemal antibody test is positive. He receives benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM.
