Five hours later he develops fever to 39.0 °C (102.2 °F), rigors, headache and myalgias; pulse is 112/min and blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg. The rash appears more prominent. There is no urticaria, wheezing or angioedema. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

options.label: C
options.html: Cytokine release triggered by lipoproteins from killed spirochetes

answerHtml: Answer: C. Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction
explanationHtml: The Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction occurs within 24 hours (typically 2–8 hours) of treating spirochetal infections, most often secondary syphilis. Lysed treponemes release lipoproteins that activate macrophages (via TLR2) to release TNF-α, IL-6 and IL-8. It is self-limited (<24 h); treat with antipyretics and reassure. Warn pregnant women: it can trigger preterm labor or fetal distress, but treatment must not be withheld.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — anaphylaxis occurs within minutes with urticaria, bronchospasm and hypotension. B — serum sickness appears 1–2 weeks after exposure, with arthralgia and urticarial rash. D — Hoigné syndrome is caused by procaine penicillin (not benzathine) and presents with immediate anxiety, hallucinations and fear of death. E — neurosyphilis does not develop within hours and does not cause fever and rigors.

stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman from Connecticut develops fatigue, myalgias and an expanding, warm, erythematous patch on her thigh 10 days after a weekend hike in June. The lesion is now 12 cm across with central clearing. She does not recall a tick bite. The vector responsible for this infection can also transmit which of the following pathogens?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Babesia microti
explanationHtml: Erythema migrans in a Northeastern hiker = early localized Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi), a clinical diagnosis treated with doxycycline without waiting for serology. The vector, Ixodes scapularis, also transmits Babesia microti, Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Borrelia miyamotoi and Powassan virus. Co-infection should be suspected when a Lyme patient has high fevers, anemia/hemolysis, leukopenia or thrombocytopenia, or fails to improve on doxycycline (which does not treat Babesia).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — RMSF is transmitted by Dermacentor (and Rhipicephalus) ticks. B — E. chaffeensis is transmitted by the lone star tick (Amblyomma americanum). C — tularemia is transmitted by Dermacentor/Amblyomma ticks, deer flies, and contact with rabbits. E — plague is transmitted by rodent fleas.

stemHtml: A 5-year-old boy in North Carolina is brought to the emergency department in July with 3 days of fever to 40 °C (104 °F), severe headache and myalgias. A blanching maculopapular rash began on his wrists and ankles yesterday and now involves his palms, soles and trunk. The family dog often has ticks. Platelets are 85,000/mm<sup>3</sup> and sodium is 129 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

options.label: D
options.html: Chloramphenicol, because doxycycline is contraindicated under age 8

answerHtml: Answer: B. Doxycycline
explanationHtml: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (R. rickettsii): Dermacentor tick exposure in the South-central/Southeastern US in summer, fever and headache, then a rash that begins on wrists and ankles and spreads centripetally to palms, soles and trunk; thrombocytopenia and hyponatremia from vasculitis. Mortality rises steeply if treatment is delayed beyond day 5. The CDC and AAP recommend doxycycline for patients of all ages; short courses do not cause clinically significant tooth staining.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — serology is often negative early; treat empirically on clinical suspicion. C and E — β-lactams have no activity against obligate intracellular rickettsiae (ceftriaxone would be reasonable only as an addition if meningococcemia were also suspected). D — chloramphenicol is associated with higher mortality in RMSF and causes aplastic anemia; age is not a contraindication to doxycycline here.

stemHtml: A 26-year-old physician who completed medical school in India is beginning residency in the United States. She received BCG vaccine at birth. She is asymptomatic and has a normal examination. As part of occupational health screening for tuberculosis, which of the following is the most appropriate test?

options.label: A
options.html: Tuberculin skin test, interpreting ≥15 mm induration as positive because of prior BCG

options.label: C
options.html: Sputum acid-fast smears on 3 consecutive mornings

options.label: D
options.html: No testing, because BCG provides lifelong protection

answerHtml: Answer: E. IGRA
explanationHtml: IGRAs (QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus, T-SPOT.TB) measure T-cell IFN-γ release to ESAT-6 and CFP-10, antigens encoded in the RD1 region that is absent from BCG strains and most nontuberculous mycobacteria. They are therefore preferred in BCG-vaccinated individuals and require only one visit. If positive, the next step is a chest radiograph; if normal and asymptomatic → treat LTBI (e.g., 3HP or 4R).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — a TST may be used, but BCG causes false positives, and the correct cutoff for a recent immigrant from a high-burden country or a health care worker is ≥10 mm; BCG history does not change the cutoff. B — CXR detects active disease but cannot identify LTBI. C — sputum testing is for suspected active TB. D — BCG mainly protects children against disseminated/meningeal TB; it does not prevent adult infection or reactivation.

stemHtml: A 45-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and alcohol use disorder has been taking rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for pulmonary tuberculosis for 2 months. He reports burning pain and numbness in both feet. Ankle reflexes are diminished. Hemoglobin is 10.8 g/dL with a low MCV, and a bone marrow aspirate shows ringed sideroblasts. Coadministration of which of the following would most likely have prevented these findings?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Pyridoxine (vitamin B6)
explanationHtml: Isoniazid is structurally similar to pyridoxine; it forms hydrazones with pyridoxal and increases its urinary excretion, and it inhibits pyridoxine phosphokinase. B6 (as pyridoxal phosphate) is a cofactor for δ-aminolevulinic acid synthase (heme synthesis → sideroblastic anemia when deficient) and for neurotransmitter synthesis (→ peripheral neuropathy, seizures). Risk is highest in diabetes, alcohol use, malnutrition, HIV, CKD, pregnancy and slow acetylators — all should receive pyridoxine 25–50 mg daily with INH.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — thiamine deficiency causes dry/wet beriberi and Wernicke encephalopathy, not sideroblastic anemia. C and D — B12 and folate deficiencies cause macrocytic (megaloblastic) anemia. E — INH-induced B6 depletion can cause pellagra (B6 is needed to make niacin from tryptophan), but niacin would not prevent the neuropathy or sideroblastic anemia.

stemHtml: A 23-year-old woman with a positive interferon-γ release assay and a normal chest radiograph completes 4 months of daily rifampin. Throughout treatment she took a combined estrogen-progestin oral contraceptive pill daily without missing doses. She now has a positive pregnancy test. Which of the following best explains the contraceptive failure?

options.label: A
options.html: Inhibition of hepatic CYP3A4, causing accumulation of inactive metabolites

options.label: B
options.html: Chelation of ethinyl estradiol in the gut, decreasing absorption

options.label: C
options.html: Induction of hepatic CYP3A4, accelerating metabolism of the contraceptive steroids

options.label: D
options.html: Increased renal tubular secretion of the hormones

options.label: E
options.html: Displacement of the hormones from sex hormone–binding globulin

answerHtml: Answer: C. CYP3A4 induction
explanationHtml: Rifampin activates the pregnane X receptor (PXR), increasing transcription of CYP3A4 (and 2C9, 2C19, UGTs and P-glycoprotein). This markedly lowers ethinyl estradiol and progestin levels, causing contraceptive failure. Women on rifamycins should use a non-hormonal method or a levonorgestrel/copper IUD or depot medroxyprogesterone. The same mechanism lowers warfarin, azoles, protease inhibitors, tacrolimus and methadone levels.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — inhibitors (azoles, macrolides, ritonavir, grapefruit) raise drug levels. B — chelation is a tetracycline/fluoroquinolone interaction with cations, not with steroids. D — rifampin does not increase renal clearance of contraceptive steroids. E — protein-binding displacement causes only transient changes in free drug and is not clinically relevant here.

stemHtml: A 30-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV-1 infection. CD4+ count is 420/mm<sup>3</sup> and HIV RNA is 85,000 copies/mL. HLA-B*57:01 testing is negative and HBsAg is negative. He is started on a single-tablet regimen of bictegravir, emtricitabine and tenofovir alafenamide. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of bictegravir?

options.label: A
options.html: Nucleoside analog that terminates viral DNA chain elongation

options.label: B
options.html: Binds a hydrophobic allosteric pocket of reverse transcriptase

options.label: C
options.html: Blocks cleavage of the gag-pol polyprotein

options.label: D
options.html: Binds CCR5 to prevent gp120 interaction

options.label: E
options.html: Blocks the strand-transfer step of insertion of viral DNA into the host genome

answerHtml: Answer: E. Integrase strand transfer inhibitor
explanationHtml: Bictegravir (like dolutegravir, raltegravir and cabotegravir) binds the integrase active site with its Mg2+ cofactors and blocks strand transfer of proviral DNA into host chromosomes. INSTI + 2 NRTIs is the preferred initial regimen (DHHS) because of potency, a high barrier to resistance and tolerability. Counsel patients to separate doses from antacids, iron or calcium supplements (polyvalent cations chelate INSTIs).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A describes emtricitabine and tenofovir (NRTIs) in the same tablet. B describes NNRTIs (efavirenz, rilpivirine, doravirine). C describes protease inhibitors (darunavir). D describes maraviroc.

stemHtml: A 37-year-old man with HIV infection is being considered for a once-daily single-tablet regimen of dolutegravir, abacavir and lamivudine. Testing for which of the following is required before this regimen is started?
answerHtml: Answer: C. HLA-B*57:01
explanationHtml: Abacavir causes a potentially fatal multisystem hypersensitivity reaction (fever, rash, GI and respiratory symptoms) within the first 6 weeks, almost exclusively in carriers of HLA-B*57:01; abacavir binds the peptide-binding groove of this HLA molecule, altering the repertoire of self-peptides presented to T cells. Patients who test positive must never receive abacavir, and rechallenge after a reaction is contraindicated. HBV status is also checked because lamivudine alone would be inadequate HBV therapy.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — HLA-B27 is associated with seronegative spondyloarthropathies. B — HLA-B*15:02 predicts carbamazepine (and phenytoin) SJS/TEN in South and Southeast Asian patients — relevant to her patients from India, but not to abacavir. D — HLA-DR4 relates to rheumatoid arthritis and type 1 diabetes. E — G6PD testing is needed before primaquine, dapsone or rasburicase.

stemHtml:
A 29-year-old man had malaise, dark urine and jaundice 10 weeks ago; he now feels better. ALT has fallen from 1,450 U/L to 180 U/L. Serologic testing shows:
HBsAgnegative
Anti-HBsnegative
IgM anti-HBcpositive
HBeAgnegative
Anti-HBepositive
Which of the following is the most likely interpretation?

options.label: A
options.html: Chronic hepatitis B infection with low replication

options.label: B
options.html: Window period of acute hepatitis B infection

options.label: E
options.html: Acute hepatitis B infection with high infectivity

answerHtml: Answer: B. Window period
explanationHtml: In the window period, HBsAg has been cleared but anti-HBs is not yet detectable; IgM anti-HBc is the only marker that reveals recent infection (anti-HBe often appears as HBeAg is cleared). This is why blood banks test for anti-HBc. Over the following weeks anti-HBs should appear, and IgM anti-HBc will be replaced by IgG anti-HBc.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — chronic infection requires HBsAg positivity for >6 months. C — vaccination produces anti-HBs only; anti-HBc remains negative because the vaccine contains only HBsAg. D — resolved infection shows anti-HBs + and IgG (not IgM) anti-HBc. E — acute infection with high infectivity would show HBsAg + and HBeAg +.

stemHtml: A 32-year-old man who injects drugs has had HBsAg-positive chronic hepatitis B for 6 years with stable mildly elevated aminotransferases. He now presents with sudden jaundice, confusion and an INR of 2.6. IgM antibody to hepatitis D virus is positive. The superinfecting virus depends on the coinfecting hepatitis B virus to provide which of the following?
answerHtml: Answer: A. HBsAg envelope
explanationHtml: HDV is a defective satellite virus with a small circular (−) ssRNA genome and a single protein, hepatitis delta antigen. It replicates its genome using host RNA polymerase II (rolling-circle replication with ribozyme self-cleavage), but it cannot make an envelope; it is packaged in HBsAg supplied by HBV (a form of complementation). It therefore can infect only people with HBV — simultaneously (coinfection, usually resolves) or on top of chronic HBV (superinfection, often severe, fulminant or rapidly cirrhotic as here). HBV vaccination prevents HDV.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — HDV does not use reverse transcription; RT is required by HBV itself. C — HDV uses host RNA polymerase II, not a viral RdRp supplied by HBV (HBV has none). D — HDV RNA is packaged with delta antigen, not HBV core. E — neither virus uses an integrase (HBV DNA integrates randomly by host mechanisms).

stemHtml: A 41-year-old man with AIDS (CD4+ count 35/mm<sup>3</sup>) has extensive painful perianal ulcers that have enlarged despite 3 weeks of high-dose valacyclovir. PCR of the lesions is positive for HSV-2, and genotypic testing shows a mutation in the viral thymidine kinase gene. Which of the following is the most appropriate next drug?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Foscarnet
explanationHtml: Acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir/penciclovir and ganciclovir all require initial monophosphorylation by HSV thymidine kinase. TK-deficient or TK-altered mutants (the usual resistance mechanism in immunocompromised hosts) are cross-resistant to all of them. Foscarnet, a pyrophosphate analog, binds viral DNA polymerase directly and needs no activation. Monitor creatinine and electrolytes (hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, phosphate abnormalities — seizures). Cidofovir (a nucleotide analog needing no viral kinase) is another option.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B and C all depend on viral TK for activation — higher doses do not overcome a TK mutation. E — ribavirin has no meaningful activity against HSV.

stemHtml: A 44-year-old man with AIDS (CD4+ count 22/mm<sup>3</sup>) reports floaters and blurred vision in his right eye. Funduscopy shows perivascular yellow-white retinal infiltrates with flame hemorrhages. He is started on intravenous ganciclovir. Which of the following laboratory parameters should be monitored most closely for the major dose-limiting toxicity of this drug?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Absolute neutrophil count
explanationHtml: CMV retinitis ("pizza-pie" or "cottage cheese and ketchup" fundus) occurs at CD4 <50. Ganciclovir (activated by the CMV UL97 kinase, then inhibits viral DNA polymerase) is also incorporated by host cells, causing dose-limiting myelosuppression — neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia. Monitor CBC 2–3 times weekly during induction; G-CSF or switching to foscarnet may be needed. Zidovudine and other marrow-toxic drugs (TMP-SMX, valganciclovir, flucytosine) add to the effect. Doses are also renally adjusted.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — hypomagnesemia is a toxicity of foscarnet (and amphotericin B). C — hyperuricemia is caused by pyrazinamide and tumor lysis. D — elevated CK is characteristic of daptomycin, raltegravir and zidovudine myopathy. E — pancreatitis is associated with didanosine and stavudine (older NRTIs) and pentamidine.

stemHtml: An 18-year-old college student has fever, severe sore throat with tonsillar exudates, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and a palpable spleen tip. He was prescribed amoxicillin and 2 days later developed a diffuse pruritic maculopapular rash. Peripheral smear shows many large lymphocytes with abundant cytoplasm, and a heterophile antibody test is positive. The causative virus enters its primary target cells by binding which of the following?
answerHtml: Answer: D. CD21
explanationHtml: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV). The EBV envelope glycoprotein gp350 binds CD21 (CR2, the C3d receptor) on B cells; HLA class II is the coreceptor. The "atypical lymphocytes" are reactive cytotoxic CD8+ T cells responding to infected B cells. The amoxicillin rash is an immune reaction during EBV infection, not a lifelong penicillin allergy. Advise avoiding contact sports for at least 3–4 weeks (splenic rupture).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — CD4 (with CCR5/CXCR4) is the HIV receptor (HHV-7 also uses CD4). B — ICAM-1 is the receptor for most rhinoviruses. C — P antigen is the receptor for parvovirus B19. E — ACE2 is the SARS-CoV-2 receptor.

stemHtml: An 8-year-old girl with sickle cell disease has 3 days of fatigue and pallor. Hemoglobin is 4.8 g/dL (baseline 8.0 g/dL) and the reticulocyte count is 0.1%. Her younger brother had bright red cheeks and a lacy rash on his arms last week. Which of the following best describes the genome of the most likely causative virus?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Single-stranded linear DNA, nonenveloped
explanationHtml: Transient aplastic crisis in a patient with chronic hemolysis, with exposure to erythema infectiosum ("slapped cheek", fifth disease) = parvovirus B19. B19 is the only medically important ssDNA virus; it is small and naked. It binds P antigen on erythroid progenitors and replicates in dividing cells, arresting erythropoiesis for ~1 week — tolerable in normal people (RBC lifespan 120 days), catastrophic when RBC survival is 10–20 days. Treat with transfusion; immunocompromised patients with chronic infection get IVIG.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B describes herpesviruses and poxviruses. C describes HBV (hepadnavirus). D describes rotavirus (reovirus). E describes picornaviruses (e.g., enteroviruses, HAV) and caliciviruses.

stemHtml: A novel influenza A strain spreads worldwide, causing severe illness in young adults who had antibodies against all recently circulating seasonal strains. Genetic analysis shows that the isolate's hemagglutinin gene is derived from an avian influenza virus, while its other gene segments match a circulating human strain. Pigs on nearby farms were found to be infected with both viruses. Which of the following processes generated this strain?

options.label: A
options.html: Accumulation of point mutations in the hemagglutinin gene

options.label: B
options.html: Complementation by a defective coinfecting virus

options.label: D
options.html: Crossover recombination within a single RNA segment

options.label: E
options.html: Reassortment of genome segments in a coinfected host cell

answerHtml: Answer: E. Reassortment (antigenic shift)
explanationHtml: Influenza A has 8 RNA segments. When a single cell (classically in pigs, which carry both avian α2,3- and human α2,6-sialic acid receptors) is infected by two different strains, progeny can package segments from both parents. Acquiring a new HA (and/or NA) subtype to which the population has no immunity = antigenic shift → pandemics (1957, 1968, 2009 H1N1 — a triple reassortant). Only influenza A undergoes shift because it has animal reservoirs.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A is antigenic drift (seasonal epidemics, partial immunity remains). B — complementation is functional help without genetic exchange (e.g., HDV and HBV). C — phenotypic mixing gives progeny a coat from another virus temporarily; the genome is unchanged, so the next generation reverts. D — homologous recombination within segments is rare in influenza and does not explain an intact avian HA segment combined with human segments.

stemHtml: A 35-year-old man from Kentucky has had fever, nonproductive cough and fatigue for 2 weeks. Three weeks ago he explored a cave inhabited by bats. Chest radiography shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with scattered small nodules. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows small (2–4 µm) oval budding yeasts within alveolar macrophages. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Histoplasma capsulatum
explanationHtml: Ohio/Mississippi River valley + bat or bird droppings (caves, chicken coops) + small intracellular yeasts in macrophages = histoplasmosis. Acute pulmonary disease is usually self-limited; moderate–severe disease is treated with itraconazole (or liposomal amphotericin B then itraconazole if severe or disseminated). Urine and serum antigen testing is the fastest diagnostic method.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — Blastomyces forms large (8–15 µm) yeasts with broad-based buds and is not intracellular. B — Coccidioides forms large spherules with endospores and is found in the Southwest. D — Cryptococcus is a larger encapsulated yeast with narrow-based budding (pigeon droppings) and is usually extracellular. E — Pneumocystis appears as cysts on silver stain in immunocompromised hosts and does not form budding yeasts in macrophages.

stemHtml: A 33-year-old man has had progressive exertional dyspnea and a dry cough for 3 weeks. Temperature is 38.2 °C (100.8 °F), respirations are 28/min, and oxygen saturation is 86% on room air. Arterial PaO<sub>2</sub> is 58 mm Hg, and serum LDH is 520 U/L. Chest radiography shows bilateral diffuse interstitial infiltrates. A fourth-generation HIV test is positive, and the CD4+ count is 68/mm<sup>3</sup>. Methenamine silver stain of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid shows cup-shaped cysts. Intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is started. Which of the following additional therapies, started now, has been shown to reduce mortality in this condition?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Adjunctive corticosteroids
explanationHtml: Pneumocystis pneumonia with PaO2 <70 mm Hg (or A–a gradient ≥35 mm Hg) → add prednisone (40 mg BID × 5 days, then taper over 21 days) within 72 hours of starting antimicrobial therapy. Killing of organisms causes an inflammatory surge in the lung that worsens hypoxemia during the first days of treatment; steroids blunt it and reduce respiratory failure and death. ART should then be started within 2 weeks.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — echinocandins inhibit β-glucan synthesis and have some activity against the cyst form, but are not standard or mortality-reducing therapy. B — combining pentamidine with TMP-SMX adds toxicity without benefit; pentamidine is an alternative for patients who cannot take TMP-SMX. D — Pneumocystis lacks ergosterol in its membrane, so amphotericin B (and azoles) are ineffective. E — azithromycin is MAC treatment/prophylaxis; MAC prophylaxis is not recommended when ART will be started promptly.

stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman with AIDS is being treated for cryptococcal meningitis with liposomal amphotericin B and flucytosine. On day 6 of therapy she reports muscle weakness and palpitations. An ECG shows prominent U waves. Creatinine has risen from 0.7 to 1.4 mg/dL. Which of the following sets of electrolyte abnormalities is most likely?

options.label: C
options.html: Hyperkalemia with type 4 renal tubular acidosis

answerHtml: Answer: E. Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia
explanationHtml: Amphotericin B binds ergosterol in fungal membranes but also binds, less avidly, to cholesterol in human cell membranes. In the distal nephron it forms pores → K+ and Mg2+ wasting and back-leak of H+ (distal/type 1 RTA, a non–anion gap acidosis with hypokalemia). It also causes afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction → ↓GFR. U waves and weakness reflect hypokalemia. Hypomagnesemia must be corrected for K+ repletion to succeed. Saline loading and the liposomal formulation lower nephrotoxicity. Flucytosine is renally cleared, so rising creatinine increases its marrow toxicity.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and C — potassium is wasted, not retained; type 4 RTA (hyperkalemic) is caused by hypoaldosteronism, trimethoprim, ACE inhibitors and other agents. B — amphotericin does not cause hypercalcemia. D — hyponatremia is not the typical amphotericin toxicity (cryptococcal meningitis itself can cause SIADH, but it does not explain U waves and weakness after starting the drug).

stemHtml: A 29-year-old man who emigrated from India 7 months ago has had fever with rigors every 48 hours for 1 week. He has not traveled since arriving in the United States. Thin blood smear shows enlarged red blood cells with fine red stippling (Schüffner dots) and ameboid trophozoites. He is started on chloroquine. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional step to prevent future episodes?

options.label: D
options.html: Measure G6PD activity, then give primaquine

answerHtml: Answer: D. G6PD testing, then primaquine (radical cure)
explanationHtml: Onset months after leaving an endemic area, a 48-hour cycle, enlarged RBCs and Schüffner dots = P. vivax (the predominant species in India). Dormant liver hypnozoites cause relapses months to years later. Blood schizonticides (chloroquine, artemisinins, atovaquone-proguanil) do not kill hypnozoites; radical cure requires an 8-aminoquinoline — primaquine for 14 days or single-dose tafenoquine — after confirming normal G6PD activity (oxidant hemolysis in deficiency). Both are avoided in pregnancy and breastfeeding of a G6PD-unknown infant.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B — suppressive blood-stage drugs do not eliminate hypnozoites; mefloquine is used for prophylaxis in travelers, not radical cure. C — IV artesunate is for severe malaria (usually falciparum). E — atovaquone-proguanil treats blood-stage parasites but does not prevent vivax relapse.

stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman who moved to the United States from rural India 2 years ago has a first-ever focal seizure with secondary generalization. She has been a lifelong strict vegetarian and has never eaten meat. MRI of the brain shows multiple small cystic lesions, some with an eccentric hyperintense nodule, and several punctate calcifications. Which of the following is the most likely route by which she acquired this infection?

options.label: A
options.html: Eating undercooked pork containing larval cysts

options.label: B
options.html: Ingesting eggs shed in human feces

options.label: D
options.html: Skin penetration by larvae in contaminated soil

options.label: E
options.html: The bite of an infected mosquito

answerHtml: Answer: B. Ingestion of Taenia solium eggs (fecal–oral)
explanationHtml: Cysts with a scolex ("hole with a dot") and calcifications = neurocysticercosis, the leading cause of acquired epilepsy in India and Latin America. Humans develop cysticercosis — larvae in tissue — when they ingest T. solium eggs from a human tapeworm carrier (contaminated food, water, or hands of a food handler). Eating pork never causes cysticercosis directly; it causes intestinal taeniasis, which then makes the carrier a source of eggs. That is why vegetarians (and Orthodox Jewish families in a famous US outbreak involving immigrant housekeepers) can acquire it. Treatment: albendazole (± praziquantel) with corticosteroids for viable cysts, antiseizure medication; screen household for a tapeworm carrier.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A causes intestinal taeniasis, not cysticercosis. C — raw fish transmits Diphyllobothrium (B12 deficiency) and Clonorchis (biliary disease). D — skin penetration is the route of hookworm and Strongyloides. E — mosquitoes transmit malaria and lymphatic filariasis.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old man who worked for many years as a farmer in rural Tamil Nadu before moving to the United States is diagnosed with giant cell arteritis. Long-term high-dose prednisone is planned. He reports intermittent epigastric discomfort and recurrent transient, itchy, serpiginous rashes on his buttocks. Absolute eosinophil count is 1,200/mm<sup>3</sup>. Which of the following drugs should be given to prevent a potentially fatal complication of the planned therapy?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Ivermectin
explanationHtml: Eosinophilia, larva currens (rapidly migrating serpiginous rash on buttocks/perianal area) and residence in an endemic tropical area = chronic Strongyloides stercoralis. Because of autoinfection, it persists for decades after emigration. Corticosteroids (and HTLV-1 coinfection) trigger hyperinfection/disseminated strongyloidiasis — massive larval migration carrying enteric gram-negative bacteria → sepsis, meningitis, ARDS, with mortality often >50%. Treat with ivermectin (or test and treat) before immunosuppression, even if stool examinations are negative.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — praziquantel treats flukes and tapeworms. C — metronidazole treats protozoa and anaerobes. D — pyrantel is for pinworm, Ascaris and hookworm; it is not effective for Strongyloides. E — DEC is for lymphatic filariasis and Loa loa.

stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with 1 day of fever, severe headache, neck stiffness and confusion. Temperature is 39.3 °C (102.7 °F), and blood pressure is 138/80 mm Hg. She has nuchal rigidity and is oriented only to person; there is no papilledema or focal deficit. Blood cultures are drawn, and a head CT is ordered before lumbar puncture. Dexamethasone is given. Which of the following empiric antimicrobial regimens should be given immediately?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Vancomycin + ceftriaxone + ampicillin
explanationHtml: In adults >50 years, the likely organisms are S. pneumoniae (#1), N. meningitidis, Listeria monocytogenes and aerobic gram-negative bacilli. Ceftriaxone covers pneumococcus, meningococcus and gram-negatives; vancomycin covers penicillin/cephalosporin-resistant pneumococci (altered PBPs); ampicillin covers Listeria, which is resistant to cephalosporins. Because the CT is indicated (altered mental status), antibiotics and dexamethasone must be given before imaging — never delay them. Acyclovir is added if HSV encephalitis is suspected.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A misses resistant pneumococci and Listeria. C is correct for ages 1 month–50 years but misses Listeria here. D is a neonatal regimen and misses resistant pneumococci and meningococci. E treats only HSV, not bacterial meningitis.

stemHtml: A 66-year-old man who takes sertraline for depression develops bacteremia with vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium. He is started on a new antibiotic. Three days later he becomes agitated and diaphoretic with tremor, hyperreflexia, inducible ankle clonus and a temperature of 38.6 °C (101.5 °F). Which of the following is the mechanism of action of the antibiotic most likely given?

options.label: A
options.html: Binds the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of cell wall precursors

options.label: B
options.html: Calcium-dependent insertion into the membrane causing depolarization

options.label: C
options.html: Binds the 30S subunit, causing misreading of mRNA

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV

options.label: E
options.html: Binds 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit, preventing formation of the 70S initiation complex

answerHtml: Answer: E. Linezolid (oxazolidinone)
explanationHtml: The two main drugs for VRE bacteremia are linezolid and daptomycin. Linezolid is a weak, reversible, nonselective monoamine oxidase inhibitor; with SSRIs, SNRIs, meperidine or tramadol it can precipitate serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia, hyperthermia, agitation). Linezolid binds the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit and prevents assembly of the functional 70S initiation complex — a mechanism distinct from other 50S inhibitors, so cross-resistance with them is uncommon. Other toxicities: thrombocytopenia (>2 weeks), optic/peripheral neuropathy, lactic acidosis. Treat serotonin syndrome by stopping the drugs, supportive care, benzodiazepines, ± cyproheptadine.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — vancomycin; the organism is resistant (D-Ala-D-Lac). B — daptomycin; it causes myopathy/CK elevation, not serotonin syndrome. C — aminoglycosides; not active alone against enterococci. D — fluoroquinolones; not used for VRE and not serotonergic.

stemHtml: A 59-year-old woman who has been hospitalized for 5 weeks after a liver transplant develops bacteremia with Enterococcus faecium. The isolate is resistant to vancomycin (MIC >256 µg/mL) and to teicoplanin. Molecular testing detects the vanA gene cluster on a transposon. Which of the following is the biochemical basis of this resistance?

options.label: B
options.html: Production of a low-affinity penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)

options.label: C
options.html: Active efflux of the drug from the cytoplasm

options.label: D
options.html: Replacement of the terminal D-Ala-D-Ala of peptidoglycan precursors with D-Ala-D-Lac

answerHtml: Answer: D. D-Ala-D-Lac substitution
explanationHtml: Vancomycin binds the D-Ala-D-Ala end of the pentapeptide side chains, sterically blocking transglycosylation and transpeptidation. The vanA operon (vanH, vanA, vanX) produces precursors ending in D-Ala-D-Lactate, reducing vancomycin binding about 1,000-fold (loss of a hydrogen bond). VanA confers high-level resistance to both vancomycin and teicoplanin; VanB spares teicoplanin. Treat with linezolid or daptomycin. Rare VRSA arises when S. aureus acquires vanA from enterococci.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — β-lactamase affects β-lactams, not glycopeptides. B — PBP2a (mecA) is MRSA's mechanism for β-lactam resistance. C — vancomycin acts outside the cytoplasmic membrane, so efflux is not its resistance mechanism (efflux is typical of tetracyclines, macrolides, fluoroquinolones). E — 23S rRNA methylation (erm) confers macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin B resistance.

stemHtml: A 74-year-old man with COPD who takes prednisone 20 mg daily is treated as an outpatient for community-acquired pneumonia with a single oral agent. On the fifth day of therapy he feels a sudden "pop" in his left heel while climbing stairs and cannot stand on his toes. Squeezing the calf does not produce plantar flexion. Which of the following drugs was he most likely taking?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Levofloxacin
explanationHtml: Single-agent therapy for CAP in a patient with comorbidities (COPD) is a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin or moxifloxacin). Fluoroquinolones cause tendinopathy and Achilles tendon rupture (positive Thompson test), with risk multiplied by age >60, concurrent corticosteroids, and solid-organ transplant; the mechanism involves chelation of Mg2+ and matrix metalloproteinase activation in tenocytes. Other boxed warnings: QT prolongation, aortic aneurysm/dissection, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects and dysglycemia.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B and E — β-lactams are used with a macrolide or doxycycline (not alone) in comorbid patients and are not associated with tendon rupture. C — doxycycline causes photosensitivity and esophagitis. D — azithromycin causes QT prolongation and GI upset, and macrolide monotherapy is not recommended for comorbid patients.

stemHtml: A 61-year-old man on mechanical ventilation in the intensive care unit for 6 days develops fever, purulent tracheal secretions and a new right lower lobe infiltrate. A tracheal aspirate grows methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. His creatinine rose while he was receiving vancomycin earlier in the admission, and a colleague suggests daptomycin, which is effective for MRSA bacteremia. Which of the following best explains why daptomycin is not appropriate for this infection?

options.label: A
options.html: High plasma protein binding prevents it from reaching lung tissue

options.label: B
options.html: MRSA strains carrying mecA enzymatically inactivate it

options.label: C
options.html: It is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant

options.label: D
options.html: Its uptake into bacteria requires oxygen-dependent transport

options.label: E
options.html: It is only bacteriostatic against S. aureus

answerHtml: Answer: C. Inactivation by pulmonary surfactant
explanationHtml: Daptomycin is a cyclic lipopeptide that inserts into gram-positive membranes in a calcium-dependent manner, causing rapid depolarization and death (bactericidal). In the alveolus, it inserts into surfactant phospholipid aggregates instead, which sequester and inactivate it; clinical trials in pneumonia showed inferior outcomes. Appropriate alternatives for MRSA pneumonia in a patient with vancomycin nephrotoxicity: linezolid (good lung penetration, non-nephrotoxic). Note the nuance: hematogenous septic pulmonary emboli from right-sided endocarditis can still respond to daptomycin, because the problem is the alveolar surfactant, not lung tissue penetration.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — protein binding is not the reason; daptomycin reaches lung tissue (and septic emboli). B — mecA encodes PBP2a, which affects β-lactams only. D — oxygen-dependent uptake explains aminoglycoside inactivity in anaerobes. E — daptomycin is rapidly bactericidal.

stemHtml: A 70-kg man with life-threatening sepsis is to receive an IV antibiotic. The target plasma concentration is 20 mg/L. The drug's volume of distribution is 0.6 L/kg, its clearance is 6 L/h, and its oral bioavailability is 50%. Which of the following is the most appropriate IV loading dose?
answerHtml: Answer: C. 840 mg
explanationHtml: LD = Ctarget × Vd / F. The total Vd is 0.6 L/kg × 70 kg = 42 L. Because the drug is given IV, F = 1. LD = 20 mg/L × 42 L / 1 = 840 mg. Clearance determines the maintenance dose, not the loading dose.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A (280 mg) and B (420 mg) result from using the wrong volume or halving the dose. D (1260 mg) has no basis in the formula. E (1680 mg) wrongly divides by the oral bioavailability (0.5), which applies only to oral dosing.

stemHtml: A 62-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation is to start an oral drug. The desired average steady-state plasma concentration is 10 mg/L. The drug's clearance is 5 L/h and its oral bioavailability is 0.5. It is to be taken every 12 hours. Which of the following is the appropriate oral maintenance dose?
answerHtml: Answer: A. 1200 mg every 12 hours
explanationHtml: MD = Css × CL × τ / F = 10 mg/L × 5 L/h × 12 h / 0.5 = 600 / 0.5 = 1200 mg. Check the units: (mg/L)(L/h)(h) = mg.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B (600 mg) forgets to divide by F. C (300 mg) multiplies by F instead of dividing. D (100 mg) omits the dosing interval and bioavailability. E (2400 mg) divides by F twice or uses a 24-hour interval.

stemHtml: A new anticonvulsant follows first-order kinetics. Its volume of distribution is 40 L and its clearance is 4 L/h. A patient is started on a constant IV infusion with no loading dose. Approximately how long will it take for the plasma concentration to reach about 97% of its eventual steady-state value?
answerHtml: Answer: E. 35 hours
explanationHtml: t½ = 0.693 × Vd/CL ≈ 0.7 × 40/4 = 7 h. After a constant infusion, the plasma level reaches 50% of steady state at 1 t½, 75% at 2, 87.5% at 3, 93.75% at 4, and 96.9% at 5 half-lives. So about 97% is reached at 5 × 7 = 35 h. Changing the infusion rate would change the steady-state level but not this time.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A (7 h) is one half-life (50%). B (14 h) is two half-lives (75%). C (3.5 h) is only half of one half-life. D (70 h) is 10 half-lives, well past steady state.

stemHtml: A 28-year-old man with focal epilepsy has a phenytoin level of 12 μg/mL on 300 mg/day (therapeutic range 10–20 μg/mL) but still has occasional seizures. His dose is increased to 400 mg/day. Two weeks later he has horizontal nystagmus and an ataxic gait, and his level is 34 μg/mL. Albumin is 4.2 g/dL. Liver and renal function are normal, and he takes no other drugs. Which of the following best explains the disproportionate rise in his phenytoin level?

options.label: A
options.html: Autoinduction of the enzymes that metabolize it

options.label: C
options.html: Displacement of phenytoin from albumin binding sites

options.label: D
options.html: Decreased glomerular filtration of unchanged drug

answerHtml: Answer: B. Saturation of hepatic metabolizing enzymes
explanationHtml: Phenytoin is metabolized mainly by CYP2C9 (and 2C19) with Michaelis–Menten kinetics, and its Km lies within the therapeutic range. As the enzymes saturate, elimination becomes zero-order: a constant amount per unit time. The half-life lengthens, so a 33% dose increase can triple the level. Toxicity causes nystagmus, then ataxia, then confusion.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, autoinduction, is typical of carbamazepine and would lower levels. C: albumin is normal and there is no displacing drug. D: phenytoin is cleared mainly by the liver, and renal function is normal. E: tolerance would reduce the effect, not raise the level.

stemHtml: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after ingesting a large number of aspirin tablets. She has tinnitus and is breathing rapidly. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.42, PaCO<sub>2</sub> 22 mm Hg, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 14 mEq/L. Anion gap 22. An IV infusion is started to increase elimination of the drug. By which of the following mechanisms does this therapy enhance salicylate excretion?

options.label: B
options.html: Chelation of salicylate in the gut lumen

options.label: C
options.html: Competitive displacement of salicylate from cyclooxygenase

options.label: D
options.html: Increasing the ionized fraction of salicylate in tubular fluid, which decreases its reabsorption

options.label: E
options.html: Acidification of the urine, which increases tubular secretion of salicylate

answerHtml: Answer: D. Increasing the ionized fraction in tubular fluid, which decreases reabsorption
explanationHtml: The blood gas shows a mixed primary respiratory alkalosis (direct stimulation of the medullary respiratory center) and a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, which is classic for salicylate toxicity. Salicylic acid is a weak acid (pKa ≈ 3). IV sodium bicarbonate raises urine pH, so more salicylate is in the ionized form (A−). That form cannot diffuse back across the tubular epithelium and is "trapped" in the urine. Alkalinizing the serum also keeps salicylate out of the CNS. Hemodialysis is used for severe toxicity.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: CYP2E1 matters in acetaminophen toxicity. B: activated charcoal adsorbs (it does not chelate) and is not an IV infusion. C: there is no such antidote at COX. E: acidification would increase reabsorption of a weak acid.

stemHtml: A 34-year-old man with opioid use disorder who last used heroin 2 hours ago is given a sublingual dose of buprenorphine in clinic. Within 45 minutes he develops yawning, rhinorrhea, piloerection, abdominal cramps and dilated pupils. Which of the following properties of buprenorphine best explains this reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: High-affinity partial agonist at μ-opioid receptors that displaces the full agonist

options.label: B
options.html: Pure competitive antagonist at μ-opioid receptors

options.label: D
options.html: Induction of CYP3A4, which accelerates the metabolism of heroin

options.label: E
options.html: Irreversible noncompetitive antagonism at δ-opioid receptors

answerHtml: Answer: A. High-affinity partial agonist at μ receptors
explanationHtml: Buprenorphine binds μ receptors with very high affinity but has lower intrinsic efficacy than heroin or morphine. When a full agonist already occupies the receptors, buprenorphine displaces it and the net receptor stimulation falls to buprenorphine's lower maximum. The result is precipitated withdrawal. For this reason, buprenorphine induction is usually started once the patient shows mild to moderate withdrawal (for example, 12 or more hours after a short-acting opioid). The low efficacy also produces a "ceiling" on respiratory depression, which makes buprenorphine safer.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: naloxone and naltrexone are pure antagonists; buprenorphine has agonist activity (it relieves withdrawal once withdrawal has started). C: buprenorphine is a κ antagonist, and κ activity would not explain the reaction. D: buprenorphine is a CYP3A4 substrate, not an inducer, and induction would take days. E: it does not act irreversibly at δ receptors.

stemHtml: In an isolated arterial ring preparation with no receptor reserve, a cumulative concentration–response curve to phenylephrine is obtained. The tissue is then incubated with phenoxybenzamine, washed thoroughly, and the phenylephrine curve is repeated. Which of the following changes in the phenylephrine curve is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Parallel shift to the right with an unchanged maximal response

options.label: B
options.html: Parallel shift to the left with an unchanged maximal response

options.label: C
options.html: Decreased maximal response with an unchanged EC<sub>50</sub>

options.label: D
options.html: Increased maximal response with a decreased EC<sub>50</sub>

options.label: E
options.html: No change, because the antagonist was washed out

answerHtml: Answer: C. Decreased maximal response, unchanged EC<sub>50</sub>
explanationHtml: Phenoxybenzamine alkylates (covalently binds) α receptors, so washing does not remove it. Fewer functional receptors remain, and no amount of agonist can restore the full response. This is noncompetitive (insurmountable) antagonism: Emax falls. With no spare receptors, the EC50 of the remaining receptors is unchanged. Clinically, phenoxybenzamine is used before surgery for pheochromocytoma because high catecholamine levels cannot overcome its blockade.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A describes a reversible competitive antagonist (phentolamine, prazosin). B describes a sensitizing drug. D is not an antagonist effect. E: the covalent bond is not reversed by washing; only new receptor synthesis restores the response.

stemHtml: Five investigational analgesics are tested in animals. The median effective dose (ED<sub>50</sub>) and median toxic dose (TD<sub>50</sub>) of each are shown. Which drug has the widest margin of safety?

options.label: A
options.html: Drug A: ED<sub>50</sub> 10 mg/kg, TD<sub>50</sub> 40 mg/kg

options.label: B
options.html: Drug B: ED<sub>50</sub> 2 mg/kg, TD<sub>50</sub> 10 mg/kg

options.label: C
options.html: Drug C: ED<sub>50</sub> 50 mg/kg, TD<sub>50</sub> 250 mg/kg

options.label: D
options.html: Drug D: ED<sub>50</sub> 1 mg/kg, TD<sub>50</sub> 8 mg/kg

options.label: E
options.html: Drug E: ED<sub>50</sub> 5 mg/kg, TD<sub>50</sub> 100 mg/kg

answerHtml: Answer: E. Drug E
explanationHtml: Therapeutic index = TD50/ED50. The values are A = 40/10 = 4, B = 10/2 = 5, C = 250/50 = 5, D = 8/1 = 8, and E = 100/5 = 20. The highest TI means the widest separation between effective and toxic doses, so Drug E is safest.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: D has the lowest ED50 (the most potent drug), but potency is not safety; its TI is 8. C has the largest absolute toxic dose, but its ratio is only 5. A and B have the narrowest ratios.

stemHtml: An investigator studies a reversible enzyme inhibitor that is structurally similar to the enzyme's natural substrate and binds the active site. Reaction velocity is measured at a range of substrate concentrations with and without the inhibitor, and the data are plotted as 1/V against 1/[S]. Compared with the uninhibited enzyme, which of the following is expected with the inhibitor?

options.label: A
options.html: Higher y-intercept, same x-intercept (↓V<sub>max</sub>, unchanged K<sub>m</sub>)

options.label: B
options.html: Same y-intercept, x-intercept closer to the origin (unchanged V<sub>max</sub>, ↑K<sub>m</sub>)

options.label: D
options.html: Same y-intercept, x-intercept farther from the origin (unchanged V<sub>max</sub>, ↓K<sub>m</sub>)

answerHtml: Answer: B. Same y-intercept; x-intercept moves toward 0
explanationHtml: A competitive inhibitor competes with the substrate for the active site. Enough substrate overcomes it, so Vmax (y-intercept = 1/Vmax) is unchanged. More substrate is needed to reach ½Vmax, so the apparent Km rises. The x-intercept (−1/Km) therefore moves toward the origin, and the slope (Km/Vmax) increases: the lines intersect on the y-axis. This is the enzyme equivalent of a competitive receptor antagonist reducing potency.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A is noncompetitive inhibition (allosteric). C is uncompetitive inhibition. D would mean increased affinity. E (higher V<sub>max</sub>) describes an activator, not an inhibitor.

stemHtml: A 45-year-old farmer is brought in 1 hour after spraying crops without protective equipment. He has vomiting, diarrhea, profuse sweating, wheezing with copious bronchial secretions, and pinpoint pupils. HR is 48/min. Repeated IV atropine is given until his bronchial secretions dry and his HR rises to 96/min. He still has diffuse muscle fasciculations and progressive weakness of his limbs and respiratory muscles. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional pharmacotherapy?

options.label: A
options.html: A further increase in the atropine dose

answerHtml: Answer: D. Pralidoxime
explanationHtml: Organophosphates phosphorylate acetylcholinesterase, so ACh accumulates at muscarinic, nicotinic (NMJ and ganglionic) and CNS synapses. Atropine blocks only muscarinic receptors, so it controls secretions, bronchospasm and bradycardia but not nicotinic effects at the NMJ (fasciculations, then depolarizing paralysis). Pralidoxime removes the phosphate group from AChE and regenerates the enzyme. It works only if given before the enzyme–phosphate bond "ages." It is the only option that treats the nicotinic weakness.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: the muscarinic endpoint (dry secretions) has been reached, and more atropine does nothing at nicotinic receptors. B and C: other AChE inhibitors would worsen the cholinergic crisis. E: succinylcholine is a depolarizing blocker metabolized by plasma cholinesterase, which is also inhibited, so paralysis would be prolonged. Use a nondepolarizing agent if he needs intubation.

stemHtml: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after drinking tea brewed from jimsonweed seeds. He is agitated and hallucinating. Temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F), HR 132/min. His skin is flushed, hot and dry, his pupils are 8 mm and poorly reactive, bowel sounds are absent, and his bladder is distended. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a normal QRS duration. Which of the following drugs would reverse both his peripheral and central findings?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Physostigmine
explanationHtml: Jimsonweed (Datura) contains atropine and scopolamine, which cause an anticholinergic toxidrome: hyperthermia, anhidrosis, flushing, mydriasis, delirium, ileus and urinary retention. Physostigmine is a tertiary amine AChE inhibitor. It is lipid-soluble and crosses the blood–brain barrier, so it raises ACh both centrally and peripherally and overcomes the competitive muscarinic blockade. The normal QRS matters: physostigmine is avoided when a TCA is suspected (wide QRS).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: neostigmine is a quaternary amine, so it acts only peripherally and would not reverse the delirium. C: pralidoxime regenerates AChE after organophosphate poisoning and is irrelevant here. D: bethanechol is peripheral and muscarinic-selective and does not enter the CNS. E: haloperidol does not reverse the muscarinic blockade, lowers the seizure threshold, and can worsen hyperthermia; benzodiazepines are preferred for agitation.

stemHtml: In an anesthetized dog, IV epinephrine raises mean arterial pressure from 100 to 140 mm Hg. The animal is then given drug X, and the same dose of epinephrine now lowers mean arterial pressure to 80 mm Hg. Drug X given alone did not change the heart rate response to isoproterenol. Which of the following receptor effects is responsible for the fall in blood pressure after drug X?

options.label: A
options.html: α1-receptor stimulation in venous capacitance vessels

options.label: B
options.html: β1-receptor stimulation in the SA node

options.label: C
options.html: M3-receptor stimulation of endothelial nitric oxide release

options.label: D
options.html: Central α2-receptor stimulation that reduces sympathetic outflow

options.label: E
options.html: β2-receptor stimulation in skeletal muscle arterioles

answerHtml: Answer: E. β2-mediated arteriolar vasodilation
explanationHtml: Drug X is an α-blocker (for example, phentolamine or phenoxybenzamine); its lack of effect on the isoproterenol response shows that β receptors are intact. Epinephrine normally causes α1 vasoconstriction, which outweighs β2 vasodilation. With α1 blocked, the remaining effect on peripheral resistance is β2-mediated dilation of skeletal muscle arterioles, so total peripheral resistance and MAP fall. This is called "epinephrine reversal."
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: α1 stimulation is blocked and would raise pressure. B: β1 stimulation increases cardiac output, which raises MAP. C: epinephrine does not act on M3 receptors. D: central α2 effects are not the mechanism of this acute response.

stemHtml: A healthy volunteer receives a continuous IV infusion of norepinephrine. Systolic and diastolic blood pressures both rise substantially, and heart rate falls from 72/min to 58/min. Which of the following best explains the change in heart rate?

options.label: A
options.html: Reflex increase in vagal tone triggered by carotid sinus baroreceptors

options.label: B
options.html: Direct stimulation of M2 receptors in the SA node by norepinephrine

options.label: C
options.html: Norepinephrine acting as a β1-receptor antagonist

options.label: D
options.html: Presynaptic α2-mediated inhibition of acetylcholine release

options.label: E
options.html: Direct α1-mediated slowing of SA node depolarization

answerHtml: Answer: A. Baroreceptor reflex (↑vagal tone)
explanationHtml: Norepinephrine acts mainly on α1 receptors (and β1), with little β2 effect. The resulting rise in peripheral resistance raises MAP. The carotid sinus baroreceptors fire more (afferents via CN IX), the nucleus tractus solitarius increases vagal outflow and decreases sympathetic outflow, and HR falls. This reflex overrides norepinephrine's direct β1 chronotropic effect. If the reflex were blocked (with atropine or a ganglionic blocker), the same infusion would cause tachycardia.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: norepinephrine is not a muscarinic agonist. C: norepinephrine is a β1 agonist. D: presynaptic α2 receptors inhibit norepinephrine release; even if ACh release fell, HR would rise. E: the SA node has no meaningful α1-mediated slowing.

stemHtml: A 78-year-old man with severe COPD is brought to the emergency department with acute hypercapnic respiratory failure. He is obtunded and cannot communicate. He failed a trial of noninvasive ventilation. His valid living will, written 1 year ago after a discussion with his pulmonologist, clearly states that he does not want endotracheal intubation or mechanical ventilation under any circumstances. He did not designate a health care proxy. His daughter arrives and insists that "everything be done," including intubation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Intubate the patient, because the daughter is the next of kin and is present

options.label: B
options.html: Intubate temporarily until the hospital ethics committee can meet

options.label: C
options.html: Obtain an emergency court order before making any decision

options.label: D
options.html: Honor the living will: do not intubate, and provide maximal non-ventilatory treatment and comfort care consistent with his wishes

options.label: E
options.html: Ask the daughter to sign a form that releases the hospital from liability, then intubate

answerHtml: Answer: D. Honor the living will
explanationHtml: A valid, specific advance directive is the patient's own autonomous decision, expressed while he had capacity. It applies exactly to this situation, and it takes precedence over the wishes of any family member or surrogate. Surrogates decide only when the patient's wishes are unknown, and then by substituted judgment. Continue treatments he did not refuse (bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics), relieve dyspnea (opioids are appropriate; double effect), and talk compassionately with the daughter about her father's documented wishes.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: next-of-kin status does not override a clear advance directive. B: intubating against his documented refusal violates autonomy, even "temporarily." C: a court order is unnecessary when the directive is valid and clear. E: the daughter's waiver of liability has no bearing on the patient's right to refuse.

stemHtml: A 67-year-old woman with a mechanical mitral valve has had a stable INR of 2.5–3.0 on warfarin for 2 years. She is treated for esophageal candidiasis, and 6 days later she presents with gum bleeding and large ecchymoses. INR is 7.8. Her diet is unchanged. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this interaction?

options.label: B
options.html: Displacement of warfarin from plasma albumin as the dominant long-term effect

options.label: D
options.html: Decreased intestinal absorption of vitamin K

options.label: E
options.html: Inhibition of renal tubular secretion of warfarin

answerHtml: Answer: C. Inhibition of CYP2C9
explanationHtml: Esophageal candidiasis is treated with oral fluconazole, which strongly inhibits CYP2C9 (and moderately inhibits 3A4). The more potent S-enantiomer of warfarin is cleared mainly by CYP2C9, so inhibition raises warfarin levels and the INR within days. Other common CYP2C9 inhibitors that interact with warfarin: TMP-SMX, metronidazole, amiodarone. Management: hold warfarin, give oral vitamin K for an INR over 10 or minor bleeding, and give 4F-PCC plus IV vitamin K for major bleeding.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: induction would lower the INR (as with rifampin or carbamazepine). B: protein-binding displacement causes only a transient rise in free drug, because clearance rises to match; it rarely explains a sustained interaction. D: antibacterial disruption of gut flora contributes slightly with some antibiotics, but not with an antifungal, and her diet is unchanged. E: warfarin is eliminated by hepatic metabolism, not renal secretion.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman taking a combined oral contraceptive (ethinyl estradiol/norethindrone) is diagnosed with latent tuberculosis infection and starts a 4-month course of daily rifampin. Five months later she has a positive pregnancy test. She reports taking her contraceptive every day. Which of the following best explains the contraceptive failure?

options.label: A
options.html: Chelation of the hormones in the gastrointestinal tract

options.label: B
options.html: Increased renal excretion of unchanged estrogen

options.label: C
options.html: Competitive antagonism at estrogen and progesterone receptors

answerHtml: Answer: E. Induction of CYP3A4
explanationHtml: Rifampin is a potent inducer of CYP3A4 (through the pregnane X receptor) and of UGT enzymes. It speeds the metabolism of ethinyl estradiol and progestins, lowers their levels, and allows ovulation. Patients on rifampin (and on carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John's wort, and others) should use a non-hormonal method or an IUD (the levonorgestrel IUD and the copper IUD are not meaningfully affected), plus backup contraception for at least 28 days after stopping the inducer, because new enzymes take weeks to decline.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: chelation affects tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones taken with cations, not OCPs. B: estrogens are cleared mainly by hepatic metabolism. C: rifampin has no hormone-receptor activity. D: rifampin is not a CYP2D6 inhibitor, and inhibition would increase hormone levels.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman with resistant hypertension has taken hydralazine for 9 months. She now has fever, arthralgias of the hands and wrists, and pleuritic chest pain with a small pleural effusion. Urinalysis is normal and she has no neurologic symptoms. Genetic testing shows she is a slow acetylator. Which of the following serologic findings is most characteristic of her condition?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Anti-histone antibodies
explanationHtml: Drug-induced lupus is caused by hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid (all acetylated by NAT2, so slow acetylators are at higher risk), minocycline and TNF-α inhibitors. It presents with arthralgia, serositis, fever and rash, and usually spares the kidneys and CNS. The ANA is positive, anti-histone antibodies are present in more than 95% of cases, and complement is usually normal. It resolves weeks to months after the drug is stopped.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and C are specific for idiopathic SLE (anti-dsDNA correlates with nephritis); TNF-α inhibitor-induced lupus can be anti-dsDNA positive, but hydralazine-induced lupus usually is not. D: limited scleroderma (CREST). E: polymyositis/dermatomyositis with antisynthetase syndrome.

stemHtml: A 22-year-old woman presents 6 hours after ingesting 40 tablets of 500 mg acetaminophen. She has mild nausea only. Her serum acetaminophen level drawn on arrival (6 hours after ingestion) is above the treatment line on the Rumack–Matthew nomogram, and IV N-acetylcysteine is started. Which of the following best describes how this antidote prevents liver injury?

options.label: A
options.html: It replenishes hepatic glutathione, which conjugates and detoxifies NAPQI

options.label: C
options.html: It chelates acetaminophen in the plasma for renal excretion

options.label: D
options.html: It alkalinizes the urine to trap acetaminophen

options.label: E
options.html: It antagonizes acetaminophen at hepatocyte receptors

answerHtml: Answer: A. It replenishes glutathione
explanationHtml: Normally, acetaminophen is mostly glucuronidated and sulfated. A small fraction is oxidized by CYP2E1 (and 3A4) to NAPQI, which glutathione detoxifies. In overdose, the conjugation pathways saturate, glutathione is depleted, and NAPQI binds hepatocyte proteins, causing centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis. N-acetylcysteine is a cysteine donor that regenerates glutathione (and may also directly reduce NAPQI). It is nearly 100% protective if given within 8 hours. Chronic alcohol use (CYP2E1 induction) and malnutrition (low glutathione) increase the risk.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B describes fomepizole (methanol and ethylene glycol). C: NAC does not chelate. D: urinary alkalinization is used for salicylates. E: acetaminophen hepatotoxicity is not receptor-mediated.

stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman with no symptoms and no personal or family history of breast cancer has a screening mammogram as part of her routine health maintenance visit. Mammography in this setting is an example of which of the following?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Secondary prevention
explanationHtml: Screening detects disease that already exists in an early, asymptomatic stage, so that treatment can reduce morbidity and mortality. This is secondary prevention. USPSTF (2024) recommends mammography every 2 years for women aged 40–74 (grade B).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: primary prevention stops disease from starting (HPV vaccine, smoking cessation). B: quaternary prevention protects patients from overmedicalization. D: tertiary prevention limits complications of established disease (rehabilitation after mastectomy, lymphedema care). E: chemoprevention (tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor in high-risk women) is a form of primary prevention, not screening.

stemHtml: A new rapid antigen test is evaluated in 1000 people; 200 have the disease by the gold standard. Of those with the disease, 180 test positive. Of those without the disease, 720 test negative. What is the positive predictive value of the test in this population?
answerHtml: Answer: D. 69%
explanationHtml: Build the 2×2 table. Diseased = 200: TP (a) = 180, FN (c) = 20. Non-diseased = 800: TN (d) = 720, FP (b) = 80. PPV = a/(a + b) = 180/(180 + 80) = 180/260 ≈ 0.69, or 69%. For completeness: sensitivity = 180/200 = 90%, specificity = 720/800 = 90%, NPV = 720/740 ≈ 97%, prevalence = 20%.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A (20%) is the prevalence. B (90%) is both the sensitivity and the specificity. C (97%) is the NPV. E (31%) is 1 − PPV, the proportion of positive results that are false positives (80/260).

stemHtml: The test in the previous question (sensitivity 90%, specificity 90%) was validated in a referral clinic where disease prevalence was 20%. It is now to be used for community screening, where prevalence is 2%. Compared with the referral clinic, which of the following best describes the test's performance in the community?

options.label: C
options.html: PPV and NPV are both unchanged

answerHtml: Answer: D. PPV decreases, NPV increases
explanationHtml: Sensitivity and specificity are intrinsic to the test (at a fixed cutoff) and do not change with prevalence. Worked example with 10,000 people at 2% prevalence: diseased = 200, giving TP 180 and FN 20. Non-diseased = 9800, giving TN 8820 and FP 980. PPV = 180/1160 ≈ 15.5% (down from 69%). NPV = 8820/8840 ≈ 99.8% (up from 97%). When a disease is rare, most positive results are false positives. This is why low-prevalence screening needs a confirmatory, highly specific second test.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and E: Sn and Sp do not depend on prevalence (unless the spectrum of disease changes, which is a separate issue). B is the reverse of the truth. C: predictive values depend on prevalence.

stemHtml: A clinical decision rule for deep venous thrombosis has a sensitivity of 80% and a specificity of 90%. What is the positive likelihood ratio of this rule?
answerHtml: Answer: A. 8.0
explanationHtml: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity) = 0.80/(1 − 0.90) = 0.80/0.10 = 8. A positive result multiplies the pretest odds by 8. For example, at a pretest probability of 20%, the pretest odds are 0.25, the post-test odds are 2, and the post-test probability is 2/3 ≈ 67%.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B (0.22) is the LR−: (1 − 0.8)/0.9 = 0.2/0.9. C (4.5) has no basis in these values. D (9.0) is 0.9/0.1, which confuses sensitivity with specificity. E (0.89) is 0.8/0.9, which mistakenly divides sensitivity by specificity.

stemHtml: To avoid missed myocardial infarctions, an emergency department lowers the high-sensitivity troponin value that it uses as the positive cutoff for diagnosing acute MI. Assuming the prevalence of MI among tested patients does not change, which of the following combinations of effects is expected?

options.label: C
options.html: Fewer false negatives and fewer false positives

answerHtml: Answer: E. ↑Sensitivity, ↓specificity, ↑NPV
explanationHtml: The distributions of troponin values in patients with and without MI overlap (Figure 6). Lowering the positive cutoff classifies more patients as positive. More true MIs are caught, so false negatives fall and sensitivity rises. More patients without MI are labeled positive, so false positives rise and specificity falls. With fewer false negatives among the negative results, NPV rises. With more false positives among the positive results, PPV generally falls.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A describes raising the cutoff. B and C: moving a single cutoff always trades sensitivity against specificity; only a better test (a higher AUC) improves both. D: PPV falls, not rises, as false positives increase.

stemHtml: Investigators identify 150 patients with newly diagnosed pleural mesothelioma and 300 age- and sex-matched patients without mesothelioma from the same hospitals. Trained interviewers use structured questionnaires and employment records to determine each participant's past occupational asbestos exposure. Which of the following is the most appropriate measure of association for this study?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Odds ratio
explanationHtml: This is a case–control study: participants are selected by outcome (mesothelioma or not), and investigators look back at exposure. Because the investigators fixed the ratio of cases to controls (1:2), the incidence of disease in exposed and unexposed people cannot be calculated, so the relative risk cannot be computed. The odds ratio, ad/bc, approximates the RR because mesothelioma is rare. Case–control designs suit rare diseases with long latency.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B require following a cohort from exposure to calculate incidence. D needs time-to-event data (Cox model) from a cohort or trial. E is used in cross-sectional studies.

stemHtml: In a case–control study of bladder cancer, 40 of 100 patients with bladder cancer and 20 of 200 controls report having worked in the aniline dye industry. What is the odds ratio for bladder cancer associated with dye-industry work?
answerHtml: Answer: B. 6.0
explanationHtml: The 2×2 table: exposed cases (a) = 40, exposed controls (b) = 20, unexposed cases (c) = 60, unexposed controls (d) = 180. OR = ad/bc = (40 × 180)/(20 × 60) = 7200/1200 = 6. Equivalently, the odds of exposure in cases are 40/60 = 0.667 and in controls 20/180 = 0.111, and 0.667/0.111 = 6. The odds of bladder cancer are 6 times higher in people exposed to aniline dyes (aromatic amines, a cause of urothelial carcinoma).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A (2.0) is 40/20, the raw counts of exposed people. C (3.3) has no basis in these values. D (4.0) is 40% ÷ 10%, the ratio of exposure proportions, which is not the odds ratio. E (0.17) is the inverted OR (1/6).

stemHtml: In a 5-year randomized controlled trial of a new lipid-lowering drug in 4000 high-risk adults, a major adverse cardiovascular event occurred in 20% of the placebo group and 15% of the drug group. How many patients must be treated for 5 years to prevent one major adverse cardiovascular event?
answerHtml: Answer: B. 20
explanationHtml: ARR = control event rate − experimental event rate = 0.20 − 0.15 = 0.05. NNT = 1/ARR = 1/0.05 = 20 patients treated for 5 years. The relative risk is 0.15/0.20 = 0.75, so the RRR is 25%. NNT always refers to the trial's duration.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A (5) uses the ARR expressed as a percentage instead of computing its reciprocal. C (25) is the RRR (as a percentage), not the NNT. D (4) is 1/RRR (1/0.25). E (15) is the event rate in the drug group.

stemHtml: In the trial described in the previous question, clinically significant myopathy occurred in 3% of patients taking the drug and 1% of those taking placebo. What is the number needed to harm for myopathy over 5 years?
answerHtml: Answer: D. 50
explanationHtml: Absolute risk increase (attributable risk) = 0.03 − 0.01 = 0.02. NNH = 1/0.02 = 50. For every 50 patients treated for 5 years, one additional case of myopathy occurs. Comparing the two calculations: treating 50 patients prevents about 2.5 cardiovascular events (50/20) and causes 1 case of myopathy.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A (2) uses the risk difference as a percentage. B (33) is 1/0.03, the event rate in the drug group alone. C (100) is 1/0.01, the placebo rate. E (67) has no basis in these values.

stemHtml: In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of a new influenza vaccine, laboratory-confirmed influenza developed in 10% of placebo recipients and 6% of vaccine recipients during the season. What is the relative risk reduction (vaccine efficacy)?
answerHtml: Answer: C. 40%
explanationHtml: RR = 0.06/0.10 = 0.6. RRR = 1 − RR = 0.4 = 40%. Equivalently, RRR = ARR/CER = (0.10 − 0.06)/0.10 = 0.04/0.10 = 40%. Vaccine efficacy is the RRR. The ARR is 4%, so the NNT is 25 people vaccinated to prevent one case.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A (4%) is the ARR. B (25%) is the NNT (25) misread as a percentage. D (60%) is the RR expressed as a percentage. E (67%) is 4/6, which divides the ARR by the vaccine-group rate instead of the control rate.

stemHtml: A new drug is approved that extends median survival in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) by 3 years but does not cure the disease or affect who develops it. If the drug is widely used, which of the following changes in the epidemiology of ALS is expected over the next decade?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Prevalence ↑, incidence unchanged
explanationHtml: Prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration of disease. The drug does not change the rate of new cases (incidence), but patients live longer with the disease (longer duration), so more people have ALS at any given time. The same logic explains why prevalence rose for HIV after antiretroviral therapy and for type 1 diabetes after insulin.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: incidence is unaffected because the drug does not cause ALS or change its onset. C: shorter duration (a cure or faster death) would lower prevalence. D: only primary prevention lowers incidence. E: prevalence changes because duration lengthens.

stemHtml: On January 1, a town of 10,000 people has 500 residents with a chronic, incurable autoimmune disease. During the following year, 190 new cases are diagnosed. No one dies or moves. What is the incidence of the disease for that year?
answerHtml: Answer: E. 2.0%
explanationHtml: Incidence = new cases / population at risk. The 500 people who already have the disease cannot develop it again, so they are excluded from the denominator: 10,000 − 500 = 9500 at risk. Incidence = 190/9500 = 0.02, or 2.0% (20 per 1000 per year). The point prevalence on January 1 is 500/10,000 = 5%. The period prevalence for the year is (500 + 190)/10,000 = 6.9%.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A (1.9%) uses the total population as the denominator, a common trap. B (5.0%) is the point prevalence on January 1. C (6.9%) is the period prevalence. D (0.19%) is a decimal-place error.

stemHtml: A study compares patients whose lung cancer was found by low-dose CT screening with patients diagnosed after symptoms appeared. The screen-detected patients survive an average of 5.2 years after diagnosis, compared with 2.9 years for symptom-detected patients. Tumors in both groups had similar histologic grade and doubling times, and the average age at death from lung cancer was the same in both groups. Which of the following best explains the apparent survival benefit?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Lead-time bias
explanationHtml: Screening moved the date of diagnosis earlier, but the age at death was unchanged. The extra "survival" is simply the time added before symptoms would have appeared (the lead time); the natural history was not altered. The way to avoid this bias is to compare disease-specific mortality between populations randomized to screening or no screening, not survival measured from diagnosis. (LDCT screening does reduce lung cancer mortality in RCTs such as NLST and NELSON; this question is about a flawed analysis.)
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: length-time bias requires screening to preferentially detect slower-growing tumors, but the growth rates here were similar. B: healthy-volunteer selection could affect outcomes, but it would not leave the age at death identical while lengthening survival from diagnosis. C: recall bias concerns remembered exposures in case–control studies. D: the Hawthorne effect is a change in behavior from being observed.

stemHtml: A cohort study finds that heavy coffee drinkers have a higher risk of lung cancer than non-coffee drinkers (crude RR 2.4). When the analysis is stratified by smoking status, the RR for coffee is 1.0 among smokers and 1.0 among nonsmokers. Coffee drinkers were much more likely to smoke. Which of the following best explains the crude association?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Confounding
explanationHtml: Smoking is associated with the exposure (coffee drinking) and is an independent cause of the outcome (lung cancer), and it is not on the causal pathway between them. After stratification, the stratum-specific RRs are similar to each other (1.0 and 1.0) but different from the crude RR (2.4). This is the signature of confounding. The crude association came entirely from smoking. It can be controlled by stratification, multivariable adjustment, restriction, matching, or randomization.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: effect modification produces stratum-specific RRs that differ from each other (for example, 3.0 in smokers and 1.0 in nonsmokers). B: no unrepresentative sampling is described. D: a cohort study records exposures before the outcome occurs, so recall bias is unlikely. E: a chance finding would not disappear in this systematic way on stratification.

stemHtml: A pilot RCT randomizes 40 adults with hypertension to a new antihypertensive or placebo. Mean systolic BP falls 4 mm Hg more with the drug, but p = 0.30. The investigators calculate that the study had 35% power to detect a 5 mm Hg difference. A later trial of 4000 patients shows a true, statistically significant 5 mm Hg reduction. Which of the following best describes the pilot study's conclusion, and how could it have been prevented?

options.label: A
options.html: Type I error; lower the α level to 0.01

options.label: B
options.html: Type II error; increase the sample size

options.label: C
options.html: Type I error; increase the sample size

options.label: D
options.html: Type II error; lower the α level to 0.01

answerHtml: Answer: B. Type II error; increase the sample size
explanationHtml: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis (missing a real effect) is a type II (β) error. Power = 1 − β, so this study had a 65% chance of missing a true 5 mm Hg difference. Power increases with a larger sample size (the most practical lever), a larger effect size, less variability, and a higher α. Investigators should calculate the sample size before the trial, typically targeting 80–90% power.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and C: a type I error is a false-positive conclusion, but this study found no significant difference. D: lowering α reduces power and makes a type II error more likely. E: randomization was used, and confounding does not explain a nonsignificant result in an underpowered trial.

stemHtml: A prospective cohort study reports that regular use of a proton pump inhibitor is associated with incident dementia, with a relative risk of 1.4 (95% confidence interval, 0.9–2.1). Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation?

options.label: A
options.html: PPI use causes a 40% increase in dementia risk, p < 0.05

options.label: B
options.html: The result is significant because the interval does not include 0

options.label: C
options.html: The result is significant because the point estimate is greater than 1

options.label: D
options.html: The association is not statistically significant at α = 0.05

options.label: E
options.html: The interval proves that PPIs do not increase dementia risk
