answerHtml: Answer: D. Not statistically significant
explanationHtml: For a ratio measure (RR, OR, HR), the null value is 1. A 95% CI that includes 1 (here 0.9–2.1) corresponds to p > 0.05, so the null hypothesis cannot be rejected. The data are compatible with anything from a 10% decrease to a 110% increase in risk. A wide CI suggests imprecision (a small sample).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: the result is not significant, and an observational cohort cannot by itself establish causation. B: 0 is the null value for differences (of means, or ARR), not for ratios. C: the point estimate alone does not determine significance. E: absence of evidence is not evidence of absence; the study may simply be underpowered.

stemHtml: Researchers randomize adults with type 2 diabetes to metformin alone, metformin plus a GLP-1 receptor agonist, or metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor. The primary outcome is the mean HbA1c (a continuous variable) after 6 months. Which statistical test is most appropriate for comparing the primary outcome among the groups?
answerHtml: Answer: A. ANOVA
explanationHtml: ANOVA compares the means of a continuous variable across three or more independent groups. Running several pairwise t-tests instead would inflate the type I error. If the ANOVA is significant, post-hoc tests (such as Tukey) identify which groups differ.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: chi-square compares proportions of categorical outcomes (for example, the % reaching HbA1c < 7%). C: a paired t-test compares two measurements in the same subjects. D: a correlation describes the relationship between two continuous variables, not group differences. E: a two-sample t-test compares only two groups.

stemHtml: In a large healthy population, a serum analyte is normally distributed with a mean of 100 mg/dL and a standard deviation of 10 mg/dL. Approximately what percentage of this population has a value greater than 120 mg/dL?
answerHtml: Answer: A. 2.5%
explanationHtml: 120 is 2 SD above the mean: (120 − 100)/10 = 2. About 95% of values lie within ±2 SD (80–120), so 5% lie outside, split equally between the two tails: 2.5% above 120. This is why laboratory "normal ranges" (mean ± 2 SD) label about 5% of healthy people as abnormal.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B (5%) counts both tails. C (16%) is the fraction above +1 SD ((100 − 68)/2). D (0.15%) is the fraction above +3 SD. E (32%) is the fraction outside ±1 SD (both tails).

stemHtml: A 54-year-old man with schizophrenia, stable for 6 years on a long-acting injectable antipsychotic, is admitted with diabetic foot osteomyelitis. The surgeon recommends below-knee amputation. The patient declines. Over three discussions on different days, he accurately describes his condition and explains that without surgery the infection could spread and he could die. He says he would rather accept that risk and try prolonged IV antibiotics, because staying able to walk on his own leg matters more to him than living longer. He has no hallucinations, and his reasoning involves no delusional content. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Petition the court for an order authorizing amputation

options.label: B
options.html: Obtain a psychiatric consultation to declare him incapable because of his diagnosis

options.label: C
options.html: Ask his sister to provide consent as his next of kin

options.label: D
options.html: Proceed with surgery under implied emergency consent

options.label: E
options.html: Respect his decision, continue IV antibiotics, and keep the option of surgery open

answerHtml: Answer: E. Respect his refusal
explanationHtml: Capacity is decision-specific and has four elements. He communicates a consistent choice, understands the information, appreciates the consequences for himself (including death), and reasons in line with his own values. A psychiatric diagnosis does not by itself mean incapacity, and a patient with capacity may refuse even life-saving treatment. The physician should accept his decision, provide the best alternative treatment, address any misunderstandings, and revisit the decision if his condition or wishes change. Document the capacity assessment.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: courts are not needed to override a patient who has capacity, and they would not do so. B: any physician can assess capacity, and declaring incapacity on the basis of a diagnosis alone is discriminatory. A consult may help in unclear cases, but this case is clear. C: surrogates decide only when the patient lacks capacity. D: this is not an emergency with an unconscious patient, and implied consent never overrides an explicit refusal.

stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl comes to her primary care physician alone and asks for a prescription for oral contraceptive pills. She has been sexually active with one male partner for 3 months and uses condoms inconsistently. She asks that her parents not be told. She has no history of migraine with aura, hypertension or thromboembolism, and her BP is 112/70 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Explain that a parent must give consent before contraception can be prescribed to a minor

options.label: B
options.html: Prescribe the pills, but notify her parents because she is under 18

options.label: C
options.html: Decline to prescribe and refer her to a gynecologist

options.label: D
options.html: Counsel her on contraception and STI prevention, encourage (but do not require) parental involvement, and prescribe contraception confidentially

options.label: E
options.html: Perform a pelvic examination and Pap test before prescribing

answerHtml: Answer: D. Counsel her and prescribe confidentially
explanationHtml: In the US, minors may consent on their own to contraception (as well as STI care, prenatal care, and substance-use treatment) in nearly all states, and federal Title X programs provide confidential contraceptive services. Requiring parental consent deters adolescents from seeking care and increases unintended pregnancy. Good care includes counseling on long-acting reversible contraception (the most effective option), consistent condom use for STI prevention, chlamydia/gonorrhea screening (recommended for sexually active females 24 and younger), and gently encouraging her to involve a trusted adult.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B: parental consent or notification is not required for contraception, and notifying her parents would breach confidentiality. C: refusing to provide routine care she is entitled to is inappropriate. E: neither a pelvic exam nor a Pap test is required before starting hormonal contraception, and cervical cancer screening does not begin until age 21.

stemHtml: During an outpatient psychotherapy session, a 32-year-old man says he recently bought a handgun and intends to kill his former girlfriend, whom he names, "this weekend" because she ended their relationship. He refuses voluntary admission. Which of the following is the psychiatrist's most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.html: Maintain confidentiality, because HIPAA prohibits disclosure of psychotherapy content

options.label: B
options.html: Take reasonable steps to protect the woman, including warning her and notifying law enforcement, and evaluate the patient for involuntary hospitalization

options.label: C
options.html: Document the statement and reassess the threat at the next scheduled session

options.label: D
options.html: Increase the patient's medication dose and schedule weekly visits

options.label: E
options.html: Report the patient to the state medical board

answerHtml: Answer: B. Protect the identifiable victim
explanationHtml: Under the Tarasoff principle, adopted by statute or case law in most states, a clinician whose patient makes a credible threat of serious violence against an identifiable person has a duty to take reasonable steps to protect that person. Those steps include warning the victim, notifying the police, and/or hospitalizing the patient. Confidentiality is not absolute when there is a serious, imminent risk of harm. HIPAA explicitly permits disclosure to prevent a serious and imminent threat to a person's health or safety.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: HIPAA permits this disclosure. C and D: the threat is specific and imminent (he has a weapon and a date), so waiting or adjusting medication is inadequate. E: the medical board licenses physicians and has no role in a patient's threats.

stemHtml: A 74-year-old man has a large left MCA stroke and is aphasic and unable to make decisions. Three years ago he completed a durable power of attorney for health care that names his niece, a nurse, as his agent. He has no living will. His wife of 40 years and his adult son disagree with the niece about whether he should have a feeding tube placed. The niece says he often told her he would never want to "live on tubes." Whose decision should guide the medical team?

options.label: A
options.html: His wife's, because the spouse is first in the surrogate hierarchy

options.label: B
options.html: His son's, because he is the closest blood relative

options.label: C
options.html: His niece's, applying her knowledge of what the patient would have wanted

options.label: D
options.html: The attending physician's, based on the patient's best medical interest

answerHtml: Answer: C. The niece (designated health care agent)
explanationHtml: A legally designated health care agent (durable power of attorney for health care) ranks above all default surrogates, including the spouse. The patient chose her when he had capacity. The agent must use substituted judgment, deciding as the patient would have, based on his values and prior statements. Here those statements are specific. The team should support the family through the disagreement, but the agent makes the decision. An ethics consultation can help mediate the conflict but does not replace the agent.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B: the default surrogate hierarchy applies only when no agent has been designated. D: physicians do not substitute their own judgment when a valid surrogate is available. E: ethics committees advise and mediate; they do not decide.

stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman hospitalized for cellulitis mistakenly receives a single oral dose of amlodipine 5 mg that was ordered for her roommate. The error is discovered 1 hour later. Her vital signs remain normal, and the pharmacist advises that no harm is expected beyond monitoring her BP. The intern asks the attending physician what to do. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.label: A
options.html: Do not tell the patient, because she was not harmed

options.label: B
options.html: Tell the patient only if she becomes hypotensive

options.label: C
options.html: Tell the patient what happened, apologize, explain the monitoring plan, and report the error through the hospital's safety reporting system

options.label: D
options.html: Document in the chart that the medication was given as ordered

options.label: E
options.html: Report the nurse to the state board of nursing

answerHtml: Answer: C. Disclose, apologize and report
explanationHtml: Errors that reach the patient should be disclosed honestly and promptly, even when no harm results. Professional standards (AMA, Joint Commission) and patients' own expectations support this, and transparency maintains trust and is associated with fewer lawsuits. Disclosure covers what happened, an apology, the possible consequences, the monitoring plan, and the steps being taken to prevent a recurrence. Reporting through the institution's non-punitive system allows a systems analysis (for example, of patient identification and barcode scanning).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B: the patient has a right to know about errors in her care, and disclosure should not depend on harm. D: falsifying the medical record is unethical and illegal. E: a punitive response to an individual is inappropriate for a system-type error in a just-culture framework, and a licensing board report is reserved for reckless or impaired practice.

stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after being struck by a car. He has a splenic laceration and is in hemorrhagic shock: BP 68/40 mm Hg, HR 160/min, hemoglobin 5.1 g/dL despite crystalloid boluses. The surgeon plans emergency laparotomy and needs to transfuse him now. His parents, who are Jehovah's Witnesses, refuse any blood products for their son. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Respect the parents' refusal and continue crystalloid resuscitation

options.label: B
options.html: Delay the transfusion until a court order is obtained

options.label: C
options.html: Request an urgent ethics committee meeting before deciding

options.label: D
options.html: Transfuse the child now, informing the parents and documenting the emergency

options.label: E
options.html: Ask the child whether he wants a blood transfusion

answerHtml: Answer: D. Transfuse now
explanationHtml: Parents cannot refuse life-saving treatment for a minor on religious grounds. A competent adult Jehovah's Witness may refuse blood for themselves, but the state's interest in protecting children overrides parental refusal when the child's life is at risk. In a true emergency where delay would cause death or serious harm, physicians should treat immediately. If time allows (for example, a planned transfusion during chemotherapy), seek a court order. Use blood-sparing strategies where possible, and treat the parents respectfully.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: withholding transfusion would likely let the child die. B and C: these are appropriate only when treatment is not urgent; here, delay is life-threatening. E: a 6-year-old does not have the capacity to make this decision, and the stem calls for action now.

stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman who speaks only Spanish returns to discuss the results of a breast biopsy that shows invasive ductal carcinoma. Her bilingual 15-year-old granddaughter and her adult son are with her, and both offer to interpret. A bilingual housekeeping staff member also offers to help. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to communicate the diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Use a trained professional medical interpreter (in person, by video or by phone)

options.label: B
options.html: Use the granddaughter, since she is fluent in both languages

options.label: C
options.html: Use the son, since he is an adult family member

options.label: D
options.html: Speak slowly in simple English and use diagrams

options.label: E
options.html: Use the bilingual housekeeping staff member

answerHtml: Answer: A. Professional medical interpreter
explanationHtml: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (and Section 1557 of the ACA) requires federally funded health care providers to offer language assistance. Trained medical interpreters convey medical terms accurately, are bound by confidentiality, and do not filter information. Family members, and especially minors, may omit or soften bad news, impose their own views, or be traumatized, and the patient may not speak freely in front of them. Afterward, ask the patient whether she would like her family present for the discussion.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: using a child as an interpreter is particularly inappropriate for serious news. C: family interpreters raise accuracy, confidentiality and bias problems; they can be used only if the patient insists after being offered a professional. D: the patient does not speak English. E: untrained staff are not qualified in medical interpretation and raise confidentiality concerns.

stemHtml: On a pediatric ward, a liquid oral medication was drawn into a standard Luer-lock syringe and accidentally injected into a child's IV line, causing harm. A root cause analysis is performed. Which of the following interventions would be most effective in preventing this type of error from happening again?

options.label: A
options.html: Mandatory annual education sessions on medication administration

options.label: B
options.html: Using oral/enteral syringes whose connectors physically cannot attach to IV ports

options.label: C
options.html: Adding "FOR ORAL USE ONLY" warning stickers to oral medication bottles

options.label: D
options.html: Disciplinary action against the nurse involved

options.label: E
options.html: A policy requiring a second nurse to double-check and co-sign all oral liquid medications

answerHtml: Answer: B. A forcing function (incompatible connectors such as ENFit)
explanationHtml: In the hierarchy of safety interventions, the strongest are forcing functions and physical design changes, which make the error impossible whatever the person's vigilance. Next come automation and standardization, then checklists and double checks, and the weakest are education, policies, and warning labels, which all depend on human memory and attention. This error came from a latent system flaw (oral medication drawn up in IV-compatible syringes). Fixing the system is better than blaming the individual.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and C: education and labels are the weakest interventions, because people still make mistakes when busy or tired. D: punishing an individual for an error the system invited does not prevent recurrence and discourages reporting (it is contrary to just culture). E: independent double checks help, but they are weaker than a forcing function and prone to "automation" of the check.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old man returns to clinic for the results of a CT-guided liver biopsy, which show metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma. The physician has arranged a private room, silenced her pager, and sat down facing the patient and his wife, who he asked to be present. Which of the following is the most appropriate next statement?

options.label: A
options.html: "I'm afraid the biopsy shows a cancer that has spread to your liver."

options.label: B
options.html: "Let's talk about which chemotherapy regimen would be best for you."

options.label: C
options.html: "Don't worry, there is a lot we can do for this nowadays."

options.label: D
options.html: "The pathology shows stage IV pancreatic adenocarcinoma with hepatic metastases."

options.label: E
options.html: "Before we go over the results, can you tell me what you understand about why we did the biopsy?"

answerHtml: Answer: E. Assess the patient's perception
explanationHtml: SPIKES: the Setting is complete (private, seated, uninterrupted, support person present). The next step is Perception: find out what the patient already knows and expects, which lets the physician correct misunderstandings and pitch the news correctly. Then comes the Invitation (how much detail he wants), then Knowledge with a warning shot, then responding to Emotions, and finally Strategy and summary.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A is an appropriate "warning shot" plus disclosure, but it skips perception and invitation. B jumps to strategy before he has heard the news. C is false reassurance, which undermines trust and blocks emotional expression. D uses jargon and delivers the news abruptly, without first assessing his understanding.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes develops crushing substernal chest pain but does not seek care until 9 hours later. ECG shows ST elevations in leads V1–V4, and troponin I is markedly elevated. He dies of a ventricular arrhythmia 2 hours after arrival. Electron microscopy of myocytes from the center of the affected region would most likely show which of the following changes that indicates the injury had become irreversible?

options.label: B
options.html: Detachment of ribosomes from rough endoplasmic reticulum

answerHtml: Answer: E. Fragmentation of the nucleus (karyorrhexis)
explanationHtml: After about 20–40 minutes of severe ischemia, myocytes cross the point of no return. Irreversible injury is defined by damage to membranes (plasma, mitochondrial, lysosomal) and by nuclear changes: pyknosis, then karyorrhexis, then karyolysis. Large amorphous Ca²⁺-rich densities in mitochondria are another marker. At 9+ hours, the infarct center shows nuclear breakdown and early coagulative necrosis.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B, C, and D are all consequences of ATP depletion (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase failure, ↓ protein synthesis, cytoskeletal changes, ↓ pH from anaerobic glycolysis). These are reversible if blood flow is restored in time.

stemHtml: A 45-year-old man with alcohol use disorder comes to the emergency department with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and repeated vomiting. Serum lipase is 1,800 U/L (normal < 60). Despite intensive care, he dies of multiorgan failure. At autopsy, the peripancreatic adipose tissue contains multiple chalky-white foci that appear basophilic on H&E staining. Which of the following best explains the formation of these foci?

options.label: A
options.html: Release of fatty acids by lipases, which then combine with calcium

options.label: B
options.html: Denaturation of structural proteins with preservation of cell outlines

options.label: C
options.html: Dystrophic calcification of caseous granulomatous debris

options.label: E
options.html: Deposition of immune complexes and fibrin in vessel walls

answerHtml: Answer: A. Release of fatty acids by lipases, which then combine with calcium
explanationHtml: Pancreatic lipases leak into surrounding fat and split triglycerides. The released fatty acids bind calcium (saponification), giving chalky-white, basophilic deposits. This is enzymatic fat necrosis. It is a form of dystrophic calcification in necrotic tissue, and it uses up serum calcium, which is why hypocalcemia is a poor prognostic sign in acute pancreatitis.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B describes coagulative necrosis (ischemic infarcts). C is caseous necrosis (TB, fungi). D: metastatic calcification needs high serum Ca²⁺ or phosphate and occurs in normal tissue; pancreatitis causes hypocalcemia. E is fibrinoid necrosis (vasculitis, malignant hypertension).

stemHtml: A 56-year-old woman has painless cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy that has waxed and waned over 2 years. Lymph node biopsy shows closely packed follicles of small cleaved and large centroblast-like cells that efface the nodal architecture. Cytogenetics shows a translocation between chromosomes 14 and 18. The translocation most directly promotes survival of the neoplastic cells by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Constitutive activation of a non-receptor tyrosine kinase

options.label: B
options.html: Overexpression of a nuclear transcription factor that drives proliferation

options.label: C
options.html: Prevention of mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization and cytochrome c release

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of Fas-mediated death receptor signaling

answerHtml: Answer: C. Prevention of mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization and cytochrome c release
explanationHtml: Follicular lymphoma carries t(14;18). This moves BCL2 next to the immunoglobulin heavy-chain (IGH) enhancer. BCL-2 overexpression blocks BAX/BAK pore formation in the mitochondrial outer membrane, so cytochrome c is not released, the apoptosome does not form, and caspase-9 is not activated. The intrinsic apoptosis pathway is shut off. The cells survive instead of dividing quickly, which explains the indolent course. Follicular lymphoma can later transform into diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A is BCR::ABL1 (CML) or JAK2. B is MYC in Burkitt t(8;14). D describes the extrinsic pathway defect in ALPS. E is the mechanism of retinoblastoma and HPV E7, not t(14;18).

stemHtml: A 5-week-old boy is brought to the clinic because his umbilical cord stump has not separated and the surrounding skin is red and indurated. He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Temperature is 38.3°C (101°F). Leukocyte count is 42,000/mm³ with 85% neutrophils. A culture from the umbilical site grows Staphylococcus aureus, yet there is no pus at the site. Growth is normal, and his red cells type as group A, Rh positive. Which of the following is most likely defective in this patient?

options.label: A
options.html: Fucosylation of the selectin ligand sialyl-Lewis X

options.label: B
options.html: The CD18 subunit of β2 integrins

answerHtml: Answer: B. The CD18 subunit of β2 integrins
explanationHtml: Delayed umbilical cord separation, omphalitis without pus, and marked neutrophilia are the classic triad of leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 (autosomal recessive ITGB2 mutation). Without CD18, LFA-1 and Mac-1 cannot bind endothelial ICAM-1. Neutrophils roll but cannot adhere firmly or migrate into tissue, so they build up in the blood and pus does not form.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A is LAD type 2. It impairs rolling, but it comes with the Bombay (hh) blood phenotype, intellectual disability, and growth delay; this infant is growing normally and his red cells express A antigen, which a Bombay (hh) phenotype cannot do (Bombay cells lack H, the A/B precursor, and type falsely as group O on routine testing). C: PECAM-1 deficiency is not a classic clinical syndrome. D is chronic granulomatous disease; neutrophils still reach tissue and abscesses form. E is Chédiak–Higashi syndrome (albinism, giant granules, neuropathy).

stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy has had a Staphylococcus aureus liver abscess, Serratia marcescens osteomyelitis, and now Aspergillus pneumonia. His maternal uncle died of recurrent infections in childhood. A dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry assay shows markedly reduced fluorescence of stimulated neutrophils. A deficiency of which of the following enzymes is the most likely cause?
answerHtml: Answer: D. NADPH oxidase
explanationHtml: This is chronic granulomatous disease. The most common form is X-linked (CYBB/gp91phox), which fits the affected maternal uncle. Without NADPH oxidase there is no respiratory burst (O₂ → superoxide), so the DHR test shows low fluorescence. Catalase-negative bacteria make their own H₂O₂, which the neutrophil can use for killing. Catalase-positive organisms (S. aureus, Serratia, Burkholderia, Nocardia, Aspergillus) destroy their own H₂O₂ and so survive. Prophylaxis is TMP-SMX plus itraconazole, with or without IFN-γ.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: MPO deficiency is usually mild (Candida infections), and the DHR test is normal because the oxidative burst still happens. B and E are antioxidant enzymes that do not cause this syndrome. C: glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency is von Gierke disease. Type Ib (a G6P transporter defect) causes neutropenia, not a burst defect.

stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman has a 3-day history of productive cough and chills. Temperature is 39.4°C (103°F). Chest x-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. She takes ibuprofen, and her temperature returns to 37.5°C within 2 hours. Which of the following mediators acts directly on hypothalamic thermoregulatory neurons to raise the temperature set point, and is reduced by the drug she took?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Prostaglandin E₂
explanationHtml: Pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6) from activated macrophages act on the endothelium near the preoptic hypothalamus and induce COX-2. The PGE₂ produced binds EP3 receptors on thermoregulatory neurons and raises the set point. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen block COX and so lower PGE₂ synthesis. This is how they reduce fever, even though the cytokine levels are unchanged.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B are endogenous pyrogens, but they work upstream by inducing PGE₂, and ibuprofen does not block their production. C causes vasodilation and increased permeability, not fever. D is a neutrophil chemoattractant made by 5-lipoxygenase, which NSAIDs do not inhibit.

stemHtml: A 72-year-old widower who lives alone and eats mostly tea, toast, and canned meat comes to the clinic because a shin laceration from 6 weeks ago has not healed. Examination shows swollen, bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages on the legs, and coiled body hairs. Which step in collagen synthesis is most likely impaired?

options.label: B
options.html: Cleavage of terminal propeptides by procollagen peptidases

options.label: C
options.html: Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues

options.label: D
options.html: Covalent cross-linking of tropocollagen by lysyl oxidase

options.label: E
options.html: Translation of α chains with glycine at every third residue

answerHtml: Answer: C. Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues
explanationHtml: This patient has scurvy. Vitamin C (ascorbate) keeps the iron in prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases in the Fe²⁺ state. These enzymes work in the rough endoplasmic reticulum. Without hydroxyproline, the triple helix forms poorly, so collagen is weak. The results are fragile vessels (perifollicular and gum hemorrhage), corkscrew hairs, and poor wound healing.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A occurs after hydroxylation, and its failure is not a vitamin C problem. B is defective in Ehlers–Danlos dermatosparaxis type. D requires copper (Menkes disease, copper deficiency). E: glycine substitutions cause osteogenesis imperfecta.

stemHtml: A 12-year-old boy with osteosarcoma of the distal femur receives a high-dose methotrexate infusion. Twenty-four hours after the infusion starts, he is given scheduled doses of leucovorin (folinic acid) along with IV hydration and urine alkalinization. Which of the following best describes how leucovorin protects his normal cells?

options.label: A
options.html: It inhibits thymidylate synthase in normal cells

options.label: B
options.html: It provides a reduced folate that bypasses dihydrofolate reductase inhibition

options.label: C
options.html: It increases renal tubular secretion of methotrexate

options.label: D
options.html: It cleaves methotrexate into inactive metabolites

options.label: E
options.html: It increases transcription of dihydrofolate reductase

answerHtml: Answer: B. It provides a reduced folate that bypasses dihydrofolate reductase inhibition
explanationHtml: Methotrexate blocks DHFR, so cells run out of tetrahydrofolate and cannot make thymidylate or purines. Leucovorin (5-formyl-THF) is already reduced and enters the folate pool downstream of DHFR. This restores DNA synthesis in normal marrow and mucosa. Timing the "rescue" after the infusion is what makes high-dose MTX tolerable.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: inhibiting TS is how 5-FU works (leucovorin actually strengthens 5-FU's binding to TS). C: hydration and alkalinization help MTX clearance, not leucovorin. D describes glucarpidase, used for MTX toxicity with renal failure. E is a mechanism of tumor resistance (DHFR gene amplification), not rescue.

stemHtml: A 77-year-old man has had progressive exertional dyspnea and ankle edema for 1 year. He had bilateral carpal tunnel release 8 years ago. Blood pressure is 108/70 mm Hg. ECG shows low QRS voltage in the limb leads. Echocardiography shows symmetric left ventricular wall thickening, a "speckled" myocardium, and an ejection fraction of 55%. Serum and urine immunofixation are negative, and the serum free light-chain ratio is normal. A technetium-99m pyrophosphate scan shows intense myocardial uptake. Which protein is most likely deposited in his heart?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Wild-type transthyretin
explanationHtml: An older man with HFpEF, thick ventricles but low ECG voltage (an infiltrative pattern), and earlier bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome has wild-type ATTR (senile systemic) amyloidosis. Negative monoclonal protein studies exclude AL amyloid. A positive PYP scan with no monoclonal protein confirms ATTR without biopsy. Treatment is tafamidis, which stabilizes the TTR tetramer.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: AL amyloid would show a monoclonal protein or an abnormal free light-chain ratio. C: AA amyloid needs chronic inflammation and mainly involves the kidneys. D: Aβ2M occurs in long-term dialysis patients. E: ANF amyloid is limited to the atria, is usually incidental, and does not cause carpal tunnel syndrome.

stemHtml: A 12-year-old boy has 3 weeks of abdominal pain and a rapidly enlarging right lower quadrant mass. Serum LDH is 2,400 U/L and uric acid is 9.8 mg/dL. Biopsy of an ileocecal mass shows sheets of medium-sized lymphocytes mixed with scattered pale macrophages containing apoptotic debris. Ki-67 stains nearly 100% of tumor cells. The product of the gene most likely dysregulated in this tumor normally functions as which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: An anti-apoptotic protein in the mitochondrial membrane

options.label: B
options.html: A cyclin that activates CDK4 during G1

options.label: D
options.html: A transcription factor that activates growth and metabolic genes

answerHtml: Answer: D. A transcription factor that activates growth and metabolic genes
explanationHtml: This is sporadic Burkitt lymphoma: an ileocecal mass, a "starry-sky" pattern of tingible-body macrophages, and a proliferation index near 100%. The defining lesion is t(8;14), which places MYC under the IGH enhancer. MYC is a nuclear transcription factor that drives ribosome biogenesis, glycolysis, and cell-cycle entry. Very rapid turnover causes high LDH and uric acid and a high risk of tumor lysis syndrome.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A is BCL-2 (follicular lymphoma). B is cyclin D1 (mantle cell lymphoma). C is ABL or JAK2. E is RAS.

stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman is diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast. Her mother died of adrenocortical carcinoma at 40, her brother had osteosarcoma at 14, and a maternal cousin had a choroid plexus carcinoma in childhood. Germline testing finds a pathogenic variant in a gene whose product normally does which of the following?

options.label: B
options.html: Induces p21 expression to arrest the cell cycle at G1/S after DNA damage

options.label: C
options.html: Repairs DNA double-strand breaks by homologous recombination

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibits mTOR signaling through a complex with hamartin

answerHtml: Answer: B. Induces p21 expression to arrest the cell cycle at G1/S after DNA damage
explanationHtml: Early breast cancer, adrenocortical carcinoma, sarcoma, and brain tumors (choroid plexus carcinoma is a hallmark) point to Li–Fraumeni syndrome, caused by germline TP53 mutation. p53 senses DNA damage and induces p21 (CDKN1A). p21 inhibits cyclin–CDK complexes, so Rb stays hypophosphorylated and the cell halts at G1/S for repair. If the damage cannot be repaired, p53 triggers apoptosis through BAX and PUMA.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A is APC (FAP). C is BRCA1/2. These cause breast and ovarian cancer, but not adrenocortical carcinoma, osteosarcoma, or choroid plexus tumors. D is TSC2/tuberin (tuberous sclerosis). E is VHL.

stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman with stage II HER2-negative breast cancer is treated with doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide followed by paclitaxel. Fourteen months later, she has orthopnea and bilateral crackles. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30%; her baseline was 62%. Which agent, given with her chemotherapy, would most likely have reduced the risk of this complication?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Dexrazoxane
explanationHtml: Anthracyclines cause cumulative, dose-dependent dilated cardiomyopathy. The mechanism involves iron-dependent free-radical injury and topoisomerase IIβ poisoning in cardiomyocytes. Dexrazoxane chelates iron and blocks topoisomerase IIβ, which reduces cardiotoxicity. Monitor LVEF with serial echocardiography. Trastuzumab cardiotoxicity, by contrast, is usually reversible and not dose-dependent; it is not relevant here because her tumor is HER2-negative.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B (mesna) prevents cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide hemorrhagic cystitis by binding acrolein. C (amifostine) protects the kidneys from cisplatin and the salivary glands during radiation. D rescues cells from methotrexate. E prevents hyperuricemia in tumor lysis syndrome.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old man with stage IIA classic Hodgkin lymphoma is receiving ABVD chemotherapy. After his fourth cycle, he has 3 weeks of dry cough and exertional dyspnea. Temperature is 37.0°C, pulse oximetry on room air is 92%, and bibasilar fine inspiratory crackles are heard. Pulmonary function tests show a restrictive pattern with a markedly reduced DLCO. CT shows subpleural reticular opacities. Which drug is most likely responsible?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Bleomycin
explanationHtml: Bleomycin binds iron and oxygen to form free radicals that break DNA strands, and it acts mainly in G2. The lungs and skin have little bleomycin hydrolase, the enzyme that inactivates it. This allows pneumonitis that progresses to fibrosis: restrictive physiology, low DLCO, and subpleural reticulation. Risk rises with cumulative dose, age, renal impairment, smoking, radiation, and high inspired oxygen concentrations (FiO₂). Myelosuppression from bleomycin is minimal.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: doxorubicin is cardiotoxic, which would cause dilated cardiomyopathy (orthopnea, low EF, pulmonary edema), not subpleural fibrosis with restriction. B: vinblastine mainly suppresses the marrow. C: dacarbazine causes nausea, myelosuppression, and flu-like symptoms. D: ondansetron is an antiemetic and can prolong the QT interval, but it is not a pulmonary toxin.

stemHtml: A 64-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history is brought to the emergency department with confusion, polyuria, and constipation. Serum calcium is 14.1 mg/dL, phosphorus 2.0 mg/dL (normal 3.0–4.5), intact PTH 8 pg/mL (normal 10–65), and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D at the low end of normal. Chest CT shows a 5-cm cavitating mass near the right hilum. Bone scan shows no lesions. Which mechanism best explains his hypercalcemia?

options.label: C
options.html: Tumor secretion of parathyroid hormone–related peptide

options.label: D
options.html: Ectopic secretion of authentic parathyroid hormone

answerHtml: Answer: C. Tumor secretion of parathyroid hormone–related peptide
explanationHtml: A central cavitating mass in a heavy smoker is typical of squamous cell carcinoma, the classic source of PTHrP (humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy). PTHrP binds the PTH1 receptor, increasing bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption and causing phosphaturia (low phosphate). Endogenous PTH is suppressed. Unlike PTH, PTHrP only weakly stimulates renal 1α-hydroxylase, so calcitriol is not elevated.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A (seen in lymphomas and granulomas) would raise 1,25-(OH)₂D. B: the bone scan is negative, and bone metastases do not lower phosphate. D: true ectopic PTH is extremely rare, and intact PTH is suppressed here. E would cause hypokalemic alkalosis and Cushing features (more typical of small cell carcinoma), not hypercalcemia.

stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman who smokes has had 3 months of difficulty climbing stairs and rising from chairs, as well as dry mouth and constipation. Proximal leg strength is 4/5 at first but improves after several seconds of repeated maximal contraction. Patellar reflexes are absent at rest but appear after brief exercise. Ptosis and diplopia are absent. Chest CT shows bulky mediastinal lymphadenopathy with a central lung mass. Her symptoms are most likely caused by antibodies directed against which of the following?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels
explanationHtml: Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome causes proximal weakness that improves with repeated effort, low reflexes that return after exercise (post-exercise facilitation), and autonomic symptoms. Antibodies block presynaptic VGCCs, so less acetylcholine is released. Repeated stimulation builds up presynaptic Ca²⁺ and temporarily improves release, which is why strength improves. About half of cases are paraneoplastic, mostly from small cell lung cancer (a central mass with bulky nodes). Treatment: treat the tumor and give amifampridine (a K⁺ channel blocker that prolongs depolarization).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B cause myasthenia gravis, which worsens with use and typically involves ocular muscles. C causes paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration (ovarian or breast cancer). D causes sensory neuronopathy or encephalomyelitis with SCLC, not fatigable proximal weakness.

stemHtml: A 52-year-old man has fatigue and early satiety. He has massive splenomegaly but no lymphadenopathy. Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL, leukocyte count 2,100/mm³ with an absolute monocyte count of 30/mm³ (normal 200–800), and platelets 64,000/mm³. Bone marrow aspiration yields a "dry tap." The peripheral smear shows a few medium-sized lymphoid cells with fine, hair-like cytoplasmic projections. Which additional finding is most likely?

options.label: B
options.html: Coexpression of CD5 and CD23 on B cells

options.label: D
options.html: Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase positivity and BRAF V600E mutation

options.label: E
options.html: CD15 and CD30 positivity of large binucleate cells

answerHtml: Answer: D. Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase positivity and BRAF V600E mutation
explanationHtml: Hairy cell leukemia, a mature B-cell neoplasm of middle-aged men, presents with pancytopenia (classically with profound monocytopenia), massive splenomegaly from red pulp infiltration, and a dry tap from reticulin fibrosis. The cells are TRAP⁺, CD11c⁺, CD25⁺, CD103⁺, and annexin A1⁺. Nearly all carry BRAF V600E. Purine analogs (cladribine, pentostatin) produce durable remissions.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A (CML) causes leukocytosis, not pancytopenia. B (CLL) causes lymphocytosis with smudge cells and lymphadenopathy. C: primary myelofibrosis also gives a dry tap and splenomegaly, but it shows teardrop cells and a leukoerythroblastic smear, not hairy lymphocytes with monocytopenia. E describes Reed–Sternberg cells of Hodgkin lymphoma.

stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman has 4 months of fatigue, exertional dyspnea, and a craving to chew ice. Her menstrual periods are heavy and last 8 days. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL, MCV 71 fL, RDW 18.5% (normal 11.5–14.5), and platelets 480,000/mm³. Which of the following additional laboratory findings is most likely?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Increased total iron-binding capacity
explanationHtml: Menorrhagia, pagophagia (ice craving), microcytosis, high RDW, and reactive thrombocytosis indicate iron deficiency anemia. When iron stores fall, the liver makes more transferrin, so TIBC rises. Ferritin falls (the most specific test), and transferrin saturation falls. Without iron, ferrochelatase cannot insert it into protoporphyrin, so free (zinc) protoporphyrin builds up.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B and C are the opposite of what happens in iron deficiency; they are seen in iron overload or sideroblastic anemia. D: protoporphyrin is increased, not decreased. E: HbA₂ is elevated in β-thalassemia trait and, if anything, falls in iron deficiency.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has increasing fatigue. Hemoglobin is 10.2 g/dL and MCV 83 fL. Serum iron is 35 μg/dL (normal 50–170), TIBC 210 μg/dL (normal 250–400), ferritin 410 ng/mL (normal 15–200), and CRP 4.8 mg/dL. Which of the following best explains her low serum iron?

options.label: A
options.html: Increased duodenal DMT1 expression with increased iron absorption

options.label: C
options.html: Impaired activity of δ-aminolevulinic acid synthase

options.label: E
options.html: Cytokine-induced hepcidin causing internalization and degradation of ferroportin

answerHtml: Answer: E. Cytokine-induced hepcidin causing internalization and degradation of ferroportin
explanationHtml: This is anemia of chronic disease (inflammation). IL-6 from active RA induces hepatic hepcidin. Hepcidin binds ferroportin, the only cellular iron exporter, and causes its internalization and degradation in macrophages and enterocytes. Iron is trapped in storage (high ferritin), serum iron falls, and transferrin (a negative acute-phase reactant) falls, so TIBC is low. This deprives bacteria of iron, but it also limits erythropoiesis.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A would raise serum iron, and hepcidin actually reduces absorption. B leads to B12 deficiency (macrocytic anemia). C causes sideroblastic anemia with high serum iron. D: nephrotic syndrome can lose transferrin, but nothing suggests it here, and it would not explain high ferritin.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old man of Greek descent has a mildly abnormal CBC on a pre-employment physical. He feels well. Hemoglobin is 11.9 g/dL, MCV 63 fL, RBC count 6.2 million/mm³, RDW 13.8% (normal), and ferritin 95 ng/mL. His younger sister needed regular transfusions from 6 months of age because of severe anemia with marked hepatosplenomegaly and frontal bossing. Hemoglobin electrophoresis of this patient is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: C
options.html: Hemoglobin A₂ 5.5% with mildly increased hemoglobin F

answerHtml: Answer: C. Hemoglobin A₂ 5.5% with mildly increased hemoglobin F
explanationHtml: Marked microcytosis with mild anemia, a high RBC count (Mentzer index 63/6.2 ≈ 10, under 13), normal RDW, and normal ferritin indicate thalassemia trait. Mediterranean ancestry and a sibling with transfusion-dependent anemia starting at 6 months (β-thalassemia major) mean he carries β-thalassemia trait. Reduced β-chain synthesis shifts production toward δ chains (HbA₂ > 3.5%) and sometimes γ chains (HbF).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A is sickle trait (normocytic, no microcytosis). B is HbH disease (three α genes deleted; moderate hemolytic anemia, not a symptom-free carrier). D is the pattern of β-thalassemia major (his sister), not a well adult. E is seen in newborns with α-thalassemia, or as hydrops fetalis when all four α genes are deleted.

stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for irritability, constipation, and intermittent abdominal pain. His family recently moved into a house built in 1950 that is being renovated. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL with MCV 70 fL. The peripheral smear shows coarse basophilic stippling of erythrocytes. Inhibition of which enzyme accounts for the increased zinc protoporphyrin in his erythrocytes?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Ferrochelatase
explanationHtml: Lead (from old paint dust during renovation) inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase. Ferrochelatase inserts Fe²⁺ into protoporphyrin IX in the mitochondria. When it is blocked, zinc is inserted instead, and zinc protoporphyrin builds up. Lead also inhibits pyrimidine 5′-nucleotidase, so ribosomal RNA is not broken down; the RNA aggregates appear as coarse basophilic stippling. Treat with succimer for moderate levels, or dimercaprol plus CaNa₂EDTA for encephalopathy or very high levels, and remove the source.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A is the rate-limiting enzyme (needs B6) and is defective in X-linked sideroblastic anemia. B is deficient in acute intermittent porphyria. C is deficient in porphyria cutanea tarda. E is deficient in congenital erythropoietic porphyria.

stemHtml: A 46-year-old man who emigrated from the Philippines was started on isoniazid monotherapy for latent tuberculosis 5 months ago. He now has fatigue and numbness of the feet. Hemoglobin is 9.0 g/dL and MCV 72 fL. Serum iron and ferritin are elevated, and transferrin saturation is 62%. A Prussian blue stain of the bone marrow shows erythroid precursors with iron granules ringing the nucleus. Besides stopping isoniazid, which treatment would most directly correct the enzymatic defect causing his anemia?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Pyridoxine
explanationHtml: Isoniazid forms an inactive complex with pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) and causes functional B6 deficiency. Pyridoxal phosphate is the required cofactor for δ-ALA synthase, the first and rate-limiting step of heme synthesis in the mitochondria. With heme synthesis blocked, iron builds up in mitochondria around the nucleus (ringed sideroblasts), and systemic iron indices rise. B6 deficiency also explains his peripheral neuropathy. This is why pyridoxine is routinely given with isoniazid.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and E treat megaloblastic (macrocytic) anemia. C would worsen iron overload. D chelates iron and may be needed for transfusional overload, but it does not fix the defect in heme synthesis.

stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis has 6 months of fatigue, tingling in both feet, and unsteady gait. Examination shows reduced vibration and position sense in the lower limbs and a positive Romberg sign. Hemoglobin is 9.3 g/dL, MCV 114 fL, and the smear shows macro-ovalocytes and neutrophils with 6 nuclear lobes. Which laboratory finding would best distinguish her condition from folate deficiency?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Elevated serum methylmalonic acid
explanationHtml: This patient has an autoimmune disease, megaloblastic anemia, and dorsal-column signs, which together suggest vitamin B12 deficiency from pernicious anemia. B12 is a cofactor for two enzymes: methionine synthase (homocysteine → methionine, shared with folate) and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA, B12 only). So methylmalonic acid rises only in B12 deficiency. Abnormal fatty acids incorporated into myelin contribute to subacute combined degeneration.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: homocysteine rises in both B12 and folate deficiency. B and E reflect ineffective erythropoiesis (intramedullary hemolysis) in both. C: both are hypoproliferative anemias.

stemHtml: A 7-year-old girl has had episodes of jaundice during viral illnesses. Her father had a splenectomy as a teenager. The spleen tip is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL, MCV 84 fL, MCHC 37.6 g/dL (normal 32–36), and reticulocytes 9%. The smear shows many small, round erythrocytes without central pallor. The direct antiglobulin test is negative. Which test is most specific for confirming the diagnosis?

options.label: D
options.html: Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59

answerHtml: Answer: B. Eosin-5-maleimide binding by flow cytometry
explanationHtml: Autosomal dominant inheritance, spherocytes, raised MCHC, splenomegaly, and a negative DAT (which excludes autoimmune spherocytosis) indicate hereditary spherocytosis. Defects in ankyrin, spectrin, band 3, or protein 4.2 cause membrane loss, and spherical cells are trapped and destroyed in the splenic cords. EMA dye binds band 3. Spherocytes have less membrane and so show lower fluorescence. EMA binding is more sensitive and specific than the classic osmotic fragility test.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A diagnoses hemoglobinopathies and thalassemias. C detects G6PD deficiency (bite cells, Heinz bodies, oxidant triggers). D diagnoses PNH. E is low in any hemolysis and does not identify the cause.

stemHtml: A 22-year-old African American man is treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a skin infection. Three days later he has dark urine and scleral icterus. Hemoglobin has fallen from 14.8 to 10.1 g/dL. LDH is elevated and haptoglobin is low. The smear shows erythrocytes with "bites" removed from their edges, and a crystal violet stain shows round intracellular inclusions. Which of the following best explains the hemolysis?

options.label: A
options.html: Defective erythrocyte cytoskeletal proteins causing membrane loss

options.label: B
options.html: Complement-mediated lysis due to absence of GPI-anchored proteins

options.label: C
options.html: Inability to regenerate reduced glutathione because of deficient NADPH production

options.label: D
options.html: IgG antibodies binding drug molecules adsorbed onto the erythrocyte membrane

options.label: E
options.html: Insufficient ATP generation from defective glycolysis

answerHtml: Answer: C. Inability to regenerate reduced glutathione because of deficient NADPH production
explanationHtml: G6PD is the rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway and is the RBC's only source of NADPH. NADPH is needed by glutathione reductase to keep glutathione reduced, which detoxifies H₂O₂. An oxidant drug (sulfonamide) denatures hemoglobin into Heinz bodies (seen with crystal violet). Splenic macrophages remove them and leave bite cells. G6PD deficiency is X-linked, and the A⁻ variant is common in people of African ancestry. Note that the G6PD level may look falsely normal during the acute episode because reticulocytes have more enzyme.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A is hereditary spherocytosis. B is PNH. D (the penicillin hapten mechanism) causes DAT-positive spherocytic hemolysis, not Heinz bodies. E is pyruvate kinase deficiency (no oxidant trigger; echinocytes).

stemHtml: A 16-year-old boy with homozygous sickle cell disease has had four hospital admissions for vaso-occlusive pain crises in the past year and one episode of acute chest syndrome. He is started on daily oral hydroxyurea. Which of the following best explains the drug's main clinical benefit in this patient?

options.label: A
options.html: It increases fetal hemoglobin, which interferes with polymerization of deoxygenated HbS

options.label: B
options.html: It blocks P-selectin–mediated adhesion of sickled cells to endothelium

options.label: C
options.html: It raises hemoglobin oxygen affinity, stabilizing oxygenated HbS

options.label: D
options.html: It increases NAD⁺ redox potential to reduce oxidative stress

options.label: E
options.html: It chelates excess iron from repeated transfusions

answerHtml: Answer: A. It increases fetal hemoglobin, which interferes with polymerization of deoxygenated HbS
explanationHtml: Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase. The resulting stress erythropoiesis reactivates γ-globin synthesis. HbF (α₂γ₂) and the α₂βSγ hybrid tetramers cannot join HbS polymers, so sickling is reduced. Hydroxyurea also lowers neutrophil and platelet counts and improves RBC hydration and NO release. It reduces pain crises, acute chest syndrome, transfusion needs, and mortality. Monitor CBC for myelosuppression and expect macrocytosis.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B is crizanlizumab. C is voxelotor, which was withdrawn from the market in 2024. D is L-glutamine. E describes deferasirox or deferoxamine.

stemHtml: A 34-year-old man has dark urine on waking, fatigue, and right upper quadrant pain. Doppler ultrasound shows hepatic vein thrombosis. Hemoglobin is 8.2 g/dL, leukocyte count 3,100/mm³, platelets 98,000/mm³, LDH 1,450 U/L, haptoglobin undetectable, urine hemosiderin positive, and the direct antiglobulin test is negative. Flow cytometry shows granulocytes and erythrocytes lacking CD55 and CD59. He is started on an intravenous humanized monoclonal antibody every 2 weeks and must receive meningococcal vaccination first. This drug binds which target?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Complement C5
explanationHtml: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria comes from an acquired PIGA mutation in a hematopoietic stem cell. Without GPI anchors, cells lack the complement regulators CD55 (DAF) and CD59 (MIRL, which blocks MAC assembly). The result is intravascular hemolysis (hemoglobinuria, hemosiderinuria), thrombosis at unusual sites, and cytopenias. Eculizumab (every 2 weeks) and ravulizumab (every 8 weeks) bind C5 and prevent formation of C5b-9 (MAC). Because terminal complement is needed against Neisseria, meningococcal vaccination is required.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A is rituximab. B is sutimlimab (cold agglutinin disease). C is tocilizumab (cytokine release syndrome, RA). D is daratumumab (myeloma).

stemHtml: A 20-year-old college student has had 2 weeks of dry cough, headache, and low-grade fever. Chest x-ray shows patchy bilateral interstitial infiltrates. She now has fatigue, and her fingertips and ears turn blue in cold weather. Hemoglobin is 8.8 g/dL, reticulocytes 8%, and indirect bilirubin 2.9 mg/dL. The blood smear shows clumped erythrocytes at room temperature that disperse when the slide is warmed. The direct antiglobulin test is positive for C3d and negative for IgG. Which mechanism is most likely responsible for her anemia?

options.label: A
options.html: IgG autoantibodies active at 37°C causing splenic phagocytosis

options.label: B
options.html: IgM autoantibodies that bind erythrocyte I antigen at low temperatures and fix complement

options.label: C
options.html: Mechanical fragmentation of erythrocytes on fibrin strands in small vessels

answerHtml: Answer: B. IgM autoantibodies that bind erythrocyte I antigen at low temperatures and fix complement
explanationHtml: Mycoplasma pneumoniae ("walking pneumonia" in a young adult) induces cross-reacting IgM against the I antigen. IgM is pentameric and causes agglutination (clumping that reverses with warming) and acrocyanosis in cooler body parts. It fixes complement. Some cells are lysed in vessels by MAC; others are coated with C3b and removed by liver Kupffer cells. When the cells return to 37°C, IgM falls off and only C3d remains, which explains the DAT pattern. Glucocorticoids work poorly; keep the patient warm and treat the cause.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A is warm AIHA (DAT IgG⁺, spherocytes). C is MAHA (schistocytes). D is G6PD deficiency. E is drug-induced immune hemolysis; she has no drug exposure.

stemHtml: A 61-year-old man has headaches, burning pain in his hands and feet, and intense itching after hot showers. He has a ruddy complexion and a palpable spleen. He does not smoke and has no sleep apnea. Hematocrit is 59%, leukocyte count 13,500/mm³, platelets 540,000/mm³, serum erythropoietin is low, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Which mechanism best explains his erythrocytosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Constitutive activation of a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase coupled to cytokine receptors, causing EPO-independent signaling

options.label: B
options.html: Ectopic erythropoietin production by a renal tumor

options.label: C
options.html: Hypoxia-driven stabilization of HIF-1α in renal interstitial cells

options.label: D
options.html: A fusion tyrosine kinase created by a reciprocal translocation

options.label: E
options.html: A hemoglobin variant with increased oxygen affinity

answerHtml: Answer: A. Constitutive activation of a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase coupled to cytokine receptors, causing EPO-independent signaling
explanationHtml: Polycythemia vera is a myeloproliferative neoplasm. About 95% of cases carry JAK2 V617F, a gain-of-function mutation in the pseudokinase domain of JAK2, the non-receptor tyrosine kinase that signals for the EPO, TPO, and G-CSF receptors. Signaling continues without EPO, so EPO is suppressed and all three lineages expand. Aquagenic pruritus (mast cell histamine), erythromelalgia, and splenomegaly are typical. Treatment: phlebotomy to Hct < 45%, low-dose aspirin, and cytoreduction (hydroxyurea, interferon, ruxolitinib) for high-risk patients.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, C, and E are secondary polycythemias with normal or high EPO and usually only RBCs increased. A high-affinity Hb also causes a left shift and lifelong erythrocytosis. D is BCR::ABL1 (CML), which causes leukocytosis with basophilia rather than isolated erythrocytosis.

stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy with severe hemophilia A has developed high-titer inhibitory antibodies against factor VIII and has recurrent knee hemarthroses. He is started on weekly subcutaneous injections of a humanized bispecific monoclonal antibody for bleeding prophylaxis. By which mechanism does this drug prevent bleeding?

options.label: A
options.html: It directly activates factor X without needing tissue factor

options.label: B
options.html: It neutralizes tissue factor pathway inhibitor

options.label: C
options.html: It bridges activated factor IX and factor X, replacing the cofactor role of factor VIIIa

options.label: D
options.html: It binds and stabilizes von Willebrand factor to prolong factor VIII half-life

answerHtml: Answer: C. It bridges activated factor IX and factor X, replacing the cofactor role of factor VIIIa
explanationHtml: Emicizumab has one arm that binds factor IXa and another that binds factor X. Holding them together the way factor VIIIa does in the tenase complex restores factor X activation. Because it is not factor VIII, inhibitors do not neutralize it, and its long half-life allows weekly or less frequent SC dosing. It falsely shortens aPTT-based assays, so monitoring requires specific assays.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A describes recombinant factor VIIa (a bypassing agent given IV, not a bispecific antibody). B describes anti-TFPI antibodies (concizumab, marstacimab), which are monospecific. D is a strategy of extended-half-life VIII products, which inhibitors would still neutralize. E describes tranexamic or aminocaproic acid, which are small-molecule adjuncts.

stemHtml: A 19-year-old woman has had heavy menstrual periods since menarche, frequent nosebleeds, and prolonged bleeding after a wisdom tooth extraction. Her mother has similar symptoms. Platelets are 255,000/mm³, PT 12 s (normal), and aPTT 38 s (normal 25–35). Von Willebrand factor antigen and ristocetin cofactor activity are both reduced proportionally to about 35% of normal. Before an upcoming dental procedure, which drug is most likely to raise her plasma von Willebrand factor level?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Desmopressin
explanationHtml: Mucocutaneous bleeding, autosomal dominant inheritance, and a proportional fall in vWF antigen and activity indicate type 1 von Willebrand disease. The aPTT is mildly prolonged because vWF carries and protects factor VIII. Desmopressin (a V2 agonist) releases stored vWF and factor VIII from endothelial Weibel–Palade bodies, raising plasma levels 2- to 5-fold. A trial dose confirms response. Adverse effects: hyponatremia (water retention), flushing, and tachyphylaxis with repeated doses.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and E are antifibrinolytics. They are useful adjuncts for mucosal bleeding and menorrhagia but do not raise vWF. B corrects deficiency of vitamin K–dependent factors (PT prolonged). C reverses heparin.

stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with confusion and petechiae. Temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F). Hemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL, platelets 16,000/mm³, LDH 1,900 U/L, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, and the smear shows many schistocytes. PT, aPTT, and fibrinogen are normal, and the direct antiglobulin test is negative. She has had no diarrhea. Which mechanism underlies her condition?

options.label: A
options.html: Tissue factor–driven consumption of clotting factors and platelets

options.label: B
options.html: Autoantibody-mediated deficiency of a von Willebrand factor–cleaving metalloprotease

options.label: C
options.html: Shiga toxin–induced injury of glomerular endothelium

options.label: D
options.html: IgG autoantibodies against platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa

options.label: E
options.html: IgG antibodies against heparin–platelet factor 4 complexes

answerHtml: Answer: B. Autoantibody-mediated deficiency of a von Willebrand factor–cleaving metalloprotease
explanationHtml: MAHA, severe thrombocytopenia, neurologic changes, fever, and mild kidney injury with normal coagulation tests indicate thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Acquired TTP comes from IgG autoantibodies that inhibit ADAMTS13. Uncleaved ultra-large vWF multimers then capture platelets in microvessels, forming platelet-rich microthrombi that shear RBCs into schistocytes. Start plasma exchange urgently (it removes the antibody and replaces ADAMTS13), along with glucocorticoids, caplacizumab, and rituximab. Avoid platelet transfusion.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A is DIC, which would prolong PT/aPTT and lower fibrinogen. C is typical HUS, which follows bloody diarrhea and mostly affects children. D is ITP, which has no schistocytes or hemolysis. E is HIT, which requires heparin exposure and rarely causes platelets this low.

stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 36 weeks' gestation is brought to the hospital with sudden painful vaginal bleeding and a rigid, tender uterus. Ultrasound shows a retroplacental hematoma. An hour later, she is oozing blood from her IV sites and has hematuria. Which set of laboratory findings is most likely?

options.label: B
options.html: ↓ Platelets, normal PT, normal aPTT, normal fibrinogen, ↑ LDH

options.label: C
options.html: Normal platelets, ↑ PT, normal aPTT, normal fibrinogen, normal D-dimer

options.label: D
options.html: Normal platelets, normal PT, ↑ aPTT, normal fibrinogen, normal D-dimer

options.label: E
options.html: Normal platelets, normal PT, normal aPTT, normal fibrinogen, prolonged bleeding time

answerHtml: Answer: A. ↓ Platelets, ↑ PT, ↑ aPTT, ↓ fibrinogen, ↑ D-dimer
explanationHtml: Placental abruption releases thromboplastin (tissue factor) into the maternal circulation and triggers disseminated intravascular coagulation. Widespread thrombin generation consumes platelets, fibrinogen, and factors V and VIII, which prolongs PT and aPTT. At the same time, plasmin breaks down cross-linked fibrin (high D-dimer). The result is microvascular thrombosis together with bleeding from puncture sites and mucosa. Manage by delivering the fetus and replacing blood products (cryoprecipitate when fibrinogen is low).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B is TTP/HUS (or HELLP), with normal coagulation times. C fits early warfarin effect or vitamin K deficiency. D fits hemophilia or a factor VIII/IX/XI deficiency. E fits a platelet function defect (vWD, aspirin, uremia).

stemHtml: A 67-year-old man is on postoperative day 7 after a total hip replacement and has been receiving subcutaneous unfractionated heparin for thromboprophylaxis. His platelet count has fallen from 265,000/mm³ before surgery to 92,000/mm³. His left calf is swollen, and Doppler ultrasound shows a popliteal vein thrombosis. Liver function tests are normal and creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. An anti-PF4/heparin immunoassay has been sent. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.html: Start warfarin and continue heparin until the INR is therapeutic

answerHtml: Answer: E. Stop heparin and start argatroban
explanationHtml: A drop in platelets of more than 50% that begins 5–10 days after starting heparin, with new thrombosis and no other cause, gives a high 4T score for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. IgG binds PF4–heparin complexes and activates platelets through FcγRIIa, making the patient highly prothrombotic. Stop all heparin immediately, without waiting for test results, and start a non-heparin anticoagulant: argatroban (hepatically cleared, suits normal liver function), bivalirudin, fondaparinux, or a DOAC.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: LMWH cross-reacts with HIT antibodies. B: platelet transfusion can fuel thrombosis and is avoided unless there is life-threatening bleeding. C: starting warfarin in acute HIT can cause venous limb gangrene (rapid protein C depletion); wait until platelets recover. D: continuing heparin worsens HIT.

stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman develops a left femoral deep venous thrombosis 3 months after starting a combined estrogen–progestin oral contraceptive. Her mother had a pulmonary embolism after childbirth. Antithrombin, protein C, and protein S activities are normal, and antiphospholipid antibody tests are negative. In a coagulation assay, adding activated protein C to her plasma prolongs the aPTT much less than in control plasma. Which of the following best explains her thrombosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Reduced inactivation of thrombin and factor Xa by a serine protease inhibitor

options.label: B
options.html: A 3′ untranslated region mutation increasing prothrombin levels

options.label: C
options.html: A point mutation making factor Va resistant to cleavage by activated protein C

options.label: E
options.html: Deficient cofactor activity for activated protein C

answerHtml: Answer: C. A point mutation making factor Va resistant to cleavage by activated protein C
explanationHtml: An abnormal APC-resistance test indicates factor V Leiden (Arg506Gln), the most common inherited thrombophilia in people of European ancestry. Activated protein C normally cleaves factor Va at Arg506. The mutant Va persists, prothrombinase activity is prolonged, and more thrombin is produced. Estrogen raises the risk further by increasing hepatic clotting factors and reducing protein S. Confirm with genetic testing.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A is antithrombin deficiency (normal levels here). B is prothrombin G20210A, which gives a normal APC-resistance test. D is antiphospholipid syndrome (tests negative). E is protein S deficiency (normal activity here).

stemHtml: A 48-year-old woman with a newly diagnosed calf DVT is started on warfarin alone. Three days later, she has painful, well-demarcated purple plaques on her thighs and breasts that become hemorrhagic bullae and then black eschars. INR is 2.4. Biopsy shows thrombi in dermal venules with surrounding necrosis. Which mechanism most likely explains her skin lesions?

options.label: B
options.html: Calcification of small arterioles in subcutaneous fat

options.label: C
options.html: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis triggered by drug hypersensitivity

options.label: D
options.html: A rapid fall in protein C activity before prothrombin and factor X decline

options.label: E
options.html: Increased hepatic synthesis of factor VIII

answerHtml: Answer: D. A rapid fall in protein C activity before prothrombin and factor X decline
explanationHtml: Warfarin blocks synthesis of all vitamin K–dependent proteins, but existing proteins disappear at rates set by their half-lives. Protein C (~8 h) and factor VII (~6 h) fall first; prothrombin (~60 h) and factor X (~40 h) fall slowly. In the first days, anticoagulant protein C is low while procoagulant II and X are still present, causing a temporary hypercoagulable state. Patients with underlying protein C deficiency are at highest risk. The INR rises early because of factor VII, and that does not mean the patient is fully anticoagulated. Prevent this by bridging with heparin for at least 5 days. Treat with vitamin K, protein C concentrate or FFP, and heparin.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A is HIT, which needs heparin exposure. B is calciphylaxis, seen in end-stage renal disease. C would cause palpable purpura with neutrophilic vessel-wall inflammation, not bland venular thrombi. E: warfarin does not raise factor VIII.

stemHtml: A 35-year-old man with a history of frequent sinusitis and giardiasis receives his first-ever packed RBC transfusion after a motorcycle crash. Within 5 minutes, he develops diffuse urticaria, lip swelling, wheezing, and a blood pressure of 72/40 mm Hg. Temperature is 37.0°C. Pretransfusion crossmatch was compatible, and post-reaction urine is not discolored. Which mechanism best explains this reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: Donor anti-HLA antibodies activating recipient neutrophils in the pulmonary microvasculature

options.label: B
options.html: Recipient anti-IgA antibodies reacting with IgA in residual donor plasma

options.label: C
options.html: Recipient preformed antibodies against donor ABO antigens

options.label: D
options.html: Cytokines released from leukocytes during storage of the donor unit

options.label: E
options.html: Circulatory volume overload from rapid infusion

answerHtml: Answer: B. Recipient anti-IgA antibodies reacting with IgA in residual donor plasma
explanationHtml: Selective IgA deficiency, the most common primary immunodeficiency, is suggested by recurrent sinopulmonary infections and giardiasis. Some patients make anti-IgA (often IgG) antibodies. Within minutes of exposure to donor IgA, they can develop anaphylaxis (hypotension, bronchospasm, angioedema) without fever or hemolysis, even with a first transfusion. Treat with epinephrine. For future transfusions, use washed cellular products or plasma from IgA-deficient donors.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A (TRALI) causes hypoxemia and bilateral infiltrates within 6 hours, with fever and hypotension but no urticaria or angioedema. C (acute hemolytic) causes fever, flank pain, hemoglobinuria, and DIC; the crossmatch was compatible. D (febrile nonhemolytic) causes fever and chills. E (TACO) causes hypertension and pulmonary edema.

stemHtml: A 54-year-old man has fatigue, night sweats, and early satiety. The spleen is palpable 10 cm below the costal margin. Leukocyte count is 148,000/mm³ with neutrophils, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, 2% blasts, and 9% basophils. Platelets are 610,000/mm³. FISH confirms the diagnosis, and he is started on an oral drug aimed at the disease-defining molecular lesion. Which mechanism best describes this drug?

options.label: A
options.html: Competitive inhibition at the ATP-binding site of a constitutively active fusion tyrosine kinase

options.label: D
options.html: Irreversible inhibition of Bruton tyrosine kinase

options.label: E
options.html: Induced degradation of a fusion retinoic acid receptor

answerHtml: Answer: A. Competitive inhibition at the ATP-binding site of a constitutively active fusion tyrosine kinase
explanationHtml: Marked leukocytosis with the full range of granulocyte maturation, basophilia, thrombocytosis, and massive splenomegaly indicate chronic myeloid leukemia in chronic phase. The Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) creates BCR::ABL1, which is always switched on. Imatinib (and dasatinib, nilotinib, bosutinib) competes with ATP at the ABL kinase domain and stops downstream signaling. The T315I "gatekeeper" mutation causes resistance to most TKIs; ponatinib or asciminib (which binds the myristoyl pocket) is used instead.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B (hydroxyurea) can lower counts temporarily but does not target BCR::ABL1. C (ruxolitinib) is used for JAK2-driven myelofibrosis and PV. D (ibrutinib) is used for CLL and mantle cell lymphoma. E (ATRA or arsenic) is used for APL.

stemHtml: A 41-year-old man has gum bleeding and large bruises. Hemoglobin is 9.0 g/dL, leukocyte count 2,800/mm³, platelets 22,000/mm³, PT 19 s, fibrinogen 90 mg/dL, and D-dimer is markedly elevated. Bone marrow shows sheets of abnormal promyelocytes with heavy granules and bundles of Auer rods. Cytogenetics confirms t(15;17). All-trans retinoic acid is started at once. What is the main mechanism of this drug's therapeutic effect?

options.label: A
options.html: Inhibition of topoisomerase II, causing double-strand DNA breaks

options.label: B
options.html: Alkylation of guanine bases, causing DNA cross-links

options.label: C
options.html: Inhibition of FMS-like tyrosine kinase 3 signaling

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibition of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL-2

options.label: E
options.html: Binding the RARα portion of the fusion protein, releasing the block in myeloid differentiation

answerHtml: Answer: E. Binding the RARα portion of the fusion protein, releasing the block in myeloid differentiation
explanationHtml: In acute promyelocytic leukemia, PML::RARA recruits corepressors and halts maturation at the promyelocyte stage. Pharmacologic doses of ATRA bind the RARα ligand-binding domain, release the corepressors, and lead to degradation of the fusion protein. The promyelocytes then mature into neutrophils. Arsenic trioxide targets the PML part. Starting ATRA quickly lowers early deaths from DIC, which is driven by tissue factor and annexin II in promyelocyte granules. Watch for differentiation syndrome (fever, dyspnea, edema, pulmonary infiltrates) and treat it with dexamethasone.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A describes anthracyclines or etoposide. B describes alkylating agents. C describes midostaurin or gilteritinib (FLT3-mutated AML). D describes venetoclax.

stemHtml: A 23-year-old woman has 2 months of dry cough, drenching night sweats, generalized pruritus, and a 6-kg weight loss. Chest x-ray shows a widened mediastinum, and CT shows an anterior mediastinal mass with enlarged supraclavicular nodes. Biopsy of a supraclavicular node shows nodules separated by broad collagen bands, containing large cells that sit in clear spaces, plus scattered large binucleate cells with prominent "owl-eye" nucleoli, in a background of lymphocytes and eosinophils. The large neoplastic cells are most likely to show which immunophenotype?
answerHtml: Answer: D. CD15⁺, CD30⁺, CD45⁻
explanationHtml: A young woman with a mediastinal mass, B symptoms, pruritus, collagen bands, and lacunar cells has nodular sclerosis classic Hodgkin lymphoma, the most common subtype. Reed–Sternberg cells and their lacunar variants come from germinal-center B cells but have lost most B-cell markers. They are CD15⁺ and CD30⁺, PAX5 weakly positive, and CD45⁻ and usually CD20⁻. Cytokines they secrete (e.g., IL-5) attract the reactive background of eosinophils and lymphocytes. Standard treatment is ABVD with or without radiation; brentuximab vedotin targets CD30.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A is adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (HTLV-1). B is CLL/SLL. C is the "popcorn" LP cell of nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, which lacks collagen bands and lacunar cells. E is T-lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia, which also causes a mediastinal mass in young people but appears as sheets of blasts without RS cells.

stemHtml: A 70-year-old African American man has 3 months of low back pain and fatigue. Calcium is 12.4 mg/dL, creatinine 2.2 mg/dL, hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, total protein 9.8 g/dL, and albumin 3.1 g/dL. The smear shows rouleaux. Skeletal survey shows multiple punched-out lytic lesions in the skull and vertebrae. Serum protein electrophoresis shows an IgG κ M spike. He starts bortezomib, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone, and he is given acyclovir prophylaxis. What is the mechanism of bortezomib?

options.label: A
options.html: Inhibition of Bruton tyrosine kinase in the B-cell receptor pathway

options.label: B
options.html: Antibody binding to CD38 on plasma cells

options.label: C
options.html: Reversible inhibition of the 26S proteasome, causing build-up of misfolded proteins and apoptosis

options.label: D
options.html: Cereblon-mediated degradation of the transcription factors Ikaros and Aiolos

answerHtml: Answer: C. Reversible inhibition of the 26S proteasome, causing build-up of misfolded proteins and apoptosis
explanationHtml: The CRAB features (hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, lytic bone lesions) with an M spike indicate plasma cell (multiple) myeloma. Myeloma cells make huge amounts of immunoglobulin and depend on the proteasome to clear misfolded protein. Bortezomib, a boronic acid, reversibly inhibits the chymotrypsin-like site of the 26S proteasome. Unfolded proteins build up, ER stress (the unfolded protein response) follows, and IκB is not degraded, so NF-κB stays inactive. The result is apoptosis. Key toxicities: peripheral neuropathy (reduced with SC dosing) and herpes zoster reactivation, which is why acyclovir prophylaxis is given.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A describes ibrutinib. B describes daratumumab. D describes lenalidomide, which he is also receiving. E describes denosumab (used for bone protection).
