stemHtml: A 74-year-old man has had two episodes of syncope while climbing stairs. Examination shows a harsh crescendo–decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to both carotids and a delayed, weak carotid upstroke. During cardiac catheterization, a left ventricular pressure–volume loop is recorded. Peak LV systolic pressure is 190 mmHg while simultaneous aortic systolic pressure is 115 mmHg; end-diastolic volume is near normal, stroke volume is reduced, and both isovolumetric phases are clearly present. Which of the following best explains this loop?

options.label: E
options.html: Increased myocardial contractility from sympathetic stimulation

answerHtml: Answer: C. Aortic stenosis
explanationHtml: A large systolic pressure gradient between the LV and aorta means the LV must generate much higher pressure to eject through a narrowed valve — the loop becomes very tall with a reduced width (stroke volume). Isovolumetric phases persist because both valves still close competently. The murmur, exertional syncope and pulsus parvus et tardus complete the picture.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — MR abolishes true isovolumetric contraction (blood leaks into the LA as soon as LV pressure exceeds LA pressure) and ↑ EDV. B — AR removes isovolumetric relaxation and markedly ↑ EDV and stroke volume. D — MS reduces EDV and LV pressures are not elevated. E — ↑ contractility steepens the ESPVR and ↑ stroke volume; it does not create an LV–aortic gradient.

stemHtml: A 63-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 30%) is taking sacubitril–valsartan, maximally tolerated metoprolol succinate, spironolactone, and dapagliflozin. He remains in NYHA class II–III. Pulse is 78/min and regular (sinus rhythm), and blood pressure is 108/68 mmHg. His cardiologist adds a drug that lowers heart rate without reducing myocardial contractility or blood pressure. Which of the following is the mechanism of this drug?

options.label: A
options.html: Decreases the slope of phase 4 depolarization in SA nodal cells by blocking HCN channels

options.label: B
options.html: Inhibits myocardial Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup>-ATPase and increases vagal tone

options.label: C
options.html: Blocks L-type Ca<sup>2+</sup> channels in nodal tissue

options.label: D
options.html: Blocks delayed rectifier K<sup>+</sup> channels, prolonging phase 3

options.label: E
options.html: Activates A<sub>1</sub> receptors, increasing K<sup>+</sup> efflux in the AV node

answerHtml: Answer: A. Blocks HCN ("funny") channels → ↓ phase 4 slope
explanationHtml: Ivabradine selectively inhibits If in the SA node, slowing spontaneous diastolic depolarization and therefore heart rate. It has no negative inotropic or vasodilator effect, which is why it is used in HFrEF patients in sinus rhythm with HR ≥70/min despite maximal β-blockade (it reduces HF hospitalizations). Side effects include luminous visual phenomena (HCN channels in retina) and bradycardia.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — digoxin is a positive inotrope (raises contractility). C — verapamil/diltiazem are negative inotropes and lower BP; avoided in HFrEF. D — class III drugs (amiodarone, dofetilide) prolong repolarization, not used to lower sinus rate. E — adenosine is an IV, seconds-long agent for terminating PSVT, not chronic rate reduction.

stemHtml: A male newborn of a mother with poorly controlled pregestational diabetes becomes deeply cyanotic within hours of birth. Oxygen saturation does not improve with 100% oxygen. A single loud S2 is heard and there is no significant murmur. Chest x-ray shows a narrow mediastinum with an egg-shaped cardiac silhouette. Failure of which embryologic process most likely caused this condition?

options.label: B
options.html: Proper alignment of the infundibular septum

options.label: C
options.html: Fusion of septum primum with septum secundum

answerHtml: Answer: E. Spiraling of the aorticopulmonary septum
explanationHtml: D-transposition of the great arteries results when the neural crest–derived aorticopulmonary septum fails to spiral, so the aorta arises from the RV and the pulmonary trunk from the LV. Systemic and pulmonary circuits run in parallel; survival requires mixing (PDA, ASD, VSD). Maternal diabetes is a classic risk factor; the narrow pedicle gives the "egg on a string." Management: PGE1 (alprostadil) to keep the ductus open, balloon atrial septostomy, arterial switch.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — endocardial cushion defects (AVSD) are acyanotic L→R lesions linked to Down syndrome. B — anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum causes tetralogy of Fallot (boot-shaped heart, systolic murmur). C — failed fusion of septa causes a PFO, which is clinically silent. D — closure of the ductus is normal and would worsen TGA, but is not its cause.

stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman is evaluated for palpitations and mild exertional dyspnea. Auscultation reveals a grade 2/6 midsystolic murmur at the left upper sternal border and a widely split S2 that does not change with respiration. She is not cyanotic. Right heart catheterization with oximetry is performed. Which of the following findings is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: An increase in O<sub>2</sub> saturation first detected in the right ventricle

options.label: B
options.html: An increase in O<sub>2</sub> saturation first detected in the right atrium

options.label: C
options.html: An increase in O<sub>2</sub> saturation first detected in the pulmonary artery

options.label: D
options.html: A decrease in O<sub>2</sub> saturation between pulmonary veins and left atrium

options.label: E
options.html: No change in O<sub>2</sub> saturation from vena cava to pulmonary artery

answerHtml: Answer: B. Step-up first in the right atrium
explanationHtml: A fixed split S2 indicates an atrial septal defect. Oxygenated LA blood shunts L→R into the RA, raising RA saturation above that of the vena cavae. The extra volume crossing the pulmonic valve produces a flow murmur at the LUSB and delays P2 regardless of respiration (RV volume stays high in both phases).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — a step-up first in the RV indicates a VSD. C — a step-up first in the pulmonary artery indicates a PDA. D — desaturation in the LA indicates R→L shunting (e.g. Eisenmenger), unlikely in an acyanotic patient. E — no step-up is expected with a PFO or no shunt, not with a fixed split S2 and flow murmur.

stemHtml: A 66-year-old man presented 5 days ago, 18 hours after symptom onset, with ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF; he did not undergo reperfusion. Today he develops abrupt severe dyspnea. Blood pressure is 88/56 mmHg, pulse 118/min. There are diffuse crackles and a new loud holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. Echocardiography shows a flail posterior mitral leaflet with severe regurgitation. Oximetry shows no O<sub>2</sub> step-up between the right atrium and pulmonary artery. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.html: Rupture of the LV free wall

options.label: D
options.html: Rupture of the posteromedial papillary muscle

options.label: E
options.html: Rupture of the anterolateral papillary muscle

answerHtml: Answer: D. Posteromedial papillary muscle rupture
explanationHtml: Inferior STEMI is usually due to RCA occlusion. The posteromedial papillary muscle depends on a single artery (the PDA, from the RCA in right-dominant hearts), so it is the one that ruptures, typically 3–7 days after MI when macrophage-mediated removal of necrotic tissue weakens it. Result: acute severe MR, pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — free wall rupture causes tamponade (JVD, muffled sounds, PEA), not a holosystolic murmur with flail leaflet. B — septal rupture produces a holosystolic murmur at the LLSB and an O<sub>2</sub> step-up in the RV. C — Dressler syndrome occurs weeks later with pleuritic pain and a friction rub. E — the anterolateral papillary muscle has dual supply (LAD + LCX) and is far less likely to rupture, especially after an inferior MI.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with a 75% stenosis of the proximal LAD reports that his chest pain reliably appears when his heart rate exceeds about 110/min. Increasing heart rate worsens his ischemia not only by raising myocardial O<sub>2</sub> demand but also by disproportionately shortening the portion of the cardiac cycle during which most left ventricular myocardial blood flow occurs. During which phase is left ventricular coronary blood flow greatest?

options.label: B
options.html: Early diastole (isovolumetric relaxation and rapid filling)

answerHtml: Answer: B. Early diastole
explanationHtml: During systole, contracting LV myocardium compresses intramyocardial vessels (most severely in the subendocardium), so LV coronary flow is low or even reversed. Flow peaks in early diastole when the myocardium relaxes while aortic pressure is still high. Tachycardia shortens diastole much more than systole, reducing perfusion time while increasing demand — the rationale for β-blockers in angina.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — isovolumetric contraction produces maximal extravascular compression and the lowest LV coronary flow (and highest O<sub>2</sub> consumption). C, D — ejection phases still involve compression; flow is reduced. E — atrial systole occurs in late diastole, when aortic pressure has fallen to its lowest point; flow is lower than in early diastole.

stemHtml: A 19-year-old college basketball player collapses briefly during practice and recovers spontaneously. Examination reveals a harsh systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that becomes louder when he stands up from a squatting position. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy with deep septal Q waves. Which of the following maneuvers would most likely decrease the intensity of this murmur?

options.label: A
options.html: Strain phase of the Valsalva maneuver

options.label: B
options.html: Abruptly standing from a supine position

answerHtml: Answer: D. Sustained handgrip
explanationHtml: In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the LVOT obstruction is dynamic: anything that makes the LV cavity larger separates the hypertrophied septum from the anterior mitral leaflet and reduces the gradient. Handgrip increases afterload (and LV size), so the murmur softens. Squatting and passive leg raise (↑ preload) also soften it.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B — Valsalva strain and standing ↓ venous return → smaller LV → louder murmur. C — amyl nitrite ↓ afterload → smaller LV, ↑ gradient → louder. E — nitroglycerin ↓ preload → louder; nitrates and other vasodilators should be avoided in obstructive HCM.

stemHtml: A 71-year-old man has taken an antiarrhythmic drug for 2 years to maintain sinus rhythm in paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. He now has a 3-month history of dry cough and progressive exertional dyspnea. There are fine bibasilar crackles and a slate-gray discoloration of his face and the backs of his hands. CT shows bilateral peripheral reticular opacities, and DLCO is reduced. This drug is also well known to cause which of the following?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Hypothyroidism
explanationHtml: Amiodarone causes pulmonary fibrosis and blue-gray skin pigmentation. It is ~37% iodine by weight and inhibits peripheral 5'-deiodinase, so it can cause either hypothyroidism (more common in iodine-sufficient regions such as the US) or thyrotoxicosis. Other toxicities: hepatotoxicity, corneal microdeposits, optic neuropathy, photosensitivity, peripheral neuropathy, bradycardia, and CYP inhibition. Monitor TSH, LFTs and PFTs.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — procainamide (and hydralazine) cause drug-induced lupus. C — cinchonism is quinidine toxicity. D — gingival hyperplasia occurs with DHP CCBs (nifedipine), phenytoin and cyclosporine. E — loop diuretics (furosemide, ethacrynic acid) are ototoxic, especially with aminoglycosides.

stemHtml: A 78-year-old woman with symptomatic HFrEF in sinus rhythm has taken digoxin 0.125 mg daily for years with stable therapeutic levels. Over the past week she has developed nausea, anorexia, and yellow halos around lights. ECG shows atrial tachycardia with 2:1 AV block. Serum digoxin is elevated. Serum K<sup>+</sup> is 4.3 mEq/L, Mg<sup>2+</sup> is normal, and creatinine is unchanged at 1.0 mg/dL. A new medication was started 2 weeks ago. Which of the following was most likely added?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Verapamil
explanationHtml: Verapamil inhibits P-glycoprotein, which mediates renal tubular secretion and intestinal efflux of digoxin; adding it raises digoxin concentrations substantially (amiodarone, quinidine, dronedarone, and some macrolides act similarly). With normal K+, Mg2+ and renal function, a drug interaction is the explanation. Verapamil also adds AV-nodal blockade, compounding the arrhythmia risk. Treatment of significant toxicity: digoxin immune Fab.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — cholestyramine binds digoxin in the gut and lowers levels. B — amlodipine (a DHP) has no clinically important effect on digoxin. C — metformin does not interact meaningfully. D — rifampin induces P-glycoprotein and lowers digoxin levels.

stemHtml: A 52-year-old man with low HDL cholesterol and elevated triglycerides is started on a new lipid-lowering medication. Within 30 minutes of each dose he experiences intense warmth, redness and itching of the face and upper trunk, which is prevented by taking aspirin beforehand. Three months later, his serum uric acid and fasting glucose have risen. Which of the following is the primary mechanism of this drug?

options.label: B
options.html: Blockade of NPC1L1-mediated intestinal cholesterol absorption

options.label: C
options.html: Inhibition of lipolysis in adipose tissue, decreasing hepatic VLDL synthesis

options.label: D
options.html: Activation of PPAR-α, increasing lipoprotein lipase activity

options.label: E
options.html: Prevention of LDL-receptor degradation by binding PCSK9

answerHtml: Answer: C. Niacin
explanationHtml: Niacin activates an adipocyte Gi-coupled receptor that suppresses hormone-sensitive lipase, reducing free fatty acid delivery to the liver and therefore VLDL (and LDL) production; it raises HDL more than any other drug. Prostaglandin-mediated (PGD2) flushing is blunted by aspirin. Hyperglycemia (insulin resistance), hyperuricemia (gout) and hepatotoxicity are classic adverse effects.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — statins cause myalgia/hepatotoxicity, not flushing. B — ezetimibe is well tolerated. D — fibrates cause gallstones and myopathy. E — PCSK9 antibodies cause injection-site reactions.

stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy of Japanese descent has had fever to 39.8°C for 6 days. He has bilateral nonexudative conjunctival injection, red cracked lips, a strawberry tongue, a 2-cm unilateral cervical lymph node, a polymorphous truncal rash, and erythema with swelling of the palms and soles. Without appropriate treatment, which of the following is the most serious potential complication?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Coronary artery aneurysm
explanationHtml: Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis of young children. Coronary aneurysms develop in ~25% of untreated children (≈4% with treatment) and can thrombose or rupture, causing MI or sudden death. Treat with IVIG plus aspirin and obtain echocardiography.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — GN is a feature of IgA vasculitis and ANCA vasculitides, not Kawasaki. C — mitral stenosis follows rheumatic fever years later. D — intussusception complicates IgA vasculitis (HSP). E — hearing loss is associated with congenital infections, meningitis, and Alport syndrome.

stemHtml: A 74-year-old Black man has progressive exertional dyspnea and bilateral leg edema. He underwent bilateral carpal tunnel release 6 years ago. Echocardiography shows concentrically thickened LV walls (septum 17 mm), biatrial enlargement, preserved ejection fraction, and a restrictive filling pattern. ECG shows low QRS voltage in the limb leads. An endomyocardial biopsy is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Disorganized, branching myocytes with interstitial fibrosis

options.label: B
options.html: Noncaseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells

options.label: C
options.html: Extracellular amorphous deposits with apple-green birefringence after Congo red staining

options.label: E
options.html: Dense eosinophilic infiltrates with endomyocardial fibrosis

answerHtml: Answer: C. Amyloid deposits
explanationHtml: Thick walls on echo with low ECG voltage is the signature of an infiltrative cardiomyopathy — amyloidosis. In an older Black man, transthyretin amyloid (V122I variant, or wild-type) is likely; carpal tunnel syndrome often precedes cardiac involvement by years. Amyloid shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light after Congo red staining. Tafamidis (TTR stabilizer) improves outcomes in ATTR cardiomyopathy.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — myofiber disarray is HCM, which typically shows high voltage. B — sarcoid granulomas present with heart block/VT and patchy wall involvement. D — Aschoff bodies with Anitschkow cells are acute rheumatic carditis. E — Löffler endocarditis occurs with marked peripheral eosinophilia.

stemHtml: A 15-year-old girl is evaluated for short stature and primary amenorrhea. She has a webbed neck and widely spaced nipples. Blood pressure in the right arm is 162/94 mmHg; thigh blood pressure is lower, and femoral pulses are weak and delayed relative to the radial pulses. Chest x-ray shows notching of the inferior margins of several posterior ribs. Which additional cardiac abnormality is most likely present?

options.label: A
options.html: Apical displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets

answerHtml: Answer: E. Bicuspid aortic valve
explanationHtml: Turner syndrome (45,X) is associated with coarctation of the aorta (arm hypertension, brachiofemoral delay, rib notching from dilated intercostal collaterals) and bicuspid aortic valve, which is also the most common cardiac lesion accompanying coarctation in general. Bicuspid valves predispose to early AS, AR, and aortic dilation/dissection.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — Ebstein anomaly is linked to maternal lithium. B — TOF is linked to 22q11 deletion. C — ostium primum ASD (endocardial cushion defect) is linked to Down syndrome. D — supravalvular AS is linked to Williams syndrome (7q11.23, elastin).

stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman with chronic hypertension well controlled on lisinopril learns she is 8 weeks pregnant. Her physician stops lisinopril and starts labetalol. If lisinopril had been continued into the second and third trimesters, the fetus would have been at greatest risk for which of the following?

options.label: B
options.html: Apical displacement of the tricuspid valve

answerHtml: Answer: D. Renal tubular dysgenesis with oligohydramnios
explanationHtml: Fetal renal perfusion and GFR depend heavily on angiotensin II. Second- and third-trimester exposure to ACE inhibitors, ARBs or aliskiren causes fetal renal failure (renal tubular dysgenesis) → oligohydramnios → Potter-type sequence (pulmonary hypoplasia, limb contractures), skull ossification defects (hypocalvaria), and neonatal anuria/hypotension. Preferred antihypertensives in pregnancy: labetalol, nifedipine, methyldopa.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — neural tube defects: valproate, carbamazepine, folate antagonists. B — Ebstein anomaly: lithium. C — cleft lip/palate: phenytoin, topiramate, isotretinoin (among others). E — ototoxicity/deafness: aminoglycosides.

stemHtml: A 67-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with fever (39.4°C), confusion, and right flank pain. Urinalysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria. After 30 mL/kg of IV crystalloid, blood pressure is 78/40 mmHg and pulse 124/min. Her skin is warm and flushed with brisk capillary refill, and peripheral pulses are bounding. Which hemodynamic profile is most characteristic of this patient's type of shock?

options.label: A
options.html: PCWP ↓, cardiac output ↓, systemic vascular resistance ↑

options.label: B
options.html: PCWP ↓, cardiac output ↑, systemic vascular resistance ↓

options.label: C
options.html: PCWP ↑, cardiac output ↓, systemic vascular resistance ↑

options.label: D
options.html: PCWP ↓, cardiac output ↓, systemic vascular resistance ↓

options.label: E
options.html: PCWP ↑, cardiac output ↑, systemic vascular resistance ↑

answerHtml: Answer: B. ↓ PCWP, ↑ CO, ↓ SVR
explanationHtml: Septic (distributive) shock from pyelonephritis: cytokine-induced NO production and vascular hyporesponsiveness lower SVR; venodilation and capillary leak lower filling pressures; the heart compensates with tachycardia and ↑ cardiac output ("warm shock"). Mixed venous O2 saturation is often high because of impaired tissue O2 extraction. Treatment: antibiotics, fluids, norepinephrine.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — hypovolemic shock (cold, clammy, flat neck veins). C — cardiogenic shock (pulmonary edema, cold extremities). D — neurogenic shock (spinal cord injury, warm but bradycardic). E — not a shock profile.

stemHtml: A 68-year-old man has 6 weeks of low-grade fevers, fatigue, and 4-kg weight loss. A new holosystolic apical murmur is heard. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL with MCV 72 fL. Three blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in chains that are nonhemolytic, grow in the presence of bile and hydrolyze esculin, but do not grow in 6.5% NaCl. Echocardiography shows a mitral valve vegetation. This patient's infection is most strongly associated with which of the following?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Colorectal neoplasia
explanationHtml: Bile-esculin–positive, salt-intolerant group D streptococci = Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis biotype I). Bacteremia/endocarditis with this organism is strongly associated with colorectal adenomas and carcinoma — colonoscopy is mandatory. The microcytic (iron-deficiency) anemia is a further clue to occult GI blood loss.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — dental procedures are linked to viridans streptococci (bile-esculin negative). B — injection drug use is linked to S. aureus (tricuspid valve). C — prosthetic valves are linked to coagulase-negative staphylococci. D — SLE causes sterile Libman–Sacks vegetations. Enterococcus would grow in 6.5% NaCl.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old man is found unresponsive with pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 6/min. Arterial blood gas on room air at sea level shows: pH 7.17, PaCO<sub>2</sub> 80 mmHg, PaO<sub>2</sub> 44 mmHg, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 28 mEq/L. Chest x-ray is clear. Which of the following is the primary mechanism of his hypoxemia?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Alveolar hypoventilation
explanationHtml: PAO2 = 150 − (80 ÷ 0.8) = 150 − 100 = 50 mmHg. A–a gradient = 50 − 44 = 6 mmHg (normal). Hypoxemia with a normal A–a gradient at sea level means the lungs are transferring O2 normally; the problem is that rising alveolar CO2 (from opioid-induced hypoventilation) displaces alveolar O2. The HCO3− of 28 matches acute respiratory acidosis (↑ ~1 per 10 mmHg PaCO2). Treat naloxone and ventilatory support.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, C, D — V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation and shunt all widen the A–a gradient. E — inspired PO2 is normal at sea level on room air; ↓ PiO2 (altitude) also has a normal A–a gradient but would show a low PaCO2 from compensatory hyperventilation.

stemHtml: In January, a family of four presents with headache, nausea, and dizziness that improve when they leave the house. They recently began using an old gas furnace. The father's pulse oximetry reading is 99% on room air, and his arterial PaO<sub>2</sub> is 98 mmHg. Which of the following best describes the effect of the toxic exposure on his blood's oxygen–hemoglobin relationship?

options.label: A
options.html: Right shift of the dissociation curve with normal O<sub>2</sub>-carrying capacity

options.label: B
options.html: No shift of the curve, with decreased O<sub>2</sub>-carrying capacity

options.label: C
options.html: Right shift of the curve with decreased O<sub>2</sub>-carrying capacity

options.label: D
options.html: Left shift of the curve with decreased O<sub>2</sub>-carrying capacity

options.label: E
options.html: Left shift of the curve with increased O<sub>2</sub>-carrying capacity

answerHtml: Answer: D. Left shift + ↓ carrying capacity
explanationHtml: Carbon monoxide occupies heme sites with ~200–250× the affinity of O2, reducing the number of sites available (↓ O2 content/capacity), and it increases the O2 affinity of the remaining sites (left shift), impairing unloading in tissues. PaO2 (dissolved O2) is normal, and standard pulse oximetry cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin — co-oximetry is required. Treat with 100% O2 or hyperbaric O2.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, C — right shifts follow ↑ CO<sub>2</sub>, ↑ H<sup>+</sup>, ↑ 2,3-BPG, ↑ temperature, not CO. B — anemia lowers capacity without shifting the curve. E — CO never increases O<sub>2</sub> capacity; polycythemia would raise capacity without a shift.

stemHtml: A 45-year-old man has right lower lobe pneumonia with complete consolidation of the lobe. Despite an FiO<sub>2</sub> of 0.6, his PaO<sub>2</sub> remains 62 mmHg. Which of the following best describes gas exchange in the consolidated lobe?

options.label: A
options.html: V/Q approaches infinity; alveolar gas approaches the composition of inspired air

options.label: B
options.html: V/Q is approximately 1; end-capillary PO<sub>2</sub> is approximately 100 mmHg

options.label: C
options.html: V/Q approaches zero; end-capillary PO<sub>2</sub> and PCO<sub>2</sub> approach mixed venous values

options.label: D
options.html: V/Q approaches infinity; end-capillary PO<sub>2</sub> approaches mixed venous values

options.label: E
options.html: Hypoxic vasoconstriction increases blood flow to the consolidated lobe

answerHtml: Answer: C. V/Q → 0 (shunt)
explanationHtml: Alveoli filled with exudate receive perfusion but no ventilation. Blood traversing them cannot exchange gas, so it leaves with mixed-venous PO2 (~40 mmHg) and PCO2 (~46 mmHg) and mixes with arterial blood. Because shunted blood never contacts the high-O2 alveolar gas, raising FiO2 corrects the hypoxemia poorly; well-ventilated units are already nearly fully saturated and cannot compensate (sigmoid curve plateau).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — V/Q → ∞ describes dead space (e.g. PE): ventilation without perfusion. B — normal matching. D — combines dead space physiology with shunt blood values; if there is no perfusion, there is no end-capillary blood. E — hypoxic vasoconstriction decreases flow to poorly ventilated regions (partially limiting the shunt).

stemHtml: A 67-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history has progressive dyspnea. He has a barrel-shaped chest, hyperresonance to percussion, and distant breath sounds. Post-bronchodilator FEV<sub>1</sub>/FVC is 0.52, total lung capacity is 125% of predicted, and DLCO is 45% of predicted. Compared with a healthy person, which of the following is increased in this patient?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Lung compliance
explanationHtml: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and their elastic fibers (protease–antiprotease imbalance). With less elastic tissue, the lung distends more for a given pressure change (↑ compliance) and recoils less. Loss of recoil and of tethering (radial traction) lets small airways collapse during expiration → air trapping, ↑ TLC, RV, FRC.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — DLCO is ↓ because capillary surface area is destroyed (stated in the stem). C — elastic recoil is ↓. D — FEV<sub>1</sub>/FVC is ↓ (0.52). E — radial traction is ↓, explaining dynamic airway collapse.

stemHtml: A 36-year-old man who has never smoked has 2 years of progressive dyspnea. CT shows panacinar emphysema predominantly in the lower lobes. Serum aminotransferases are mildly elevated. Liver biopsy shows periportal hepatocytes containing PAS-positive, diastase-resistant cytoplasmic globules. Which of the following best explains his liver disease?

options.label: B
options.html: Copper accumulation due to a defective hepatocyte ATPase

options.label: C
options.html: Iron deposition due to increased intestinal absorption

options.label: D
options.html: Accumulation of a misfolded protein in the endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes

options.label: E
options.html: Autoantibody-mediated destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts

answerHtml: Answer: D. Misfolded α<sub>1</sub>-antitrypsin retained in hepatocyte ER
explanationHtml: The PiZ allele of SERPINA1 produces an α1-antitrypsin that polymerizes and is trapped in the hepatocyte ER (PAS+ globules) — a toxic gain of function causing hepatitis, cirrhosis and HCC. The lung disease is a loss of function: too little circulating antiprotease reaches the lung, so neutrophil elastase destroys alveolar walls (panacinar, lower lobes, early onset).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — unopposed elastase explains the lung injury, not the liver injury. B — Wilson disease (ATP7B). C — hereditary hemochromatosis (HFE). E — primary biliary cholangitis (anti-mitochondrial antibodies).

stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman with moderate persistent asthma and recurrent nasal polyps develops severe wheezing, nasal congestion, and facial flushing 1 hour after taking ibuprofen for a headache. She has had similar reactions to aspirin. Which of the following best explains her reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: Drug-specific IgE cross-linking on mast cells

options.label: B
options.html: Shunting of arachidonic acid toward 5-lipoxygenase with increased cysteinyl leukotrienes

options.label: C
options.html: Decreased thromboxane A<sub>2</sub> synthesis in platelets

options.label: D
options.html: Accumulation of bradykinin due to inhibition of kininase II

options.label: E
options.html: Direct antagonism of β<sub>2</sub>-adrenergic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle

answerHtml: Answer: B. Leukotriene overproduction after COX-1 inhibition
explanationHtml: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (asthma + chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps + reactions to COX-1 inhibitors) is a pseudoallergic, non-IgE reaction. Blocking COX-1 removes protective PGE2 (which normally restrains 5-lipoxygenase and mast cells) and diverts arachidonic acid to leukotrienes C4/D4/E4, causing bronchoconstriction and mucosal edema. Because it is class-based, cross-reactivity with all strong COX-1 inhibitors is expected. Leukotriene modifiers (montelukast, zileuton) and aspirin desensitization help; selective COX-2 inhibitors are usually tolerated.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — the reaction is not IgE-mediated (reacts to structurally unrelated NSAIDs). C — ↓ TXA<sub>2</sub> impairs platelet aggregation; it does not cause bronchospasm. D — bradykinin accumulation explains ACE-inhibitor cough/angioedema. E — NSAIDs have no β-blocking activity (β-blockers cause bronchospasm by that mechanism).

stemHtml: A 58-year-old man who worked for 30 years in sandblasting has progressive dyspnea. Chest x-ray shows multiple small nodules predominantly in the upper lobes and "eggshell" calcification of hilar lymph nodes. This patient is at significantly increased risk for which of the following?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Tuberculosis
explanationHtml: Silicosis: inhaled crystalline silica is ingested by alveolar macrophages and disrupts phagolysosomes, releasing cytokines (fibrosis via IL-1, TNF, TGF-β) and impairing killing of intracellular mycobacteria. Silicosis carries a markedly increased risk of TB (screen with TB testing) and an increased risk of lung cancer.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — mesothelioma is linked to asbestos. C — hepatic angiosarcoma is linked to vinyl chloride, arsenic, Thorotrast. D — Langerhans cell histiocytosis is linked to cigarette smoking. E — bronchial carcinoids are not associated with occupational dusts.

stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with a 60-pack-year smoking history has 2 weeks of confusion, polyuria, and constipation. Serum calcium is 13.4 mg/dL and PTH is 8 pg/mL (low). Chest x-ray shows a 5-cm cavitating mass adjacent to the right hilum. A biopsy of the mass is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Small cells with scant cytoplasm and nuclear molding, chromogranin positive

options.label: B
options.html: Tumor cells growing along intact alveolar septa without invasion

options.label: C
options.html: Mucin-producing glands that stain for TTF-1

options.label: D
options.html: Large pleomorphic cells without glandular or squamous differentiation

options.label: E
options.html: Nests of cells with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges

answerHtml: Answer: E. Squamous cell carcinoma
explanationHtml: A central (hilar), cavitating lung mass in a heavy smoker with PTH-independent hypercalcemia (suppressed PTH) is squamous cell carcinoma secreting PTH-related peptide. Histology: keratinization (pearls) and intercellular bridges (desmosomes); p40/p63 positive.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — small cell carcinoma is central but causes SIADH, ACTH, and Lambert–Eaton, not PTHrP hypercalcemia classically. B — adenocarcinoma in situ (lepidic). C — invasive adenocarcinoma is usually peripheral. D — large cell carcinoma is peripheral and undifferentiated.

stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman who smokes has 3 months of difficulty climbing stairs and rising from chairs, along with dry mouth and constipation. On examination, hip flexor strength is reduced but improves after several seconds of sustained effort; deep tendon reflexes are diminished and become brisker after brief exercise. Ocular movements are normal. CT shows a central lung mass with bulky mediastinal adenopathy. Which of the following best explains her weakness?

options.label: A
options.html: Antibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors

options.label: C
options.html: Antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels

options.label: D
options.html: Ectopic ACTH secretion causing steroid myopathy

options.label: E
options.html: Antibodies against a neuronal nuclear antigen causing encephalomyelitis

answerHtml: Answer: C. Anti-P/Q-type VGCC antibodies (Lambert–Eaton)
explanationHtml: Small cell lung carcinoma is associated with Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome: antibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type Ca2+ channels reduce ACh release. Repetitive effort increases presynaptic Ca2+ and transiently improves strength and reflexes (incremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation). Autonomic symptoms (dry mouth, constipation) are typical; ocular involvement is less prominent than in myasthenia gravis.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B — myasthenia gravis (anti-AChR, anti-MuSK) worsens with repeated use and prominently affects ocular muscles; associated with thymoma. D — steroid myopathy causes proximal weakness but does not improve with effort and has normal reflexes; Cushingoid features would be expected. E — anti-Hu causes sensory neuronopathy/encephalomyelitis, not effort-related improvement.

stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman on postoperative day 4 after total knee arthroplasty develops sudden dyspnea and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Pulse is 118/min and respirations are 28/min. Arterial blood gas on room air: pH 7.50, PaCO<sub>2</sub> 29 mmHg, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 22 mEq/L, PaO<sub>2</sub> 64 mmHg. Which of the following best describes her acid–base status?

options.label: B
options.html: Chronic respiratory alkalosis with appropriate renal compensation

options.label: C
options.html: Acute respiratory alkalosis with appropriate compensation

options.label: D
options.html: Respiratory alkalosis with a concurrent metabolic acidosis

options.label: E
options.html: Respiratory acidosis with a concurrent metabolic alkalosis

answerHtml: Answer: C. Acute respiratory alkalosis, appropriately compensated
explanationHtml: Alkalemia with low PaCO2 = primary respiratory alkalosis (hyperventilation driven by hypoxemia and J-receptor stimulation from pulmonary embolism). Acute compensation (cellular buffering): HCO3− falls ~2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg ↓ PaCO2 → expected 24 − 2.2 ≈ 22. Measured 22 matches. Chronic compensation (renal, 2–3 days) would lower HCO3− ~4–5 per 10 → ≈19.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> is not elevated. B — HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> is higher than expected for chronic compensation, and onset was sudden. D — a concurrent metabolic acidosis would lower HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> below ~22 (e.g., lactic acidosis from shock). E — PaCO<sub>2</sub> is low, not high.

stemHtml: A 54-year-old man is admitted with severe acute pancreatitis. On hospital day 2 he develops worsening dyspnea, and chest x-ray shows new bilateral diffuse opacities. PaO<sub>2</sub>/FiO<sub>2</sub> is 110 on PEEP 8 cmH<sub>2</sub>O. Echocardiography shows normal LV function, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is 10 mmHg. He dies despite intensive care. Microscopic examination of the lungs would most likely show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Mucus plugs containing spiral shed epithelium

options.label: C
options.html: Fibroblastic foci with subpleural honeycomb change

answerHtml: Answer: E. Hyaline membranes (diffuse alveolar damage)
explanationHtml: ARDS (onset within 1 week, bilateral opacities, PaO2/FiO2 ≤300 on PEEP ≥5, not explained by cardiac failure — normal PCWP) results from neutrophil-mediated injury to capillary endothelium and type I pneumocytes; protein-rich fluid and necrotic debris form hyaline membranes. Moderate ARDS here (101–200). Management: lung-protective low tidal-volume ventilation and prone positioning.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — Curschmann spirals are seen in asthma. B — "heart failure cells" reflect chronic pulmonary venous congestion (PCWP would be high). C — fibroblastic foci and honeycombing are IPF (usual interstitial pneumonia). D — sarcoidosis.

stemHtml: A male infant is born at 29 weeks' gestation by cesarean delivery to a mother with type 1 diabetes; she did not receive antenatal corticosteroids. Within minutes he develops grunting, nasal flaring, and subcostal retractions. Chest x-ray shows diffuse ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms. His condition is due to deficiency of a substance produced primarily by which cell type?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Type II pneumocytes
explanationHtml: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome reflects surfactant deficiency. Surfactant (mainly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) is made and stored in lamellar bodies of type II pneumocytes; it lowers surface tension, preventing end-expiratory alveolar collapse. Risk factors here: prematurity, maternal diabetes (fetal hyperinsulinemia inhibits surfactant synthesis), cesarean delivery without labor, no antenatal steroids.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — type I pneumocytes form the thin gas-exchange surface but do not secrete surfactant. C — ciliated cells move mucus. D — macrophages clear debris (and recycle surfactant). E — goblet cells secrete mucus in conducting airways.

stemHtml: A 64-year-old woman who has never smoked has 3 months of progressive dyspnea and a 6-kg weight loss. She takes no medications and has no history of heart, liver, or kidney disease. Chest x-ray shows a large right pleural effusion. Thoracentesis results: pleural protein 4.2 g/dL (serum 6.8 g/dL), pleural LDH 420 U/L (serum 210 U/L; upper limit of normal 250 U/L), glucose 85 mg/dL, lymphocyte-predominant cells. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Malignant effusion from lung adenocarcinoma
explanationHtml: Light's criteria: protein ratio 4.2/6.8 = 0.62 (>0.5), LDH ratio 420/210 = 2.0 (>0.6), and pleural LDH 420 > ⅔ × 250 (167) — all indicate an exudate. Weight loss in a never-smoker woman with a lymphocytic exudate points to malignancy; adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer in never-smokers and frequently involves the pleura. Cytology/pleural biopsy confirms.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, C, D, E — all cause transudates (↑ hydrostatic or ↓ oncotic pressure) that fail Light's criteria (HF can mimic an exudate only after aggressive diuresis, and she has no HF).

stemHtml: A 70-year-old man with severe COPD has taken an oral maintenance medication for many years. He is started on ciprofloxacin for community-acquired pneumonia. Three days later he develops nausea, vomiting, tremor, and palpitations; ECG shows a narrow-complex tachycardia at 150/min. Shortly afterward he has a generalized tonic–clonic seizure. Toxicity of which of the following drugs is most likely?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Theophylline
explanationHtml: Theophylline (PDE inhibitor and adenosine receptor antagonist) has a narrow therapeutic index and is metabolized by CYP1A2. Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2, raising theophylline levels. Toxicity: GI upset, tachyarrhythmias (adenosine antagonism + catecholamine effects), hypokalemia, and seizures (fluoroquinolones themselves lower the seizure threshold). Treat with activated charcoal, benzodiazepines, β-blockade for arrhythmia, and hemodialysis if severe.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — montelukast causes neuropsychiatric effects, not tachyarrhythmia/seizures from this interaction. B — tiotropium is inhaled; anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, urinary retention). C — inhaled steroid/LABA; not an oral drug and not affected by ciprofloxacin. E — omalizumab is an injectable anti-IgE antibody (anaphylaxis risk).

stemHtml: A 26-year-old man is evaluated for infertility. He has had chronic sinusitis and recurrent pneumonias since childhood and produces copious purulent sputum daily. Heart sounds are loudest to the right of the sternum. CT shows bronchiectasis. Semen analysis shows a normal sperm count, but the sperm are immotile. Which structure is most likely defective?

options.label: A
options.html: Dynein arms of the microtubule axoneme

options.label: C
options.html: A serine protease inhibitor synthesized by hepatocytes

answerHtml: Answer: A. Axonemal dynein arms (primary ciliary dyskinesia)
explanationHtml: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (AR) impairs ciliary beating → poor mucociliary clearance (sinusitis, otitis, bronchiectasis), immotile sperm and ↑ ectopic pregnancy risk in women, and randomized left–right orientation during embryonic nodal flow — half have situs inversus (Kartagener syndrome; dextrocardia here). Nasal nitric oxide is low.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — CFTR defects (cystic fibrosis) cause infertility via absent vas deferens (azoospermia), not immotile sperm with normal count, and do not cause situs inversus. C — α<sub>1</sub>-antitrypsin deficiency → emphysema, liver disease. D — Alport syndrome. E — Marfan syndrome.

stemHtml: A 35-year-old Black woman has 4 months of fatigue, dry cough, and increased thirst and urination. Chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Serum calcium is 11.8 mg/dL, PTH is 9 pg/mL (low), 25-hydroxyvitamin D is normal, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is elevated. Which of the following best explains her hypercalcemia?

options.label: E
options.html: Excessive intake of vitamin D supplements

answerHtml: Answer: D. Macrophage 1α-hydroxylase (sarcoidosis)
explanationHtml: In sarcoidosis, interferon-γ–activated macrophages within granulomas express 1α-hydroxylase that is not regulated by PTH, converting 25-OH vitamin D to calcitriol → ↑ intestinal Ca2+ absorption → hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria with suppressed PTH. Glucocorticoids inhibit this enzyme and are effective. The same mechanism occurs in TB, fungal infections, and lymphomas.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — PTHrP (squamous cell carcinoma) would not raise 1,25-(OH)2D. B — primary hyperparathyroidism has high PTH. C — osteolytic metastases have suppressed PTH and usually suppressed calcitriol. E — vitamin D intoxication raises 25-hydroxyvitamin D, which is normal here.

stemHtml: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has eGFR 55 mL/min/1.73 m² and a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 600 mg/g. He is started on lisinopril. Two weeks later, his serum creatinine has risen from 1.4 to 1.6 mg/dL and albuminuria has decreased. Which set of changes best describes the drug's direct effect on glomerular hemodynamics?

options.label: A
options.html: GFR ↓, renal plasma flow ↓, filtration fraction unchanged

options.label: B
options.html: GFR ↑, renal plasma flow ↑, filtration fraction unchanged

options.label: C
options.html: GFR ↓, renal plasma flow ↑, filtration fraction ↓

options.label: D
options.html: GFR ↑, renal plasma flow ↓, filtration fraction ↑

options.label: E
options.html: GFR ↓, renal plasma flow ↓, filtration fraction ↑

answerHtml: Answer: C. GFR ↓, RPF ↑, FF ↓
explanationHtml: Angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole. ACE inhibition dilates the efferent arteriole: resistance downstream of the glomerulus falls, so glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure drops (↓ GFR) while total renal vascular resistance falls (↑ RPF); FF = GFR/RPF therefore falls. The reduced intraglomerular pressure is exactly what lowers albuminuria and slows diabetic nephropathy. A creatinine rise of ≤30% is expected and acceptable; therapy should be continued.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — afferent constriction (NSAIDs, sympathetic). B — afferent dilation (e.g., high-protein meal, early diabetic hyperfiltration). D — efferent constriction (Ang II itself). E — the pattern of volume depletion: RPF falls more than GFR (Ang II-mediated efferent constriction), so FF rises.

stemHtml: In a renal physiology study, a healthy volunteer receives a continuous infusion of inulin. Measurements show: urine inulin 15 mg/mL, plasma inulin 0.25 mg/mL, urine flow 2 mL/min. Substance X is freely filtered at the glomerulus; its plasma concentration is 0.1 mg/mL and its urine concentration is 10 mg/mL. Which of the following best describes the net renal handling of substance X?

options.label: D
options.html: Filtration only, with no net tubular transport

answerHtml: Answer: B. Net secretion of 8 mg/min
explanationHtml: GFR = Cinulin = (15 × 2) ÷ 0.25 = 120 mL/min. Filtered load of X = GFR × PX = 120 × 0.1 = 12 mg/min. Excretion of X = UX × V̇ = 10 × 2 = 20 mg/min. Excretion exceeds filtration by 8 mg/min → net secretion. (Equivalently, CX = 200 mL/min > GFR.)
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, E — reabsorption would require excretion < filtered load. C — 20 mg/min is the total excretion rate, not the secreted amount. D — no net transport would require C<sub>X</sub> = GFR (120 mL/min).

stemHtml: A 45-year-old man has had three calcium oxalate kidney stones in 4 years. Serum calcium and PTH are normal; 24-hour urine calcium is 350 mg (elevated). He is started on a drug that reduces urinary calcium excretion by acting on the early distal convoluted tubule. Which additional laboratory change is most likely to develop with this drug?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Hyperuricemia
explanationHtml: Thiazides (e.g., chlorthalidone, HCTZ) block NCC in the DCT; the lower intracellular Na+ enhances basolateral Na+/Ca2+ exchange and apical Ca2+ entry, and mild volume contraction increases proximal Ca2+ reabsorption — reducing urinary calcium and stone recurrence. Volume contraction also increases proximal urate reabsorption, and thiazides compete with urate for secretion → hyperuricemia (can precipitate gout). Other effects: hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemia, hypercalcemia.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — thiazides cause hypokalemia (↑ distal Na+ delivery). B — they cause hypomagnesemia. C — they cause metabolic alkalosis. D — they raise glucose.

stemHtml: A 19-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes presents with abdominal pain and deep, rapid respirations after missing several insulin doses. She has not vomited. Labs: Na<sup>+</sup> 135 mEq/L, K<sup>+</sup> 5.4 mEq/L, Cl<sup>−</sup> 100 mEq/L, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 10 mEq/L, glucose 520 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.26, PaCO<sub>2</sub> 23 mmHg. Albumin is normal. Which of the following best describes her acid–base status?

options.label: A
options.html: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation

options.label: B
options.html: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation

options.label: C
options.html: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with a concurrent respiratory acidosis

options.label: D
options.html: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with a concurrent respiratory alkalosis

options.label: E
options.html: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with a concurrent metabolic alkalosis

answerHtml: Answer: B. HAGMA with appropriate respiratory compensation
explanationHtml: Anion gap = 135 − (100 + 10) = 25 (high) — ketoacids (β-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate). Winter's formula: expected PaCO2 = 1.5(10) + 8 ± 2 = 21–25; measured 23 → appropriate (Kussmaul breathing). Delta–delta: ΔAG = 25 − 12 = 13; ΔHCO3− = 24 − 10 = 14; ratio ≈ 0.9 (≈1) → no hidden second metabolic disorder.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — the gap is elevated. C — PaCO<sub>2</sub> would be >25. D — PaCO<sub>2</sub> would be <21. E — a concurrent metabolic alkalosis (e.g., from vomiting) would make ΔAG/ΔHCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> >2.

stemHtml: A 22-year-old woman reports fatigue and muscle weakness. BMI is 19 kg/m². She has erosion of the lingual surfaces of her teeth, bilateral parotid enlargement, and calluses on the dorsum of her right hand. She denies diuretic or laxative use, and a urine diuretic screen is negative. Labs: Na<sup>+</sup> 138 mEq/L, K<sup>+</sup> 2.9 mEq/L, Cl<sup>−</sup> 92 mEq/L, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 34 mEq/L; arterial pH 7.49, PaCO<sub>2</sub> 46 mmHg. Which additional finding is most likely?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Low urine chloride (saline-responsive alkalosis)
explanationHtml: Self-induced vomiting (bulimia nervosa — enamel erosion, parotid hypertrophy, Russell sign) causes loss of HCl → metabolic alkalosis (expected PaCO2 ≈ 40 + 0.7 × 10 = 47; measured 46, appropriate). Volume depletion activates RAAS; the kidney avidly reabsorbs NaCl, so urine Cl− is low (<20). Urine Na+ can be misleadingly high because bicarbonaturia drags Na+ out, making urine Cl− the better marker. Hypokalemia results mainly from aldosterone-driven renal K+ wasting. Treatment: isotonic saline with KCl.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — high urine Cl− suggests active diuretic use, Bartter/Gitelman, or mineralocorticoid excess. B — magnesium tends to be normal or low (GI and renal losses), not elevated. C — the anion gap is 138 − (92 + 34) = 12, which is normal. D — renin and aldosterone are elevated from volume depletion.

stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman with dry eyes and dry mouth (anti-SSA positive) has recurrent flank pain. CT shows bilateral nephrocalcinosis and several small stones. Labs: Na<sup>+</sup> 140 mEq/L, K<sup>+</sup> 3.1 mEq/L, Cl<sup>−</sup> 114 mEq/L, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 16 mEq/L. Urine pH is 6.6 and the urine anion gap is positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Distal (type 1) RTA
explanationHtml: Normal anion gap (140 − 130 = 10) hyperchloremic acidosis with hypokalemia, an inappropriately alkaline urine (>5.5) despite systemic acidosis, and a positive urine anion gap (failure to excrete NH4+) = distal RTA. Sjögren syndrome causes autoimmune injury to α-intercalated cell H+-ATPase. Alkaline urine, hypocitraturia and bone-derived hypercalciuria cause calcium phosphate stones and nephrocalcinosis. Treat with potassium citrate.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — proximal RTA can acidify urine (<5.5) once HCO3− is below threshold and rarely causes stones. B — type 4 RTA causes hyperkalemia. D — diarrhea gives a negative urine anion gap (appropriately ↑ NH4Cl excretion). E — hyperaldosteronism causes metabolic alkalosis.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old man has 2 months of progressive leg swelling and foamy urine. Blood pressure is 132/84 mmHg. Urine protein is 7 g/day without RBC casts; serum albumin is 2.2 g/dL and LDL cholesterol is elevated. ANA, hepatitis B and C serologies, and age-appropriate cancer screening are negative. Renal biopsy shows diffuse thickening of capillary walls; electron microscopy shows subepithelial electron-dense deposits separated by projections of basement membrane material. Which circulating autoantibody is most likely present?

options.label: A
options.html: Anti-α3 chain of type IV collagen

answerHtml: Answer: D. Anti-PLA2R
explanationHtml: Nephrotic syndrome with GBM thickening and subepithelial deposits with "spikes" (spike-and-dome) is membranous nephropathy. Primary membranous nephropathy is caused in ~70–80% of cases by IgG4 autoantibodies to the podocyte phospholipase A2 receptor; titers track disease activity. It has the highest thrombosis risk among nephrotic diseases (renal vein thrombosis). Secondary causes (SLE, HBV/HCV, tumors, drugs) were excluded.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — anti-GBM disease is nephritic/RPGN with linear IgG. B — PR3-ANCA is granulomatosis with polyangiitis (pauci-immune crescentic GN). C — ASO indicates recent streptococcal infection (PSGN, nephritic, subepithelial humps without spikes). E — anti-dsDNA indicates SLE (lupus class V can be membranous, but ANA is negative).

stemHtml: An 8-year-old boy is brought in with puffy eyelids and dark, cola-colored urine. Three weeks ago he had crusted, honey-colored lesions on his legs. Blood pressure is 138/90 mmHg. Urinalysis shows RBC casts and mild proteinuria. Serum C3 is low and C4 is normal; anti-DNase B titer is elevated. If a renal biopsy were performed, electron microscopy would most likely show which of the following?

options.label: B
options.html: Diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes as the only abnormality

options.label: D
options.html: Splitting of the GBM by mesangial interposition

options.label: E
options.html: Irregular thinning and lamellation of the GBM

answerHtml: Answer: A. Subepithelial humps (PSGN)
explanationHtml: Post-streptococcal GN follows impetigo by 3–6 weeks (pharyngitis by 2–4 weeks). Nephritogenic streptococcal antigens form immune complexes that deposit on the subepithelial side of the GBM and activate the alternative pathway (↓ C3, normal C4). Anti-DNase B is the best marker after skin infection (ASO is often low after impetigo). Children usually recover fully with supportive care.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — minimal change disease (nephrotic, normal complement). C — diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis (↓ C3 and C4). D — MPGN "tram-track." E — Alport syndrome (hereditary, basket-weave GBM, normal complement).

stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman has muscle cramps, salt craving, and fatigue. Blood pressure is 104/66 mmHg. She takes no medications and denies vomiting; a urine diuretic screen is negative. Labs: K<sup>+</sup> 2.8 mEq/L, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 32 mEq/L, Mg<sup>2+</sup> 1.2 mg/dL (low), urine calcium-to-creatinine ratio low, urine Cl<sup>−</sup> 60 mEq/L; plasma renin and aldosterone are elevated. A defect in which transporter is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup>/2Cl<sup>−</sup> cotransporter in the thick ascending limb

options.label: B
options.html: Epithelial Na<sup>+</sup> channel in the collecting duct (gain of function)

options.label: E
options.html: Thiazide-sensitive Na<sup>+</sup>/Cl<sup>−</sup> cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule

answerHtml: Answer: E. NCC (Gitelman syndrome)
explanationHtml: Gitelman syndrome (AR, SLC12A3) behaves like chronic thiazide use: hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with high urine Cl− (renal salt wasting), secondary hyperaldosteronism with normal/low BP, hypocalciuria and hypomagnesemia. Low urine calcium is the key discriminator from Bartter syndrome. Treatment: K+ and Mg2+ supplements, liberal salt, ± amiloride/spironolactone.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — Bartter syndrome (NKCC2) mimics loop diuretics: hypercalciuria, often nephrocalcinosis, earlier onset. B — Liddle syndrome causes hypertension with ↓ renin and aldosterone. C — apparent mineralocorticoid excess causes hypertension with ↓ renin and aldosterone. D — distal RTA causes metabolic acidosis.

stemHtml: A 72-year-old man has prolonged hypotension during emergency repair of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. The next day he is oliguric and serum creatinine rises from 1.0 to 3.2 mg/dL. Urine osmolality is 300 mOsm/kg, FENa is 3.5%, and urine sediment shows numerous muddy brown granular casts. Which nephron segments are most vulnerable to this type of injury?

options.label: B
options.html: Thin descending limb of the loop of Henle

options.label: D
options.html: Proximal straight tubule and medullary thick ascending limb

answerHtml: Answer: D. Proximal straight tubule (S3) and medullary TAL
explanationHtml: Ischemic acute tubular necrosis: isosthenuric urine, high FENa (tubules can't reabsorb Na+), and muddy brown granular casts of sloughed epithelium. The outer medulla is relatively hypoxic even normally (vasa recta countercurrent exchange), and the S3 segment and medullary TAL have high ATP demands for active transport, making them most susceptible. Necrosis is patchy; basement membrane is preserved, allowing regeneration (recovery often has a polyuric phase).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — glomeruli are relatively resistant to ischemia. B — thin limbs perform passive transport with low O<sub>2</sub> demand. C, E — distal segments are less metabolically vulnerable to ischemia; the inner medullary collecting duct is adapted to low O<sub>2</sub>.

stemHtml: A 38-year-old man has hypertension, intermittent gross hematuria, and bilateral palpable flank masses. His father started dialysis at age 50, and a paternal uncle died suddenly of a subarachnoid hemorrhage. Ultrasound shows bilaterally enlarged kidneys with numerous cysts and several hepatic cysts. A mutation in which gene is most likely?
answerHtml: Answer: B. PKD1
explanationHtml: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (vertical transmission, adult onset, hepatic cysts, berry aneurysms) is caused by PKD1 mutations (~85%, polycystin-1, chromosome 16; earlier ESRD) or PKD2 (chromosome 4). Hypertension results from cyst-related intrarenal ischemia activating RAAS. Tolvaptan slows cyst growth in rapidly progressive disease.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — PKHD1 causes autosomal recessive PKD (infancy, Potter sequence, congenital hepatic fibrosis). C — VHL causes clear cell RCC, hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytoma (cysts in kidneys can occur, but the family history and phenotype fit ADPKD). D — WT1 causes Wilms tumor syndromes. E — COL4A5 causes Alport syndrome.

stemHtml: A 61-year-old man who smokes has gross hematuria and a 5-kg weight loss. Hematocrit is 56%. He has a left scrotal swelling that feels like a "bag of worms" and does not decrease in size when he lies supine. CT shows a 7-cm solid left renal mass with tumor extending into the left renal vein. From which cells does this tumor most likely arise?

options.label: A
options.html: Intercalated cells of the collecting duct

options.label: E
options.html: Perivascular epithelioid cells forming vessels, smooth muscle and fat

answerHtml: Answer: C. Proximal tubule epithelium (clear cell RCC)
explanationHtml: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma arises from PCT cells, typically in older male smokers. Polycythemia reflects ectopic EPO; the non-reducing left varicocele indicates tumor obstruction of the left renal vein (into which the left gonadal vein drains). Sporadic and VHL-associated tumors share 3p (VHL) loss with HIF accumulation.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — intercalated cells give rise to oncocytoma (benign) and chromophobe RCC. B — metanephric blastema gives rise to Wilms tumor in children. D — urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis causes hematuria but not EPO-driven polycythemia or typical renal vein invasion of this type. E — angiomyolipoma (PEComa) is benign, fat-containing, associated with tuberous sclerosis.

stemHtml: A 54-year-old woman has had recurrent urinary tract infections over the past year. CT shows a large branched stone filling the left renal pelvis and calyces. Urine pH is 8.0, and urine culture grows a gram-negative, urease-positive rod that swarms across the agar plate. Which of the following is the most likely composition of the stone?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate)
explanationHtml: Proteus mirabilis (swarming motility) produces urease, which hydrolyzes urea into NH3 and CO2, alkalinizing the urine and supplying ammonium; struvite precipitates and can grow into a staghorn calculus that harbors bacteria. Treatment requires complete stone removal plus antibiotics.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — calcium oxalate stones are the most common overall but are not caused by urease-producing infection. C — uric acid stones form in acidic urine and are radiolucent. D — cystine stones form in acidic urine in cystinuria. E — calcium phosphate forms in alkaline urine (distal RTA, hyperparathyroidism), but the infection-driven staghorn picture is struvite.

stemHtml: A 4-week-old firstborn boy is brought to the clinic because of forceful, nonbilious vomiting after every feed for 5 days. He was treated with oral erythromycin for pertussis exposure at 1 week of age. He appears dehydrated, and a firm, mobile 2-cm mass is palpated in the epigastrium after he vomits. Which of the following sets of laboratory findings is most likely?

options.label: B
options.html: Anion-gap metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate

options.label: D
options.html: Respiratory alkalosis with normal serum chloride

answerHtml: Answer: C. Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
explanationHtml: This is hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (early macrolide exposure is a known risk factor). Persistent vomiting of gastric contents loses HCl → hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. Volume depletion activates RAAS; aldosterone drives Na⁺ reabsorption in exchange for K⁺ and H⁺ in the collecting duct → hypokalemia and a "paradoxical aciduria." Because the obstruction is proximal to the ampulla of Vater, vomitus is nonbilious.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — hyperchloremic acidosis follows lower GI (bicarbonate) loss such as diarrhea. B — lactic acidosis would appear only with shock or bowel ischemia, a late finding. D — primary respiratory alkalosis is not caused by vomiting. E — vomiting lowers, not raises, chloride, and K⁺ falls.

stemHtml: A 20-year-old college student notices yellow eyes during a week of final examinations in which he has been skipping meals. He feels well. Examination shows scleral icterus only. Total bilirubin is 3.1 mg/dL with direct bilirubin 0.2 mg/dL. Hemoglobin, reticulocyte count, haptoglobin, LDH, AST, ALT and alkaline phosphatase are normal. Urinalysis is negative for bilirubin. Which of the following best explains his condition?

options.label: A
options.html: Reduced activity of hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase due to a promoter variant

options.label: C
options.html: Defective canalicular transport of conjugated bilirubin by MRP2

options.label: D
options.html: Increased heme turnover from extravascular hemolysis

options.label: E
options.html: Obstruction of the common bile duct

answerHtml: Answer: A. Reduced activity of hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase due to a promoter variant
explanationHtml: Mild isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia triggered by fasting/stress in an otherwise healthy young adult with normal hemolysis markers and liver enzymes is Gilbert syndrome — a TA-repeat variant in the UGT1A1 promoter lowers enzyme expression (~30% of normal). Fasting further reduces conjugation capacity. It is benign and needs no treatment.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — Crigler-Najjar type I presents in the neonatal period with very high bilirubin and kernicterus. C — Dubin-Johnson causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with bilirubinuria. D — hemolysis is excluded by normal hemoglobin, reticulocytes, haptoglobin and LDH. E — obstruction raises conjugated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase.

stemHtml: A 61-year-old man with chronic knee osteoarthritis who takes naproxen daily presents with melena and hematemesis. Blood pressure is 88/56 mm Hg, pulse 124/min. Upper endoscopy shows a deep ulcer with a visible vessel on the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum. Erosion of which of the following arteries is most likely responsible for the bleeding?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Gastroduodenal artery
explanationHtml: The gastroduodenal artery (branch of the common hepatic artery from the celiac trunk) runs directly behind the first part of the duodenum. A posterior duodenal ulcer can erode into it, producing brisk upper GI hemorrhage. NSAIDs promote ulcers by inhibiting COX-1–dependent prostaglandin synthesis (↓ mucus and bicarbonate, ↓ mucosal blood flow).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — the left gastric artery bleeds from lesser-curvature gastric ulcers (and supplies esophageal varices territory). B — the splenic artery runs along the superior pancreas; posterior gastric ulcers can rarely erode it, not duodenal ulcers. C — short gastrics supply the fundus. D — the SMA lies behind the third part of the duodenum and pancreas neck, not the first part.

stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman with Crohn disease underwent resection of 100 cm of terminal ileum 2 years ago. She now has steatorrhea and presents with right flank pain and hematuria. CT shows a radiopaque stone in the right ureter; stone analysis reveals calcium oxalate. Which of the following best explains the formation of her stone?

options.label: A
options.html: Increased hepatic synthesis of oxalate from glycine

options.label: B
options.html: Binding of intestinal calcium by unabsorbed fatty acids, leaving free oxalate to be absorbed in the colon

options.label: D
options.html: Chronic metabolic alkalosis increasing urinary citrate

options.label: E
options.html: Reduced renal ammonium excretion acidifying the urine

answerHtml: Answer: B. Binding of intestinal calcium by unabsorbed fatty acids, leaving free oxalate to be absorbed in the colon
explanationHtml: Ileal resection disrupts enterohepatic bile-acid recycling → bile-acid pool depletion → fat malabsorption. Luminal fatty acids saponify with calcium, so dietary oxalate is no longer precipitated as insoluble calcium oxalate in the gut. Free oxalate is absorbed by the colon (whose permeability is further increased by unabsorbed bile acids) → hyperoxaluria → calcium oxalate stones ("enteric hyperoxaluria"). Chronic diarrhea also causes volume depletion and hypocitraturia (from metabolic acidosis), which contribute.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — increased endogenous oxalate synthesis is primary hyperoxaluria (an inherited enzyme defect). C — malabsorption actually lowers vitamin D and calcium absorption. D — chronic diarrhea produces metabolic acidosis, which lowers urinary citrate; higher citrate would protect against stones. E — acidic urine favors uric acid stones, not calcium oxalate, and is not the primary mechanism here.

stemHtml: A 28-year-old man presents with 3 weeks of fatigue, nausea and dark urine. He had unprotected intercourse with a new partner 3 months ago. ALT is 1,250 U/L. Hepatitis B serology shows: HBsAg negative, anti-HBs negative, HBeAg negative, anti-HBe positive, IgM anti-HBc positive. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation?

options.label: B
options.html: Chronic hepatitis B with high infectivity

options.label: D
options.html: Acute hepatitis B in the window period

options.label: E
options.html: Chronic inactive hepatitis B carrier state

answerHtml: Answer: D. Acute hepatitis B in the window period
explanationHtml: During the window period HBsAg has fallen below detection but anti-HBs has not yet appeared. IgM anti-HBc (marker of recent infection) remains positive and is often the only clue; anti-HBe may also be present as HBeAg clears. The timing (3 months after exposure) and markedly elevated ALT fit acute infection.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — vaccination produces anti-HBs only (no anti-HBc because the vaccine contains only HBsAg). B and E — chronic infection requires HBsAg positivity >6 months with IgG (not IgM) anti-HBc. C — resolved infection shows anti-HBs and IgG anti-HBc.

stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman has had intermittent bloating and loose stools for 2 years. She also reports an intensely itchy rash of grouped vesicles on her elbows and knees. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL with MCV 72 fL and low ferritin. Serum IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody is markedly elevated. An endoscopic biopsy of the distal duodenum would most likely show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Lamina propria filled with PAS-positive foamy macrophages

options.label: C
options.html: Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes

options.label: D
options.html: Lipid-laden enterocytes with normal villous architecture

options.label: E
options.html: Crypt abscesses with inflammation confined to the mucosa

answerHtml: Answer: C. Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes
explanationHtml: Celiac disease (with dermatitis herpetiformis and iron deficiency from impaired duodenal absorption) is a T-cell–mediated response to deamidated gliadin presented by HLA-DQ2/DQ8. The classic histologic triad is villous blunting/atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis, most marked in the distal duodenum and proximal jejunum.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — Whipple disease. B — Crohn disease. D — abetalipoproteinemia (MTTP deficiency). E — crypt abscesses confined to the mucosa describe ulcerative colitis in the colon.

stemHtml: A 46-year-old man has recurrent peptic ulcers despite eradication of H. pylori and high-dose PPI therapy. He also has chronic watery diarrhea. Endoscopy shows ulcers in the third part of the duodenum and proximal jejunum with thickened gastric folds. After PPIs are held, fasting serum gastrin is 820 pg/mL (normal <100) and gastric pH is 1.5. Which of the following results is most likely after intravenous administration of secretin?

options.label: A
options.html: A marked rise in serum gastrin

options.label: B
options.html: A marked fall in serum gastrin

options.label: C
options.html: No change in gastrin but a rise in serum calcium

answerHtml: Answer: A. A marked rise in serum gastrin
explanationHtml: Refractory, distal ulcers with diarrhea and markedly elevated gastrin in the presence of acid indicate Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma). Normal G cells are inhibited by secretin, but gastrinoma cells express secretin receptors and respond with a paradoxical increase in gastrin (rise ≥120 pg/mL is diagnostic). The diarrhea results from acid inactivating pancreatic lipase and damaging the mucosa. About 25% are associated with MEN1, so serum calcium/PTH should be checked.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — gastrin falls or stays the same in normal people or in hypergastrinemia from atrophic gastritis/PPIs. C — secretin does not change calcium; hypercalcemia from MEN1 would be present at baseline. D — secretin does not stimulate CCK. E — hypoglycemia would suggest insulinoma, not provoked by secretin.

stemHtml: A 33-year-old man with an 8-year history of pancolonic ulcerative colitis has pruritus and fatigue. Alkaline phosphatase is 480 U/L, GGT is elevated and bilirubin is normal. Antimitochondrial antibodies are negative; p-ANCA is positive. MRCP shows multifocal strictures and dilations of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. In addition to colorectal cancer, this patient is at greatest risk for which of the following malignancies?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Cholangiocarcinoma
explanationHtml: Beaded intra- and extrahepatic ducts with a cholestatic pattern in a young man with UC is primary sclerosing cholangitis. Chronic biliary inflammation and concentric "onion-skin" periductal fibrosis carry a lifetime cholangiocarcinoma risk of roughly 10–15%; gallbladder carcinoma and colorectal carcinoma (with UC) are also increased, which is why annual colonoscopy and gallbladder imaging are recommended.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — hepatic adenoma relates to OCPs/anabolic steroids. B — acinar cell carcinoma is not linked to PSC. C — angiosarcoma relates to vinyl chloride, arsenic, Thorotrast. D — gastric MALT lymphoma relates to H. pylori.

stemHtml: A 70-year-old man is resuscitated after a cardiac arrest with 25 minutes of hypotension. Two days later, AST is 4,800 U/L and ALT 3,900 U/L; both fall rapidly over the following week. A liver biopsy obtained on day 2 would show necrosis concentrated in the hepatocytes surrounding the central veins. Which of the following best explains why this region is preferentially injured?

options.label: A
options.html: It receives blood first from the portal triad and therefore the highest concentration of absorbed toxins

options.label: B
options.html: It has the lowest oxygen tension, being farthest along the sinusoid from the hepatic arteriole

options.label: D
options.html: It is the site of bile acid synthesis and accumulates toxic bile

options.label: E
options.html: It contains the highest density of Kupffer cells that release cytokines

answerHtml: Answer: B. It has the lowest oxygen tension, being farthest along the sinusoid from the hepatic arteriole
explanationHtml: Blood flows from the portal triad (zone 1) through sinusoids to the central vein (zone 3). Oxygen is extracted along the way, so zone 3 hepatocytes are the most hypoxic and are the first to die in ischemic hepatitis ("shock liver"), producing transaminases in the thousands that fall quickly once perfusion is restored. Zone 3 is also rich in CYP450 (CYP2E1), explaining its vulnerability to acetaminophen and alcohol.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — describes zone 1 (periportal), affected by viral hepatitis and ingested toxins such as cocaine. C — zone 3 has the highest CYP450 content. D — bile acid secretion is not the cause of ischemic necrosis. E — Kupffer cells are distributed throughout the lobule (more periportal) and are not the explanation for hypoxic zone 3 injury.

stemHtml: A 52-year-old man of Irish descent has new-onset diabetes, erectile dysfunction, darkening of his skin and pain in the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints. Serum ferritin is 2,400 ng/mL and transferrin saturation 78%. Genetic testing shows homozygosity for HFE C282Y. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of iron overload in this patient?

options.label: A
options.html: Excess hepcidin causes internalization of ferroportin in enterocytes

options.label: B
options.html: Loss of a copper-transporting ATPase impairs biliary iron excretion

options.label: C
options.html: Decreased hepatic transferrin synthesis increases free plasma iron

options.label: D
options.html: Inappropriately low hepcidin allows unregulated ferroportin-mediated iron export from enterocytes and macrophages

options.label: E
options.html: Increased degradation of duodenal DMT1 enhances apical iron uptake

answerHtml: Answer: D. Inappropriately low hepcidin allows unregulated ferroportin-mediated iron export from enterocytes and macrophages
explanationHtml: HFE normally helps hepatocytes sense body iron (via transferrin receptor signaling) to upregulate hepcidin. In HFE hemochromatosis, hepcidin is inappropriately low for the iron load. Hepcidin normally binds ferroportin and triggers its degradation; without it, ferroportin on the basolateral enterocyte membrane and on macrophages keeps exporting iron into plasma, increasing absorption and saturating transferrin. Iron deposits in liver (cirrhosis, HCC), pancreas (diabetes), pituitary (hypogonadism), heart and joints. Treatment is phlebotomy.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — excess hepcidin causes the opposite (anemia of chronic disease). B — ATP7B loss causes Wilson disease (copper). C — transferrin levels are normal or low; low transferrin is not the cause. E — DMT1 degradation would decrease, not increase, apical uptake.

stemHtml: A 69-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history presents with painless jaundice, pruritus, a 9-kg weight loss and new-onset diabetes. Examination shows a palpable, nontender gallbladder. CT shows a 3-cm hypodense mass in the head of the pancreas with dilation of both the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct. Which of the following genetic alterations is most likely present in the tumor?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Activating KRAS mutation
explanationHtml: Painless obstructive jaundice with a palpable nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) and a "double-duct sign" indicates pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the head. KRAS activating mutations occur in >90% of cases and are an early event in PanIN progression, followed by CDKN2A (p16), TP53 and SMAD4 loss. Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — APC loss is the initiating event in colorectal adenomas. B — BRAF V600E characterizes papillary thyroid carcinoma, melanoma, hairy cell leukemia and serrated colon lesions. D — RET gain of function causes MEN2/medullary thyroid carcinoma. E — MEN1 loss causes pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, not ductal adenocarcinoma.

stemHtml: A 55-year-old woman receiving cisplatin for ovarian carcinoma is given an antiemetic before each infusion. A baseline ECG is obtained because the drug can prolong the QT interval, and she later develops constipation and headache. The drug most likely acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Antagonism of 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents and in the chemoreceptor trigger zone

options.label: B
options.html: Antagonism of D2 receptors with stimulation of 5-HT4 receptors in the gut

options.label: C
options.html: Antagonism of neurokinin-1 receptors in the brainstem

options.label: D
options.html: Antagonism of H1 receptors in the vestibular nuclei

answerHtml: Answer: A. Antagonism of 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents and in the chemoreceptor trigger zone
explanationHtml: Cisplatin damages enterochromaffin cells, releasing serotonin that activates 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents and in the area postrema. Ondansetron (a 5-HT3 antagonist) is the standard premedication; its characteristic adverse effects are headache, constipation and dose-related QT prolongation.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — metoclopramide; adverse effects are extrapyramidal symptoms and tardive dyskinesia, and it causes diarrhea rather than constipation. C — aprepitant is used for delayed CINV; QT prolongation and constipation are not its signature. D — meclizine/dimenhydrinate are for motion sickness and cause sedation. E — dronabinol causes euphoria, dizziness, appetite stimulation.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman with long-standing type 1 diabetes and gastroparesis has taken a prokinetic agent for 9 months. She now has involuntary lip smacking, tongue protrusion and choreiform finger movements. She also noticed breast tenderness and milky nipple discharge. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Metoclopramide
