explanationHtml: Metoclopramide is a central and peripheral D2 antagonist (and 5-HT4 agonist) used for diabetic gastroparesis. Because it crosses the blood–brain barrier, chronic use causes tardive dyskinesia (boxed warning: avoid use >12 weeks). Blocking D2 receptors on pituitary lactotrophs removes dopaminergic inhibition → hyperprolactinemia (galactorrhea, gynecomastia).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — erythromycin (motilin agonist) causes GI upset, QT prolongation and tachyphylaxis, not TD. B — ondansetron is an antiemetic without prokinetic or dopaminergic effects. C — domperidone blocks D2 receptors but barely crosses the blood–brain barrier (can raise prolactin but rarely causes TD) and is not FDA approved in the US. D — prucalopride is a selective 5-HT4 agonist without antidopaminergic effects.

stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman with moderate-to-severe ileocolonic Crohn disease has failed corticosteroids. Her gastroenterologist plans to start infliximab. Which of the following tests is most important to perform before the first infusion?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Interferon-γ release assay
explanationHtml: TNF-α is essential for macrophage activation and granuloma maintenance. Anti-TNF agents (infliximab, adalimumab) can reactivate latent tuberculosis, often as disseminated or extrapulmonary disease, so latent TB must be screened for (IGRA or tuberculin skin test, plus chest radiograph if positive) and treated before therapy. Hepatitis B serology is also required.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — TPMT/NUDT15 testing precedes azathioprine/6-MP. C — G6PD testing matters for sulfasalazine's sulfapyridine moiety, dapsone, primaquine, rasburicase. D — HLA-B*58:01 predicts allopurinol hypersensitivity. E — ceruloplasmin is for Wilson disease.

stemHtml: A 3-day-old boy with trisomy 21 has not passed meconium and has progressive abdominal distension and bilious vomiting. Abdominal radiograph shows dilated loops of bowel without rectal gas. On digital rectal examination, the rectum feels tight, and withdrawal of the finger is followed by an explosive release of gas and stool. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?

options.label: A
options.html: Failure of recanalization of the duodenal lumen

options.label: B
options.html: Inspissated meconium due to defective chloride transport

options.label: C
options.html: Intrauterine vascular occlusion of a segment of jejunum

options.label: D
options.html: Failure of neural crest cells to migrate to the distal colon

options.label: E
options.html: Incomplete rotation of the midgut around the superior mesenteric artery

answerHtml: Answer: D. Failure of neural crest cells to migrate to the distal colon
explanationHtml: Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon) results from failed craniocaudal migration of neural crest–derived ganglion cells, so the distal segment (always including the rectum) lacks Meissner and Auerbach plexuses and cannot relax. Delayed meconium passage, distension and the "squeeze sign" are characteristic; associations include trisomy 21 and RET mutations. Diagnosis is by rectal suction biopsy showing absent ganglion cells.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — duodenal atresia (also trisomy 21) presents within hours of birth with a "double bubble" and does not cause the squeeze sign; meconium may still pass. B — meconium ileus (CF) obstructs the ileum; rectal exam does not produce explosive stool. C — jejunal atresia causes early bilious vomiting with few air-fluid levels and a microcolon. E — malrotation with volvulus causes sudden bilious vomiting, usually without delayed meconium as the main feature.

stemHtml: A 10-day-old infant with ambiguous genitalia (clitoromegaly and fused labioscrotal folds) is brought to the emergency department with vomiting and lethargy. Blood pressure is 58/30 mm Hg. Serum sodium is 126 mEq/L and potassium 7.1 mEq/L. Pelvic ultrasound shows a uterus and ovaries. Which of the following serum findings is most likely?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone
explanationHtml: A virilized 46,XX infant with salt-wasting crisis (hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia) has classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Blocked conversion of progesterone → 11-deoxycorticosterone and 17-OH progesterone → 11-deoxycortisol causes deficiency of aldosterone and cortisol. Low cortisol raises ACTH, and the accumulated 17-OH progesterone is shunted to adrenal androgens, causing virilization. 17-OH progesterone is the newborn screening marker.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — DOC is low in 21-OH deficiency; it is high in 11β- and 17α-hydroxylase deficiency (which cause hypertension). B — cortisol is low. D — aldosterone is low (salt wasting). E — renin is markedly elevated because of volume depletion and absent aldosterone.

stemHtml: A 6-year-old girl is evaluated for early pubic hair, clitoromegaly and accelerated growth. Blood pressure is 138/90 mm Hg (above the 99th percentile). Serum potassium is 3.1 mEq/L and plasma renin activity is suppressed. Serum cortisol is low and ACTH is elevated. Accumulation of which of the following steroids best explains her hypertension?
answerHtml: Answer: A. 11-Deoxycorticosterone
explanationHtml: Virilization plus hypertension and hypokalemia with low renin points to 11β-hydroxylase deficiency. The block prevents 11-deoxycorticosterone → corticosterone (and 11-deoxycortisol → cortisol). ACTH-driven accumulation of DOC, a mineralocorticoid agonist, causes sodium retention, hypertension and hypokalemia, and suppresses renin (so aldosterone itself is low). The precursors also flow into androgens, causing virilization.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — aldosterone is low because aldosterone synthase lies downstream and renin is suppressed. C — corticosterone is distal to the block and is decreased. D — cortisol is low (stem). E — 17-OH progesterone has negligible mineralocorticoid activity; it is the key marker of 21-hydroxylase deficiency, which causes salt wasting rather than hypertension.

stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman has gained 15 kg over 2 years, mainly in her trunk, with wide purple abdominal striae, proximal muscle weakness and hypertension. She takes no medications. Two 24-hour urine free cortisol measurements are elevated, and a 1-mg overnight dexamethasone test fails to suppress morning cortisol. Plasma ACTH is mildly elevated. After 8 mg of dexamethasone, serum cortisol falls by 70%. Which of the following is the most likely source of her disease?

options.label: B
options.html: Small cell carcinoma of the lung

options.label: E
options.html: Corticotroph adenoma of the anterior pituitary

answerHtml: Answer: E. Corticotroph adenoma of the anterior pituitary
explanationHtml: Hypercortisolism is confirmed; an elevated ACTH makes it ACTH-dependent. Pituitary corticotroph adenomas retain partial glucocorticoid feedback, so high-dose dexamethasone suppresses cortisol (and CRH stimulation increases ACTH). This is Cushing disease, the most common endogenous cause. Next steps are pituitary MRI and, if equivocal, inferior petrosal sinus sampling.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and D — adrenal sources suppress ACTH (low ACTH). B — ectopic ACTH from small cell lung carcinoma is not suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone and usually produces very high ACTH with rapid onset and severe hypokalemia. C — exogenous glucocorticoids suppress ACTH, and most synthetic steroids are not measured as cortisol (except hydrocortisone).

stemHtml: A 44-year-old man has hypertension requiring three medications. Blood pressure is 168/102 mm Hg; there is no peripheral edema. Serum potassium is 2.9 mEq/L and bicarbonate 31 mEq/L. Which of the following combinations of plasma aldosterone and plasma renin activity is most likely?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Aldosterone increased, renin decreased
explanationHtml: Resistant hypertension with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis suggests primary hyperaldosteronism (bilateral adrenal hyperplasia or an aldosterone-producing adenoma). Autonomous aldosterone causes sodium retention and volume expansion, which suppresses renin; the aldosterone-to-renin ratio is the screening test. Edema is absent because of "aldosterone escape" (pressure natriuresis and ANP).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — high renin with high aldosterone is secondary hyperaldosteronism (renal artery stenosis, renin-secreting tumor, diuretics). C — low aldosterone and low renin with hypertension suggests a non-aldosterone mineralocorticoid (11β/17α CAH, licorice, Liddle syndrome). D — low aldosterone with high renin is primary adrenal insufficiency, which causes hyperkalemia and hypotension. E — normal values would not explain hypokalemic alkalosis.

stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman presents 4 months after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery with palpitations, anxiety and a 3-kg weight loss. She is breastfeeding. Pulse is 112/min. The thyroid is mildly enlarged and nontender; there is no exophthalmos. TSH is <0.01 µU/mL, free T4 is elevated, ESR is normal, serum thyroglobulin is elevated, and anti-TPO antibodies are strongly positive. Radioactive iodine uptake measured with a tracer dose is 2% at 24 hours (low). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Postpartum (painless lymphocytic) thyroiditis
explanationHtml: Thyrotoxicosis with low iodine uptake means preformed hormone is leaking from a damaged gland (or is exogenous). A painless, nontender goiter within a year of delivery, positive anti-TPO, normal ESR and elevated thyroglobulin indicate postpartum lymphocytic thyroiditis, an autoimmune destructive process. It often progresses to a hypothyroid phase before recovery; the hyperthyroid phase is treated with β-blockers only (thionamides are ineffective because synthesis is not increased).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — Graves (which can also flare postpartum) shows diffusely increased uptake. B — toxic MNG shows patchy increased uptake and occurs in older patients. C — subacute granulomatous thyroiditis is painful and tender with a high ESR. E — exogenous T4 suppresses thyroglobulin (low), and the gland is small.

stemHtml: A 37-year-old woman with untreated Graves disease develops a temperature of 40.1°C, atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 170/min, agitation and vomiting after an emergency appendectomy. In addition to propranolol and hydrocortisone, a drug is given that inhibits both thyroid peroxidase and peripheral 5′-deiodinase. Which drug was given?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Propylthiouracil
explanationHtml: Thyroid storm requires blockade of synthesis, release, peripheral conversion and adrenergic effects. Both thionamides inhibit TPO-mediated oxidation, organification and coupling, but only PTU also inhibits peripheral 5′-deiodinase (T4 → T3), giving a faster fall in active hormone. This is why PTU is often preferred in storm (and in the first trimester of pregnancy) despite its hepatotoxicity.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — methimazole inhibits TPO but not peripheral deiodinase. B — iodide blocks hormone release (Wolff-Chaikoff) and should be given ≥1 hour after a thionamide; it does not inhibit TPO enzymatically or deiodinase. D — levothyroxine would worsen thyrotoxicosis. E — RAI takes weeks to work and is contraindicated in storm.

stemHtml: A 59-year-old woman is found to have serum calcium of 11.4 mg/dL (normal 8.4–10.2) on routine testing. She has had a kidney stone and mild depression. Albumin is normal. Phosphate is 2.2 mg/dL (low), intact PTH is 98 pg/mL (normal 10–65), and 24-hour urinary calcium is elevated; the calcium/creatinine clearance ratio is 0.03. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Primary hyperparathyroidism due to a parathyroid adenoma

options.label: E
options.html: Secondary hyperparathyroidism due to chronic kidney disease

answerHtml: Answer: A. Primary hyperparathyroidism due to a parathyroid adenoma
explanationHtml: Hypercalcemia with an elevated (inappropriately non-suppressed) PTH, low phosphate (PTH reduces proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption) and hypercalciuria is primary hyperparathyroidism; a single adenoma accounts for ~85% of cases. Although PTH increases distal calcium reabsorption, the filtered calcium load is so high that urinary calcium rises — hence stones.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — FHH has a Ca/Cr clearance ratio <0.01 (low urinary calcium). C — PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia suppresses intact PTH. D — vitamin D toxicity suppresses PTH and usually raises phosphate. E — CKD-related secondary hyperparathyroidism has low or normal calcium with high phosphate.

stemHtml: An 11-year-old boy is evaluated for muscle cramps and a seizure. He is short with a round face, obesity, and shortened fourth and fifth metacarpals. Serum calcium is 6.9 mg/dL, phosphate 7.0 mg/dL, and PTH markedly elevated. Infusion of PTH fails to increase urinary cyclic AMP. His mother has the same skeletal features and also has hypothyroidism with an elevated TSH. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.html: Failed development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches

options.label: B
options.html: Activating mutation of the calcium-sensing receptor

options.label: C
options.html: Mutation of the vitamin D receptor

options.label: D
options.html: Paternally inherited GNAS mutation without hormone resistance

options.label: E
options.html: Maternally inherited inactivating GNAS mutation causing end-organ PTH resistance

answerHtml: Answer: E. Maternally inherited inactivating GNAS mutation causing end-organ PTH resistance
explanationHtml: Hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia despite high PTH, with no cAMP response to PTH, indicate renal PTH resistance at the Gsα-coupled receptor — pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a. Albright hereditary osteodystrophy (short stature, round face, brachydactyly of metacarpals 4–5) accompanies it. Because GNAS is paternally imprinted (silenced) in renal proximal tubule and thyroid, a mutation inherited from the mother causes hormone resistance (PTH, TSH, gonadotropins).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — DiGeorge causes low PTH. B — activating CaSR mutations (autosomal dominant hypocalcemia) suppress PTH. C — vitamin D receptor defects (hereditary vitamin D–resistant rickets) cause low phosphate, rickets and alopecia, and PTH-induced cAMP rises normally. D — pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism (paternal transmission) shows the AHO phenotype with normal calcium and PTH.

stemHtml: A 32-year-old nurse is brought to the emergency department after being found confused in the hospital locker room. Fingerstick glucose is 34 mg/dL; she improves with IV dextrose. She has had three similar episodes. A blood sample drawn before dextrose shows serum insulin markedly elevated, C-peptide undetectable, proinsulin low, and a negative sulfonylurea/meglitinide screen. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

options.label: E
options.html: Anti-insulin receptor antibodies blocking insulin action

answerHtml: Answer: B. Surreptitious injection of exogenous insulin
explanationHtml: Endogenous insulin is cleaved from proinsulin in equimolar amounts with C-peptide. High insulin with suppressed C-peptide during hypoglycemia means the insulin did not come from β cells: pharmaceutical insulin lacks C-peptide, and the exogenous insulin suppresses the patient's own secretion. Access to insulin (health care worker) is a common clue in factitious disorder.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — insulinoma raises insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin. C — sulfonylureas raise insulin and C-peptide, with a positive drug screen. D — adrenal insufficiency causes hypoglycemia with appropriately low insulin. E — receptor-blocking antibodies cause hyperglycemia (type B insulin resistance); antibodies that activate the receptor cause hypoglycemia with low insulin.

stemHtml: A 57-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction was started on a new oral agent 2 months ago; since then he has had two episodes of genital candidiasis. He now presents with nausea, abdominal pain and tachypnea after 3 days of poor oral intake from gastroenteritis. Glucose is 192 mg/dL, bicarbonate 11 mEq/L, anion gap 24, and serum β-hydroxybutyrate is markedly elevated. Which of the following is the mechanism of the drug most likely responsible?

options.label: B
options.html: Closure of ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels on β cells

options.label: C
options.html: Activation of PPAR-γ in adipose tissue

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibition of the sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 in the proximal tubule

answerHtml: Answer: D. Inhibition of the sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 in the proximal tubule
explanationHtml: SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., empagliflozin, dapagliflozin — indicated in HFrEF) cause glucosuria, predisposing to genital mycotic infections. By lowering glucose through urinary loss, they reduce insulin requirement and secretion and raise glucagon; with fasting, dehydration or illness this favors lipolysis and ketogenesis, producing euglycemic DKA (glucose <250 mg/dL with ketoacidosis). Patients should hold the drug during acute illness ("sick-day rules").
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — DPP-4 inhibitors are weight neutral and not linked to genital infections or DKA. B — sulfonylureas cause hypoglycemia, not ketoacidosis. C — TZDs cause fluid retention and are contraindicated in symptomatic HF. E — α-glucosidase inhibitors cause flatulence and diarrhea.

stemHtml: A 36-year-old woman has a 2-cm thyroid nodule. Fine-needle aspiration shows spindle and polygonal cells in an amyloid-rich stroma that stains with Congo red, and serum calcitonin is elevated. She reports episodic pounding headaches, sweating and palpitations. Her father died suddenly during surgery for a "neck tumor." Which of the following should be done before thyroidectomy?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Measurement of plasma free metanephrines
explanationHtml: Medullary thyroid carcinoma (C cells, calcitonin, amyloid) with paroxysmal adrenergic symptoms and a family history suggests MEN2A (RET gain of function). A coexisting pheochromocytoma must be excluded (plasma free or urine fractionated metanephrines) and, if present, resected first after α-blockade; anesthetic induction with an unrecognized pheochromocytoma can precipitate fatal hypertensive crisis — the likely cause of her father's death.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and D — gastrinoma and prolactinoma belong to MEN1. B — C cells do not concentrate iodine, so RAI scanning and therapy are useless in MTC. E — 5-HIAA evaluates carcinoid syndrome.

stemHtml: A 63-year-old man has episodic facial flushing, watery diarrhea and wheezing. Examination reveals a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration, and hepatomegaly. CT shows a small ileal mass and multiple liver lesions; urinary 5-HIAA is elevated. He also develops a scaly, hyperpigmented rash on sun-exposed skin. Deficiency of which of the following is most likely responsible for the rash?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Niacin
explanationHtml: Carcinoid syndrome (here from an ileal NET with hepatic metastases that release serotonin directly into the systemic circulation, bypassing hepatic MAO) produces flushing, diarrhea, bronchospasm and right-sided valvular fibrosis (tricuspid regurgitation). The tumor diverts large amounts of dietary tryptophan to serotonin synthesis, leaving too little for nicotinic acid (niacin) synthesis → pellagra (photosensitive dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — thiamine deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff. C — B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neuropathy (ileal resection could cause it, but not a photosensitive rash). D — vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding. E — folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia without dermatitis.

stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman has had amenorrhea for 7 months and bilateral milky nipple discharge. Pregnancy test is negative, TSH is normal, and she takes no medications. Serum prolactin is 180 ng/mL (normal <25). MRI shows a 7-mm pituitary adenoma. She wishes to become pregnant in the future. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of the first-line drug?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Dopamine D2 receptor agonism
explanationHtml: Prolactin is under tonic inhibition by hypothalamic dopamine acting on lactotroph D2 receptors (Gi). D2 agonists — cabergoline (preferred; more effective and better tolerated) or bromocriptine — lower prolactin and shrink the adenoma, restoring GnRH pulsatility and ovulation. Hyperprolactinemia causes amenorrhea by suppressing GnRH.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — octreotide is used for acromegaly/NETs. B — pegvisomant treats acromegaly. C — D2 antagonists (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) cause hyperprolactinemia. D — mifepristone treats hypercortisolism.

stemHtml: A 35-year-old man develops polyuria (8 L/day) and intense thirst a week after a motorcycle accident with a basal skull fracture. Serum sodium is 149 mEq/L, serum osmolality 305 mOsm/kg and urine osmolality 110 mOsm/kg. After 6 hours of supervised water deprivation, urine osmolality is 130 mOsm/kg. One hour after subcutaneous desmopressin, urine osmolality rises to 480 mOsm/kg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: D
options.html: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

answerHtml: Answer: B. Arginine vasopressin deficiency (central diabetes insipidus)
explanationHtml: Trauma damaging the hypothalamus/pituitary stalk causes deficient ADH release. The kidney cannot concentrate urine during dehydration (dilute urine despite hypernatremia), but its V2 receptors and aquaporin-2 respond normally to exogenous ADH — urine osmolality rises far more than 50% after desmopressin. Treatment is desmopressin.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — primary polydipsia causes low-normal sodium and concentrates urine with water deprivation. C — nephrogenic DI shows little response to desmopressin. D — SIADH causes hyponatremia with concentrated urine. E — osmotic diuresis produces urine osmolality typically >300 mOsm/kg, and no hyperglycemia is described.

stemHtml: A 42-year-old woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis on levothyroxine has had 4 months of fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, salt craving and dizziness on standing. Blood pressure is 92/60 mm Hg supine with a postural drop. Her palmar creases and buccal mucosa are hyperpigmented. Sodium is 128 mEq/L and potassium 5.9 mEq/L. Which of the following additional findings is most likely?

options.label: D
options.html: High plasma ACTH and a subnormal cortisol response to cosyntropin

answerHtml: Answer: D. High plasma ACTH and a subnormal cortisol response to cosyntropin
explanationHtml: Hyperpigmentation, hypotension, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia in a woman with another autoimmune endocrinopathy indicate primary adrenal insufficiency (autoimmune adrenalitis — the most common cause in the US; part of autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2). Loss of cortisol feedback raises ACTH (and POMC-derived MSH, causing pigmentation); the destroyed cortex cannot respond to cosyntropin (synthetic ACTH). Loss of aldosterone causes hyperkalemia and volume depletion.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — low ACTH indicates secondary/tertiary AI, which lacks hyperpigmentation and hyperkalemia. B — renin is high because aldosterone is deficient and volume is low. C — cortisol deficiency causes eosinophilia, not eosinopenia. E — aldosterone deficiency impairs H⁺ secretion and produces a non-anion-gap (type 4 RTA–like) metabolic acidosis.

stemHtml: A 17-year-old girl is evaluated for primary amenorrhea. She is 172 cm tall with well-developed breasts (Tanner 5) but sparse pubic and axillary hair. Pelvic examination reveals a short, blind-ending vagina; ultrasound shows no uterus, and bilateral oval masses are present in the inguinal canals. Karyotype is 46,XY. Which of the following hormone profiles is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Testosterone low, LH low, estradiol low

options.label: B
options.html: Testosterone high, LH low, estradiol low

options.label: C
options.html: Testosterone high, LH high, estradiol high (for a male)

options.label: D
options.html: Testosterone normal, LH normal, dihydrotestosterone low

options.label: E
options.html: Testosterone low, FSH high, estradiol low

answerHtml: Answer: C. Testosterone high, LH high, estradiol high (for a male)
explanationHtml: Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome: a defective androgen receptor (X-linked) prevents Wolffian development and masculinization of external genitalia, while testicular AMH still regresses the Müllerian ducts (no uterus, upper vagina). The hypothalamus and pituitary are also androgen-insensitive, so testosterone fails to suppress LH → high LH and high testosterone, which is aromatized to estradiol → breast development. Sparse androgen-dependent hair is a key clue. Gonads should be removed after puberty because of germ cell tumor risk.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (e.g., Kallmann) would give poor breast development. B — in AIS the hypothalamus and pituitary cannot sense testosterone, so LH is high rather than low, and aromatization raises estradiol. D — 5α-reductase deficiency causes ambiguous genitalia with virilization at puberty and no breast development. E — gonadal dysgenesis (e.g., Swyer or Turner) has low sex steroids and no breast development without therapy, and a uterus is present.

stemHtml: A 14-year-old child raised as a girl in a consanguineous family presents with deepening voice, increased muscle mass and enlargement of the phallus. At birth, the external genitalia were ambiguous with a blind vaginal pouch. Karyotype is 46,XY. Testes are found in the labioscrotal folds, and the epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicles are present. Serum testosterone and LH are within the normal adult male range, and the testosterone-to-DHT ratio is markedly elevated. Which of the following is the most likely defect?

options.label: E
options.html: Complete loss of androgen receptor function

answerHtml: Answer: A. Deficiency of 5α-reductase type 2
explanationHtml: Testosterone itself drives Wolffian structures (present here), but the external genitalia and prostate require DHT. With type 2 enzyme deficiency (autosomal recessive), genitalia are undervirilized at birth. At puberty, the surge of testosterone (acting directly and via residual type 1 isozyme) produces virilization. The high testosterone:DHT ratio is diagnostic.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — aromatase deficiency virilizes XX fetuses (and mothers) and causes tall stature from failure of epiphyseal closure. C — 17α-hydroxylase deficiency causes low testosterone and hypertension. D — 21-hydroxylase deficiency virilizes XX infants; XY infants have normal genitalia. E — complete AIS shows no Wolffian structures and no pubertal virilization.

stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman who is trying to conceive charts her basal body temperature and uses urinary LH kits. Her cycles are regular at 28 days. On day 12, serum estradiol has risen to 300 pg/mL and has been above 200 pg/mL for 2 days. Which of the following best explains the hormonal event that will occur in the next 24–36 hours?

options.label: A
options.html: A fall in progesterone removes negative feedback on GnRH

options.label: B
options.html: Rising inhibin A stimulates gonadotroph LH release

options.label: C
options.html: A decline in FSH allows LH receptor upregulation in the pituitary

options.label: E
options.html: Sustained high estradiol switches estrogen feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary from negative to positive

answerHtml: Answer: E. Sustained high estradiol switches estrogen feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary from negative to positive
explanationHtml: The dominant follicle's estradiol output rises late in the follicular phase. When estradiol exceeds ~200 pg/mL for about 36–48 hours, feedback flips from negative to positive: GnRH pulse frequency increases and gonadotrophs become more sensitive, producing the LH surge. Ovulation follows ~24–36 hours after surge onset; afterwards, progesterone from the corpus luteum raises basal body temperature.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — progesterone is low throughout the follicular phase; it rises after ovulation. B — inhibin A is mainly a luteal product that suppresses FSH. C — the surge is not caused by falling FSH; FSH declines in the late follicular phase because of estradiol and inhibin B negative feedback, and this does not trigger LH release. D — prolactin is not the trigger of the surge.

stemHtml: A 26-year-old man is evaluated for infertility. He is 190 cm tall with long limbs, sparse facial hair and bilateral gynecomastia. Testes are small (2 mL each) and firm. Semen analysis shows azoospermia. Which of the following sets of laboratory results is most likely?
answerHtml: Answer: B. FSH ↑, LH ↑, testosterone ↓, inhibin B ↓
explanationHtml: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) causes primary testicular failure: hyalinization of seminiferous tubules destroys Sertoli cells (↓ inhibin B → ↑ FSH) and Leydig dysfunction lowers testosterone (→ ↑ LH). Elevated LH stimulates aromatase, raising the estradiol:testosterone ratio and causing gynecomastia; delayed epiphyseal closure produces eunuchoid proportions.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — low gonadotropins with low testosterone indicate hypothalamic or pituitary disease (e.g., Kallmann syndrome), not primary testicular failure. C — high testosterone does not fit hypogonadism. D — isolated LH elevation with low FSH does not fit tubular failure. E — estradiol is relatively increased, not decreased.

stemHtml: A 23-year-old woman at 12 weeks' gestation by dates presents with vaginal bleeding and severe nausea and vomiting. The uterus is the size of a 17-week gestation. Blood pressure is 152/96 mm Hg with proteinuria. TSH is 0.05 µU/mL and free T4 is elevated. Serum β-hCG is 310,000 mIU/mL. Ultrasound shows a heterogeneous intrauterine mass with multiple small cystic spaces and no fetal tissue, and bilateral multiloculated ovarian cysts. Uterine evacuation is performed; the villi are diffusely edematous with circumferential trophoblast proliferation and are negative for p57 immunostaining. Which of the following best describes the genetic origin of this lesion?

options.label: A
options.html: 69,XXY from fertilization of a normal ovum by two sperm

options.label: B
options.html: 46,XX with one maternal and one paternal haploid set

options.label: D
options.html: 46,XX with all chromosomes paternal, from duplication of one sperm's genome in an ovum lacking maternal chromosomes

options.label: E
options.html: 45,X from loss of the paternal sex chromosome

answerHtml: Answer: D. 46,XX with all chromosomes paternal, from duplication of one sperm's genome in an ovum lacking maternal chromosomes
explanationHtml: Absence of fetal parts, diffuse hydropic villi, very high hCG, uterus large for dates, early-onset preeclampsia (<20 weeks), hyperthyroidism and theca lutein cysts define a complete hydatidiform mole. Complete moles are androgenetic — usually 46,XX from an "empty" egg fertilized by one sperm that duplicates (less often dispermy, giving 46,XX or 46,XY). p57 (KIP2) is a paternally imprinted, maternally expressed gene, so its absence confirms the lack of maternal DNA. hCG, sharing the α subunit with TSH and having a structurally similar β subunit, stimulates the TSH receptor.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — triploid partial moles contain fetal parts and are p57 positive (maternal genome present). B — a biparental diploid conceptus is a normal (or nonmolar) pregnancy. C — 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome. E — 45,X conceptuses usually abort with cystic hygroma/hydrops, not trophoblastic proliferation.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with vaginal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a thickened endometrial stripe and a 9-cm solid right ovarian mass. Endometrial biopsy shows complex hyperplasia without atypia. The resected ovarian tumor consists of cuboidal cells with grooved "coffee-bean" nuclei arranged around small spaces containing eosinophilic material. Which of the following serum markers would be most useful for monitoring recurrence of this tumor?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Inhibin
explanationHtml: Call-Exner bodies (rosettes around eosinophilic secretions) and coffee-bean nuclei identify an adult granulosa cell tumor, a sex cord–stromal tumor that secretes estrogen (causing endometrial hyperplasia and postmenopausal bleeding) and inhibin. Granulosa cells normally produce inhibin, so serum inhibin (A and B) is the standard tumor marker; anti-Müllerian hormone is also used.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — hCG marks choriocarcinoma. B — AFP marks yolk sac tumor (and some immature teratomas). D — LDH marks dysgerminoma. E — chromogranin A marks neuroendocrine tumors (e.g., carcinoid in a teratoma).

stemHtml: A 27-year-old man notices a painless, firm enlargement of his left testis. Ultrasound shows a heterogeneous intratesticular mass. Serum AFP is 1,850 ng/mL (markedly elevated), β-hCG is mildly elevated, and LDH is elevated. Which of the following statements about this tumor is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.html: It contains a nonseminomatous germ cell component

options.label: B
options.html: It is most likely a pure classic seminoma

options.label: C
options.html: Transscrotal needle biopsy is the preferred diagnostic procedure

options.label: D
options.html: It most likely arises from Leydig cells

options.label: E
options.html: It is most likely a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

answerHtml: Answer: A. It contains a nonseminomatous germ cell component
explanationHtml: Pure seminomas never secrete AFP (some secrete modest hCG from syncytiotrophoblastic cells). A markedly raised AFP indicates a yolk sac tumor element, typically within a mixed nonseminomatous germ cell tumor (often with embryonal carcinoma). Any AFP elevation reclassifies a "seminoma" as nonseminomatous for treatment. Diagnosis and treatment begin with radical inguinal orchiectomy.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — AFP excludes pure seminoma. C — transscrotal procedures are avoided because they can seed scrotal skin and redirect lymphatic spread to inguinal nodes. D — Leydig cell tumors produce sex steroids, not AFP. E — testicular lymphoma occurs in men >60 and does not secrete AFP.

stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman has a vague thickening in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast that is difficult to see on mammography. Core biopsy shows small, uniform, discohesive tumor cells infiltrating the stroma in single-file lines; immunohistochemistry shows loss of membranous E-cadherin. The tumor is estrogen receptor positive. MRI shows a second lesion in the right breast. Loss of function of which of the following genes is characteristic of this tumor?
answerHtml: Answer: E. CDH1
explanationHtml: Invasive lobular carcinoma is defined by loss of E-cadherin (encoded by CDH1), a calcium-dependent adhesion molecule. Without it, cells are discohesive and infiltrate in single files, often without forming a discrete mass (mammographically subtle). It is frequently multicentric and bilateral and metastasizes to unusual sites (peritoneum, GI tract, ovaries). Germline CDH1 mutations cause hereditary diffuse gastric cancer and lobular breast cancer.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — ERBB2 (HER2) is an oncogene amplified (gain of function), not lost, mainly in ductal carcinomas. B — BRCA2 increases breast cancer risk (including male) but does not define lobular morphology. C — TP53 mutations are common in triple-negative and high-grade tumors. D — PTEN loss (Cowden) raises risk of breast cancer without a specific single-file phenotype.

stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman has taken tamoxifen for 3 years after lumpectomy for estrogen receptor–positive breast cancer. She now presents with postmenopausal vaginal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 14 mm. Which of the following best explains the effect of the drug on her endometrium?

options.label: A
options.html: Pure antagonism of endometrial estrogen receptors

options.label: B
options.html: Partial agonism at endometrial estrogen receptors

answerHtml: Answer: B. Partial agonism at endometrial estrogen receptors
explanationHtml: Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator whose effect depends on tissue co-regulator context: it antagonizes ER in breast tissue but acts as a partial agonist in endometrium (and bone), causing endometrial hyperplasia, polyps and endometrial carcinoma. Postmenopausal bleeding on tamoxifen requires endometrial sampling. Raloxifene, in contrast, is an endometrial antagonist.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — pure endometrial antagonism describes raloxifene and would not stimulate the endometrium. C — aromatase inhibition (anastrozole, letrozole) lowers estrogen and thins the endometrium. D — tamoxifen is not a progestin; progestins protect the endometrium. E — tamoxifen does not act mainly by GnRH suppression (in premenopausal women it can even raise estradiol).

stemHtml: A 64-year-old man with stable angina treated with isosorbide mononitrate takes a tablet given to him by a friend before sexual activity. Thirty minutes later he becomes lightheaded and collapses; blood pressure is 70/40 mm Hg. Which of the following best explains his hypotension?

options.label: B
options.html: Increased cAMP in vascular smooth muscle from phosphodiesterase-3 inhibition

options.label: C
options.html: Inhibition of endothelial nitric oxide synthase

options.label: D
options.html: Synergistic accumulation of cGMP in vascular smooth muscle from increased synthesis and decreased degradation

answerHtml: Answer: D. Synergistic accumulation of cGMP in vascular smooth muscle from increased synthesis and decreased degradation
explanationHtml: Nitrates release NO, which activates soluble guanylyl cyclase and increases cGMP synthesis. PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) block cGMP hydrolysis. Together they produce marked cGMP accumulation → protein kinase G activation → ↓ intracellular Ca²⁺ and myosin light-chain dephosphorylation → profound venous and arterial dilation and hypotension. Coadministration is contraindicated (nitrates should be avoided for 24 h after sildenafil and 48 h after tadalafil).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — α1-blockers also cause hypotension with PDE5 inhibitors but are not the drug class taken here. B — PDE3 inhibitors (milrinone, cilostazol) increase cAMP. C — inhibiting NO synthase would cause vasoconstriction. E — β2 agonism is not the mechanism of either drug.

stemHtml: A 30-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks' gestation has headache and visual scintillations. Blood pressure is 166/112 mm Hg on repeat measurement. Urine protein:creatinine ratio is 1.4, platelets 88,000/mm³, AST 140 U/L and ALT 165 U/L. Which of the following best describes the underlying pathogenesis of her condition?

options.label: A
options.html: Increased placental secretion of placental growth factor causing vascular leak

options.label: B
options.html: Excess maternal prostacyclin production causing vasodilation

options.label: C
options.html: Abnormal trophoblastic invasion with failure of spiral artery remodeling, placental ischemia and release of antiangiogenic factors

options.label: D
options.html: Maternal autoantibodies against platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa

options.label: E
options.html: Entry of amniotic fluid into the maternal circulation

answerHtml: Answer: C. Abnormal trophoblastic invasion with failure of spiral artery remodeling, placental ischemia and release of antiangiogenic factors
explanationHtml: Preeclampsia with severe features (severe-range BP, cerebral symptoms, thrombocytopenia, transaminitis — approaching HELLP) originates in the placenta. Cytotrophoblasts fail to invade and convert maternal spiral arteries into wide, low-resistance vessels, so the placenta becomes ischemic and releases soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1, which sequesters VEGF and PlGF) and soluble endoglin → systemic endothelial dysfunction, vasoconstriction, glomerular endotheliosis and platelet consumption. Delivery is the definitive treatment; magnesium sulfate prevents seizures.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — free PlGF is decreased (sFlt-1:PlGF ratio rises). B — prostacyclin is relatively reduced and thromboxane increased. D — anti-GPIIb/IIIa antibodies cause immune thrombocytopenia, without hypertension or transaminitis. E — amniotic fluid embolism causes sudden cardiorespiratory collapse and DIC during labor.

stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman with preeclampsia with severe features is receiving an intravenous infusion for seizure prophylaxis. Six hours later she is drowsy, her patellar reflexes are absent, and her respiratory rate is 8/min. Urine output over the last 4 hours was 40 mL. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate pharmacologic treatment?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Calcium gluconate
explanationHtml: Magnesium sulfate is renally excreted, so oliguria causes accumulation. Rising levels sequentially cause loss of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory depression and cardiac arrest, because Mg²⁺ antagonizes Ca²⁺-dependent acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction. Stop the infusion and give IV calcium gluconate, which directly counteracts magnesium's membrane effects.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — naloxone reverses opioids. C — flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines. D — protamine reverses heparin. E — physostigmine reverses anticholinergic toxicity.

stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman who has never been screened presents with postcoital bleeding. Biopsy of a friable cervical mass shows invasive squamous cell carcinoma, and in situ hybridization detects high-risk HPV-16 DNA integrated into the host genome. One viral oncoprotein directly binds a host protein, releasing E2F transcription factors and driving cells from G1 into S phase. Which host protein is bound?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Retinoblastoma protein (Rb)
explanationHtml: HPV E7 binds hypophosphorylated Rb, displacing E2F and allowing transcription of S-phase genes (unregulated G1/S transition). HPV E6 promotes ubiquitin-mediated degradation of p53 (via E6-AP), removing the G1 checkpoint and apoptosis. Integration of viral DNA (often disrupting E2, the repressor of E6/E7) increases oncoprotein expression; high-risk types (16, 18) bind these targets with high affinity.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — p53 is targeted by E6, not E7, and its loss does not directly release E2F. B — BRCA1 is involved in homologous recombination repair. C — APC regulates β-catenin (Wnt pathway). D — cyclin D1 normally promotes Rb phosphorylation; it is not the viral target.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman has had irregular menses every 2–4 months since menarche, worsening facial hirsutism and acne. BMI is 34 kg/m², and she has velvety hyperpigmentation of the posterior neck. Serum total testosterone is mildly elevated, LH:FSH ratio is 3:1, and prolactin, TSH and 17-hydroxyprogesterone are normal. Without treatment, she is at greatest risk for which of the following malignancies?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Endometrial carcinoma
explanationHtml: Polycystic ovary syndrome causes chronic anovulation: without ovulation there is no corpus luteum, so the endometrium is exposed to continuous estrogen (from ovarian follicles and peripheral aromatization of androgens in adipose tissue) without progesterone opposition. Unopposed estrogen drives endometrial hyperplasia and endometrioid adenocarcinoma. Combined OCPs or cyclic progestins protect the endometrium; insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans) also increases T2DM risk.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — dysgerminoma is linked to gonadal dysgenesis (Y-chromosome material), not PCOS. C — cervical SCC is driven by HPV. D — phyllodes tumors have no PCOS association. E — leiomyosarcoma arises de novo, mainly in postmenopausal women.

stemHtml: A healthy 29-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation has arterial blood gas testing as part of a research protocol. She has no symptoms; respiratory rate is 16/min and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Results: pH 7.44, PaCO₂ 30 mm Hg, PaO₂ 104 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 20 mEq/L. Which of the following best explains these findings?

options.label: A
options.html: Primary metabolic acidosis from starvation ketosis

options.label: D
options.html: Physiologic, renally compensated respiratory alkalosis caused by progesterone stimulation of the respiratory center

options.label: E
options.html: Respiratory acidosis from diaphragmatic elevation by the gravid uterus

answerHtml: Answer: D. Physiologic, renally compensated respiratory alkalosis caused by progesterone stimulation of the respiratory center
explanationHtml: Progesterone increases the sensitivity of the medullary respiratory center to CO₂, raising tidal volume (and minute ventilation by ~30–50%) with little change in respiratory rate. PaCO₂ falls to ~28–32 mm Hg; the kidneys compensate by excreting bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻ ~18–21), leaving pH mildly alkaline. The low maternal PaCO₂ creates a gradient that favors CO₂ transfer from fetus to mother. PaO₂ rises slightly.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — a primary metabolic acidosis would produce pH <7.35 (and she is not fasting/ill). B — PE would cause symptoms, tachypnea, hypoxemia and a widened A–a gradient; this is an asymptomatic patient with normal oxygenation. C — vomiting raises HCO₃⁻. E — despite reduced FRC, PaCO₂ falls rather than rises in pregnancy.

stemHtml: A 64-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes develops sudden vertigo, nausea and difficulty swallowing. Examination shows hoarseness, a diminished gag reflex on the left, a left-sided ptosis and miosis, loss of pain and temperature sensation over the left face and the right side of the body, and left-sided limb ataxia. Strength is 5/5 in all limbs. Occlusion of which of the following arteries most likely explains these findings?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Left posterior inferior cerebellar artery
explanationHtml: This is lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome. Dysphagia, hoarseness and reduced gag point to the nucleus ambiguus (CN IX, X), which lies in the lateral medulla. Ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss = spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract; contralateral body pain/temperature loss = already-crossed spinothalamic tract; Horner = descending hypothalamospinal sympathetic fibers; vertigo = vestibular nuclei; ataxia = inferior cerebellar peduncle. Lateral structures with intact strength (medial pyramid spared) → PICA (or intracranial vertebral artery).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — medial medullary syndrome: contralateral hemiparesis, contralateral loss of proprioception, ipsilateral tongue deviation. B — AICA (lateral pons) produces ipsilateral LMN facial paralysis and hearing loss, not nucleus ambiguus signs. D — paramedian basilar occlusion gives ventral pontine signs (hemiparesis/locked-in). E — PCA causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia.

stemHtml: A 25-year-old man is stabbed in the back. Neurologic examination reveals weakness and hyperreflexia of the left leg with an upgoing left toe, loss of vibration and joint-position sense in the left leg, and loss of pain and temperature sensation in the right leg beginning about two dermatomes below the umbilicus. Which of the following best describes the lesion?

options.label: A
options.html: Right hemisection of the cord at T10

options.label: B
options.html: Left hemisection of the cord at about T10

options.label: C
options.html: Left dorsal column transection at L1

answerHtml: Answer: B. Left hemisection of the cord at about T10
explanationHtml: Brown-Séquard syndrome: the corticospinal tract and dorsal columns travel ipsilaterally in the cord, so a left lesion causes left UMN weakness and left loss of vibration/proprioception. Spinothalamic fibers cross within 1–2 segments of entry, so pain/temperature loss is on the right, starting a level or two below the lesion. The umbilicus is T10.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — a right lesion would give right-sided weakness. C — isolated dorsal column damage would not cause weakness or contralateral pain loss. D — anterior cord syndrome is bilateral and spares dorsal columns. E — central cord lesions are bilateral and spare dorsal columns.

stemHtml: A 70-year-old man undergoes open repair of a thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm. On postoperative day 1 he cannot move his legs. Patellar and ankle reflexes are absent, and he has lost pain and temperature sensation below the umbilicus bilaterally. He has urinary retention. Which of the following findings would most likely also be present on careful examination?

options.label: B
options.html: Loss of light touch in a saddle distribution only

options.label: C
options.html: Bilateral loss of vibration sense in the toes

options.label: E
options.html: Preserved vibration and joint-position sense in both feet

answerHtml: Answer: E. Preserved vibration and joint-position sense in both feet
explanationHtml: Interruption of the artery of Adamkiewicz during aortic surgery infarcts the territory of the anterior spinal artery — the anterior two-thirds of the cord (corticospinal tracts, spinothalamic tracts, anterior horns). The dorsal columns are supplied by the paired posterior spinal arteries and are spared, so vibration and proprioception remain intact. Acute spinal shock explains the initially absent reflexes.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — the lesion is in the lower thoracic cord, below the sympathetic outflow to the head (T1–T2). B — saddle-only loss suggests a conus/cauda lesion and would not explain bilateral sensory level at T10. C — vibration loss would require dorsal column (posterior spinal artery) involvement. D — the lesion is bilateral and spares proprioception.

stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman reports burning her hands on a stove several times without feeling it. Examination shows loss of pain and temperature sensation over both shoulders and arms in a cape-like distribution with preserved light touch, vibration, and proprioception. She has wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles. MRI of the brain shows the cerebellar tonsils 7 mm below the foramen magnum. Damage to which of the following structures accounts for her sensory loss?

options.label: D
options.html: Lateral spinothalamic tracts in the lateral funiculi

options.label: E
options.html: Posterior limb of the internal capsule

answerHtml: Answer: A. Anterior white commissure
explanationHtml: A Chiari I malformation is associated with a cervical syrinx. The expanding central cavity first interrupts second-order pain/temperature fibers as they cross in the anterior white commissure, producing bilateral, segmental (cape) loss of pain and temperature with preserved dorsal column modalities ("dissociated sensory loss"). Extension into the ventral horns causes LMN hand wasting.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — DRG damage would affect all modalities. C — cuneatus carries vibration/proprioception, which are preserved. D — damage to the already-formed lateral spinothalamic tracts produces loss below the level, not a segmental cape. E — internal capsule lesions are unilateral and affect all modalities with motor deficits.

stemHtml: A 48-year-old woman presents with a severe headache and double vision that began 2 days ago. Her left eye is positioned down and out, there is left ptosis, and the left pupil is 7 mm and unreactive to light. The right eye is normal. Her hemoglobin A1c is 5.4%. Which of the following best explains why the pupil is involved in this patient?

options.label: A
options.html: The Edinger–Westphal nucleus lies outside the midbrain and is compressed first

options.label: B
options.html: Diabetic microvascular infarction preferentially affects the core of the nerve

options.label: C
options.html: Sympathetic fibers travel within CN III and are compressed

options.label: D
options.html: Parasympathetic fibers lie on the periphery of CN III and are vulnerable to external compression

options.label: E
options.html: The ciliary ganglion is supplied by the posterior communicating artery

answerHtml: Answer: D. Parasympathetic fibers lie on the periphery of CN III and are vulnerable to external compression
explanationHtml: A painful, pupil-involving CN III palsy suggests compression, classically from a posterior communicating artery aneurysm (an emergency — rule out with CTA/MRA). Preganglionic parasympathetic pupillomotor fibers run superficially on the nerve and are affected early by compression; ischemic (diabetic) palsies infarct the central fibers and typically spare the pupil.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — the Edinger–Westphal nucleus is within the midbrain. B — this is true but explains pupil sparing, and her A1c is normal. C — sympathetic fibers to the pupil travel on the ICA/V1, not CN III; sympathetic loss causes miosis, not mydriasis. E — the ciliary ganglion's blood supply is not the explanation.

stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman has sudden weakness of the right arm and leg. On examination the tongue deviates to the left on protrusion, with left-sided tongue atrophy and fasciculations developing over the following weeks. She has decreased vibration and proprioception on the right side of the body. Pain and temperature are intact, and facial strength is symmetric. Which of the following structures is most likely infarcted?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Left medial medulla
explanationHtml: Medial medullary syndrome (anterior spinal artery or vertebral branches): left pyramid (above the decussation) → right hemiparesis; left medial lemniscus (already crossed) → right loss of vibration/proprioception; left hypoglossal nucleus/fibers → LMN palsy with the tongue deviating toward the lesion (left). The crossed pattern (ipsilateral cranial nerve, contralateral body) localizes the brainstem.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — a right lesion would cause left hemiparesis and rightward tongue deviation. C — lateral medulla spares the pyramid and causes pain/temperature loss. D — ventral pons would involve CN VI/VII rather than XII. E — a capsular lesion causes UMN tongue weakness without atrophy/fasciculations and would deviate toward the weak (right) side.

stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman has 3 days of horizontal double vision. When asked to look to the left, her right eye fails to move medially and her left eye shows nystagmus as it abducts. Convergence is normal. Eight months ago she had an episode of painful vision loss in the left eye that resolved. Which of the following is the most likely location of her current lesion?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Right medial longitudinal fasciculus
explanationHtml: On left gaze, the left PPRF drives the left abducens nucleus, which sends fibers up the contralateral (right) MLF to the right oculomotor nucleus to adduct the right eye. A right MLF lesion causes right internuclear ophthalmoplegia: impaired right adduction on left gaze with nystagmus of the abducting left eye. Convergence is preserved because it does not use the MLF — proving CN III and the medial rectus are intact. Prior optic neuritis plus INO in a young woman suggests multiple sclerosis.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — a right abducens nucleus lesion causes a right horizontal gaze palsy (neither eye goes right). B — left CN VI palsy impairs left abduction. C — CN III palsy would also impair convergence and cause ptosis/vertical deficits. D — a left PPRF lesion causes inability of both eyes to look left.

stemHtml: A 68-year-old man with resting tremor, bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity is started on a combination tablet containing levodopa and a second agent. The second agent allows a lower levodopa dose and reduces nausea and orthostatic hypotension. Which of the following is the mechanism of the second agent?

options.label: B
options.html: Selective inhibition of monoamine oxidase B in the striatum

options.label: C
options.html: Inhibition of peripheral aromatic L-amino acid (DOPA) decarboxylase

options.label: D
options.html: Direct agonism at D2 receptors in the striatum

answerHtml: Answer: C. Inhibition of peripheral aromatic L-amino acid (DOPA) decarboxylase
explanationHtml: Carbidopa does not cross the blood–brain barrier. It blocks conversion of levodopa to dopamine in the periphery, so more levodopa reaches the brain and less peripheral dopamine is available to stimulate the area postrema (nausea, outside the BBB) and vascular receptors (hypotension, arrhythmias).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — entacapone is a peripheral COMT inhibitor; tolcapone acts centrally but is not co-formulated as the standard partner. B — selegiline/rasagiline are MAO-B inhibitors given separately. D — pramipexole/ropinirole are D2 agonists, not levodopa partners. E — benztropine/trihexyphenidyl are antimuscarinics.

stemHtml: A 42-year-old man has 2 years of irritability, depression and progressively worsening involuntary, dance-like movements of his face and limbs. His father had similar symptoms beginning at age 50 and died by suicide. MRI shows enlarged lateral ventricles with flattening of their lateral walls. A drug is prescribed to reduce his involuntary movements. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this drug?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Inhibition of vesicular monoamine transporter 2
explanationHtml: Huntington disease (autosomal dominant CAG repeat expansion in HTT with anticipation, especially paternal transmission) causes loss of GABAergic striatal neurons, particularly in the caudate (flattened lateral ventricular walls = caudate atrophy). Loss of the indirect pathway leads to relative dopaminergic excess and chorea. Tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine and valbenazine inhibit VMAT2, depleting presynaptic dopamine.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — AChE inhibitors treat Alzheimer disease. C — baclofen treats spasticity. D — carbidopa raises central dopamine availability from levodopa and would worsen chorea. E — amantadine/memantine (NMDA antagonists) are not first-line for HD chorea.

stemHtml: A 19-year-old man is hit on the side of the head by a baseball. He loses consciousness briefly, then is alert and talking for 2 hours before becoming drowsy. His right pupil becomes dilated and he develops left-sided weakness. Noncontrast CT shows a biconvex hyperdense collection over the right temporal lobe that does not cross suture lines. Which of the following vessels is most likely the source of bleeding?

options.label: C
options.html: A ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm

answerHtml: Answer: D. Middle meningeal artery
explanationHtml: A blow to the pterion fractures the thin temporal bone and tears the middle meningeal artery (branch of the maxillary artery entering through the foramen spinosum). Arterial blood strips the dura from the skull, forming a lens-shaped epidural hematoma limited by sutures where the dura is tightly attached. The lucid interval is followed by rapid deterioration and uncal herniation (ipsilateral CN III, contralateral hemiparesis). Emergency surgical evacuation.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — bridging veins cause crescentic subdural hematomas that cross sutures. B — MCA rupture would cause intraparenchymal or subarachnoid blood. C — AComm aneurysm causes SAH. E — lenticulostriate rupture causes hypertensive basal ganglia hemorrhage.

stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman is admitted with a sudden "thunderclap" headache. CT shows blood in the basal cisterns, and an anterior communicating artery aneurysm is coiled. On hospital day 6 she becomes confused and develops weakness of the right leg. Repeat CT shows no new blood. Which of the following agents, started on admission, is intended to reduce the risk of this complication?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Nimodipine
explanationHtml: Delayed cerebral ischemia from vasospasm typically occurs 3–14 days after aneurysmal SAH, likely triggered by blood breakdown products. New leg weakness fits ACA territory near the AComm. Oral nimodipine, a dihydropyridine L-type calcium channel blocker, given for 21 days improves neurologic outcome (thought to be partly neuroprotective rather than purely reversing angiographic spasm).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — antifibrinolytics reduce rebleeding but increase ischemic complications and do not improve outcome. C — steroids have no role in vasospasm. D — mannitol lowers ICP but does not prevent vasospasm. E — BP control before aneurysm securing reduces rebleeding; it does not prevent vasospasm.

stemHtml: A 66-year-old right-handed man is brought in by his wife because his speech "makes no sense." He speaks fluently with normal rhythm but uses invented words and incorrect words, and he cannot follow simple commands or repeat phrases. He appears unconcerned. Strength is normal. Which of the following is the most likely site of infarction?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Left posterior superior temporal gyrus
explanationHtml: Fluent aphasia with poor comprehension and poor repetition and lack of insight is Wernicke (receptive) aphasia, from a lesion of the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere (inferior division of the left MCA). The absence of weakness fits because the motor cortex is supplied by the superior division.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — Broca area: nonfluent speech with intact comprehension. B — conduction aphasia: comprehension preserved, repetition impaired. C — angular gyrus: Gerstmann syndrome or alexia with agraphia. D — in a right-handed man the right hemisphere is almost always nondominant.

stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation who stopped her anticoagulant notices she keeps bumping into objects on her left side. Visual field testing shows a left homonymous hemianopia; central vision is preserved in both left hemifields. Strength, sensation and language are normal. Which of the following best explains the preserved central vision?

options.label: A
options.html: The occipital pole representing the macula receives collateral supply from the middle cerebral artery

options.label: B
options.html: Macular fibers travel in Meyer loop, which is supplied by the anterior choroidal artery

options.label: C
options.html: Macular fibers decussate in the optic chiasm and are spared by occipital lesions

options.label: D
options.html: The lateral geniculate nucleus represents the macula bilaterally

options.label: E
options.html: Embolic strokes spare cortical layers receiving macular input

answerHtml: Answer: A. The occipital pole representing the macula receives collateral supply from the middle cerebral artery
explanationHtml: A right PCA (cardioembolic) infarct of the occipital lobe gives a contralateral homonymous hemianopia. The macular representation at the occipital pole has dual supply from the PCA and the MCA, so it is often spared — "macular sparing" is a clue to a cortical PCA infarct rather than an optic tract lesion.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — Meyer loop carries the contralateral superior quadrant fibers through the temporal lobe; lesions cause "pie in the sky." C — chiasmal crossing determines which hemifield is affected, not macular sparing. D — the LGN represents only the contralateral hemifield. E — embolic infarcts are not selective for cortical layers.

stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman has episodes of blurred vision in the right eye that worsen after a hot shower, and an electric shock sensation down her spine when she flexes her neck. MRI shows multiple periventricular T2 hyperintensities oriented perpendicular to the lateral ventricles. Destruction of which cell type is primarily responsible for her symptoms?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Oligodendrocytes
explanationHtml: Multiple sclerosis is an immune-mediated destruction of CNS myelin and the oligodendrocytes that produce it (Dawson fingers on MRI). Heat worsening symptoms (Uhthoff phenomenon) reflects impaired conduction in demyelinated axons as temperature rises; Lhermitte sign reflects cervical dorsal column demyelination. The optic nerve is CNS tissue myelinated by oligodendrocytes, explaining optic neuritis.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — astrocytes form gliotic scars in plaques but are not the primary target. B — Schwann cells myelinate the PNS (targeted in Guillain–Barré). D — ependymal cells line the ventricles. E — microglia participate in demyelination as effectors but are not the destroyed cell type.

stemHtml: A 34-year-old man develops tingling in his feet followed over 5 days by symmetric weakness of the legs that ascends to involve his arms. Three weeks ago he had bloody diarrhea after eating undercooked chicken. Deep tendon reflexes are absent. Heart rate fluctuates between 50 and 130/min. Which of the following cerebrospinal fluid findings is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Elevated neutrophils, elevated protein, low glucose

options.label: B
options.html: Elevated lymphocytes, normal protein, normal glucose

options.label: C
options.html: Oligoclonal IgG bands with mild lymphocytic pleocytosis

options.label: D
options.html: Normal cell count with markedly elevated protein

options.label: E
options.html: Xanthochromia with elevated red blood cells

answerHtml: Answer: D. Normal cell count with markedly elevated protein
explanationHtml: Guillain–Barré syndrome after Campylobacter jejuni infection results from molecular mimicry: antibodies against bacterial lipooligosaccharide cross-react with peripheral nerve gangliosides, causing demyelination (or axonal injury) of nerve roots and peripheral nerves. Inflamed roots leak protein into CSF without many cells — albuminocytologic dissociation. Autonomic instability is common; treat with IVIG or plasmapheresis and monitor vital capacity.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — bacterial meningitis. B — viral meningitis. C — multiple sclerosis. E — subarachnoid hemorrhage.

stemHtml: A 76-year-old man has had 8 months of slowly progressive forgetfulness and urinary urgency with incontinence. His gait is broad-based and slow, and his feet appear "stuck to the floor." CT shows enlarged lateral and third ventricles out of proportion to sulcal atrophy. Lumbar opening pressure is 14 cm H₂O. Which of the following is most likely to predict benefit from definitive therapy?

options.label: B
options.html: Low CSF β-amyloid-42 with high phosphorylated tau

options.label: C
options.html: Presence of the APOE ε4 allele

options.label: E
options.html: Improvement in gait after removal of 30–50 mL of CSF

answerHtml: Answer: E. Improvement in gait after removal of 30–50 mL of CSF
explanationHtml: Normal pressure hydrocephalus (gait apraxia, incontinence, dementia; ventriculomegaly; normal opening pressure) is a reversible dementia caused by impaired CSF absorption; ventricular expansion stretches periventricular corona radiata fibers to the legs and bladder. Improvement after a high-volume lumbar tap predicts response to a ventriculoperitoneal shunt. Gait typically responds best.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and D — markers of Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (rapid course, myoclonus). B — CSF biomarker profile of Alzheimer disease; it does not predict shunt response. C — APOE ε4 increases Alzheimer risk.

stemHtml: A 7-year-old girl's teacher reports that she "zones out" many times a day for several seconds, with eyelid fluttering, and then resumes her activity with no confusion. An EEG during hyperventilation shows generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges. Physical examination is normal. The drug of choice acts primarily by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Prolonging inactivation of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels

options.label: B
options.html: Blocking T-type Ca²⁺ channels in thalamic neurons

options.label: C
options.html: Increasing the frequency of GABA<sub>A</sub> chloride channel opening

options.label: E
options.html: Binding the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels

answerHtml: Answer: B. Blocking T-type Ca²⁺ channels in thalamic neurons
explanationHtml: Childhood absence epilepsy results from oscillatory thalamocortical firing driven by low-threshold T-type calcium currents. Ethosuximide blocks these channels and is first-line for isolated absence seizures (valproate if generalized tonic-clonic seizures coexist).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — phenytoin/carbamazepine (sodium channel blockers) can worsen absence seizures. C — benzodiazepines are used for status epilepticus. D — levetiracetam. E — gabapentin/pregabalin, ineffective for absence.

stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, well controlled on a single agent that also inhibits GABA transaminase and has caused weight gain and tremor, asks about planning a pregnancy. Which of the following fetal abnormalities is most strongly associated with her medication?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Lumbosacral myelomeningocele
explanationHtml: Valproate (inhibits GABA transaminase, prolongs Na⁺ channel inactivation, blocks T-type Ca²⁺ channels) is the most teratogenic common antiepileptic, with roughly 1–2% risk of neural tube defects (folate antagonism and histone deacetylase inhibition are proposed), plus other malformations and reduced IQ. Women of childbearing potential should preferably use lamotrigine or levetiracetam and take folic acid.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — lithium. C — thalidomide. D — chloramphenicol in neonates. E — tetracyclines.

stemHtml: A 35-year-old woman of Han Chinese ancestry is diagnosed with trigeminal neuralgia. Before her physician prescribes the first-line agent, a genetic test is ordered. Which of the following adverse effects is this test intended to help prevent?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis
explanationHtml: Carbamazepine is first-line for trigeminal neuralgia. The HLA-B*15:02 allele, common in Han Chinese, Thai, Malaysian and some South Asian populations, strongly predicts carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN (a T-cell–mediated reaction where the drug binds directly to the HLA molecule). FDA labeling recommends testing patients of at-risk ancestry before starting therapy.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B — carbamazepine can cause agranulocytosis/aplastic anemia and SIADH, but these are monitored with CBC and sodium, not HLA typing. D — hepatotoxicity is not predicted by HLA-B*15:02. E — gingival hyperplasia is a phenytoin effect.

stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy has 2 months of morning headaches, vomiting and a wide-based gait. MRI shows a well-circumscribed cystic mass with an enhancing mural nodule in the right cerebellar hemisphere. Biopsy shows bipolar cells with hair-like processes and eosinophilic corkscrew-shaped fibers. Which of the following is most likely true of this tumor?

options.label: A
options.html: It is derived from small round blue cells forming Homer Wright rosettes

options.label: B
options.html: It frequently spreads through CSF to cause drop metastases

options.label: C
options.html: It stains negative for glial fibrillary acidic protein

options.label: D
options.html: It carries a favorable prognosis after complete resection

options.label: E
options.html: It is associated with bilateral vestibular schwannomas

answerHtml: Answer: D. It carries a favorable prognosis after complete resection
explanationHtml: Pilocytic astrocytoma — the most common pediatric brain tumor — is a WHO grade 1 glioma of the cerebellum with a cyst and mural nodule, piloid (hair-like) cells, and Rosenthal fibers (corkscrew eosinophilic aggregates of GFAP). It is often associated with BRAF alterations; gross total resection is usually curative.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B — describe medulloblastoma, a midline vermis tumor with CSF dissemination. C — pilocytic astrocytoma is GFAP positive. E — bilateral vestibular schwannomas define NF2; pilocytic astrocytomas (optic pathway) are associated with NF1.

stemHtml: A 61-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history reports difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a chair, and a dry mouth. On examination, hip flexor strength is reduced but improves transiently after 10 seconds of sustained effort. Patellar reflexes are absent at rest but appear after brief exercise. Ptosis is minimal. Which of the following is the most likely target of the pathogenic antibodies?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels
explanationHtml: Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome is often a paraneoplastic disorder of small cell lung cancer. Antibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type calcium channels reduce Ca²⁺ entry and ACh release. Repeated stimulation builds up presynaptic Ca²⁺, so strength and reflexes transiently improve (incremental response on high-frequency repetitive stimulation). Cholinergic autonomic dysfunction (dry mouth) is common. Amifampridine (K⁺ channel blocker) prolongs depolarization to increase Ca²⁺ entry.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B — myasthenia gravis: ocular/bulbar fatigable weakness that worsens with use, normal reflexes. C — antibodies to voltage-gated K⁺ channel complexes cause neuromyotonia and limbic encephalitis, not this picture. D — anti-GQ1b defines Miller Fisher variant of GBS (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia).

stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy is evaluated for infantile spasms that began at 6 months and developmental delay. Examination shows several hypopigmented, leaf-shaped macules on the trunk best seen under ultraviolet light. A fetal echocardiogram during the pregnancy had shown intracardiac masses that have since regressed. The causative mutation most directly leads to overactivity of which of the following?

options.label: B
options.html: Ras–MAPK signaling due to loss of a GTPase-activating protein

options.label: E
options.html: Gαq signaling from an activating somatic mutation

answerHtml: Answer: A. mTOR complex 1 signaling
explanationHtml: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC1/hamartin or TSC2/tuberin; autosomal dominant with frequent de novo mutations) features ash-leaf macules, cortical tubers with seizures/infantile spasms, intellectual disability, cardiac rhabdomyomas (which regress), facial angiofibromas, renal angiomyolipomas and subependymal giant cell astrocytomas. Hamartin–tuberin normally inhibits Rheb, so loss causes unchecked mTORC1 activity; mTOR inhibitors (everolimus) shrink SEGAs and angiomyolipomas.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — NF1 (neurofibromin). C — von Hippel–Lindau. D — Gorlin syndrome (PTCH1), basal cell carcinoma, medulloblastoma. E — Sturge–Weber (GNAQ).

stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman has recurrent unilateral throbbing headaches with nausea and photophobia lasting 12–24 hours. She also has chest pain on exertion, and a stress test is positive for inducible ischemia. Which of the following abortive agents is most appropriate to avoid in her, and why?

options.label: A
options.html: Ibuprofen, because it inhibits CGRP release

options.label: B
options.html: Sumatriptan, because 5-HT1B agonism can constrict coronary arteries

options.label: C
options.html: Ubrogepant, because CGRP receptor blockade raises heart rate

options.label: D
options.html: Metoclopramide, because D2 antagonism causes coronary vasospasm

options.label: E
options.html: Acetaminophen, because it reduces prostacyclin synthesis in coronary endothelium

answerHtml: Answer: B. Sumatriptan, because 5-HT1B agonism can constrict coronary arteries
explanationHtml: Triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists: 5-HT1D on trigeminal terminals inhibits release of CGRP and substance P, and 5-HT1B constricts dilated meningeal vessels. Because 5-HT1B receptors are also present on coronary arteries, triptans can cause coronary vasospasm and are contraindicated in coronary artery disease, Prinzmetal angina, uncontrolled hypertension and prior stroke. Gepants (CGRP receptor antagonists) and lasmiditan (5-HT1F agonist) lack vasoconstriction and are alternatives.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — NSAIDs work by COX inhibition (caution with CAD, but the mechanism stated is wrong and they are not the classic contraindication). C — gepants are not vasoconstrictive and are preferred in vascular disease. D — metoclopramide is an antiemetic adjunct without coronary vasospasm. E — acetaminophen does not have this effect.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old engineer is told that his biopsy shows pancreatic adenocarcinoma. He calmly asks for the exact staging criteria, the median survival with and without chemotherapy, and the names of recent clinical trials, and spends the next week reading oncology journal articles. When asked how he feels about the diagnosis, he again begins discussing hazard ratios. Which defense mechanism is he most likely using?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Intellectualization
explanationHtml: Intellectualization is retreat into abstract reasoning and facts to avoid experiencing distressing emotions. He fully accepts the diagnosis (not denial) but deflects every invitation to discuss feelings toward data.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — denial would involve refusing to accept the diagnosis. B — suppression is a conscious decision to postpone thinking about something. D — sublimation channels an unacceptable impulse into a socially valued activity. E — rationalization offers a self-serving logical explanation for an event or behavior ("the job wasn't right for me anyway").

stemHtml: A mother brings her son for a well-child visit. He walks independently, says "mama," "dada," and "ball" with meaning, stacks two blocks, and imitates adults clapping. He does not yet run or combine words into phrases. Assuming normal development, which of the following is his most likely age?
answerHtml: Answer: D. 12 months
explanationHtml: At about 12 months children walk (often with cruising before), have 1–3 meaningful words, build a 2-block tower, use a mature pincer grasp, and imitate. Running and a 4-block tower appear around 18 months; 2-word phrases by 2 years.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — at 6 months, infants sit with support and babble. B — at 9 months, infants crawl, pull to stand and say "mama/dada" nonspecifically. C — at 2 years, children run, climb stairs and use 2-word phrases. E — at 3 years, children ride tricycles and speak 3-word sentences.

stemHtml: A 19-year-old college student falls asleep during lectures despite sleeping 8 hours each night. When she laughs at a joke, her knees buckle and she sometimes falls, remaining fully conscious. She reports vivid dream-like images as she falls asleep. Polysomnography shows REM sleep within 10 minutes of sleep onset. A deficiency of which of the following is most likely responsible?

options.label: D
options.html: GABA from the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus

answerHtml: Answer: E. Orexin (hypocretin) from the lateral hypothalamus
explanationHtml: Narcolepsy type 1 (with cataplexy) results from autoimmune loss of orexin-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus (strong HLA-DQB1*06:02 association). Orexin stabilizes wakefulness and suppresses REM; without it REM intrudes into wakefulness — cataplexy (REM atonia triggered by emotion), hypnagogic hallucinations, sleep paralysis, and sleep-onset REM periods.
