CSF hypocretin is low.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — melatonin deficiency affects circadian phase, not cataplexy. B, C — these monoamines change during REM but are not the deficient substance. D — VLPO GABA promotes sleep; loss causes insomnia.

stemHtml: A 5-year-old boy's parents report that about 2 hours after he falls asleep, he sits up screaming, is sweaty and tachycardic, and cannot be consoled. After a few minutes he goes back to sleep and has no memory of the episode in the morning. During which stage of sleep do these episodes most likely occur?
answerHtml: Answer: A. N3
explanationHtml: Sleep terrors are a non-REM parasomnia arising from slow-wave (N3, delta) sleep, which dominates the first third of the night. The child is difficult to arouse and is amnestic for the event, unlike nightmares (REM, later in the night, vivid recall). Sleepwalking and enuresis also arise from N3. Most are outgrown.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — N1 is light transitional sleep (theta waves). C — N2 (spindles, K complexes) is associated with bruxism. D — REM is associated with nightmares (recalled) and REM sleep behavior disorder. E — the child is asleep.

stemHtml: A 22-year-old man is brought in by his roommate because for the past 3 months he has believed that the government implanted a chip in his teeth, hears voices commenting on his actions, and has stopped attending classes. He has no history of mood episodes, substance use or medical illness. Urine toxicology is negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Schizophreniform disorder
explanationHtml: He meets the symptomatic criteria for schizophrenia (delusions + hallucinations, functional decline) but the total duration is between 1 and 6 months, which defines schizophreniform disorder. If symptoms persist beyond 6 months the diagnosis changes to schizophrenia.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — brief psychotic disorder lasts less than 1 month. C — schizophrenia requires ≥ 6 months of disturbance. D — delusional disorder involves delusions without prominent hallucinations and with preserved function. E — schizoaffective disorder requires a concurrent major mood episode.

stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder stable on lithium for 6 years is started on hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension. Three weeks later she has a coarse tremor, diarrhea, slurred speech and unsteady gait. Which of the following best explains her condition?

options.label: A
options.html: Thiazide inhibition of hepatic lithium metabolism by CYP3A4

options.label: B
options.html: Thiazide displacement of lithium from plasma albumin

options.label: C
options.html: Volume contraction increasing proximal tubular reabsorption of sodium and lithium

options.label: D
options.html: Thiazide-induced hypokalemia increasing lithium entry into neurons through ENaC

options.label: E
options.html: Increased distal tubular secretion of lithium by the Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter

answerHtml: Answer: C. Volume contraction increasing proximal tubular reabsorption of sodium and lithium
explanationHtml: Lithium is not metabolized or protein bound; it is filtered and handled like sodium. Thiazides cause mild volume depletion, which triggers compensatory proximal tubular sodium reabsorption — and lithium is reabsorbed along with it, raising serum levels into the toxic range (tremor, GI upset, ataxia, dysarthria, confusion). ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs and dehydration act similarly.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — lithium is not hepatically metabolized. B — lithium is not protein bound. D — hypokalemia is not the mechanism; ENaC relates to lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus in principal cells. E — the NCC is the thiazide target; thiazides reduce, not increase, lithium excretion.

stemHtml: A 37-year-old man taking sertraline for depression is prescribed tramadol for back pain. The next evening he is agitated and diaphoretic. Temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F), pulse 124/min and blood pressure 162/94 mm Hg. Pupils are dilated. He has hyperactive bowel sounds, hyperreflexia, and sustained clonus at both ankles. Besides stopping the offending drugs and giving benzodiazepines, which of the following is the most appropriate specific pharmacotherapy?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Cyproheptadine
explanationHtml: Serotonin syndrome from an SSRI plus tramadol (which inhibits serotonin reuptake) presents within 24 hours with the triad of altered mental status, autonomic hyperactivity and neuromuscular hyperexcitability (hyperreflexia, clonus worse in the legs). Cyproheptadine, a first-generation antihistamine with 5-HT2A antagonism, is the specific antidote.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — dantrolene (RyR1 blocker) treats malignant hyperthermia and sometimes NMS; it does not address serotonin excess. B — bromocriptine treats NMS (dopamine blockade, lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia) and could worsen serotonin toxicity. C — physostigmine reverses anticholinergic toxicity, which features dry skin and absent bowel sounds. E — naloxone reverses opioid respiratory depression; the picture is not opioid intoxication.

stemHtml: A 30-year-old man with schizophrenia has persistent hallucinations despite adequate trials of risperidone and olanzapine and has made two suicide attempts. His psychiatrist begins the antipsychotic reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Which of the following laboratory tests should be monitored regularly with this drug?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Absolute neutrophil count
explanationHtml: Clozapine is the only antipsychotic proven effective in treatment-resistant schizophrenia and reduces suicidal behavior. It can cause severe neutropenia/agranulocytosis (immune-mediated or toxic to myeloid precursors), so ANC is checked weekly for the first 6 months, then every 2 weeks, then monthly. Other toxicities: seizures, myocarditis (early), constipation/ileus, sialorrhea, metabolic syndrome.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — prolactin elevation is a risperidone/typical antipsychotic issue; clozapine spares prolactin. B — TSH monitoring is for lithium. C — creatinine for lithium. D — CK is checked if NMS is suspected, not routinely.

stemHtml: A 20-year-old man is given intramuscular haloperidol in the emergency department for acute agitation and psychosis. Four hours later his neck twists to the right, his eyes deviate upward and he has difficulty opening his jaw. Vital signs are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Benztropine
explanationHtml: Acute dystonia (torticollis, oculogyric crisis, trismus) occurs within hours to days of starting a high-potency D2 antagonist, especially in young men. D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway produces a relative excess of striatal cholinergic activity. An anticholinergic (benztropine) or diphenhydramine IM/IV rapidly reverses it.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia/NMS; vital signs are normal. C — propranolol treats akathisia. D — VMAT2 inhibitors treat tardive dyskinesia. E — benzodiazepines are adjuncts (and for akathisia), not first-line for dystonia.

stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman treated with risperidone for 4 months reports milky nipple discharge and absent menses. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Blockade of dopamine receptors in which of the following pathways explains her symptoms?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Tuberoinfundibular
explanationHtml: Dopamine released from arcuate nucleus neurons into the hypophyseal portal system tonically inhibits lactotrophs via D2 receptors. Blocking this pathway raises prolactin → galactorrhea, and prolactin suppresses GnRH → amenorrhea, infertility and reduced bone density. Risperidone (and its metabolite paliperidone) raises prolactin the most among atypicals; the pituitary lies outside the BBB, so drugs with relatively high peripheral exposure act strongly there.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — mesolimbic blockade is the antipsychotic effect. C — mesocortical blockade may worsen negative symptoms. D — nigrostriatal blockade causes EPS. E — area postrema blockade is antiemetic.

stemHtml: A 33-year-old man with opioid use disorder who last injected heroin 4 hours ago is given a sublingual dose of buprenorphine in clinic. Within 30 minutes he develops yawning, rhinorrhea, piloerection, abdominal cramps, diarrhea and dilated pupils. Which property of buprenorphine best explains this reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: Full μ-receptor agonism with rapid tolerance

options.label: C
options.html: High μ-receptor affinity with low intrinsic activity, displacing the full agonist

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibition of norepinephrine reuptake in the locus ceruleus

answerHtml: Answer: C. High μ-receptor affinity with low intrinsic activity, displacing the full agonist
explanationHtml: Buprenorphine is a high-affinity partial μ agonist. When given while a full agonist (heroin) still occupies receptors, it displaces the full agonist but produces less receptor activation, so net μ signaling falls abruptly — precipitated withdrawal. Therefore induction is started only once moderate withdrawal is present (or by low-dose "micro-induction" strategies). Its ceiling effect on respiratory depression makes it safer than methadone.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — buprenorphine is not a full agonist. B — it is actually a κ antagonist; κ effects would not produce this autonomic withdrawal syndrome. D — this is tramadol/tapentadol pharmacology. E — methadone has some NMDA antagonism; not relevant here.

stemHtml: A 52-year-old man is admitted for a hip fracture. On hospital day 3 he becomes acutely confused, picks at the bedsheets, reports seeing insects on the walls, and is tremulous and diaphoretic. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), pulse 128/min and blood pressure 172/100 mm Hg. His AST is 140 U/L and ALT 60 U/L. Which of the following describes the mechanism of the most appropriate first-line drug class?

options.label: D
options.html: Increased frequency of GABA<sub>A</sub> chloride channel opening

options.label: E
options.html: Increased duration of GABA<sub>A</sub> chloride channel opening

answerHtml: Answer: D. Increased frequency of GABA<sub>A</sub> chloride channel opening
explanationHtml: Delirium tremens typically begins 48–96 hours after the last drink, with hallucinations, autonomic hyperactivity and fever; AST:ALT > 2 suggests alcohol use. Chronic alcohol use down-regulates GABAA and up-regulates NMDA signaling; abrupt cessation produces CNS hyperexcitability. Benzodiazepines (cross-tolerant with alcohol) increase the frequency of GABAA channel opening and are first-line; symptom-triggered dosing with lorazepam is preferred in liver disease.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and are only adjuncts. B, C — clonidine/dexmedetomidine and β-blockers blunt autonomic signs but do not prevent seizures or DTs. E — barbiturates (phenobarbital) are an alternative in refractory cases, but the first-line class is benzodiazepines.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old man is brought by police after assaulting a stranger. He is combative and appears not to feel pain from a deep laceration on his hand. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse 118/min, blood pressure 168/98 mm Hg. He has both horizontal and vertical nystagmus. Pupils are 4 mm and reactive. The substance he most likely used acts primarily as which of the following?

options.label: B
options.html: Inhibitor of dopamine, norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake

answerHtml: Answer: E. Noncompetitive NMDA receptor antagonist
explanationHtml: Phencyclidine (PCP) intoxication: violence, agitation, analgesia, psychosis, hypertension, tachycardia and characteristic vertical (plus horizontal/rotatory) nystagmus. PCP (and ketamine) block the NMDA receptor channel pore. Complications include rhabdomyolysis, seizures and trauma; manage with benzodiazepines and a calm environment.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — LSD causes perceptual distortions with mydriasis, not vertical nystagmus or violent analgesia. B — cocaine causes sympathomimetic toxicity with marked mydriasis but not vertical nystagmus. C — cannabis causes conjunctival injection and increased appetite. D — opioids cause miosis and CNS depression.

stemHtml: A 40-year-old man involved in a minor car accident 2 months ago complains of severe neck pain that prevents him from working. He has filed a lawsuit against the other driver. In the clinic he grimaces and cannot turn his neck, but he is later observed in the parking lot turning his head freely to back out his car. Examination and imaging are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Malingering
explanationHtml: Malingering is the intentional production or exaggeration of symptoms for external (secondary) gain — here, financial compensation and avoiding work. Symptoms are inconsistent and improve when the patient believes he is unobserved or once the gain is achieved. It is not a mental disorder in DSM-5-TR (it is a "condition that may be a focus of clinical attention").
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — factitious disorder involves conscious symptom production motivated by assuming the sick role (internal/primary gain), without obvious external incentives. C, D, E — symptoms in somatic symptom, conversion and illness anxiety disorders are not consciously produced.

stemHtml: A 4.6-kg newborn is delivered vaginally after a difficult delivery complicated by shoulder dystocia that required strong lateral traction on the head. The infant's right arm hangs adducted and internally rotated at the shoulder, with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated. Grasp is intact. The Moro reflex is absent on the right. Which part of the brachial plexus was most likely injured?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Upper trunk
explanationHtml: Erb palsy: lateral traction that widens the angle between neck and shoulder stretches the C5–C6 roots/upper trunk. Paralysis of the deltoid and supraspinatus (abduction), infraspinatus/teres minor (lateral rotation), and biceps/brachialis (elbow flexion, supination) yields the "waiter's tip" posture. Hand function (C8–T1) is preserved, so grasp is intact; the Moro reflex is asymmetric because it requires shoulder abduction.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — posterior cord injury affects axillary and radial nerves (wrist drop, deltoid paralysis) but not biceps. C — lower trunk (Klumpke) causes claw hand with absent grasp. D — medial cord damages ulnar/median contributions to the hand. E — long thoracic injury causes a winged scapula.

stemHtml: A 30-year-old man falls off a ladder and sustains a midshaft fracture of the right humerus. Afterward he cannot extend his wrist or fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joints and has decreased sensation over the dorsum of the hand between the thumb and index finger. Elbow extension is preserved. Which of the following best explains why elbow extension is spared?

options.label: A
options.html: The triceps is innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve

options.label: B
options.html: The triceps is innervated by the axillary nerve

options.label: C
options.html: Branches to the triceps arise from the radial nerve proximal to the spiral groove

options.label: D
options.html: The deep radial nerve innervates the triceps distal to the elbow

options.label: E
options.html: The triceps receives dual supply from the median and ulnar nerves

answerHtml: Answer: C. Branches to the triceps arise from the radial nerve proximal to the spiral groove
explanationHtml: The radial nerve runs in the radial (spiral) groove with the deep brachial artery and is injured by midshaft humeral fractures. The branches to the long, lateral and most of the medial head of the triceps arise in the axilla or before the nerve enters the groove, so elbow extension is largely preserved. Distal radial-innervated muscles (wrist and finger extensors, brachioradialis) are paralyzed → wrist drop, and the superficial radial nerve sensory territory is lost. By contrast, an axillary ("crutch") compression affects triceps as well.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — musculocutaneous supplies the elbow flexors. B — axillary supplies deltoid and teres minor. D — the deep (posterior interosseous) branch supplies forearm extensors, not triceps. E — the median and ulnar nerves do not supply the triceps.

stemHtml: A 55-year-old woman develops a limp after an intramuscular injection into the buttock. When she stands on her left leg alone, her right hip drops. When she walks, she leans her trunk to the left during left-leg stance. Which of the following nerves was most likely injured?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Left superior gluteal nerve
explanationHtml: The superior gluteal nerve (L4–S1) supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae, which abduct the hip and keep the pelvis level during single-leg stance. If the left abductors are weak, standing on the left leg lets the opposite (right) hemipelvis sag — a positive Trendelenburg sign — and patients compensate by leaning toward the affected side (Trendelenburg/lurching gait). IM injections should be given in the superolateral quadrant (or ventrogluteal site) to avoid this nerve and the sciatic nerve.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — a right-sided lesion would cause the left hip to drop when standing on the right leg. B — inferior gluteal injury weakens gluteus maximus (difficulty climbing stairs/rising from a chair), not pelvic stability. C — sciatic injury causes foot drop and hamstring/below-knee weakness. E — obturator injury weakens adduction.

stemHtml: A 50-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis treated with a weekly oral drug for 2 years presents with mouth ulcers, fatigue and easy bruising. CBC shows hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, MCV 108 fL, leukocyte count 2,400/mm³ and platelet count 70,000/mm³. She admits to taking the medication daily for the past 2 weeks by mistake. Which of the following is the primary target of the drug responsible?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Dihydrofolate reductase
explanationHtml: Methotrexate, the first-line DMARD for RA, is dosed once weekly; daily dosing errors cause dangerous toxicity. By inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase it depletes tetrahydrofolate, impairing thymidylate and purine synthesis in rapidly dividing cells → mucositis, megaloblastic pancytopenia. Leucovorin (folinic acid) bypasses the blocked enzyme and is the rescue agent; routine folic acid reduces adverse effects.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — leflunomide inhibits DHODH (pyrimidine synthesis), dosed daily. B — 5-fluorouracil inhibits thymidylate synthase. C — mycophenolate inhibits IMP dehydrogenase. D — hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase.

stemHtml: A 60-year-old man with a kidney transplant maintained on azathioprine and tacrolimus has recurrent gout flares and tophi. Serum uric acid is 9.4 mg/dL. His physician starts allopurinol without modifying other medications. Six weeks later he has pancytopenia. Which of the following best explains this outcome?

options.label: A
options.html: Inhibition of xanthine oxidase, which normally inactivates 6-mercaptopurine

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibition of CYP3A4, raising tacrolimus levels

answerHtml: Answer: A. Inhibition of xanthine oxidase, which normally inactivates 6-mercaptopurine
explanationHtml: Azathioprine is converted to 6-mercaptopurine, which is inactivated mainly by xanthine oxidase (to 6-thiouric acid) and by TPMT. Allopurinol (and febuxostat) block xanthine oxidase, shunting 6-MP toward cytotoxic 6-thioguanine nucleotides and causing severe myelosuppression. The azathioprine dose must be reduced to about 25–33% or an alternative used.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — allopurinol does not inhibit TPMT (TPMT deficiency is a separate genetic risk). C — oxypurinol is not intrinsically myelotoxic at these doses. D — allopurinol is not a meaningful CYP3A4 inhibitor; tacrolimus toxicity would cause nephrotoxicity/neurotoxicity. E — HLA-B*58:01 predicts severe cutaneous reactions (SJS/TEN, DRESS), not isolated pancytopenia.

stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman has painful erosions of the buccal mucosa for 2 months, followed by flaccid blisters on her trunk that rupture easily. Gentle lateral pressure on normal-appearing skin causes the epidermis to separate. Biopsy shows a suprabasal split with basal cells remaining attached to the basement membrane. Direct immunofluorescence would most likely show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone

options.label: B
options.html: Intercellular IgG deposition in a net-like pattern throughout the epidermis

options.label: C
options.html: Granular IgA deposits in the dermal papillae

options.label: D
options.html: Granular IgG and C3 at the dermal–epidermal junction in sun-exposed skin only

answerHtml: Answer: B. Intercellular IgG deposition in a net-like pattern throughout the epidermis
explanationHtml: Pemphigus vulgaris is a type II hypersensitivity reaction with IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 (mucosal) and desmoglein 1 (skin). Loss of desmosomal adhesion causes acantholysis just above the basal layer ("row of tombstones"), flaccid intraepidermal bullae, oral involvement and a positive Nikolsky sign. Direct IF shows IgG outlining keratinocytes in a fishnet pattern. Treatment: systemic glucocorticoids plus rituximab.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — bullous pemphigoid (hemidesmosomes, tense subepidermal blisters, elderly, Nikolsky negative). C — dermatitis herpetiformis. D — lupus band pattern in SLE. E — immune deposits are characteristic of pemphigus; SJS/TEN or staphylococcal scalded skin would lack them.

stemHtml: A 57-year-old woman has 3 months of difficulty combing her hair and climbing stairs. She has a violaceous rash on her upper eyelids with periorbital edema and scaly erythematous papules over the dorsal knuckles. Serum creatine kinase is 3,200 U/L. Muscle biopsy shows perifascicular atrophy with perivascular CD4⁺ lymphocytes. Which of the following is the most important next step in her evaluation, given this diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.html: Genetic testing for dystrophin gene deletions

options.label: C
options.html: Age-appropriate and targeted screening for occult malignancy

options.label: D
options.html: Thyroid function testing to exclude hypothyroid myopathy as the cause

options.label: E
options.html: Measurement of serum aldolase to confirm the diagnosis

answerHtml: Answer: C. Age-appropriate and targeted screening for occult malignancy
explanationHtml: Dermatomyositis (heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, symmetric proximal weakness, high CK, perifascicular atrophy from complement-mediated capillary injury with CD4⁺ T cells) is associated with underlying malignancy in roughly 15–25% of adults — especially ovarian, lung, gastric, colorectal and pancreatic cancers and lymphoma; anti-TIF1-γ antibodies carry the highest risk. Cancer screening (including CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, and pelvic ultrasound/CA-125 in women) is a key step after diagnosis.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — myasthenia gravis does not cause rash or a high CK. B — dystrophinopathies present in childhood/adolescence in males. D — hypothyroidism can raise CK but does not cause heliotrope rash or this biopsy finding. E — aldolase is often elevated but adds little once biopsy confirms the diagnosis.

stemHtml: A 38-year-old man from India with ankylosing spondylitis has persistent inflammatory back pain and morning stiffness despite two different full-dose NSAIDs. His physician plans to start a biologic that is a recombinant fusion protein of the TNF receptor linked to the Fc portion of human IgG1. Which of the following is the most important test before starting this drug, and why?

options.label: A
options.html: Serum ANA, because the drug commonly causes drug-induced lupus that must be excluded beforehand

options.label: B
options.html: HLA-B27 typing, because it predicts response to the drug

options.label: C
options.html: Echocardiography, because the drug causes aortic regurgitation

options.label: D
options.html: Interferon-γ release assay, because TNF is essential for granuloma maintenance and latent TB may reactivate

options.label: E
options.html: Thiopurine methyltransferase activity, because deficiency causes myelosuppression

answerHtml: Answer: D. Interferon-γ release assay, because TNF is essential for granuloma maintenance and latent TB may reactivate
explanationHtml: Etanercept is a soluble TNF receptor–Fc fusion "decoy" that binds TNF-α (and TNF-β/lymphotoxin). TNF-α from macrophages is required to form and maintain granulomas; blocking it permits reactivation of latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis (often extrapulmonary/disseminated) and histoplasmosis. Screening for latent TB (IGRA preferred in BCG-vaccinated individuals, plus chest radiograph) and hepatitis B is mandatory before anti-TNF therapy; latent TB is treated before or alongside initiation.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — anti-TNF agents can induce antinuclear/antihistone antibodies and occasionally lupus-like syndromes, but ANA is not a required pre-treatment test. B — HLA-B27 supports the diagnosis but does not determine eligibility. C — aortic regurgitation is a manifestation of AS itself, not a drug toxicity. E — TPMT testing is for azathioprine/6-MP.

stemHtml: A new point-of-care antigen test for streptococcal pharyngitis is evaluated in 500 children with sore throat. Throat culture, the reference standard, is positive in 200 children. Of these 200, the new test is positive in 160. Of the 300 children with negative cultures, the new test is negative in 270. Which of the following is the sensitivity of the new test?
answerHtml: Answer: B. 80%
explanationHtml: Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN) = 160 / 200 = 80%. It is calculated only from people who truly have the disease (culture positive).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: C (84%) is the PPV = 160 / (160 + 30). D (90%) is the specificity = 270 / 300. A and E do not match any standard measure from this 2×2 table (NPV = 270/310 ≈ 87%, accuracy = 430/500 = 86%).

stemHtml: A 19-year-old college basketball player faints during a game. His uncle died suddenly at age 30. On examination there is a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that does not radiate to the carotids. The murmur gets louder when he bears down against a closed glottis and softer when he squats. Which of the following best explains why the murmur gets louder during the strain maneuver?

options.label: B
options.html: Increased venous return to the right heart

answerHtml: Answer: D. Decreased left ventricular end-diastolic volume
explanationHtml: This is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction (asymmetric septal hypertrophy plus systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflet). The Valsalva strain phase raises intrathoracic pressure and reduces venous return. With less preload the LV cavity gets smaller, the septum and mitral leaflet come closer together, obstruction worsens, and the murmur gets louder. Squatting raises preload and afterload, which enlarges the cavity and softens the murmur.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and E (higher afterload or aortic pressure) enlarge the LV and decrease the HCM murmur, as with handgrip. B: Valsalva reduces venous return. C: a larger end-diastolic volume reduces obstruction.

stemHtml:
A 42-year-old woman has had dry eyes and dry mouth for several years and has now passed her third kidney stone. Abdominal x-ray shows bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis. Laboratory studies:
TestResult
Na+140 mEq/L
K+2.9 mEq/L
Cl−115 mEq/L
HCO3−15 mEq/L
Arterial pH7.30
Urine pH6.4
Impairment of which of the following is the most likely cause of her acid–base disorder?

options.label: A
options.html: H<sup>+</sup> secretion by α-intercalated cells of the collecting duct

options.label: B
options.html: HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule

options.label: D
options.html: Na<sup>+</sup>–K<sup>+</sup>–2Cl<sup>−</sup> cotransport in the thick ascending limb

options.label: E
options.html: Na<sup>+</sup>–Cl<sup>−</sup> cotransport in the distal convoluted tubule

answerHtml: Answer: A. H<sup>+</sup> secretion by α-intercalated cells
explanationHtml: The anion gap is 140 − (115 + 15) = 10, so this is a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis. Urine pH stays above 5.5 despite systemic acidemia, along with hypokalemia, calcium phosphate stones and nephrocalcinosis. That pattern is distal (type 1) RTA, which is classically linked to Sjögren syndrome. Calcium phosphate precipitates easily in alkaline urine, and the acidosis also lowers urinary citrate, which normally inhibits stones.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: proximal (type 2) RTA can still acidify urine below 5.5 once serum HCO3− falls below the lowered threshold, and it rarely causes stones. C: type 4 RTA causes hyperkalemia. D and E: loop-like (Bartter) and thiazide-like (Gitelman) defects cause metabolic alkalosis.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman comes to the emergency department on the fourth day of her menstrual period with fever of 39.8°C (103.6°F), vomiting, and confusion. Blood pressure is 78/44 mm Hg. She has diffuse blanching macular erythema like a sunburn and conjunctival hyperemia. A tampon is removed. Blood cultures are negative. Ten days later, the skin of her palms and soles peels. The toxin responsible for this illness acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: B
options.html: Cleavage of SNARE proteins at the neuromuscular junction

options.label: C
options.html: ADP-ribosylation of the G<sub>s</sub>α subunit, increasing cAMP

options.label: D
options.html: Cleavage of desmoglein-1 in the stratum granulosum

options.label: E
options.html: Binding MHC class II and the T-cell receptor Vβ region outside the antigen groove

answerHtml: Answer: E. Superantigen cross-linking of MHC II and the TCR Vβ region
explanationHtml: This is menstrual toxic shock syndrome from Staphylococcus aureus TSST-1. A superantigen bridges MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells to the Vβ chain of the TCR without being processed. That nonspecifically activates up to about 20% of T cells, and the resulting flood of IL-2, IFN-γ and TNF-α causes shock. Blood cultures are usually negative because the disease is caused by the toxin, not by bacteria in the blood.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A. B: botulinum and tetanus toxins. C: cholera toxin and heat-labile E. coli toxin. D: exfoliative toxins of staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. SSSS causes superficial blistering, mostly in infants, and not this degree of shock.

stemHtml: A 45-year-old man has blood pressure of 168/102 mm Hg despite taking three antihypertensive drugs. He reports muscle cramps. Serum K<sup>+</sup> is 3.0 mEq/L, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> is 31 mEq/L, and Na<sup>+</sup> is 144 mEq/L. Plasma renin activity is suppressed and the plasma aldosterone concentration is markedly elevated. CT of the abdomen shows a 1.5-cm low-density mass in the left adrenal gland. This mass most likely arises from which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla

answerHtml: Answer: C. Zona glomerulosa
explanationHtml: Resistant hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, high aldosterone, and suppressed renin together mean primary hyperaldosteronism. An aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn syndrome) arises from the zona glomerulosa, the outermost cortical layer and the one that expresses aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2). Escape from aldosterone's sodium effect keeps the serum Na+ high-normal and prevents edema.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: a pheochromocytoma causes episodic catecholamine symptoms and no aldosterone excess. B: a fasciculata adenoma makes cortisol (Cushing syndrome), and aldosterone would not be high. D: the reticularis makes androgens. E: a reninoma would raise renin, not suppress it.

stemHtml: A 35-year-old woman is hospitalized with a bleeding duodenal ulcer. Her hemoglobin is 6.5 g/dL and she is hemodynamically stable after crystalloid. She is alert and oriented, and she correctly explains that she could die without a blood transfusion. As a Jehovah's Witness, she refuses all blood products. Her husband, who does not share her faith, tells the physician to transfuse her anyway. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Respect her refusal and maximize blood-conserving alternatives such as IV iron, erythropoietin, and endoscopic hemostasis

options.label: B
options.html: Transfuse because the spouse is the legal surrogate

options.label: C
options.html: Obtain an emergency court order to transfuse

options.label: D
options.html: Transfuse once she loses consciousness, under implied consent

options.label: E
options.html: Request a psychiatric evaluation before accepting the refusal

answerHtml: Answer: A. Respect the refusal and use alternatives
explanationHtml: An adult with decision-making capacity can refuse any treatment, including life-saving treatment, and that refusal stays valid if she later loses consciousness. She shows capacity: she understands, appreciates the consequences, reasons, and states a consistent choice. Good care still means offering every acceptable alternative.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: a surrogate decides only when the patient lacks capacity, and even then the surrogate must follow her known wishes. C: courts step in for minors, not for adults with capacity. D: an informed refusal carries over after she loses consciousness, so implied consent does not apply. E: a religious belief is not evidence of incapacity, and nothing here suggests a psychiatric illness.

stemHtml: A 68-year-old man with hypertension has sudden vertigo, vomiting, hoarseness, and difficulty swallowing. Examination shows a left ptosis and miosis, loss of pain and temperature sensation over the left face and over the right arm, trunk, and leg, and left-sided limb ataxia. The palate deviates to the right when he says "ah." Limb strength is normal. Occlusion of which of the following arteries is most likely?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Left posterior inferior cerebellar artery
explanationHtml: This is lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome on the left. The lesion damages the nucleus ambiguus (dysphagia, hoarseness, uvula deviating away from the lesion), the spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract (ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss), the spinothalamic tract (contralateral body pain/temperature loss), descending sympathetic fibers (ipsilateral Horner), the inferior cerebellar peduncle (ipsilateral ataxia), and the vestibular nuclei (vertigo). The pyramids are medial and spared, so strength is normal.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: AICA (lateral pontine) causes ipsilateral facial paralysis and hearing loss. B: anterior spinal artery occlusion (medial medullary) causes contralateral hemiparesis, contralateral loss of proprioception, and ipsilateral tongue deviation. C: a right-sided lesion would put the Horner syndrome and ataxia on the right. D: basilar occlusion causes quadriplegia and locked-in syndrome.

stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman receives unfractionated heparin after a total knee replacement. Her platelet count is 250,000/mm<sup>3</sup> preoperatively and 90,000/mm<sup>3</sup> on postoperative day 7. She now has a painful swollen left calf, and duplex ultrasound shows a femoral vein thrombus. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of her thrombocytopenia?

options.label: B
options.html: IgG antibodies to platelet factor 4–heparin complexes that activate platelets through Fc receptors

options.label: D
options.html: IgG autoantibodies to glycoprotein IIb/IIIa with splenic clearance

options.label: E
options.html: Consumption of platelets and clotting factors from tissue factor release

answerHtml: Answer: B. Anti-PF4–heparin IgG that activates platelets
explanationHtml: Immune heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (type 2 HIT) starts 5–10 days after heparin is begun. The platelet count falls by more than 50%, and paradoxical arterial or venous thrombosis develops. The IgG–PF4–heparin immune complexes bind platelet FcγRIIa, which activates platelets, releases procoagulant microparticles, and generates thrombin. Stop all heparin, including flushes, and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban, bivalirudin, or fondaparinux.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: non-immune HIT (type 1) occurs within 1–2 days, is mild, and does not cause thrombosis. C: TTP has hemolysis with schistocytes and is unrelated to heparin. D: in ITP the antibodies do not cause thrombosis. E: DIC needs a trigger such as sepsis, and it prolongs the PT/PTT.

stemHtml: A 55-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has taken warfarin for 2 years, and his INR has been stable at 2.5. After a positive interferon-γ release assay with a normal chest x-ray, he starts a 4-month daily course of rifampin. Three weeks later his INR is 1.3. He has been taking his warfarin every day. Which of the following best explains the change in INR?

options.label: A
options.html: Competition with warfarin for vitamin K epoxide reductase

options.label: B
options.html: Displacement of warfarin from plasma albumin

options.label: D
options.html: Induction of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes that metabolize warfarin

options.label: E
options.html: Inhibition of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes that metabolize warfarin

answerHtml: Answer: D. CYP induction
explanationHtml: Rifampin is one of the strongest inducers of CYP enzymes (2C9, 3A4, 1A2 and others) through the nuclear pregnane X receptor. Warfarin's active S-enantiomer is cleared by CYP2C9, so faster metabolism lowers its levels and the INR falls. Induction takes 1–2 weeks to develop fully because new enzyme must be made. Warfarin doses usually need to be raised substantially, and the INR checked closely, including after rifampin is stopped.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A is how warfarin itself works, not the interaction. B: displacement from albumin briefly raises free drug and the INR. C: this is not rifampin's mechanism. E: CYP inhibitors such as fluconazole, amiodarone, and metronidazole raise the INR.

stemHtml: A 38-year-old man who has never smoked has had progressive exertional dyspnea for 2 years. His serum ALT is mildly elevated. Pulmonary function tests show FEV<sub>1</sub>/FVC of 0.55, total lung capacity at 125% of predicted, and DLCO at 45% of predicted. High-resolution CT shows panlobular emphysema that is most severe in the lower lobes. Which of the following best explains the lung damage?

options.label: A
options.html: Smoke-induced recruitment of neutrophils and macrophages to respiratory bronchioles

options.label: B
options.html: Thickening of the alveolar–capillary membrane by collagen deposition

options.label: C
options.html: Unopposed neutrophil elastase activity due to deficiency of a hepatic protease inhibitor

options.label: D
options.html: Hyperplasia of submucosal mucous glands in large airways

options.label: E
options.html: Hypertrophy of bronchial smooth muscle from Th2-mediated inflammation

answerHtml: Answer: C. α<sub>1</sub>-antitrypsin deficiency
explanationHtml: A young nonsmoker with panlobular (panacinar), lower-lobe emphysema and liver abnormalities most likely has α1-antitrypsin deficiency (PiZZ). The obstructive pattern (low FEV1/FVC), air trapping (high TLC), and low DLCO reflect destroyed alveolar walls, which leave less capillary surface for gas exchange. The misfolded Z protein also accumulates in hepatocytes as PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules, which can cause cirrhosis.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: smoking causes centriacinar, upper-lobe emphysema. B: interstitial fibrosis gives a restrictive pattern with a normal or high FEV1/FVC. D: this describes chronic bronchitis, with a normal DLCO. E: this describes asthma, with a normal or high DLCO.

stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman has bloating and loose stools and iron-deficiency anemia that has not responded to 6 months of oral iron. She has intensely itchy grouped vesicles on both elbows. Duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. Her condition is most strongly associated with which of the following?
answerHtml: Answer: E. HLA-DQ2
explanationHtml: This is celiac disease with dermatitis herpetiformis, the itchy vesicles on extensor surfaces with IgA deposits in the dermal papillae. Over 90% of patients carry HLA-DQ2 and most of the rest carry DQ8. These MHC II molecules bind gluten peptides that tissue transglutaminase has deamidated, which makes them strong triggers of CD4 T cells. Iron is absorbed in the duodenum, so iron deficiency that does not respond to oral iron is a classic presentation.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: seronegative spondyloarthropathies. B: rheumatoid arthritis and type 1 diabetes (with DR3). C: multiple sclerosis and Goodpasture syndrome. D: hereditary hemochromatosis.

stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman has had 4–5 menstrual periods a year since menarche, with acne and coarse hair on her chin and lower abdomen. BMI is 33 kg/m<sup>2</sup>, and there is velvety hyperpigmentation of the posterior neck. Serum LH is elevated relative to FSH, and free testosterone is mildly elevated. Pelvic ultrasound shows enlarged ovaries with many peripheral follicles. Without treatment, she is at greatest increased risk for which of the following?

options.label: C
options.html: Squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix

answerHtml: Answer: A. Endometrial carcinoma
explanationHtml: Polycystic ovary syndrome causes chronic anovulation. Without ovulation there is no corpus luteum and so no progesterone. Estrogen from peripheral aromatization of androgens in adipose tissue then stimulates the endometrium unopposed, causing endometrial hyperplasia and endometrioid (type 1) carcinoma. Insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans) adds risk of type 2 diabetes and dyslipidemia. Cyclic progestins or combined oral contraceptives protect the endometrium.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: a germ-cell tumor not linked to PCOS. C: driven by HPV. D: estrogen is preserved in PCOS, so bone is protected (contrast with hypothalamic amenorrhea). E: not related to PCOS.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old man wakes with excruciating pain, redness, and swelling of his right first metatarsophalangeal joint after a night of heavy drinking. Joint aspiration shows needle-shaped crystals that are yellow when parallel to the axis of the compensator under polarized light. He had an upper GI bleed from a gastric ulcer last month. He is given an oral drug that is also first-line therapy for familial Mediterranean fever. Which of the following is the mechanism of this drug?

options.label: B
options.html: Inhibition of URAT1-mediated uric acid reabsorption in the proximal tubule

options.label: C
options.html: Binding of tubulin, preventing microtubule polymerization in neutrophils

options.label: E
options.html: Enzymatic conversion of uric acid to allantoin

answerHtml: Answer: C. Tubulin binding (colchicine)
explanationHtml: Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals (yellow when parallel) are monosodium urate, so this is acute gout. His recent GI bleed rules out NSAIDs. Colchicine binds tubulin and blocks microtubule assembly, which impairs neutrophil chemotaxis, degranulation, and NLRP3 inflammasome activation. The same anti-neutrophil action is why it is first-line for FMF. Its main toxicity is diarrhea. Doses must be reduced in renal impairment and with strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors such as clarithromycin.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: allopurinol or febuxostat, urate-lowering drugs that are not started in the middle of an acute flare. B: probenecid. D: NSAIDs, contraindicated after his GI bleed. E: pegloticase (rasburicase is used for tumor lysis).

stemHtml: A 9-month-old boy has had three episodes of otitis media and one of pneumococcal pneumonia since age 6 months. His maternal uncle died of "infections" in childhood. On examination, tonsils cannot be seen and no lymph nodes are palpable. Serum IgG, IgA, and IgM are all markedly low. Flow cytometry shows normal CD3<sup>+</sup> T-cell counts and almost no CD19<sup>+</sup> cells. A defect in which of the following is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.html: CD40 ligand on activated T cells

answerHtml: Answer: B. Bruton tyrosine kinase (X-linked agammaglobulinemia)
explanationHtml: BTK signaling is needed for pre-B cells to mature. Without it, B cells stop at the pre-B stage, so mature CD19+ B cells and all immunoglobulin classes are absent, as are germinal centers (no tonsils or nodes). Infections begin after about 6 months, once maternal IgG has waned, and are mostly encapsulated bacteria and enteroviruses. Inheritance is X-linked recessive (the maternal uncle). Treat with IVIG and avoid live vaccines.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: hyper-IgM syndrome has B cells and a normal or high IgM. C: ADA-SCID causes profound T-cell lymphopenia. D: WAS causes eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, and low IgM. E: CGD causes catalase-positive infections with normal immunoglobulins.

stemHtml: A 62-year-old man delays seeking care for chest pain and is found to have a completed anterior wall ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Five days later, he suddenly becomes hypotensive with jugular venous distention and muffled heart sounds, and he progresses to pulseless electrical activity. Which of the following histologic findings is most likely in the infarcted myocardium at this time?

options.label: B
options.html: Coagulative necrosis with a dense neutrophilic infiltrate as the predominant finding

options.label: D
options.html: Macrophages phagocytosing necrotic myocytes, with early granulation tissue at the margins

options.label: E
options.html: Mature granulation tissue with abundant collagen and contracting scar

answerHtml: Answer: D. Macrophage phase
explanationHtml: The sudden tamponade (Beck triad, then PEA) points to free wall rupture, which peaks 3–14 days after MI. In this window macrophages clear the necrotic myocytes and the wall is at its weakest, before collagen is laid down. At day 5, macrophages dominate (days 3–7) and granulation tissue begins at the edges.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: 0–4 hours. B: neutrophils dominate at 1–3 days, which is the setting for fibrinous pericarditis. E: weeks 2–8, as the scar matures. C: more than 2 months, the setting for ventricular aneurysm and Dressler syndrome.

stemHtml: During morning rounds, an attending physician sharply criticizes a second-year resident in front of the team. Later that day, the resident angrily berates a medical student for a minor mistake in a progress note. The resident has never treated the student this way before. Which of the following defense mechanisms is the resident most likely using?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Displacement
explanationHtml: In displacement, feelings about a threatening target (the attending) are redirected onto a safer, less powerful one (the student). The emotion stays the same, but its object changes.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: projection attributes one's own unacceptable feelings to someone else. B: reaction formation means acting the opposite of what one feels, such as being excessively polite to the attending. C: sublimation channels an impulse into a socially valued activity, a mature defense. D: passive aggression expresses hostility indirectly toward the original target, for example by "forgetting" the attending's request.

stemHtml: A 67-year-old woman with hypertension started a new once-daily antihypertensive 2 months ago. Laboratory studies now show serum calcium 10.9 mg/dL, K<sup>+</sup> 3.2 mEq/L, Na<sup>+</sup> 133 mEq/L, glucose 128 mg/dL, and uric acid 8.1 mg/dL. Serum PTH is low-normal. The drug most likely acts on which of the following transporters?

options.label: A
options.html: Na<sup>+</sup>–K<sup>+</sup>–2Cl<sup>−</sup> cotransporter in the thick ascending limb

options.label: B
options.html: Na<sup>+</sup>–Cl<sup>−</sup> cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule

options.label: C
options.html: Epithelial Na<sup>+</sup> channel in the collecting duct

options.label: D
options.html: Carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule

answerHtml: Answer: B. NCC in the DCT (thiazide)
explanationHtml: The adverse-effect pattern of thiazides is hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, and hyponatremia. Blocking NCC lowers intracellular Na+ in the DCT cell. That increases basolateral Na+/Ca2+ exchange and apical Ca2+ entry, so more calcium is reabsorbed. This is why thiazides help prevent calcium stones. Thiazides are the classic cause of hyponatremia because they impair urinary dilution while leaving the medullary gradient intact.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: loop diuretics increase calcium excretion ("loops lose calcium"). C and E: potassium-sparing agents cause hyperkalemia. D: acetazolamide causes a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis and does not raise calcium.

stemHtml: A 3-day-old boy born at term stops feeding well and becomes lethargic with vomiting and rapid breathing. Plasma ammonia is 450 μmol/L (normal <50), BUN is low, and arterial blood gas shows a respiratory alkalosis. Plasma citrulline is low and urinary orotic acid is markedly elevated. Blood glucose and the anion gap are normal. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Ornithine transcarbamylase
explanationHtml: OTC deficiency is the most common urea cycle disorder and is X-linked (a sick boy). Carbamoyl phosphate cannot combine with ornithine, so it builds up in the mitochondria and spills into the cytosol. There it enters pyrimidine synthesis through CPS II/aspartate transcarbamoylase, producing excess orotic acid. Ammonia stimulates the respiratory center, causing the respiratory alkalosis. Citrulline is low because it is made downstream of OTC.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: CPS I deficiency also causes hyperammonemia but orotic acid is normal or low, since carbamoyl phosphate is never made. C: hereditary orotic aciduria causes megaloblastic anemia without hyperammonemia. D: maple syrup urine disease causes ketoacidosis with a high anion gap and sweet-smelling urine. E: PKU does not cause neonatal hyperammonemia.

stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with resting tremor and bradykinesia is started on levodopa alone. He develops marked nausea and orthostatic lightheadedness, and his motor symptoms improve only at high doses. A second drug is added. His nausea and orthostasis resolve, and a much lower levodopa dose now controls his symptoms. The added drug most likely acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Inhibition of catechol-O-methyltransferase in the periphery

options.label: B
options.html: Selective inhibition of monoamine oxidase type B in the brain

options.label: C
options.html: Inhibition of aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase outside the CNS

options.label: D
options.html: Direct agonism at striatal D<sub>2</sub> receptors

answerHtml: Answer: C. Peripheral DOPA decarboxylase inhibition (carbidopa)
explanationHtml: Carbidopa does not cross the blood–brain barrier. It stops levodopa from being converted to dopamine in the periphery. That conversion causes the nausea (the area postrema lies outside the BBB) and the orthostatic hypotension. With conversion blocked, more levodopa reaches the brain, so a lower dose works. In the US it is given as the fixed combination carbidopa–levodopa (Sinemet).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: entacapone prolongs levodopa's effect ("wearing-off") but does not mainly prevent peripheral dopamine side effects. B: selegiline and rasagiline. D: pramipexole and ropinirole, which themselves cause nausea and orthostasis. E: trihexyphenidyl helps tremor but does not interact with levodopa this way.

stemHtml: A 55-year-old woman has had painful oral erosions for 2 months. She now has flaccid blisters on her trunk that rupture easily and leave raw erosions. Gentle lateral pressure on normal-looking skin makes the epidermis slide off. Skin biopsy shows a blister just above the basal layer, with rounded, detached keratinocytes in the blister cavity. Direct immunofluorescence shows IgG in a net-like pattern between keratinocytes. The autoantibodies are most likely directed against which of the following?

options.label: B
options.html: Type VII collagen in anchoring fibrils

answerHtml: Answer: D. Desmoglein 3
explanationHtml: Pemphigus vulgaris is a type II hypersensitivity against desmosomal cadherins (desmoglein 3, plus desmoglein 1 in mucocutaneous disease). Loss of cell–cell adhesion (acantholysis) gives a suprabasal, intraepidermal split, with basal cells still attached ("row of tombstones"). The result is a positive Nikolsky sign, oral involvement, and intercellular "fishnet" IgG.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: bullous pemphigoid causes tense subepidermal bullae, linear IgG/C3 along the basement membrane, a negative Nikolsky sign, and rare oral lesions. B: epidermolysis bullosa acquisita. C: dermatitis herpetiformis, with granular IgA in the dermal papillae. E: these are mutated (not autoantibody targets) in epidermolysis bullosa simplex.

stemHtml:
A 60-year-old woman with long-standing, active rheumatoid arthritis has fatigue. She has no GI symptoms, and stool guaiac is negative. Laboratory studies:
TestResultReference
Hemoglobin10.2 g/dL12–16
MCV82 fL80–100
Serum iron35 μg/dL50–170
TIBC210 μg/dL250–400
Ferritin390 ng/mL15–200
Transferrin saturation17%20–50%
Which of the following is the primary mechanism of her anemia?

options.label: A
options.html: IL-6–induced hepatic hepcidin causing degradation of ferroportin

options.label: C
options.html: Inhibition of δ-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase and ferrochelatase

options.label: D
options.html: Defective DNA synthesis from cobalamin deficiency

answerHtml: Answer: A. Hepcidin-mediated iron sequestration (anemia of chronic disease)
explanationHtml: Low serum iron with a low TIBC and a high ferritin is anemia of inflammation. IL-6 drives hepatic hepcidin, which binds ferroportin and causes it to be internalized and degraded. Iron is then trapped in macrophages and enterocytes and is unavailable for erythropoiesis. In this "iron-restricted" state, the anemia is normocytic or mildly microcytic.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: iron deficiency gives a high TIBC and low ferritin. C: lead poisoning causes basophilic stippling and ringed sideroblasts. D: B12 deficiency is macrocytic. E: hemochromatosis causes iron overload with high transferrin saturation, not anemia.

stemHtml: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 8 hours after swallowing about 60 tablets of an over-the-counter analgesic after a breakup. She has nausea but is otherwise well. A drug level plotted on the treatment nomogram is above the treatment line. If she is not treated, liver biopsy 3 days later would show necrosis concentrated around the central veins. The antidote she should be given works mainly by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: B
options.html: Chelation of the parent drug in plasma

options.label: D
options.html: Adsorption of the drug in the gut lumen

options.label: E
options.html: Replenishment of hepatic glutathione to detoxify the reactive metabolite

answerHtml: Answer: E. N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione
explanationHtml: In acetaminophen overdose, glucuronidation and sulfation are saturated, so more drug goes through CYP2E1 to the reactive metabolite NAPQI. Glutathione normally conjugates NAPQI, but it runs out, and NAPQI then binds hepatocyte proteins. Zone 3 (centrilobular) hepatocytes have the most CYP2E1 and the least oxygen, so necrosis concentrates there. N-acetylcysteine supplies cysteine for glutathione synthesis. It works best when started within 8–10 hours, but it is still given to late presenters. The Rumack–Matthew nomogram applies to a single acute ingestion from 4 hours onward.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: fomepizole for methanol or ethylene glycol. B: chelators (e.g., deferoxamine, dimercaprol) are for metals. C: inducing conjugating enzymes is not the antidote mechanism. D: activated charcoal helps only within about 1–4 hours and is not the specific antidote.

stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes has abdominal pain and Kussmaul respirations. Glucose is 540 mg/dL, arterial pH 7.12, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 9 mEq/L, serum K<sup>+</sup> 5.8 mEq/L, and serum β-hydroxybutyrate is markedly elevated. Four hours after starting IV normal saline and a continuous infusion of regular insulin, her serum K<sup>+</sup> is 3.1 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most direct cause of the fall in serum potassium?

options.label: A
options.html: Increased aldosterone secretion in response to volume depletion

options.label: C
options.html: Insulin-stimulated Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup>-ATPase activity in skeletal muscle and liver

options.label: D
options.html: Cotransport of K<sup>+</sup> with glucose through GLUT4

answerHtml: Answer: C. Insulin stimulates Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup>-ATPase
explanationHtml: DKA patients are depleted of total-body K+ (osmotic diuresis, vomiting) but often have a normal or high serum K+. Insulin deficiency and hyperosmolality shift K+ out of cells. Insulin quickly reverses this by stimulating the Na+/K+-ATPase, moving K+ into cells and unmasking the deficit. Under ADA guidance, insulin is held if K+ is below 3.3 mEq/L, and K+ is added to fluids once it is below about 5.0–5.2.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and E: these contribute to total-body losses over time but do not explain a sharp fall within hours of starting insulin. B: unrelated to insulin. D: GLUT4 carries glucose, not K<sup>+</sup>.

stemHtml: A healthy 30-year-old woman flies from sea level to a mountain town at 4,000 m (13,000 ft). Six hours after arrival she has a mild headache. Which of the following arterial blood gas patterns is most likely at this time, compared with her sea-level values?

options.label: D
options.html: pH normal, PaCO<sub>2</sub> normal, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> normal

answerHtml: Answer: B. Acute respiratory alkalosis
explanationHtml: Low inspired PO2 lowers PaO2, which stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies). Ventilation rises and PaCO2 falls. In the acute phase, the only buffering is a small, immediate drop in HCO3− from intracellular buffers. Renal compensation (bicarbonaturia) takes 2–3 days. Acetazolamide speeds acclimatization by causing a mild metabolic acidosis, which allows ventilation to rise further.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: respiratory acidosis (hypoventilation). C: primary metabolic acidosis. D: plasma values do not stay unchanged at altitude. E: metabolic alkalosis with compensatory hypoventilation.

stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl comes to a clinic in the United States with vaginal discharge. Nucleic acid amplification testing is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis. She asks the physician not to tell her parents, who have her on their health insurance. She is otherwise healthy and not pregnant. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.html: Obtain parental consent before giving antibiotics

options.label: B
options.html: Treat her and tell her parents, because she is a minor

options.label: C
options.html: Defer treatment until she is 18 years old

options.label: D
options.html: Treat her confidentially, without parental consent or notification

options.label: E
options.html: Seek a court order to authorize treatment

answerHtml: Answer: D. Confidential treatment
explanationHtml: Every US state lets minors consent to diagnosis and treatment of sexually transmitted infections without a parent. Confidentiality should be kept, and the physician should encourage, but not require, her to involve a trusted adult. Exceptions to confidentiality include risk of serious harm to self or others and suspected abuse. Chlamydia is reported to the public health department, which is not the same as telling parents. Counsel her on partner treatment and retesting.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B, and E: parental involvement is not legally required for STI, contraception, or substance-use care in most states, and a court order is unnecessary. C: delaying treatment risks PID and infertility.

stemHtml: A 19-year-old man is hospitalized with his second episode of meningitis in 3 years. CSF Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci, and culture grows an oxidase-positive organism that ferments maltose and glucose. He has no other history of serious infection. Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?

options.label: A
options.html: Deficiency of a terminal complement component (C5–C9)

answerHtml: Answer: A. Terminal complement (membrane attack complex) deficiency
explanationHtml: Recurrent infection with Neisseria meningitidis (maltose and glucose fermenter) points to a defect in forming the membrane attack complex (C5b–C9). Lysis by MAC is essential against Neisseria because of their thin peptidoglycan and outer membrane. US practice: screen with CH50 and vaccinate with MenACWY and MenB. Eculizumab and ravulizumab, which block C5, carry the same risk and require meningococcal vaccination.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: hereditary angioedema (C4 low, no infections). C: usually asymptomatic or Candida infections. D: leukocyte adhesion deficiency with delayed separation of the umbilical cord and infections without pus. E: early classical-pathway deficiencies cause SLE-like disease.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes with microalbuminuria starts a new medication. Three weeks later he has a persistent, dry, nonproductive cough. Lung examination and chest x-ray are normal. His physician changes him to a drug that blocks the AT<sub>1</sub> receptor, and the cough resolves. The original drug caused the cough by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Increased angiotensin II levels in bronchial tissue

options.label: C
options.html: Blockade of β<sub>2</sub>-adrenergic receptors in bronchial smooth muscle

answerHtml: Answer: E. Decreased bradykinin breakdown
explanationHtml: Angiotensin-converting enzyme is the same enzyme as kininase II. ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril therefore raise bradykinin and substance P, which sensitize airway C-fibers and cause cough in about 5–20% of patients. They also predispose to angioedema. ARBs such as losartan leave kininase activity alone, so cough is rare.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: ACE inhibitors lower angiotensin II. B: lower aldosterone does occur, causing hyperkalemia, but it does not cause cough. C: nonselective β-blockers cause bronchospasm, not an isolated dry cough. D: not the mechanism.

stemHtml: A 25-year-old man and his wife have been unable to conceive for 2 years. He is 191 cm (6 ft 3 in) tall with long legs, sparse body hair, and bilateral gynecomastia. Both testes are small and firm. Semen analysis shows azoospermia. Serum testosterone is low, and LH and FSH are elevated. Testicular biopsy shows hyalinized seminiferous tubules with clusters of Leydig cells. Which of the following karyotypes is most likely?
answerHtml: Answer: C. 47,XXY (Klinefelter syndrome)
explanationHtml: Klinefelter syndrome is primary hypogonadism. Seminiferous tubules degenerate (low inhibin, so FSH rises) and Leydig cells fail (low testosterone, so LH rises). A high estrogen:testosterone ratio causes gynecomastia. Delayed epiphyseal closure gives eunuchoid proportions. It results from meiotic nondisjunction, of paternal or maternal origin in roughly equal proportions. Patients have a higher risk of male breast cancer.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Turner syndrome is phenotypically female. B: androgen insensitivity gives a female phenotype with testes and high or normal testosterone. D: XYY men are tall with normal fertility and testes. E: 46,XX testicular DSD gives small testes and azoospermia but usually short or normal stature, because extra X/Y growth genes are absent. Tall stature with eunuchoid proportions fits XXY best.

stemHtml: A 30-year-old man is thrown from a motorcycle. X-ray shows a displaced fracture of the midshaft of the right humerus. He cannot extend his wrist or fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joints, but he can extend his elbow against resistance. Sensation is reduced over the dorsum of the hand between the thumb and index finger. Which of the following nerves is most likely injured?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Radial nerve (spiral groove)
explanationHtml: The radial nerve winds around the humerus in the spiral (radial) groove, so it is at risk with midshaft fractures. The result is wrist drop and loss of sensation over the dorsal first web space. Triceps strength is usually preserved because the branches to triceps leave the nerve proximal to the groove.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: surgical neck fracture or anterior shoulder dislocation, with deltoid weakness and loss of the "regimental badge" sensation. C: supracondylar fracture or carpal tunnel. D: medial epicondyle fracture, with claw hand. E: rare, with weak elbow flexion and loss of lateral forearm sensation.

stemHtml: A 35-year-old Black woman has a dry cough, tender red nodules on both shins, and ankle pain. Chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Serum calcium is 11.8 mg/dL, PTH is suppressed, PTH-related peptide is undetectable, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is elevated. Transbronchial biopsy shows tightly packed epithelioid granulomas without central necrosis. Which of the following best explains her hypercalcemia?

options.label: A
options.html: Secretion of PTH-related peptide by lung epithelial cells

answerHtml: Answer: D. Macrophage 1α-hydroxylase
explanationHtml: In sarcoidosis, IFN-γ–activated macrophages in granulomas express 1α-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) that does not respond to PTH or calcium. They convert 25-OH vitamin D to calcitriol, which increases intestinal calcium absorption and bone resorption. The same mechanism occurs in TB, fungal granulomas, and some lymphomas. Glucocorticoids suppress it. Bilateral hilar adenopathy with erythema nodosum and arthritis is Löfgren syndrome.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: PTHrP is undetectable (it typically comes from squamous cell carcinoma). B: there is no malignancy. C: 24-hydroxylase inactivates vitamin D. E: PTH is suppressed.

stemHtml: Investigators identify 200 patients with newly diagnosed pancreatic adenocarcinoma and 400 people of similar age without the disease from the same hospitals. They interview all participants about lifetime cigarette smoking. Which of the following is the most appropriate measure of association for this study?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Odds ratio
explanationHtml: Participants are selected by outcome (disease vs. no disease) and then asked about past exposure, which makes this a case-control study. The investigators set the ratio of cases to controls, so incidence, and therefore relative risk, cannot be calculated. The odds ratio is (a×d)/(b×c), and it approximates the RR when the disease is rare. This design is prone to recall bias.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B, and C need an incidence, which comes from following a cohort forward. D: hazard ratios come from time-to-event (survival) analyses in cohort studies or RCTs.

stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy has had puffy eyes for a week, starting a few days after a cold, and his scrotum and legs are now swollen. Blood pressure is normal. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein, no red cells, and fatty casts. Serum albumin is 1.8 g/dL, cholesterol is 340 mg/dL, and C3 and C4 are normal. Which of the following findings would most likely be seen on renal biopsy?

options.label: A
options.html: Diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy, with normal light microscopy

options.label: D
options.html: Splitting and lamination of the glomerular basement membrane

options.label: E
options.html: "Spike and dome" thickening of the GBM with subepithelial deposits

answerHtml: Answer: A. Foot-process effacement (minimal change disease)
explanationHtml: Pure nephrotic syndrome in a young child after an upper respiratory infection, with normal complement and no hematuria or hypertension, is minimal change disease. Light microscopy and immunofluorescence are normal, and the only finding is podocyte foot-process effacement on electron microscopy. It responds well to glucocorticoids, so children with typical features are treated empirically without biopsy. Selective loss of albumin follows loss of the GBM's negative charge.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: post-streptococcal GN (nephritic, low C3). C: lupus nephritis. D: Alport syndrome (hematuria, deafness). E: membranous nephropathy in adults (anti-PLA2R).

stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman has had drooping eyelids and double vision for 3 months, worse in the evening. She tires while chewing and has trouble climbing stairs late in the day. Holding an ice pack over her eyes for 2 minutes improves the ptosis. Deep tendon reflexes and sensation are normal. Further evaluation is most likely to show an abnormality of which of the following structures?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Anterior mediastinum (thymus)
explanationHtml: Fatigable ptosis, diplopia, and bulbar and proximal weakness with normal reflexes point to myasthenia gravis. Autoantibodies to the postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptor block it, cross-link it, and destroy it through complement. Cold improves transmission by slowing acetylcholinesterase. Most patients with AChR antibodies have a thymic abnormality: lymphoid hyperplasia in about 65% and thymoma in about 10–15%. All should have chest CT or MRI. Thymectomy helps in generalized AChR-positive disease and is required for thymoma.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: C: small cell carcinoma usually arises centrally and causes Lambert–Eaton syndrome, in which proximal weakness improves with use and reflexes are depressed. A, B, and E do not cause fluctuating fatigable weakness.

stemHtml: A 70-year-old man in the ICU is treated with gentamicin and a β-lactam for Pseudomonas bacteremia. He is also receiving IV furosemide. On day 9, he reports ringing in his ears and difficulty hearing, and his serum creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 2.1 mg/dL. Which of the following is the antibacterial mechanism of the drug most likely responsible?

options.label: A
options.html: Inhibition of peptidyltransferase on the 50S subunit

options.label: B
options.html: Binding of the 30S subunit, causing mRNA misreading and blocking formation of the initiation complex

answerHtml: Answer: B. 30S binding (aminoglycoside)
explanationHtml: Aminoglycosides bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and cause misreading and faulty initiation. They kill bacteria in a concentration-dependent way and have a post-antibiotic effect. Uptake is oxygen-dependent, so they do not work against anaerobes. Their toxicities are nephrotoxicity (acute tubular necrosis), ototoxicity (worse with loop diuretics), neuromuscular blockade, and teratogenicity. Monitor trough levels.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: chloramphenicol (peptidyltransferase); linezolid, macrolides, and clindamycin also act on the 50S subunit. C: fluoroquinolones (tendon rupture, QT prolongation). D: β-lactams, rarely the cause of this toxicity pattern. E: sulfonamides.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old man has had crampy right lower quadrant pain, nonbloody diarrhea, and 6-kg weight loss for 8 months. Examination shows a perianal fistula. Colonoscopy shows a cobblestone pattern and deep linear ulcers in the terminal ileum, with segments of normal colon in between. Biopsy shows transmural inflammation with non-caseating granulomas. This patient is at increased risk of forming which of the following kidney stones?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Calcium oxalate (enteric hyperoxaluria)
explanationHtml: Crohn disease of the terminal ileum causes bile acid and fat malabsorption. Fatty acids left in the lumen bind calcium (saponification), so dietary oxalate stays free and is absorbed in the colon. Bile salts also make the colon more permeable to oxalate. The result is hyperoxaluria and calcium oxalate stones. Chronic diarrhea adds volume depletion and hypocitraturia.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: inherited aminoaciduria. B: urease-producing organisms such as Proteus. D: distal RTA or hyperparathyroidism. E: xanthine oxidase deficiency or allopurinol in tumor lysis.

stemHtml: A 50-year-old man has fatigue, early satiety, and a spleen palpable 8 cm below the costal margin. WBC count is 120,000/mm<sup>3</sup> with neutrophils at all stages of maturation, including myelocytes, and absolute basophilia. Blasts make up 2%. FISH shows a fusion gene formed by a reciprocal translocation. He starts an oral drug that targets the protein product of this fusion gene. The drug acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Competitive blockade of the ATP-binding site of a constitutively active tyrosine kinase

options.label: C
options.html: Induction of differentiation by binding a retinoic acid receptor fusion protein

options.label: D
options.html: Complement- and antibody-dependent lysis of CD20<sup>+</sup> cells

answerHtml: Answer: A. BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibition (imatinib)
explanationHtml: Chronic myeloid leukemia comes from t(9;22), the Philadelphia chromosome, which creates BCR-ABL1, a constitutively active tyrosine kinase. Imatinib, dasatinib, and nilotinib occupy its ATP-binding pocket. Resistance comes from kinase-domain mutations such as T315I, which ponatinib or asciminib may overcome.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: ruxolitinib for JAK2-mutant myelofibrosis or polycythemia vera. C: all-trans retinoic acid for APL t(15;17). D: rituximab for B-cell neoplasms. E: hydroxyurea can be used for short-term cytoreduction but does not target BCR-ABL.

stemHtml: A 28-year-old man has sudden tearing chest pain that radiates to his back. He is 198 cm (6 ft 6 in) tall, his arm span is greater than his height, and he has a pectus excavatum. Both lenses are displaced upward. CT angiography shows a dissection of the ascending aorta. Pathology of the aortic wall would show fragmentation of elastic fibers. The disorder is most likely caused by a mutation in the gene for which of the following?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Fibrillin-1 (FBN1)
explanationHtml: Marfan syndrome is autosomal dominant. Fibrillin-1 is a microfibril glycoprotein that scaffolds elastin and holds TGF-β in a latent form. Defective fibrillin allows excess TGF-β signaling and weakens connective tissue. That produces cystic medial degeneration of the aorta (root dilation, dissection), mitral valve prolapse, superotemporal (upward) lens subluxation, and skeletal overgrowth. Losartan and β-blockers slow aortic root dilation.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: osteogenesis imperfecta. B: vascular Ehlers–Danlos (arterial and bowel rupture, no lens displacement or tall stature). C: Williams syndrome (supravalvular aortic stenosis). D: homocystinuria, where the lenses dislocate downward (inferonasally), with thrombosis and intellectual disability.

stemHtml: A 40-year-old woman has a firm left thyroid nodule. She reports episodes of pounding headache, sweating, and palpitations, and her blood pressure during one episode was 210/115 mm Hg. Her father died of a "thyroid tumor" in his 40s. Fine-needle aspiration shows nests of spindle and polygonal cells in a stroma that stains with Congo red and shows apple-green birefringence. Serum calcitonin is markedly elevated. Germline testing would most likely show a mutation in which of the following genes?
answerHtml: Answer: D. RET
explanationHtml: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells, which make calcitonin. The amyloid comes from calcitonin. MTC together with pheochromocytoma is MEN2A (with hyperparathyroidism) or MEN2B (with mucosal neuromas and a marfanoid habitus). Both are caused by activating germline mutations of the RET receptor tyrosine kinase, inherited as autosomal dominant. Before thyroid surgery, pheochromocytoma must be excluded with plasma free metanephrines and removed first. Carriers of high-risk RET mutations undergo prophylactic thyroidectomy in childhood.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: MEN1 (parathyroid, pituitary, pancreatic tumors). B: papillary thyroid carcinoma. C: follicular carcinoma. E: VHL causes pheochromocytoma but not MTC.

stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman returns to discuss biopsy results with her physician. After a warning that the news is serious, she is told that she has pancreatic adenocarcinoma that has spread to the liver. She looks down, becomes tearful, and says nothing. Which of the following is the most appropriate next response from the physician?

options.label: A
options.html: Immediately describe the available chemotherapy regimens and their response rates

options.label: B
options.html: Allow a period of silence, then acknowledge her emotion, such as "This is very hard news to hear."

options.label: C
options.html: Reassure her that many patients with this cancer do well with treatment

options.label: D
options.html: Refer her to a psychiatrist to manage her reaction

options.label: E
options.html: Leave the room so she can be alone and return the next day

answerHtml: Answer: B. Silence and empathic acknowledgment
explanationHtml: The SPIKES protocol (Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, Strategy and Summary) calls for responding to emotion with empathy before giving more information. A patient who is in shock retains very little factual detail. Sitting with her, allowing silence, and naming the emotion builds trust. The treatment discussion can follow once she is ready.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: gives information too early, and she will not absorb it. C: false reassurance, since metastatic pancreatic cancer has a poor prognosis. D: grief is a normal reaction, not a psychiatric disorder. E: abandons the patient at a vulnerable moment.

stemHtml: A 46-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease receives a deceased-donor kidney transplant. Minutes after the vascular clamps are released, the graft, which had turned pink, becomes mottled and cyanotic and stops producing urine. Biopsy shows widespread thrombosis of glomerular capillaries and arterioles with neutrophil infiltration. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism?

options.label: A
options.html: Recipient CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells recognizing donor MHC class I

options.label: B
options.html: Donor T cells attacking recipient tissues

options.label: C
options.html: Preformed recipient antibodies binding donor endothelial antigens and activating complement

options.label: D
options.html: Progressive intimal fibrosis of graft arteries over months

options.label: E
options.html: Recipient IgE bound to mast cells reacting with donor antigens
