answerHtml: Answer: C. Preformed antibodies (hyperacute rejection)
explanationHtml: Hyperacute rejection begins within minutes of reperfusion. It is a type II hypersensitivity: preformed anti-ABO or anti-HLA antibodies, from prior transfusion, pregnancy, or transplant, bind graft endothelium and activate complement, causing thrombosis and ischemic necrosis. The graft must be removed. ABO matching and pre-transplant crossmatching prevent it.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: acute cellular rejection occurs weeks to months after transplant. B: graft-versus-host disease occurs mainly after hematopoietic stem cell transplant and targets the recipient's skin, gut, and liver, not the graft. D: chronic rejection develops over months to years. E: graft rejection is not mediated by IgE.

stemHtml: In a 5-year randomized controlled trial of adults with atrial fibrillation, ischemic stroke occurs in 10% of patients given placebo and 6% of patients given a new oral anticoagulant. How many patients need to be treated with the new drug for 5 years to prevent one stroke?
answerHtml: Answer: D. 25
explanationHtml: Absolute risk reduction = 10% − 6% = 4% = 0.04. NNT = 1 / ARR = 1 / 0.04 = 25, over the 5-year trial period.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: E (40) is the relative risk reduction as a percentage (0.04 / 0.10 = 40%), not the NNT. A (4) is the ARR as a percentage, not its reciprocal. B (6) is the treated-group event rate, and C (10) is 1 / the placebo event rate. Neither is an NNT.

stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman who emigrated from India had several months of joint pain and fever as a child. She now has progressive exertional dyspnea, difficulty swallowing solid food, and a hoarse voice. Pulse is irregularly irregular. Auscultation shows a loud S1, an early diastolic opening snap, and a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex. Laryngoscopy shows left vocal cord paralysis. Her hoarseness is most likely caused by enlargement of which of the following structures?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Left atrium
explanationHtml: Rheumatic mitral stenosis causes pressure overload of the left atrium and LA dilation, which predisposes to atrial fibrillation and LA thrombus. The LA is the most posterior chamber. When enlarged it presses on the esophagus (dysphagia) and can compress the left recurrent laryngeal nerve against the pulmonary artery (Ortner syndrome, hoarseness). On auscultation, a shorter S2–opening snap interval indicates more severe stenosis.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: the LV is underfilled in mitral stenosis. C and D: these enlarge later with pulmonary hypertension but do not lie next to the recurrent laryngeal nerve or esophagus. E: the left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch, not the ascending aorta, and the stem points to mitral stenosis.

stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman develops sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea on day 3 after hip surgery. Heart rate is 118/min and respirations 28/min. Arterial blood gas on room air: pH 7.48, PaCO<sub>2</sub> 30 mm Hg, PaO<sub>2</sub> 62 mm Hg. Chest x-ray is clear. CT angiography shows a large embolus occluding the right lower lobe pulmonary artery. In the right lower lobe alveoli supplied by the occluded artery, which of the following best describes gas exchange?

options.label: B
options.html: Diffusion limitation from a thickened alveolar–capillary membrane

options.label: D
options.html: V/Q ratio lower than normal, with alveolar gas resembling mixed venous blood

options.label: E
options.html: V/Q ratio approaching infinity, with alveolar gas resembling inspired air

answerHtml: Answer: E. Dead space (V/Q → ∞)
explanationHtml: Alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused are physiologic dead space. No gas is exchanged, so alveolar PO2 and PCO2 approach those of humidified inspired air (about 150 and 0 mm Hg). The patient's systemic hypoxemia and widened A–a gradient come from blood being diverted to the rest of the lung, creating areas of low V/Q, plus atelectasis and bronchoconstriction. Hyperventilation causes the respiratory alkalosis.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and D: shunt and low V/Q (pneumonia, atelectasis, edema) describe perfused but poorly ventilated alveoli, the opposite. B: fibrosis. C: alveolar hypoventilation raises PaCO<sub>2</sub>.

stemHtml:
A 22-year-old woman has fatigue and palpitations. She has calluses on the dorsum of her right hand, bilateral parotid enlargement, and dental enamel erosion. She is normotensive with dry mucous membranes. Laboratory studies:
TestResult
Na+136 mEq/L
K+2.9 mEq/L
Cl−86 mEq/L
HCO3−36 mEq/L
Arterial pH7.51
PaCO247 mm Hg
Urine Cl−8 mEq/L (low)
Which of the following best explains why her alkalosis persists?

options.label: A
options.html: Ongoing renal loss of H<sup>+</sup> caused by a diuretic

options.label: B
options.html: Autonomous aldosterone secretion by an adrenal adenoma

options.label: C
options.html: Volume and chloride depletion activating the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, which increases renal HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> reabsorption and H<sup>+</sup> secretion

answerHtml: Answer: C. Volume/Cl<sup>−</sup> depletion maintains the alkalosis
explanationHtml: Self-induced vomiting (bulimia nervosa: Russell sign, parotid hypertrophy, enamel erosion) generates the alkalosis by removing gastric HCl. The alkalosis is maintained by the kidney. Volume contraction activates RAAS, angiotensin II increases proximal Na+/H+ exchange and HCO3− reabsorption, and aldosterone increases distal H+ and K+ secretion. Low filtered Cl− also limits pendrin-mediated HCO3− excretion. A low urine Cl− marks it as "saline-responsive", and it corrects with NaCl and KCl. Expected compensation: PaCO2 rises by about 0.7 × ΔHCO3−, giving about 48 mm Hg, which is appropriate here.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: during active diuretic use urine Cl− is high. B: primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension, a high urine Cl−, and volume expansion. D: GI bicarbonate loss (diarrhea) causes acidosis. E: hypoventilation is appropriate compensation and does not keep the HCO3− high.

stemHtml: A 45-year-old man has multiple ulcers in the distal duodenum and jejunum that have not responded to standard-dose proton pump inhibitor therapy, along with chronic watery diarrhea. He has had two calcium-containing kidney stones and serum calcium of 11.2 mg/dL. His brother has a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma. Fasting serum gastrin, measured after PPIs were held, is markedly elevated. Which of the following results is expected after IV secretin is given?

options.label: A
options.html: A marked decrease in serum gastrin

options.label: B
options.html: A further rise in serum gastrin

options.label: C
options.html: No change in gastrin with a large rise in somatostatin

options.label: D
options.html: A rise in serum insulin with hypoglycemia

answerHtml: Answer: B. Paradoxical rise in gastrin
explanationHtml: Refractory distal ulcers with diarrhea suggest gastrinoma (Zollinger–Ellison syndrome). Hyperparathyroidism and a family pituitary adenoma point to MEN1 (menin, autosomal dominant). Gastrinoma cells express secretin receptors, so secretin stimulates them, and gastrin rises by more than about 120 pg/mL. Normal G cells, and the hypergastrinemia caused by achlorhydria or PPIs, are inhibited by secretin or show little change. Diarrhea occurs because excess acid inactivates pancreatic lipase and damages the mucosa.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: this is the normal response or the response to non-tumor hypergastrinemia. C: somatostatinoma is not suggested and this is not the secretin-test result. D: insulinoma (also part of MEN1) is diagnosed by a supervised fast, not a secretin test. E: calcitonin relates to medullary thyroid cancer in MEN2.

stemHtml:
A 42-year-old woman has gained 15 kg over a year, mostly in her trunk, with wide purple abdominal striae, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness, and new hypertension. She takes no medications. Results:
TestResult
24-h urinary free cortisol3× upper limit of normal
Late-night salivary cortisolElevated
Plasma ACTH (8 AM)Mildly elevated
Low-dose (1 mg) dexamethasone suppressionNo suppression of cortisol
High-dose (8 mg) dexamethasone suppressionCortisol suppressed by >50%
Which of the following is the most likely cause?

options.label: C
options.html: Ectopic ACTH secretion by small cell lung carcinoma

answerHtml: Answer: D. Pituitary corticotroph adenoma (Cushing disease)
explanationHtml: Hypercortisolism is confirmed, and an inappropriately normal or high ACTH means it is ACTH-dependent. Pituitary corticotroph adenomas keep some glucocorticoid feedback, so high-dose dexamethasone suppresses them. Ectopic ACTH sources usually do not suppress. In current practice, MRI of the pituitary and, when needed, inferior petrosal sinus sampling have largely replaced the high-dose test, but the physiology is still tested. Women are affected more often than men.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B, and E: ACTH would be suppressed by the exogenous steroid or by autonomous adrenal cortisol, and adrenal carcinoma often adds androgen excess. C: ectopic ACTH typically gives very high ACTH, hypokalemia, and no suppression on high-dose dexamethasone.

stemHtml: A 25-year-old woman at 14 weeks' gestation by dates has painless vaginal bleeding and severe nausea and vomiting. Her uterus is at the level of the umbilicus. She has a fine tremor and heart rate of 112/min. Serum β-hCG is 250,000 mIU/mL and TSH is suppressed. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a heterogeneous "snowstorm" pattern with many cystic spaces, no fetus, and bilateral multiloculated ovarian cysts. Cytogenetic analysis of the evacuated tissue would most likely show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: 46,XX with all chromosomes of paternal origin

options.label: B
options.html: 69,XXY with two paternal sets and one maternal set

options.label: C
options.html: 46,XX with one maternal and one paternal set

answerHtml: Answer: A. 46,XX androgenetic (complete mole)
explanationHtml: A complete hydatidiform mole forms when an "empty" ovum, without maternal DNA, is fertilized by one sperm that duplicates (usually 46,XX) or, less often, by two sperm (46,XY). There is no fetal tissue. hCG is very high, causing theca-lutein cysts, hyperemesis, and hyperthyroidism, because hCG shares an α-subunit with TSH and its β-subunit is similar enough to activate the TSH receptor. Complete moles do not express p57 (a maternally expressed gene) and carry about a 15–20% risk of persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, including choriocarcinoma. hCG is followed to zero after evacuation.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: a partial mole is triploid with fetal parts and lower hCG. C: a normal conceptus. D and E: common karyotypes in spontaneous abortions (trisomy 16 is the most common autosomal trisomy in miscarriages), not molar pregnancy.

stemHtml: A 26-year-old man is stabbed in the back. MRI shows a lesion that cuts the right half of the spinal cord at the T10 level. Which of the following sets of findings is most likely below the level of the lesion?

options.label: A
options.html: Bilateral loss of pain and temperature in a band at T10 only, with preserved vibration

options.label: B
options.html: Left-sided weakness and left-sided loss of vibration; right-sided loss of pain and temperature

options.label: C
options.html: Bilateral weakness and bilateral loss of pain and temperature with preserved vibration and proprioception

options.label: D
options.html: Bilateral loss of vibration and proprioception only

options.label: E
options.html: Right-sided weakness and right-sided loss of vibration and proprioception; left-sided loss of pain and temperature

answerHtml: Answer: E. Brown-Séquard syndrome
explanationHtml: Below a hemisection, the lateral corticospinal tract (already crossed in the medulla) causes ipsilateral UMN weakness, and the dorsal columns (which cross in the medulla) cause ipsilateral loss of vibration and proprioception. The spinothalamic tract crosses within 1–2 segments of entry through the anterior white commissure, so pain and temperature are lost contralaterally, starting 1–2 levels below the lesion. At the level of the lesion there may be ipsilateral LMN signs and a band of complete sensory loss.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: central cord or syringomyelia ("cape" distribution in the cervical cord). B: a left hemisection (the sides are reversed). C: anterior spinal artery syndrome. D: posterior column disease (tabes dorsalis or B12 deficiency, though B12 deficiency also involves the corticospinal tracts).

stemHtml: A 5-year-old boy falls often and has trouble climbing stairs. To stand up from the floor, he pushes on his thighs with his hands. Both calves are enlarged and firm. Serum creatine kinase is 15,000 U/L. Muscle biopsy shows fiber necrosis, regeneration, and replacement by fat and fibrous tissue, and immunostaining shows no dystrophin. Which of the following types of mutation is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: In-frame deletion in the dystrophin gene

options.label: B
options.html: CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion in DMPK

options.label: C
options.html: Frameshift deletion in the dystrophin gene

options.label: E
options.html: Missense mutation in the β-myosin heavy chain gene

answerHtml: Answer: C. Frameshift deletion (Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
explanationHtml: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is X-linked recessive and most often caused by deletions in the very large DMD gene that shift the reading frame. The result is a truncated, unstable protein, and dystrophin is absent. Without dystrophin, the sarcolemma is no longer linked to the extracellular matrix, and fibers are damaged by contraction. Signs are the Gowers sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, and death from cardiomyopathy or respiratory failure. Exon-skipping antisense drugs are designed to restore the reading frame.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Becker dystrophy has reduced or abnormal dystrophin and a milder, later course. B: myotonic dystrophy (myotonia, cataracts, frontal balding). D: spinal muscular atrophy causes LMN weakness with fasciculations and a normal or mildly raised CK. E: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old man of Mediterranean ancestry is given an antimalarial drug to eradicate liver-stage parasites after returning from a deployment. Two days later he has dark urine, jaundice, and fatigue. Hemoglobin has fallen from 14.5 to 9.1 g/dL, and indirect bilirubin and LDH are elevated. Peripheral smear shows red cells with "bites" taken from their edges, and supravital staining shows small dark inclusions. Direct antiglobulin test is negative. Which of the following best explains his hemolysis?

options.label: A
options.html: Defective spectrin in the red cell cytoskeleton

options.label: B
options.html: Insufficient NADPH to keep glutathione reduced

options.label: C
options.html: ATP depletion from deficient pyruvate kinase

options.label: D
options.html: Warm IgG autoantibodies against red cell antigens

options.label: E
options.html: Absence of GPI-anchored complement regulatory proteins

answerHtml: Answer: B. G6PD deficiency
explanationHtml: Primaquine (and tafenoquine), which clear hypnozoites, are oxidant stresses. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is the rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway and the red cell's only source of NADPH. Without NADPH, glutathione cannot be regenerated and H2O2 oxidizes hemoglobin. Denatured hemoglobin precipitates as Heinz bodies, which splenic macrophages "bite" out. The disorder is X-linked. G6PD testing is required before giving primaquine or tafenoquine. Results can be falsely normal during acute hemolysis because older, deficient cells have already lysed.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: hereditary spherocytosis (spherocytes, osmotic fragility test or EMA binding). C: pyruvate kinase deficiency causes chronic hemolysis that is not triggered by oxidants. D: the DAT is negative. E: PNH (CD55/CD59, flow cytometry).

stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman is in the hospital on day 6 of IV ceftriaxone for pneumonia. She develops 8 watery stools a day, crampy abdominal pain, and a temperature of 38.4°C (101.1°F). WBC count is 22,000/mm<sup>3</sup>. Stool testing is positive for glutamate dehydrogenase antigen and toxin. The organism's major toxins cause disease by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Glucosylation of Rho-family GTPases, disrupting the actin cytoskeleton of colonocytes

options.label: B
options.html: ADP-ribosylation of the G<sub>s</sub>α subunit, raising cAMP

options.label: C
options.html: Removal of an adenine from 28S rRNA of the 60S ribosomal subunit

options.label: D
options.html: Activation of guanylate cyclase, raising cGMP

answerHtml: Answer: A. Glucosylation of Rho GTPases (C. difficile toxins A and B)
explanationHtml: Clostridioides difficile toxin A (enterotoxin) and toxin B (cytotoxin) are glucosyltransferases that inactivate Rho, Rac, and Cdc42. Actin depolymerizes, tight junctions open, colonocytes die, and inflammation forms pseudomembranes. The 2021 IDSA/SHEA update recommends oral fidaxomicin as preferred, with oral vancomycin as an acceptable alternative, for an initial episode. Metronidazole is no longer first-line.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: cholera toxin and E. coli LT. C: Shiga toxin and Shiga-like toxins. D: E. coli heat-stable toxin. E: C. perfringens α-toxin (lecithinase).

stemHtml: A resident realizes that a hospitalized 60-year-old man was given a second dose of subcutaneous enoxaparin 4 hours after his first because of an order-entry error. The patient has no bleeding, and his hemoglobin and platelet count are unchanged. The attending physician tells the resident that the patient does not need to be told because no harm occurred. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.html: Do not tell the patient, since there were no adverse consequences

options.label: B
options.html: File an institutional incident report and do not tell the patient

options.label: C
options.html: Tell the patient's family but not the patient

options.label: D
options.html: Tell the patient about the error honestly, explain the monitoring plan, and report it through the institution's safety system

options.label: E
options.html: Wait until discharge and tell the patient only if bleeding develops

answerHtml: Answer: D. Disclose the error to the patient
explanationHtml: Physicians must disclose medical errors to patients, including errors that have not caused harm, especially when the error carries ongoing risk that needs monitoring, as here with bleeding risk. Disclosure means saying what happened, its possible consequences, what is being done, and how it will be prevented. An apology is appropriate. Reporting through the safety system supports systems improvement, but it does not replace telling the patient.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B, and E: withholding the information violates honesty and the patient's autonomy. C: the patient has capacity, and telling his family instead breaches confidentiality.

stemHtml: A new oral antiarrhythmic drug has a volume of distribution of 40 L, an elimination half-life of 12 hours, and an oral bioavailability of 50%. A target plasma concentration of 4 mg/L is needed quickly. Which of the following oral loading doses is most appropriate?
answerHtml: Answer: E. 320 mg
explanationHtml: Loading dose = (Cp × Vd) / F = (4 mg/L × 40 L) / 0.5 = 320 mg. The loading dose depends on volume of distribution, not half-life or clearance. Without a loading dose, steady state takes about 4–5 half-lives, here 2–2.5 days. Maintenance dose = (Cp × CL × τ) / F.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: C (160 mg) is the IV loading dose, which ignores bioavailability. B (80 mg) wrongly multiplies by F instead of dividing. A and D come from other arithmetic errors.

stemHtml: A 68-year-old man has 3 weeks of fevers, night sweats, and fatigue. He has a new holosystolic murmur at the apex and splinter hemorrhages. He does not use injection drugs, has no dental problems, and has no prosthetic valves. Blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in chains that are nonhemolytic, grow in 40% bile, and hydrolyze esculin, but do not grow in 6.5% NaCl. Transesophageal echocardiography shows a mitral valve vegetation. Further evaluation is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: E
options.html: Urinary tract obstruction from prostatic hyperplasia

answerHtml: Answer: B. Colorectal neoplasia (Streptococcus gallolyticus)
explanationHtml: A group D streptococcus that grows in bile and hydrolyzes esculin but does not grow in 6.5% NaCl is S. gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis biotype I). Bacteremia or endocarditis with this organism is strongly associated with colorectal adenomas and carcinoma, so colonoscopy is required.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: D: viridans streptococci (α-hemolytic, optochin-resistant) after dental work. E: Enterococcus grows in 6.5% NaCl and often follows GU instrumentation. C: catheter-related endocarditis is usually S. aureus or coagulase-negative staphylococci. A: rheumatic valves predispose to viridans-streptococcal endocarditis.

stemHtml: A 64-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history becomes confused. He appears euvolemic. Serum Na<sup>+</sup> is 121 mEq/L, serum osmolality 255 mOsm/kg, and urine osmolality 520 mOsm/kg. CT of the chest shows a large central mass next to the right main bronchus with bulky mediastinal nodes. Bronchoscopic biopsy shows sheets of small cells with scant cytoplasm, finely granular chromatin, nuclear molding, and crush artifact, and the cells stain for chromogranin and synaptophysin. This tumor type is most often associated with which other paraneoplastic disorder?

options.label: C
options.html: Proximal weakness from antibodies to presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels

options.label: E
options.html: Fatigable ptosis from antibodies to postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors

answerHtml: Answer: C. Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome
explanationHtml: Small cell (neuroendocrine) lung carcinoma is central, strongly linked to smoking, and positive for chromogranin and synaptophysin. Its typical paraneoplastic syndromes are SIADH (this patient's euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine), ectopic ACTH, Lambert–Eaton syndrome (anti-P/Q-type VGCC antibodies, proximal weakness that improves with repeated effort, autonomic symptoms, depressed reflexes), and anti-Hu paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: squamous cell carcinoma. B: most often lung adenocarcinoma and other non-small cell cancers. D: renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, and hemangioblastoma. E: myasthenia gravis, associated with thymoma.

stemHtml: An 8-year-old boy has cola-colored urine and puffy eyelids. Three weeks ago he had a sore throat and fever that resolved without treatment. Blood pressure is 142/92 mm Hg. Urinalysis shows red cell casts and 1+ protein. Serum C3 is low, C4 is normal, and anti-DNase B titer is elevated. Which of the following is most likely on electron microscopy of a renal biopsy?

options.label: C
options.html: No deposits, with linear IgG along the GBM on immunofluorescence

options.label: D
options.html: Isolated effacement of podocyte foot processes

options.label: E
options.html: Mesangial deposits only, with IgA on immunofluorescence

answerHtml: Answer: A. Subepithelial humps (post-streptococcal GN)
explanationHtml: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis follows pharyngitis by 1–3 weeks or skin infection by 3–6 weeks. It is an immune complex (type III) disease that activates the alternative pathway and lowers C3. Light microscopy shows enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with neutrophils. Immunofluorescence shows granular "lumpy-bumpy" IgG, IgM, and C3. EM shows subepithelial humps. Children usually recover completely, and C3 returns to normal within about 8 weeks.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis. C: anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease. D: minimal change disease, which is nephrotic. E: IgA nephropathy, which causes hematuria during or within days of infection (synpharyngitic) with normal C3.

stemHtml:
A 30-year-old man had jaundice and dark urine 2 months ago, and these are now improving. He had unprotected sex with a new partner 4 months ago. He has never been vaccinated against hepatitis B. Hepatitis serologies:
MarkerResult
HBsAgNegative
Anti-HBsNegative
IgM anti-HBcPositive
HBeAgNegative
Anti-HAV IgMNegative
Anti-HCVNegative
Which of the following best describes his hepatitis B status?

options.label: E
options.html: Recent acute infection in the window period

answerHtml: Answer: E. Window period of acute hepatitis B
explanationHtml: In the window period, HBsAg has cleared but anti-HBs cannot yet be detected. IgM anti-HBc is then the only positive marker and the only proof of recent infection. Chronic infection is defined as HBsAg persisting for more than 6 months. In adults, more than 90% of acute infections resolve.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: vaccination gives anti-HBs only, with no anti-HBc, because the vaccine contains HBsAg alone. B: requires HBsAg positivity. C: shows IgG anti-HBc plus anti-HBs. D: anti-HBc is positive, so he has been infected.

stemHtml: A 56-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is taking metformin. A second oral agent is added. Three months later her HbA1c has fallen from 8.4% to 7.5%, she has lost 3 kg, and her systolic blood pressure has fallen by 5 mm Hg. She now has vulvar itching with a thick white discharge, and KOH preparation shows budding yeast and pseudohyphae. Urine glucose is strongly positive with a serum glucose of 140 mg/dL. The added drug most likely acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibition of the sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 in the proximal tubule

options.label: E
options.html: Closure of ATP-sensitive K<sup>+</sup> channels in β cells

answerHtml: Answer: D. SGLT2 inhibition (e.g., empagliflozin, dapagliflozin)
explanationHtml: SGLT2 reabsorbs about 90% of filtered glucose in the S1–S2 segments of the proximal tubule. Blocking it causes glucosuria at normal glucose levels, which leads to calorie loss (weight loss), mild osmotic diuresis and natriuresis (lower BP), and genital mycotic infections. SGLT2 inhibitors reduce heart failure hospitalization and slow CKD progression, so they are preferred in HFrEF (ADA Standards of Care). Other risks: euglycemic DKA, volume depletion, and rarely Fournier gangrene.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: GLP-1 agonists cause weight loss but not glucosuria or yeast infections, and their main effects are GI. B: DPP-4 inhibitors are weight-neutral. C: thiazolidinediones cause weight gain and fluid retention and are contraindicated in heart failure. E: sulfonylureas cause weight gain and hypoglycemia.

stemHtml: A 55-year-old woman has a poorly defined thickening in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast, and mammography shows subtle architectural distortion without calcifications. Core biopsy shows small, uniform, discohesive tumor cells invading the stroma in single-file lines and in concentric rings around normal ducts, with no gland formation. The tumor is strongly estrogen-receptor positive. The tumor cells have most likely lost expression of which of the following proteins?
answerHtml: Answer: B. E-cadherin (invasive lobular carcinoma)
explanationHtml: Invasive lobular carcinoma results from loss of the CDH1 gene product E-cadherin, a calcium-dependent adhesion molecule of adherens junctions. Without it the cells come apart (discohesion) and invade in single file and "targetoid" rings. These tumors are often multicentric and bilateral, usually ER/PR positive, and can be hard to see on mammography. Germline CDH1 mutations also cause hereditary diffuse gastric (signet ring) cancer.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: HER2 is amplified, not lost, in a subset of breast cancers and is uncommon in classic lobular carcinoma. C: the stem states ER is strongly positive. D: carcinomas are epithelial and keep cytokeratin. E: lobular carcinomas are usually PR positive as well.

stemHtml: A 50-year-old man with long-standing alcohol use disorder is found confused and is given IV 5% dextrose in the emergency department. Over the next hours he becomes more disoriented. Examination shows horizontal nystagmus, bilateral lateral rectus weakness, and a wide-based, unsteady gait. Deficiency of a cofactor needed by which of the following enzymes is most likely responsible?
answerHtml: Answer: C. α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (thiamine/TPP)
explanationHtml: Wernicke encephalopathy, with confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia, is caused by thiamine deficiency. Thiamine pyrophosphate is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase, and transketolase. A glucose load increases flux through these enzymes, consumes the remaining thiamine, and worsens brain energy failure, especially in the mammillary bodies and periaqueductal gray. Give IV thiamine before or together with glucose. Untreated, it can progress to Korsakoff syndrome (amnesia, confabulation).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: biotin. B: vitamin B12 (adenosylcobalamin). D: riboflavin (FAD). E: vitamin C.

stemHtml: A 60-year-old fair-skinned man has a 9-mm pigmented lesion on his upper back that has grown over the past year. It is asymmetric, with irregular borders and areas of brown, black, and blue-gray. Excisional biopsy shows atypical melanocytes in nests and single cells spreading through the epidermis and invading the dermis. Which of the following features of this lesion is the most important predictor of metastasis?

options.label: A
options.html: Depth of invasion measured from the granular layer of the epidermis

options.label: C
options.html: Number of colors in the lesion

options.label: E
options.html: Presence of a BRAF V600E mutation

answerHtml: Answer: A. Breslow thickness
explanationHtml: For primary cutaneous melanoma, the most important prognostic factor is tumor thickness (Breslow depth, in mm, from the top of the granular layer to the deepest invasive cell). Thickness reflects the vertical growth phase, which brings the tumor into contact with dermal lymphatics and vessels. Ulceration is the second T-stage factor in AJCC staging, and sentinel lymph node status is the strongest predictor overall once it is known.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, C (ABCDE features), and D help with clinical suspicion or modestly affect prognosis, but they are far weaker predictors than depth. E: BRAF V600E is present in about half of melanomas and predicts response to BRAF/MEK inhibitors (e.g., vemurafenib, dabrafenib plus trametinib), not metastasis.

stemHtml:
A 32-year-old woman has fever, confusion, and new petechiae. Her neurologic findings change over hours, including transient right-arm weakness. She has not had diarrhea. Laboratory studies:
TestResult
Hemoglobin7.8 g/dL
Platelets18,000/mm3
Peripheral smearNumerous schistocytes
LDH1,450 U/L (high)
HaptoglobinUndetectable
Indirect bilirubin3.2 mg/dL
PT / aPTTNormal
FibrinogenNormal
Creatinine1.6 mg/dL
Direct antiglobulin testNegative
Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism?

options.label: A
options.html: Shiga toxin–mediated injury to glomerular endothelium

options.label: B
options.html: Tissue factor–driven consumption of coagulation factors

options.label: D
options.html: IgG antibodies to platelet factor 4–heparin complexes

options.label: E
options.html: Autoantibody-mediated deficiency of a von Willebrand factor–cleaving metalloprotease

answerHtml: Answer: E. ADAMTS13 deficiency (TTP)
explanationHtml: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes, high LDH, low haptoglobin, DAT negative) with severe thrombocytopenia, changing neurologic deficits, fever, and mild renal injury, but normal coagulation tests, is thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Acquired TTP is caused by IgG autoantibodies that inhibit ADAMTS13. Ultra-large vWF multimers then remain uncleaved and form platelet-rich microthrombi. It is an emergency treated with plasma exchange, glucocorticoids, and often caplacizumab or rituximab. Platelet transfusion is avoided unless there is life-threatening bleeding.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: HUS follows bloody diarrhea and causes more severe renal failure. B: DIC prolongs PT/PTT and lowers fibrinogen. C: ITP causes no hemolysis or schistocytes. D: HIT requires heparin exposure and does not cause MAHA.

stemHtml: A 34-year-old man receives antivenom made from sheep immunoglobulin after a rattlesnake bite and recovers. Ten days later he has fever, an itchy urticarial rash, painful swollen knees and wrists, and lymphadenopathy. Urinalysis shows mild proteinuria. Serum C3 and C4 are low. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: Cross-linking of IgE on mast cells by sheep proteins

options.label: B
options.html: IgG antibodies binding antigens fixed to the patient's own cell surfaces

options.label: C
options.html: CD4<sup>+</sup> Th1 cells releasing cytokines and activating macrophages

options.label: D
options.html: Deposition of circulating antigen–antibody complexes in vessel walls with complement activation

answerHtml: Answer: D. Immune complex deposition (serum sickness, type III)
explanationHtml: About 1–2 weeks after foreign protein is given (antivenom, antithymocyte globulin, chimeric monoclonal antibodies), the host makes IgG while antigen is still in excess. Small and intermediate-sized immune complexes form, deposit in vessels, synovium, and glomeruli, activate complement (low C3/C4), and recruit neutrophils. The result is fever, rash, arthralgia, and glomerulonephritis. Symptoms resolve as the antigen is cleared.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: anaphylaxis occurs within minutes. B: type II (for example, autoimmune hemolysis). C: type IV delayed hypersensitivity does not involve complement consumption. E: anaphylactoid reactions (vancomycin, opioids, radiocontrast) are immediate.

stemHtml: A new imaging test detects a type of lung cancer an average of 2 years earlier than symptoms would. In a study, patients diagnosed by the test survive an average of 4 years from diagnosis, compared with 2 years for patients diagnosed after symptoms appear. Average age at death from the cancer is the same in both groups. Which of the following best explains the apparent survival benefit?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Lead-time bias
explanationHtml: Earlier detection starts the survival clock earlier without delaying death. The 2 "extra" years equal the lead time, and the unchanged age at death shows there is no real benefit. Compare mortality rates, or adjust for lead time, rather than survival from diagnosis.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: length-time bias means screening preferentially finds slow-growing, less aggressive tumors, which improves survival statistics in a different way. C: selection bias comes from nonrandom selection of participants, such as healthier volunteers. D: recall bias applies to retrospective exposure data. E: observer bias comes from unblinded assessment of outcomes.

stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman taking sertraline for depression is admitted with an abscess and cellulitis caused by methicillin-resistant S. aureus, and IV linezolid is started. The next day she is agitated, diaphoretic, and has diarrhea. Temperature is 39.4°C (103°F), heart rate 128/min, and she has inducible ankle clonus and hyperreflexia that is worse in the legs. Which property of linezolid most likely caused this reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: Inhibition of CYP2D6, raising sertraline levels

options.label: E
options.html: Inhibition of the serotonin reuptake transporter

answerHtml: Answer: C. MAO inhibition
explanationHtml: Linezolid is a weak, reversible, nonselective MAO inhibitor in addition to binding the 50S subunit (23S rRNA) to prevent the initiation complex. Combined with an SSRI, it can cause serotonin syndrome: autonomic instability, altered mental status, and neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia worse in the lower limbs). Management is to stop the serotonergic drugs, give supportive care and benzodiazepines, and give cyproheptadine (a 5-HT2A antagonist) if needed. Similar MAOI interactions occur with methylene blue.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: linezolid is not a significant CYP inhibitor (fluoxetine and paroxetine inhibit CYP2D6). B: D<sub>2</sub> blockade causes neuroleptic malignant syndrome, with lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, and slower onset. D: anticholinergic toxicity causes dry skin, hyperthermia, and no clonus. E: this is sertraline's own action, not linezolid's.

stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy with a congenital heart defect has episodes of sudden cyanosis and rapid breathing while playing. During these episodes he stops and squats, and his color improves. Examination shows a harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border and a single S2. Chest x-ray shows an upturned cardiac apex with decreased pulmonary vascular markings. Squatting most likely improves his oxygenation by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Increasing systemic vascular resistance, which reduces right-to-left flow across the ventricular septal defect

options.label: B
options.html: Decreasing venous return to the right heart

options.label: E
options.html: Increasing right ventricular outflow tract obstruction

answerHtml: Answer: A. Increased SVR reduces the right-to-left shunt
explanationHtml: Tetralogy of Fallot consists of pulmonary (infundibular) stenosis, RV hypertrophy (boot-shaped heart), overriding aorta, and VSD. It arises from anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum. Shunt direction across the VSD depends on the balance between RVOT obstruction and SVR. Squatting kinks the femoral arteries and raises SVR, which pushes more RV blood into the pulmonary artery. During a "tet spell," treatment includes knee-to-chest positioning, oxygen, morphine, IV fluids, β-blockers, and phenylephrine.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: squatting increases venous return. C: PVR is not the main variable, since the obstruction is fixed and dynamic in the infundibulum. D: squatting does not affect the ductus. E: more RVOT obstruction (infundibular spasm) triggers the spells.

stemHtml: A 35-year-old woman with adult-onset asthma and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps develops severe wheezing, nasal congestion, and facial flushing 45 minutes after taking ibuprofen for a headache. She has had similar reactions to aspirin. Skin testing for ibuprofen-specific IgE is negative. Which of the following best explains her reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: Drug-specific IgE cross-linking on mast cells

options.label: B
options.html: Increased production of bronchoprotective prostaglandin E<sub>2</sub>

options.label: D
options.html: Shunting of arachidonic acid through 5-lipoxygenase, increasing cysteinyl leukotriene production

options.label: E
options.html: Downregulation of β<sub>2</sub>-adrenergic receptors in airway smooth muscle

answerHtml: Answer: D. Arachidonic acid shunted to the leukotriene pathway
explanationHtml: In aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (Samter triad), COX-1 inhibition removes PGE2, which normally restrains mast cells and 5-lipoxygenase. Arachidonic acid is then diverted to LTC4/D4/E4, which cause bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, and vascular leak. The reaction is pharmacologic, not IgE-mediated. Leukotriene modifiers (montelukast, zileuton) help, and aspirin desensitization is an option. Selective COX-2 inhibitors are generally tolerated.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: the reaction is not IgE-mediated, and her reactions to several chemically unrelated NSAIDs point to COX inhibition. B: PGE2 decreases. C: not an immune complex disease. E: not the mechanism of acute NSAID sensitivity.

stemHtml:
A 30-year-old man has polyuria (about 7 L/day) and constant thirst since a motorcycle crash with a basilar skull fracture 3 weeks ago. A water deprivation test is performed:
MeasurementBaselineAfter 8 h water deprivation1 h after desmopressin
Urine osmolality (mOsm/kg)110140510
Serum Na+ (mEq/L)143149147
Serum osmolality (mOsm/kg)292306302
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Central diabetes insipidus (arginine vasopressin deficiency)
explanationHtml: The urine does not concentrate despite rising serum osmolality, so ADH action is deficient. A large rise in urine osmolality after desmopressin (more than about 50%) shows the collecting duct responds normally, which puts the defect in ADH secretion. Head trauma, especially basilar skull fracture, can damage the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary. Treat with desmopressin. Current nomenclature: central DI is "AVP deficiency" and nephrogenic DI is "AVP resistance."
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: in primary polydipsia, urine concentrates with deprivation and serum Na<sup>+</sup> stays low-normal. B: nephrogenic DI shows little or no response to desmopressin. C: SIADH causes hyponatremia and concentrated urine. D: an osmotic diuresis has high urine osmolality.

stemHtml: A term newborn boy with Down syndrome has not passed meconium by 48 hours of age. His abdomen is distended and he has bilious vomiting. Digital rectal examination is followed by an explosive release of stool and gas. Contrast enema shows a narrow rectosigmoid segment with dilated colon above it. Rectal suction biopsy shows no ganglion cells in the submucosal plexus and hypertrophied nerve fibers. Which of the following embryologic events failed?

options.label: B
options.html: Craniocaudal migration of neural crest cells into the bowel wall

options.label: C
options.html: Blood supply to a segment of the midgut

answerHtml: Answer: B. Neural crest migration (Hirschsprung disease)
explanationHtml: Enteric ganglion cells come from vagal neural crest that migrates craniocaudally. When migration stops early, the distal segment (always including the rectum) is aganglionic and stays tonically contracted, with absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex. The bowel above dilates (megacolon). The disease is associated with RET mutations and Down syndrome. The "squirt sign" is the explosive stool after rectal exam. Treatment is resection of the aganglionic segment with a pull-through procedure.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: duodenal atresia (double-bubble sign, also seen in Down syndrome) has no distal colonic findings. C: jejunoileal atresia ("apple-peel"). D: Meckel diverticulum. E: malrotation and volvulus.

stemHtml: A 10-day-old infant with ambiguous genitalia (clitoromegaly and partially fused labioscrotal folds, no palpable gonads) is brought in with poor feeding, vomiting, and lethargy. Blood pressure is 58/30 mm Hg. Serum Na<sup>+</sup> is 126 mEq/L, K<sup>+</sup> 7.0 mEq/L, and glucose 48 mg/dL. Karyotype is 46,XX, and pelvic ultrasound shows a uterus. Serum concentration of which of the following is most likely increased?
answerHtml: Answer: C. 17-Hydroxyprogesterone (21-hydroxylase deficiency)
explanationHtml: Classic salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency (CYP21A2, autosomal recessive) blocks conversion of progesterone to 11-deoxycorticosterone and of 17-OH progesterone to 11-deoxycortisol. Cortisol and aldosterone are deficient, so hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia develop in the second week. ACTH rises and pushes precursors into androgens, which virilizes a 46,XX fetus. 17-OH progesterone is the precursor that accumulates and is measured on US newborn screening. Treat with hydrocortisone, fludrocortisone, and salt.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and E: these accumulate in 11β-hydroxylase deficiency, which causes virilization with hypertension and hypokalemia. B and D: both are deficient in this condition.

stemHtml: A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman had a lumpectomy for estrogen receptor–positive invasive ductal carcinoma 3 years ago and has taken an oral adjuvant drug since then. She now has vaginal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial stripe of 14 mm, and biopsy shows endometrial hyperplasia with atypia. She also had a DVT last year. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of her adjuvant drug?

options.label: A
options.html: Inhibition of peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogens

options.label: C
options.html: Pure estrogen receptor antagonism with receptor degradation

options.label: D
options.html: Continuous GnRH receptor stimulation causing pituitary desensitization

options.label: E
options.html: Estrogen receptor antagonism in breast with partial agonism in endometrium

answerHtml: Answer: E. Selective estrogen receptor modulator (tamoxifen)
explanationHtml: Tamoxifen blocks the estrogen receptor in breast tissue but acts as a partial agonist in the endometrium, raising the risk of hyperplasia and endometrial carcinoma, and in the liver and coagulation system, raising the risk of VTE. It also acts as an agonist in bone and helps preserve it. Raloxifene is an antagonist in the endometrium, so it does not raise endometrial cancer risk, but it does carry VTE risk.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: aromatase inhibitors (anastrozole, letrozole) cause bone loss and arthralgias but do not stimulate the endometrium or cause VTE. B: trastuzumab is cardiotoxic. C: fulvestrant has no agonist activity and is given IM. D: leuprolide does not stimulate the endometrium.

stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman had an episode of painful vision loss in her right eye a year ago that resolved over 6 weeks. She now has double vision. When she looks to the right, her left eye does not adduct and her right eye shows nystagmus on abduction. Convergence is normal. MRI shows multiple ovoid T2-hyperintense lesions in the periventricular white matter, oriented perpendicular to the ventricles. A lesion in which of the following structures best explains her eye findings?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Left MLF
explanationHtml: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia is named for the side of the eye that fails to adduct. On right gaze, the right PPRF and CN VI nucleus fire. The right lateral rectus abducts, and interneurons cross to travel in the left MLF to the left CN III nucleus (medial rectus). A left MLF lesion therefore blocks left-eye adduction. Convergence is preserved because it does not use the MLF. Bilateral INO in a young adult strongly suggests multiple sclerosis, here with previous optic neuritis and periventricular lesions ("Dawson fingers").
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: a right MLF lesion impairs right-eye adduction on left gaze. C: a CN III nucleus lesion also impairs convergence and causes ptosis and pupil involvement. D: a PPRF lesion abolishes conjugate gaze to that side in both eyes. E: a CN VI lesion impairs abduction of the left eye.

stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis still has active synovitis despite maximal methotrexate. Her rheumatologist plans to add infliximab, a chimeric monoclonal antibody against a cytokine. Before starting, she has an interferon-γ release assay. Treatment with this drug most directly increases the risk of reactivating which of the following infections, and why?

options.label: A
options.html: Herpes simplex virus, from impaired NK-cell cytotoxicity

options.label: B
options.html: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, from impaired formation and maintenance of granulomas

options.label: C
options.html: Giardia lamblia, from loss of secretory IgA

options.label: D
options.html: Clostridioides difficile, from disruption of gut flora

options.label: E
options.html: JC virus, from blocking lymphocyte entry into the CNS through α<sub>4</sub>-integrin

answerHtml: Answer: B. TB reactivation (TNF-α is needed for granulomas)
explanationHtml: TNF-α from macrophages and T cells keeps granulomas intact and walls off latent M. tuberculosis. TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept, certolizumab, golimumab) can break down granulomas and cause reactivation, often extrapulmonary or disseminated TB. Screen with an IGRA or TST before starting, and treat latent TB first. Screen for hepatitis B as well.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: not the hallmark risk of TNF inhibitors. C: linked to selective IgA deficiency and CVID. D: linked to antibiotics. E: PML risk is specific to natalizumab, which blocks α<sub>4</sub>-integrin.

stemHtml: A 60-year-old Black man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction has taken a fixed-dose combination of an arteriolar vasodilator and a nitrate for 8 months. He now has polyarthralgia, low-grade fever, a pleural friction rub, and a mild rash on sun-exposed skin. Renal function and urinalysis are normal, and he has no neurologic symptoms. ANA is positive. He is a slow acetylator. Which of the following autoantibodies is most likely present?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Anti-histone (drug-induced lupus)
explanationHtml: Isosorbide dinitrate plus hydralazine (BiDil) is indicated in Black patients with HFrEF. Hydralazine, procainamide, and isoniazid are metabolized by N-acetylation, so slow acetylators have higher levels and higher risk of drug-induced lupus. It presents with serositis, arthralgias, fever, and rash, and it rarely involves the kidneys or CNS. Anti-histone antibodies are present in more than 95% of cases. It resolves after the drug is stopped.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B: specific for idiopathic SLE (anti-dsDNA correlates with nephritis) and usually absent in drug-induced lupus. C: limited scleroderma (CREST). E: polymyositis and dermatomyositis with interstitial lung disease.

stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman who recently immigrated from Southeast Asia is treated for latent tuberculosis with a 9-month course of a single drug that inhibits mycolic acid synthesis. She also has poorly controlled diabetes and drinks alcohol daily. After 3 months she reports burning pain and numbness in both feet in a stocking distribution. Deficiency of which of the following vitamins is most likely contributing to her symptoms?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Pyridoxine (B<sub>6</sub>)
explanationHtml: Isoniazid forms a hydrazone with pyridoxal and increases its excretion, and it competes with pyridoxal phosphate, which is needed for neurotransmitter synthesis (GABA, serotonin, norepinephrine). The result is peripheral neuropathy, and in overdose, seizures (treated with IV pyridoxine). Prophylactic B6 is given to patients at risk: those with diabetes, alcohol use, malnutrition, HIV, pregnancy, CKD, or slow acetylator status.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: thiamine deficiency (dry beriberi) is possible with alcohol use but is not caused by INH. B: INH can cause pellagra by depleting B<sub>6</sub>, which is needed for niacin synthesis from tryptophan, but neuropathy is the classic and direct consequence of B<sub>6</sub> loss. D and E: not caused by INH. B<sub>12</sub> deficiency is linked to metformin, but it is not the best answer given the timing with INH.

stemHtml: A 17-year-old girl of Ashkenazi Jewish descent has fatigue, easy bruising, and episodes of severe bone pain. Her spleen and liver are markedly enlarged. CBC shows pancytopenia. Femur x-ray shows flaring of the distal metaphysis ("Erlenmeyer flask"). Bone marrow aspirate shows large macrophages with abundant fibrillar cytoplasm resembling crumpled tissue paper. Her intellect is normal. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Glucocerebrosidase (Gaucher disease type 1)
explanationHtml: Gaucher disease is the most common lysosomal storage disorder and is autosomal recessive. Glucocerebroside accumulates in macrophages ("Gaucher cells") in the spleen, liver, and marrow. It causes hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, bone crises, avascular necrosis, and Erlenmeyer flask deformity. Type 1 does not involve the CNS. Treatment is enzyme replacement (imiglucerase) or substrate reduction (eliglustat).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Tay–Sachs (cherry-red spot, neurodegeneration, no hepatosplenomegaly). B: Niemann–Pick (cherry-red spot, hepatosplenomegaly, foamy macrophages, neurodegeneration). C: Fabry (X-linked, painful neuropathy, angiokeratomas, renal and cardiac disease). D: Krabbe (globoid cells, peripheral neuropathy, optic atrophy).

stemHtml:
A 68-year-old man has had low back pain for 3 months and increasing fatigue. Laboratory studies:
TestResult
Hemoglobin9.5 g/dL (normocytic)
Calcium12.4 mg/dL
Creatinine2.6 mg/dL (1.0 six months ago)
Total protein / albumin10.2 / 3.2 g/dL
Serum protein electrophoresisMonoclonal spike in the γ region
Urine dipstick proteinNegative
24-h urine protein3.1 g (mostly κ light chains)
Peripheral smear shows red cells stacked like coins. Which of the following is the most likely primary cause of his kidney injury?

options.label: A
options.html: Light chains forming obstructive casts with Tamm–Horsfall protein in the distal tubules

options.label: B
options.html: Subendothelial immune complex deposition with complement activation

options.label: D
options.html: Glomerular deposition of serum amyloid A protein

answerHtml: Answer: A. Light-chain cast nephropathy ("myeloma kidney")
explanationHtml: Hypercalcemia, renal failure, anemia, bone pain, an M-spike, and rouleaux point to multiple myeloma. Excess free light chains (Bence Jones proteins) are filtered and bind uromodulin (Tamm–Horsfall protein) in the distal tubule. They form obstructive, fractured casts surrounded by multinucleated giant cells and are directly toxic to tubules. The urine dipstick detects albumin, not light chains, which explains the gap between a negative dipstick and a large 24-hour protein. Hypercalcemia, dehydration, and NSAIDs make the injury worse.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: lupus nephritis or MPGN. C: Goodpasture syndrome with nephritic urine sediment. D: AA amyloid comes from chronic inflammation (myeloma causes AL amyloid), and glomerular amyloid causes albuminuria that the dipstick would detect. E: does not explain the M-protein findings.

stemHtml: A 75-year-old woman with heart failure and atrial fibrillation takes digoxin. Two weeks after her furosemide dose is doubled for worsening edema, she has nausea, anorexia, confusion, and blurry yellow-tinged vision. ECG shows frequent premature ventricular beats and runs of bidirectional ventricular tachycardia. Which electrolyte abnormality most likely contributed to her toxicity, and through what mechanism?

options.label: A
options.html: Hyperkalemia, which increases digoxin binding to Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup>-ATPase

options.label: B
options.html: Hypocalcemia, which increases sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release

options.label: C
options.html: Hypermagnesemia, which slows AV nodal conduction

options.label: D
options.html: Hypokalemia, which reduces competition with digoxin for its binding site on Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup>-ATPase

options.label: E
options.html: Hypernatremia, which increases the intracellular Na<sup>+</sup> gradient

answerHtml: Answer: D. Hypokalemia
explanationHtml: Digoxin binds the extracellular K+-binding site of the Na+/K+-ATPase. Low K+ means less competition, so more pump is inhibited, intracellular Ca2+ rises through reduced Na+/Ca2+ exchange, and delayed afterdepolarizations trigger arrhythmias. Loop diuretics cause hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia, both of which predispose to toxicity. Renal impairment and drugs such as amiodarone, verapamil, and quinidine also raise digoxin levels. Treat with digoxin immune Fab. In acute toxicity, hyperkalemia is a marker of severity.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: high K+ reduces digoxin binding, although hyperkalemia develops in acute overdose. B: hypercalcemia predisposes to toxicity. C: hypomagnesemia predisposes. E: not a recognized contributor.

stemHtml: A 78-year-old woman with advanced Alzheimer disease is hospitalized with aspiration pneumonia and lacks decision-making capacity. Five years ago, while competent, she signed a durable power of attorney for health care naming her niece. The niece declines a feeding tube, saying her aunt often said she would never want to be "kept alive by tubes." The patient's two sons insist on the feeding tube. Which of the following should make the decision?

options.label: A
options.html: The patient's elder son, as closest next of kin

options.label: B
options.html: The niece, as the designated health care agent

options.label: C
options.html: The attending physician, using best medical judgment

options.label: D
options.html: A majority vote of the family members

answerHtml: Answer: B. The designated health care agent (niece)
explanationHtml: A durable power of attorney for health care names a surrogate who takes priority over the default hierarchy of next of kin (spouse, adult children, parents, siblings). The agent must use substituted judgment, meaning what the patient would want, which the niece is doing. An ethics consult can help mediate the family conflict, but it does not override a valid agent who is acting on the patient's wishes. Feeding tubes are not recommended in advanced dementia, since they do not prolong survival or prevent aspiration.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and D: next of kin and family consensus apply only when no agent was designated. C: the physician advises but does not override the surrogate. E: ethics committees advise and mediate but do not make the decision.

stemHtml: An autosomal recessive disorder affects 1 in 2,500 newborns in a population that is in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium. Which of the following is closest to the frequency of heterozygous carriers in this population?
answerHtml: Answer: E. 1 in 25
explanationHtml: q2 = 1/2,500, so q = 1/50 and p ≈ 1. Carrier frequency = 2pq ≈ 2 × 1/50 = 1/25. This is a typical figure for cystic fibrosis in people of Northern European ancestry. A common follow-up: if a woman known to be a carrier has a child with an unrelated man from this population, the risk the child is affected is 1/25 × 1/4 = 1/100 (option C is the answer to that question, not this one).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: q<sup>2</sup>, the disease frequency. B: 2q<sup>2</sup>, which has no meaning. C: carrier × ¼, the risk for a child of one known carrier as described above. D: q, the allele frequency.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old man has 2 hours of crushing substernal chest pain and goes to a rural emergency department that has no catheterisation laboratory. BP is 142/86 mm Hg and pulse is 92/min. ECG shows 3-mm ST elevation in V1–V4. He has no history of bleeding, stroke or recent surgery. He has received aspirin. The nearest PCI-capable hospital is a ground transfer of about 150 minutes from first medical contact to device. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Administer tenecteplase and arrange transfer to the PCI-capable center

options.label: B
options.html: Transfer immediately for primary PCI without fibrinolysis

options.label: C
options.html: Start IV heparin and repeat troponin in 3 hours

options.label: D
options.html: Obtain CT angiography of the chest to exclude aortic dissection

options.label: E
options.html: Start IV metoprolol and observe for 6 hours

answerHtml: Answer: A. Fibrinolysis, then transfer (pharmacoinvasive strategy).
explanationHtml: This is a STEMI with symptoms for less than 12 hours. Primary PCI is preferred only if first-medical-contact-to-device time is ≤120 minutes when transfer is needed. Here it is about 150 minutes and he has no contraindications, so give a fibrinolytic within 30 minutes of arrival. Then transfer him for angiography at 2–24 h, or for rescue PCI if reperfusion fails.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B accepts a delay beyond the 120-minute benchmark and loses myocardium. C manages him like NSTE-ACS; a STEMI needs reperfusion now, not serial troponins. D: nothing suggests dissection (no tearing back pain, pulse deficit or mediastinal widening), and routine CT delays reperfusion. E: β-blockers do not reperfuse, and IV β-blockers are not routine in STEMI.

stemHtml: A 64-year-old woman with diabetes is admitted with chest pressure. hs-troponin rises from 40 to 410 ng/L. ECG shows new 2-mm horizontal ST depression in V4–V6, with no ST elevation. She has received aspirin, ticagrelor, IV heparin and three doses of sublingual nitroglycerin, and an IV nitroglycerin infusion is running. She still has 8/10 chest pain. BP is 108/68 mm Hg, pulse 98/min, and lungs are clear. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.html: Coronary angiography within the next 72 hours

answerHtml: Answer: C. Immediate invasive strategy.
explanationHtml: She has an NSTEMI with refractory angina despite maximal medical therapy. That is an indication for an immediate invasive strategy (<2 h). The others are hemodynamic instability or cardiogenic shock, acute HF, sustained VT/VF and mechanical complications. Without these features, high-risk NSTEMI would get angiography within 24 hours.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and E are for low-risk patients, and stress testing during active ischemia is dangerous. B: fibrinolytics are contraindicated in NSTE-ACS because they increase harm without benefit. D: 72 hours is too slow for ongoing ischemia.

stemHtml: A 61-year-old man has chest pain and an ECG showing ST elevation in II, III and aVF, with 1-mm ST elevation in right-sided lead V4R. After sublingual nitroglycerin, BP falls from 112/70 to 78/50 mm Hg. Pulse is 64/min. JVP is 12 cm H₂O and lungs are clear on auscultation. Emergent PCI is being arranged. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate step for his hypotension?
answerHtml: Answer: E. IV isotonic fluid bolus.
explanationHtml: He has an inferior STEMI with RV involvement (ST↑ in V4R, raised JVP, clear lungs). The ischemic RV depends on preload. Nitrates cause venodilation and drop preload, which leads to hypotension. Treat with volume loading. If hypotension persists, add inotropes and proceed with urgent reperfusion.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B and D all reduce preload and worsen shock. C: a β-blocker in hypotension and possible evolving AV block (inferior MI) is contraindicated.

stemHtml: A 59-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 30%) has NYHA class II symptoms. He takes lisinopril 20 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 200 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, dapagliflozin 10 mg daily and furosemide 20 mg daily. BP is 118/72 mm Hg and pulse is 62/min. He is euvolemic. Serum potassium is 4.4 mEq/L and eGFR is 58 mL/min/1.73 m². He has no history of angioedema. Which of the following changes is most likely to reduce his mortality further?

options.label: B
options.html: Stop lisinopril and start sacubitril-valsartan 36 hours later

answerHtml: Answer: B. Switch the ACE inhibitor to an ARNI after a 36-hour washout.
explanationHtml: In PARADIGM-HF, sacubitril-valsartan reduced cardiovascular death and HF hospitalisation compared with enalapril. Guidelines recommend replacing an ACEi/ARB with an ARNI in NYHA II–III HFrEF to reduce morbidity and mortality further. A 36-hour gap is required because neprilysin inhibition plus an ACEi raises bradykinin and the risk of angioedema. He is already on the other three pillars (β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: digoxin reduces hospitalisation but not mortality. C: amlodipine is neutral in HFrEF and is used only for HTN or angina. D: hydralazine-nitrate benefits self-identified Black patients with NYHA III–IV on optimal therapy, or those who cannot take ACEi/ARB/ARNI. An ARNI comes first. E: he is euvolemic, and loop diuretics do not reduce mortality.

stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman with hypertension and obesity has exertional dyspnea and ankle edema. She does not have diabetes. Echocardiography shows LVEF 60%, concentric LV hypertrophy and grade II diastolic dysfunction. NT-proBNP is raised. She feels better on furosemide, but she was hospitalised twice for HF this year. BP is 128/76 mm Hg and eGFR is 52 mL/min/1.73 m². Which of the following additional medications is most likely to reduce her risk of HF hospitalisation?
answerHtml: Answer: D. An SGLT2 inhibitor.
explanationHtml: This is HFpEF. Empagliflozin (EMPEROR-Preserved) and dapagliflozin (DELIVER) reduced the composite of cardiovascular death or worsening HF, driven mainly by fewer HF hospitalisations, whether or not the patient has diabetes. Guidelines give SGLT2i a 2a recommendation in HFpEF, and it is the agent with the most consistent evidence.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: digoxin has no role in HFpEF without AF. B: diltiazem has no proven outcome benefit here. C: ivabradine is for HFrEF in sinus rhythm with HR ≥70 and has no benefit in HFpEF. E: hydralazine alone has no outcome data in HFpEF.

stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman with hypertension is found on routine examination to have an irregularly irregular pulse. ECG confirms atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 84/min. She has no heart failure, diabetes, prior stroke or vascular disease. Echocardiography shows normal valves and LVEF 60%. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term therapy to prevent stroke?

options.label: D
options.html: Warfarin with a target INR of 2.5–3.5

answerHtml: Answer: A. Apixaban (a DOAC).
explanationHtml: Her CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is HTN 1 + age 65–74 1 + female 1 = 3. For women, a score ≥3 is a Class 1 indication for oral anticoagulation. In non-valvular AF, DOACs are preferred over warfarin because they cause less intracranial hemorrhage and need no INR monitoring.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B and C: antiplatelet therapy is inferior for stroke prevention in AF, and dual antiplatelet therapy bleeds about as much as anticoagulation. D: warfarin is acceptable but not preferred, and 2.5–3.5 is the wrong INR target for AF (2–3). E: her risk is high enough to treat.

stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman who emigrated from India 3 years ago has 2 weeks of palpitations and exertional dyspnea. She had "rheumatic fever" as a child. ECG shows atrial fibrillation at 112/min. Echocardiography shows a thickened mitral valve with commissural fusion, mitral valve area 1.1 cm² and an enlarged left atrium. Which of the following is the most appropriate anticoagulant?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Warfarin (INR 2–3).
explanationHtml: AF with moderate–severe mitral stenosis is one of the two settings (with mechanical valves) where DOACs are not recommended. In the INVICTUS trial in rheumatic heart disease, rivaroxaban led to more deaths and strokes than a VKA. She needs anticoagulation regardless of her CHA₂DS₂-VASc score, because MS with AF carries a very high thromboembolic risk. Her severe symptomatic MS also needs evaluation for percutaneous balloon commissurotomy once LA thrombus has been excluded by TEE.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B and E are DOACs, which are not recommended in moderate–severe rheumatic MS. D: aspirin gives inadequate protection.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old man has had palpitations for 1 hour. BP is 124/78 mm Hg and he is alert. ECG shows an irregularly irregular, wide-complex tachycardia at 230/min with varying QRS morphology. A prior ECG showed a short PR interval and a slurred QRS upstroke. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Procainamide.
explanationHtml: This is pre-excited AF in a patient with WPW. Blocking the AV node with adenosine, CCBs, β-blockers or digoxin removes the node's protective filtering and sends impulses preferentially down the accessory pathway. That can degenerate into VF. Procainamide (or ibutilide) slows conduction in the accessory pathway. If he becomes unstable, give synchronized cardioversion. The definitive treatment is catheter ablation.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B, C and D are AV-nodal blocking agents, which are contraindicated in pre-excited AF. Digoxin also shortens the accessory pathway's refractory period.

stemHtml: A 66-year-old man collapses in the hospital corridor. He is pulseless, and CPR begins at once. The monitor shows ventricular fibrillation. He receives one 200-J biphasic shock, followed by 2 minutes of CPR and placement of IV access. At the rhythm check, VF persists. A second shock is delivered and CPR is resumed immediately. Which of the following medications should be given now?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Epinephrine 1 mg IV, repeated every 3–5 minutes.
explanationHtml: In the AHA VF/pulseless VT algorithm, epinephrine is given during the CPR cycle after the 2nd shock. Amiodarone 300 mg (or lidocaine) follows if VF persists after the 3rd shock. Epinephrine's α-agonist effect raises coronary perfusion pressure during CPR.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: amiodarone comes after the 3rd shock in shock-refractory VF. C: atropine is not used in cardiac arrest. D: adenosine is for stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia. E: bicarbonate is reserved for hyperkalemia, TCA overdose or known severe acidosis, not routine arrest.

stemHtml: A 72-year-old man is brought to the ED because he is light-headed. BP is 78/48 mm Hg and pulse is 34/min. He is diaphoretic and slow to respond. ECG shows P waves at 80/min completely dissociated from a wide-complex escape rhythm at 34/min. He received atropine 1 mg IV twice, with no change in rate. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: E
options.html: Observation with repeat ECG in 1 hour

answerHtml: Answer: D. Transcutaneous pacing.
explanationHtml: He has third-degree AV block with an infranodal (wide) escape rhythm and signs of poor perfusion. When atropine fails, the next step is transcutaneous pacing, or a dopamine or epinephrine infusion. Atropine often fails in infranodal block because it acts on the vagally innervated sinus and AV nodes. He will then need transvenous pacing and a permanent pacemaker.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and C slow conduction further and can cause asystole. B: cardioversion treats tachyarrhythmias. E: an unstable patient cannot be observed.

stemHtml: An 84-year-old man has had two episodes of exertional syncope and new exertional angina. Examination shows a late-peaking crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border, with a soft single S2. Echocardiography shows a calcified trileaflet aortic valve: peak velocity 4.6 m/s, mean gradient 52 mm Hg, valve area 0.7 cm² and LVEF 55%. Coronary angiography shows no significant CAD. His STS surgical risk is intermediate. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: Balloon aortic valvuloplasty as definitive therapy

options.label: D
options.html: Start metoprolol and nitrates for angina

options.label: E
options.html: Surgical aortic valve replacement with a mechanical valve

answerHtml: Answer: A. TAVR.
explanationHtml: He has severe symptomatic aortic stenosis (Vmax ≥4 m/s, mean gradient ≥40 mm Hg, AVA ≤1.0 cm² with syncope and angina), which is a Class 1 indication for AVR. Untreated, symptomatic severe AS has a very poor survival. For patients over 80, the 2020 ACC/AHA guideline favours transfemoral TAVR over surgical AVR when anatomy is suitable.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: watchful waiting is only for asymptomatic AS with preserved EF. C: valvuloplasty is a temporary bridge with early restenosis. D: vasodilators such as nitrates can cause dangerous hypotension in severe AS, and drugs do not change outcome. E: at 84, a mechanical valve with lifelong warfarin and surgical risk is not preferred.

stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman is followed for mitral valve prolapse with mitral regurgitation. She runs 5 km three times a week without symptoms. Echocardiography shows a flail posterior leaflet with severe MR (effective regurgitant orifice 0.5 cm²). LVEF is 57% (65% last year) and LV end-systolic diameter is 42 mm. She is in sinus rhythm. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Start lisinopril and repeat echocardiography in 1 year

options.label: C
options.html: Referral for surgical mitral valve repair

options.label: E
options.html: Mitral valve replacement with a mechanical prosthesis

answerHtml: Answer: C. Surgical mitral valve repair.
explanationHtml: In asymptomatic severe primary MR, surgery is indicated once LV dysfunction appears: LVEF ≤60% or LVESD ≥40 mm. She meets both. A posterior-leaflet flail is highly repairable, and repair is preferred over replacement because it preserves LV function and avoids anticoagulation. Waiting risks irreversible LV dysfunction.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: vasodilators do not delay surgery in primary MR without HTN, and waiting is inappropriate. B: she has already met the surgical triggers. D: TEER is reserved for patients at high or prohibitive surgical risk. E: replacement is inferior to repair when the valve is repairable.

stemHtml: A 49-year-old man with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.1% on metformin) has an average home BP of 134/84 mm Hg over 2 weeks, consistent with office readings. He has no known cardiovascular disease. BMI is 29 kg/m². Creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL, potassium 4.3 mEq/L and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 90 mg/g. He has been following a low-sodium diet and exercising for 3 months. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue lifestyle changes and recheck BP in 12 months

options.label: C
options.html: Start hydrochlorothiazide plus amlodipine as a single pill

answerHtml: Answer: E. Start an ACE inhibitor.
explanationHtml: He has stage 1 hypertension (130–139/80–89) with diabetes. Under both the 2017 and 2025 ACC/AHA guidelines, diabetes alone is enough to start drug therapy, with a target below 130/80. With albuminuria (UACR 30–300 mg/g), an ACEi or ARB is the preferred first agent because it lowers intraglomerular pressure and slows nephropathy.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: lifestyle alone is inadequate for a patient with stage 1 HTN and diabetes. B: β-blockers are not first-line without a compelling indication. C: starting two drugs is for stage 2 HTN, and this combination skips the RAAS blocker his albuminuria calls for. D: nothing suggests pheochromocytoma.

stemHtml: A 60-year-old man had an anterior STEMI treated with PCI 3 months ago. He takes aspirin, ticagrelor, metoprolol succinate, lisinopril and atorvastatin 80 mg daily, and is adherent with no muscle symptoms. Fasting LDL-C is 92 mg/dL (it was 168 mg/dL before the statin). Triglycerides are 140 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in lipid management?

options.label: E
options.html: Make no changes; he is on high-intensity statin therapy

answerHtml: Answer: B. Add ezetimibe.
explanationHtml: After ACS, both the 2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline and the 2026 dyslipidemia guideline recommend adding a nonstatin if LDL-C stays ≥70 mg/dL on a maximally tolerated statin. The 2026 goal for most secondary-prevention patients is <55 mg/dL. Ezetimibe is the usual first add-on (IMPROVE-IT). A PCSK9 monoclonal antibody is the next step if he remains above goal.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: pravastatin is a moderate-intensity statin, which is a step down. C and D: fibrates and niacin do not reduce events when added to statins, and his triglycerides are normal. E: he is above goal, so the plan needs to change.

stemHtml: A 19-year-old college basketball player collapses during practice and wakes within a minute, with no confusion afterward. He had no prodrome. His uncle died suddenly at age 30. Examination shows a harsh systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that gets louder with the Valsalva maneuver and softer with squatting. ECG shows sinus rhythm with LV hypertrophy and deep narrow Q waves in the lateral leads. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Transthoracic echocardiography.
explanationHtml: Exertional syncope without prodrome, a family history of sudden death, and a murmur that rises with reduced preload all point to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with LV outflow obstruction. TTE confirms asymmetric septal hypertrophy and the outflow gradient. Cardiac MRI and ambulatory monitoring then help stratify sudden death risk (ICD decision). He must stop competitive sports until he has been evaluated.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: tilt-table testing evaluates reflex syncope, which this is not. B and C: he had no seizure features or neurologic deficits. E: exertional syncope is cardiac until proven otherwise, and returning to play could be fatal.

stemHtml: A 57-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has 3 days of worsening dyspnea. BP is 82/60 mm Hg, pulse 124/min and respiratory rate 26/min. Systolic BP falls by 18 mm Hg with inspiration. JVP is raised to the angle of the jaw, and heart sounds are distant. Lungs are clear. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with low voltage and beat-to-beat variation in QRS amplitude. Bedside echocardiography shows a large circumferential pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse. She has received a 500-mL saline bolus. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: CT scan of the chest with contrast

answerHtml: Answer: A. Urgent pericardiocentesis.
explanationHtml: She has cardiac tamponade: Beck triad, pulsus paradoxus >10 mm Hg, electrical alternans and RV diastolic collapse on echo. This is obstructive shock. Fluid is only a temporizing bridge. The definitive treatment is drainage, ideally echo-guided needle pericardiocentesis. A pericardial window or catheter may follow for a recurrent malignant effusion.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: diuretics reduce preload and can precipitate arrest. C: unstable patients should not go to the CT scanner, and the diagnosis is already made. D: waiting a week is far too long. E: positive-pressure ventilation lowers venous return and can cause collapse in tamponade, so avoid it before drainage if at all possible.

stemHtml: A 31-year-old man who injects heroin has 5 days of fever, rigors and pleuritic chest pain. Temperature is 39.6 °C, BP 104/62 mm Hg and pulse 118/min. A holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border increases with inspiration. Chest CT shows multiple peripheral nodules, some cavitating. Three sets of blood cultures have just been drawn. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Wait for transesophageal echocardiography before starting antibiotics

answerHtml: Answer: C. Empiric IV vancomycin.
explanationHtml: This is likely right-sided (tricuspid) endocarditis with septic pulmonary emboli. The most likely organism in IV drug use is S. aureus, including MRSA. In a septic, acutely ill patient, start empiric antibiotics immediately after cultures are drawn. Vancomycin covers MRSA. Many regimens add a gram-negative agent such as cefepime.
