Narrow therapy once susceptibilities are known (e.g., cefazolin or nafcillin for MSSA). Echo can be done afterward.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: delaying antibiotics in a septic patient is harmful. The "hold antibiotics" approach applies only to stable, subacute presentations while extra cultures are collected. B: sepsis needs IV therapy in hospital. D: penicillin does not cover S. aureus, which mostly produces penicillinase. E: tricuspid endocarditis is usually managed medically; surgery is for specific indications such as refractory right HF or persistent bacteremia.

stemHtml: A dentist plans tooth extractions for five patients. For which of the following patients is antibiotic prophylaxis against infective endocarditis recommended before the procedure?

options.label: A
options.html: A 30-year-old woman with mitral valve prolapse and mild mitral regurgitation

options.label: B
options.html: A 45-year-old man with a bicuspid aortic valve and mild aortic stenosis

options.label: D
options.html: A 12-year-old girl whose secundum ASD was closed surgically 3 years ago with no residual defect

options.label: E
options.html: A 60-year-old man who had viridans streptococcal endocarditis of a native valve 4 years ago

answerHtml: Answer: E. Prior infective endocarditis.
explanationHtml: AHA/ADA guidance limits prophylaxis (amoxicillin 2 g, 30–60 min before the procedure) to the highest-risk groups. These are prosthetic valves or prosthetic repair material, prior IE, certain congenital heart disease (unrepaired cyanotic CHD, within 6 months of complete repair, or residual defects at prosthetic sites) and cardiac transplant recipients with valvulopathy.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B and C carry increased lifetime risk but do not qualify, because prophylaxis has not been shown to help them. D: a fully repaired ASD more than 6 months after repair with no residual defect does not qualify.

stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension has sudden tearing pain between his shoulder blades. BP is 192/108 mm Hg in the right arm and 186/104 mm Hg in the left, and pulse is 96/min. Distal pulses are intact. Creatinine and lactate are normal. CT angiography shows a dissection flap starting distal to the left subclavian artery and extending to the renal arteries, with no malperfusion or rupture. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
answerHtml: Answer: B. An IV β-blocker (esmolol or labetalol) first.
explanationHtml: This is an uncomplicated Stanford type B (descending) dissection, which is managed medically. The aim is to reduce aortic wall stress (dP/dt): first lower the heart rate to ≤60/min with an IV β-blocker, then bring SBP to about 100–120 mm Hg. Add a vasodilator such as nicardipine or nitroprusside if BP stays high after β-blockade. TEVAR is reserved for complicated type B dissection.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: emergency surgery is for type A dissection or complicated type B. C: a vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia, increases shear force and can extend the tear. D and E: anticoagulants and thrombolytics are contraindicated in dissection.

stemHtml: A 77-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation stopped her apixaban 2 weeks ago because of cost. For the past 3 hours her right leg has been painful and numb. The right foot is cool and pale, with absent popliteal, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses. She has reduced sensation over the toes, and motor function is intact. No Doppler signal is heard over the pedal arteries. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.label: D
options.html: Give an IV unfractionated heparin bolus and start an infusion

answerHtml: Answer: D. Immediate systemic anticoagulation with IV heparin.
explanationHtml: This is acute limb ischemia, probably embolic from AF. The limb is viable but threatened (Rutherford IIa: minimal sensory loss, no motor loss). The first step is an IV heparin bolus and infusion to stop clot propagation. Urgent vascular surgery consultation and revascularisation follow, by catheter-directed thrombolysis or embolectomy, with imaging if it does not delay treatment.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: an ABI is for chronic PAD, and the absent Doppler signal already shows severe ischemia. B and C treat chronic claudication. E: amputation is for an irreversibly ischemic limb, which shows profound sensory loss, paralysis and absent venous and arterial signals.

stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman with asthma uses her albuterol inhaler about 3 times a week for wheezing. She wakes at night with cough about twice a month. She takes no other medication. Her inhaler technique is good, and spirometry shows FEV₁ 88% predicted. Per GINA, which of the following is the preferred treatment change?
answerHtml: Answer: A. As-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol (GINA Track 1, steps 1–2).
explanationHtml: Her symptoms are fewer than 4–5 days a week, which fits GINA steps 1–2. GINA prefers as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol as the reliever. It reduces severe exacerbations compared with SABA alone, and is about as effective as daily low-dose ICS while exposing her to much less steroid. Daily low-dose ICS with PRN SABA (Track 2) is the alternative.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: SABA-only treatment is no longer recommended for adults and adolescents, because it raises the risk of severe and fatal exacerbations. C: leukotriene antagonists are less effective and carry a boxed warning for neuropsychiatric effects. D: high-dose ICS-LABA is step 4–5 therapy, far too much for her. E: maintenance oral steroids are a last resort at step 5.

stemHtml: A 67-year-old man with COPD (post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC 0.58, FEV₁ 48% predicted) has a CAT score of 19. Over the past year he had two exacerbations treated as an outpatient with prednisone and antibiotics. He currently uses only albuterol as needed. His blood eosinophil count is 380/µL. He quit smoking 2 years ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate maintenance therapy?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Triple therapy (LABA + LAMA + ICS).
explanationHtml: Two moderate exacerbations in a year place him in GOLD group E. The initial therapy for group E is LABA + LAMA. GOLD recommends going straight to LABA + LAMA + ICS when blood eosinophils are ≥300 cells/µL, because these patients' exacerbations respond best to ICS. A single-inhaler triple regimen also reduced mortality in exacerbation-prone patients.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: LAMA monotherapy is inadequate for group E. B: ICS monotherapy is not recommended in COPD. D: roflumilast is an add-on for patients with chronic bronchitis and FEV₁ <50%, not a stand-alone therapy. E: he needs maintenance therapy.

stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman with severe COPD (FEV₁ 32% predicted) is seen in clinic when stable, 6 weeks after an exacerbation. She is on LABA/LAMA/ICS, has quit smoking and has completed pulmonary rehabilitation. At rest on room air, SpO₂ is 86% and ABG shows pH 7.38, PaCO₂ 48 mm Hg and PaO₂ 53 mm Hg. Hematocrit is 49%. Which intervention is most likely to prolong her survival?

options.label: E
options.html: Supplemental oxygen for at least 15 hours per day

answerHtml: Answer: E. Long-term oxygen therapy (≥15 h/day).
explanationHtml: She has severe resting hypoxemia (PaO₂ ≤55 mm Hg / SaO₂ ≤88%) while stable on optimal therapy. Long-term oxygen for at least 15 h/day, and ideally continuously, reduces mortality, as shown in the NOTT and MRC trials. Smoking cessation, which she has already done, is the other classic mortality-reducing intervention.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: rehab improves symptoms and exercise capacity, but repeating it is not the survival-changing step. B: oxygen at night only was inferior to continuous oxygen in NOTT. C: theophylline has a narrow therapeutic window and no mortality benefit. D: azithromycin reduces exacerbations but has no proven survival benefit.

stemHtml: A 69-year-old man with severe COPD is admitted with 3 days of increased dyspnea and purulent sputum. He has received nebulised albuterol-ipratropium, prednisone 40 mg and doxycycline. On 2 L/min nasal cannula, SpO₂ is 90% and respiratory rate is 28/min, with use of accessory muscles. He is alert, follows commands and is protecting his airway. ABG shows pH 7.29, PaCO₂ 64 mm Hg and PaO₂ 60 mm Hg. BP is 138/80 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: E
options.html: Chest physiotherapy and repeat ABG in 6 hours

answerHtml: Answer: B. NIPPV.
explanationHtml: He has acute hypercapnic respiratory failure (pH ≤7.35, PaCO₂ ≥45) from a COPD exacerbation. He is alert, cooperative and hemodynamically stable. NIPPV cuts the need for intubation, mortality and length of stay. Reassess the ABG at 1–2 hours.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: intubate if NIV fails or is contraindicated (coma, vomiting, inability to protect the airway, shock), and none of these apply. C: high-concentration oxygen worsens hypercapnia, so titrate to SpO₂ 88–92%. D: aminophylline adds toxicity without benefit. E: waiting with no ventilatory support is unsafe.

stemHtml: A 71-year-old retired accountant who formerly smoked has 18 months of progressive exertional dyspnea and a dry cough. He has digital clubbing and fine end-inspiratory "Velcro" crackles at both bases. PFTs show FEV₁/FVC 0.86, FVC 61% predicted, TLC 64% predicted and DLCO 42% predicted. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
explanationHtml: A normal-to-high FEV₁/FVC with reduced TLC defines restriction. A reduced DLCO places the problem in the parenchyma (interstitial disease). An older ex-smoking man with clubbing and basal Velcro crackles is classic for IPF. The next step is HRCT looking for a UIP pattern, plus serologies to exclude CTD-ILD. Treatment is with antifibrotics (nintedanib or pirfenidone).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and C cause obstruction (low ratio), and emphysema has high TLC. B and E cause extraparenchymal restriction, where DLCO is normal or near normal.

stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with COPD and type 2 diabetes has 3 days of fever, productive cough and right-sided pleuritic pain. Temperature is 38.4 °C, BP 132/80 mm Hg, pulse 96/min, RR 22/min and SpO₂ 94% on room air. He is alert and eating. BUN is 16 mg/dL. Chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. He has had no antibiotics or hospitalisations in the past 90 days. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: D
options.html: ICU admission with IV ceftriaxone plus azithromycin

options.label: E
options.html: Hospital admission with IV vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam

answerHtml: Answer: A. Outpatient β-lactam plus macrolide.
explanationHtml: His CURB-65 is 1 (age only), so outpatient treatment is appropriate. Because he has comorbidities (chronic lung disease, diabetes), the 2019 ATS/IDSA guideline recommends amoxicillin-clavulanate (or a cephalosporin) plus a macrolide or doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: amoxicillin alone is for healthy outpatients without comorbidities. C: macrolide monotherapy is for healthy adults only, and only where pneumococcal macrolide resistance is <25%. D: he meets no severe-CAP criteria. E: he has no MRSA or Pseudomonas risk factors, so broad coverage is unnecessary.

stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has 2 days of sharp left-sided chest pain that worsens with deep breaths, starting after a week of viral URI symptoms. She uses a copper IUD and takes no medications. She has no history of VTE, recent surgery, trauma or travel. Temperature is 37.2 °C, pulse 84/min, BP 118/74 mm Hg, RR 16/min and SpO₂ 98% on room air. She has no hemoptysis and her legs are symmetric without swelling. ECG and chest X-ray are normal. The physician judges the pretest probability of PE to be low. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step regarding PE?
answerHtml: Answer: C. No further testing. PERC is negative.
explanationHtml: When gestalt pretest probability is low, a patient who meets all 8 PERC criteria needs no testing, because her probability of PE is below the testing threshold. She meets them: age <50, HR <100, SpO₂ ≥95%, no hemoptysis, no estrogen use (a copper IUD is non-hormonal), no prior VTE, no unilateral leg swelling and no recent surgery or trauma. Ordering a D-dimer risks false positives that lead to needless CT and radiation.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: a D-dimer would be next if any PERC criterion were positive, or if pretest probability were not low. B, D and E are imaging tests, unjustified when PE has effectively been ruled out.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman develops sudden dyspnea and syncope 2 days after a 14-hour flight. BP is 78/50 mm Hg after 1 L of IV crystalloid, pulse is 128/min and SpO₂ is 86% on 6 L/min. CT pulmonary angiography shows a saddle embolus with RV/LV ratio 1.4. Troponin is raised. She has no history of bleeding, stroke, recent surgery or uncontrolled hypertension. IV heparin has been started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Place an inferior vena cava filter

options.label: D
options.html: Continue heparin alone and observe in the ICU

options.label: E
options.html: Give systemic thrombolysis with IV alteplase

answerHtml: Answer: E. Systemic thrombolysis.
explanationHtml: She has high-risk (massive) PE with sustained hypotension (SBP <90) and no contraindication to fibrinolysis. The guidelines recommend systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours) to reverse RV failure quickly. If thrombolysis is contraindicated or fails, the options are catheter-directed therapy or surgical embolectomy.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: an IVC filter is for patients who cannot be anticoagulated, and it does not treat the clot already in the lungs. B and C do not lyse the clot. D: heparin alone is appropriate for intermediate-risk (normotensive) PE, not for shock.

stemHtml: A 55-year-old man is in hospital on day 5 of IV ceftriaxone and azithromycin for left lower lobe pneumonia. He still has fever (38.8 °C). Chest X-ray shows a new moderate left pleural effusion, and ultrasound shows septations. Thoracentesis yields turbid fluid: pH 7.02, glucose 38 mg/dL, LDH 1,650 U/L (serum ULN 220), protein 4.6 g/dL (serum 6.8 g/dL). Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in chains. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue the current antibiotics and repeat chest X-ray in 1 week

answerHtml: Answer: B. Chest tube drainage.
explanationHtml: The fluid is an exudate by Light's criteria (protein ratio 0.68, LDH far above 2/3 of the ULN). It is a complicated parapneumonic effusion (pH <7.2, glucose <60, LDH >1,000, organisms on Gram stain) and is loculated. Antibiotics alone will not clear it, and it needs drainage. Intrapleural tPA plus DNase can be added for loculations, and VATS decortication follows if drainage fails.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and C delay drainage of an infected space, which leads to fibrothorax or sepsis. D: this is not a transudate. E: pleurodesis is for recurrent malignant effusions, never for an active infection.

stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman who has never smoked and has no family history of lung cancer has a CT of the abdomen for renal colic. It shows a 5-mm smooth solid nodule in the right lower lobe. She has no history of cancer and is not immunocompromised. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for the nodule?

options.label: A
options.html: CT of the chest in 3 months

answerHtml: Answer: D. No routine follow-up.
explanationHtml: Under the Fleischner 2017 guidelines, a single solid nodule <6 mm in a low-risk patient (never-smoker, no family history, smooth margins) carries a malignancy risk below 1%. Routine follow-up is not recommended. Even in high-risk patients, follow-up is only optional, at 12 months.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: a 3-month CT is for nodules >8 mm or part-solid nodules. B: PET is unreliable below about 8 mm. C: biopsy is not indicated. E: this is screening logic (Lung-RADS), and she is not eligible for screening.

stemHtml: A 63-year-old man comes for a health maintenance visit. He smoked 1.5 packs per day for 20 years and quit 12 years ago. He has no symptoms. His medical history is hypertension, which is well controlled. He is otherwise healthy and would accept surgery if needed. Which of the following is the most appropriate lung cancer screening recommendation?

options.label: A
options.html: Annual low-dose CT of the chest

options.label: B
options.html: No screening, because he quit more than 10 years ago

answerHtml: Answer: A. Annual LDCT.
explanationHtml: USPSTF (2021, grade B) recommends annual low-dose CT for adults aged 50–80 with ≥20 pack-years who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years. He has 30 pack-years (1.5 × 20) and quit 12 years ago, so he qualifies. Screening stops once he reaches 15 years since quitting, or if his health no longer permits curative treatment.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: the cutoff is 15 years, not 10. C and D do not reduce lung cancer mortality and are not recommended. E: the recommended interval is annual.

stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman is in the ED with fever, right flank pain and confusion. Temperature is 39.4 °C, BP 82/44 mm Hg (MAP 57), pulse 122/min and RR 24/min. Blood and urine cultures have been drawn, and IV piperacillin-tazobactam was given within 40 minutes of arrival. Over the past 2 hours she has received 30 mL/kg of lactated Ringer's solution. Repeat BP is 84/46 mm Hg (MAP 58). Lactate is 4.6 mmol/L. She has two large-bore peripheral IV lines and no central line yet. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Give another 3 L of 0.9% saline over 1 hour

options.label: C
options.html: Start a norepinephrine infusion through a peripheral IV

options.label: E
options.html: Delay vasopressors until a central venous catheter is placed

answerHtml: Answer: C. Norepinephrine, which can be started peripherally.
explanationHtml: She is in septic shock: hypotension persisting after adequate fluids, with lactate >2. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends norepinephrine as the first-line vasopressor, titrated to an initial MAP target of about 65 (60–65 at age ≥65). Starting it through a well-functioning proximal peripheral IV is acceptable, so treatment is not delayed. Add vasopressin if norepinephrine needs keep rising. Hydrocortisone is added if the vasopressor requirement persists.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: further fluid should be guided by dynamic measures of fluid responsiveness, and large volumes of saline cause hyperchloremic acidosis and fluid overload. B: dopamine causes more arrhythmias than norepinephrine. D: steroids are adjuncts to vasopressors, not a substitute. E: waiting for a central line delays treatment of shock.

stemHtml: A 50-year-old man (height 170 cm, predicted body weight ~66 kg) is intubated for severe pancreatitis. Chest X-ray shows new bilateral diffuse opacities, and echocardiography shows normal LV function. Ventilator settings are volume control, tidal volume 550 mL, RR 18/min, PEEP 8 cm H₂O and FiO₂ 0.7. ABG shows pH 7.36, PaCO₂ 42 mm Hg and PaO₂ 77 mm Hg. Plateau pressure is 33 cm H₂O. Which of the following is the most appropriate ventilator change?

options.label: A
options.html: Increase tidal volume to 650 mL to improve oxygenation

options.label: B
options.html: Decrease PEEP to 0 cm H₂O to lower plateau pressure

options.label: C
options.html: Give IV furosemide without changing the ventilator

options.label: D
options.html: Switch to pressure-support ventilation with no backup rate

options.label: E
options.html: Decrease tidal volume to about 400 mL and increase the respiratory rate

answerHtml: Answer: E. Low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg PBW) with a higher rate.
explanationHtml: He has moderate ARDS (P/F = 77/0.7 = 110). His tidal volume of 550 mL is about 8.3 mL/kg PBW and his plateau pressure is above 30. Lung-protective ventilation means about 6 mL/kg PBW (≈400 mL) and a plateau of 30 cm H₂O or less, which reduces mortality (ARDSNet). Raise the RR to maintain minute ventilation, accepting permissive hypercapnia. With P/F <150, prone positioning is also indicated.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: a larger tidal volume causes volutrauma. B: dropping PEEP to zero worsens derecruitment and hypoxemia. C: diuresis alone ignores injurious ventilator settings, and conservative fluid management comes after shock resolves. D: pressure support without a backup rate is unsafe in severe, sedated ARDS.

stemHtml: A 64-year-old man with severe COPD was intubated 30 minutes ago for hypercapnic respiratory failure. Ventilator settings are tidal volume 500 mL, RR 26/min and PEEP 5 cm H₂O. His BP falls from 128/76 to 72/40 mm Hg. Peak airway pressure is high. Breath sounds are present bilaterally with diffuse wheezes, and the trachea is midline. The ventilator flow waveform shows expiratory flow not returning to baseline before the next breath. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Briefly disconnect the patient from the ventilator, then lower the respiratory rate

options.label: D
options.html: Bilateral needle decompression of the chest

options.label: E
options.html: Start an epinephrine infusion and leave the settings unchanged

answerHtml: Answer: B. Disconnect from the ventilator to release trapped air, then lengthen expiratory time.
explanationHtml: This is dynamic hyperinflation (auto-PEEP). A high rate in obstructed lungs leaves too little time to exhale, so breaths stack. Intrathoracic pressure rises, venous return falls and the patient becomes hypotensive. Disconnecting the circuit lets the trapped gas escape. Then reduce the RR and tidal volume and shorten inspiratory time (higher flow), accepting permissive hypercapnia, and treat bronchospasm.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and C worsen air trapping. D: bilateral breath sounds and a midline trachea argue against tension pneumothorax, so needle decompression is not indicated. E: vasopressors without fixing the cause leave the mechanical problem in place.

stemHtml: A 78-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia has had 2 days of decreased urine output and lower abdominal discomfort. He recently started diphenhydramine for sleep. He has suprapubic fullness and tenderness. Creatinine is 2.6 mg/dL (baseline 1.1) and potassium 5.2 mEq/L. Bedside bladder ultrasound shows 950 mL of urine. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: CT of the abdomen with IV contrast

options.label: C
options.html: Start tamsulosin and recheck creatinine in 1 week

answerHtml: Answer: D. Bladder catheterization.
explanationHtml: This is postrenal AKI from bladder outlet obstruction (BPH plus an anticholinergic antihistamine). Relieving the obstruction treats it and confirms the diagnosis. After decompression, watch for post-obstructive diuresis and electrolyte shifts, and stop the diphenhydramine. Tamsulosin can then be started with a trial of voiding.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: fluids do not relieve obstruction and can cause overload. B: contrast is a nephrotoxic risk and unnecessary, since bedside ultrasound has already shown retention. C: a week is too long to leave 950 mL of retention and rising creatinine. E: he has no dialysis indication, and the AKI should reverse with drainage.

stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with CKD stage G4 and diabetes takes lisinopril and spironolactone. He has generalised weakness. BP is 136/82 mm Hg and pulse 58/min. Serum potassium is 7.4 mEq/L (the sample is not hemolysed), glucose 162 mg/dL and HCO₃ 20 mEq/L. ECG shows peaked T waves, a prolonged PR interval and QRS duration of 140 ms. Which of the following is the most appropriate first step?

options.label: E
options.html: Arrange hemodialysis within the next 24 hours

answerHtml: Answer: A. IV calcium gluconate.
explanationHtml: Severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes, especially QRS widening, is an emergency. The first priority is to stabilise the cardiac membrane with IV calcium, which acts within minutes, though it does not lower K. Next, shift K into cells with insulin plus dextrose and nebulised albuterol. Then remove K from the body with a binder (sodium zirconium cyclosilicate or patiromer), diuretics or dialysis. Stop lisinopril and spironolactone.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B is slow and carries a risk of bowel necrosis. C is the correct second step but takes 15–30 minutes, and it comes after membrane stabilisation. D is slow and only partially effective in CKD G4. E: dialysis may be needed, but a 24-hour delay is unacceptable when the ECG has already changed, and membrane stabilisation comes first in any case.

stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure at the finish line of a marathon, during which she drank large volumes of water. She is now post-ictal and vomiting. BP is 124/76 mm Hg. Serum sodium is 118 mEq/L (it was normal 1 month ago) and glucose 98 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
answerHtml: Answer: C. 3% saline bolus.
explanationHtml: She has acute (<48 h), severely symptomatic hyponatremia (seizure, vomiting) from exercise-associated hyponatremia, with risk of cerebral edema and herniation. The treatment is a 100-mL bolus of 3% saline over about 10 minutes, repeated up to twice more if symptoms persist, aiming for a 4–6 mEq/L rise. Acute hyponatremia carries little risk of ODS, but the usual daily limits still guide later correction.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: fluid restriction is far too slow for a seizing patient. B: isotonic saline raises Na too little in the presence of non-osmotic ADH (stress, nausea) and can make things worse. D: tolvaptan is for chronic euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia, not emergencies. E: desmopressin would worsen water retention. It is used only as a rescue to prevent overcorrection.

stemHtml: A 70-year-old man with newly diagnosed small cell lung cancer has a serum sodium of 127 mEq/L. He has no symptoms. He appears euvolemic, with normal BP, no orthostasis and no edema. Serum osmolality is 262 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg and urine sodium 55 mEq/L. TSH and morning cortisol are normal. He takes no diuretics. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Fluid restriction.
explanationHtml: This is SIADH from ectopic ADH: euvolemic hypotonic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine and urine Na >30, after hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency have been excluded. For mild to moderate asymptomatic SIADH, the first step is fluid restriction (<800–1,000 mL/day). Oral salt tablets with a loop diuretic, oral urea or tolvaptan are added if needed. Treating the cancer often resolves it.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: hypertonic saline is reserved for severe or symptomatic hyponatremia. B: with a fixed high urine osmolality, normal saline can lower Na further, because the salt is excreted and the water retained. C: IV vaptans are for hospitalised patients needing a faster rise and are not first line for an asymptomatic patient. D: demeclocycline is a slow, nephrotoxic second-line drug.

stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman with alcohol use disorder and poor nutrition is admitted with confusion and a serum sodium of 108 mEq/L. Serum potassium is 2.9 mEq/L. She is treated with isotonic saline and potassium. Ten hours later she has passed 4 L of dilute urine (urine osmolality 90 mOsm/kg), and her sodium is 120 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue current therapy and recheck sodium in 24 hours

options.label: B
options.html: Start D5W and give IV desmopressin

answerHtml: Answer: B. Re-lower the sodium with D5W ± desmopressin.
explanationHtml: She is at high risk for osmotic demyelination syndrome: initial Na ≤105–110, alcohol use disorder, malnutrition and hypokalemia. Her correction limit is ≤8 mEq/L in 24 hours. In 10 hours she has risen 12 mEq/L because of a brisk water diuresis: once volume was restored, ADH switched off. Give free water (D5W) and desmopressin to stop the aquaresis and bring Na back toward the limit.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: continuing allows further dangerous overcorrection. C and E would raise Na further. D: furosemide promotes free-water loss, which also raises Na.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is brought in drowsy after missing insulin doses. He also took several oxycodone tablets. RR is 10/min. Labs show Na 134, Cl 98 and HCO₃ 10 mEq/L, glucose 520 mg/dL and positive serum β-hydroxybutyrate. ABG shows pH 7.12 and PaCO₂ 32 mm Hg. Which of the following best describes his acid–base status?

options.label: A
options.html: Anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation

options.label: B
options.html: Anion gap metabolic acidosis with concomitant respiratory alkalosis

options.label: C
options.html: Non-anion gap metabolic acidosis with concomitant metabolic alkalosis

options.label: D
options.html: Anion gap metabolic acidosis with concomitant respiratory acidosis

options.label: E
options.html: Primary respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation

answerHtml: Answer: D. High-AG metabolic acidosis (DKA) with superimposed respiratory acidosis.
explanationHtml: The anion gap is 134 − (98 + 10) = 26, which is high (ketoacidosis). Winter's formula predicts PaCO₂ = 1.5(10) + 8 ± 2 = 21–25 mm Hg. His actual PaCO₂ of 32 is higher than expected, so ventilation is inadequate: a second, respiratory acidosis from opioid-induced hypoventilation. The delta ratio is (26 − 12)/(24 − 10) = 1.0, so there is no added metabolic disorder. He needs his airway assessed and naloxone, alongside DKA treatment.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: compensation would bring PaCO₂ to 21–25. B: respiratory alkalosis would push PaCO₂ below 21. C: the gap is high, and a delta ratio of 1 indicates no metabolic alkalosis. E: HCO₃ is low, not high, so the primary process is metabolic.

stemHtml: A 45-year-old man is found confused in his garage. BP is 142/88 mm Hg, RR 28/min, and he has no visual complaints. Labs: Na 138, Cl 100, HCO₃ 8 mEq/L, BUN 28 mg/dL, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, glucose 90 mg/dL. Measured serum osmolality is 330 mOsm/kg. Ethanol is undetectable. Urinalysis shows envelope-shaped crystals. In addition to nephrology consultation for hemodialysis, which of the following should be given?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Fomepizole.
explanationHtml: The anion gap is 138 − 108 = 30. Calculated osmolality is 2(138) + 90/18 + 28/2.8 = 276 + 5 + 10 = 291, giving an osmolar gap of about 39. Calcium oxalate (envelope) crystals and AKI identify ethylene glycol poisoning. Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase and stops conversion to glycolic and oxalic acids. Severe acidosis and AKI are indications for hemodialysis, which removes both the parent alcohol and its toxic metabolites. Thiamine and pyridoxine are adjuncts.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B is the antidote for acetaminophen. C: charcoal does not bind alcohols, and they are absorbed quickly. D: thiamine is an adjunct, not the main antidote. E: methylene blue treats methemoglobinemia.

stemHtml: A 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has an eGFR of 38 mL/min/1.73 m² (stable over 1 year) and a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 650 mg/g. She takes losartan 100 mg daily (maximum dose), metformin 500 mg twice daily and atorvastatin. BP is 126/78 mm Hg, potassium 4.6 mEq/L and HbA1c 7.4%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to slow progression of her kidney disease?

options.label: E
options.html: Stop losartan because of her reduced eGFR

answerHtml: Answer: C. Add an SGLT2 inhibitor.
explanationHtml: KDIGO and ADA recommend an SGLT2 inhibitor for patients with T2DM and CKD with eGFR ≥20, on top of maximally tolerated RAAS blockade. It reduces kidney failure, cardiovascular death and HF hospitalisation (CREDENCE, DAPA-CKD, EMPA-KIDNEY). Its kidney benefit does not depend on glucose lowering. Finerenone and a GLP-1 RA (semaglutide) are further add-ons for persistent albuminuria.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and D: dual RAAS blockade (ACEi + ARB, or adding aliskiren) causes hyperkalemia and AKI without benefit. B: severe protein restriction risks malnutrition; KDIGO suggests about 0.8 g/kg/day. E: RAAS blockade should continue in albuminuric CKD despite a reduced eGFR.

stemHtml: A 40-year-old man has 1 day of severe right flank pain radiating to the groin, with fever and rigors. Temperature is 39.2 °C, BP 104/64 mm Hg and pulse 112/min. WBC count is 18,000/mm³ and creatinine is 1.3 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows pyuria, nitrites and bacteria. Non-contrast CT shows a 7-mm proximal right ureteral stone with moderate hydronephrosis. Blood and urine cultures have been sent. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: D
options.html: 24-hour urine collection for stone risk analysis

options.label: E
options.html: IV antibiotics and urgent decompression with a ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy

answerHtml: Answer: E. Urgent drainage plus IV antibiotics.
explanationHtml: An obstructed, infected upper urinary tract (obstructive pyelonephritis heading toward urosepsis) is a urologic emergency. Antibiotics cannot sterilise an obstructed collecting system, so it must be drained urgently by retrograde ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy. Definitive stone treatment is postponed until the infection has cleared.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: medical expulsive therapy is only for uncomplicated stones without infection. B: lithotripsy of an infected obstructed system can cause sepsis and is deferred. C: a septic patient with obstruction needs admission and drainage. D: metabolic evaluation is done later, for prevention.

stemHtml: A 28-year-old man who smokes has 1 week of hemoptysis and dark urine. BP is 150/94 mm Hg. Creatinine has risen from 1.6 to 3.8 mg/dL over 4 days. Urinalysis shows dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts and 1.5 g/day of protein. Chest X-ray shows bilateral alveolar infiltrates. Serum anti-GBM antibodies are strongly positive, ANCA is negative and C3/C4 are normal. A kidney biopsy is scheduled for tomorrow. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment to start now?

options.label: A
options.html: Lisinopril and repeat creatinine in 1 week

options.label: B
options.html: Plasma exchange with high-dose glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide

options.label: D
options.html: Supportive care until biopsy results are available

options.label: E
options.html: IV ceftriaxone and azithromycin for pneumonia

answerHtml: Answer: B. Plasma exchange + glucocorticoids + cyclophosphamide.
explanationHtml: This is anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome) with pulmonary hemorrhage and RPGN. Treat urgently with plasma exchange to remove circulating antibody, pulse then oral glucocorticoids, and cyclophosphamide to stop antibody production. Positive serology with a typical picture justifies starting before the biopsy, because outcomes depend on the creatinine and dialysis dependence at the start of treatment. The biopsy will show linear IgG deposition along the GBM.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and D delay treatment of a rapidly progressive, organ-threatening disease. C: rituximab is the induction agent for ANCA vasculitis. In anti-GBM disease, plasma exchange plus cyclophosphamide is the standard. E: this is not infection, and antibiotics do not treat it.

stemHtml: A 70-year-old man with HFrEF is admitted with decompensated heart failure. He has received IV furosemide 80 mg twice daily for 3 days, losing 6 kg, and is now orthostatic. Creatinine has risen from 1.2 to 2.1 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows a few hyaline casts with no cells or granular casts. Fractional excretion of sodium is 2.4%. Which of the following tests would best distinguish prerenal azotemia from acute tubular necrosis in this patient?

options.label: C
options.html: Repeat fractional excretion of sodium in 6 hours

answerHtml: Answer: D. Fractional excretion of urea (FEUrea).
explanationHtml: Loop diuretics block sodium reabsorption and falsely raise FENa, so FENa misleads in patients taking them. Urea is reabsorbed mainly in the proximal tubule and is largely unaffected by loop diuretics. An FEUrea <35% supports a prerenal state, here from over-diuresis. FEUrea >50% suggests ATN. The bland sediment with hyaline casts also favours a prerenal cause. Hold the diuretic and reassess his volume status.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: biopsy is invasive and not indicated for a likely hemodynamic AKI. B: urine eosinophils are a poor test, even for AIN. C: repeating FENa while the diuretic effect persists remains unreliable. E: cystatin C estimates GFR but does not tell prerenal from intrinsic injury.

stemHtml: A 29-year-old man comes to the emergency department after vomiting a small amount of coffee-ground material once this morning. He has taken ibuprofen 800 mg three times daily for 1 week for an ankle sprain. He has had no melena or syncope and has no history of liver disease or heart failure. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 82/min, and blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg. The epigastrium is mildly tender. Hemoglobin is 14.8 g/dL, BUN is 14 mg/dL, and creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Admission to the intensive care unit and upper endoscopy within 12 hours

options.label: B
options.html: Discontinue ibuprofen, start an oral proton pump inhibitor, and discharge with outpatient endoscopy

options.label: C
options.html: Transfusion of 1 unit of packed red blood cells

answerHtml: Answer: B. Stop the NSAID, oral PPI, discharge with outpatient endoscopy.
explanationHtml: His Glasgow-Blatchford score is 0: BUN <18.2 mg/dL, hemoglobin ≥13 g/dL in a man, systolic BP ≥110, pulse <100, and no melena, syncope, liver disease or heart failure. ACG guidance supports outpatient management of patients with GBS 0–1 because their risk of needing intervention or dying is very low. The likely lesion is an NSAID-induced ulcer or erosions, so stopping ibuprofen and starting a PPI is the right treatment, with H. pylori testing as part of follow-up.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — ICU care and urgent EGD are for high-risk or unstable bleeding. C — Hb 14.8 is far above the restrictive threshold of 7 g/dL. D — octreotide is for suspected variceal bleeding (cirrhosis). E — CT angiography is for brisk ongoing bleeding when the source can't be found, usually in the lower GI tract.

stemHtml: A 54-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis has two episodes of large-volume hematemesis. Pulse is 118/min and blood pressure is 88/56 mm Hg. Two large-bore IV lines are placed, 1 L of crystalloid is infused, and transfusion of packed red cells is started. Hemoglobin is 7.6 g/dL, platelet count is 68,000/µL, and INR is 1.7. He is alert and protecting his airway. In addition to resuscitation, which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Fresh frozen plasma to correct the INR to <1.5 before endoscopy

options.label: D
options.html: Intravenous octreotide and intravenous ceftriaxone, followed by upper endoscopy within 12 hours

answerHtml: Answer: D. Vasoactive therapy plus antibiotic prophylaxis, then EGD within 12 hours.
explanationHtml: Suspected acute variceal hemorrhage calls for a bundle: a splanchnic vasoconstrictor (octreotide) to lower portal pressure, prophylactic ceftriaxone (which lowers bacterial infection, rebleeding and mortality in cirrhosis), restrictive transfusion to a hemoglobin of about 7–8 g/dL, and endoscopic band ligation within 12 hours.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — the INR does not reflect bleeding risk in cirrhosis because both pro- and anticoagulant factors are reduced; FFP expands volume and raises portal pressure. B — beta-blockers lower blood pressure and are contraindicated during acute hemorrhage with hypotension; they are started later for secondary prophylaxis. C — TIPS is rescue therapy (or pre-emptive in Child C/high-risk B after endoscopic control), not first-line before endoscopy. E — balloon tamponade is only a temporary bridge (≤24 h) for uncontrollable bleeding.

stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman has 2 months of epigastric pain. Upper endoscopy shows a 7-mm clean-based duodenal ulcer, and antral biopsy shows Helicobacter pylori. She developed hives after taking amoxicillin as a child. She took azithromycin for sinusitis last year. She takes no NSAIDs. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: PPI, bismuth subsalicylate, tetracycline, and metronidazole for 14 days

options.label: B
options.html: PPI, clarithromycin, and amoxicillin for 14 days

options.label: C
options.html: PPI, clarithromycin, and metronidazole for 14 days

options.label: E
options.html: PPI alone for 8 weeks, then serology to confirm eradication

answerHtml: Answer: A. Bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days.
explanationHtml: The ACG 2024 guideline makes bismuth quadruple therapy the preferred first-line regimen for treatment-naive patients, and it is the obvious choice here: she has a penicillin allergy, and her earlier macrolide use makes clarithromycin resistance likely. Afterward, confirm eradication with a urea breath test, stool antigen, or biopsy at least 4 weeks after antibiotics and 2 weeks after stopping the PPI.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B and D both contain amoxicillin, which she is allergic to. B and C use clarithromycin. US resistance is over 15%, and prior macrolide exposure predicts resistance, so clarithromycin triple therapy is only used when susceptibility has been documented. E — a PPI alone does not eradicate H. pylori, and serology stays positive after cure, so it cannot confirm eradication.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old man comes to the emergency department 3 hours after a piece of steak became stuck while he was eating. He is drooling, spitting out saliva, and unable to swallow water. He has had two similar episodes in the past year that resolved on their own. He has asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis. Vital signs are normal, and there is no subcutaneous crepitus. Chest x-ray shows no free air. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Intravenous glucagon and observation for 24 hours

options.label: C
options.html: CT of the chest with oral contrast

answerHtml: Answer: E. Urgent upper endoscopy.
explanationHtml: A food bolus causing complete obstruction (he cannot handle his own secretions) needs endoscopic removal urgently, ideally within 6 hours, because of the risks of aspiration, pressure necrosis and perforation. A young atopic man with repeated impactions most likely has eosinophilic esophagitis, so esophageal biopsies (≥6) should be taken during or after the procedure.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and C — contrast studies delay treatment, risk aspiration, and barium coats the mucosa so that endoscopy becomes harder. B — glucagon may be tried briefly but must not delay endoscopy, and observing for 24 hours with a complete obstruction is unsafe. D — enzymatic meat tenderizers can damage the esophagus and are contraindicated.

stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis is admitted with 12 bloody stools per day. On admission, pulse is 108/min and temperature is 38.0 °C (100.4 °F). Stool testing for C. difficile is negative, and flexible sigmoidoscopy biopsies show no CMV inclusions. Abdominal x-ray shows a transverse colon diameter of 4.5 cm. She receives IV methylprednisolone 60 mg/day and enoxaparin prophylaxis. On hospital day 4 she still has 9 bloody stools per day, and C-reactive protein is 58 mg/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: E
options.html: Continue the current regimen for 7 more days

answerHtml: Answer: C. Rescue therapy with infliximab (cyclosporine is the alternative).
explanationHtml: This is acute severe UC (Truelove-Witts criteria) that has not responded after 3–5 days of IV corticosteroids. More than 8 stools per day, or 3–8 stools with CRP >45 mg/L, on day 3 predicts colectomy. Infectious causes (C. difficile, CMV) have been excluded, so medical rescue with infliximab or cyclosporine is indicated, with early surgical consultation. Colectomy follows if rescue fails or toxic megacolon or perforation develops.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — higher steroid doses add no benefit. B — mesalamine is too weak for acute severe colitis. D — thiopurines take 2–3 months to work and are maintenance drugs. E — continuing steroids that are failing delays rescue therapy and increases surgical complications and mortality.

stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman who was born in India and received BCG at birth has moderate-to-severe ileocolonic Crohn disease that has not responded to budesonide. Her gastroenterologist plans to start adalimumab. She has no fever, cough, or weight loss. Which of the following should be done before the first dose?

options.label: B
options.html: Interferon-γ release assay and hepatitis B serologies (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs)

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat colonoscopy to define disease extent

options.label: E
options.html: No testing is needed; begin adalimumab

answerHtml: Answer: B. IGRA plus hepatitis B serologies.
explanationHtml: TNF inhibitors impair granuloma maintenance and can reactivate latent TB, and they can also reactivate HBV. Every patient needs screening for latent TB and HBV (HCV and HIV are also reasonable) before starting. An IGRA is preferred in BCG-vaccinated people because BCG does not affect it. If latent TB is found, treatment should begin, ideally about 1 month before the biologic. Live vaccines must also be given before immunosuppression starts.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — a TST can be falsely positive after BCG and does not screen for HBV. C — TPMT testing is needed before azathioprine or 6-MP, not adalimumab. D — colonoscopy does not change the need to screen for infection. E — skipping screening risks disseminated TB or fulminant HBV.

stemHtml: A 50-year-old woman has had fatigue and generalized itching for 6 months, worse at night. She does not drink alcohol and takes no medications. Examination shows excoriations without jaundice. Labs: alkaline phosphatase 410 U/L (ULN 120), GGT 290 U/L, ALT 48 U/L, AST 44 U/L, total bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL, albumin 4.0 g/dL. Right upper quadrant ultrasound shows normal liver echotexture and no biliary dilation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Antimitochondrial antibody.
explanationHtml: This is a cholestatic pattern (R ratio well below 2), the raised GGT confirms the ALP comes from the liver, and the ducts are not dilated. In a middle-aged woman with pruritus and fatigue, the leading diagnosis is primary biliary cholangitis. A positive AMA (≥1:40) with ALP ≥1.5× ULN is diagnostic without biopsy. Treatment is ursodeoxycholic acid, with a PPAR agonist (elafibranor, seladelpar) for an inadequate response. Obeticholic acid was withdrawn from the US market in 2025.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — ERCP is invasive and is used to treat obstruction; MRCP would be the next test if AMA were negative (to look for PSC). C — biopsy is reserved for AMA-negative cases after a normal MRCP or unclear overlap. D and E — hemochromatosis and Wilson disease give hepatocellular, not cholestatic, patterns.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis and ascites is admitted with temperature 38.2 °C (100.8 °F), mild diffuse abdominal tenderness, and new confusion. Diagnostic paracentesis shows a polymorphonuclear count of 420/µL. Gram stain shows no organisms, and culture is pending. Creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL (baseline 1.0), and total bilirubin is 3.4 mg/dL. Blood pressure is 104/66 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: B
options.html: No antibiotics until ascitic fluid culture results return

answerHtml: Answer: D. IV third-generation cephalosporin plus IV albumin (1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3).
explanationHtml: An ascitic PMN count of ≥250/µL is diagnostic of SBP, and treatment starts before culture results. Albumin significantly reduces hepatorenal syndrome and mortality in patients with creatinine >1 mg/dL, BUN >30 mg/dL, or bilirubin >4 mg/dL. He meets the creatinine criterion. After recovery, he needs lifelong secondary prophylaxis.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — antibiotics alone leave him at high risk of renal failure. B — delaying treatment raises mortality. C — oral norfloxacin is a prophylaxis drug, not treatment for active SBP, and it is no longer available in the US. E — therapeutic large-volume paracentesis is avoided during active SBP with AKI, and it does not treat infection.

stemHtml: A 61-year-old man with cirrhosis is admitted for the second time in 4 months with overt hepatic encephalopathy. Evaluation finds no infection, GI bleeding, electrolyte abnormality, or sedative use. Before admission he took lactulose reliably, with 2–3 soft stools daily. His mental status returns to normal after lactulose is titrated in the hospital. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to prevent recurrence?

options.label: D
options.html: Lorazepam at bedtime to restore the sleep–wake cycle

answerHtml: Answer: E. Rifaximin added to lactulose.
explanationHtml: Lactulose is first-line for treatment and secondary prevention of hepatic encephalopathy. After a recurrence on adequate lactulose, adding rifaximin (550 mg BID), a minimally absorbed antibiotic that reduces ammonia-producing gut bacteria, lowers recurrence and hospitalizations. It is also important to look for, and remove, precipitants.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — neomycin causes ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity with long-term use. B — protein restriction worsens sarcopenia and outcomes; cirrhotic patients need 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day. C — long-term metronidazole causes peripheral neuropathy. D — benzodiazepines precipitate encephalopathy.

stemHtml: A 57-year-old woman with cirrhosis and tense ascites is hospitalized when her creatinine rises from 1.0 to 2.4 mg/dL over 3 days. Diuretics are stopped, and she receives IV albumin 1 g/kg/day for 2 days, but creatinine is now 2.6 mg/dL. She has received no NSAIDs or contrast. Mean arterial pressure is 72 mm Hg, oxygen saturation is 97% on room air, and lungs are clear. Urinalysis is bland with no proteinuria, urine sodium is <10 mEq/L, and renal ultrasound is normal. Diagnostic paracentesis shows no SBP. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue albumin alone and recheck creatinine in 48 hours

answerHtml: Answer: C. Terlipressin plus albumin.
explanationHtml: She meets the criteria for hepatorenal syndrome–AKI: cirrhosis with ascites, an AKI that did not respond to 48 hours of diuretic withdrawal plus albumin, no shock, no nephrotoxins, and no evidence of parenchymal kidney disease. Terlipressin, a vasopressin analog that constricts splanchnic vessels, is FDA-approved and improves HRS reversal. It requires adequate oxygenation (avoid if SpO2 <90% or volume overloaded). Norepinephrine is an ICU alternative, and midodrine plus octreotide is used only when neither is available. Liver transplant is the definitive treatment.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — continuing albumin alone after a failed challenge delays effective therapy. B — diuretics worsen renal perfusion. D — dialysis is a bridge for refractory cases or urgent indications (none here). E — large saline volumes worsen ascites and are inappropriate after an adequate albumin challenge.

stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman, gravida 1, at 24 weeks' gestation, is HBsAg-positive on prenatal screening. HBeAg is positive, HBV DNA is 3.4 × 10<sup>7</sup> IU/mL, and ALT is 28 U/L. Liver elastography is normal. The pediatric team will give the newborn hepatitis B immune globulin and the first vaccine dose within 12 hours of birth. Which of the following additional measures most reduces the risk of perinatal transmission?

options.label: A
options.html: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate starting at 28–32 weeks' gestation

answerHtml: Answer: A. Tenofovir (TDF) from 28–32 weeks through delivery.
explanationHtml: With HBV DNA >200,000 IU/mL, immunoprophylaxis alone fails in roughly 8–10% of infants. Adding maternal TDF in the third trimester lowers transmission substantially and is safe in pregnancy. It can be stopped at delivery to 3 months postpartum, with monitoring for flares, if she does not otherwise meet treatment criteria.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — entecavir has limited pregnancy safety data, and TDF is the drug of choice. C — cesarean delivery is not recommended for HBV. D — interferon is contraindicated in pregnancy. E — breastfeeding is permitted, including while taking TDF, once the infant has received immunoprophylaxis.

stemHtml: A 46-year-old man has a positive HCV antibody on routine one-time screening. HCV RNA is 1.8 million IU/mL, ALT is 64 U/L, platelet count is 240,000/µL, FIB-4 is 0.9, and transient elastography is 5.8 kPa. HBsAg and anti-HBc are negative, anti-HBs is positive, and HIV testing is negative. He takes no medications and has never been treated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Pegylated interferon plus ribavirin for 48 weeks

options.label: B
options.html: Liver biopsy to stage fibrosis before treatment

options.label: C
options.html: Repeat HCV RNA in 6 months and treat if still detectable

answerHtml: Answer: D. A pangenotypic direct-acting antiviral regimen (sofosbuvir-velpatasvir 12 weeks; glecaprevir-pibrentasvir 8 weeks is equivalent).
explanationHtml: The simplified AASLD/IDSA approach treats every viremic, treatment-naive patient without cirrhosis using a pangenotypic DAA. Genotyping is not required, and noninvasive fibrosis testing (FIB-4, elastography) replaces biopsy. HBV status has been checked (no reactivation risk). Cure is SVR12, an undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks after therapy, and occurs in more than 95% of patients.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — interferon-based regimens are obsolete (toxic, less effective). B — biopsy is unnecessary when noninvasive tests are clearly low. C — there is no reason to wait; acute and chronic HCV are both treated promptly. E — ribavirin alone is ineffective.

stemHtml: A 44-year-old man is hospitalized with alcohol-associated acute pancreatitis (lipase 2,400 U/L, typical pain). He has received goal-directed lactated Ringer solution at a moderate rate. On day 2 his pain is 3/10 on oral analgesics, he has no nausea, bowel sounds are present, and he asks for food. Pulse is 88/min, BUN has fallen from 26 to 16 mg/dL, and lipase is 900 U/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Keep him NPO until lipase normalizes

options.label: B
options.html: Start an oral low-fat solid diet

options.label: C
options.html: Place a nasojejunal tube for enteral feeding

answerHtml: Answer: B. Early oral feeding with a low-fat solid diet.
explanationHtml: In mild acute pancreatitis, oral feeding within 24–48 hours, as tolerated, shortens hospital stay and is safe. There is no need to wait for lipase to normalize or for pain to resolve fully. A low-fat solid diet is as safe as clear liquids. Enteral tube feeding is used only when oral intake fails, and it is preferred over TPN, which raises infectious complications.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — lipase does not guide feeding, and prolonged NPO harms gut barrier function. C — tube feeding is unnecessary when he can eat. D — TPN is the last resort. E — prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended, even for necrotizing pancreatitis; use them only for documented infection.

stemHtml: A 41-year-old man asks about colon cancer screening. His father was diagnosed with colorectal adenocarcinoma at age 55 and is alive after resection. No other relatives have had cancer. He has no GI symptoms, and his examination and CBC are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.label: A
options.html: Fecal immunochemical test annually starting now

options.label: B
options.html: Colonoscopy at age 45, then every 10 years

answerHtml: Answer: E. Colonoscopy now, then every 5 years.
explanationHtml: A first-degree relative diagnosed with CRC before age 60 puts him at increased risk. Screening should be by colonoscopy (not stool tests) starting at age 40 or 10 years before the relative's age at diagnosis (55 − 10 = 45), whichever is earlier. That makes the start age 40, so at 41 he is already due. The interval is every 5 years.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and C — stool tests and CT colonography are average-risk options. B — this is the average-risk schedule (USPSTF age 45). D — age 50 is the outdated average-risk start age.

stemHtml: A 64-year-old man with type 2 diabetes takes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily. His A1c is 7.4%. He has heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 30%, NYHA class II), treated with sacubitril-valsartan, carvedilol, and spironolactone. eGFR is 52 mL/min/1.73 m², and BMI is 29 kg/m². Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his regimen?
answerHtml: Answer: C. An SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin or dapagliflozin).
explanationHtml: The ADA recommends an SGLT2 inhibitor for any patient with type 2 diabetes and heart failure, regardless of A1c or baseline therapy, because it reduces heart failure hospitalization and cardiovascular death (it is also one of the four pillars of HFrEF therapy). It also slows CKD progression, which fits his eGFR of 52. Counsel him about genital mycotic infection and euglycemic DKA, and to hold the drug for 3 days before surgery.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — pioglitazone causes fluid retention and is contraindicated in symptomatic HF. B — saxagliptin increased HF hospitalizations (SAVOR-TIMI). D — sulfonylureas cause hypoglycemia and weight gain and have no cardiorenal benefit. E — insulin is not needed at A1c 7.4% and has no cardiorenal benefit.

stemHtml: A 57-year-old woman had a myocardial infarction treated with PCI 2 years ago. She has type 2 diabetes treated with maximum-dose metformin, and her A1c is 8.3%. BMI is 37 kg/m², and eGFR is 88 mL/min/1.73 m². She has no history of pancreatitis, gastroparesis, or thyroid cancer, and no family history of medullary thyroid cancer. She wants to lose weight. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition?
answerHtml: Answer: A. A GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven cardiovascular benefit (semaglutide).
explanationHtml: She has established ASCVD and obesity. The ADA recommends a GLP-1 RA (or an SGLT2 inhibitor) with proven cardiovascular benefit regardless of A1c. Semaglutide also lowers A1c substantially and produces major weight loss, which suits her goals. Tirzepatide would also be reasonable for weight and glucose.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — sulfonylureas cause weight gain and hypoglycemia without CV benefit. C — pioglitazone causes weight gain and edema. D — sitagliptin is weight-neutral and CV-neutral, with modest potency. E — insulin causes weight gain and is not needed before a GLP-1 RA at this A1c.

stemHtml: A 20-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes has vomited for 1 day after missing insulin doses. Pulse is 120/min, blood pressure is 100/62 mm Hg, and respirations are 30/min and deep. Labs: glucose 486 mg/dL, Na<sup>+</sup> 131 mEq/L, K<sup>+</sup> 3.1 mEq/L, Cl<sup>−</sup> 96 mEq/L, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 8 mEq/L, BUN 28 mg/dL, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, venous pH 7.10, β-hydroxybutyrate 6.8 mmol/L. She has received a 1-L bolus of 0.9% saline. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Start a regular insulin infusion at 0.1 U/kg/h

options.label: B
options.html: Give a regular insulin IV bolus of 0.1 U/kg followed by an infusion

options.label: D
options.html: Switch IV fluids to 5% dextrose in 0.45% saline

options.label: E
options.html: Give intravenous potassium chloride and withhold insulin until K<sup>+</sup> is ≥3.5 mEq/L

answerHtml: Answer: E. Replete potassium first and hold insulin until K<sup>+</sup> ≥3.5 mEq/L.
explanationHtml: Despite acidosis, which shifts K+ out of cells, her serum K+ is already low, so total-body potassium is severely depleted. Insulin drives K+ into cells and could cause life-threatening hypokalemia, arrhythmia and respiratory muscle weakness. Fluids continue, IV KCl (about 10–20 mEq/h) is given with cardiac monitoring, and the insulin infusion starts once K+ is at least 3.5.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B — starting insulin with K<sup>+</sup> 3.1 is dangerous. C — bicarbonate is reserved for pH <7.0 and would further lower K<sup>+</sup>. D — dextrose is added only once glucose falls below about 250 mg/dL.

stemHtml: A 19-year-old man with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes is being treated for DKA with a regular insulin infusion at 0.1 U/kg/h and 0.9% saline with 20 mEq/L KCl. Six hours later, glucose is 228 mg/dL, anion gap is 17 mEq/L, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> is 13 mEq/L, venous pH is 7.22, and K<sup>+</sup> is 4.2 mEq/L. He is nauseated and not yet eating. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Stop the insulin infusion until glucose rises above 250 mg/dL

options.label: B
options.html: Add dextrose to the IV fluids and continue the insulin infusion

options.label: C
options.html: Give subcutaneous insulin glargine and stop the infusion now

options.label: E
options.html: Continue the current fluids and insulin unchanged

answerHtml: Answer: B. Add dextrose (e.g., D5 in 0.45% saline) and continue insulin, reducing the rate to about 0.05 U/kg/h if needed.
explanationHtml: Insulin is given in DKA to suppress ketogenesis and close the anion gap, not just to lower glucose. Glucose normalizes well before the ketoacidosis resolves. Once glucose falls below about 250 mg/dL, dextrose is added so insulin can continue without causing hypoglycemia until the resolution criteria are met (pH ≥7.3, HCO3− ≥18, BHB <0.6 mmol/L). The transition to subcutaneous basal insulin then overlaps the infusion by ≥2 hours.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — stopping insulin lets ketogenesis continue. C — he has not met resolution criteria and is not eating, and stopping the drip without overlap causes rebound DKA. D — pH 7.22 does not warrant bicarbonate. E — continuing unchanged risks hypoglycemia.

stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman has a palpable nodule in the right thyroid lobe. She reports mild heat intolerance. TSH is 0.05 µU/mL (normal 0.4–4.0), and free T4 is 1.9 ng/dL (normal 0.8–1.8). Neck ultrasound shows a 2.2-cm solid, isoechoic, well-circumscribed nodule without microcalcifications and no abnormal lymph nodes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Radionuclide thyroid scan.
explanationHtml: When a nodule is found with a subnormal TSH, the ATA recommends a radionuclide scan next. A hyperfunctioning ("hot") nodule is almost never malignant and does not need FNA. This one is probably a toxic adenoma, which is treated with radioactive iodine, lobectomy, or (temporarily) methimazole. If the nodule is cold or isointense, it is biopsied according to its ultrasound criteria.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — FNA of a hot nodule is unnecessary, and the cytology is often indeterminate and misleading. B — surgery without functional characterization is premature. C — she is hyperthyroid and needs a diagnosis now. E — levothyroxine would worsen hyperthyroidism.

stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman has a thyroid nodule found incidentally on a carotid ultrasound. She has no symptoms and no history of radiation exposure. TSH is 1.8 µU/mL. Dedicated thyroid ultrasound shows a 1.3-cm solid, markedly hypoechoic nodule with irregular margins and microcalcifications. No cervical lymphadenopathy is present. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Ultrasound-guided FNA.
explanationHtml: With a normal TSH, the decision depends on the ultrasound pattern and size. A solid hypoechoic nodule with irregular margins and microcalcifications has a high-suspicion pattern (70–90% malignancy risk, most often papillary carcinoma), and FNA is recommended at ≥1 cm. The Bethesda category then guides management.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — a scan is used only when TSH is low. B — observation is for very-low-suspicion or subcentimeter nodules. D — tissue diagnosis comes before surgery to plan its extent. E — thyroglobulin is a postoperative tumor marker for differentiated cancer, not a diagnostic test.

stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman with Graves disease stopped methimazole 2 months ago. She now has community-acquired pneumonia and presents with agitation and delirium. Temperature is 40.1 °C (104.2 °F), pulse is 156/min and irregularly irregular, and blood pressure is 142/60 mm Hg. She has mild jaundice. TSH is undetectable, and free T4 is 6.2 ng/dL. IV fluids, cooling blankets, antibiotics, and propranolol have been started. Which of the following should be given next?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Propylthiouracil.
explanationHtml: Thyroid storm is treated in sequence: a β-blocker, then a thionamide to block new hormone synthesis (PTU is preferred in storm because it also blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion), then iodine at least 1 hour after the thionamide, plus glucocorticoids (hydrocortisone), supportive care, and treatment of the trigger.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — iodine given before a thionamide supplies substrate for more hormone synthesis (Jod-Basedow) and can worsen the storm. C — radioactive iodine releases preformed hormone and takes weeks to work, so it is never used in storm. D — salicylates displace T4 from TBG and raise free hormone; use acetaminophen. E — surgery is reserved for refractory cases after medical stabilization.

stemHtml: A 54-year-old man has CT for renal colic, which incidentally shows a 2.4-cm homogeneous left adrenal mass with an unenhanced attenuation of 6 Hounsfield units. He has no headaches, palpitations, or sweating. Blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg, and serum potassium is 4.3 mEq/L. He has no cushingoid features. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Repeat CT in 6 months with no further testing

answerHtml: Answer: E. 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test.
explanationHtml: Every adrenal incidentaloma needs to be checked for autonomous cortisol secretion (mild autonomous cortisol secretion is common and linked to hypertension, diabetes and osteoporosis), even without overt Cushing features. A morning cortisol >1.8 µg/dL after dexamethasone is abnormal. This mass has a benign imaging phenotype (<10 HU, homogeneous, <4 cm), so no follow-up imaging is needed. ESE 2023 allows skipping metanephrines for clearly lipid-rich adenomas, although many clinicians still check them. Aldosterone screening is reserved for patients with hypertension or hypokalemia.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — surgery is for functional tumors, size >4 cm, or suspicious imaging. B — biopsy is rarely indicated and is dangerous if the mass is a pheochromocytoma. C — imaging follow-up is unnecessary here, and hormonal evaluation cannot be skipped. D — he is normotensive and normokalemic.

stemHtml: A 36-year-old woman has 1 year of weight gain, wide purple abdominal striae, proximal muscle weakness, new hypertension, and diabetes. She takes no glucocorticoids in any form. 24-hour urinary free cortisol is 3 times the upper limit of normal on two collections, and late-night salivary cortisol is elevated twice. Morning plasma ACTH is 74 pg/mL (normal 10–60). Dedicated high-resolution pituitary MRI shows no adenoma. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH or desmopressin stimulation

answerHtml: Answer: A. Inferior petrosal sinus sampling.
explanationHtml: Hypercortisolism is confirmed, and the normal-to-high ACTH makes it ACTH-dependent. Pituitary Cushing disease is the most common cause, but many corticotroph adenomas are too small to see on MRI. When the MRI is negative (or shows a lesion under 6–10 mm), IPSS separates a pituitary source (central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient ≥2 at baseline or ≥3 after stimulation) from ectopic ACTH. With no gradient, the next step is CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis (small-cell carcinoma, bronchial carcinoid).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — adrenal imaging is for ACTH-independent (low-ACTH) disease. C — operating without localization risks failure if the source is ectopic. D — bilateral adrenalectomy is a last resort and risks Nelson syndrome. E — waiting leaves dangerous hypercortisolism untreated.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis has taken prednisone 15 mg daily for 2 years. He has had vomiting and diarrhea for 3 days and has not been able to keep his medications down. After 2 L of 0.9% saline, blood pressure is 76/44 mm Hg and pulse is 118/min. Temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F). Na<sup>+</sup> is 130 mEq/L, K<sup>+</sup> is 4.4 mEq/L, and glucose is 58 mg/dL. Blood for cortisol and ACTH has been drawn. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Cosyntropin stimulation test, then treat according to the result

options.label: B
options.html: Start norepinephrine and reassess in 1 hour

options.label: E
options.html: CT of the abdomen and pelvis

answerHtml: Answer: D. Immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg (then 200 mg/24 h) along with fluids and dextrose.
explanationHtml: Chronic supraphysiologic glucocorticoids suppress the HPA axis. Not taking the drug during acute illness has produced adrenal crisis: shock that does not respond to fluids, hypoglycemia, and hyponatremia. Treatment should never wait for confirmatory testing. Potassium is normal because the renin–aldosterone axis is intact in secondary (exogenous) adrenal insufficiency.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — testing would delay life-saving therapy, and the HPA suppression is already explained. B — vasopressors fail without glucocorticoid, which is needed for vascular catecholamine responsiveness. C — fludrocortisone is not needed in secondary AI, and at 100 mg/day hydrocortisone provides mineralocorticoid effect anyway. E — imaging does not treat the shock.

stemHtml: A 67-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history has 2 weeks of increasing confusion, polyuria, and constipation. His mucous membranes are dry, and blood pressure is 104/62 mm Hg. Serum calcium is 14.9 mg/dL, albumin 3.9 g/dL, intact PTH 6 pg/mL (normal 10–65), and PTH-related peptide elevated. Creatinine is 1.5 mg/dL (baseline 0.9). Chest x-ray shows a right hilar mass. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: C
options.html: Intravenous 0.9% saline plus calcitonin, followed by intravenous zoledronic acid

answerHtml: Answer: C. Saline, calcitonin, and then a bisphosphonate.
explanationHtml: This is humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy (PTHrP, probably squamous cell lung cancer) with severe, symptomatic hypercalcemia and prerenal AKI from calcium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Saline restores volume and promotes calciuresis. Calcitonin lowers calcium within hours but loses effect after about 48 hours (tachyphylaxis). Zoledronic acid, dose-adjusted for renal function, takes 2–4 days and provides lasting control. Denosumab is preferred if renal failure is severe.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — loop diuretics given before volume repletion worsen dehydration; they are used only for volume overload. B — cinacalcet is for PTH-mediated hypercalcemia (parathyroid carcinoma, secondary HPT). D — glucocorticoids work for 1,25-(OH)<sub>2</sub>D-mediated hypercalcemia (granulomatous disease, lymphoma), not PTHrP. E — dialysis is for refractory cases or severe renal failure.

stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman has a serum calcium of 10.9 mg/dL (normal 8.5–10.2) on two occasions. She has no symptoms. Intact PTH is 96 pg/mL, 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 36 ng/mL, phosphate is 2.5 mg/dL, and eGFR is 98 mL/min/1.73 m². 24-hour urine calcium is 240 mg, and the calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio is 0.024. DXA T-scores are −1.4 at the spine and −1.1 at the hip, and renal ultrasound shows no stones. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.label: B
options.html: Observation with yearly calcium and creatinine

options.label: E
options.html: Genetic testing for a calcium-sensing receptor mutation

answerHtml: Answer: A. Parathyroidectomy.
explanationHtml: She has primary hyperparathyroidism: high calcium with a non-suppressed (high) PTH, replete vitamin D, and a clearance ratio above 0.02, which effectively excludes FHH. Even without symptoms, surgery is recommended if any criterion is met: calcium >1 mg/dL above the upper limit, T-score ≤ −2.5 or vertebral fracture, eGFR <60, nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis, hypercalciuria, or age <50. Her age alone qualifies her. Localization imaging (sestamibi, ultrasound, 4D-CT) is done after the biochemical diagnosis to plan the operation.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — observation is for asymptomatic patients who meet no surgical criteria. C — cinacalcet lowers calcium but is not curative and is used when surgery is not possible. D — her bone density does not warrant a bisphosphonate, and surgery is the definitive treatment. E — FHH is unlikely with a ratio of 0.024 (FHH is typically <0.01).

stemHtml: A 69-year-old man has 3 months of fatigue and exertional dyspnea. He has no visible bleeding and takes no NSAIDs or anticoagulants. He has always declined colon cancer screening. Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL, MCV 71 fL, ferritin 7 ng/mL, and platelets 460,000/µL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Oral iron and repeat CBC in 3 months, with no further testing

answerHtml: Answer: D. Bidirectional endoscopy.
explanationHtml: A ferritin below 30 ng/mL confirms iron deficiency (reactive thrombocytosis supports it). In a man or postmenopausal woman, iron deficiency anemia is GI blood loss until proven otherwise, especially colorectal cancer, so AGA guidance recommends both colonoscopy and EGD (and celiac serology). Iron replacement starts at the same time, but it does not replace the search for a source.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — treating without investigating can miss cancer. B — thalassemia trait has a normal or high ferritin. C — a negative occult blood test does not exclude a lesion because bleeding is intermittent, so it should not be used to decide on endoscopy. E — marrow biopsy is unnecessary once the iron deficiency is proven.

stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman had an unprovoked proximal left femoral DVT 3 months ago and has been taking rivaroxaban since. She has no features of SLE. A lupus anticoagulant was positive on a sample drawn before anticoagulation. Anticardiolipin IgG and anti-β2-glycoprotein I IgG antibodies are present at high titer on two measurements 12 weeks apart. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term anticoagulation plan?

options.label: C
options.html: Stop anticoagulation and start low-dose aspirin

options.label: D
options.html: Stop anticoagulation now that 3 months are complete

options.label: E
options.html: Switch to warfarin with a target INR of 2–3, continued indefinitely

answerHtml: Answer: E. Warfarin (INR 2–3), indefinite.
explanationHtml: She has thrombotic antiphospholipid syndrome with triple positivity, the highest-risk profile. Trials (TRAPS, with rivaroxaban, and others with apixaban) showed more thrombotic events, especially arterial, with DOACs than with warfarin. Vitamin K antagonists remain the standard, and because the event was unprovoked in the setting of APS, therapy is long term.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B — DOACs are not recommended in APS, particularly triple-positive disease. C — aspirin alone is inadequate after a venous thrombosis in APS. D — stopping anticoagulation carries a high risk of recurrence.

stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman hospitalized for pneumonia receives subcutaneous unfractionated heparin 5,000 units three times daily for VTE prophylaxis. Her platelet count was 260,000/µL on admission and is 98,000/µL on day 7. She has new left calf swelling, and ultrasound shows a popliteal vein DVT. She has received no other new drugs and has no signs of sepsis or bleeding. Creatinine and liver enzymes are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Stop heparin and start an argatroban infusion

options.label: E
options.html: Stop heparin and give no anticoagulant until the PF4 antibody result returns

answerHtml: Answer: B. Stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant.
explanationHtml: Her 4T score is high: a 62% fall in platelets (2 points), onset on day 7 (2), new thrombosis (2), and no other cause (2) = 8. When HIT is suspected at intermediate or high probability, all heparin must stop immediately and a non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux, or a DOAC) must start, even before PF4 ELISA and serotonin release assay results, because the thrombosis risk is very high.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — LMWH cross-reacts with HIT antibodies. C — platelet transfusion may fuel thrombosis and is not indicated without serious bleeding. D — warfarin started during acute HIT lowers protein C and can cause venous limb gangrene; begin it only after platelets recover to ≥150,000/µL, overlapping with a parenteral agent. E — leaving her without anticoagulation risks new thrombosis.

stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman has 2 days of confusion and petechiae. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F). Hemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL, platelets 14,000/µL, LDH 1,100 U/L, haptoglobin undetectable, creatinine 1.2 mg/dL, and PT/INR and aPTT normal. The direct antiglobulin test is negative, and the peripheral smear shows numerous schistocytes. ADAMTS13 activity has been sent and will take 3 days. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Wait for the ADAMTS13 result before starting treatment

answerHtml: Answer: C. Emergent plasma exchange plus glucocorticoids.
explanationHtml: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with severe thrombocytopenia, neurologic findings and normal coagulation studies is TTP until proven otherwise (PLASMIC score high). Untreated, mortality is about 90%. Plasma exchange removes the ADAMTS13 inhibitor and replaces the enzyme, and glucocorticoids suppress the autoantibody. Caplacizumab and rituximab are commonly added. Treatment starts on clinical suspicion.
