whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — platelet transfusion may worsen microvascular thrombosis and is avoided unless bleeding is life-threatening. B — waiting 3 days could be fatal. D — eculizumab is for complement-mediated (atypical) HUS. E — IVIG is used for ITP, which does not cause MAHA.

stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman with acute myeloid leukemia is on day 12 after induction chemotherapy. She develops a temperature of 38.7 °C (101.7 °F). Pulse is 104/min, blood pressure 116/70 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Her PICC insertion site is clean, her skin and mucosa show no lesions, and her lungs are clear. She has no history of MRSA. Absolute neutrophil count is 100/µL. Blood cultures have been drawn from the PICC and a peripheral vein. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Oral ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin-clavulanate with outpatient follow-up

options.label: C
options.html: Withhold antibiotics until culture results are available

answerHtml: Answer: E. Empiric IV antipseudomonal β-lactam monotherapy (cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or meropenem) within 60 minutes.
explanationHtml: Neutropenic fever is a medical emergency, and gram-negative bacteremia (including Pseudomonas) can be fatal within hours. She is high risk (hematologic malignancy, expected prolonged profound neutropenia) and needs inpatient IV therapy. Vancomycin is added only for specific indications: hemodynamic instability, pneumonia, a suspected catheter-related or skin/soft-tissue infection, MRSA colonization, or gram-positive bacteremia. She has none.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — oral outpatient therapy is for low-risk patients (MASCC ≥21, usually solid tumors with short neutropenia). B — empiric vancomycin without an indication adds toxicity and resistance. C — delaying antibiotics increases mortality. D — empiric antifungals are added for fever persisting 4–7 days despite antibiotics.

stemHtml: A 72-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer has 3 weeks of thoracic back pain that is worse when lying down. For 2 days he has had bilateral leg weakness (4/5 strength), decreased pinprick sensation below the umbilicus, and urinary hesitancy. Emergency MRI of the entire spine has been ordered. Which of the following should be done now, while awaiting the MRI?
answerHtml: Answer: A. High-dose IV dexamethasone.
explanationHtml: He has malignant epidural spinal cord compression (sensory level around T10, weakness, early bladder dysfunction). Glucocorticoids reduce vasogenic edema and preserve neurologic function, and they should be given as soon as compression is suspected in a patient with deficits, without waiting for imaging. Whole-spine MRI (multiple levels are common) then guides decompressive surgery plus radiation, or radiation alone. Ambulatory status at the start of treatment is the strongest predictor of outcome.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — LP has no role and could worsen herniation below a block. C — bisphosphonates reduce skeletal events over months, not acute compression. D — a bone scan cannot show cord compression. E — starting a GnRH agonist alone causes a testosterone flare that can worsen compression; if androgen deprivation is needed urgently, a GnRH antagonist (degarelix) or antiandrogen cover is used.

stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman comes for a health maintenance visit. She has no breast symptoms, no personal history of breast disease, no chest radiation, and no family history of breast, ovarian, or other cancers. Breast examination is normal. According to current USPSTF recommendations, which of the following is the most appropriate breast cancer screening plan?

options.label: A
options.html: Annual clinical breast examination only, with mammography starting at age 50

options.label: C
options.html: Mammography starting at age 45, then yearly

answerHtml: Answer: D. Biennial screening mammography starting at age 40.
explanationHtml: The USPSTF's 2024 update recommends biennial mammography for all average-risk women aged 40–74 (grade B), down from age 50, because of rising incidence in women in their 40s and its effect on mortality, particularly in Black women. Evidence is insufficient for screening at 75 and older and for supplemental imaging in dense breasts.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — this is the outdated starting age, and clinical breast examination alone is not a screening strategy. B — MRI is for high-risk women (BRCA carriers, lifetime risk >20%, chest radiation). C — this follows ACS-style timing, not USPSTF. E — genetic testing is offered only when a familial risk assessment tool is positive.

stemHtml: A 28-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV-1 infection (reactive antigen/antibody test confirmed by differentiation assay). He feels well and has no thrush. CD4 count is 160 cells/µL and HIV RNA is 92,000 copies/mL. HBsAg is negative and anti-HBs is positive. Creatinine is normal. IGRA and Toxoplasma IgG are negative. A resistance genotype has been sent and will take 2 weeks. He is eager to start treatment. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Start TMP-SMX now and begin ART after the genotype returns

options.label: B
options.html: Start bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide today plus daily TMP-SMX

options.label: C
options.html: Start ART today; no prophylaxis is needed because his CD4 is above 100 cells/µL

options.label: D
options.html: Start TMP-SMX and azithromycin, and defer ART until CD4 falls below 100 cells/µL

options.label: E
options.html: Start dolutegravir/lamivudine today plus daily TMP-SMX

answerHtml: Answer: B. Rapid ART start with BIC/FTC/TAF plus PJP prophylaxis.
explanationHtml: DHHS guidelines recommend ART for everyone with HIV regardless of CD4 count, ideally the same day or within 7 days of diagnosis, before baseline results return. Bictegravir- or dolutegravir-based regimens with a tenofovir backbone are preferred for rapid start because transmitted integrase resistance is rare and they cover HBV. A CD4 count below 200 cells/µL calls for PJP prophylaxis with TMP-SMX.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — delaying ART for genotype results is no longer recommended. C — PJP prophylaxis is triggered by CD4 <200, not <100 (the toxoplasma threshold). D — deferring ART is harmful, and MAC prophylaxis is not needed when ART starts promptly. E — the two-drug DTG/3TC regimen requires a known genotype (no lamivudine resistance), VL <500,000, and no HBV, so it is not used for rapid start before the genotype returns.

stemHtml: A 34-year-old man with untreated HIV (CD4 28 cells/µL) has 2 weeks of headache and fever. Lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 34 cm H<sub>2</sub>O and a positive CSF cryptococcal antigen. He is started on liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine and has daily therapeutic lumbar punctures. When should antiretroviral therapy be started?

options.label: D
options.html: Only after CSF cultures are sterile and CD4 exceeds 100 cells/µL

options.label: E
options.html: After completing 12 months of fluconazole maintenance

answerHtml: Answer: C. Delay ART 4–6 weeks after starting antifungal therapy.
explanationHtml: For most opportunistic infections, ART begins within 2 weeks. Cryptococcal meningitis is the main exception: trials (e.g., COAT) showed higher mortality when ART started within 1–2 weeks, from CNS immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome inside the closed cranial space. Guidelines therefore delay ART for 4–6 weeks after induction begins.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B — early ART increases fatal IRIS in cryptococcal meningitis. D and E — waiting this long exposes him to other OIs and death; ART is the only way to restore immunity, and the CD4 count rises after ART, not before.

stemHtml: A 29-year-old nurse who emigrated from the Philippines 2 years ago has a positive interferon-γ release assay on pre-employment screening. She received BCG as a child. She has no cough, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Chest x-ray is normal. HIV test is negative, liver enzymes are normal, and she is not pregnant. She uses depot medroxyprogesterone for contraception. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 2 months, then rifampin and isoniazid for 4 months

options.label: B
options.html: Three induced sputum samples for AFB smear and culture before deciding

options.label: C
options.html: No treatment because the result reflects prior BCG vaccination

options.label: E
options.html: Isoniazid plus rifapentine once weekly for 12 weeks

answerHtml: Answer: E. 3HP (once-weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine for 12 doses).
explanationHtml: A positive IGRA with no symptoms and a normal chest x-ray means latent TB infection. Treatment is indicated in a recent immigrant from a high-burden country and healthcare worker, because the lifetime risk of reactivation is about 5–10%. The CDC prefers short rifamycin-based regimens (3HP, 4 months of rifampin, or 3 months of isoniazid plus rifampin) because of better completion and less hepatotoxicity. Rifamycins reduce the effect of oral contraceptives, but depot medroxyprogesterone remains effective.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — four-drug therapy is for active TB. B — sputum testing is unnecessary when the patient has no symptoms and a normal CXR (unless HIV-positive or the CXR is abnormal). C — an IGRA is not affected by BCG. D — retesting does not address her current infection.

stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with 1 day of fever, severe headache, and neck stiffness. Temperature is 39.2 °C (102.6 °F), pulse 112/min, and blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg. She is confused (Glasgow Coma Scale 13) and has nuchal rigidity. There is no papilledema or focal neurologic deficit. She has no rash. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Blood cultures, then dexamethasone with vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and ampicillin, followed by head CT

options.label: B
options.html: Head CT, then lumbar puncture, then antibiotics guided by the CSF Gram stain

options.label: D
options.html: Blood cultures, then vancomycin and ceftriaxone, followed by head CT

options.label: E
options.html: Intravenous acyclovir alone until CT results are available

answerHtml: Answer: A.
explanationHtml: An altered level of consciousness is an IDSA indication for CT before LP, so the LP will be delayed and antibiotics must come first. At age >50, empiric coverage must include Listeria (ampicillin) in addition to vancomycin and ceftriaxone for pneumococcus and meningococcus. Dexamethasone given before or with the first antibiotic dose reduces death and neurologic sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis. Acyclovir can be added if encephalitis is suspected.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — delaying antibiotics until after CT and LP increases mortality. C — her altered mental status calls for CT first. D — it omits ampicillin (Listeria coverage at >50) and dexamethasone. E — acyclovir alone does not treat bacterial meningitis.

stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman develops 7 watery stools per day with mild cramping 5 days after finishing a course of cephalexin for cellulitis. Temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F), and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft and mildly tender, with normal bowel sounds. WBC is 11,800/µL and creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL (baseline 0.9). Stool C. difficile NAAT and toxin EIA are both positive. This is her first episode. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Oral fidaxomicin (oral vancomycin 125 mg QID is the acceptable alternative).
explanationHtml: This is a first episode of non-severe CDI (WBC <15,000, creatinine <1.5). The 2021 IDSA/SHEA update prefers fidaxomicin over oral vancomycin because recurrence rates are lower. Oral metronidazole is now used only for non-severe disease when neither is available. Contact precautions and soap-and-water hand hygiene are also needed.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — IV vancomycin is not excreted into the colon. B — IV metronidazole is an adjunct only in fulminant CDI. C — FMT is for multiple recurrences (≥2). E — antimotility agents without antibiotic therapy risk toxic megacolon, and probiotics do not treat CDI.

stemHtml: A 22-year-old man has had dysuria and purulent urethral discharge for 3 days. Urine NAAT is positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and negative for Chlamydia trachomatis. He weighs 78 kg and has no drug allergies. HIV and syphilis testing have been sent. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: C
options.html: Ceftriaxone 250 mg intramuscularly plus azithromycin 1 g orally once

options.label: E
options.html: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly once

answerHtml: Answer: B. Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM as a single dose.
explanationHtml: The CDC 2021 guidelines changed uncomplicated gonorrhea treatment to ceftriaxone monotherapy, 500 mg (1 g if ≥150 kg), because of rising azithromycin resistance and concern about antimicrobial stewardship. Doxycycline 100 mg BID for 7 days is added only when chlamydia has not been excluded; here it has been. Partners should be treated, and he should be retested in 3 months.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — azithromycin monotherapy has high resistance and is not recommended. C — this is the outdated 2015 dual regimen. D — fluoroquinolone resistance has made ciprofloxacin obsolete for gonorrhea. E — penicillin treats syphilis, not gonorrhea.

stemHtml: A 25-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 14 weeks' gestation, has had a painless, indurated vulvar ulcer for 10 days. RPR is reactive at 1:32, and TP-PA is positive. At age 12 she had throat swelling and hypotension after an injection of penicillin. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days

options.label: C
options.html: Ceftriaxone 1 g intramuscularly daily for 10 days

options.label: E
options.html: Penicillin desensitization, followed by benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once

answerHtml: Answer: E. Desensitize, then give penicillin.
explanationHtml: Primary syphilis in pregnancy must be treated with penicillin, the only therapy proven to prevent congenital syphilis. With a history of anaphylaxis, she should undergo desensitization in a monitored setting and then receive a single dose of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU for primary syphilis. Monthly titers follow, along with a fetal ultrasound after 20 weeks. Jarisch-Herxheimer reactions can trigger preterm contractions.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy (fetal teeth and bone). B — azithromycin has high resistance and does not prevent congenital syphilis. C — ceftriaxone is not an adequate substitute in pregnancy. D — deferring treatment risks stillbirth and congenital syphilis.

stemHtml: A 31-year-old man has had a painful swelling on his left thigh for 3 days. Examination shows a 4-cm fluctuant, tender nodule with a 1-cm rim of surrounding erythema. Temperature is 37.3 °C (99.1 °F) and pulse is 78/min. He has no medical conditions and no history of injection drug use. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Incision and drainage (send pus for culture).
explanationHtml: A purulent skin abscess, usually caused by S. aureus including community MRSA, needs source control. I&D is the primary treatment. Antibiotics active against MRSA (TMP-SMX or doxycycline) are added when there are systemic signs, extensive cellulitis, multiple lesions, immunosuppression, extremes of age, difficult sites (face, hand, genitalia), or failure of I&D. Newer trials show a modest added cure benefit even for simple abscesses, but drainage remains essential.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — cephalexin covers streptococci and MSSA, but no antibiotic can sterilize an undrained abscess. B — TMP-SMX alone without drainage is inadequate for a 4-cm fluctuant abscess. D — he has no systemic toxicity requiring IV therapy. E — a fluctuant abscess of this size will not resolve with compresses.

stemHtml: An 82-year-old nursing-home resident with mild dementia is evaluated because staff noticed cloudy, foul-smelling urine. She is at her baseline mental status and has no fever, dysuria, urgency, suprapubic pain, or flank tenderness. Vital signs are normal. Urinalysis shows 25 WBC/hpf and positive nitrite, and urine culture grows >100,000 CFU/mL Escherichia coli. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat urine culture in 1 week and treat if still positive

options.label: E
options.html: Straight catheterization to obtain a sterile specimen, then treat

answerHtml: Answer: A. Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria.
explanationHtml: Bacteriuria with pyuria is common in elderly and institutionalized patients (up to 50%). Treating it does not reduce symptomatic infection or mortality, and it does cause C. difficile infection, adverse drug events and resistance. Cloudy or malodorous urine is not a symptom of UTI. IDSA 2019 recommends screening and treating asymptomatic bacteriuria only in pregnancy and before urologic procedures that cause mucosal bleeding.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B and C — antibiotics are not indicated. D — screening cultures should not be sent in the first place, and a repeat would not change management. E — the problem is not contamination, and she would not need treatment even with a clean specimen.

stemHtml: A 73-year-old woman has had a new right temporal headache for 3 weeks, scalp tenderness when combing her hair, and jaw pain while chewing. She has no visual symptoms. Her right temporal artery is tender with a reduced pulse. Fundoscopic examination is normal. ESR is 92 mm/h and CRP is 64 mg/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Temporal artery biopsy, starting glucocorticoids only if the biopsy is positive

options.label: C
options.html: Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days

options.label: D
options.html: Prednisone 40–60 mg daily now, then temporal artery biopsy (or ultrasound) within 1–2 weeks

answerHtml: Answer: D. Start high-dose oral glucocorticoids immediately, then confirm the diagnosis.
explanationHtml: Giant cell arteritis threatens irreversible blindness from anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, and jaw claudication is a strong risk predictor. Glucocorticoids are started on clinical suspicion. Biopsy findings persist for at least 1–2 weeks after steroids begin, so treatment does not reduce diagnostic yield. Tocilizumab is added to spare steroids and reduce relapse.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — waiting for biopsy risks vision loss. B — 15 mg is the PMR dose and is inadequate for GCA. C — IV pulse methylprednisolone is reserved for active visual loss or amaurosis, which she does not have. E — NSAIDs do not treat vasculitis.

stemHtml: A 54-year-old man of Korean descent has had three attacks of podagra in the past year, confirmed by monosodium urate crystals on aspiration. His most recent flare resolved 1 week ago. Serum urate is 9.4 mg/dL, and eGFR is 48 mL/min/1.73 m². He has no tophi and no history of cardiovascular disease. Urate-lowering therapy is planned. Which of the following should be done next?

options.label: E
options.html: Continue colchicine prophylaxis alone without urate-lowering therapy

answerHtml: Answer: B. HLA-B*58:01 testing before allopurinol.
explanationHtml: Two or more flares a year is a strong indication for urate-lowering therapy, and allopurinol is first-line even in CKD. HLA-B*58:01 is common in people of Korean, Han Chinese, and Thai descent and in African Americans, and it greatly increases the risk of allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (SJS/TEN, DRESS). ACR recommends testing these patients first. If the test is negative, allopurinol is started at ≤100 mg/day (lower in CKD), titrated to urate <6 mg/dL, with colchicine flare prophylaxis for 3–6 months. If positive, febuxostat is used instead.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — 300 mg is too high a starting dose (especially at eGFR 48) and skips genetic screening in a high-risk ancestry. C — uricosurics are less effective with reduced GFR and are second-line. D — pegloticase is for refractory tophaceous gout. E — prophylaxis without urate lowering leaves the disease progressing.

stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman has 4 months of pain and swelling in the MCP and PIP joints of both hands and both wrists, with 2 hours of morning stiffness. Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies are strongly positive, ESR is 48 mm/h, and hand x-rays show periarticular osteopenia and two marginal erosions. Disease activity is moderate to high. Liver enzymes, creatinine, and CBC are normal. Hepatitis B and C serologies are negative and chest x-ray is normal. She does not drink alcohol, has a levonorgestrel IUD, and does not plan pregnancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy?

options.label: B
options.html: NSAIDs alone and reassess in 3 months

answerHtml: Answer: C. Methotrexate (titrated to 15–25 mg weekly) with folic acid; a short low-dose glucocorticoid bridge is optional.
explanationHtml: She has seropositive, erosive RA with moderate–high activity. ACR 2021 strongly recommends methotrexate monotherapy as initial DMARD therapy over other conventional DMARDs and over biologic or JAK inhibitor monotherapy. The goal is low disease activity or remission. If that is not reached in about 3 months at an optimal dose, a biologic (TNF inhibitor) or JAK inhibitor is added. Reliable contraception matters because methotrexate is teratogenic.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — hydroxychloroquine is for low disease activity. B — NSAIDs relieve symptoms but do not prevent erosions, and delay worsens outcomes. D — biologic monotherapy is less effective than MTX-based therapy and is not first-line. E — long-term glucocorticoids cause cumulative toxicity and are not a DMARD strategy.

stemHtml: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a motorcycle collision. He is wearing a cervical collar. He moans to painful stimuli and does not open his eyes; he withdraws his arm from pain. There are gurgling sounds with respiration and blood in the oropharynx. Pulse is 118/min, blood pressure 104/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 8/min, and SpO<sub>2</sub> 86% on a non-rebreather mask. Breath sounds are equal bilaterally. Suctioning briefly clears the airway but blood re-accumulates. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Rapid sequence intubation with manual in-line cervical stabilization

options.label: B
options.html: CT scan of the head and cervical spine

options.label: D
options.html: Needle decompression of the right chest

options.label: E
options.html: Two large-bore IV lines and 1 L of warmed crystalloid before any airway intervention

answerHtml: Answer: A. Rapid sequence intubation with manual in-line stabilization
explanationHtml: The GCS is 7 (E1, V2, M4), the airway is not maintainable (ongoing oropharyngeal bleeding), and he is hypoxic and hypoventilating. "A" comes first in the primary survey, and GCS ≤ 8 with an unprotected airway mandates a definitive airway. The cervical collar's anterior portion is removed and an assistant holds the head in line during laryngoscopy.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — the patient cannot leave the resuscitation bay for CT with an unsecured airway. C — nasal airways are a temporizing adjunct, contraindicated with possible basilar skull/midface fracture, and do not protect against aspiration of blood. D — breath sounds are equal; there is no evidence of tension pneumothorax. E — IV access is done in parallel, but circulation does not take priority over a failing airway.

stemHtml: A 34-year-old man is brought in after falling from a ladder onto his right side. He is anxious and short of breath. Pulse is 132/min, blood pressure 78/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min, and SpO<sub>2</sub> 84% on 15 L/min oxygen. The trachea is deviated to the left, neck veins are distended, breath sounds are absent on the right, and the right hemithorax is hyperresonant. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST)

options.label: C
options.html: Needle decompression of the right chest, followed by tube thoracostomy

answerHtml: Answer: C. Needle decompression of the right chest, followed by tube thoracostomy
explanationHtml: Hypotension, distended neck veins, contralateral tracheal deviation, absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on one side define tension pneumothorax — a clinical diagnosis. Immediate decompression (adult site per ATLS 10th ed: 4th–5th intercostal space anterior to the mid-axillary line; or finger thoracostomy) converts it to a simple pneumothorax, and a chest tube is then placed.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B — imaging delays a life-saving procedure; the patient may arrest while waiting. D — tamponade also gives JVD and hypotension, but breath sounds are equal and the trachea midline. E — thoracotomy is for traumatic arrest or massive hemorrhage, not for a problem a needle fixes.

stemHtml: A 22-year-old man is brought in 10 minutes after being stabbed once just left of the sternum at the level of the 4th intercostal space. Pulse is 128/min and blood pressure 82/64 mmHg; systolic pressure falls by 18 mmHg during inspiration. His jugular veins are distended. Heart sounds are faint. Breath sounds are present and equal bilaterally, and the trachea is midline. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Cardiac tamponade
explanationHtml: A penetrating wound in the cardiac box with Beck triad (hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds) and pulsus paradoxus (> 10 mmHg inspiratory fall) indicates pericardial tamponade. Equal breath sounds and a midline trachea argue against a pleural process. FAST (pericardial view) confirms; management is operative (sternotomy/thoracotomy) with pericardiocentesis as a bridge if a surgeon is not immediately available.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — would have absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation. B — gives flat neck veins and a dull, silent hemithorax. C — blunt deceleration mechanism, not a stab; JVD and pulsus are not features. D — needs a spinal cord injury and produces bradycardia, not tachycardia with JVD.

stemHtml: A 41-year-old man is brought in after a gunshot wound to the right lateral chest. Pulse is 126/min and blood pressure 86/58 mmHg. The right chest is dull to percussion with absent breath sounds; neck veins are flat. A right chest tube is placed and immediately drains 1,700 mL of blood. Two units of O-negative packed red cells are being transfused through a rapid infuser. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Place a second chest tube on the right

options.label: D
options.html: Observe chest tube output for 4 hours, then decide

options.label: E
options.html: Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) evacuation in 48 hours

answerHtml: Answer: B. Thoracotomy in the operating room
explanationHtml: Massive hemothorax is defined by ≥ 1,500 mL immediately on chest-tube insertion (or > 200 mL/h for 2–4 h), or persistent need for transfusion/instability. This patient meets the immediate-volume criterion and is unstable: he needs operative control of the bleeding source (usually intercostal/internal mammary artery, lung parenchyma, or hilar vessels).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — a second tube will not stop bleeding. C — unstable patients do not go to the CT scanner. D — the 4-hour criterion applies to ongoing output when the initial drainage is < 1,500 mL and the patient is stable. E — VATS is for retained hemothorax in a stable patient days later.

stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman is brought in after a high-speed head-on car crash. Airway is patent and breath sounds are equal. After 1 L of warmed crystalloid and 2 units of packed red cells, her pulse is 134/min and blood pressure 76/48 mmHg. The abdomen is distended and diffusely tender. The pelvis is stable on examination and pelvic x-ray shows no fracture. FAST examination shows free fluid in Morison pouch and the splenorenal recess. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast

answerHtml: Answer: D. Exploratory laparotomy
explanationHtml: A hemodynamically unstable blunt trauma patient who does not respond to resuscitation and has a positive FAST has intra-abdominal hemorrhage until proven otherwise; the next step is laparotomy (with continued massive transfusion).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — CT is only for hemodynamically stable patients. B — DPL adds nothing once FAST already shows hemoperitoneum. C — angioembolization is used for stable patients with a contrast blush (or pelvic arterial bleeding), not for unstable patients with blood in multiple quadrants. E — delaying is dangerous in a non-responder.

stemHtml: A 19-year-old man is hit in the left flank during a football game. He has left upper quadrant pain radiating to the left shoulder. Pulse is 96/min and blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, and they remain stable over 2 hours. Hemoglobin is 13.1 g/dL. The abdomen is tender in the left upper quadrant without rigidity or rebound. CT of the abdomen with IV contrast shows a grade III splenic laceration with a moderate perisplenic hematoma and no contrast extravasation. There is no free air. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Admission for close monitoring with serial abdominal examinations and serial hemoglobin measurements

options.label: D
options.html: Discharge home with instructions to avoid contact sports for 2 weeks

options.label: E
options.html: Prophylactic splenic artery embolization and pneumococcal vaccination

answerHtml: Answer: A. Admission for close monitoring with serial examinations and hemoglobin measurements
explanationHtml: Hemodynamically stable patients with blunt splenic injury (any grade) and no peritonitis are managed nonoperatively: admission (often ICU/step-down for higher grades), bed rest initially, serial exams and hemoglobin, with laparotomy if they become unstable. Angioembolization is added when CT shows a contrast blush/pseudoaneurysm or there is ongoing bleeding.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, C — operation is for instability, peritonitis or failure of nonoperative management. D — a grade III laceration requires inpatient observation; activity restriction typically lasts several weeks to months. E — routine embolization without a blush is not indicated, and vaccination is required after splenectomy (or extensive embolization), not now.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman is struck by a car. On arrival, pulse is 140/min and blood pressure 72/40 mmHg. Airway and breathing are adequate. Chest x-ray is normal. Pelvic x-ray shows widening of the pubic symphysis and disruption of the left sacroiliac joint. A pelvic binder is placed at the level of the greater trochanters and massive transfusion is started. FAST is negative in all views. After 4 units of packed red cells, 4 units of plasma and 1 unit of platelets, blood pressure is 80/46 mmHg. There are no long-bone fractures or external bleeding. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis

options.label: D
options.html: Open reduction and internal fixation of the pelvis

answerHtml: Answer: C. Pelvic angiography with embolization
explanationHtml: The source of shock is the unstable pelvic fracture (chest clear, FAST negative, no other sources). When hypotension persists despite a binder and blood products, the next step is hemorrhage control by angioembolization (or preperitoneal pelvic packing, where angiography is not immediately available). Arterial bleeders are embolized; venous bleeding responds to stabilization/packing.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — laparotomy with a negative FAST is non-therapeutic and opening the abdomen can release the tamponade of the pelvic hematoma. B — the patient is unstable. D — definitive fixation happens after physiologic stabilization (external fixation may be used acutely). E — urethral assessment is important (if blood at meatus) but does not address shock.

stemHtml: A 30-year-old man is brought in after a motor vehicle collision. He is hemodynamically stable after 1 L of crystalloid. Pelvic x-ray shows bilateral superior and inferior pubic rami fractures. Examination shows blood at the urethral meatus and a scrotal hematoma. He has not voided. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Insert a Foley catheter to monitor urine output

answerHtml: Answer: E. Retrograde urethrogram
explanationHtml: Blood at the meatus, perineal/scrotal hematoma, a high-riding prostate or a pelvic fracture with inability to void suggests urethral injury. A retrograde urethrogram must be performed before any urethral catheter. If the urethra is disrupted, a suprapubic catheter is placed.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, D — blind catheterization can convert a partial tear into a complete transection and introduce infection. B — a CT cystogram evaluates the bladder and requires a catheter, so the urethra must be cleared first. C — IVP is obsolete and assesses the upper tracts.

stemHtml: A 21-year-old man is struck on the right side of the head by a baseball. He briefly loses consciousness, then is alert and talking for about 1 hour. He then becomes progressively drowsy and vomits. In the emergency department, GCS is 9, blood pressure 168/90 mmHg, pulse 54/min, and the right pupil is 6 mm and nonreactive. Non-contrast CT of the head shows a 2.5-cm biconvex hyperdense collection in the right temporal region with 7 mm of midline shift and an overlying skull fracture. After airway management, which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Emergency craniotomy and evacuation of the hematoma

options.label: C
options.html: Admission to the ICU for repeat CT in 6 hours

options.label: E
options.html: Prophylactic hyperventilation to PaCO<sub>2</sub> 25 mmHg for 24 hours

answerHtml: Answer: B. Emergency craniotomy and evacuation
explanationHtml: The lucid interval, temporal fracture, biconvex lens-shaped hematoma (middle meningeal artery) and signs of uncal herniation (ipsilateral blown pupil, Cushing response with hypertension and bradycardia) define an epidural hematoma needing immediate surgical evacuation. Osmotherapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline) and brief hyperventilation may bridge to the OR.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — steroids worsen outcomes in TBI. C — a large symptomatic hematoma with herniation cannot be observed. D — lumbar puncture with a mass lesion can precipitate herniation. E — prolonged aggressive hyperventilation causes cerebral vasoconstriction and ischemia; it is only a short bridge with a target of 30–35 mmHg.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old man dives into a shallow pool. On arrival, he cannot move his arms or legs and has no sensation below the clavicles. Pulse is 48/min, blood pressure 76/40 mmHg, and his extremities are warm and dry. FAST is negative, chest and pelvic x-rays are normal, and there is no external bleeding. Hemoglobin is 14.2 g/dL. CT shows a C5 burst fracture. Blood pressure remains 78/42 mmHg after 2 L of crystalloid. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Norepinephrine infusion
explanationHtml: Hypotension with bradycardia and warm, dry skin after a cervical cord injury, with hemorrhage excluded, is neurogenic shock (loss of sympathetic outflow → vasodilation and unopposed vagal tone). After adequate volume, vasopressors with both α and β activity (norepinephrine; or phenylephrine plus atropine for bradycardia) restore perfusion; MAP is typically maintained at 85–90 mmHg for 7 days to protect the injured cord.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — high-dose methylprednisolone is not recommended (infection, GI bleeding, no clear benefit). B — further volume risks pulmonary edema without fixing vasodilation. C — there is no evidence of hemorrhage. E — FAST is negative and the hemoglobin is normal.

stemHtml: An 80-kg man is pulled from a burning car. He has blistered partial-thickness and leathery full-thickness burns covering the entire anterior trunk, the entire right arm, and the entire right leg (front and back). He also has red, painful, non-blistered burns of the face. Paramedics start lactated Ringer's solution at the scene at the time of injury. Using the Parkland formula, which of the following is the appropriate infusion rate for the first 8 hours?
answerHtml: Answer: C. 900 mL/h
explanationHtml: Count only partial- and full-thickness burns: anterior trunk 18% + right arm 9% + entire right leg 18% = 45% TBSA. The facial burn is superficial (first-degree) and is excluded. Parkland: 4 mL × 80 kg × 45 = 14,400 mL over 24 h; half (7,200 mL) in the first 8 hours from the time of burn = 900 mL/h, then 7,200 mL over the next 16 h (450 mL/h). The rate is then titrated to urine output of 0.5 mL/kg/h (~40 mL/h).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — 450 mL/h is the rate for hours 8–24. B — 600 mL/h spreads the total evenly over 24 h, under-resuscitating early. D — 1,080 mL/h results from wrongly including the superficial facial burn (54%). E — 1,800 mL/h gives the entire 24-h volume in 8 h.

stemHtml: A 36-year-old man is rescued from a burning apartment where he was trapped in a closed bedroom for 15 minutes. He has partial-thickness burns of the face and neck (about 6% TBSA). His voice is hoarse, his nasal hairs are singed, and there is black soot in the oropharynx and sputum. Pulse is 110/min, respiratory rate 22/min, and SpO<sub>2</sub> 97% on a non-rebreather mask. There is no stridor yet. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue 100% oxygen by non-rebreather mask and reassess in 4 hours

options.label: D
options.html: Calculate Parkland fluids and obtain a CT scan of the chest

answerHtml: Answer: B. Endotracheal intubation
explanationHtml: Enclosed-space fire with hoarseness, singed nasal hair, carbonaceous sputum and facial burns indicates inhalation injury. Supraglottic edema progresses over hours (worse with fluid resuscitation) and can make later intubation impossible; the airway should be secured early, before stridor develops. A normal SpO2 offers no reassurance — it does not exclude airway edema and is falsely normal with carbon monoxide.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — waiting allows the airway to swell shut (100% O<sub>2</sub> should continue after intubation for CO). C — hydroxocobalamin is for suspected cyanide toxicity (severe lactic acidosis, shock, coma), which this alert patient does not show. D — 6% TBSA does not need formal Parkland resuscitation, and CT does not secure the airway. E — bronchodilators do not treat upper airway edema.

stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman at 20 weeks' gestation has had 18 hours of periumbilical pain that moved to the right side of her abdomen, with nausea and anorexia. Temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F) and pulse 104/min. She is tender in the right mid-abdomen with voluntary guarding. Leukocyte count is 14,800/mm<sup>3</sup>. Urinalysis is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast

options.label: B
options.html: MRI of the abdomen with gadolinium

options.label: D
options.html: Graded-compression ultrasonography of the right abdomen

options.label: E
options.html: Serum lipase and observation for 24 hours

answerHtml: Answer: D. Graded-compression ultrasonography
explanationHtml: Suspected appendicitis in pregnancy is evaluated first with ultrasound (no ionizing radiation). If ultrasound is non-diagnostic, MRI without gadolinium is next; CT is used if MRI is unavailable. The appendix is displaced upward by the gravid uterus, explaining the mid/right-flank location. Delay increases perforation, which raises fetal loss substantially.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — CT is not first-line in pregnancy when US/MRI are available. B — gadolinium crosses the placenta and is avoided; non-contrast MRI suffices. C — plain films are non-specific. E — observation risks perforation.

stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman has had constant right upper quadrant pain for 14 hours that began after a fatty meal. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F). She has a positive Murphy sign. Leukocyte count is 14,200/mm<sup>3</sup>; total bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 98 U/L, AST 38 U/L, and lipase normal. Ultrasound shows multiple gallstones, a gallbladder wall thickness of 5 mm, pericholecystic fluid, and a common bile duct of 4 mm. IV fluids and antibiotics are started. She has no significant medical history. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.html: Discharge on oral antibiotics with elective cholecystectomy in 6–8 weeks

answerHtml: Answer: A. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy during this hospitalization
explanationHtml: Ultrasound confirms acute calculous cholecystitis. In a fit patient, early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (ideally within 72 hours of presentation) reduces total hospital stay and recurrent attacks compared with delayed surgery and has equal or lower complication rates.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — normal bilirubin and ALP with a non-dilated duct make choledocholithiasis unlikely. C — HIDA is used when ultrasound is equivocal; here it is diagnostic. D — delayed ("interval") cholecystectomy is inferior for a good surgical candidate. E — cholecystostomy is for patients too ill for surgery (septic shock, severe comorbidity).

stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman is brought in with fever, chills and confusion. Temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F), pulse 118/min, and blood pressure 84/50 mmHg. Her sclerae are icteric and she is tender in the right upper quadrant. Total bilirubin is 5.8 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 420 U/L, and leukocyte count 19,000/mm<sup>3</sup>. Ultrasound shows gallstones and a common bile duct of 11 mm. Blood cultures are drawn, and she receives 30 mL/kg of crystalloid and IV piperacillin–tazobactam; blood pressure improves to 98/60 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: E
options.html: Continue antibiotics and reassess in 72 hours

answerHtml: Answer: B. Urgent ERCP with biliary decompression
explanationHtml: Fever, jaundice and RUQ pain (Charcot triad) plus hypotension and confusion (Reynolds pentad) indicate severe acute cholangitis from an obstructing common duct stone. After resuscitation and antibiotics, the definitive treatment is urgent biliary drainage, preferably ERCP with sphincterotomy/stone extraction or stent (percutaneous transhepatic drainage if ERCP fails). Cholecystectomy follows later, once she recovers.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — cholecystectomy does not decompress the obstructed common duct and is dangerous in septic shock. C — MRCP delays therapy when the diagnosis is already clear. D — HIDA evaluates cystic duct patency (cholecystitis), not cholangitis. E — severe cholangitis with shock needs drainage within about 24 hours.

stemHtml: A 64-year-old man has had left lower quadrant pain for 3 days; for the past 6 hours the pain has become severe and generalized. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse 122/min, and blood pressure 92/58 mmHg after 2 L of crystalloid. The abdomen is rigid with rebound tenderness in all quadrants. CT shows sigmoid wall thickening with diverticula, extensive free intraperitoneal air, and diffuse free fluid; there is no discrete abscess. IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole are started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Continued IV antibiotics and bowel rest for 72 hours

answerHtml: Answer: D. Emergency laparotomy with sigmoid resection
explanationHtml: Free perforation with generalized peritonitis (Hinchey III/IV) and sepsis requires emergency source control: resection of the diseased sigmoid with an end colostomy (Hartmann procedure), or primary anastomosis with a diverting ileostomy in selected stable patients.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — percutaneous drainage treats a contained abscess, not diffuse peritonitis with free air. B — colonoscopy is contraindicated acutely (perforation risk); it is done 6–8 weeks after recovery. C, E — antibiotics alone cannot control a free perforation; outpatient management is only for uncomplicated disease.

stemHtml: A 79-year-old thin woman has had crampy abdominal pain, bilious vomiting and abdominal distension for 24 hours. She has never had abdominal surgery. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F) and pulse 112/min. There is a 3-cm firm, exquisitely tender, irreducible mass in the right groin below the inguinal ligament and lateral to the pubic tubercle; the overlying skin is erythematous. Leukocyte count is 15,600/mm<sup>3</sup> and lactate 3.8 mmol/L. Abdominal x-ray shows dilated small-bowel loops with air–fluid levels. IV fluids and nasogastric decompression are started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Water-soluble contrast challenge with serial abdominal radiographs

options.label: B
options.html: Manual reduction of the mass under sedation, followed by elective repair

options.label: C
options.html: Ultrasound of the groin and observation for 24 hours

options.label: E
options.html: Emergency surgical exploration and hernia repair

answerHtml: Answer: E. Emergency surgical exploration and hernia repair
explanationHtml: A groin mass below the inguinal ligament in an elderly woman is a femoral hernia — the hernia with the highest incarceration and strangulation risk. Fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, elevated lactate, a tender erythematous mass and SBO indicate strangulation; she needs emergency operation to repair the hernia and inspect/resect the trapped bowel.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — the contrast challenge is for adhesive SBO without strangulation; this is a hernia with ischemia and no prior surgery. B — reducing a strangulated hernia can return gangrenous bowel to the abdomen ("reduction en masse") and is contraindicated. C, D — delay risks perforation and death.

stemHtml: A 76-year-old man with atrial fibrillation, who stopped warfarin 2 months ago because of cost, develops sudden severe periumbilical pain 3 hours ago, followed by vomiting and one loose bowel movement. He is writhing in pain. Pulse is 108/min and irregularly irregular; blood pressure is 142/84 mmHg. The abdomen is soft and only mildly tender, without guarding or rebound. Leukocyte count is 15,400/mm<sup>3</sup>, and lactate is 2.3 mmol/L (upper limit 2.0). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Oral proton pump inhibitor and reassessment in 24 hours

answerHtml: Answer: C. CT angiography of the abdomen
explanationHtml: Sudden severe pain out of proportion to examination, "gut emptying" (vomiting/diarrhea), atrial fibrillation without anticoagulation and leukocytosis suggest acute mesenteric ischemia from an SMA embolus. CT angiography is the diagnostic test of choice; IV heparin, fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics should be started, followed by embolectomy/endovascular revascularization. Peritonitis would mandate going straight to laparotomy.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, D — endoscopy does not evaluate the mesenteric arteries; colonoscopy may be used for ischemic colitis but can worsen ischemia and is not the test here. B — delay leads to infarction; mortality rises with each hour. E — biliary ultrasound does not fit the presentation. Note that lactate may be normal or only mildly elevated early.

stemHtml: A 53-year-old man who takes naproxen daily for knee osteoarthritis develops sudden, severe epigastric pain 4 hours ago that is now generalized. Pulse is 112/min, blood pressure 108/70 mmHg, and temperature 38.0°C (100.4°F). The abdomen is rigid with diffuse rebound tenderness. Upright chest x-ray shows free air under the right hemidiaphragm. IV fluids, an IV proton pump inhibitor, and broad-spectrum antibiotics are started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Upper endoscopy to locate the ulcer

options.label: B
options.html: Emergency surgical repair with an omental patch

options.label: C
options.html: H. pylori stool antigen and triple therapy

options.label: D
options.html: CT of the abdomen with oral contrast before deciding

answerHtml: Answer: B. Emergency surgical repair with an omental patch
explanationHtml: Perforated peptic ulcer with free air and diffuse peritonitis requires emergent operative repair (laparoscopic or open Graham omental patch) after initial resuscitation. H. pylori testing and eradication and stopping NSAIDs follow.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — insufflation at endoscopy can enlarge the perforation and worsen pneumoperitoneum. C — appropriate later but does not treat a perforation. D — free air with peritonitis is already diagnostic; more imaging only delays. E — nonoperative management is reserved for selected sealed perforations without peritonitis, typically in poor surgical candidates.

stemHtml: A 66-year-old man is evaluated before elective total knee arthroplasty. He had a drug-eluting stent placed in the right coronary artery 4 years ago and has had no angina since. He climbs two flights of stairs carrying groceries without symptoms and does yard work. He takes aspirin, atorvastatin, and metoprolol. Blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg and pulse 62/min. Cardiac examination is normal. ECG shows Q waves in leads II, III and aVF, unchanged from 3 years ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.html: Stop metoprolol 48 hours before surgery to avoid intraoperative bradycardia

options.label: E
options.html: Proceed with surgery, continuing metoprolol and atorvastatin

answerHtml: Answer: E. Proceed with surgery, continuing metoprolol and atorvastatin
explanationHtml: Per the ACC/AHA algorithm, a patient with elevated risk but functional capacity ≥ 4 METs (climbing two flights of stairs) and no active cardiac condition proceeds to surgery without further testing. β-blockers and statins should be continued perioperatively; aspirin is usually continued in patients with coronary stents if bleeding risk allows.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B — stress testing or angiography is only indicated if functional capacity is poor/unknown and the result would change management; prophylactic revascularization before noncardiac surgery does not improve outcomes. C — echo is for unexplained dyspnea, a change in heart failure status or suspected significant valve disease. D — abrupt β-blocker withdrawal increases ischemia and MI risk.

stemHtml: A 71-year-old man is scheduled for elective laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair in 2 weeks. He has nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, hypertension and type 2 diabetes, and takes warfarin (INR consistently 2–3), lisinopril and metformin. He has never had a stroke or TIA, and he has no prosthetic valves or history of venous thromboembolism. Creatinine is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate perioperative anticoagulation plan?

options.label: A
options.html: Stop warfarin 5 days before surgery without bridging; resume 12–24 hours after surgery when hemostasis is secure

options.label: B
options.html: Stop warfarin 5 days before surgery and bridge with therapeutic enoxaparin until 24 hours before surgery

options.label: C
options.html: Continue warfarin through surgery with a target INR of 2–3

options.label: D
options.html: Stop warfarin 1 day before surgery and give fresh frozen plasma on the morning of surgery

options.label: E
options.html: Stop warfarin 5 days before and place a temporary IVC filter

answerHtml: Answer: A. Stop warfarin 5 days before without bridging
explanationHtml: His CHA2DS2-VASc score is 3 (age 65–74, hypertension, diabetes) with no prior stroke. In the BRIDGE trial, bridging AF patients with LMWH did not reduce arterial thromboembolism but doubled major bleeding. Warfarin is stopped 5 days preoperatively (INR checked the day before), and restarted 12–24 hours after surgery.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — bridging is reserved for high thrombotic risk (mechanical mitral valve, recent stroke/VTE within 3 months, severe thrombophilia). C — continuing therapeutic warfarin is acceptable only for minimal-bleeding procedures (dental, cataract, skin). D — using FFP to reverse warfarin electively is inappropriate (volume, transfusion risks); emergency reversal uses 4-factor PCC and vitamin K. E — IVC filters prevent PE in VTE patients who cannot be anticoagulated; they do not prevent AF-related stroke.

stemHtml: A 56-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis who has taken prednisone 20 mg daily for the past year undergoes right hemicolectomy for cancer. Her morning prednisone dose was not given. One hour into the operation, blood pressure falls to 72/40 mmHg and pulse rises to 118/min. Estimated blood loss is 150 mL, and there is no bleeding in the field. End-tidal CO<sub>2</sub> and temperature are normal. Hypotension persists despite 3 L of crystalloid and phenylephrine boluses. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Transfuse 2 units of packed red blood cells

options.label: E
options.html: Obtain a stat transthoracic echocardiogram before further therapy

answerHtml: Answer: D. IV hydrocortisone 100 mg
explanationHtml: Chronic prednisone ≥ 20 mg/day for ≥ 3 weeks suppresses the HPA axis. Under surgical stress, especially when the usual dose is missed and no stress dose was given, acute adrenal insufficiency causes vasodilatory shock refractory to fluids and pressors. Stress-dose hydrocortisone (100 mg IV, then 50 mg every 6–8 hours) treats it and should have been given at induction.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — blood loss is minimal. B — dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia, which would raise end-tidal CO<sub>2</sub> and temperature. C — protamine reverses heparin; there is no heparin-related bleeding. E — echocardiography may be useful later but should not delay a simple, likely life-saving treatment.

stemHtml: A 62-year-old man underwent low anterior resection with primary colorectal anastomosis for rectal cancer 5 days ago. He was tolerating clear liquids until today, when he developed lower abdominal pain and distension. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse 118/min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, and SpO<sub>2</sub> 96% on room air. The incision looks clean. He is tender in the left lower quadrant and suprapubic region without diffuse rigidity. Leukocyte count is 17,800/mm<sup>3</sup> (11,000 yesterday). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Immediate return to the operating room for re-laparotomy

options.label: B
options.html: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV and rectal (water-soluble) contrast

options.label: C
options.html: Flexible sigmoidoscopy to inspect the anastomosis

options.label: D
options.html: Duplex ultrasound of the lower extremities

answerHtml: Answer: B. CT with IV and rectal water-soluble contrast
explanationHtml: Fever, tachycardia, abdominal pain and rising leukocytosis on postoperative day 3–7 after a colorectal anastomosis are an anastomotic leak until proven otherwise. In a hemodynamically stable patient without generalized peritonitis, CT with contrast defines whether there is a contained collection (→ percutaneous drainage + antibiotics) or a large leak (→ re-operation with diversion).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — immediate re-laparotomy is indicated for diffuse peritonitis or instability, not yet present here. C — endoscopic insufflation can disrupt a fresh anastomosis and does not show extraluminal collections. D — DVT does not explain localized abdominal tenderness. E — atelectasis does not cause this picture.

stemHtml: A 68-year-old man with obesity and COPD underwent an emergency midline laparotomy for a perforated sigmoid colon 6 days ago. During a coughing fit, he felt something "give way." The nurse notes a large amount of pink, watery fluid soaking the dressing, and loops of small bowel are visible through the separated wound. Pulse is 98/min and blood pressure 134/80 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Push the bowel back into the abdomen and staple the skin at the bedside

options.label: B
options.html: CT scan of the abdomen to assess for an abscess

options.label: C
options.html: Wet-to-dry dressings with an abdominal binder, allowing healing by secondary intention

options.label: E
options.html: Cover the bowel with sterile saline-moistened dressings and return to the operating room urgently

answerHtml: Answer: E. Moist sterile dressing and urgent return to the OR
explanationHtml: Salmon-colored (serosanguinous) drainage around postoperative day 5–8 heralds fascial dehiscence; protrusion of bowel is evisceration, a surgical emergency. The exposed viscera are covered with sterile saline-soaked gauze to prevent desiccation and contamination, the patient is kept supine with flexed knees, and the fascia is closed in the operating room (often with retention sutures or temporary abdominal closure).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — bedside reduction and skin closure do not repair the fascia and risk contamination and bowel injury. B — imaging delays treatment. C — wet-to-dry dressings on exposed bowel risk enterocutaneous fistula; secondary intention is for superficial wound separation with intact fascia. D — antibiotics do not repair the abdominal wall.

stemHtml: A 19-year-old man undergoes laparoscopic appendectomy under general anesthesia with sevoflurane after induction with propofol and succinylcholine. Thirty minutes into the case, end-tidal CO<sub>2</sub> rises from 38 to 74 mmHg despite doubling minute ventilation. Pulse is 146/min, and the masseter and limb muscles are rigid. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F) and rising. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.12; potassium is 6.3 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Discontinue sevoflurane and administer IV dantrolene

options.label: B
options.html: Administer IV acetaminophen and apply cooling blankets

options.label: C
options.html: Administer IV diltiazem to control the heart rate

options.label: D
options.html: Deepen anesthesia with a higher sevoflurane concentration

answerHtml: Answer: A. Discontinue sevoflurane and give IV dantrolene
explanationHtml: Rising end-tidal CO2 despite increased ventilation (the earliest sign), muscle rigidity, tachycardia, hyperthermia, acidosis and hyperkalemia after a volatile agent and succinylcholine are malignant hyperthermia (RYR1-mediated uncontrolled Ca2+ release). Stop all triggers, hyperventilate with 100% O2, give dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV (repeat as needed), cool, and treat hyperkalemia.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — antipyretics do not work because the heat is generated by muscle, not a hypothalamic set-point change; cooling is supportive only. C — calcium-channel blockers given with dantrolene can cause hyperkalemia and cardiovascular collapse. D — more volatile agent worsens the crisis. E — bromocriptine is used in neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman finds a lump in her left breast. She has no nipple discharge and no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Examination shows a 2-cm firm, smooth, rubbery, freely mobile, non-tender mass in the upper outer quadrant. There are no skin changes or axillary lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Targeted breast ultrasound
explanationHtml: A palpable mass in a woman younger than 30 is first evaluated with ultrasound: breast tissue is dense (mammography is less sensitive), radiation is avoided, and US distinguishes cyst from solid mass. This presentation is most consistent with a fibroadenoma; typical US features permit observation, while suspicious or enlarging lesions undergo core needle biopsy.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — mammography is first-line from age 30 (it may be added if US is suspicious). B — MRI is for high-risk screening or extent of known cancer. C — excision is not the first step; image-guided core biopsy is preferred when tissue is needed. E — a discrete mass always requires imaging.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman has a 2.5-cm hard, irregular, non-tender mass in the upper outer quadrant of her right breast. There is a palpable 1-cm mobile right axillary node. Diagnostic mammography shows a spiculated mass with pleomorphic microcalcifications (BI-RADS 5), and ultrasound confirms an irregular solid mass. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy of the mass and the axillary node

options.label: D
options.html: Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the mass only

answerHtml: Answer: A. Image-guided core needle biopsy of the mass and node
explanationHtml: BI-RADS 4–5 lesions require tissue diagnosis, and image-guided core needle biopsy is the standard: it gives histology (invasive vs in situ), grade and receptor status (ER/PR/HER2), which determines whether neoadjuvant therapy is used. A clinically suspicious axillary node is sampled at the same time.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — definitive surgery is never performed without a tissue diagnosis, and receptor status may favor neoadjuvant systemic therapy. C — short-interval follow-up is for BI-RADS 3. D — FNA cannot distinguish invasive from in-situ carcinoma and gives unreliable receptor data. E — systemic staging follows diagnosis and is not routine for early-stage disease.

stemHtml: A 32-year-old man has a 2-cm firm left thyroid nodule. Fine-needle aspiration shows medullary thyroid carcinoma, and serum calcitonin is markedly elevated. He reports episodes of pounding headache, palpitations and sweating over the past 6 months. Blood pressure is 168/102 mmHg. His father had "thyroid cancer" and died suddenly during surgery. Serum calcium is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection this week

answerHtml: Answer: C. Plasma free metanephrines
explanationHtml: Medullary thyroid carcinoma with paroxysmal headaches, palpitations, sweating and hypertension — and a father who died during surgery — suggests MEN 2A (RET mutation) with pheochromocytoma. Pheochromocytoma must be excluded (and, if present, resected first after α-blockade) before thyroidectomy; otherwise anesthesia can precipitate a fatal hypertensive crisis. RET testing and serum calcium/PTH (hyperparathyroidism) complete the workup.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — thyroidectomy is correct eventually but not before excluding pheochromocytoma. B — C cells do not concentrate iodine, so radioiodine is ineffective in MTC. D — MTC requires total thyroidectomy (often multifocal/bilateral in hereditary disease). E — TSH suppression has no role in MTC, which is not TSH-dependent.

stemHtml: A 68-year-old man comes for a routine health maintenance visit. He smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years and quit 20 years ago. He has hypertension controlled with amlodipine. He has no symptoms. Abdominal examination is normal, and there is no carotid bruit. Colonoscopy 4 years ago was normal. Which of the following screening tests is recommended for this patient?
answerHtml: Answer: E. One-time abdominal ultrasonography
explanationHtml: USPSTF recommends a one-time ultrasound screen for abdominal aortic aneurysm in men aged 65–75 who have ever smoked (grade B). Ultrasound is safe, inexpensive and highly sensitive. (He is not eligible for low-dose CT lung screening because he quit more than 15 years ago.)
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — CT involves radiation and contrast and is not the screening test. B — USPSTF recommends against screening for asymptomatic carotid stenosis (grade D). C — evidence is insufficient (grade I) for ABI screening in asymptomatic adults. D — AAA screening is indicated.

stemHtml: A 74-year-old man with a known 5.2-cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm, under surveillance, develops sudden severe abdominal and back pain and faints at home. In the emergency department, pulse is 132/min and blood pressure 74/42 mmHg. He is pale and diaphoretic, and a tender pulsatile mass is palpable above the umbilicus. Two large-bore IV lines are placed and type-specific blood is ordered. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Immediate transfer to the operating room (or hybrid suite) for repair

options.label: B
options.html: CT angiography of the abdomen to confirm rupture

options.label: C
options.html: Abdominal ultrasonography to confirm the aneurysm size

options.label: D
options.html: Rapid infusion of 4 L of crystalloid to a systolic blood pressure of 130 mmHg

options.label: E
options.html: IV esmolol infusion to lower the heart rate

answerHtml: Answer: A. Immediate transfer to the OR for repair
explanationHtml: A known AAA with the triad of pain, hypotension and a pulsatile mass is a ruptured AAA. The unstable patient goes directly to the operating room for open repair or EVAR; blood products are given en route with permissive hypotension (SBP ~ 70–90 mmHg, maintaining mentation) to avoid disrupting the retroperitoneal tamponade.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, C — imaging delays definitive hemorrhage control in an unstable patient with a known aneurysm (CTA is used only if the patient is stable and the diagnosis is uncertain). D — aggressive crystalloid to normal BP worsens bleeding, dilutes clotting factors and causes hypothermia. E — rate control is the approach to aortic dissection, not to a hypotensive ruptured AAA.

stemHtml: A 69-year-old right-handed man had two episodes of weakness of the left arm and slurred speech lasting 20 minutes each, 5 days ago. Neurologic examination is now normal. MRI of the brain shows no infarct. Carotid duplex ultrasonography shows 80% stenosis of the right internal carotid artery and 30% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. ECG shows sinus rhythm. He is started on aspirin and high-intensity atorvastatin. His surgical risk is average. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Right carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks
explanationHtml: Left arm weakness and dysarthria localize to the right carotid territory, which has a 70–99% stenosis — a symptomatic, high-grade lesion. Carotid endarterectomy (with continued antiplatelet and statin therapy) markedly reduces recurrent stroke, with maximal benefit when performed within 2 weeks of the event. Stenting is an alternative for high surgical risk.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — surveillance alone leaves a high early recurrent stroke risk. B — warfarin is not superior to antiplatelet therapy for atherosclerotic stenosis and there is no AF. D, E — the left 30% stenosis is asymptomatic and below the threshold for revascularization.

stemHtml: A 71-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation, who stopped apixaban 3 weeks ago because of bruising, develops sudden severe pain in her right leg 2 hours ago. The right foot is cold and pale, with absent popliteal and pedal pulses. Sensation is mildly reduced over the toes; ankle and toe movement is normal. Doppler signals are absent at the dorsalis pedis but present in the popliteal vein. The left leg has normal pulses. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step?

options.label: B
options.html: IV unfractionated heparin bolus followed by an infusion

options.label: C
options.html: Aspirin and cilostazol with a supervised walking program

options.label: D
options.html: Elevation of the leg and warm compresses

options.label: E
options.html: Transthoracic echocardiography to locate the embolic source

answerHtml: Answer: B. IV unfractionated heparin
explanationHtml: Sudden onset of the Ps (pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paresthesia) in a patient with AF off anticoagulation and a normal contralateral limb indicates acute embolic limb ischemia, Rutherford IIa (marginally threatened: minimal sensory loss, no motor deficit). Immediate systemic heparin prevents clot propagation; then urgent imaging (CTA/angiography) and revascularization (embolectomy or catheter-directed thrombolysis).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — amputation is for irreversible ischemia (Rutherford III: paralysis, profound anesthesia, no Doppler signals). C — this regimen treats chronic claudication. D — elevation reduces arterial perfusion; heat increases metabolic demand of ischemic tissue. E — echocardiography is part of the later workup and should not delay anticoagulation and revascularization.

stemHtml: A 27-year-old man sustained a closed fracture of the right tibial shaft in a motorcycle crash and was placed in a long-leg splint 8 hours ago. He now has severe leg pain unrelieved by IV morphine. The splint has been removed and the dressing loosened, without improvement. The anterior compartment is tense, and passive plantar flexion of the toes causes severe pain. Dorsalis pedis pulse is palpable, and capillary refill is normal. Blood pressure is 124/70 mmHg. Anterior compartment pressure is 44 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Elevate the leg well above the level of the heart

options.label: B
options.html: Increase the opioid dose and reassess in 2 hours

answerHtml: Answer: E. Emergency fasciotomy
explanationHtml: Pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch of the compartment's muscles (passive toe plantar flexion stretches the anterior compartment) are the earliest signs of acute compartment syndrome. The compartment pressure of 44 mmHg (> 30 mmHg) and ΔP of 70 − 44 = 26 mmHg (≤ 30) confirm it. Fasciotomy of all four leg compartments must be performed promptly to prevent muscle necrosis and Volkmann-type contracture.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — elevation above the heart lowers arterial inflow pressure and worsens perfusion; keep the limb at heart level. B — delay causes irreversible damage within hours. C — external constriction has already been removed without benefit. D — palpable pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome (pulselessness is a late sign), and DVT does not explain these findings.

stemHtml: A 15-year-old boy is awakened by sudden, severe left scrotal pain that began 2 hours ago, accompanied by two episodes of vomiting. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F). The left testis is high-riding with a horizontal lie and is diffusely, exquisitely tender. The cremasteric reflex is absent on the left, and elevating the testis does not relieve the pain. Urinalysis is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Color Doppler ultrasonography of the scrotum

options.label: C
options.html: Scrotal elevation, ice and NSAIDs with follow-up in 24 hours

answerHtml: Answer: D. Immediate surgical exploration
explanationHtml: A classic presentation of testicular torsion (adolescent, abrupt pain, vomiting, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex, negative Prehn sign) warrants immediate surgical exploration with detorsion and bilateral orchiopexy. Testicular salvage is about 90% within 6 hours and falls sharply after that; imaging should not delay surgery when the clinical picture is clear.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — Doppler US is appropriate when the diagnosis is uncertain, but it costs time in a classic case. B — antibiotics treat epididymitis (gradual onset, cremasteric reflex present, pyuria). C — conservative care is for torsion of the appendix testis or epididymitis. E — nuclear scans are slow and essentially obsolete for this purpose.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old man has had gradually worsening right scrotal pain for 3 days with dysuria. He has had two new female sexual partners in the past 2 months. Temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F). The right epididymis is swollen and tender posterior to the testis; lifting the scrotum relieves the pain, and the cremasteric reflex is present. Urinalysis shows pyuria. Color Doppler ultrasound shows increased blood flow to the right epididymis. Nucleic acid amplification testing is sent. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 10 days

answerHtml: Answer: A. Ceftriaxone IM plus doxycycline
explanationHtml: Acute epididymitis in a sexually active man under 35 is most often due to Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae. CDC treatment is ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 10 days; partners are treated, and an HIV/syphilis screen is offered. Gradual onset, positive Prehn sign, preserved cremasteric reflex and increased flow on Doppler exclude torsion.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — levofloxacin alone is for enteric organisms (older men, after instrumentation, low risk of gonorrhea); it does not reliably cover gonorrhea. C — surgery is for torsion or abscess. D — single-dose azithromycin is inadequate for epididymitis and does not cover gonorrhea. E — TMP-SMX does not cover the sexually transmitted pathogens.

stemHtml: A 13-year-old boy has had a limp and pain in his left knee for 3 weeks. There was no trauma. He is afebrile, and his BMI is at the 98th percentile. Knee examination is normal. Passive flexion of the left hip causes the thigh to rotate externally, and internal rotation of the hip is limited and painful. He can bear weight with a limp. Anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral x-rays of the pelvis show posterior and medial displacement of the left femoral epiphysis relative to the metaphysis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Physical therapy to strengthen the hip abductors

options.label: C
options.html: Ultrasound-guided aspiration of the left hip

options.label: D
options.html: Closed manipulation to reduce the epiphysis, followed by a spica cast

options.label: E
options.html: Non-weight-bearing and surgical fixation in situ with a screw

answerHtml: Answer: E. Non-weight-bearing and surgical pinning in situ
explanationHtml: An obese adolescent with referred knee pain, obligatory external rotation with hip flexion, and epiphyseal displacement on the frog-leg view has a slipped capital femoral epiphysis. He should immediately stop weight-bearing (crutches/wheelchair) to prevent further slippage and undergo in-situ screw fixation. The contralateral hip should be monitored (bilateral in up to ~ 20–40%).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — physical therapy allows progression of the slip. B — the knee is normal; the pain is referred via the obturator nerve. C — he is afebrile, and there is no clinical suspicion of septic arthritis. D — forceful reduction increases the risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

stemHtml: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her roommate, who found an empty bottle of acetaminophen 500-mg tablets in her room. The patient says she took "a bunch of pills" sometime last night or early this morning but cannot say when or how many. She has nausea and has vomited twice. Vital signs are normal. Serum acetaminophen level is 38 mcg/mL, AST 640 U/L, ALT 710 U/L, and INR 1.4. Salicylate level is undetectable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Plot the level on the Rumack–Matthew nomogram using an estimated time of ingestion

options.label: B
options.html: Administer activated charcoal and observe without N-acetylcysteine

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat the acetaminophen level in 4 hours before deciding on treatment

answerHtml: Answer: C. Begin intravenous N-acetylcysteine now
explanationHtml: The Rumack–Matthew nomogram is valid only for a single acute ingestion with a known time. When the time is unknown, NAC is indicated if the acetaminophen level is detectable or aminotransferases are elevated — both are true here. NAC replenishes glutathione to detoxify NAPQI and is beneficial even after liver injury has begun; it is continued until acetaminophen is undetectable, aminotransferases are improving, the INR is < 2 and she is clinically well. Psychiatric evaluation follows medical stabilization.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — guessing the ingestion time can falsely place a toxic level below the line. B — charcoal is useful only within ~ 1–2 hours of ingestion, and withholding NAC risks fulminant hepatic failure. D — delaying NAC worsens outcome; levels are repeated during treatment, not instead of it. E — hemodialysis is reserved for massive ingestions with coma, severe lactic acidosis and very high levels.

stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman is brought in 6 hours after ingesting a large quantity of aspirin. She has tinnitus, vomiting and is now confused and agitated. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), pulse 118/min, and respiratory rate 32/min. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.38, PaCO<sub>2</sub> 22 mmHg, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 13 mEq/L. Anion gap is 26. Potassium 3.4 mEq/L, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, and glucose 102 mg/dL. Serum salicylate level is 104 mg/dL. A sodium bicarbonate infusion and potassium replacement have been started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Increase the bicarbonate infusion and recheck levels in 2 hours

options.label: C
options.html: Intubation with standard ventilator settings (respiratory rate 14/min)

answerHtml: Answer: B. Hemodialysis
explanationHtml: The mixed respiratory alkalosis and anion-gap metabolic acidosis is typical of salicylate poisoning. Altered mental status (neurotoxicity reflects high brain salicylate) and a level > 100 mg/dL are each indications for emergency hemodialysis, which removes salicylate and corrects the acid–base disturbance. Alkalinization and dextrose (for CNS hypoglycemia) continue until dialysis begins.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — bicarbonate alone is insufficient with neurologic toxicity and a level above 100 mg/dL. C — intubation with a normal respiratory rate removes the compensatory hyperventilation, causing abrupt acidemia, more salicylate entry into the brain, and death; if intubation is unavoidable, match her high minute ventilation. D — NAC treats acetaminophen toxicity. E — acetazolamide causes systemic metabolic acidosis, increasing CNS salicylate penetration.
