stemHtml: A 40-year-old woman with depression is found drowsy next to an empty bottle of amitriptyline. Pulse is 128/min, blood pressure 90/56 mmHg, and temperature 37.9°C (100.2°F). Pupils are dilated, the skin is dry and flushed, and bowel sounds are decreased. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 136 ms and an R wave of 5 mm in lead aVR. She is intubated for airway protection. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
answerHtml: Answer: E. IV sodium bicarbonate
explanationHtml: Tricyclic antidepressants block cardiac fast sodium channels, widening the QRS (> 100 ms predicts seizures, > 160 ms ventricular arrhythmias) and producing a terminal R wave in aVR. Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate boluses (1–2 mEq/kg, repeated) provide a sodium load and alkalinize the serum, decreasing drug binding to the channel and narrowing the QRS while improving blood pressure. Benzodiazepines are used for seizures.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — physostigmine can precipitate bradyasystole and seizures in TCA poisoning, despite anticholinergic features. B — flumazenil lowers the seizure threshold. C — procainamide (class IA) is itself a sodium-channel blocker and worsens toxicity. D — gastric lavage is not recommended routinely and does not address the immediate cardiotoxicity.

stemHtml: A 45-year-old farmer is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after spraying pesticide on his crops. He is confused and has profuse salivation, sweating, tearing, vomiting and diarrhea. Pupils are pinpoint. He has diffuse wheezing with copious bronchial secretions, and fasciculations of the chest and thigh muscles. Pulse is 44/min, blood pressure 92/60 mmHg, and SpO<sub>2</sub> 88% on oxygen. Staff are wearing protective equipment, and his clothing has been removed. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Atropine and pralidoxime
explanationHtml: Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing muscarinic excess (secretions, bronchospasm, bradycardia, miosis, GI hypermotility) and nicotinic effects (fasciculations, weakness, respiratory muscle paralysis). Atropine competitively blocks muscarinic receptors and is titrated (doubling doses every 5 minutes) until bronchial secretions dry; pralidoxime reactivates cholinesterase before "aging" and reverses the nicotinic weakness that atropine cannot.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — miosis and CNS depression mimic opioids, but the wet cholinergic syndrome does not respond to naloxone. B — physostigmine is a cholinesterase inhibitor and would worsen toxicity. C — succinylcholine is metabolized by plasma cholinesterase, which is inhibited, causing prolonged paralysis; use a non-depolarizing agent (e.g., rocuronium) if intubation is required. E — epinephrine does not treat cholinergic excess.

stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation and her husband are brought in after both developed headaches and nausea during a cold night in an apartment heated by an old gas heater. She briefly lost consciousness in the bathroom. She is now alert with a headache. Pulse is 110/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, and SpO<sub>2</sub> 99% on room air by pulse oximetry. Carboxyhemoglobin is 18%. Fetal heart rate tracing shows recurrent late decelerations. She has been placed on 100% oxygen by non-rebreather mask. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Continue non-rebreather oxygen and discharge when carboxyhemoglobin is < 5%

options.label: E
options.html: Emergency cesarean delivery under general anesthesia

answerHtml: Answer: A. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy
explanationHtml: Carbon monoxide poisoning (household cluster, faulty heater, SpO2 falsely normal) is confirmed by co-oximetry. Fetal hemoglobin binds CO even more avidly and fetal elimination is slower, so fetal COHb exceeds maternal levels. Hyperbaric O2 is indicated for loss of consciousness, pregnancy with COHb > 15–20%, or evidence of fetal distress — she meets all three. It shortens the CO half-life to ~ 20 minutes and may reduce delayed neurologic sequelae.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B — normobaric O<sub>2</sub> alone is insufficient with syncope and fetal compromise in pregnancy. C — hydroxocobalamin treats cyanide, mainly in smoke inhalation with severe lactic acidosis. D — methylene blue treats methemoglobinemia. E — the fetal distress is caused by maternal/fetal CO toxicity; treating the mother (with HBO, which is safe in pregnancy) is the priority; delivery is reconsidered if fetal distress persists.

stemHtml: A 30-year-old man is found unresponsive in a public restroom. Respiratory rate is 4/min, pulse 58/min, blood pressure 104/66 mmHg, and SpO<sub>2</sub> 78% on room air. Pupils are pinpoint, and there are needle marks on both forearms. Fingerstick glucose is 96 mg/dL. Bag-valve-mask ventilation with 100% oxygen is started, and SpO<sub>2</sub> rises to 94%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Naloxone, titrated to adequate spontaneous respiration

answerHtml: Answer: B. Naloxone titrated to adequate respiration
explanationHtml: Respiratory depression, miosis and coma in a person who injects drugs indicate opioid overdose. After oxygenation with BVM, naloxone (e.g., 0.04–0.4 mg IV, repeated and escalated, or 2–4 mg intranasally) reverses the respiratory depression; the goal is adequate breathing, not full arousal, to limit precipitated withdrawal. Observe for recurrence because naloxone's duration is shorter than many opioids; offer take-home naloxone and buprenorphine.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and can provoke seizures. C — intubation is reserved for failure to respond to naloxone or other indications; most patients avoid it. D — atropine treats symptomatic bradycardia or cholinergic toxicity. E — charcoal is inappropriate with an unprotected airway and injected drugs.

stemHtml: A 19-year-old military recruit collapses during a 10-km training run on a hot, humid afternoon. He is confused and combative. Rectal temperature is 41.6°C (106.9°F), pulse 152/min, blood pressure 100/58 mmHg, and respiratory rate 30/min. His skin is hot and sweaty. Fingerstick glucose is 110 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.html: CT scan of the head, then cooling blankets

options.label: E
options.html: Room-temperature IV saline and transport to an ICU before cooling

answerHtml: Answer: C. Immediate cold-water immersion
explanationHtml: Core temperature ≥ 40°C with CNS dysfunction after exertion is exertional heat stroke. Mortality and organ damage depend on the duration of hyperthermia, so rapid cooling is the priority — cold- or ice-water immersion gives the fastest cooling rate ("cool first, transport second"), stopping at about 38.5–39°C. Sweating may persist in exertional heat stroke and does not exclude it.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — antipyretics act on the hypothalamic set point, which is normal in heat stroke. B — dantrolene has no proven benefit outside malignant hyperthermia. D — imaging delays cooling; blankets cool too slowly. E — delaying cooling for transport increases mortality; IV fluids are given alongside cooling.

stemHtml: A 45-year-old man is found outdoors on a winter morning after a night of heavy drinking. He is pulseless, and the monitor shows ventricular fibrillation. Core (esophageal) temperature is 25°C (77°F). CPR is started, and one defibrillation attempt is unsuccessful. Serum potassium is 4.8 mEq/L. The hospital has extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) capability. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Pronounce death, because he is in cardiac arrest with a temperature of 25°C

options.label: B
options.html: Passive external rewarming with dry blankets while continuing CPR

options.label: C
options.html: Forced warm-air blanket as the sole rewarming method

options.label: D
options.html: Continue CPR and initiate rewarming with ECMO (extracorporeal circulation)

options.label: E
options.html: Standard ACLS with epinephrine every 3 minutes; stop if no return of circulation in 20 minutes

answerHtml: Answer: D. Continue CPR and rewarm with ECMO
explanationHtml: Severe hypothermia (< 28°C) with cardiac arrest is best treated with extracorporeal rewarming (ECMO or cardiopulmonary bypass), which supports circulation and oxygenation while raising core temperature rapidly. Hypothermia protects the brain, so prolonged resuscitation can succeed; death should not be declared until the patient is rewarmed (≥ 32–35°C) — "not dead until warm and dead." A potassium of 4.8 mEq/L does not suggest a non-survivable injury.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A — he cannot be declared dead while severely hypothermic. B, C — passive or external rewarming alone is far too slow for a patient in arrest at 25°C. E — the cold myocardium responds poorly to drugs and defibrillation, and drugs may accumulate (European guidelines withhold epinephrine below 30°C and double the interval at 30–35°C; AHA allows considering standard dosing); above all, stopping resuscitation after 20 minutes in a severely hypothermic patient is inappropriate.

stemHtml: A 62-year-old woman with hypertension treated with metoprolol develops diffuse urticaria, wheezing and lightheadedness 5 minutes after receiving IV contrast for a CT scan. Blood pressure is 70/40 mmHg and pulse 96/min. She receives two doses of epinephrine 0.5 mg IM in the thigh 5 minutes apart, 2 L of normal saline, IV diphenhydramine and nebulized albuterol. Her wheezing improves, but blood pressure remains 74/44 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: E
options.html: A second dose of IV diphenhydramine

answerHtml: Answer: C. IV glucagon
explanationHtml: Anaphylaxis in a patient taking a β-blocker can be refractory to epinephrine because β-receptors are blocked. Glucagon activates adenylyl cyclase through its own receptor, independent of β-receptors, increasing cardiac contractility and heart rate. It is given as an IV bolus (1–5 mg) followed by an infusion. An IV epinephrine infusion is the other key option for refractory anaphylactic shock.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B, E — glucocorticoids and H1/H2 antihistamines are adjuncts that do not reverse shock. D — atropine treats bradycardia, which she does not have (pulse 96/min), and does not raise vascular tone.

stemHtml: A 20-hour-old boy born at 39 weeks' gestation by uncomplicated vaginal delivery is noted by the nurse to be jaundiced to the level of the chest. He is breastfeeding every 2–3 hours. His mother's blood type is O, Rh-positive, with a negative antibody screen; other prenatal labs were normal. Temperature 37.0 °C, heart rate 140/min, respirations 40/min. There is no cephalohematoma or bruising, and the examination is otherwise normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Reassure the parents that this is physiologic jaundice and arrange follow-up in 2 days

options.label: C
options.html: Measure the total serum bilirubin and obtain the infant's blood type and direct antiglobulin test

options.label: D
options.html: Advise indirect sunlight exposure at home after discharge

answerHtml: Answer: C. Measure TSB and obtain the infant's blood type and DAT.
explanationHtml: Jaundice that is visible in the first 24 hours is pathologic until proven otherwise. The most common cause is hemolysis. With a type O mother, ABO isoimmunization (infant type A or B) is the leading concern even though the maternal antibody screen is negative, because anti-A/anti-B are naturally occurring IgG and are not detected by the routine screen. Quantify the bilirubin (TSB, plotted by hour of age on the AAP 2022 curves) and look for hemolysis: blood type, DAT, and CBC with reticulocytes. A positive DAT is a neurotoxicity risk factor that lowers the phototherapy threshold.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Physiologic jaundice appears after 24 h. B: Water or dextrose supplements do not lower bilirubin and can cause hyponatremia; they are contraindicated. D: Sunlight is unsafe and unreliable and is not recommended. E: Exchange transfusion is reserved for a TSB at the exchange threshold or for signs of bilirubin encephalopathy, and no level has been measured yet.

stemHtml: A 16-day-old girl born at 40 weeks is brought for a follow-up visit because of persistent yellow skin. She is exclusively breastfed 10 times daily, has 6–8 wet diapers and several yellow seedy stools daily, and now weighs 400 g more than her birth weight. She is alert and vigorous. Examination shows jaundice to the abdomen with no hepatosplenomegaly. Stools are yellow. Total serum bilirubin is 13.8 mg/dL, and direct (conjugated) bilirubin is 0.3 mg/dL. Hemoglobin and reticulocyte count are normal. The state newborn screen, including thyroid and galactosemia testing, was normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue breastfeeding and reassess the bilirubin level

options.label: B
options.html: Discontinue breastfeeding permanently and switch to formula

answerHtml: Answer: A. Continue breastfeeding and reassess.
explanationHtml: This infant has breast-milk jaundice: prolonged unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in a thriving, well-fed infant. It starts after the first week and can last 2–3 months. The required evaluation of prolonged jaundice has already been done, and it is reassuring: the conjugated bilirubin is normal (excluding cholestasis/biliary atresia), there is no hemolysis, and the newborn screen excludes hypothyroidism and galactosemia. Her TSB is well below the AAP phototherapy threshold for her age. The correct management is to continue breastfeeding and follow the bilirubin until it resolves.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: Stopping breastfeeding is unnecessary and harmful. Even the historic diagnostic 24–48-hour interruption is no longer recommended. C and E: HIDA and US evaluate cholestasis (direct bilirubin >1.0 mg/dL, acholic stools), which is absent. D: Phototherapy is indicated only at or above the hour- and GA-specific threshold, which for a term infant beyond 4 days is about 20 mg/dL or higher.

stemHtml: An 18-day-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a rectal temperature of 38.3 °C at home. He was born at 39 weeks after an uncomplicated pregnancy; maternal GBS status was negative. He has been feeding well with no vomiting, cough, or rash. Temperature 38.4 °C, heart rate 160/min, respirations 42/min. He is alert and well-appearing with a flat anterior fontanelle and no focal findings. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Urinalysis, blood culture, and inflammatory markers; discharge home with follow-up in 24 hours if all are normal

options.label: C
options.html: Oral amoxicillin and follow-up in 48 hours

options.label: D
options.html: Acetaminophen and home observation, returning if the fever persists

options.label: E
options.html: Urinalysis and urine culture, blood culture, lumbar puncture, hospital admission, and parenteral antibiotics

answerHtml: Answer: E. Full sepsis evaluation including LP, admission, and empiric parenteral antibiotics.
explanationHtml: Under the AAP 2021 guideline for well-appearing febrile infants, 8–21 days old is the highest-risk group (invasive bacterial infection rate ~3–4% even when well-appearing). These infants need a catheterized UA and culture, blood culture, CSF analysis and culture, admission, and parenteral antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin + ceftazidime or gentamicin), regardless of inflammatory markers. Add acyclovir if there are HSV risk factors.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, C, D: All under-evaluate an infant at high risk of bacteremia and meningitis, and empiric oral antibiotics without cultures would obscure the diagnosis. B: This is an acceptable pathway for some well-appearing infants aged 29–60 days (and some 22–28 days), but not for an 18-day-old.

stemHtml: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department at 2 AM with a "seal-like" cough and noisy breathing that began tonight after 2 days of rhinorrhea and low-grade fever. Temperature 38.0 °C, heart rate 130/min, respirations 36/min, SpO<sub>2</sub> 96% on room air. He sits comfortably on his mother's lap and is not drooling. There is inspiratory stridor at rest with mild suprasternal retractions. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Oral dexamethasone and nebulized racemic epinephrine

answerHtml: Answer: B. Dexamethasone plus nebulized racemic epinephrine.
explanationHtml: This is croup (parainfluenza laryngotracheobronchitis) with stridor at rest, which makes it moderate. Every child with croup gets a single dose of dexamethasone, which reduces airway edema within hours. Nebulized racemic epinephrine (α-adrenergic vasoconstriction of the subglottic mucosa) is added for stridor at rest or moderate–severe distress. Observe for 2–4 hours afterward because the epinephrine effect wears off.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Croup is a clinical diagnosis, and a steeple sign adds nothing. C: Intubation is for impending respiratory failure, which is not present. D: The illness is viral. Antibiotics are for bacterial tracheitis or epiglottitis. E: Albuterol treats lower-airway bronchospasm, not subglottic edema.

stemHtml: A 3-year-old girl has had fever up to 39.8 °C for 6 days despite antipyretics. She is irritable. Examination shows bilateral nonexudative conjunctival injection sparing the limbus, red cracked lips, a strawberry tongue, a polymorphous truncal rash, firm swelling and erythema of the hands and feet, and a single 2-cm left cervical lymph node. Rapid streptococcal antigen test is negative. CRP is 9 mg/dL, platelets 480,000/μL, and ALT 68 U/L. An echocardiogram is ordered. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
answerHtml: Answer: D. IVIG (2 g/kg) plus aspirin.
explanationHtml: Fever ≥5 days with all five principal features is complete Kawasaki disease. IVIG given within 10 days of fever onset reduces coronary artery aneurysms from ~25% to ~4%. Aspirin is given at a moderate–high anti-inflammatory dose until afebrile, then a low antiplatelet dose for 6–8 weeks (longer if aneurysms). Echocardiography is done at diagnosis and repeated at 1–2 and 4–6 weeks.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Ibuprofen does not prevent aneurysms and antagonizes aspirin's antiplatelet effect. B: Steroids are an adjunct for high-risk or refractory cases, not monotherapy. C: There is no bacterial infection. Scarlet fever does not cause limbic-sparing conjunctivitis or hand edema, and the strep test is negative. E: Infliximab is used for IVIG-resistant disease.

stemHtml: A 4-week-old firstborn boy has had 4 days of progressively forceful, nonbilious vomiting after every feed. He seems hungry immediately afterward. Mucous membranes are dry and capillary refill is 3 seconds. Labs: Na<sup>+</sup> 133 mEq/L, K<sup>+</sup> 2.9 mEq/L, Cl<sup>−</sup> 86 mEq/L, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 35 mEq/L, BUN 24 mg/dL, creatinine 0.4 mg/dL. Ultrasound shows a pyloric muscle thickness of 5 mm and a channel length of 19 mm. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Intravenous isotonic saline resuscitation followed by dextrose-containing fluids with potassium until the electrolytes normalize

answerHtml: Answer: A. Correct dehydration and the hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis first.
explanationHtml: US confirms hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Vomiting of gastric HCl causes hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. Volume depletion activates aldosterone, which causes renal K+ wasting and, late, paradoxical aciduria. Pyloromyotomy is not an emergency. Operating on an alkalotic infant raises the risk of postoperative apnea (compensatory hypoventilation and anesthetic sensitivity). Give an NS bolus, then D5-½NS with KCl once the infant voids, until HCO3− is below ~30 and Cl− and K+ are normal. Then operate.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: Surgery comes after metabolic correction. C: The diagnosis is already confirmed by US, and an UGI adds nothing. D: An air enema treats intussusception. E: Early macrolide exposure is a risk factor for pyloric stenosis, not a treatment.

stemHtml: A 6-day-old girl born at term fed well until this morning, when she had three episodes of dark green emesis. Temperature 37.1 °C, heart rate 165/min, blood pressure 70/45 mm Hg. Her abdomen is soft, nondistended, and nontender. Plain abdominal radiographs show a nonspecific gas pattern with some distal bowel gas. A nasogastric tube is placed and IV fluids are started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Abdominal ultrasonography to measure pyloric muscle thickness

options.label: E
options.html: Observation with reintroduction of feeds in 24 hours

answerHtml: Answer: C. Emergent upper GI contrast series.
explanationHtml: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise. Volvulus can infarct the entire midgut within hours. A soft, nondistended abdomen does not exclude it, because the obstruction is proximal. In a stable infant, the UGI series is the diagnostic test of choice: the duodenojejunal junction lies right of midline or low, the duodenum does not cross the midline, and there may be a "corkscrew" appearance. If it is positive, or if the infant becomes unstable or develops peritonitis, the next step is an emergent Ladd procedure.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Pyloric stenosis causes nonbilious vomiting at 3–6 weeks. B: A contrast enema evaluates distal obstruction (Hirschsprung, meconium ileus, small left colon) and can miss malrotation. D: Rectal biopsy diagnoses Hirschsprung, which presents with failure to pass meconium and distension. E: Observation risks catastrophic bowel loss.

stemHtml: A 10-month-old boy has had 8 hours of episodic inconsolable crying every 15–20 minutes, during which he draws his knees to his chest. Between episodes he is quiet and drowsy. He has vomited twice and passed one stool with blood and mucus. He had an upper respiratory infection last week. Temperature 37.6 °C, heart rate 140/min, blood pressure 90/55 mm Hg. A sausage-shaped mass is palpated in the right upper quadrant; there is no guarding or rebound. Ultrasonography shows a "target" sign. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: CT of the abdomen with contrast

options.label: E
options.html: Air (pneumatic) enema reduction under imaging guidance

answerHtml: Answer: E. Pneumatic (or hydrostatic) enema reduction.
explanationHtml: This is ileocolic intussusception, with a lead point of hypertrophied Peyer patches after a viral illness. The child is hemodynamically stable with no peritonitis, so an air or hydrostatic contrast enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic and succeeds in ~80–90%. Surgical consultation should be available in case of perforation.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Surgery is for peritonitis, perforation, shock, or failed enema reduction. B: US is the diagnostic test of choice. CT adds radiation and delays treatment. C: Delay risks bowel ischemia. D: An UGI series evaluates malrotation.

stemHtml: A 4-month-old girl is brought to the clinic for fussiness. Her mother says the infant "rolled off the couch" onto a carpeted floor yesterday. On examination she is alert and consolable, the anterior fontanelle is flat, and the neurologic examination is normal. There are two 1-cm bruises on the left pinna and a 2-cm bruise on the right cheek. There is no family history of bleeding disorders. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Reassure the mother, because the injuries are consistent with the history

options.label: B
options.html: Obtain a CBC and coagulation studies; discharge home if normal

options.label: C
options.html: Tell the mother abuse is suspected and ask her to explain the injuries again

options.label: D
options.html: Obtain a skeletal survey, head imaging, and coagulation studies, and report to child protective services

options.label: E
options.html: Obtain parental consent before notifying child protective services

answerHtml: Answer: D. Full medical workup for occult injury plus a report to CPS.
explanationHtml: Bruising of the ears and cheek in an infant ≤4 months meets the TEN-4-FACESp decision rule. A short fall onto carpet does not explain bruises on several planes of the head. These are sentinel injuries. Children <2 y need a skeletal survey. Infants this young often have occult intracranial injury despite a normal exam, so neuroimaging is indicated. Coagulation studies exclude a bleeding disorder. Physicians must report on reasonable suspicion; proof is not required.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: The history does not fit the injury pattern. B: Coagulation testing is part of the workup, but discharging without a skeletal survey, imaging, and a report could return the infant to an unsafe home. C: A confrontational interview is not the physician's role and can endanger the child. Report and let CPS/law enforcement investigate. E: Reporting does not require parental consent.

stemHtml: A 12-month-old boy is seen for a well-child visit in October. At 10 months he developed hives and lip swelling within minutes of eating scrambled egg; he had no respiratory or cardiovascular symptoms. His immunizations are up to date, and he is due for MMR, varicella, hepatitis A, PCV, Hib, and his first-season influenza vaccine. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.label: A
options.html: Defer the influenza vaccine until an allergist has evaluated him

options.label: B
options.html: Give the influenza vaccine only in an allergist's office with 30 minutes of observation

options.label: C
options.html: Perform skin testing with the influenza vaccine before administration

options.label: D
options.html: Give MMR but withhold influenza vaccine this season

options.label: E
options.html: Administer all due vaccines, including MMR and influenza, in the usual manner

answerHtml: Answer: E. Vaccinate routinely.
explanationHtml: Egg allergy of any severity is not a contraindication or precaution for influenza vaccination. Since the 2023–24 season, ACIP and AAP recommend no extra measures beyond those for any vaccine (standard 15-minute observation and readiness to treat anaphylaxis). The ovalbumin content of current vaccines is negligible. MMR is grown in chick embryo fibroblast culture and contains essentially no egg protein, so it is also given routinely. Anaphylaxis to MMR is usually due to gelatin or neomycin. As a child <9 y receiving influenza vaccine for the first time, he needs a second dose ≥4 weeks later.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B, D: Deferring or restricting vaccination leaves an infant unprotected during influenza season without any benefit. C: Vaccine skin testing for egg allergy is not recommended.

stemHtml: A healthy infant born at term is brought for a routine visit. She sits without support, crawls, and pulls to stand but does not yet walk while holding onto furniture. She picks up a piece of cereal between her thumb and the side of her index finger. She babbles "mamama" and "dadada" but does not use these words for a specific parent. She cries when her mother leaves the room and enjoys peek-a-boo. Her development is normal. Which of the following is the most likely age of this infant?
answerHtml: Answer: A. 9 months.
explanationHtml: Sitting alone, crawling, pulling to stand, an immature (inferior) pincer grasp, nonspecific "mama/dada," separation anxiety, and object-permanence games (peek-a-boo) all fit a 9-month-old.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: A 12-month-old cruises or takes first steps, has a fine (fingertip) pincer, and uses "mama/dada" specifically plus 1–3 words. C: A 6-month-old sits with support (tripod), rakes objects, and babbles without pulling to stand. D: An 18-month-old runs and has 10–25 words. E: A 4-month-old rolls front to back and cannot sit independently.

stemHtml: At an 18-month well-child visit, the parents of a boy say he rarely responds to his name. He says no words, does not point to show them objects, makes little eye contact, and spends long periods lining up toy cars. He passed his newborn hearing screen. Growth and physical examination are normal. The M-CHAT-R/F, including the follow-up interview, indicates high risk. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Reassure the parents that boys often speak later and repeat the M-CHAT at 24 months

options.label: D
options.html: Refer for formal audiologic evaluation, comprehensive developmental evaluation, and early intervention services

answerHtml: Answer: D. Audiology, diagnostic ASD evaluation, and early intervention referral all at once.
explanationHtml: A positive M-CHAT-R/F with red flags (no pointing by 12 months, no words by 16 months, poor response to name, restricted/repetitive play) needs prompt referral. Get a formal audiologic evaluation, because a passed newborn screen does not exclude later or mild hearing loss. Refer for a comprehensive diagnostic evaluation for autism spectrum disorder, and refer to early intervention right away, without waiting for a formal diagnosis. Outcomes are best when behavioral therapy starts early. Genetic testing (chromosomal microarray, Fragile X) is part of the subsequent etiologic workup.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Waiting delays intervention. "Wait and see" is the classic wrong answer. B, E: EEG and MRI are for seizures, regression, or focal neurologic findings, not routine ASD workup. C: Risperidone treats irritability/aggression in diagnosed ASD, not core symptoms, and is not a first step.

stemHtml: A 6-hour-old boy born at 39 weeks to a mother with poorly controlled pregestational diabetes becomes cyanotic. SpO<sub>2</sub> is 70% in both the right hand and the foot. On 100% oxygen, arterial PaO<sub>2</sub> is 38 mm Hg. He is tachypneic without retractions. There is no murmur, and S2 is single and loud. Chest radiograph shows a narrow mediastinum with an "egg-on-a-string" cardiac silhouette and increased pulmonary vascular markings. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Prostaglandin E<sub>1</sub>.
explanationHtml: Transposition of the great arteries creates parallel circulations. Survival depends on mixing through the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale. A failed hyperoxia test (PaO2 <150 on 100% O2) indicates cyanotic heart disease. PGE1 keeps the ductus open to improve mixing. Watch for apnea. Next comes balloon atrial septostomy if mixing remains inadequate, then an arterial switch operation. Maternal diabetes is a classic association.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Indomethacin closes the ductus and would be fatal here. B, D: Digoxin and diuretics treat heart failure from left-to-right shunts, not cyanotic mixing lesions. E: Inhaled NO treats PPHN, which typically shows differential (pre- versus post-ductal) saturations and lung or meconium history. Equal right-hand and foot saturations with "egg on a string" point to TGA.

stemHtml: A 4-month-old girl born at term has had 3 days of rhinorrhea and cough and now has wheezing. She is feeding about 75% of her usual volume and has a normal number of wet diapers. Temperature 38.1 °C, heart rate 150/min, respirations 52/min, SpO<sub>2</sub> 94% on room air. There are mild subcostal retractions with diffuse expiratory wheezes and fine crackles bilaterally. She has had no apneic episodes. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Supportive care with nasal suctioning and hydration, with close follow-up and return precautions

options.label: E
options.html: Nebulized hypertonic saline in the emergency department

answerHtml: Answer: A. Supportive care.
explanationHtml: This is bronchiolitis (most likely RSV). AAP guidance is supportive care only: nasal suctioning, maintaining hydration, and supplemental O2 if SpO2 persistently falls below 90%. She is feeding adequately, has no apnea, and has SpO2 ≥90%, so outpatient care with return precautions is appropriate.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: Bronchodilators do not improve outcomes in bronchiolitis and are not recommended. C: Corticosteroids are ineffective. D: Routine CXR leads to unnecessary antibiotics, and the illness is viral. Crackles are expected in bronchiolitis. E: Hypertonic saline is not recommended in the ED and has only a possible role in hospitalized infants with expected stays >72 h.

stemHtml: A 3-year-old girl has had 1 day of right ear pain and fever. She has had no antibiotics in the past 6 months, has no drug allergies, and has no eye discharge. Temperature 39.4 °C. The right tympanic membrane is erythematous, opaque, and markedly bulging with no mobility on pneumatic otoscopy; the left is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
answerHtml: Answer: E. High-dose amoxicillin (80–90 mg/kg/day in two divided doses).
explanationHtml: She has acute otitis media (moderate–severe TM bulging). A temperature ≥39 °C makes it severe, so antibiotics are indicated at any age and the observation option does not apply. High-dose amoxicillin overcomes intermediate penicillin resistance in S. pneumoniae. Duration is 10 days for children <2 y or with severe symptoms (as here), and 7 days for ages 2–5 with mild–moderate AOM.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Observation applies only to non-severe AOM in eligible children. B: Amoxicillin–clavulanate is for amoxicillin use in the past 30 days, concurrent purulent conjunctivitis, or treatment failure. C: Macrolides are poorly effective against pneumococcus and H. influenzae and are used only in severe penicillin allergy. D: Cefdinir is an alternative for non-severe penicillin allergy.

stemHtml: A 4-year-old unvaccinated boy who recently immigrated has had 6 hours of high fever and sore throat. He is sitting upright, leaning forward on his hands, and drooling, with a muffled voice and soft inspiratory stridor. Temperature 40.0 °C, heart rate 160/min, respirations 32/min, SpO<sub>2</sub> 93% on room air. He appears toxic and anxious. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Examine the oropharynx with a tongue depressor

options.label: C
options.html: Place an intravenous line, draw blood cultures, and give ceftriaxone in the emergency department

options.label: D
options.html: Keep the child calm with his parent and arrange for anesthesia and otolaryngology to secure the airway in the operating room

answerHtml: Answer: D. Secure the airway in a controlled setting.
explanationHtml: Abrupt high fever, toxicity, drooling, tripod posture, and a muffled voice in an unvaccinated child indicate epiglottitis (Hib). Any agitation (throat exam, needles, separation from the parent, lying supine) can provoke complete obstruction. Keep him calm and upright with the parent and supplemental O2 as tolerated. Get the most skilled airway team to intubate (or perform a surgical airway) in the OR. Cultures and IV ceftriaxone + vancomycin follow once the airway is secure.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: A tongue depressor can trigger laryngospasm and obstruction. B: Imaging delays definitive care and requires leaving a monitored setting. C: IV placement and phlebotomy agitate the child, and antibiotics should come after the airway is secured. E: This is croup treatment and does not address supraglottic infection.

stemHtml: A 3-day-old boy born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy fed normally for 48 hours, then developed poor feeding, vomiting, and progressive lethargy. He is now tachypneic. Temperature 36.9 °C. Labs: glucose 82 mg/dL; arterial pH 7.50, PCO<sub>2</sub> 28 mm Hg, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> 22 mEq/L; anion gap 12; plasma ammonia 420 μmol/L (normal <50); urine ketones negative. Plasma citrulline is low, and urine orotic acid is markedly elevated. Which of the following is the most likely enzyme deficiency?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency.
explanationHtml: Severe hyperammonemia with respiratory alkalosis (ammonia stimulates the respiratory center), no metabolic acidosis or ketosis, and normal glucose points to a urea cycle defect. Low citrulline places the block before citrulline formation (CPS I or OTC). In OTC deficiency, the accumulated carbamoyl phosphate leaks into the cytosol and enters pyrimidine synthesis, producing orotic aciduria. OTC deficiency is X-linked, so the classic patient is a male neonate. Management: stop protein, give high-rate IV dextrose, IV sodium phenylacetate/benzoate + arginine, and hemodialysis for this degree of hyperammonemia.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: CPS I deficiency gives the same picture but with low/normal orotic acid, because no carbamoyl phosphate is made. B: MSUD causes ketoacidosis and a maple-syrup odor without marked hyperammonemia. D: MCAD causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia with fasting. E: Propionic acidemia causes anion-gap metabolic acidosis with ketosis (hyperammonemia may accompany it).

stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl comes to the clinic alone and requests contraception. She has been sexually active with one male partner for 4 months and uses condoms inconsistently. She asks that her parents not be told. She is healthy and takes no medications. Blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg. Urine hCG is negative. State law permits minors to consent to contraceptive services. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Explain that parental consent is required before contraception can be prescribed

options.label: B
options.html: Counsel her on options, including long-acting reversible contraception, provide her chosen method confidentially, and offer STI screening

options.label: C
options.html: Prescribe contraception but inform her parents because she is a minor

options.label: D
options.html: Perform a pelvic examination and Pap test before prescribing

answerHtml: Answer: B. Confidential contraceptive counseling and provision, with STI screening.
explanationHtml: Where minors may consent to contraception (most states and all Title X clinics), confidentiality should be maintained unless there is a risk of serious harm. AAP and ACOG recommend LARC (implant, IUD) as first-line for adolescents because of very low failure rates, while respecting her choice. Encourage continued condom use. Screen for chlamydia/gonorrhea (all sexually active females ≤24 y) and offer HIV testing and HPV vaccination if not done. Encourage, but do not require, communication with a trusted adult.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, C: Requiring or forcing parental involvement violates the minor's legal right to consent and drives teens away from care. D: Neither a pelvic exam nor cytology is required to start contraception, and cervical screening does not begin until 21. E: Judicial bypass applies to abortion parental-involvement laws in some states, not to contraception.

stemHtml: A boy born at 28 weeks' gestation is now 12 days old in the neonatal ICU, receiving advancing formula feeds. He develops abdominal distension, bilious gastric residuals, temperature instability, and grossly bloody stools. Platelets 90,000/μL; there is metabolic acidosis on blood gas. Abdominal radiograph shows pneumatosis intestinalis without free intraperitoneal air. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Stop enteral feeds, decompress with an orogastric tube, give IV fluids, obtain a blood culture, and start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics

options.label: D
options.html: Continue feeds with an added probiotic

answerHtml: Answer: A. Medical management of necrotizing enterocolitis.
explanationHtml: Pneumatosis intestinalis in a formula-fed preterm infant confirms NEC (modified Bell stage II). Without perforation, treatment is medical: bowel rest (NPO), gastric decompression, IV fluids/parenteral nutrition, cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin + gentamicin ± metronidazole), and serial abdominal radiographs every 6–12 h to detect perforation.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: Surgery (laparotomy or peritoneal drain) is indicated for pneumoperitoneum or clinical deterioration despite medical therapy. C: A contrast enema risks perforating inflamed bowel. D: Continuing feeds worsens NEC. E: Oral vancomycin treats C. difficile colitis, which is not the issue in neonates.

stemHtml: A term infant is delivered vaginally after a prolonged second stage; the amniotic fluid is clear. At birth he is limp and apneic. He is placed under a radiant warmer, dried, stimulated, and his airway is positioned and cleared. At 30 seconds he remains apneic, and his heart rate by auscultation is 80/min. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Intravenous epinephrine via an umbilical venous catheter

answerHtml: Answer: E. Positive-pressure ventilation (21% O<sub>2</sub> at term).
explanationHtml: Apnea, gasping, or HR <100 after the initial steps calls for PPV within the first minute. Most neonatal bradycardia is caused by hypoxia from inadequate ventilation, and effective ventilation is the single most important intervention. Term infants start in room air, and O2 is titrated to pre-ductal saturation targets.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Compressions start only if HR stays <60 after 30 s of effective ventilation. B: Epinephrine is for HR <60 despite ventilation and compressions. C: Tracheal suctioning is not indicated (clear fluid; even for meconium, routine suctioning is no longer recommended). Intubation may be an alternative airway for PPV but not for suctioning. D: Blow-by O<sub>2</sub> does not ventilate an apneic infant.

stemHtml: A 12-month-old girl is seen for a well-child visit. She is enrolled in Medicaid and lives with her family in an apartment built in 1955. She was born at term, is growing along the 40th percentile, and is meeting milestones. She has no history of travel, known TB exposure, or recurrent infections. In addition to routine immunizations, which of the following screening tests are indicated at this visit?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Hemoglobin and blood lead level.
explanationHtml: AAP recommends universal hemoglobin screening at 12 months for iron deficiency anemia. Federal law requires blood lead testing at 12 and 24 months for all Medicaid-enrolled children, and pre-1978 housing (lead paint) is an additional risk factor. Lead and iron deficiency often coexist and worsen each other's neurodevelopmental effects.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Universal lipid screening is at 9–11 and 17–21 y (selective from age 2 for family history). B: Routine screening UA is not recommended. D: Congenital hypothyroidism is covered by the newborn screen. E: TB testing is risk-based, and she has no risk factors.

stemHtml: A 27-year-old primigravida at 35 weeks' gestation has a severe frontal headache that has not responded to acetaminophen. Blood pressure is 166/112 mm Hg and, 15 minutes later, 168/110 mm Hg. Pulse 88/min. She has 2+ pedal edema and 3+ patellar reflexes. Urine protein/creatinine ratio is 0.6. Platelets 168,000/μL, AST 32 U/L, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL. The fetal heart rate tracing is Category I, and the fetus is cephalic. The cervix is 2 cm dilated and 50% effaced. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Betamethasone and expectant management until 37 weeks

options.label: B
options.html: Intravenous labetalol and magnesium sulfate, followed by induction of labor

options.label: C
options.html: Magnesium sulfate alone, with delivery planned at 37 weeks

options.label: D
options.html: Oral methyldopa and outpatient follow-up in 1 week

options.label: E
options.html: Immediate cesarean delivery under general anesthesia

answerHtml: Answer: B. Treat severe-range BP, start magnesium, and deliver.
explanationHtml: She has preeclampsia with severe features: severe-range BP confirmed within minutes, plus a new headache unresponsive to analgesics. Management: (1) treat acute severe hypertension within 30–60 minutes with IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or oral immediate-release nifedipine; (2) give magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis; (3) at ≥34 weeks, deliver after maternal stabilization. Vaginal delivery (induction) is appropriate, and cesarean is for the usual obstetric indications.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Expectant management is an option only for stable severe preeclampsia at <34 weeks, and late-preterm steroids should not delay an indicated delivery. C: Magnesium does not treat hypertension, and waiting until 37 weeks is appropriate only without severe features. D: Outpatient management is unsafe with severe features. E: Severe preeclampsia is not itself an indication for cesarean, and general anesthesia carries extra risk (hypertensive response to intubation, difficult airway).

stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman at 37 weeks' gestation with preeclampsia with severe features is undergoing induction of labor. She has received a magnesium sulfate infusion at 2 g/h for 10 hours. The nurse reports that she is drowsy and difficult to arouse. Respirations are 9/min, SpO<sub>2</sub> 93% on room air, and blood pressure 150/96 mm Hg. Patellar reflexes are absent. Urine output has been 15 mL/h over the past 4 hours. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Decrease the magnesium infusion to 1 g/h

options.label: B
options.html: Draw a serum magnesium level and continue the infusion pending the result

options.label: D
options.html: Stop the magnesium infusion and administer intravenous calcium gluconate

options.label: E
options.html: Administer intravenous furosemide to enhance magnesium excretion

answerHtml: Answer: D. Stop magnesium and give IV calcium gluconate (1 g of a 10% solution over ~3 min).
explanationHtml: Magnesium is renally excreted. Oliguria led to accumulation. Loss of deep tendon reflexes (~7–10 mEq/L) followed by respiratory depression (~10–13 mEq/L) means life-threatening toxicity, and cardiac arrest can follow. Calcium directly antagonizes magnesium at the neuromuscular junction and myocardium. Also give supportive airway care, check a serum level, and resume only at a reduced dose once the level is known and renal function recovers.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B: Continuing any infusion during respiratory depression is dangerous. Act on clinical signs; do not wait for a level. C: Naloxone reverses opioids, and nothing suggests opioid toxicity. E: Loop diuretics may help clearance later but are not the immediate antidote and can worsen volume status.

stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 31 weeks' gestation has had epigastric and right upper quadrant pain with nausea for 12 hours. Blood pressure 152/98 mm Hg. Labs: hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, platelets 72,000/μL, AST 290 U/L, ALT 260 U/L, LDH 920 U/L, glucose 88 mg/dL, fibrinogen 310 mg/dL; peripheral smear shows schistocytes. The fetal heart rate tracing is Category I, and estimated fetal weight is at the 25th percentile. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Magnesium sulfate, antihypertensive therapy as needed, and delivery after maternal stabilization

options.label: B
options.html: Expectant management with twice-weekly laboratory monitoring until 34 weeks

options.label: E
options.html: High-dose dexamethasone to raise the platelet count and allow continuation of pregnancy

answerHtml: Answer: A. Stabilize (magnesium, BP control) and deliver.
explanationHtml: Hemolysis (schistocytes, LDH >600), elevated transaminases (≥2× ULN), and platelets <100,000 define HELLP syndrome, a severe form of preeclampsia that can progress rapidly to hepatic hematoma/rupture, DIC, abruption, and death. Prolonged expectant management is not appropriate at any GA. After maternal stabilization, deliver. At <34 weeks, a delay of 24–48 h to complete antenatal corticosteroids for fetal benefit is acceptable only if mother and fetus remain stable. Platelet transfusion is given before cesarean if platelets are <50,000 (or for bleeding).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: Expectant management to 34 weeks exposes the mother to catastrophic complications. C: Transfusion does not treat the disease. D: Plasma exchange is for TTP. Normal glucose and fibrinogen and prominent transaminitis favor HELLP, and HELLP resolves with delivery. E: Steroids do not improve maternal outcomes in HELLP and must not be used to prolong pregnancy.

stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 26 weeks' gestation has a routine 1-hour 50-g glucose challenge test result of 152 mg/dL (institutional cutoff 140 mg/dL). She has no polyuria or polydipsia. BMI is 27 kg/m². Her first pregnancy was uncomplicated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Perform a 3-hour 100-g oral glucose tolerance test

options.label: E
options.html: Repeat the 50-g glucose challenge test at 32 weeks

answerHtml: Answer: C. Diagnostic 3-hour 100-g OGTT.
explanationHtml: In the two-step approach, the 50-g GCT is only a screen. An abnormal result leads to a diagnostic fasting 100-g 3-hour OGTT. GDM is diagnosed if ≥2 values meet Carpenter–Coustan thresholds (95/180/155/140 mg/dL). Only then are nutrition therapy and, if needed, medication started.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B: Treatment before diagnosis is premature. D: A1c is insensitive for GDM in the second/third trimester (it is used early in pregnancy for overt diabetes). E: Delaying the diagnosis loses the window to treat and reduce macrosomia and shoulder dystocia.

stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, with two prior cesarean deliveries, presents at 32 weeks' gestation with sudden painless bright-red vaginal bleeding of about 100 mL after intercourse; it has now stopped. Blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg, pulse 88/min. The uterus is soft and nontender. The fetal heart rate is 145/min with moderate variability and accelerations, and there are no contractions. She missed her 20-week anatomy ultrasound. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Digital cervical examination to assess dilation

answerHtml: Answer: B. Ultrasound for placental location before any digital examination.
explanationHtml: Painless bright-red third-trimester bleeding with a soft uterus in a woman with prior cesareans suggests placenta previa. A digital exam can provoke massive hemorrhage, so placental location must be established first (transabdominal, then transvaginal US, which is safe). With previa and two prior cesareans, also evaluate for placenta accreta spectrum. Mother and fetus are stable, so management would be expectant: admission, betamethasone (<34 wk), RhIG if Rh-negative, and planned cesarean at 36 0/7–37 6/7 wk if previa is confirmed.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: A digital exam is contraindicated until previa is excluded. C: Emergent cesarean is for uncontrolled bleeding or fetal compromise, and neither is present. D, E: Induction and amniotomy are contraindicated if previa is present, and they are inappropriate at 32 weeks without an indication.

stemHtml: A 26-year-old primigravida at 30 weeks' gestation has had regular painful contractions every 4 minutes for 3 hours. Sterile speculum examination shows intact membranes. The cervix is 4 cm dilated and 80% effaced; it was long and closed 2 weeks ago. She is afebrile with normal vital signs, and the uterus is nontender between contractions. GBS status is unknown. The fetal heart rate tracing is Category I. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Betamethasone only and discharge home on pelvic rest

options.label: B
options.html: Oral terbutaline maintenance therapy and bed rest

options.label: D
options.html: Betamethasone, magnesium sulfate, nifedipine, and intravenous penicillin G

answerHtml: Answer: D. Steroids, magnesium for neuroprotection, short-term tocolysis, and GBS prophylaxis.
explanationHtml: This is preterm labor at 30 weeks (contractions with cervical change). Each component has a purpose. Betamethasone (24 0/7–33 6/7 wk) reduces RDS, IVH, NEC, and death. Magnesium sulfate at <32 weeks reduces cerebral palsy. Tocolysis (nifedipine, or indomethacin at <32 wk) for up to 48 h buys time for steroids and transfer. IV penicillin because GBS status is unknown and she is preterm. Get a GBS culture and stop prophylaxis if it is negative or labor stops.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: She is in active preterm labor and needs inpatient care. B: Maintenance tocolysis is ineffective, and oral terbutaline carries an FDA boxed warning. Bed rest is not recommended. C: Hydroxyprogesterone caproate (Makena) was withdrawn from the US market in 2023. It was a preventive agent for women with a prior preterm birth, never a treatment for active labor. E: Prematurity alone is not an indication for cesarean.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 29 weeks' gestation reports a gush of clear fluid from the vagina 3 hours ago. She is afebrile with a pulse of 84/min, the uterus is nontender, and she has no contractions. Sterile speculum examination shows pooling of fluid in the posterior fornix; nitrazine is positive, and ferning is seen on microscopy. Ultrasonography shows a cephalic fetus, an amniotic fluid index of 4 cm, and an estimated fetal weight at the 50th percentile. The fetal heart rate is 140/min with moderate variability. GBS status is unknown. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.html: Discharge home with bed rest and weekly visits

options.label: E
options.html: Hospitalize; give betamethasone and latency antibiotics (IV ampicillin and erythromycin); manage expectantly until 34 weeks

answerHtml: Answer: E. Inpatient expectant management with corticosteroids and latency antibiotics.
explanationHtml: PPROM at 24 0/7–33 6/7 weeks without infection, labor, abruption, or fetal compromise is managed expectantly in the hospital. Latency antibiotics (IV ampicillin + erythromycin for 48 h, then oral amoxicillin + erythromycin for 5 days; azithromycin is an accepted substitute) prolong latency and reduce chorioamnionitis and neonatal morbidity. Ampicillin also covers GBS. Give a single course of betamethasone. Give magnesium for neuroprotection only if delivery becomes imminent before 32 weeks. Deliver at 34 0/7 weeks, or sooner if intraamniotic infection, abruption, or nonreassuring status develops.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Immediate delivery is the standard at ≥34 weeks, not at 29 weeks without complications. B: Outpatient management of PPROM is not recommended because of the risks of infection, cord prolapse, and abruption. C: Tocolysis is not beneficial in PPROM and may mask infection. Prolonged indomethacin also risks ductal constriction and oligohydramnios. D: Cerclage is contraindicated with ruptured membranes.

stemHtml: A 25-year-old primigravida at 28 weeks' gestation is seen for a routine visit. Her blood type is O, Rh(D)-negative. Antibody screens at the first visit and today are negative. Her partner's blood type is unknown. She has had no bleeding or trauma. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Administer Rh immune globulin only after delivery if the newborn is Rh-positive

options.label: B
options.html: Administer 300 μg of Rh immune globulin now, and again within 72 hours of delivery if the newborn is Rh(D)-positive

options.label: D
options.html: Perform amniocentesis to determine fetal Rh status

options.label: E
options.html: No intervention is needed because her antibody screen is negative

answerHtml: Answer: B. Antenatal RhIG at 28 weeks plus postpartum RhIG if the newborn is Rh-positive.
explanationHtml: She is unsensitized (negative antibody screen). About 1–2% of Rh-negative women become sensitized during the third trimester from silent fetomaternal hemorrhage, so routine 28-week prophylaxis reduces third-trimester sensitization substantially. A second dose within 72 h of delivery covers the fetomaternal hemorrhage at birth. The dose can be adjusted by Kleihauer–Betke testing if the rosette screen is positive.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Postpartum-only prophylaxis misses antenatal sensitization. C: KB testing quantifies a known or suspected large hemorrhage, such as after delivery or trauma. D: Amniocentesis is invasive and can itself sensitize. Noninvasive cfDNA fetal RhD genotyping exists, but prophylaxis is the standard here. E: A negative screen is exactly why she still benefits from prophylaxis. Once sensitized, RhIG is useless.

stemHtml: A 29-year-old primigravida at 40 weeks' gestation is undergoing oxytocin induction. Her cervix is 5 cm dilated, and an epidural was placed 1 hour ago; blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg. Over the past 30 minutes, the fetal heart rate tracing shows a baseline of 150/min, minimal variability, and late decelerations with every contraction. Contractions average 7 per 10 minutes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Discontinue oxytocin, reposition the patient to a lateral position, and give an intravenous fluid bolus

options.label: B
options.html: Increase the oxytocin infusion to expedite delivery

answerHtml: Answer: A. Intrauterine resuscitation, starting with stopping oxytocin.
explanationHtml: Recurrent late decelerations with minimal (not absent) variability make this a Category II tracing. It is caused here by tachysystole (>5 contractions/10 min averaged over 30 min), which reduces intervillous perfusion. First steps: stop oxytocin, reposition laterally (relieves aortocaval compression), give an IV fluid bolus (especially after an epidural), and consider terbutaline if tachysystole persists. Reassess. If the tracing progresses to Category III (absent variability with recurrent lates) or does not improve, expedite delivery.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: More oxytocin worsens uteroplacental insufficiency. C: Amnioinfusion treats recurrent variable decelerations (cord compression), not lates. D: Immediate cesarean is premature before correcting a reversible cause in a Category II tracing. E: Operative vaginal delivery requires full cervical dilation.

stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman, gravida 4, para 4, with moderate persistent asthma and preeclampsia without severe features (blood pressure 152/98 mm Hg) has a vaginal delivery of a 4.3-kg infant. The placenta delivers intact. Fifteen minutes later she has brisk bleeding, with estimated blood loss of 1200 mL. The uterus is soft and boggy above the umbilicus. Bimanual massage and an oxytocin infusion have been started, tranexamic acid has been given, the bladder is emptied, and inspection shows no lacerations. The uterus remains boggy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next pharmacologic agent?

options.label: E
options.html: No further medication; proceed to immediate hysterectomy

answerHtml: Answer: C. Misoprostol.
explanationHtml: This is PPH from uterine atony (macrosomia and grand multiparity are risk factors) that has not responded to massage and oxytocin. The second-line uterotonic depends on contraindications. Methylergonovine (an ergot vasoconstrictor) is contraindicated in hypertension/preeclampsia. Carboprost (PGF2α) causes bronchoconstriction and is contraindicated in asthma. Misoprostol (PGE1) has neither problem. Resuscitation continues in parallel. If bleeding persists, escalate to balloon tamponade, embolization, or surgery.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Methylergonovine risks hypertensive crisis and stroke. B: Carboprost risks severe bronchospasm. D: rFVIIa is a last-resort hemostatic for refractory coagulopathic bleeding, not atony. E: Hysterectomy is definitive but is reserved for failure of uterotonics and conservative measures (tamponade, embolization, compression sutures) when fertility-sparing options remain.

stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman has had 6 weeks of amenorrhea, light vaginal spotting, and mild left lower quadrant pain. Blood pressure 118/76 mm Hg, pulse 82/min. There is mild left adnexal tenderness without peritoneal signs. Serum β-hCG is 2,900 mIU/mL. Transvaginal ultrasound shows no intrauterine gestational sac and a 2.5-cm complex left adnexal mass, separate from the ovary, with a hyperechoic ring and no embryonic cardiac activity; there is minimal free fluid. CBC, creatinine, and liver enzymes are normal. She is not breastfeeding and can reliably return for follow-up. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Repeat the β-hCG level in 48 hours

options.label: D
options.html: Expectant management with weekly β-hCG levels

answerHtml: Answer: E. Single-dose methotrexate (50 mg/m² IM).
explanationHtml: An extra-ovarian adnexal mass with a tubal ring ("bagel sign"), no IUP, and a positive hCG is a tubal ectopic pregnancy. She is an ideal methotrexate candidate: hemodynamically stable, unruptured, hCG <5,000, no cardiac activity, mass <3.5–4 cm, normal labs, not breastfeeding, and reliable. Check hCG on days 4 and 7. A ≥15% fall between them indicates response.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Serial hCG is for a pregnancy of unknown location. Here the ectopic is visualized. B: D&C is used to distinguish a failed IUP from ectopic when no mass is seen. It does not treat a tubal pregnancy. C: Surgery (preferably laparoscopic) is for instability, rupture, MTX contraindications, or failure. Laparotomy is unnecessary in a stable patient. D: Expectant management is reserved for very low and falling hCG (e.g., <200 mIU/mL).

stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 12 weeks' gestation is told that her cell-free DNA screening result is "high risk for trisomy 21." Ultrasound today shows a nuchal translucency of 2.1 mm and no structural anomalies. She is distressed and wants to know for certain whether the fetus is affected. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Counsel her regarding termination of pregnancy

options.label: B
options.html: Provide genetic counseling and offer chorionic villus sampling now or amniocentesis at or after 15 weeks

options.label: C
options.html: Repeat cell-free DNA screening in 2 weeks

options.label: D
options.html: Perform a quadruple screen at 16 weeks

options.label: E
options.html: Reassure her because the nuchal translucency is normal

answerHtml: Answer: B. Genetic counseling and diagnostic testing.
explanationHtml: Cell-free DNA is a screening test that analyzes placental DNA. Its positive predictive value, although high at age 38, is not 100%, because of confined placental mosaicism, vanishing twin, and maternal mosaicism or malignancy. ACOG recommends diagnostic testing before any irreversible decision. CVS (10–13 wk) gives an earlier answer, with a small risk that placental mosaicism will mislead. Amniocentesis (≥15 wk) samples fetal cells.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Termination should never be based on a screening result alone. C: Repeating the screen does not confirm the diagnosis. D: A serum screen is less sensitive than cfDNA and is not diagnostic. Sequential screening after cfDNA is not recommended. E: A normal NT does not exclude trisomy 21.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old primigravida at 40 weeks' gestation is in spontaneous labor with an epidural. At 08:00 her cervix is 6 cm dilated, 100% effaced, at −1 station, and amniotomy is performed. An intrauterine pressure catheter shows 230–250 Montevideo units since then. At 12:30 the cervical examination is unchanged. The fetus is in occiput anterior position, and the fetal heart rate tracing has remained Category I. She is afebrile. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Cesarean delivery for active-phase arrest.
explanationHtml: Under ACOG–SMFM criteria, active-phase arrest is cervical dilation ≥6 cm with ruptured membranes and no cervical change for ≥4 hours despite adequate contractions (≥200 MVUs), or ≥6 hours of inadequate contractions despite oxytocin. She meets the first definition (4.5 h with adequate MVUs), so cesarean is indicated.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Further observation is not supported once arrest criteria are met. B: Oxytocin is for inadequate contractions, and hers are already adequate. C: Operative vaginal delivery requires full dilation. E: Membranes are already ruptured.

stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman at 9 weeks' gestation has 1 month of palpitations, heat intolerance, and a 3-kg weight loss despite good appetite, with only mild nausea. Pulse 112/min. She has a diffuse nontender goiter with a bruit and bilateral proptosis. TSH is <0.01 μU/mL, free T4 is markedly elevated, and thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin is positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: E
options.html: No antithyroid treatment, because this is gestational transient thyrotoxicosis

answerHtml: Answer: B. PTU (first trimester) plus a β-blocker for symptoms.
explanationHtml: Goiter with bruit, ophthalmopathy, and positive TSI mean Graves disease, not hCG-mediated thyrotoxicosis. During organogenesis, PTU is preferred because methimazole is linked to aplasia cutis and choanal/esophageal atresia (methimazole embryopathy). After the first trimester, switch to methimazole because of PTU's hepatotoxicity. Use the lowest dose that keeps free T4 at the upper limit of normal, because both drugs cross the placenta. Propranolol controls adrenergic symptoms short-term.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Methimazole is avoided in the first trimester. C: RAI is contraindicated in pregnancy because it ablates the fetal thyroid (which takes up iodine after ~10–12 weeks). D: Surgery is reserved for drug failure or intolerance and is best done in the second trimester. E: Gestational transient thyrotoxicosis has no goiter, ophthalmopathy, or TSI, and usually accompanies hyperemesis.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman whose menopause occurred at age 51 had a single episode of light vaginal bleeding 1 week ago. She has never taken hormone therapy. BMI is 34 kg/m², and she has type 2 diabetes. Pelvic examination shows no vulvar, vaginal, or cervical lesions. Her cervical screening is current and normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Reassurance, because a single episode is usually due to atrophy

options.label: E
options.html: Transvaginal ultrasonography to measure endometrial thickness

answerHtml: Answer: E. Evaluate the endometrium (TVUS or endometrial biopsy).
explanationHtml: Any postmenopausal bleeding requires evaluation for endometrial cancer, which is present in ~10%, and she has obesity and diabetes as risk factors. Either TVUS or office endometrial biopsy is an acceptable first step. An endometrial stripe ≤4 mm has a >99% negative predictive value. A thicker stripe, persistent bleeding, or a poorly visualized endometrium → EMB.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Atrophy is the most common cause, but it is a diagnosis of exclusion. B: Hormones could mask or worsen a malignancy. C: CA-125 is not a test for endometrial cancer. D: Hysterectomy without a tissue diagnosis is inappropriate.

stemHtml: A 34-year-old nulligravid woman has had no menses for 8 months, with hot flashes and vaginal dryness. Menarche was at age 12, and cycles were previously regular. She takes no medications and has not had chemotherapy or radiation. Urine hCG is negative. TSH and prolactin are normal. FSH is 68 mIU/mL, and 4 weeks later 74 mIU/mL; estradiol is low. Karyotype and FMR1 premutation testing have been ordered. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional management?

options.label: A
options.html: No therapy, because symptoms will resolve spontaneously

options.label: D
options.html: Estrogen with cyclic progestin, continued until about the average age of natural menopause

answerHtml: Answer: D. Hormone therapy until ~age 50–51.
explanationHtml: Amenorrhea with menopausal-range FSH on two occasions before age 40 is primary ovarian insufficiency. Workup includes karyotype (Turner mosaicism, Y material), FMR1 premutation, and autoimmune screening (TSH/anti-TPO, 21-hydroxylase antibodies for adrenal insufficiency). Estrogen deficiency this early causes bone loss, cardiovascular risk, and urogenital atrophy. Physiologic estrogen replacement plus a progestin (she has a uterus) is recommended until the average age of menopause. The WHI risk data for older menopausal women do not apply here. A DEXA scan is also indicated.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Untreated POI causes osteoporosis and increases cardiovascular disease and mortality. B: Clomiphene requires functioning follicles and fails in POI. Donor oocytes are the effective fertility option, and spontaneous pregnancy occurs in only ~5–10%. C: Bromocriptine treats hyperprolactinemia, and her prolactin is normal. E: A high FSH places the problem in the ovary, not the pituitary.

stemHtml: A 28-year-old nulligravid woman has been trying to conceive for 14 months. Her menstrual cycles occur every 45–90 days. She has acne and coarse hair on her chin and lower abdomen. BMI is 31 kg/m². TSH, prolactin, and early-morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone are normal. Her partner's semen analysis is normal, and hysterosalpingography shows bilateral tubal patency. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to achieve pregnancy?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Letrozole.
explanationHtml: She has PCOS (oligo-ovulation and clinical hyperandrogenism, with mimics excluded) with anovulatory infertility. The male and tubal factors are normal. Letrozole, an aromatase inhibitor that lowers estrogen negative feedback and raises FSH, is first-line for ovulation induction in PCOS. It produces higher ovulation and live-birth rates than clomiphene (PPCOS II trial). Lifestyle-based weight loss also improves ovulation.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Clomiphene is now second-line (lower live-birth rate, antiestrogenic endometrial effects). C: Metformin alone is a weak ovulation inducer and is used mainly for metabolic indications. D: IVF is reserved for failure of ovulation induction or other factors. E: Ovarian drilling is a second-line surgical option.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old nulligravid woman requests contraception. She has migraines about twice a month that are preceded by 20 minutes of flashing zigzag lines in her vision. She does not smoke, and her blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. She wants a highly effective reversible method and would prefer lighter periods. Which of the following is the most appropriate method?

options.label: E
options.html: Combined oral contraceptive containing 20 μg ethinyl estradiol

answerHtml: Answer: A. LNG-IUD.
explanationHtml: Migraine with aura is US MEC category 4 for all estrogen-containing methods because it increases the risk of ischemic stroke. Progestin-only methods and IUDs are category 1–2. The LNG-IUD is highly effective (failure <1%), reversible, and reduces menstrual bleeding. The implant would also be acceptable but often causes unpredictable bleeding.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, C, D, E: All contain estrogen. A lower estrogen dose (E) does not remove the contraindication.

stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman reports that a condom broke during intercourse 4 days (96 hours) ago. Her last menstrual period began 12 days ago, and her cycles are regular. BMI is 34 kg/m². Urine hCG is negative. She wants the most effective emergency contraception and is also interested in long-term contraception. She has no medical problems. Which of the following is the most appropriate option?

options.label: D
options.html: High-dose combined oral contraceptive pills (Yuzpe regimen)

options.label: E
options.html: Reassurance that pregnancy is unlikely at this point in her cycle

answerHtml: Answer: C. Copper IUD.
explanationHtml: The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraceptive (>99%) when inserted within 5 days. Its efficacy is not reduced by BMI, and it provides up to 10–12 years of ongoing contraception, which matches both of her goals. (The 52-mg LNG-IUD is now an accepted alternative per the 2024 US SPR.)
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Levonorgestrel is labeled for use within 72 h, is least effective late in the window, and loses efficacy at BMI ≥30. B: Ulipristal works up to 120 h and is the best oral option (and better than LNG at higher BMI), but it is less effective than an IUD. D: The Yuzpe regimen is the least effective and causes the most nausea. E: Intercourse on cycle day 8 falls within the fertile window, so reassurance is inappropriate.

stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman has routine cervical cytology showing atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US). Reflex high-risk HPV testing is positive for a type other than 16 or 18. Her previous cytology 3 years ago was normal; HPV testing was not done. She is not pregnant and is immunocompetent. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Colposcopy.
explanationHtml: Under ASCCP 2019 risk-based guidelines, HPV-positive ASC-US (without a documented prior negative HPV test) carries an immediate CIN3+ risk of about 4%. That meets the ≥4% threshold for colposcopy, regardless of HPV genotype.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: Repeat testing in 1 year is for lower-risk results (e.g., HPV-negative LSIL, or HPV-positive NILM non-16/18). Repeat cytology at 1 year is also the plan for ASC-US/LSIL in 21–24-year-olds. C: A 3-year return is for HPV-negative ASC-US. D: Excision without histology is acceptable only for HSIL in selected patients aged ≥25 (immediate risk ≥60%). E: Six-month cytology is not part of current algorithms for this result.

stemHtml: A 22-year-old woman has her first cervical cytology, which shows a low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL). She is healthy, HIV-negative, not pregnant, and not immunosuppressed. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Repeat cytology in 1 year.
explanationHtml: In patients aged 21–24, transient HPV infection is very common and most LSIL regresses spontaneously, while the risk of invasive cancer is extremely low. ASCCP 2019 therefore recommends repeat cytology at 1 year for ASC-US or LSIL in this age group. If the 1-year result is ASC-H, AGC, or HSIL, go to colposcopy. If ASC-US/LSIL persists at 2 years, also go to colposcopy. This avoids overtreatment, because excision increases later preterm-birth risk.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Colposcopy is for ASC-H/HSIL/AGC in this age group, or for abnormalities that persist after 2 years. B: HPV testing is not recommended in women <25 (high prevalence, low specificity). If one were performed, a positive result would not change management. C: Excision is not indicated for LSIL in young women. D: A 3-year return is for normal cytology.

stemHtml: A 22-year-old woman has had 3 days of lower abdominal pain, dyspareunia, and increased vaginal discharge. Temperature 38.2 °C, blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg. She is tolerating oral intake and does not appear severely ill. Examination shows mucopurulent cervical discharge, cervical motion tenderness, and bilateral adnexal tenderness; there is no rebound tenderness. Urine hCG is negative. Transvaginal ultrasound shows no adnexal mass or tubo-ovarian abscess. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: B
options.html: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once plus oral doxycycline and metronidazole for 14 days

options.label: C
options.html: Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM once plus doxycycline for 7 days

options.label: D
options.html: Hospital admission for IV cefoxitin and doxycycline

answerHtml: Answer: B. CDC 2021 outpatient PID regimen.
explanationHtml: Pelvic pain with cervical motion and adnexal tenderness meets the minimum criteria for pelvic inflammatory disease. She has none of the criteria for admission (TOA, pregnancy, severe illness, inability to take oral medications, a surgical emergency not excluded, or failure of oral therapy). The CDC 2021 outpatient regimen is ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once + doxycycline 100 mg BID ×14 days + metronidazole 500 mg BID ×14 days. Metronidazole was added to cover anaerobes and BV-associated organisms. Re-examine within 72 h, test for HIV and syphilis, and treat partners.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: A single azithromycin dose treats uncomplicated chlamydial cervicitis only, not polymicrobial upper-tract infection. C: This is an outdated dose and duration and lacks anaerobic coverage. D: Inpatient therapy is unnecessary without admission criteria. E: Laparoscopy is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or failure of therapy. PID is treated empirically on clinical grounds.

stemHtml: A 25-year-old woman noticed a painless lump in her right breast 1 month ago. It has not changed through her menstrual cycle. She has no nipple discharge and no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Examination shows a 2-cm firm, rubbery, well-circumscribed, mobile, nontender mass in the upper outer quadrant, with no skin changes or axillary lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Targeted breast ultrasound.
explanationHtml: For a palpable breast mass in a woman <30 years, ultrasound is the initial imaging test. Young breast tissue is dense, which limits mammographic sensitivity, and US distinguishes cystic from solid lesions without radiation. The likely diagnosis is a fibroadenoma. A solid lesion with benign features may be followed or sampled by core biopsy. Suspicious features → core needle biopsy (with mammography added).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Diagnostic mammography (plus US) is first for women ≥30. B: MRI is for high-risk screening or problem-solving, not the initial evaluation. D: Excisional biopsy is invasive and comes after imaging, and core biopsy is preferred when tissue is needed. E: She has no family history or other indication for genetic testing.

stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman whose last menstrual period was 14 months ago has about 10 hot flashes daily that disrupt her sleep and work despite layered clothing, cooler room temperatures, and avoiding triggers. She has an intact uterus. She has no history of breast or endometrial cancer, venous thromboembolism, stroke, liver disease, or coronary disease. She does not smoke. Blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg; BMI 26 kg/m²; her screening mammogram this year was normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: E
options.html: Avoid all hormone therapy because of breast cancer risk
