answerHtml: Answer: D. Combined estrogen–progestogen therapy.
explanationHtml: Systemic hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for moderate–severe vasomotor symptoms. For a healthy woman <60 years and within 10 years of menopause, benefits outweigh risks. Because she has a uterus, a progestogen (e.g., micronized progesterone) must be added to prevent estrogen-induced endometrial hyperplasia and cancer. Transdermal estradiol carries less VTE risk than oral. Use the lowest effective dose and reassess yearly.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: Unopposed estrogen in a woman with a uterus causes endometrial hyperplasia and cancer. It is appropriate only after hysterectomy. B: Testosterone is not a treatment for vasomotor symptoms (its only evidence-based use is hypoactive sexual desire disorder). C: Black cohosh is not more effective than placebo and has been linked to hepatotoxicity. E: Her small absolute breast-cancer risk with E+P does not outweigh the benefits in a symptomatic, low-risk woman in this age window. Nonhormonal options (SSRIs/SNRIs, fezolinetant, elinzanetant) are for women who decline or cannot use HT.

stemHtml: A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after his wife noticed sudden right-sided weakness and difficulty speaking. He was normal at breakfast. BP is 196/112 mm Hg, pulse 84/min and regular. Fingerstick glucose is 128 mg/dL. NIHSS is 14. Noncontrast CT of the head shows no hemorrhage or early hypodensity. He takes no anticoagulants. CT angiography is being arranged. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: IV alteplase immediately without antihypertensive treatment

options.label: C
options.html: IV labetalol to lower BP below 185/110 mm Hg, then IV thrombolysis

options.label: D
options.html: IV nicardipine to lower BP below 140/90 mm Hg before any further therapy

options.label: E
options.html: Withhold thrombolysis and allow permissive hypertension

answerHtml: Answer: C. IV labetalol to <185/110, then thrombolysis
explanationHtml: He is within 4.5 h of last known well, has a disabling deficit, and has no hemorrhage. He is eligible for IV thrombolysis (alteplase or tenecteplase). The only obstacle is BP above 185/110, which is modifiable. Lower it with IV labetalol, nicardipine or clevidipine, then lyse, and keep BP <180/105 for 24 h. If CTA shows an LVO, he also goes to thrombectomy.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: aspirin is withheld for 24 h after a lytic, and aspirin alone would deny him an effective reperfusion therapy. B: lysing at BP >185/110 increases hemorrhagic transformation. D: a target of <140/90 is unnecessarily aggressive and may extend the infarct. E: permissive hypertension (treat only >220/120) applies to patients not receiving reperfusion therapy.

stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman went to bed feeling well at 10 PM and awoke at 6 AM with left hemiplegia and neglect. She arrives at the ED at 9 AM. NIHSS is 17. Noncontrast CT shows no hemorrhage; ASPECTS is 8. CT angiography shows occlusion of the right middle cerebral artery M1 segment. CT perfusion shows an ischemic core of 15 mL with a large surrounding penumbra (mismatch volume 110 mL). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: IV alteplase as the sole reperfusion therapy

options.label: D
options.html: MRI to look for DWI–FLAIR mismatch before deciding on any therapy

answerHtml: Answer: E. Mechanical thrombectomy
explanationHtml: Last known well was 11 h ago (bedtime), so she is beyond the 4.5-h thrombolysis window. She has an anterior-circulation LVO, a small core and a large penumbra, which meets DAWN/DEFUSE-3–type criteria. Thrombectomy is recommended up to 24 h from LKW in such patients and produces large reductions in disability.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: she is outside the standard lytic window, and a lytic alone is inferior for M1 occlusion. Extended-window lysis before thrombectomy has not been shown to add benefit (TIMELESS). B and C: antithrombotics do not reperfuse an M1 occlusion, and heparin has no role in acute stroke. D: DWI–FLAIR mismatch MRI selects unknown-onset patients for thrombolysis when no LVO is being treated. Here thrombectomy eligibility is already established, and delay costs brain tissue.

stemHtml: A 55-year-old man presents 7 hours after the onset of clumsiness of his left hand. Examination shows mild left hand incoordination; NIHSS is 2. MRI shows a small acute right subcortical infarct. CTA shows no large-vessel occlusion and no significant carotid stenosis. ECG shows sinus rhythm. LDL is 142 mg/dL. In addition to starting a high-intensity statin, which of the following is the most appropriate antithrombotic regimen?

options.label: A
options.html: Aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days, followed by single antiplatelet therapy

options.label: C
options.html: Warfarin with a target INR of 2–3

options.label: E
options.html: No antithrombotic therapy for 2 weeks to avoid hemorrhagic transformation

answerHtml: Answer: A. Short-term DAPT, then a single agent
explanationHtml: A minor non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke (NIHSS ≤3) or high-risk TIA has a high early recurrence risk. Aspirin + clopidogrel started within 24 h of symptom onset and continued for 21 days (CHANCE/POINT) lowers recurrent stroke. After that, single antiplatelet therapy continues long term, because prolonged DAPT increases bleeding without added benefit.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: he is outside the 4.5-h window, and lysis is not recommended for minor non-disabling deficits. C: anticoagulation is for cardioembolic sources such as AF, not small-vessel disease. D: indefinite DAPT increases major bleeding (MATCH, CHARISMA). E: antiplatelet therapy should start promptly; small infarcts carry minimal hemorrhagic-transformation risk.

stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman has a 30-minute episode of right arm weakness and aphasia that fully resolves. MRI shows no infarct. ECG shows atrial fibrillation, which is new. She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Creatinine clearance is 68 mL/min. She has no history of bleeding and no valvular disease on echocardiography. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term therapy to prevent stroke?

options.label: C
options.html: Warfarin with a target INR of 3–4

options.label: E
options.html: Percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion as first-line therapy

answerHtml: Answer: D. Apixaban
explanationHtml: TIA with nonvalvular AF: her CHA2DS2-VASc is 6 (hypertension 1, diabetes 1, stroke/TIA 2, age 65–74 1, female sex 1). Oral anticoagulation is indicated. DOACs are preferred over warfarin in nonvalvular AF because they cause less intracranial hemorrhage and are at least as effective.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B: antiplatelets are markedly inferior to anticoagulation for AF-related embolism, and DAPT bleeds about as much as a DOAC. C: the AF target INR is 2–3, and 3–4 increases bleeding. E: LAA occlusion is reserved for patients who cannot take long-term anticoagulation.

stemHtml: A 66-year-old man had two episodes of transient monocular vision loss in the left eye ("a curtain coming down") and one 20-minute episode of right hand weakness over the past 5 days. Neurologic exam is now normal. Carotid duplex and CTA show 80% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery and 30% stenosis of the right. He is a good surgical candidate. He has been started on aspirin and atorvastatin 80 mg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Left carotid endarterectomy within the next 2 weeks

options.label: E
options.html: Continue medical therapy and operate only if symptoms recur

answerHtml: Answer: B. Left CEA within 2 weeks
explanationHtml: Amaurosis fugax and hand weakness are left carotid territory symptoms. Symptomatic 70–99% stenosis is a clear indication for carotid endarterectomy. Benefit is greatest when surgery is done early, ideally within 2 weeks of the event, because recurrence risk is front-loaded.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and E: delaying exposes him to a high early stroke risk. C: the 30% asymptomatic right-sided stenosis does not need surgery. D: anticoagulation is not superior to antiplatelets for atherosclerotic carotid disease.

stemHtml: A 28-year-old man with known epilepsy is brought in by EMS with a generalized tonic-clonic seizure that has lasted 12 minutes. He has received IV lorazepam 4 mg twice, 5 minutes apart, and continues to convulse. Oxygen saturation is 95% on a nonrebreather mask, and his airway is maintained with positioning. Fingerstick glucose is 96 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: A third dose of IV lorazepam 4 mg

options.label: C
options.html: Rapid-sequence intubation and continuous propofol infusion

answerHtml: Answer: B. IV levetiracetam (second-line agent)
explanationHtml: This is established status epilepticus that has failed two adequate benzodiazepine doses. The next phase is a single second-line IV antiseizure medication. Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg and valproate 40 mg/kg were equally effective in ESETT.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: further benzodiazepines beyond two doses add respiratory depression with little efficacy. C: anesthetic infusions are for refractory status, after a second-line agent fails. His oxygenation is currently adequate, though intubation for airway failure is always allowed. D: oral drugs cannot be given to a convulsing patient and absorb too slowly. E: imaging comes after seizure control.

stemHtml: Paramedics arrive at the home of a 35-year-old woman (weight 62 kg) who has been having a generalized convulsion for 7 minutes. Two attempts at IV access fail. Glucose is 110 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: D
options.html: Wait until IV access is obtained in the hospital before giving any medication

answerHtml: Answer: A. IM midazolam 10 mg
explanationHtml: In prehospital status epilepticus without IV access, IM midazolam (10 mg for >40 kg) is at least as effective as IV lorazepam and is faster to give (RAMPART). Intranasal or buccal midazolam and rectal diazepam are alternatives.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: IM phenytoin is erratically absorbed and causes tissue injury. C: she cannot swallow, and an oral agent acts too slowly. D: every minute of delay makes status harder to stop. E: there is no evidence of opioid toxicity, and naloxone does not stop seizures.

stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman comes to the ED because of a headache that began abruptly 9 hours ago while she was lifting a box. She describes it as "the worst headache of my life," reaching maximal intensity within a minute. She vomited twice. Temperature is 37.0 °C, BP 148/88 mm Hg. Neurologic exam, including fundoscopy, is normal, and there is mild neck stiffness. Noncontrast head CT is read as normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Discharge with an NSAID and neurology follow-up

answerHtml: Answer: E. Lumbar puncture
explanationHtml: A thunderclap headache is SAH until proven otherwise. CT is nearly 100% sensitive only within 6 h of onset. At 9 h a normal CT does not exclude SAH, so perform an LP looking for xanthochromia or a non-clearing RBC count. CTA is an acceptable alternative strategy. If either is positive, get angiography to find the aneurysm.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and C: they miss a possible sentinel bleed, which carries a high risk of catastrophic rebleeding. B: triptans are contraindicated until SAH and RCVS are excluded, because they are vasoconstrictors. D: CT sensitivity falls with time, so a delayed repeat is less useful.

stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman has a 3-week history of new right temporal headache, scalp tenderness when brushing her hair, pain in her jaw when chewing, and morning shoulder stiffness. Visual acuity is normal bilaterally. The right temporal artery is tender with reduced pulsation. ESR is 88 mm/h and CRP 6.2 mg/dL. Temporal artery biopsy can be scheduled in 5 days. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Await biopsy results before starting treatment

options.label: B
options.html: Temporal artery ultrasound and treat only if a halo sign is present

answerHtml: Answer: D. Start high-dose glucocorticoids now
explanationHtml: Giant cell arteritis threatens irreversible blindness from anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. When clinical suspicion is high, start prednisone (40–60 mg/day) immediately. The biopsy remains diagnostic for at least 1–2 weeks after steroids begin. With visual loss, IV methylprednisolone pulses are used.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B: confirming the diagnosis should not delay treatment. C: NSAIDs do not prevent ischemic complications. E: tocilizumab is a steroid-sparing adjunct, not a replacement for initial glucocorticoids.

stemHtml: A 34-year-old man is admitted with 4 days of tingling in his feet and progressive leg weakness that has ascended to his arms. Two weeks ago he had bloody diarrhea. He has absent reflexes throughout. CSF shows protein 160 mg/dL and 2 WBCs/µL. On hospital day 2, he cannot count to 20 in one breath. Forced vital capacity has fallen from 30 to 14 mL/kg, and negative inspiratory force is −22 cm H2O. Oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Begin IV immunoglobulin and continue monitoring on the general ward

options.label: C
options.html: Elective endotracheal intubation in the ICU

options.label: E
options.html: Repeat lumbar puncture to confirm the diagnosis

answerHtml: Answer: C. Elective intubation in the ICU
explanationHtml: Guillain-Barré syndrome (post-Campylobacter, albuminocytologic dissociation) causes neuromuscular respiratory failure. Normal oxygen saturation is falsely reassuring, because hypoxemia appears late. FVC <20 mL/kg and NIF weaker than −30 cm H2O (here −22) are indications for elective intubation before crisis. IVIG or plasma exchange should also be given, but the airway comes first.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: IVIG is indicated, but leaving this patient on the ward risks a respiratory arrest. B: corticosteroids are ineffective in GBS. D: pyridostigmine treats myasthenia gravis, not demyelinating neuropathy. E: the diagnosis is already supported, and repeat LP delays airway protection.

stemHtml: A 39-year-old woman with generalized acetylcholine receptor antibody–positive myasthenia gravis, maintained on pyridostigmine, was prescribed ciprofloxacin for cystitis 3 days ago. She now has worsening ptosis, nasal speech, difficulty swallowing secretions, and dyspnea. FVC is 1.0 L (16 mL/kg). She is intubated in the ICU, and ciprofloxacin is stopped. Which of the following is the most appropriate disease-directed therapy?

options.label: D
options.html: High-dose prednisone as the sole immunotherapy

answerHtml: Answer: A. Plasma exchange
explanationHtml: This is myasthenic crisis triggered by a fluoroquinolone. Rapid-acting immunotherapy, either plasma exchange or IVIG, is the treatment. PLEX works slightly faster and is often preferred in crisis. Corticosteroids are usually started at the same time for durable control.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors are usually held during crisis while intubated, because they increase secretions, and higher doses risk cholinergic weakness. C: thymectomy is elective, done once the patient is stable. D: high-dose steroids alone can transiently worsen weakness and act over weeks. E: rituximab is a slow-onset maintenance option, mainly for MuSK-positive disease.

stemHtml: A 70-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer has 3 weeks of thoracic back pain that is worse when lying down. Since yesterday he has had difficulty walking and has not urinated since this morning. Examination shows 3/5 strength in both legs, brisk patellar reflexes, bilateral extensor plantar responses, and decreased sensation below the umbilicus. Bladder scan shows 800 mL. While an emergent MRI is being arranged, which of the following should be administered immediately?

options.label: D
options.html: Empiric radiation therapy to the lumbar spine before imaging

answerHtml: Answer: E. IV dexamethasone
explanationHtml: A sensory level at T10 with upper motor neuron signs and urinary retention in a patient with cancer indicates malignant epidural spinal cord compression. High-dose IV dexamethasone reduces vasogenic edema and preserves function. It should be given without waiting for imaging. Next come emergent MRI of the whole spine and definitive radiation and/or surgical decompression. Place a Foley catheter as well.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: analgesia alone does nothing for cord edema. B: there is no evidence of infection such as an epidural abscess. C: androgen deprivation is part of prostate cancer therapy, but its effect is too slow for an emergency. D: radiation needs imaging to define the level, and the exam suggests a thoracic lesion.

stemHtml: A 22-year-old man is in the ICU 3 days after a severe traumatic brain injury with massive cerebral edema. He has received no sedatives or paralytics for 48 hours, and toxicology is negative. On examination he has no response to noxious stimuli, fixed pupils, and absent corneal, oculocephalic, cough and gag reflexes. Core temperature is 34.2 °C, BP 112/70 mm Hg on low-dose norepinephrine, and serum sodium 141 mEq/L. The family asks whether he has died. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in determining death by neurologic criteria?

options.label: B
options.html: Declare brain death on the basis of the current examination

options.label: C
options.html: Warm the patient to a core temperature of at least 36 °C

options.label: D
options.html: Obtain the family's consent before performing apnea testing

options.label: E
options.html: Obtain an EEG as the required confirmatory test

answerHtml: Answer: C. Correct hypothermia first
explanationHtml: Before the brain-death exam and apnea test, confounders must be excluded. Under the 2023 consensus guideline, core temperature must be ≥36 °C, because hypothermia can depress brainstem reflexes. His BP (SBP ≥100) and electrolytes are acceptable.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B: the exam is invalid while he is hypothermic. D: family consent is not required to determine death, though families should be informed and supported. E: ancillary tests are needed only when the exam or apnea test cannot be completed, and EEG is not the preferred ancillary test in adults (blood-flow studies are).

stemHtml: A 76-year-old man with an 8-year history of Parkinson disease, treated only with carbidopa-levodopa, has had 2 months of vivid visual hallucinations of people in his house and a belief that his wife is stealing from him. These are distressing him. Urinalysis, CBC, metabolic panel and medication review show no other cause, and he has no delirium. Lowering the levodopa dose last month worsened his rigidity and falls. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Pimavanserin
explanationHtml: Parkinson disease psychosis that persists after excluding delirium and minimizing dopaminergic and anticholinergic drugs is treated with pimavanserin. It is a 5-HT2A inverse agonist without D2 blockade and is FDA-approved for PD psychosis. Low-dose quetiapine or clozapine are alternatives.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B: potent D2 blockade severely worsens parkinsonism. Antipsychotics also carry an increased-mortality warning in elderly patients, so the least harmful agent should be chosen. C: metoclopramide is a D2 antagonist antiemetic, contraindicated in PD. E: dopamine agonists worsen hallucinations.

stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman has 6 weeks of low mood, fatigue, poor concentration, and loss of interest in her hobbies. PHQ-9 is 16. She denies suicidal ideation and has never had manic symptoms. She smokes 1 pack per day and wants to quit. She stopped a previous SSRI because of sexual dysfunction and is worried about weight gain. She has no history of seizures, head trauma, or eating disorders. Which of the following is the most appropriate medication?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Bupropion
explanationHtml: Bupropion is a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor. It is effective for MDD, causes little sexual dysfunction, is weight-neutral or causes weight loss, and is FDA-approved for smoking cessation. It fits all three of her priorities. Its main contraindications are seizure disorders and bulimia or anorexia, because it lowers the seizure threshold.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: paroxetine has the most sexual dysfunction and weight gain among SSRIs. C: mirtazapine causes weight gain. D: MAOIs are reserved for refractory cases because of dietary and drug interactions. E: venlafaxine (SNRI) causes sexual dysfunction similar to SSRIs.

stemHtml: A 70-year-old widow is brought in by her son. For 6 weeks she has been withdrawn and tearful and has lost 7 kg. For the last 5 days she has refused all food and most fluids, stating that her "intestines have rotted away" and that she deserves to die. BP is 98/60 mm Hg, HR 108/min; creatinine has risen from 0.8 to 1.9 mg/dL. She is admitted and IV fluids are started. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive treatment?

options.label: B
options.html: Sertraline plus olanzapine, with reassessment in 6 weeks

answerHtml: Answer: A. ECT
explanationHtml: She has major depression with psychotic features (mood-congruent nihilistic delusions) and life-threatening refusal of food and fluids, with AKI. ECT is the most effective and fastest-acting treatment, with response often within 1–2 weeks. It is first-line for psychotic depression with medical compromise, catatonia, or acute suicidality, and it is safe in the elderly.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: antidepressant + antipsychotic is the pharmacologic option for psychotic depression, but it takes weeks, which she does not have. C: an antidepressant alone is inadequate for psychotic depression. D: outpatient therapy is unsafe. E: lithium is an augmentation agent, not monotherapy for unipolar psychotic depression.

stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium for 10 years. Six weeks ago her PCP started hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension. For 3 days she has had vomiting, diarrhea, and a coarse tremor. Today she is confused and ataxic and had a brief generalized seizure in the ED. Serum lithium is 4.3 mEq/L (therapeutic 0.6–1.2). Creatinine is 1.9 mg/dL (baseline 0.9). Lithium is stopped and IV normal saline is started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Switch to valproate and recheck the lithium level in 24 hours

options.label: D
options.html: Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate as definitive therapy

answerHtml: Answer: E. Hemodialysis
explanationHtml: This is chronic lithium toxicity precipitated by a thiazide (increased proximal reabsorption) and volume loss. Lithium is small, water-soluble and not protein-bound, so dialysis removes it well. EXTRIP recommends hemodialysis when the level is >4.0 mEq/L with impaired kidney function, or when there is a seizure or decreased consciousness at any level. She meets both.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: charcoal does not bind lithium. B: loop diuretics cause volume depletion and can worsen lithium retention. C: switching mood stabilizers does not treat the toxicity. D: SPS has only experimental data and is not definitive therapy.

stemHtml: A 29-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been taking clozapine for 4 months with marked improvement. His baseline ANC was 3,500/µL. A routine ANC today is 850/µL. He is afebrile and has no signs of infection. He has no history of benign ethnic neutropenia. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue clozapine and recheck ANC in 1 week

options.label: B
options.html: Discontinue clozapine permanently; rechallenge is contraindicated

options.label: C
options.html: Interrupt clozapine and monitor ANC daily until it is ≥1,000/µL; resumption may then be considered

options.label: D
options.html: Add filgrastim and continue clozapine at the same dose

answerHtml: Answer: C. Interrupt, monitor daily, consider resuming
explanationHtml: An ANC of 500–999/µL is moderate neutropenia. Clozapine labeling directs interrupting therapy, checking ANC daily until it is ≥1,000/µL, at which point clozapine may be resumed, with ANC three times weekly until ≥1,500/µL and then closer-than-baseline monitoring. Because clozapine is uniquely effective for treatment-resistant illness, abandoning it permanently is avoided when possible. The FDA eliminated the clozapine REMS in 2025; the labeled ANC thresholds still guide management, so the answer does not depend on the REMS.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: continuing is appropriate only for mild neutropenia (1,000–1,499). B: permanent discontinuation is for severe neutropenia (<500), and even then rechallenge may be considered when benefit outweighs risk. D: G-CSF is not standard for asymptomatic moderate neutropenia while continuing the drug. E: he has treatment-resistant illness, so first-generation agents previously failed or are unlikely to work.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old man with schizophrenia was given IM haloperidol for agitation on three consecutive days. He now has temperature 40.2 °C, HR 124/min, and BP fluctuating between 170/100 and 110/60 mm Hg. He is diaphoretic, mute, and confused, with diffuse "lead-pipe" rigidity. Reflexes are diminished, there is no clonus, and pupils are 4 mm and reactive. CK is 14,500 U/L and WBC 15,000/µL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Discontinue haloperidol, begin aggressive cooling and IV fluids in the ICU

options.label: C
options.html: Switch from haloperidol to IM olanzapine

answerHtml: Answer: B. Stop the D2 blocker, supportive ICU care
explanationHtml: This is neuroleptic malignant syndrome: subacute onset after a dopamine antagonist, hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability, altered mental status, very high CK and leukocytosis. The cornerstone is stopping the offending agent, plus active cooling, IV fluids (to protect the kidneys from rhabdomyolysis) and ICU monitoring. Benzodiazepines, dantrolene and bromocriptine are added for moderate–severe cases.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: cyproheptadine treats serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia, rapid onset). C: any antipsychotic can perpetuate NMS. Rechallenge is delayed at least 2 weeks after recovery and uses a low-potency agent. D: anticholinergics treat dystonia and parkinsonism, not NMS. E: the heat comes from muscle, so antipyretics are ineffective, and observation is dangerous.

stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman taking sertraline 150 mg/day is hospitalized for MRSA cellulitis and started on linezolid. Eight hours later she is agitated and tremulous with diarrhea. Temperature is 38.6 °C, HR 122/min, BP 158/94 mm Hg. Pupils are 7 mm, and she has hyperreflexia with sustained inducible ankle clonus that is worse in the lower extremities. Linezolid and sertraline are stopped, and she receives IV lorazepam with supportive care. One hour later she remains agitated with persistent clonus. Which of the following is the most appropriate next pharmacotherapy?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Cyproheptadine
explanationHtml: Linezolid is a weak MAO inhibitor. Combined with an SSRI, it caused serotonin syndrome, which meets Hunter criteria (inducible clonus + agitation + diaphoresis/hyperthermia). When symptoms persist despite stopping the drugs and giving benzodiazepines, the oral 5-HT2A antagonist cyproheptadine is given (12 mg load, then 2 mg every 2 h). If temperature exceeds 41.1 °C, sedation, paralysis with a nondepolarizing agent, and intubation are needed.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia or NMS rigidity. B: bromocriptine is a serotonergic dopamine agonist that can worsen serotonin syndrome and is used for NMS. C: haloperidol has no antiserotonergic benefit, can impair heat dissipation, and risks adding NMS to the picture. E: physostigmine treats anticholinergic toxicity (dry skin, absent bowel sounds), not this.

stemHtml: A 50-year-old man admitted 3 days ago for acute cholecystitis becomes acutely agitated and disoriented. He is pulling at his IV and says insects are crawling on the walls. Temperature is 38.4 °C, HR 128/min, BP 172/100 mm Hg, RR 22/min, and he is drenched in sweat. His wife says he drinks a fifth of vodka daily, and his last drink was the night before admission. He received IV thiamine on admission. Glucose is 112 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Escalating doses of IV benzodiazepine (e.g., diazepam) titrated to light somnolence, in a monitored setting

answerHtml: Answer: A. Aggressive IV benzodiazepines
explanationHtml: Delirium tremens develops about 48–96 h after the last drink. It presents with disorientation, hallucinations, fever and autonomic hyperactivity, and can be fatal. Treatment is rapid escalating IV benzodiazepines in an ICU or step-down unit, plus phenobarbital or propofol for refractory cases, together with thiamine, electrolyte repletion (Mg, K, PO4) and fluids. The fever needs evaluation, but DTs treatment cannot wait.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: antipsychotics alone lower the seizure threshold and do not treat the underlying GABA deficit. They are only adjuncts. C: restraints without sedation increase hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis. D and E: α2 agonists and β-blockers blunt vital signs but mask, rather than prevent, seizures and delirium.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis (ascites, INR 2.0, albumin 2.3 g/dL, bilirubin 4.1 mg/dL) presents 14 hours after his last drink with tremor, anxiety, sweating and nausea. CIWA-Ar score is 17. He is oriented. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent to treat his withdrawal?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Lorazepam
explanationHtml: In severe hepatic impairment, benzodiazepines that need oxidative (CYP) metabolism and have long-acting active metabolites (chlordiazepoxide, diazepam) accumulate and can precipitate prolonged sedation or hepatic encephalopathy. Lorazepam (like oxazepam and temazepam, the "LOT" drugs) undergoes only glucuronidation, which is relatively preserved in cirrhosis, and has no active metabolites.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B: long-acting agents are preferred in withdrawal except in liver disease or the elderly. D: alprazolam is short-acting and CYP3A4-metabolized, with rebound and abuse potential, and is not used for alcohol withdrawal. E: clonazepam is CYP-metabolized and long-acting.

stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman, G1P0 at 14 weeks' gestation, presents for prenatal care. She has injected heroin, now mixed with fentanyl, daily for 2 years and wants help to stop. She is in mild withdrawal. Hepatitis C antibody is positive; HIV is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for her opioid use disorder?

options.label: C
options.html: Abrupt cessation with counseling and Narcotics Anonymous

answerHtml: Answer: E. Buprenorphine
explanationHtml: ACOG and SAMHSA recommend opioid agonist therapy (buprenorphine or methadone) for OUD in pregnancy. It reduces relapse, overdose, infections and obstetric complications such as preterm birth and fetal withdrawal in utero. Buprenorphine causes a less severe neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome than methadone and can be prescribed in the office. She should also get naloxone, and hepatitis C treatment can be offered after delivery.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, C and D: withdrawal-based approaches have high relapse rates, and relapse raises overdose and fetal risk. B: naltrexone requires opioid abstinence, and data on starting it during pregnancy are limited, so it is not the first-line choice.

stemHtml: A 17-year-old girl with anorexia nervosa (BMI 13.8 kg/m², HR 42/min) is admitted for medical stabilization. Nutrition is started by nasogastric tube. On hospital day 3 she develops generalized weakness, confusion, dyspnea, bilateral leg edema, and new ventricular ectopy on telemetry. Which of the following laboratory abnormalities is most likely responsible?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Hypophosphatemia
explanationHtml: This is refeeding syndrome. Carbohydrate stimulates insulin, which drives phosphate (along with K and Mg) into cells for glycolysis and ATP synthesis, on top of depleted total-body stores. Severe hypophosphatemia depletes ATP and 2,3-BPG, causing muscle weakness, respiratory failure, heart failure (with sodium and water retention producing edema), arrhythmias and delirium. Prevention: check electrolytes before and daily during feeding, replete phosphate, potassium and magnesium, give thiamine, and use telemetry.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, C, D, E: refeeding drives low potassium and magnesium, not high levels. Calcium is not the hallmark disturbance, and insulin-mediated sodium retention causes edema, not hypernatremia.

stemHtml: A 5-year-old boy is evaluated because his preschool teachers and parents report that for the past year he cannot sit for circle time, runs around constantly, interrupts others, and does not finish tasks. Vanderbilt rating scales from both settings meet criteria for ADHD, combined presentation. Hearing, vision and development are otherwise normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Parent training in behavior management (PTBM)
explanationHtml: The AAP guideline recommends evidence-based behavioral therapy, specifically parent training and classroom interventions, as first-line treatment for preschool children aged 4–5 with ADHD. Methylphenidate is added if behavioral treatment does not produce significant improvement and functional impairment remains moderate–severe. For age 6 and older, medication plus behavioral therapy is first-line.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: methylphenidate is the medication of choice in preschoolers, but only after a trial of PTBM. B and C: nonstimulants are second-line and have less evidence in preschoolers. E: amphetamines are not preferred in this age group.

stemHtml: A 30-year-old Army veteran was sexually assaulted 5 months ago. Since then she has had intrusive memories, nightmares, avoidance of crowded places, feeling detached from her family, irritability, and exaggerated startle. She is not suicidal and does not use alcohol or drugs. She asks for the treatment "with the best evidence." Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Cognitive processing therapy
explanationHtml: Symptoms lasting more than 1 month across all four clusters (intrusion, avoidance, negative cognition/mood, hyperarousal) mean PTSD. VA/DoD and APA guidelines give the strongest recommendation to trauma-focused psychotherapies: cognitive processing therapy, prolonged exposure and EMDR. SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) or venlafaxine are alternatives or adjuncts.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: benzodiazepines are not recommended in PTSD. They may worsen outcomes and interfere with extinction learning, and they risk dependence. B: prazosin has mixed evidence for nightmares and does not treat the core disorder. C: antipsychotic monotherapy is not recommended. D: single-session debriefing does not prevent PTSD and may increase symptoms.

stemHtml: A 27-year-old man with bipolar I disorder, who had a manic episode requiring hospitalization 2 years ago, now has 4 weeks of depressed mood, hypersomnia, hopelessness and anhedonia. He has no psychotic symptoms and no suicidal plan. He stopped all medications a year ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Quetiapine
explanationHtml: FDA-approved treatments for bipolar depression are quetiapine, lurasidone, lumateperone, cariprazine and olanzapine-fluoxetine. Quetiapine has evidence for both depressive and manic poles and for maintenance. Lithium or lamotrigine are also used, particularly for maintenance.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B–E: antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar I disorder can precipitate mania or mixed states and rapid cycling, and it has not proven effective. If an antidepressant is used at all, it must be combined with a mood stabilizer. Venlafaxine carries the highest switch risk.

stemHtml: A 45-year-old man is brought to the ED by his sister after he texted her a goodbye message. He recently lost his job and divorced. He says he plans to shoot himself tonight with the handgun in his apartment, and that "nothing will change my mind." He is not intoxicated, is oriented, and has no psychotic symptoms. He refuses admission and asks to leave. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Discharge with a written safety plan and outpatient follow-up in 1 week

options.label: B
options.html: Initiate an involuntary emergency psychiatric hold

options.label: C
options.html: Have him sign a no-suicide contract before discharge

options.label: D
options.html: Start sertraline and arrange follow-up in 2 weeks

options.label: E
options.html: Ask his sister to remove the firearm, then discharge him home

answerHtml: Answer: B. Involuntary emergency hold
explanationHtml: He has high imminent suicide risk: a specific plan, access to a lethal means (a firearm), stated intent, and several risk factors (male sex, recent losses). He refuses voluntary care, and he poses a danger to himself due to a mental illness, which meets criteria for an emergency involuntary hold in every state. Capacity to refuse does not override this statutory exception when there is imminent danger from a psychiatric condition.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and D: outpatient care is appropriate only for low risk. C: no-suicide contracts have no proven protective value. E: means restriction is important, but removing one firearm does not make this high-intent patient safe to discharge.

stemHtml: A 54-year-old man with decompensated alcohol-associated cirrhosis (ascites, bilirubin 3.8 mg/dL, INR 1.9) completed inpatient alcohol withdrawal management 10 days ago and has remained abstinent. Creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL. He asks for a medication to help prevent relapse. He has no opioid use. Which of the following is the most appropriate medication?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Acamprosate
explanationHtml: Acamprosate modulates glutamate/NMDA signaling. It is renally excreted and not hepatically metabolized, so it is safe in advanced liver disease provided renal function is adequate (avoid if CrCl ≤30). Baclofen is another option studied in cirrhosis.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: disulfiram is hepatotoxic and the disulfiram–alcohol reaction is dangerous in cirrhosis. B: naltrexone is generally avoided in decompensated liver disease and acute hepatitis because of hepatotoxicity concerns, and it would complicate opioid analgesia. C: chronic benzodiazepines cause dependence and hepatic encephalopathy. E: methadone treats opioid, not alcohol, use disorder.

stemHtml: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has wet gangrene of the right foot. The surgeon recommends below-knee amputation and explains that without it he will likely develop sepsis and could die. Over 2 days of discussion he consistently refuses. He accurately restates the risks and says, "I know I might die, but I have lived with my body intact and I will not lose my leg." He is alert and oriented, with no depression, delirium or psychosis. His wife urges the team to "do the surgery anyway." Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.label: A
options.html: Obtain a psychiatric consultation to declare him incompetent

options.label: B
options.html: Petition the court for authorization to operate

options.label: C
options.html: Respect his refusal, continue antibiotics and other care, and keep the discussion open

options.label: D
options.html: Obtain surgical consent from his wife

options.label: E
options.html: Perform surgery under the emergency exception once he becomes septic

answerHtml: Answer: C. Respect the informed refusal
explanationHtml: He shows all four elements of capacity: he communicates a consistent choice, understands the information, appreciates the consequences for himself, and reasons according to his values. An adult with capacity may refuse even life-saving treatment. The team should continue all other indicated care, address his fears, offer palliative support, and periodically revisit the decision, documenting carefully.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: disagreeing with medical advice is not incapacity, and competence is a legal, not psychiatric, determination. B: there is no legal basis to override a capacitated adult. D: surrogates decide only when the patient lacks capacity. E: if he later loses capacity, his previously expressed, informed refusal still guides care. The emergency exception cannot override a known refusal.

stemHtml: An 80-year-old widow has a large left-hemispheric stroke with global aphasia and lacks decision-making capacity. Two years ago she completed a durable power of attorney for health care naming her niece as her agent, and told her physician she "never wanted to be kept alive on machines." The niece requests transition to comfort care. The patient's son, who lives out of state, insists on intubation and a feeding tube. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.html: Follow the son's wishes, because he is the closest blood relative

options.label: B
options.html: Have the ethics committee make the treatment decision

options.label: C
options.html: Petition for a court-appointed guardian before any decision is made

options.label: D
options.html: Follow the physician's own judgment of the patient's best interests

options.label: E
options.html: Follow the niece's decision as the patient's designated health care agent

answerHtml: Answer: E. Follow the designated agent
explanationHtml: A health care agent named in a valid DPOA-HC outranks all relatives in the surrogate hierarchy. Here the agent's request also matches the patient's documented wishes (substituted judgment). The team should still meet with the son, empathize, explain the patient's prior wishes, and offer palliative care and chaplaincy support. An ethics consult can help with mediation but does not take the decision away from the agent.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: next-of-kin status matters only when no agent exists. B: ethics committees advise and mediate; they do not decide. C: a guardian is unnecessary when a valid agent is available. D: a best-interests standard applies only when the patient's wishes are unknown and no surrogate is available.

stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl comes to the clinic alone and requests oral contraceptive pills. She has been sexually active with one partner and uses condoms inconsistently. She asks that her parents not be told. Her BP is 112/70 mm Hg, and she has no history of migraine with aura or thromboembolism. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Prescribe contraception, counsel on condom use for STI prevention, and keep the visit confidential

options.label: B
options.html: Tell her that parental consent is required before contraception can be prescribed

options.label: C
options.html: Prescribe contraception but inform her parents because she is a minor

options.label: D
options.html: Require a pelvic examination before prescribing

options.label: E
options.html: Advise abstinence and schedule a family meeting

answerHtml: Answer: A. Provide confidential contraceptive care
explanationHtml: In most US states, and under Title X–funded programs, minors may consent to contraception and STI care without parental involvement. The AAP and ACOG support confidential adolescent reproductive care because requiring parental notification deters teens from seeking care and increases unintended pregnancy. Offer chlamydia/gonorrhea screening (recommended for sexually active females <25), HPV vaccination, and condom counseling. A few states restrict this, but the USMLE answer is confidential care.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B and C: these breach the confidentiality that adolescents are entitled to for reproductive care. D: a pelvic exam is not needed to start hormonal contraception. E: this is moralizing, and abstinence-only counseling is ineffective.

stemHtml: During an outpatient psychotherapy session, a 35-year-old man becomes enraged discussing his ex-girlfriend, who recently obtained a restraining order. He names her and states, "I know where she works. I bought a knife, and tonight I'm going to make her pay." He then leaves the office abruptly before any further assessment. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Document the statement and address it at the next scheduled session

options.label: B
options.html: Maintain confidentiality, because the statement was made in therapy

options.label: C
options.html: Notify the ex-girlfriend and law enforcement

options.label: D
options.html: Call the patient's mother to ask her to watch him

options.label: E
options.html: Report the patient to the state medical board

answerHtml: Answer: C. Warn the identifiable victim and notify police
explanationHtml: Under the Tarasoff doctrine, a credible threat of serious violence against an identifiable person creates a duty to protect. This overrides confidentiality and is satisfied by warning the intended victim and/or notifying police, and seeking hospitalization if the patient can be reached. Details vary by state, but on the exam warning plus police notification is correct.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B: the threat is imminent and specific, so waiting is negligent. D: informing a relative does not protect the victim and is an unnecessary disclosure. E: the medical board licenses physicians and has no role in a patient's threat.

stemHtml: A 41-year-old Spanish-speaking woman with limited English proficiency is returning for results of a breast biopsy that shows invasive ductal carcinoma. Her 11-year-old son, who is fluently bilingual, accompanies her, and she says, "My son always translates for me." The physician speaks basic conversational Spanish. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to communicate the results?

options.label: A
options.html: Use the son as interpreter, since the patient prefers it

options.label: B
options.html: Use a professional medical interpreter (in person, phone or video)

options.label: D
options.html: Ask a nurse who took 2 years of high school Spanish to interpret

options.label: E
options.html: Provide a written Spanish-language handout about breast cancer instead of a discussion

answerHtml: Answer: B. Professional medical interpreter
explanationHtml: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act and Section 1557 of the ACA require meaningful language access. Trained medical interpreters reduce clinically significant errors. Using a child to interpret is especially inappropriate: it burdens the child emotionally, compromises accuracy and the mother's privacy, and distorts family roles, particularly for bad news. Remote video or phone interpreters are acceptable.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: a minor family member should not interpret, except in an emergency when nothing else is available. C and D: limited proficiency leads to errors in a high-stakes conversation. E: written materials supplement a discussion but cannot replace one, and literacy may be limited.

stemHtml: A hospitalized 67-year-old man is mistakenly given 50 mg of metoprolol intended for his roommate. The error is discovered 1 hour later. His HR is 64/min and BP 124/76 mm Hg, and he has no symptoms. Monitoring is planned, and harm is not expected. The attending physician says, "No harm was done, so there is no need to upset him." Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Do not disclose, because no harm resulted

options.label: B
options.html: File an incident report but do not inform the patient

options.label: C
options.html: Disclose the error only if the patient asks about the medication

options.label: D
options.html: Disclose the error to the patient with an apology and explanation, and report it through the safety system

options.label: E
options.html: Inform the patient's family but not the patient

answerHtml: Answer: D. Disclose and report
explanationHtml: Physicians have an ethical duty (AMA Code) to promptly and honestly disclose errors that reach the patient, whether or not harm results. Disclosure should explain what happened, the expected consequences (monitoring), an apology, and steps taken to prevent recurrence. The event should also go into the institution's reporting system so system causes (e.g., lack of barcode scanning) can be analyzed. Transparency preserves trust and lowers litigation risk.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B and C: concealment violates honesty and autonomy. An incident report is necessary but not sufficient. E: disclosing to the family without the patient's permission breaches confidentiality, and the capacitated patient is entitled to know.

stemHtml: A surgical resident arrives in the operating room for a scheduled cholecystectomy. The attending surgeon smells strongly of alcohol, has slurred speech, and fumbles while gowning. The patient is already anesthetized, and the surgeon tells the team to begin. Which of the following is the most appropriate action by the resident?

options.label: A
options.html: Assist with the operation and report the surgeon after the case

options.label: B
options.html: Stop the case from proceeding and immediately notify the chief of surgery or the OR director

options.label: C
options.html: Speak privately with the surgeon next week

options.label: D
options.html: Report the surgeon only to the state medical board

answerHtml: Answer: B. Prevent immediate harm and escalate now
explanationHtml: When an impaired colleague poses an imminent risk to a patient, the first duty is to protect the patient: stop the procedure and immediately involve a supervisor with authority (chief of surgery, department chair, OR medical director) to arrange a replacement surgeon. Later, the surgeon should be referred to the physician health program for evaluation and treatment.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and C: they knowingly expose the patient to danger. D: a board report may follow, but it does not stop the harm in progress. E: law enforcement is not the appropriate first response to a patient-safety issue within the hospital.

stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman comes to the ED with a wrist injury that she says happened when she "fell down the stairs." Examination shows a distal radius fracture and bruises of different ages on her upper arms and neck. Her husband remains in the room, answers questions for her, and declines to leave when asked casually. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Use a standard department policy (e.g., the need for an x-ray or private exam) to see the patient alone and ask directly about her safety

options.label: B
options.html: Report the husband to the police without her consent

options.label: C
options.html: Confront the husband about the suspected abuse

options.label: D
options.html: Accept the explanation and treat the fracture

answerHtml: Answer: A. Interview her alone and screen for IPV
explanationHtml: Bruises of different ages, neck bruising (concerning for strangulation, a lethality marker), an injury that does not fit the story, and a controlling partner all suggest intimate partner violence. The essential step is to speak to her privately, ask directly and non-judgmentally, assess immediate danger, document, and offer resources and safety planning. A competent adult decides whether to report or leave.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: mandatory reporting of adult IPV is not required in most states, apart from specific weapon injuries in some, and reporting against her wishes may increase danger. C: confronting the partner can escalate violence. D: this misses the abuse. E: no children are mentioned; if children are at risk, CPS involvement may be appropriate.

stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the ED after a bicycle crash. He is pale and confused, with HR 160/min and BP 70/40 mm Hg. FAST examination shows a large hemoperitoneum consistent with splenic rupture. He is not responding to crystalloid boluses. His parents, who are Jehovah's Witnesses, refuse blood transfusion on his behalf. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Obtain a court order before giving any blood products

options.label: B
options.html: Respect the parents' refusal and continue crystalloids

options.label: C
options.html: Request an ethics consultation and await its recommendation

options.label: D
options.html: Give additional crystalloid and albumin only

answerHtml: Answer: E. Transfuse immediately
explanationHtml: Parents may not refuse life-saving treatment for their minor child on religious grounds, under the "best interest" standard. In an emergency where delay would risk death or serious harm, the physician should transfuse without waiting for legal authorization. Use blood-conservation strategies where possible and treat the family respectfully. For non-emergent situations, such as planned chemotherapy, a court order is obtained.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and C: both waste time a child in hemorrhagic shock does not have, though they are appropriate in non-urgent conflicts. B and D: refusing to transfuse lets a child die from a treatable condition and does not restore oxygen-carrying capacity.

stemHtml: A new serum test for a disease is evaluated in 1,000 people, 100 of whom have the disease by the gold standard. The test has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 80%. A patient from this population tests positive. Which of the following is the approximate probability that she has the disease?
answerHtml: Answer: D. 33%
explanationHtml: The question asks for PPV. Diseased = 100, so TP = 90 and FN = 10. Non-diseased = 900; specificity 80% gives TN = 720 and FP = 180. PPV = TP/(TP+FP) = 90/270 ≈ 33%. At a low prevalence (10%), even a good test produces many false positives.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: 10% is the prevalence (pre-test probability). B: 80% is the specificity. C: 90% is the sensitivity. E: about 99% is the NPV (720/730 ≈ 98.6%).

stemHtml: A pharmaceutical advertisement for a new lipid-lowering drug states: "Reduces heart attacks by 40%!" The footnote reports a 5-year randomized trial in which myocardial infarction occurred in 5.0% of the placebo group and 3.0% of the drug group (p < 0.001). How many patients must be treated for 5 years to prevent one myocardial infarction?
answerHtml: Answer: C. 50
explanationHtml: ARR = 5.0% − 3.0% = 2.0% (0.02). NNT = 1/ARR = 1/0.02 = 50 over 5 years. The headline "40%" is the relative risk reduction (2/5). Relative figures make benefits look larger. On CK, always convert to absolute measures before counseling patients.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: 2 is the ARR expressed as a percentage, not the NNT. B: 25 would correspond to an ARR of 4%. D: 40 is the RRR percentage. E: 100 would correspond to an ARR of 1%.

stemHtml: A rapid antigen test for a viral infection was validated in a specialty clinic where the prevalence was 40%. A primary care network plans to use the same test, with the same cutoff, to screen asymptomatic adults in a community where the prevalence is 2%. Compared with its performance in the specialty clinic, which of the following changes in the test's characteristics is expected in the community?

options.label: E
options.html: Positive predictive value decreases and negative predictive value increases

answerHtml: Answer: E. PPV falls, NPV rises
explanationHtml: Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test at a given cutoff and do not depend on prevalence (assuming similar disease spectrum). Predictive values do depend on prevalence. When prevalence falls, false positives make up a larger share of positive results (PPV ↓), and negative results become even more reliable (NPV ↑). This is why screening low-risk populations yields many false positives.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B: intrinsic test characteristics are unchanged by prevalence alone. Spectrum bias could alter them, but that is not what is described. C and D: these are the opposite of the actual effect of lower prevalence.

stemHtml: A health system introduces annual screening with a new imaging test for pancreatic cancer in high-risk adults. Over 10 years, median survival measured from the date of diagnosis increases from 1.0 to 2.5 years in screened patients compared with historical controls. However, the stage and growth rate of screen-detected tumors are similar to those of symptomatic tumors, and the age at death from pancreatic cancer and the disease-specific mortality rate are unchanged. Which of the following best explains the apparent survival benefit?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Lead-time bias
explanationHtml: Screening moves the date of diagnosis earlier without changing the date of death. This lengthens measured survival from diagnosis while mortality is unchanged. The way to avoid lead-time bias is to compare mortality rates between randomized screened and unscreened groups.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: selection bias (e.g., healthier volunteers) would not explain longer survival from diagnosis with an unchanged age at death and unchanged mortality. C: length-time bias requires screening to preferentially detect slower-growing tumors, but tumor biology was similar. D: recall bias affects retrospective exposure history in case-control studies. E: the Hawthorne effect is behavior change from being observed.

stemHtml: An abstract of a randomized controlled trial of a new SGLT2 inhibitor versus placebo in patients with heart failure reports that the primary composite outcome of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization occurred in 18.2% vs 20.8% of patients (hazard ratio 0.86; 95% CI, 0.72–1.02; p = 0.09). The sponsor's press release states that the drug "reduced the risk of death or hospitalization by 14%." Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation?

options.label: A
options.html: The trial did not demonstrate a statistically significant difference in the primary outcome

options.label: B
options.html: The drug has been proven to reduce the primary outcome by 14%

options.label: C
options.html: The drug increases the risk of the primary outcome

options.label: D
options.html: The trial proves the drug is equivalent to placebo

options.label: E
options.html: There is a 9% probability that the drug is effective

answerHtml: Answer: A. Not statistically significant
explanationHtml: For a ratio measure, a 95% CI that includes 1.0 (0.72–1.02), with p > 0.05, means the null hypothesis of no difference cannot be rejected. The point estimate suggests possible benefit, but the trial may have been underpowered. The press release misleadingly presents a non-significant relative reduction as a proven effect.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B: a non-significant point estimate is not proof. C: the HR is below 1, so the estimate leans toward benefit, not harm. D: failing to show a difference is not proof of equivalence, which requires a prespecified equivalence or non-inferiority design. E: the p-value is the probability of data this extreme if the null were true, not the probability that the drug works.

stemHtml: An 82-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation and an eGFR of 25 mL/min/1.73 m² asks about a newly approved anticoagulant she saw advertised on television. The advertisement cites a large, well-conducted, double-blind randomized trial showing fewer strokes and fewer major bleeds than warfarin. The trial's exclusion criteria included age >75 years and eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m². Which of the following is the most important limitation of applying these results to this patient?

options.label: B
options.html: The trial results are confounded by indication

options.label: C
options.html: The results may not be generalizable to her (limited external validity)

options.label: D
options.html: The trial has a high risk of recall bias

options.label: E
options.html: The trial likely has a type I error

answerHtml: Answer: C. Limited external validity
explanationHtml: A well-designed, randomized, blinded trial can have excellent internal validity yet not apply to patients outside its eligibility criteria. She would have been excluded on two counts (age and renal function), and both strongly affect bleeding risk and drug clearance. So the benefit–risk balance shown may not hold for her. Checking whether "my patient would have been enrolled" is a core CK skill for reading drug ads.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A: nothing suggests flawed randomization, blinding or follow-up. B: randomization eliminates confounding by indication. D: recall bias is a case-control problem. E: there is no reason to suspect a false-positive result in a large trial with consistent findings.

stemHtml: A hospital performs a root cause analysis after a wrong-side knee arthroscopy. Contributing factors included an unmarked operative site, a consent form that listed the side in an abbreviation, a rushed time-out during a busy schedule, and a surgeon who began before the circulating nurse had completed verification. Each team member assumed someone else had confirmed the side. Which of the following interventions would be the most effective at preventing recurrence?

options.label: A
options.html: Mandatory re-education of the operating room staff on the Universal Protocol

options.label: C
options.html: An email reminder to all surgeons to perform careful time-outs

options.label: D
options.html: A hard-stop system in which instruments are not released and incision cannot proceed until the site is marked and the time-out is documented as complete

options.label: E
options.html: Hiring additional OR nurses to reduce workload

answerHtml: Answer: D. Forcing function (hard stop)
explanationHtml: This is the Swiss cheese model in action: several defensive layers (marking, consent, time-out, verification) failed and the holes lined up. In the hierarchy of safety interventions, forcing functions and physical constraints are strongest, because they make the error impossible or very difficult regardless of vigilance. Standardization and checklists come next. Education, reminders and policies are weakest because they depend on human memory and attention.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and C: they rely on memory and fade quickly. B: blame-focused responses contradict just culture and discourage reporting. They do not fix the latent system flaws. E: staffing may help with workload but does not directly block the specific failure.
tags: Patient safety – RCA / Swiss cheese / forcing functions

stemHtml: A 62-year-old man comes to the emergency department 40 minutes after the onset of crushing substernal chest pain with diaphoresis. He was given sublingual nitroglycerin by paramedics, after which he became lightheaded. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 52/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Jugular venous pressure is elevated to 12 cm H<sub>2</sub>O. The lungs are clear to auscultation. ECG shows 3-mm ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF, with ST elevation in right-sided lead V4R. The cardiac catheterization team has been activated. In addition to aspirin, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Intravenous 0.9% saline bolus
explanationHtml: Inferior STEMI with ST elevation in V4R, hypotension, a raised JVP, and clear lungs is right ventricular infarction. A failing RV depends on preload to fill the left heart, so hypotension is treated with an IV fluid bolus while the patient goes for emergent PCI. If he stays hypotensive after adequate fluids, an inotrope (dobutamine) is added.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, nitrates lower preload and caused his collapse; they are contraindicated in RV infarction. B, diuretics also lower preload and make the hypotension worse. D, a beta-blocker is contraindicated with hypotension, bradycardia, and signs of shock. E, morphine causes venodilation and lowers preload. It is avoided here.

stemHtml:
A 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes for follow-up. She takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily. Two years ago, she was diagnosed with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (ejection fraction 35%) and takes sacubitril-valsartan, carvedilol, and spironolactone. She has no history of genital infections or ketoacidosis. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg and BMI is 29 kg/m2. Laboratory studies show:
TestResult
Hemoglobin A1c8.3%
Creatinine1.1 mg/dL
eGFR55 mL/min/1.73 m2
Potassium4.4 mEq/L
Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio40 mg/g
Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to her regimen?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Empagliflozin
explanationHtml: The ADA Standards of Care recommend an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven benefit for any patient with type 2 diabetes and heart failure (HFrEF or HFpEF) or CKD, whatever the A1c. SGLT2 inhibitors reduce heart failure hospitalization and cardiovascular death, and they slow CKD progression (she has albuminuria and eGFR 55). They are also one of the four pillars of HFrEF therapy.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, a sulfonylurea lowers A1c but has no cardiorenal benefit and causes hypoglycemia and weight gain. B, thiazolidinediones cause fluid retention and are contraindicated in symptomatic heart failure. C, saxagliptin (and alogliptin) increased heart failure hospitalization in trials. D, insulin would lower A1c but should not come before an agent with proven organ protection when the A1c is only 8.3% and she has no catabolic symptoms.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman comes for a health maintenance examination. She smoked 1.5 packs of cigarettes daily from age 20 to 50 and has not smoked since. She has hypertension controlled with amlodipine. She has no cough, hemoptysis, or weight loss. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding lung cancer screening?

options.label: A
options.html: No screening, because she quit smoking more than 5 years ago

options.label: B
options.html: Annual low-dose CT scan of the chest

options.label: E
options.html: A single low-dose CT scan of the chest, repeated only if abnormal

answerHtml: Answer: B. Annual low-dose CT scan of the chest
explanationHtml: USPSTF (2021): annual LDCT for adults aged 50–80 with a ≥20 pack-year history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years. She has 45 pack-years (1.5 packs × 30 years) and quit 8 years ago, so she qualifies. Screening stops once a person has not smoked for 15 years or has a health problem that limits life expectancy or ability to have curative surgery.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, the cutoff is 15 years since quitting, not 5. C and D, chest x-ray and sputum cytology do not reduce lung cancer mortality. E, screening is annual, not one-time.

stemHtml: A 45-year-old man is admitted with melena. After IV fluids, he is alert and oriented, and blood pressure is 108/68 mm Hg. Hemoglobin is 6.8 g/dL. He is a Jehovah's Witness. After the physician explains that he may die without a transfusion, he clearly states that he understands the risks and refuses all blood products, and he repeats his reasons accurately. His wife, who is not a Jehovah's Witness, asks the team to transfuse him. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Transfuse packed red blood cells because the condition is life-threatening

options.label: B
options.html: Seek an emergency court order to permit transfusion

options.label: C
options.html: Obtain consent for transfusion from his wife

options.label: D
options.html: Respect his refusal and use blood-sparing measures such as urgent endoscopy and IV iron

options.label: E
options.html: Request a psychiatric consultation to override his decision

answerHtml: Answer: D. Respect his refusal and use blood-sparing measures such as urgent endoscopy and IV iron
explanationHtml: An adult with decision-making capacity can refuse any treatment, including life-saving treatment. He shows capacity: he understands, appreciates the consequences, reasons, and states a consistent choice. The team should document the discussion, ask which alternatives he accepts (some patients accept certain fractions or cell salvage), and treat the bleeding source aggressively with endoscopic hemostasis, IV iron, and possibly erythropoiesis-stimulating agents.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, transfusing a capacitated patient against his will is battery. B, court orders are used for minors (parents refusing for a child), not for a competent adult. C, a surrogate decides only when the patient lacks capacity. E, disagreeing with a choice is not evidence of incapacity, and a psychiatry consult cannot override a capacitated refusal.

stemHtml: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of fever for 6 days that has not responded to acetaminophen. He has been irritable. Temperature is 39.6°C (103.3°F), pulse is 150/min, and respirations are 28/min. Examination shows bilateral nonexudative conjunctival injection that spares the limbus, cracked red lips, a strawberry tongue, a 2-cm unilateral nontender cervical lymph node, a diffuse polymorphous rash on the trunk, and edema of the hands and feet. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 16,000/mm<sup>3</sup>, platelet count of 520,000/mm<sup>3</sup>, C-reactive protein of 9 mg/dL, and ALT of 85 U/L. Echocardiography is scheduled. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Intravenous immune globulin and aspirin
explanationHtml: Fever for ≥5 days plus at least 4 of the 5 principal features (conjunctivitis, oral changes, cervical lymphadenopathy, rash, extremity changes) is complete Kawasaki disease. AHA treatment is a single infusion of IVIG (2 g/kg), ideally within 10 days of fever onset, plus aspirin. This lowers the risk of coronary artery aneurysm from about 25% to under 5%. Echo is done at diagnosis and repeated at 1–2 and 4–6 weeks.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, this is not a bacterial infection. C, corticosteroids may be added for high-risk or IVIG-resistant cases but do not replace IVIG. D, infliximab is a second-line option for IVIG-resistant disease. E, antipyretics do not prevent coronary aneurysms. Ibuprofen also blocks the antiplatelet effect of aspirin and is avoided.

stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 32 weeks' gestation comes to labor and delivery because of a severe frontal headache and spots in front of her eyes for 3 hours. Her pregnancy had been uncomplicated, and blood pressure was 112/70 mm Hg at 28 weeks. Blood pressure is 164/112 mm Hg, and 15 minutes later it is 166/110 mm Hg. Pulse is 92/min. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+. Urine dipstick shows 2+ protein. Fetal heart rate tracing is category I. Platelet count is 168,000/mm<sup>3</sup>, AST is 32 U/L, and creatinine is 0.7 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.html: Oral methyldopa and outpatient follow-up in 1 week

options.label: E
options.html: 24-hour urine protein collection before any treatment

answerHtml: Answer: B. Intravenous labetalol and magnesium sulfate
explanationHtml: New hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria, severe-range BP (≥160/110 on two readings), and cerebral/visual symptoms is preeclampsia with severe features. ACOG says severe-range BP should be treated within 30–60 minutes with IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or immediate-release oral nifedipine, and magnesium sulfate should be started for seizure prophylaxis. At <34 weeks, if mother and fetus are stable, give antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone). If her headache and visual symptoms resolve and she remains stable, expectant management to 34 weeks in a tertiary center is possible. If cerebral symptoms persist despite treatment, expectant management is contraindicated and she is delivered after maternal stabilization (steroids are given but delivery is not delayed for them). Either way, stabilization comes first.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, delivery may be indicated, but the mother must be stabilized first (control BP, start Mg) and cesarean is not automatically the route. C, severe features need inpatient care. D, ACE inhibitors are teratogenic (fetal renal toxicity). E, proteinuria does not need quantifying before treatment; severe features alone make the diagnosis.

stemHtml:
A 51-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has taken lithium for 10 years. Her family brings her to the emergency department because of 2 days of confusion, unsteady gait, and diarrhea. Three weeks ago she started a new medication for hypertension and has been taking ibuprofen for back pain. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 64/min, and blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. She is disoriented to time and place. Examination shows a coarse tremor, dysarthria, ataxia, and myoclonic jerks. Laboratory studies show:
TestResultBaseline (6 months ago)
Serum lithium3.6 mEq/L0.8 mEq/L
Creatinine2.3 mg/dL0.9 mg/dL
Sodium134 mEq/L139 mEq/L
IV 0.9% saline is started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Continue IV saline and recheck lithium in 12 hours

answerHtml: Answer: C. Hemodialysis
explanationHtml: This is chronic lithium toxicity, most likely set off by a thiazide or ACE inhibitor plus an NSAID, all of which reduce renal lithium clearance. She has a markedly raised level, severe neurotoxicity (confusion, myoclonus), and acute kidney injury. Lithium is small, water-soluble, and not protein-bound, so it is easily dialyzable. EXTRIP expert criteria recommend extracorporeal removal for impaired kidney function with a level >4.0 mEq/L, or for decreased consciousness, seizures, or life-threatening dysrhythmias whatever the level. They also suggest it for confusion. Many references use a simpler rule: a level >2.5 mEq/L with severe neurologic signs or renal failure. Her confusion, myoclonus, AKI, and level of 3.6 meet these indications. Stop the lithium and the offending drugs.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, charcoal does not bind lithium or other metals. B, fluids are supportive but not enough with severe neurotoxicity and AKI; waiting risks permanent cerebellar damage (SILENT syndrome). D, sodium polystyrene can bind lithium but works slowly, is unreliable, and causes hypokalemia. It is not the next step. E, furosemide causes volume depletion, which increases proximal lithium reabsorption.

stemHtml:
A 68-year-old man with severe COPD comes to the emergency department because of 3 days of increased dyspnea and purulent sputum. He is using accessory muscles but is alert, follows commands, and can protect his airway. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 142/86 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 89% on 2 L/min oxygen by nasal cannula. He has been given nebulized albuterol-ipratropium, IV methylprednisolone, and oral azithromycin. Arterial blood gas on 2 L/min oxygen shows:
TestResult
pH7.28
PaCO268 mm Hg
PaO258 mm Hg
HCO3−31 mEq/L
Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Switch to 100% oxygen by nonrebreather mask

answerHtml: Answer: E. Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (BiPAP)
explanationHtml: This is a COPD exacerbation with acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (pH 7.28, PaCO2 68). GOLD and ATS/ERS recommend NIV for a pH ≤7.35 with PaCO2 ≥45, provided the patient is alert, cooperative, and protecting the airway. NIV reduces intubation and mortality. Recheck the ABG in 1–2 hours. Target an SpO2 of 88–92%.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, intubation is for patients who fail or cannot tolerate NIV, or who have a reduced level of consciousness, cannot protect the airway, or are hemodynamically unstable. B, high-flow oxygen worsens hypercapnia through V/Q mismatch and the Haldane effect. C, methylxanthines add toxicity without benefit in exacerbations. D, bicarbonate does not treat respiratory acidosis and can increase CO<sub>2</sub>.

stemHtml:
A pharmaceutical advertisement in a medical journal reads:

"NEUROVANT (fictional anticoagulant): Cuts the risk of stroke by 25%! In a 2-year randomized trial of 10,000 patients with atrial fibrillation, stroke occurred in 8% of patients taking placebo and 6% of patients taking Neurovant. Major bleeding: 2.1% vs 1.9%."

Based on these data, how many patients must be treated with Neurovant for 2 years to prevent one stroke?
answerHtml: Answer: D. 50
explanationHtml: Absolute risk reduction (ARR) = 8% − 6% = 2% = 0.02. NNT = 1/ARR = 1/0.02 = 50 patients treated for 2 years to prevent one stroke. The ad's "25%" is the relative risk reduction (2%/8%), which makes a small absolute benefit look bigger. Drug ads in Step questions often feature RRR.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, 4 = 1/0.25, which wrongly uses the RRR in the NNT formula. B, 25 is the RRR as a percentage. C, 2 is the ARR as a percentage. E, 13 ≈ 1/0.08, the reciprocal of the control event rate.

stemHtml: A 34-year-old man is brought to the trauma bay after a high-speed motor vehicle collision in which he was the restrained driver. He has diffuse abdominal pain. The airway is patent, and breath sounds are equal bilaterally. Pulse is 132/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 78/44 mm Hg. There is a seat-belt ecchymosis across the lower abdomen, and the abdomen is distended and diffusely tender. Pelvic x-ray and chest x-ray show no pelvic fracture and no hemothorax. After 1 L of crystalloid and 2 units of uncrossmatched O-negative packed red blood cells through a massive transfusion protocol, blood pressure is 82/48 mm Hg. Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) shows free fluid in the hepatorenal space and pelvis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast

options.label: D
options.html: Serial abdominal examinations in the ICU

answerHtml: Answer: A. Exploratory laparotomy
