explanationHtml: ATLS: blunt abdominal trauma with a positive FAST in a hemodynamically unstable patient who does not respond to resuscitation goes straight to the operating room. The free fluid is presumed to be hemorrhage, and there is no time for further imaging.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, CT is for hemodynamically stable patients; "the CT scanner is no place for an unstable patient." C, DPL is used when FAST is unavailable or equivocal; FAST here is already positive. D, observation is not appropriate in shock. E, angioembolization is useful for pelvic arterial bleeding or selected solid-organ injuries in patients who respond to resuscitation, not for refractory shock with hemoperitoneum.

stemHtml:
A 56-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis is brought to the emergency department after vomiting large amounts of bright red blood. Pulse is 124/min and blood pressure is 86/52 mm Hg. He has spider angiomas, gynecomastia, and shifting dullness. Two large-bore IV lines are placed, and a restrictive transfusion strategy is started. He is intubated for airway protection. Laboratory studies show:
TestResult
Hemoglobin6.9 g/dL
Platelet count78,000/mm3
INR1.7
Albumin2.6 g/dL
Total bilirubin3.1 mg/dL
Upper endoscopy is being arranged. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy at this time?

options.label: D
options.html: Fresh frozen plasma to correct the INR to below 1.5

answerHtml: Answer: B. Intravenous octreotide and intravenous ceftriaxone
explanationHtml: Suspected acute variceal hemorrhage in cirrhosis (AASLD) is treated before endoscopy with (1) a vasoactive drug (octreotide or terlipressin) to lower portal pressure, and (2) prophylactic antibiotics (ceftriaxone 1 g/day for up to 7 days), which reduce bacterial infection, rebleeding, and mortality. Endoscopic band ligation is then done within 12 hours of presentation. A restrictive transfusion target (Hb ~7 g/dL) avoids raising portal pressure.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, nonselective beta-blockers are for primary and secondary prophylaxis, not acute bleeding. They worsen hypotension. C, a PPI is often given until a peptic source is excluded, but on its own it does not treat variceal bleeding. D, the INR does not reflect bleeding risk in cirrhosis (rebalanced hemostasis), and giving FFP to correct it adds volume and can raise portal pressure. E, these treat or prevent hepatic encephalopathy but do not address the bleeding.

stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease, type 2 diabetes, and heart failure comes to the emergency department because of generalized weakness. His medications include lisinopril, spironolactone, and furosemide. Pulse is 54/min and blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show a potassium of 7.1 mEq/L (repeat sample without hemolysis: 7.0 mEq/L), creatinine of 3.4 mg/dL, and glucose of 140 mg/dL. ECG shows peaked T waves, a widened QRS complex, and flattened P waves. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Intravenous calcium gluconate
explanationHtml: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes is an emergency. The first step is membrane stabilization with IV calcium (gluconate or chloride). It acts within minutes, does not lower K+, and protects against arrhythmia. Next, shift K+ into cells (insulin + glucose, albuterol). Then remove it from the body (loop diuretic, potassium binders such as patiromer or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate, or dialysis). Stop the lisinopril and spironolactone.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and D, these shift potassium but come after calcium when the ECG is abnormal. B, resins act over hours and carry a risk of colonic necrosis. They are not first-line in emergencies. C, dialysis may be needed for refractory hyperkalemia in advanced CKD, but setting it up takes time and the myocardium needs protecting now.

stemHtml: A previously healthy 38-year-old man comes to the clinic because of 3 days of fever, productive cough, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. He has no chronic medical conditions, takes no medications, has not received antibiotics or been hospitalized in the past year, and does not drink alcohol excessively. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. Crackles are heard at the right lung base. Chest x-ray shows a right lower lobe consolidation. BUN is 14 mg/dL and he is oriented. Local pneumococcal macrolide resistance exceeds 25%. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

options.label: E
options.html: Hospital admission for intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin

answerHtml: Answer: C. Oral high-dose amoxicillin
explanationHtml: His CURB-65 score is 0, so he can be treated as an outpatient. For an outpatient with no comorbidities and no MRSA or Pseudomonas risk factors, ATS/IDSA 2019 recommends amoxicillin 1 g three times daily, or doxycycline, or a macrolide only if local pneumococcal macrolide resistance is <25%. High-dose amoxicillin covers S. pneumoniae, the most common cause.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, respiratory fluoroquinolones are kept for outpatients with comorbidities (or beta-lactam allergy) because of adverse effects (tendinopathy, QT prolongation, C. difficile). B, macrolide monotherapy is not advised when local resistance is ≥25%. D, combination therapy is for outpatients with comorbidities (chronic heart, lung, liver, or renal disease, diabetes, alcoholism, malignancy, asplenia). E, he does not need admission.

stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation and a mechanical mitral valve takes warfarin 5 mg daily. Routine INR monitoring shows an INR of 6.8; her target is 2.5–3.5. Two weeks ago, she finished a course of an antibiotic for a urinary tract infection. She has no bleeding, bruising, melena, or hematuria, and has no history of falls. Vital signs are within normal limits, and hemoglobin is stable at 12.8 g/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Hold warfarin for 1–2 doses, then resume at a lower dose with INR recheck

options.label: E
options.html: Continue warfarin at the same dose and recheck INR in 4 weeks

answerHtml: Answer: A. Hold warfarin for 1–2 doses, then resume at a lower dose with INR recheck
explanationHtml: When the INR is 4.5–10 and there is no bleeding, CHEST guidance is to hold warfarin and monitor, without routine vitamin K. Oral vitamin K is reserved for an INR >10 without bleeding. Reversal is needed only for bleeding. This matters even more with a mechanical valve, because overcorrecting raises the risk of valve thrombosis. The likely cause is the antibiotic interaction (e.g., TMP-SMX or a fluoroquinolone inhibiting warfarin metabolism).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, high-dose IV vitamin K is for serious bleeding. It causes warfarin resistance for days and risks valve thrombosis, and IV vitamin K can cause anaphylactoid reactions. C and D, rapid reversal agents are for major or life-threatening bleeding. E, she needs a closer response than continuing the same dose with a 4-week recheck.

stemHtml:
A 4-week-old girl is brought to the clinic because of yellow skin that has gradually worsened since age 2 weeks. She was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and is breastfed. Her mother notes that her stools have become pale, almost white, and her urine stains the diaper dark yellow. She is feeding well and has regained her birth weight. Examination shows jaundice and a firm liver palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. Laboratory studies show:
TestResult
Total bilirubin8.2 mg/dL
Direct (conjugated) bilirubin5.9 mg/dL
GGT480 U/L (elevated)
AST / ALT110 / 95 U/L
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Biliary atresia
explanationHtml: Jaundice after 2 weeks of age must be fractionated. A direct bilirubin >1.0 mg/dL (or >20% of total) is cholestasis and is never normal. Acholic stools, dark urine, hepatomegaly, and a high GGT in a thriving infant suggest biliary atresia. Workup: ultrasound (absent or abnormal gallbladder, "triangular cord" sign), hepatobiliary scintigraphy, and intraoperative cholangiogram to confirm. The Kasai portoenterostomy works best when done before about 60 days of life, so the diagnosis is time-critical.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B, C, and E all cause unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normally pigmented stools. Gilbert presents later (adolescence, with stress or fasting). Crigler-Najjar I causes severe unconjugated jaundice from birth. Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated and benign, and physiologic jaundice peaks at days 3–5.

stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, comes for follow-up of a routine cervical cancer screening. Her previous screening was cytology alone 3 years ago, which was normal; she has never had HPV testing. She has no history of abnormal results. Today's co-test shows atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US) on cytology and a positive high-risk HPV test (non-16/18 types). She is not pregnant and is not immunocompromised. According to current risk-based management guidelines, which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Colposcopy
explanationHtml: Under ASCCP 2019 risk-based guidelines, HPV-positive ASC-US with no prior HPV test (or unknown history) carries an immediate CIN3+ risk of about 4.4%, which reaches the ≥4% colposcopy threshold. So colposcopy is recommended, whatever the HPV genotype. (A documented negative HPV test or co-test within the past 5 years would lower the risk enough to allow a 1-year return instead.)
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, a 1-year return applies to HPV-positive NILM (normal cytology) with a non-16/18 type, or to low-risk results. B and D, these are routine intervals for normal results. C, expedited treatment without colposcopy is an option only for HSIL cytology with HPV 16 positivity (or very high immediate risk), not for ASC-US.

stemHtml: A 31-year-old man comes to the clinic because of 2 months of low mood, poor concentration, fatigue, hypersomnia, and loss of interest in his hobbies. He has gained 4 kg during this time. He denies suicidal ideation. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 12 years and would like to quit. He says that a friend had "sexual problems" on an antidepressant and he is worried about this, as well as about gaining more weight. He has no history of seizures, head trauma, or eating disorders, and drinks alcohol rarely. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Bupropion
explanationHtml: Bupropion is a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor. It is an effective first-line antidepressant, has almost no sexual side effects, is weight-neutral or causes mild weight loss, and is FDA-approved for smoking cessation. It suits this patient's priorities. It lowers the seizure threshold, so it is contraindicated with seizure disorders, bulimia or anorexia (electrolyte shifts), and abrupt alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and E, SSRIs and SNRIs commonly cause sexual dysfunction. C, paroxetine has the highest rates of sexual dysfunction and weight gain among SSRIs, plus anticholinergic effects. D, mirtazapine causes marked weight gain and sedation through H1 blockade and appetite stimulation.

stemHtml: A 71-year-old man comes to the clinic because of yellowing of his eyes and itching for 3 weeks. He has lost 7 kg over 3 months and has had vague epigastric discomfort that radiates to the back. He has no fever. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history. He was recently diagnosed with diabetes mellitus. Examination shows scleral icterus and a nontender, palpable gallbladder in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory studies show total bilirubin of 9.8 mg/dL (direct 7.9 mg/dL), alkaline phosphatase of 620 U/L, AST of 88 U/L, and ALT of 102 U/L. Right upper quadrant ultrasound shows dilated intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts without gallstones. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Serum CA 19-9 measurement to confirm the diagnosis

options.label: C
options.html: Contrast-enhanced, pancreas-protocol CT scan of the abdomen

answerHtml: Answer: C. Contrast-enhanced, pancreas-protocol CT scan of the abdomen
explanationHtml: Painless (or vague) obstructive jaundice, weight loss, new-onset diabetes in an older smoker, and a palpable nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) point to carcinoma of the pancreatic head. The best next test is multiphasic pancreas-protocol CT, which shows the mass and stages resectability (vascular involvement, metastases) before any intervention. EUS with fine-needle aspiration can then obtain tissue if needed.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, routine preoperative biliary drainage is not recommended for resectable disease without cholangitis, and doing ERCP before CT degrades staging images. B, CA 19-9 is used for prognosis and monitoring, not diagnosis; it is neither sensitive nor specific. D, HIDA is used for cholecystitis. E, resectability must be staged first.

stemHtml: A 67-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 90 minutes after the sudden onset of right arm and face weakness and difficulty speaking. She takes no anticoagulants. Pulse is 88/min and regular, and blood pressure is 196/108 mm Hg on two measurements. Examination shows expressive aphasia, right facial droop, and 2/5 strength in the right arm. Fingerstick glucose is 128 mg/dL. Noncontrast CT of the head shows no hemorrhage. Platelet count and INR are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Intravenous labetalol, then thrombolysis once blood pressure is below 185/110 mm Hg

options.label: B
options.html: Administer intravenous alteplase immediately without treating blood pressure

options.label: C
options.html: Oral aspirin 325 mg and admission to a stroke unit

options.label: D
options.html: MRI of the brain with diffusion-weighted imaging before any treatment

answerHtml: Answer: A. Intravenous labetalol, then thrombolysis once blood pressure is below 185/110 mm Hg
explanationHtml: She is within the 4.5-hour window with a disabling deficit and no hemorrhage, so she is a candidate for IV thrombolysis (alteplase or tenecteplase). AHA/ASA requires BP <185/110 before lytics and <180/105 for 24 hours afterward, using IV labetalol, nicardipine, or clevidipine. She should also have CT angiography to look for a large-vessel occlusion that could be treated with thrombectomy, but this must not delay lytics.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, giving lytics with BP >185/110 raises the risk of hemorrhage. C, aspirin is withheld for 24 hours after thrombolysis. It would be the choice only for a patient who is not a lytic candidate. D, MRI is not needed before lytics within the time window and would delay treatment ("time is brain"). E, full anticoagulation has no role in acute ischemic stroke.

stemHtml:
A 19-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department because of 2 days of vomiting, abdominal pain, and lethargy after she ran out of insulin. Pulse is 124/min, respirations are 30/min and deep, and blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg. Mucous membranes are dry. A 1-L bolus of 0.9% saline has been started. Laboratory studies show:
TestResult
Glucose520 mg/dL
Sodium131 mEq/L
Potassium3.0 mEq/L
Chloride96 mEq/L
Bicarbonate8 mEq/L
Arterial pH7.12
β-Hydroxybutyrate7.2 mmol/L (elevated)
Creatinine1.3 mg/dL
Urine output is adequate. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Start an intravenous regular insulin infusion at 0.1 U/kg/h

options.label: C
options.html: Intravenous regular insulin bolus of 0.1 U/kg

options.label: D
options.html: Withhold insulin and add intravenous potassium chloride to the fluids

answerHtml: Answer: D. Withhold insulin and add intravenous potassium chloride to the fluids
explanationHtml: She has DKA (glucose >250, pH <7.3, HCO3− <18, anion gap 131 − 96 − 8 = 27, ketonemia). Total-body potassium is always depleted in DKA. Insulin drives K+ into cells, so if the serum K+ is <3.3 mEq/L, insulin is held and potassium is replaced (about 20–30 mEq/h) until K+ is ≥3.3. Otherwise there is a risk of fatal arrhythmia and respiratory muscle weakness. If K+ is 3.3–5.2, add K+ to the fluids and start insulin. If K+ is >5.2, start insulin and recheck K+ every 2 hours.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and C, insulin with K<sup>+</sup> 3.0 can cause dangerous hypokalemia. B, bicarbonate is considered only for severe acidemia (pH <7.0 in the 2024 ADA-led consensus; <6.9 in older ADA guidance) and also lowers K<sup>+</sup>. E, subcutaneous long-acting insulin alone is not used to treat moderate-to-severe DKA, and it still shifts potassium.

stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman comes to the clinic for follow-up after an episode of palpitations. ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 82/min. She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She has no history of stroke, heart failure, or vascular disease. Echocardiography shows no mitral stenosis and no prosthetic valve. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL, and she has no history of bleeding. Her rate is controlled with metoprolol. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional pharmacotherapy?

options.label: D
options.html: Referral for left atrial appendage occlusion instead of medication

answerHtml: Answer: E. Apixaban
explanationHtml: CHA2DS2-VASc = age 65–74 (1) + female sex (1) + hypertension (1) + diabetes (1) = 4. The 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS guideline recommends oral anticoagulation for a score ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women. A DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, or dabigatran) is preferred over warfarin in AF without moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve, because it causes less intracranial hemorrhage.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B, antiplatelet therapy prevents strokes poorly in AF, and dual antiplatelet therapy bleeds about as much as a DOAC. C, her stroke risk clearly justifies anticoagulation. D, LAA occlusion is for patients who have a contraindication to long-term anticoagulation, which she does not.

stemHtml: A second-year resident realizes that a hospitalized 58-year-old man received 10 times his prescribed dose of subcutaneous enoxaparin the previous evening because of a decimal-point error in the order she entered. She checks on the patient. He has no bleeding, his hemoglobin and platelet count are unchanged, and his next dose has been held. The patient is alert and has full decision-making capacity. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Do not disclose the error because no harm has occurred

options.label: B
options.html: Tell the patient about the error, apologize, explain the monitoring plan, and file an incident report

options.label: C
options.html: Inform only the attending physician and let the attending decide whether to tell the patient

options.label: D
options.html: Document the event in the chart without telling the patient, to avoid anxiety

options.label: E
options.html: Wait 24 hours, and disclose the error only if complications develop

answerHtml: Answer: B. Tell the patient about the error, apologize, explain the monitoring plan, and file an incident report
explanationHtml: Medical errors should be disclosed promptly and honestly to the patient, whether or not harm has occurred. Disclosure covers what happened, the possible consequences, what is being done (monitoring for bleeding, holding doses), an apology, and steps to prevent a recurrence. The event should also go into the institution's safety reporting system so that system factors can be found and fixed, for example computerized order-entry dose alerts. The attending should be informed too, but that does not replace disclosure to the patient.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, D, and E, withholding information violates patient autonomy and trust. Lack of harm or a wish to avoid anxiety does not justify it. C, notifying the attending is appropriate, but handing off disclosure to avoid it is not.

stemHtml: A 12-month-old boy is brought to the clinic for a well-child visit. Two months ago, he developed generalized hives and lip swelling within minutes of eating scrambled egg. The symptoms resolved with oral diphenhydramine. He has had no other reactions and has received all recommended vaccines to date. He is due for the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine. His mother is concerned because she read that the vaccine is related to eggs. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Defer MMR vaccination until egg allergy has been outgrown

options.label: B
options.html: Skin-prick testing with the MMR vaccine before administration

options.label: C
options.html: Administer the MMR vaccine in the routine manner

options.label: D
options.html: Administer the MMR vaccine in graded divided doses over several hours

options.label: E
options.html: Premedicate with oral prednisone, then administer the MMR vaccine

answerHtml: Answer: C. Administer the MMR vaccine in the routine manner
explanationHtml: The MMR vaccine is grown in chick embryo fibroblast cultures and contains negligible egg protein. CDC/ACIP and AAP say children with egg allergy, including anaphylaxis, can receive MMR routinely without testing or special precautions. The rare reactions to MMR are usually caused by gelatin or neomycin. Influenza vaccines can also be given to egg-allergic patients routinely.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, delaying leaves the child unprotected against measles, and there is no valid reason to defer. B, D, and E, none of these is needed for egg allergy.

stemHtml: A 63-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis three times weekly comes to the emergency department because of severe pain and swelling of the left knee that began overnight. He had a similar episode in the first metatarsophalangeal joint 1 year ago. He has a history of a bleeding duodenal ulcer. Temperature is 37.8°C (100.0°F). The left knee is warm, erythematous, swollen, and exquisitely tender. Arthrocentesis shows a leukocyte count of 22,000/mm<sup>3</sup> (80% neutrophils), needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals, and a negative Gram stain; culture is pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this acute episode?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Oral prednisone
explanationHtml: This is an acute gout flare (monosodium urate crystals). First-line flare options per ACR 2020 are NSAIDs, colchicine, or glucocorticoids (oral, intra-articular, or IM). In dialysis patients, colchicine is not removed by dialysis and builds up, causing neuromyotoxicity and myelosuppression, so it should be avoided. NSAIDs are contraindicated with ESRD and a prior bleeding ulcer. A short course of oral glucocorticoids is therefore the safest choice. An intra-articular steroid injection would also be reasonable for a single large joint once infection is excluded.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, colchicine accumulates in ESRD on dialysis and is avoided. C, NSAIDs are contraindicated (ESRD, prior GI bleed). D, allopurinol is urate-lowering therapy. It may be started during a flare under the 2020 ACR guideline, but it does not treat the flare itself. E, uricosurics do not work at low GFR and do not treat flares.

stemHtml: A 59-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of 18 hours of crampy periumbilical pain, nausea, and bilious vomiting. Her last bowel movement was yesterday, and she is still passing some flatus. She had an open hysterectomy 10 years ago. Temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg. The abdomen is mildly distended with high-pitched bowel sounds, and there is mild diffuse tenderness without guarding or rebound. There are no hernias. Leukocyte count is 9,800/mm<sup>3</sup>, and serum lactate is 1.1 mmol/L. CT scan with IV contrast shows dilated proximal small-bowel loops with a transition point in the lower abdomen and gas and stool in the colon; there is no bowel wall thickening, pneumatosis, mesenteric swirl, or free fluid. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.html: Nasogastric decompression, nothing by mouth, and intravenous fluids

answerHtml: Answer: D. Nasogastric decompression, nothing by mouth, and intravenous fluids
explanationHtml: This is a partial adhesive small-bowel obstruction (prior surgery; still passing flatus; colonic gas) with no signs of strangulation: no fever, tachycardia out of proportion, peritonitis, leukocytosis, raised lactate, or ischemic CT features. Initial management is nonoperative: bowel rest, NG decompression, IV fluids, electrolyte correction, and serial exams. A water-soluble contrast challenge (Gastrografin) has both diagnostic and therapeutic value. About 70–90% of partial adhesive SBOs resolve without surgery. Surgery is for signs of ischemia or failure to resolve, usually within 3–5 days.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B, immediate surgery is for complete obstruction with strangulation signs, peritonitis, or a failed nonoperative trial. C and E, these evaluate the colon and are not indicated for an SBO already characterized by CT.

stemHtml:
A new rapid serum assay for detecting bacterial (vs viral) pneumonia is evaluated in 1,000 adults with pneumonia. The reference standard is a combination of cultures and PCR. The results are:
Bacterial pneumoniaNonbacterial pneumonia
Assay positive9040
Assay negative10860
A patient from this population has a positive assay result. Which of the following is the closest to the probability that this patient has bacterial pneumonia?
answerHtml: Answer: B. 69%
explanationHtml: The question asks for the positive predictive value: TP/(TP + FP) = 90/(90 + 40) = 90/130 ≈ 69%. PPV depends on prevalence (here 100/1,000 = 10%), which is why a test with high sensitivity and specificity can still give a modest PPV in a low-prevalence population.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, 90% is sensitivity (90/100). C, 96% is specificity (860/900 = 95.6%). D, 99% is NPV (860/870 = 98.9%). E, 10% is prevalence.

stemHtml:
A 36-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV infection after presenting with oral thrush. He feels well otherwise. Vital signs are within normal limits. Laboratory studies show:
TestResult
CD4+ T-lymphocyte count150/mm3
HIV RNA viral load88,000 copies/mL
Toxoplasma gondii IgGNegative
Interferon-γ release assayNegative
HLA-B*5701Negative
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activityNormal
Antiretroviral therapy is being started today. In addition, which of the following is the most appropriate prophylactic regimen?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
explanationHtml: Primary Pneumocystis prophylaxis is indicated for a CD4 count <200/mm3 (or <14%) or oropharyngeal candidiasis. He has both. TMP-SMX is first-line and also gives toxoplasma prophylaxis (toxo prophylaxis is indicated for seropositive patients with CD4 <100). Prophylaxis can stop once CD4 is >200 for ≥3 months on ART.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B and C, MAC prophylaxis is no longer recommended (DHHS) for patients who start ART right away, and in any case it was indicated only at CD4 <50. D, routine primary antifungal prophylaxis is not recommended. E, this is an alternative toxoplasma/PCP regimen for patients who cannot take sulfa drugs, and he is toxo-seronegative.

stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 28 weeks' gestation comes for a routine prenatal visit. Her blood type is O, Rh(D)-negative. Her antibody screen at the first prenatal visit and again today is negative. She has had no vaginal bleeding or abdominal trauma. The father of the baby is not available for testing, and his blood type is unknown. Her 1-hour glucose challenge test today is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Administer anti-D immune globulin only after delivery if the newborn is Rh-positive

options.label: C
options.html: Repeat the antibody screen at 36 weeks without other intervention

options.label: D
options.html: Amniocentesis to determine the fetal blood type

answerHtml: Answer: E. Administer anti-D immune globulin now
explanationHtml: ACOG recommends routine anti-D immune globulin (300 μg) at about 28 weeks for unsensitized Rh-negative women (negative antibody screen), unless the father is known to be Rh-negative. A second dose is given within 72 hours of delivering an Rh-positive infant, with the dose guided by a quantitative fetomaternal hemorrhage test. Anti-D is also given after any sensitizing event: bleeding, trauma, amniocentesis, ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage, or external cephalic version.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, postpartum-only dosing misses antepartum sensitization (about 1–2% of Rh-negative women would otherwise become sensitized). B, Kleihauer-Betke measures the size of a fetomaternal hemorrhage to guide dosing after a sensitizing event or delivery; it is not a routine 28-week test. C, repeating the screen alone does not prevent alloimmunization. D, invasive fetal typing has procedure risks (including sensitization) and is not indicated for routine prophylaxis decisions.

stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman is admitted 4 days after a total knee arthroplasty. She suddenly develops severe dyspnea and lightheadedness while walking to the bathroom. Temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure is 76/44 mm Hg; after 1 L of IV saline, it is 78/46 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 84% on room air. Jugular veins are distended. Bedside echocardiography shows a dilated, hypokinetic right ventricle with septal flattening and a normal left ventricle. Compression ultrasound shows a thrombus in the right popliteal vein. Her surgery was uncomplicated, and she has no history of intracranial disease or active bleeding. Norepinephrine is being started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.html: CT pulmonary angiography before any treatment

answerHtml: Answer: C. Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase
explanationHtml: This is high-risk (massive) PE: sustained hypotension (SBP <90) with RV dysfunction. Bedside echo showing RV strain plus a confirmed DVT is enough to act on in an unstable patient who cannot safely go to CT. CHEST, ESC, and AHA recommend systemic thrombolysis unless contraindicated, alongside unfractionated heparin. Surgery 4 days ago is a relative contraindication (major surgery within 3 weeks), but a knee arthroplasty is not intracranial or spinal surgery, and the risk of death from obstructive shock outweighs the bleeding risk. Catheter-directed therapy or surgical embolectomy are alternatives when lytics are absolutely contraindicated or have failed. A multidisciplinary PE response team should be involved when available.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, IVC filters are for patients with acute VTE who cannot be anticoagulated. They do not treat obstructive shock. B, heparin alone does not restore RV function quickly enough in massive PE. D, an unstable patient should not be moved to the CT scanner when bedside findings support the diagnosis. E, oral agents are for stable patients.

stemHtml: A 67-year-old woman develops 6 watery stools daily 5 days after finishing a course of clindamycin for a dental infection. She has mild lower abdominal cramping. This is her first such episode. Temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse is 88/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft and nondistended, with mild diffuse tenderness. Leukocyte count is 11,200/mm3 and creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL (baseline 0.8 mg/dL). Stool testing is positive for Clostridioides difficile glutamate dehydrogenase antigen and toxin. Fidaxomicin is not covered by her insurance. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Oral vancomycin
explanationHtml: This is an initial, non-severe C. difficile infection (WBC <15,000/mm3 and creatinine <1.5 mg/dL). IDSA/SHEA 2021 prefers fidaxomicin 200 mg twice daily for 10 days. Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for 10 days is an acceptable alternative and the right choice when fidaxomicin is unavailable. Oral metronidazole is used only for non-severe disease when neither of these is available.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, IV metronidazole is added to oral or rectal vancomycin for fulminant disease (hypotension, ileus, megacolon); it is not monotherapy for a first episode. C, IV vancomycin is not excreted into the colon and is ineffective for CDI. D, FMT is for multiple recurrences (usually the second or later recurrence). E, antimotility agents may increase the risk of toxic megacolon and are avoided until CDI is treated.

stemHtml: A 28-year-old man with schizophrenia was admitted 3 days ago for acute psychosis and treated with intramuscular haloperidol. Today he is confused and diaphoretic. Temperature is 40.3°C (104.5°F), pulse is 128/min, and blood pressure fluctuates between 170/100 and 110/60 mm Hg. Examination shows generalized "lead-pipe" rigidity with normal reflexes and no clonus. Pupils are normal in size. Laboratory studies show a creatine kinase of 14,500 U/L, leukocyte count of 15,000/mm<sup>3</sup>, and creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL. Haloperidol is discontinued, and he is transferred to the ICU for cooling and IV fluids. Fever and rigidity persist despite these measures. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Dantrolene
explanationHtml: Hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability, and a very high CK days after a high-potency antipsychotic is neuroleptic malignant syndrome, caused by D2 blockade. Management: stop the drug, give aggressive supportive care (cooling, fluids to protect the kidneys from rhabdomyolysis), and give benzodiazepines for agitation. In moderate-to-severe cases that do not respond, add dantrolene (a ryanodine receptor blocker that reduces muscle heat production) and/or bromocriptine (a D2 agonist).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, cyproheptadine is a 5-HT2A antagonist for serotonin syndrome, which causes hyperreflexia, clonus, and mydriasis and develops over hours rather than days. B, anticholinergics do not treat NMS and worsen hyperthermia by impairing sweating. C, physostigmine reverses anticholinergic toxicity, which causes dry skin, not diaphoresis. D, beta-blockers do not treat the underlying problem and may worsen autonomic instability.

stemHtml: A 52-year-old man has a CT scan of the abdomen for evaluation of suspected nephrolithiasis. It shows a 2.4-cm, homogeneous, well-circumscribed left adrenal mass with an unenhanced attenuation of 6 Hounsfield units. He has no headaches, palpitations, diaphoresis, weight gain, or muscle weakness. Blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg, pulse is 72/min, and BMI is 25 kg/m<sup>2</sup>. Examination shows no striae, moon facies, or proximal muscle weakness. Serum potassium is 4.3 mEq/L and fasting glucose is 92 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: No further evaluation is needed because the imaging appears benign

options.label: C
options.html: CT-guided biopsy of the adrenal mass

options.label: D
options.html: 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test and plasma free metanephrines

answerHtml: Answer: D. 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test and plasma free metanephrines
explanationHtml: Every adrenal incidentaloma needs (1) assessment of malignancy risk on imaging and (2) a hormonal workup. Imaging here (<4 cm, homogeneous, <10 HU) is benign and lipid-rich, typical of an adenoma, so no imaging follow-up is required. Biochemical screening is still needed. Mild autonomous cortisol secretion is screened with a 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test in all patients. Pheochromocytoma is screened with plasma free metanephrines (ESE 2023 guidance allows this to be omitted for lesions <10 HU, but it remains standard in many US algorithms and is expected on exams). Aldosterone-to-renin ratio is added only if the patient has hypertension or hypokalemia.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, a benign imaging appearance does not exclude hormone production. B, VMA is less sensitive than metanephrines. C, biopsy is almost never indicated and is dangerous if the lesion is a pheochromocytoma. It is used mainly for suspected metastasis after pheochromocytoma is excluded. E, surgery is for functional tumors or suspicious imaging.

stemHtml: A 67-year-old man comes for a health maintenance examination. He smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 25 years and quit 15 years ago. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia treated with lisinopril and atorvastatin. He has no abdominal or back pain. Pulse is 70/min and blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows no pulsatile mass or bruit. He has never had abdominal imaging. Which of the following is the most appropriate screening recommendation?

options.label: A
options.html: No screening, because he no longer smokes

options.label: E
options.html: Screening only if a bruit or pulsatile mass develops

answerHtml: Answer: B. One-time abdominal ultrasonography
explanationHtml: USPSTF (2019) recommends a one-time ultrasound to screen for abdominal aortic aneurysm in men aged 65–75 who have ever smoked (≥100 lifetime cigarettes), grade B. Former smokers qualify. For men 65–75 who never smoked, screening is selective (grade C). For women who never smoked, USPSTF recommends against it (grade D). For women who have smoked, evidence is insufficient (I).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, "ever smoked" includes former smokers. C, repeat screening is not recommended after a normal scan; surveillance intervals apply only once an aneurysm is found. D, CT exposes him to radiation and contrast and is not the screening test. E, physical exam is insensitive for AAA.

stemHtml:
A 61-year-old man comes to the clinic because of fatigue and exertional dyspnea for 3 months. He has no overt bleeding, abdominal pain, or change in bowel habits. He eats a varied diet with meat. He has never had colorectal cancer screening. He takes no medications. Examination shows conjunctival pallor; the abdomen is nontender, and rectal examination shows brown stool. Laboratory studies show:
TestResult
Hemoglobin9.1 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume71 μm3
Red cell distribution width18.5% (elevated)
Ferritin6 ng/mL
Platelet count460,000/mm3
Tissue transglutaminase IgANegative (normal total IgA)
Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Oral iron supplementation and recheck hemoglobin in 3 months, without further testing

answerHtml: Answer: E. Colonoscopy and upper endoscopy
explanationHtml: Iron deficiency anemia (microcytosis, high RDW, ferritin <30–45 ng/mL, reactive thrombocytosis) in a man or a postmenopausal woman is presumed to be from gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise. The AGA recommends bidirectional endoscopy to look for colorectal cancer, gastric cancer, peptic ulcer, and angiodysplasia. Iron replacement should be started as well, but it must not replace the search for a cause.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, treating without investigating can miss a cancer. B, a negative fecal test does not rule out a GI lesion in IDA (bleeding is intermittent), and a positive one would lead to colonoscopy anyway, so stool testing is not appropriate here. C, ferritin already confirms iron deficiency. D, thalassemia trait has a normal or high ferritin and a normal RDW. (NEET PG bridge: US guidance discourages using stool occult blood tests to evaluate IDA.)

stemHtml:
A 64-year-old white man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction 30%) comes for follow-up. He has dyspnea when climbing one flight of stairs (NYHA class II–III). His medications are sacubitril-valsartan, carvedilol at target dose, empagliflozin, and furosemide as needed. Pulse is 58/min and regular, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Lungs are clear, and there is no peripheral edema. Laboratory studies show:
TestResult
Sodium138 mEq/L
Potassium4.2 mEq/L
Creatinine1.1 mg/dL
eGFR68 mL/min/1.73 m2
ECG shows sinus bradycardia with a QRS duration of 104 msec. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his regimen?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Spironolactone
explanationHtml: The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline lists four drug classes ("four pillars") for HFrEF that reduce mortality: ARNI (or ACEi/ARB), evidence-based beta-blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and SGLT2 inhibitor. He is missing the MRA. Spironolactone (or eplerenone) is indicated for NYHA II–IV with eGFR >30 and K+ <5.0 mEq/L. Check potassium and creatinine within 1 week and periodically after that.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, digoxin reduces hospitalizations but not mortality and is a later add-on. B, ivabradine requires sinus rhythm with resting HR ≥70 despite maximal beta-blockade; his HR is 58. D, H-ISDN is added for self-identified Black patients on optimal therapy, or for patients who cannot take ARNI/ACEi/ARB. E, amlodipine has no HFrEF benefit (it is neutral), and his BP does not need more lowering.

stemHtml: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department at 2 AM because of a "barking" cough and noisy breathing that began tonight. He had rhinorrhea and a low-grade fever for 2 days. Temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), pulse is 140/min, and respirations are 38/min. Oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. He is alert, sitting in his mother's lap, and not drooling. There is inspiratory stridor at rest with moderate suprasternal and subcostal retractions. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.html: Intravenous ceftriaxone and immediate intubation in the operating room

options.label: C
options.html: Lateral neck x-ray before any treatment

options.label: D
options.html: Oral dexamethasone and nebulized racemic epinephrine

answerHtml: Answer: D. Oral dexamethasone and nebulized racemic epinephrine
explanationHtml: Viral prodrome, barking cough, and inspiratory stridor in a toddler is croup (laryngotracheobronchitis, usually parainfluenza). Stridor at rest with retractions means moderate croup. It is treated with a single dose of dexamethasone (0.15–0.6 mg/kg) plus nebulized epinephrine, which reduces airway edema quickly through alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction. After epinephrine, observe for 2–4 hours because symptoms can rebound. Mild croup (no stridor at rest) needs dexamethasone alone.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, croup is upper-airway (subglottic) obstruction, not bronchospasm. B, this approach is for epiglottitis (toxic appearance, drooling, tripod position, high fever, no barking cough). C, croup is a clinical diagnosis. The steeple sign is not needed, and imaging delays treatment. E, the cause is not influenza-specific.

stemHtml:
A 66-year-old man with recently diagnosed small cell lung cancer is found to have a low serum sodium on routine pre-chemotherapy laboratory studies. He has mild fatigue but no confusion, headache, nausea, or seizures. He is euvolemic on examination, with no orthostasis, edema, or jugular venous distention. He takes no diuretics. Laboratory studies show:
TestResult
Serum sodium125 mEq/L (130 mEq/L 3 weeks ago)
Serum osmolality262 mOsm/kg H2O
Urine osmolality520 mOsm/kg H2O
Urine sodium58 mEq/L
TSH and morning cortisolNormal
Glucose98 mg/dL
Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Fluid restriction
explanationHtml: Euvolemic hypotonic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine (Uosm >100) and urine Na >30, with normal thyroid and adrenal function, is SIADH. Here it is from ectopic ADH produced by small cell lung cancer. For chronic, mildly symptomatic hyponatremia, the first step is fluid restriction (<800–1,000 mL/day). Second-line options include salt tablets with a loop diuretic, urea, or vaptans (tolvaptan, used cautiously with liver-monitoring limits). Treating the cancer often helps. Correct by no more than 8–10 mEq/L in 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, hypertonic saline is for severe symptoms (seizure, obtundation, vomiting). C, in SIADH with a urine osmolality above the saline's 308 mOsm/kg, the sodium is excreted and the free water is retained, which worsens hyponatremia. D, demeclocycline is rarely used because it is nephrotoxic and slow, and it is not first-line. E, thiazides cause hyponatremia.

stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 0, comes to the clinic because she has been unable to conceive after 14 months of regular unprotected intercourse. Menses occur every 45–90 days. She has acne and coarse hair on her chin and upper lip. BMI is 31 kg/m<sup>2</sup>. Serum total testosterone is mildly elevated; TSH, prolactin, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone are normal. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows enlarged ovaries with more than 20 follicles each. Her partner's semen analysis is normal, and hysterosalpingography shows patent fallopian tubes. In addition to lifestyle modification, which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Letrozole
explanationHtml: She meets the Rotterdam criteria for PCOS (oligo-ovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovarian morphology) with infertility from anovulation. The international evidence-based PCOS guideline (2023) and ACOG recommend letrozole, an aromatase inhibitor, as first-line ovulation induction. Compared with clomiphene, it gives higher live-birth rates, more monofollicular ovulation, and fewer multiple pregnancies. Tubal patency and semen analysis were checked appropriately before starting.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, clomiphene is now second-line, with lower live-birth rates. B, metformin alone is less effective than letrozole for ovulation induction; it is mainly a metabolic adjunct. D, OCPs are first-line for PCOS in women who do not want pregnancy (cycle control, endometrial protection, acne and hirsutism). E, spironolactone is a teratogenic antiandrogen (risk of feminizing a male fetus) and is not used when trying to conceive.

stemHtml: A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of 12 hours of fever, severe headache, and neck stiffness. He has no medical history and takes no medications. Temperature is 39.8°C (103.6°F), pulse is 118/min, and blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. He is drowsy but oriented. Kernig and Brudzinski signs are present. There is no papilledema, focal neurologic deficit, or rash. Blood cultures have been drawn, and lumbar puncture will be performed promptly. Which of the following is the most appropriate empiric pharmacotherapy to administer now?

options.label: C
options.html: Intravenous dexamethasone, vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and ampicillin

options.label: E
options.html: Withhold antibiotics until cerebrospinal fluid results are available

answerHtml: Answer: B. Intravenous dexamethasone, vancomycin, and ceftriaxone
explanationHtml: IDSA empiric therapy for suspected bacterial meningitis in an immunocompetent adult aged 2–50 years is vancomycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime), covering S. pneumoniae (including resistant strains) and N. meningitidis. Dexamethasone is given just before or with the first antibiotic dose. It reduces mortality and hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis and is continued only if pneumococcus is confirmed. Antibiotics must not be delayed; if CT is needed first (papilledema, focal deficit, immunocompromise, seizure, decreased consciousness), give them after blood cultures and before imaging.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, ceftriaxone alone does not cover cephalosporin-resistant pneumococcus. C, ampicillin (for Listeria) is added for age >50, immunocompromise, pregnancy, or alcoholism, none of which applies. D, acyclovir is added if HSV encephalitis is suspected (altered behavior, focal signs, temporal lobe findings). Bacterial meningitis must still be covered. E, delay increases mortality.

stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman underwent total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma 20 hours ago. She now reports tingling around her mouth and in her fingertips, and muscle cramps. Pulse is 88/min and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Tapping anterior to the ear causes twitching of the ipsilateral facial muscles, and inflating a blood pressure cuff causes carpal spasm. ECG shows a QTc of 510 msec. Laboratory studies show a total serum calcium of 6.6 mg/dL, albumin of 4.0 g/dL, magnesium of 2.0 mg/dL, and an undetectable PTH. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: E
options.html: Observation and repeat calcium measurement in 24 hours

answerHtml: Answer: D. Intravenous calcium gluconate
explanationHtml: Acute postsurgical hypoparathyroidism is a common complication of total thyroidectomy (inadvertent removal or devascularization of the parathyroids). Symptomatic hypocalcemia with a positive Chvostek sign, a positive Trousseau sign, and QT prolongation is an emergency. It needs IV calcium gluconate (bolus followed by infusion), with cardiac monitoring. Oral calcium plus calcitriol is then started for maintenance, since calcitriol is needed when PTH is absent.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B, oral therapy alone is too slow for symptomatic, severe hypocalcemia with ECG changes, though both are part of maintenance therapy. C, her magnesium is normal; hypomagnesemia would have to be corrected for hypocalcemia to resolve. E, observation risks laryngospasm, seizures, and arrhythmia.

stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension comes to the emergency department because of sudden, severe, tearing pain between his shoulder blades that began 1 hour ago. Pulse is 104/min. Blood pressure is 188/108 mm Hg in the right arm and 182/104 mm Hg in the left arm. He is alert, with no focal neurologic deficits. Peripheral pulses are intact, abdominal examination is benign, and urine output is normal. Creatinine and lactate are normal, and troponin is negative. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy without ST changes. CT angiography shows an aortic dissection that begins distal to the left subclavian artery and extends to the renal arteries, with no malperfusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Intravenous esmolol
explanationHtml: This is an uncomplicated Stanford type B dissection (descending aorta only, no rupture or malperfusion). It is managed medically. The first step is IV beta-blockade (esmolol or labetalol) to reduce heart rate (<60/min) and aortic wall stress (dP/dt), then lower systolic BP to about 100–120 mm Hg. Add IV opioid analgesia. A vasodilator (nicardipine, nitroprusside) is added only after beta-blockade if BP is still high.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, emergent surgery is for type A (ascending) dissection. Complicated type B (rupture, malperfusion, refractory pain, rapid expansion) is usually treated with endovascular TEVAR. C, a vasodilator without prior beta-blockade causes reflex tachycardia, raises shear stress, and can extend the dissection. D and E, anticoagulants and thrombolytics are contraindicated and can be fatal.

stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman with primary hypothyroidism from Hashimoto thyroiditis comes to the clinic after a positive home pregnancy test. Her last menstrual period was 5 weeks ago. She takes levothyroxine 100 μg daily, and her TSH 2 months ago was 1.8 μU/mL. She feels well. Pulse is 76/min and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue the current dose and recheck TSH at 20 weeks' gestation

options.label: D
options.html: Increase the levothyroxine dose by about 25–30% now and check TSH in 4 weeks

options.label: E
options.html: Discontinue levothyroxine until the first-trimester TSH is available

answerHtml: Answer: D. Increase the levothyroxine dose by about 25–30% now and check TSH in 4 weeks
explanationHtml: Thyroid hormone needs rise by 25–50% early in pregnancy (estrogen raises thyroxine-binding globulin, hCG stimulation changes, placental deiodinase, larger volume of distribution). The fetus depends entirely on maternal T4 until about 12 weeks for neurodevelopment. ATA and ACOG recommend that hypothyroid women increase levothyroxine as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, typically by taking 2 extra doses per week (about a 29% increase). Check TSH every 4 weeks through mid-pregnancy, aiming for the lower half of the trimester-specific range (TSH <2.5).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, waiting risks maternal hypothyroxinemia during critical fetal brain development. B, this is the wrong direction. C, T3 does not cross into the fetal brain adequately, and levothyroxine is the drug of choice. E, stopping is harmful.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of episodic wheezing and chest tightness for 6 months. Symptoms occur 3–4 days each week and wake her from sleep about 3 times per month. She uses an albuterol inhaler on those days. She has no limitation in daily activities and has never required oral corticosteroids or an emergency department visit. Spirometry shows an FEV<sub>1</sub> of 84% of predicted with a 15% increase after bronchodilator. She does not smoke. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term management?

options.label: C
options.html: Daily low-dose inhaled corticosteroid, with as-needed albuterol

options.label: E
options.html: A 10-day course of oral prednisone, then as-needed albuterol

answerHtml: Answer: C. Daily low-dose inhaled corticosteroid, with as-needed albuterol
explanationHtml: Symptoms >2 days/week but not daily, nighttime awakenings 3–4 times/month, and FEV1 >80% classify as mild persistent asthma. The preferred NAEPP 2020 step 2 therapy is a daily low-dose ICS with a SABA as needed (or as-needed concomitant ICS + SABA). GINA prefers as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol, but lists daily low-dose ICS as an alternative. Both guidelines agree that all patients with persistent asthma need ICS-containing therapy.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, SABA-only treatment raises the risk of severe exacerbations and death. GINA no longer recommends it at any step, and under NAEPP it is only for intermittent asthma. B, LABA monotherapy is contraindicated (increased asthma deaths). D, montelukast is a less effective alternative and carries an FDA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric events. E, there is no exacerbation to justify systemic steroids.

stemHtml: An 18-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home that lasted 2 minutes. She had developed a fever and runny nose earlier that day. She has no previous seizures, her development is normal, and her immunizations are up to date. Temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F), pulse is 136/min, and respirations are 28/min. Forty minutes after the seizure, she is alert, playful, and interactive. Examination shows rhinorrhea and mild pharyngeal erythema. There is no nuchal rigidity, bulging fontanelle, or focal neurologic deficit. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Reassurance, parental education, and treatment of fever for comfort

answerHtml: Answer: B. Reassurance, parental education, and treatment of fever for comfort
explanationHtml: A simple febrile seizure is generalized, lasts <15 minutes, happens once in 24 hours, occurs between 6 months and 5 years of age, and is followed by a return to baseline. In a well-appearing, fully immunized child with a normal exam, the AAP does not recommend routine EEG, neuroimaging, or labs. LP is considered if meningeal signs are present, and is an option for infants 6–12 months who are not up to date on Hib or pneumococcal vaccines or who were pretreated with antibiotics. The recurrence risk is about 30%, and the risk of later epilepsy is only slightly above the general population. Antipyretics are for comfort and do not prevent recurrence.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and D, these are not indicated for simple febrile seizures. C, she has no meningeal signs and is fully immunized and back to baseline. E, prophylactic antiseizure drugs are not recommended, because their adverse effects outweigh any benefit.

stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation who stopped taking apixaban 2 months ago because of cost comes to the emergency department 3 hours after the sudden onset of severe pain in her left leg. Pulse is 96/min and irregularly irregular, and blood pressure is 146/88 mm Hg. The left leg is cool and pale from mid-calf downward. Femoral pulse is palpable, but popliteal, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses are absent on the left and present on the right. There is decreased light-touch sensation over the toes and mild weakness of toe dorsiflexion. Doppler arterial signals are inaudible in the left foot; venous signals are audible. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Measurement of the ankle-brachial index and outpatient vascular referral

options.label: D
options.html: Elevation of the leg and observation for 6 hours

options.label: E
options.html: Intravenous unfractionated heparin bolus and infusion

answerHtml: Answer: E. Intravenous unfractionated heparin bolus and infusion
explanationHtml: Sudden pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, and early paralysis in a patient with AF off anticoagulation is acute limb ischemia from embolism (likely to the popliteal artery bifurcation). Mild sensory loss with mild weakness and absent arterial Doppler signals is Rutherford class IIb (immediately threatened). Immediate IV heparin stops clot propagation. It is followed by urgent revascularization (surgical embolectomy, or endovascular thrombectomy/thrombolysis) within about 6 hours, with imaging only if it does not delay treatment.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, ABI and outpatient care are for chronic PAD. B, antiplatelets and cilostazol are for claudication. C, primary amputation is for a nonviable limb (class III: profound sensory loss, paralysis, absent arterial and venous signals). D, elevation worsens perfusion, and delay causes tissue loss.

stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl comes to the clinic alone and asks to start contraception. She has been sexually active with one male partner for 3 months, and they use condoms inconsistently. She asks that her parents not be told. She lives in a state with no specific law requiring parental involvement for contraceptive services. She has no medical problems, migraine, or family history of thrombosis. Blood pressure is 108/68 mm Hg. Urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Provide confidential contraceptive counseling, including long-acting reversible contraception, and offer STI screening

options.label: B
options.html: Obtain written consent from a parent before prescribing contraception

options.label: C
options.html: Contact her parents because she is a minor

options.label: D
options.html: Decline to prescribe until she is 18 years of age

options.label: E
options.html: Refer her to a court for a judicial bypass

answerHtml: Answer: A. Provide confidential contraceptive counseling, including long-acting reversible contraception, and offer STI screening
explanationHtml: US minors can generally consent on their own to contraception, STI testing and treatment, prenatal care, and substance-use treatment, without parental notification. AAP and ACOG support confidential care, encourage (but do not require) the adolescent to involve a trusted adult, and recommend LARC (implant or IUD) as first-line because it is the most effective. Sexually active females under 25 should have annual chlamydia and gonorrhea screening (USPSTF/CDC). Condom use should also be encouraged for STI protection.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, C, and D, requiring parental involvement goes against minors' consent rights for contraception, and breaking confidentiality discourages adolescents from seeking care. E, judicial bypass applies to abortion consent laws in some states, not to contraception.

stemHtml:
Read the following abstract:

"Background: Whether drug Z reduces cardiovascular events in patients with chronic kidney disease is unknown. Methods: In this double-blind trial, 1,200 adults with stage 3 CKD were randomly assigned to drug Z or placebo and followed for a median of 3 years. The primary outcome was a composite of myocardial infarction, stroke, or cardiovascular death. Results: The primary outcome occurred in 9.6% of the drug Z group and 11.8% of the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.80; 95% confidence interval, 0.62 to 1.04; P = 0.09). The trial was designed to have 80% power to detect a 30% relative risk reduction. Conclusions: ..."

Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of these results?

options.label: A
options.html: Drug Z significantly reduced cardiovascular events by 20%

options.label: B
options.html: The reduction was not statistically significant, and a clinically meaningful benefit cannot be excluded

options.label: C
options.html: Drug Z was shown to be equivalent to placebo

options.label: E
options.html: The study had a type I error

answerHtml: Answer: B. The reduction was not statistically significant, and a clinically meaningful benefit cannot be excluded
explanationHtml: The 95% CI for the hazard ratio (0.62–1.04) crosses 1.0 and P > 0.05, so the result is not statistically significant. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. The CI includes up to a 38% risk reduction, and the trial was powered only for a large (30%) effect, so a smaller real benefit could have been missed (possible type II error). Equivalence or non-inferiority would need a trial designed for it with prespecified margins.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, 20% is the point estimate, but it is not significant. C, a nonsignificant superiority trial does not show equivalence. D, the point estimate favors drug Z, and the CI allows at most a 4% increase. E, a type I error is a false positive. You can only commit one by rejecting the null hypothesis, and these investigators did not.
tags: Confidence intervals and type II error (abstract)

stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman was admitted 3 days ago with acute pancreatitis. She had epigastric pain radiating to the back, a lipase 12 times the upper limit of normal, and gallstones with a normal-caliber common bile duct on ultrasound. She does not drink alcohol, and her triglyceride level is normal. She was treated with goal-directed IV lactated Ringer's solution and analgesia. Today her pain has resolved, she is tolerating a low-fat solid diet, and she is afebrile. Liver enzymes and bilirubin have normalized. She has no signs of cholangitis or organ failure. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Discharge with elective cholecystectomy in 6–8 weeks

options.label: C
options.html: Ursodeoxycholic acid long term and no surgery

answerHtml: Answer: E. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy before discharge
explanationHtml: For mild gallstone pancreatitis, ACG, AGA, and IAP/APA guidelines recommend cholecystectomy during the same admission once the patient has recovered. Delaying surgery leads to recurrent biliary events (pancreatitis, cholecystitis, cholangitis) in up to about 30% of patients within weeks. Delayed cholecystectomy is reserved for necrotizing or severe pancreatitis with peripancreatic collections, where surgery waits until collections resolve or mature (usually >6 weeks).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, urgent ERCP is indicated for cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction, not routinely. B, delayed surgery is appropriate only after severe or necrotizing pancreatitis. C, ursodiol does not prevent recurrence well enough, and it is reserved for patients who are not surgical candidates. D, without cholecystectomy the risk of recurrence is high.

stemHtml:
A 52-year-old man with decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis is admitted for treatment of cellulitis. Thirty hours after admission (about 36 hours after his last drink), he becomes anxious, tremulous, and diaphoretic. He reports seeing "bugs" on the wall but is oriented to person, place, and time. Temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse is 118/min, and blood pressure is 158/94 mm Hg. He has a coarse tremor of the outstretched hands. Laboratory studies show:
TestResult
Albumin2.4 g/dL
Total bilirubin3.8 mg/dL
INR2.0
Glucose104 mg/dL
Magnesium1.8 mg/dL
Ascites is present on examination. Thiamine has been given. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Lorazepam
explanationHtml: Alcohol withdrawal with alcoholic hallucinosis (hallucinations with a clear sensorium) and autonomic hyperactivity is treated with benzodiazepines, given symptom-triggered by CIWA-Ar score. In significant liver disease, choose benzodiazepines that need only glucuronidation and have no active metabolites: lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam ("LOT"). Long-acting agents (chlordiazepoxide, diazepam) go through hepatic CYP oxidation to active metabolites and can accumulate and cause oversedation or precipitate hepatic encephalopathy.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, chlordiazepoxide is a good choice for withdrawal in patients with normal liver function, but it is avoided in decompensated cirrhosis. B, antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and do not treat withdrawal; they are used only as adjuncts for refractory agitation. C, phenytoin does not prevent alcohol withdrawal seizures. E, naltrexone is for long-term relapse prevention after withdrawal and is hepatotoxic (avoid in decompensated cirrhosis; acamprosate or baclofen are options in liver disease).

stemHtml:
A 70-year-old man is admitted to the ICU with septic shock from pyelonephritis. He received norepinephrine for 36 hours and IV contrast for a CT scan on admission. On hospital day 3, his urine output has fallen to 300 mL/24 hours despite restoration of normal blood pressure and adequate volume status. Laboratory studies show:
TestResult
Serum creatinine3.6 mg/dL (0.9 mg/dL on admission)
BUN48 mg/dL
Urine sodium56 mEq/L
Fractional excretion of sodium3.2%
Urine osmolality290 mOsm/kg H2O
Urine sedimentNumerous granular "muddy brown" casts and renal tubular epithelial cells
Bladder ultrasound shows no retention, and renal ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answerHtml: Answer: C. Acute tubular necrosis
explanationHtml: Ischemic and septic ATN, possibly with a contrast contribution, damages tubules so they cannot reabsorb sodium or concentrate urine. This gives FENa >2%, urine Na >40, isosthenuric urine (about 300 mOsm/kg), a BUN:Cr ratio <20, and the hallmark muddy brown granular casts with renal tubular epithelial cells. Management is supportive: avoid nephrotoxins, adjust drug doses, manage volume and electrolytes, and dialyze for standard indications (AEIOU).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, prerenal AKI has FENa <1%, urine Na <20, urine osmolality >500, BUN:Cr >20, and bland sediment or hyaline casts. B, AIN causes WBC casts, sterile pyuria, and sometimes eosinophiluria, typically after a drug exposure (beta-lactams, PPIs, NSAIDs). D, obstruction is excluded by ultrasound. E, RPGN causes dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts.

stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 3, has heavy vaginal bleeding 20 minutes after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery of a 4.2-kg (9.3-lb) infant at term. She has moderate persistent asthma treated with an inhaled corticosteroid. The placenta was delivered intact, and there are no lacerations on inspection. Estimated blood loss is 1,100 mL. Pulse is 112/min and blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. Her antepartum blood pressures were normal. The uterus is soft and boggy above the umbilicus despite bimanual massage and an IV oxytocin infusion. Tranexamic acid has been given. Which of the following is the most appropriate next pharmacotherapy?
answerHtml: Answer: A. Intramuscular methylergonovine
explanationHtml: Uterine atony is the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage (≥1,000 mL). Risk factors here include macrosomia and multiparity. After massage and oxytocin, the next uterotonics are methylergonovine (an ergot alkaloid, contraindicated in hypertension or preeclampsia), carboprost (PGF2α, contraindicated in asthma because it causes bronchoconstriction), or misoprostol (PGE1). She is normotensive and asthmatic, so methylergonovine is the correct choice. If uterotonics fail, use a uterine balloon tamponade or a vacuum-induced hemorrhage-control device, then embolization or surgery (B-Lynch suture, uterine artery ligation, hysterectomy).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, carboprost can trigger severe bronchospasm in asthma. C and D, terbutaline and magnesium are tocolytics that relax the uterus and would worsen atony. E, nifedipine is a tocolytic and antihypertensive, and it also relaxes the uterus.

stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman at 16 weeks' gestation has a reactive rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test (titer 1:32) at her first prenatal visit, confirmed by a positive treponemal antibody test. She has a painless, clean-based ulcer on the labia that appeared 1 week ago. She had a severe allergic reaction with hives, wheezing, and hypotension after receiving penicillin as a child. HIV test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: Penicillin desensitization followed by intramuscular benzathine penicillin G

answerHtml: Answer: C. Penicillin desensitization followed by intramuscular benzathine penicillin G
explanationHtml: This is primary syphilis (painless chancre, reactive nontreponemal and treponemal tests) in pregnancy. Penicillin is the only treatment proven to prevent congenital syphilis. The CDC recommends that pregnant women with penicillin allergy be desensitized and then treated with penicillin. For primary syphilis this is benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once. Warn her about the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, which can cause preterm contractions or fetal distress. Follow RPR titers, and her partner(s) should be treated.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, doxycycline is an alternative only in nonpregnant patients. It is avoided in pregnancy because of fetal tooth and bone effects, and it does not treat the fetus reliably. B, ceftriaxone has limited data in pregnancy and is not recommended for preventing congenital syphilis. D, azithromycin resistance is common and it does not treat the fetus. E, delay risks congenital syphilis and fetal death.

stemHtml:
A 64-year-old man with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is brought to the emergency department because of 4 days of confusion, constipation, polyuria, and decreased oral intake. Pulse is 104/min and blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. Mucous membranes are dry. He is lethargic but arousable. Laboratory studies show:
TestResult
Calcium14.6 mg/dL
Albumin3.8 g/dL
Phosphorus2.1 mg/dL
Creatinine1.9 mg/dL (baseline 1.0 mg/dL)
Intact PTH8 pg/mL (low)
PTH-related peptideElevated
Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: E
options.html: Intravenous 0.9% saline, subcutaneous calcitonin, and intravenous zoledronic acid

answerHtml: Answer: E. Intravenous 0.9% saline, subcutaneous calcitonin, and intravenous zoledronic acid
explanationHtml: Severe, symptomatic hypercalcemia (>14 mg/dL with altered mental status) from humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy (PTHrP from squamous cell carcinoma, with suppressed PTH) needs three treatments together. (1) IV isotonic saline corrects the volume depletion caused by hypercalcemia-induced nephrogenic DI and increases calcium excretion. (2) Calcitonin lowers calcium within hours, but tachyphylaxis develops after 48 hours. (3) A bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid, dose-adjusted for renal function) or denosumab gives a sustained effect starting in 2–4 days. Denosumab is preferred if the creatinine is markedly impaired.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, loop diuretics are used only after volume repletion and only for fluid overload, never as monotherapy. B, oral bisphosphonates are absorbed poorly and act too slowly. C, dialysis is for severe renal failure or heart failure that prevents saline therapy. D, glucocorticoids work for calcitriol-mediated hypercalcemia (lymphoma, granulomatous disease) or myeloma, not PTHrP-mediated disease.

stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman comes to the clinic because she noticed drooping of the right side of her face when she woke up this morning. She has had pain behind her right ear since yesterday, and food tastes "different." Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows inability to close the right eye, loss of the right nasolabial fold, drooping of the right corner of the mouth, and inability to wrinkle the right forehead. There are no vesicles in the ear canal or on the palate. The remainder of the neurologic examination, including the other cranial nerves and limb strength, shows no abnormalities. She is not pregnant and does not have diabetes. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.html: MRI of the brain with contrast before treatment

answerHtml: Answer: D. Oral prednisone and eye protection
explanationHtml: An acute unilateral lower motor neuron facial palsy (forehead involved) with retroauricular pain and taste change, and no other deficits, is Bell palsy. AAN and AAO-HNS guidelines recommend oral corticosteroids within 72 hours of onset, which improves complete recovery. Adding an antiviral is optional and is considered only with steroids. Lubricating drops, ointment, and taping the eye at night prevent exposure keratopathy. Most patients recover within 3–6 months.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, an antiviral alone is not effective. B, imaging is not routine; it is reserved for atypical features (forehead sparing, other neurologic deficits, slow progression, no improvement by 3–4 months). C, observation gives up the benefit of steroids. E, LP and IV steroids are not indicated for typical Bell palsy. Vesicles would suggest Ramsay Hunt syndrome (VZV), which is treated with an antiviral plus steroids.

stemHtml: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being stabbed in the left chest. He is anxious and short of breath. Pulse is 136/min, respirations are 36/min, and blood pressure is 74/40 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 82% on a nonrebreather mask. The trachea is deviated to the right, the neck veins are distended, and breath sounds are absent over the left hemithorax, with hyperresonance to percussion. Heart sounds are audible. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Needle decompression of the left chest

options.label: C
options.html: Endotracheal intubation with positive pressure ventilation

options.label: E
options.html: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST)

answerHtml: Answer: B. Needle decompression of the left chest
explanationHtml: Hypotension, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, JVD, absent breath sounds, and hyperresonance is tension pneumothorax. It is a clinical diagnosis and needs immediate decompression. ATLS (10th edition) recommends a needle or finger thoracostomy at the 4th–5th intercostal space just anterior to the midaxillary line in adults (the 2nd ICS midclavicular line remains an option, especially in children). This is followed by definitive tube thoracostomy.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, waiting for an x-ray delays a life-saving procedure. C, positive pressure ventilation before decompression worsens a tension pneumothorax and can cause cardiac arrest. D, tamponade causes JVD and hypotension but with muffled heart sounds, bilateral breath sounds, and no tracheal deviation. E, FAST (eFAST can show absent lung sliding) must not delay treatment of a clinically obvious tension pneumothorax.

stemHtml: A 10-day-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of 6 episodes of green vomiting since this morning. He was born at term and had been feeding well and passing meconium and stools normally. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 158/min, and blood pressure is 74/48 mm Hg. He is fussy but consolable. Capillary refill is 2 seconds. The abdomen is soft and mildly distended, without erythema or peritoneal signs. Abdominal x-ray shows a nonspecific gas pattern with some distal bowel gas. IV fluids are started, and a nasogastric tube is placed. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: D
options.html: Observation and repeat x-ray in 24 hours

answerHtml: Answer: B. Upper gastrointestinal contrast series
explanationHtml: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise, and malrotation with midgut volvulus is the critical diagnosis. In a hemodynamically stable infant, the gold-standard test is an emergent upper GI series. It shows an abnormally positioned duodenojejunal junction (to the right of the spine or below the pylorus) or a "corkscrew" duodenum in volvulus. Treatment is the emergent Ladd procedure. An infant with peritonitis or shock goes straight to laparotomy. A normal x-ray does not exclude volvulus.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, ultrasound of the pylorus is for nonbilious projectile vomiting (pyloric stenosis, typically at 3–6 weeks). Ultrasound can suggest volvulus (whirlpool sign, reversed SMA/SMV relationship), but UGI remains the definitive test. C, contrast enema evaluates distal obstruction (Hirschsprung disease, meconium ileus) and is unreliable for malrotation. D, delay risks necrosis of the entire midgut. E, bilious vomiting is not consistent with simple gastroenteritis.

stemHtml: A 76-year-old man comes to the clinic because of 2 episodes of lightheadedness and one episode of fainting while walking uphill over the past month. He also reports chest tightness with exertion. Pulse is 72/min and regular, and blood pressure is 118/90 mm Hg. Carotid upstrokes are weak and delayed. There is a grade 3/6 late-peaking crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to both carotids, and the second heart sound is soft and single. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Coronary angiography as the initial test

answerHtml: Answer: E. Transthoracic echocardiography
