explanationHtml: Exertional syncope, angina, pulsus parvus et tardus, a late-peaking systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids, and a soft single S2 indicate severe aortic stenosis. The diagnostic test is TTE, which gives valve area, mean gradient (≥40 mm Hg), peak velocity (≥4 m/s), and LV function. Symptomatic severe AS is a class 1 indication for aortic valve replacement (TAVR or SAVR chosen by a heart team, 2020 ACC/AHA). Untreated, the average survival after syncope is about 3 years.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, exercise testing is contraindicated in symptomatic severe AS. It is used only to unmask symptoms in apparently asymptomatic patients. B, coronary assessment comes as part of planning for valve replacement, after the valve diagnosis is established. C, a Holter monitor looks for arrhythmia, but the exam already points to a structural cause. D, the history is not neurologic.

stemHtml: A 67-year-old woman has a bone mineral density scan for routine screening. Her lowest T-score is −2.7 at the femoral neck. She has never had a fracture and has no back pain. She went through menopause at age 51 and has never used hormone therapy. She has gastroesophageal reflux controlled with lifestyle changes, can sit upright, and has no esophageal stricture or dysphagia. Serum calcium, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, creatinine, and TSH are normal. She takes calcium and vitamin D supplements. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

options.label: B
options.html: Continue calcium and vitamin D alone

answerHtml: Answer: A. Oral alendronate
explanationHtml: A T-score ≤−2.5 defines osteoporosis. USPSTF recommends DXA screening for all women ≥65 and for younger postmenopausal women at increased risk. The AACE and ACP first-line treatment for most postmenopausal osteoporosis is a bisphosphonate (alendronate, risedronate, or zoledronic acid), which reduces vertebral and hip fractures. Instruct her to take it with a full glass of water on an empty stomach and stay upright for 30 minutes. Consider a drug holiday after about 5 years (oral) if risk is low, because of the risks of atypical femoral fracture and osteonecrosis of the jaw.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, supplements alone do not treat osteoporosis. C, estrogen is not recommended mainly for osteoporosis in a 67-year-old (cardiovascular, thromboembolic, and breast cancer risks). D, anabolic agents (teriparatide, abaloparatide, romosozumab) are first-line only for very high risk patients (recent or multiple fractures, T-score <−3.0). E, calcitonin is weak and is not used for fracture prevention.

stemHtml: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because his teacher reports that he cannot stay in his seat, interrupts others, loses his belongings, and does not finish assignments. His parents report the same behaviors at home for the past 2 years, including difficulty waiting his turn and frequent careless mistakes on homework. Vanderbilt rating scales completed by parents and teacher are consistent with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, combined presentation. He has no history of cardiac disease, syncope, or tics, and there is no family history of sudden cardiac death. Physical examination, including blood pressure and cardiac auscultation, shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: A
options.html: Behavioral parent training alone, deferring medication until adolescence

answerHtml: Answer: C. Methylphenidate, along with behavioral interventions
explanationHtml: The AAP 2019 guideline recommends FDA-approved medication for children aged 6–11 years with ADHD, together with parent training in behavior management and/or behavioral classroom interventions. Stimulants (methylphenidate or amphetamine preparations) are first-line because they have the largest effect size. Monitor growth, appetite, sleep, heart rate, and blood pressure. A routine ECG is not required without cardiac risk factors. For preschoolers (4–5 years), behavioral therapy comes first.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, behavioral therapy alone is first-line only at preschool age. B and D, nonstimulants (atomoxetine, viloxazine, guanfacine ER, clonidine ER) are second-line, or are used when stimulants are not tolerated or there are comorbidities (e.g., tics, substance-use concerns). E, antipsychotics are not ADHD treatments.

stemHtml:
A 28-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, comes to the emergency department because of mild left lower abdominal pain and light vaginal spotting. Her last menstrual period was 6½ weeks ago. Pulse is 78/min and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft, with mild left lower quadrant tenderness and no rebound. Pelvic examination shows a closed cervical os and mild left adnexal tenderness. Laboratory studies and imaging show:
TestResult
Serum β-hCG2,800 mIU/mL (repeat in 48 hours: 3,100 mIU/mL)
Transvaginal ultrasonographyNo intrauterine pregnancy; 2.4-cm left adnexal mass separate from the ovary, without cardiac activity; no free fluid
Hemoglobin12.6 g/dL
Creatinine, AST, ALTNormal
Blood typeA, Rh-positive
She is not breastfeeding, has no known contraindications to any medication, understands the need for follow-up, and lives 10 minutes from the hospital. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Expectant management with repeat β-hCG in 1 week

answerHtml: Answer: D. Intramuscular methotrexate
explanationHtml: No intrauterine pregnancy, an extraovarian adnexal mass on TVUS, and an abnormal hCG rise (about 11% in 48 hours, where a viable early pregnancy usually rises at least 35–50%) point to tubal ectopic pregnancy. An adnexal mass is diagnostic even though the hCG (2,800) is still below the conservative discriminatory level (ACOG cites up to 3,500 mIU/mL). She is a good methotrexate candidate per ACOG: hemodynamically stable, unruptured, hCG <5,000, mass <3.5–4 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, normal labs, and reliable follow-up. Check hCG on days 4 and 7. A drop of ≥15% between them means success. She is Rh-positive, so no anti-D is needed.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, expectant management is reserved for very low and declining hCG (e.g., <200 mIU/mL). B, laparotomy is for unstable or ruptured ectopic; laparoscopic salpingectomy is the surgical choice in stable patients who are not candidates for methotrexate. C, D&C does not treat a tubal pregnancy. E, mifepristone with misoprostol is for intrauterine pregnancy loss or abortion and is contraindicated in ectopic pregnancy.

stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of recurrent episodes of sudden intense fear with palpitations, sweating, trembling, chest tightness, and a feeling that she is "going to die." Each episode peaks within 10 minutes and resolves within 30 minutes. They occur 2–3 times weekly without a trigger, including once while she was asleep. For the past 2 months, she has constantly worried about having another attack and has stopped driving on highways. Two emergency department evaluations with ECG, troponin, TSH, and toxicology screening were normal. She drinks one glass of wine weekly and does not use drugs or caffeine. She is not pregnant. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term pharmacotherapy?
answerHtml: Answer: D. Sertraline
explanationHtml: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks followed by ≥1 month of persistent worry and avoidance is panic disorder (with agoraphobic avoidance), with medical causes excluded. First-line treatment is CBT and/or an SSRI (sertraline, paroxetine, fluoxetine, escitalopram) or the SNRI venlafaxine. Start at a low dose, because patients with panic disorder are sensitive to initial jitteriness, and titrate up. A short benzodiazepine bridge can be used during the first weeks while the SSRI takes effect.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, long-term benzodiazepine monotherapy carries risks of dependence, tolerance, withdrawal, and cognitive impairment, and is not first-line. B, propranolol blunts somatic symptoms in performance anxiety but does not treat panic disorder. C, buspirone is used for generalized anxiety disorder and does not work for panic. E, hydroxyzine is an antihistamine used for short-term GAD symptoms, not panic disorder.

stemHtml: An 83-year-old woman is on hospital day 2 after surgical repair of a hip fracture. The night nurse reports that she has been pulling at her IV line, talking to people who are not in the room, and trying to climb out of bed. In the morning she is drowsy, cannot keep track of the conversation, and cannot recite the months of the year backward. By the afternoon she is calmer but disoriented to date. Her daughter says she lived alone, managed her own finances, and had "a perfectly sharp mind" before the fall. Medications include scheduled oxycodone and as-needed diphenhydramine for sleep. She has a urinary catheter. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F). Urinalysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.html: Major neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer disease

options.label: C
options.html: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features

answerHtml: Answer: A. Delirium
explanationHtml: An acute onset with a fluctuating course, inattention (cannot do months backward), and altered level of consciousness in an older inpatient who was cognitively normal at baseline is delirium (Confusion Assessment Method positive). Precipitants here include surgery, opioids, an anticholinergic (diphenhydramine, which is on the Beers list), a urinary catheter, possible infection, and the hospital environment. Management: find and treat the causes, stop deliriogenic drugs, remove tethers such as catheters, reorient her, maintain her sleep-wake cycle, and provide glasses and hearing aids. Use low-dose antipsychotics only if agitation endangers her. Avoid benzodiazepines unless the cause is alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, dementia develops gradually over months to years, attention is relatively preserved early on, and she had a normal baseline. C, D, and E, primary psychotic and mood disorders do not cause fluctuating consciousness or inattention, and a new psychosis in an 83-year-old is organic until proven otherwise.

stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman comes to the clinic because she found a lump in her left breast 2 weeks ago while showering. It has not changed in size during her menstrual cycle. She has no nipple discharge. Her last screening mammogram 2 years ago was normal. Her mother was diagnosed with breast cancer at age 68. Examination shows a 2-cm, firm, nontender, mobile mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. There is no skin change or axillary lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Reassurance and re-examination after her next menstrual period

options.label: B
options.html: Diagnostic mammography and targeted breast ultrasonography

answerHtml: Answer: B. Diagnostic mammography and targeted breast ultrasonography
explanationHtml: A palpable breast mass in a woman ≥30 years old is evaluated first with a diagnostic mammogram plus targeted ultrasound (ACR Appropriateness Criteria and NCCN). A suspicious lesion (BI-RADS 4–5) then has an image-guided core-needle biopsy. For women <30, ultrasound is the first test. Imaging comes before biopsy so that the post-biopsy changes do not obscure the images and so that other lesions can be found.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, observing through a cycle may be reasonable in a young woman with a soft, cyclic mass, but this is a persistent, firm mass at age 45 and needs imaging. C, MRI is not an initial test for a palpable mass. It is used for high-risk screening or for staging after a cancer diagnosis. D, core-needle biopsy has replaced excisional biopsy as the first tissue diagnosis, and imaging comes first. E, a screening exam is the wrong test for a symptomatic patient.

stemHtml: A 34-year-old man comes to the clinic in July because of a rash on his thigh for 4 days. He went hiking in Connecticut 10 days ago. He has mild fatigue, myalgia, and headache. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F). Examination shows a 9-cm, round, erythematous, slightly warm patch with central clearing on the right posterior thigh. There is no joint swelling, facial weakness, or murmur, and the neurologic examination is normal. ECG is normal. He has no drug allergies and is not immunocompromised. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Lyme serology, with treatment only if the result is positive

answerHtml: Answer: E. Oral doxycycline
explanationHtml: An expanding erythema migrans lesion of ≥5 cm after exposure in an endemic area (the northeastern US) in summer is early localized Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi). It is a clinical diagnosis, and serology is often negative this early. IDSA/AAN/ACR 2020 recommends oral doxycycline for 10 days. Amoxicillin or cefuroxime axetil for 14 days are alternatives (amoxicillin is used in pregnancy, and doxycycline for short courses is now acceptable in children of any age).
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, IV ceftriaxone is for neurologic Lyme disease with parenchymal involvement or severe carditis (high-degree AV block). B, serology lacks sensitivity in early disease, and waiting delays needed treatment. C, first-generation cephalosporins are ineffective against B. burgdorferi. D, macrolides are less effective and are reserved for patients who cannot take first-line agents.

stemHtml: A hospital's quality committee reviews data showing that the medical ICU's central line–associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) rate is twice the national benchmark. A review of recent cases shows that lines are often inserted in the femoral vein, maximal sterile barrier precautions are used inconsistently, and some lines remain in place days after the patient no longer needs them. Which of the following interventions is most likely to reduce the CLABSI rate?

options.label: A
options.html: Scheduled replacement of all central venous catheters every 7 days

options.label: B
options.html: Prophylactic systemic antibiotics for all patients with a central line

options.label: C
options.html: An evidence-based insertion and maintenance bundle with a checklist and empowerment of nurses to stop nonadherent procedures

options.label: D
options.html: Disciplinary action against physicians whose patients develop CLABSI

options.label: E
options.html: Routine surveillance blood cultures every 48 hours in all patients with central lines

answerHtml: Answer: C. An evidence-based insertion and maintenance bundle with a checklist and empowerment of nurses to stop nonadherent procedures
explanationHtml: The CLABSI bundle covers hand hygiene, maximal sterile barrier precautions, chlorhexidine-alcohol skin antisepsis, avoiding the femoral site in adults (subclavian is preferred), and daily review of whether the line is still needed with prompt removal. Combined with a checklist and a culture that lets any team member stop a breach, this has been shown to reduce CLABSI dramatically. It is a systems-based approach that builds safety into standard work.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, routine scheduled replacement does not lower infection rates and adds insertion risks (CDC recommends against it). B, prophylactic antibiotics promote resistance and C. difficile without preventing CLABSI. D, a blame culture discourages reporting and does not fix system causes. E, surveillance cultures increase false positives and costs without preventing infection.

stemHtml: A 4-month-old girl, born at term, is brought to the emergency department in January because of 3 days of rhinorrhea and cough, followed by increased work of breathing since yesterday. She is feeding about 70% of her usual volume and has had 5 wet diapers in the past 24 hours. Temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F), pulse is 150/min, and respirations are 52/min. Oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. She has copious nasal secretions, mild subcostal retractions, and diffuse fine crackles and expiratory wheezes bilaterally. She is alert and consolable. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: Nasal suctioning, monitoring of hydration, and supportive care

answerHtml: Answer: C. Nasal suctioning, monitoring of hydration, and supportive care
explanationHtml: A viral URI prodrome followed by tachypnea, retractions, crackles, and wheezes in an infant during winter is bronchiolitis, most often caused by RSV. AAP guidance says it is a clinical diagnosis and management is supportive: nasal suctioning, hydration (NG or IV if intake is inadequate), and supplemental oxygen only if SpO2 is persistently <90%. Hospitalize for hypoxemia, dehydration, apnea, or severe distress. Prevention for infants is maternal RSV vaccination at 32–36 weeks, or nirsevimab for infants entering their first RSV season.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, B, and E, bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and epinephrine do not improve meaningful outcomes in bronchiolitis, and the AAP recommends against them. D, routine chest x-ray and antibiotics are not recommended, since she has no evidence of a secondary bacterial infection.

stemHtml: A 42-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of 6 hours of severe, colicky right flank pain that radiates to the groin, with nausea. He has no fever or dysuria. After IV ketorolac, his pain is well controlled and he can tolerate oral fluids. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 84/min, and blood pressure is 132/84 mm Hg. Urinalysis shows 30 RBCs/hpf, no leukocyte esterase, no nitrites, and no bacteria. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. Noncontrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis shows a 6-mm stone in the right distal ureter with mild hydronephrosis. The left kidney is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: E
options.html: Oral NSAID, tamsulosin, hydration, and urine straining with follow-up imaging

answerHtml: Answer: E. Oral NSAID, tamsulosin, hydration, and urine straining with follow-up imaging
explanationHtml: An uncomplicated distal ureteral stone ≤10 mm, with controlled pain, no infection, normal renal function, and two functioning kidneys, can be managed with observation and medical expulsive therapy. Per AUA guidelines, an alpha-blocker (tamsulosin) relaxes ureteral smooth muscle and helps passage, particularly for distal stones of 5–10 mm. NSAIDs are the first-line analgesic. Strain the urine so the stone can be analyzed to guide prevention, and reimage. Intervention is indicated if the stone has not passed in about 4–6 weeks.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and B, intervention is for failure of conservative therapy, uncontrolled pain, AKI, an obstructed solitary kidney, or patient preference. C, PCNL is for large renal stones (>2 cm) or staghorn calculi. D, prevention should be tailored to stone and urine analysis, and it does not deal with the current stone. Note: an obstructing stone with infection (fever, pyuria) is a urologic emergency that needs decompression with a ureteral stent or nephrostomy.

stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 26 weeks' gestation comes for a prenatal visit. Her BMI before pregnancy was 29 kg/m<sup>2</sup>. Her first-trimester HbA<sub>1c</sub> was 5.4%. A nonfasting 1-hour 50-g oral glucose challenge test performed last week showed a plasma glucose concentration of 152 mg/dL; the threshold used by her practice is 140 mg/dL. She feels well. Fundal height is 26 cm. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.html: Repeat the 1-hour glucose challenge test in 4 weeks

options.label: D
options.html: Measure HbA<sub>1c</sub> to establish the diagnosis

options.label: E
options.html: Medical nutrition therapy and rescreening at 36 weeks

answerHtml: Answer: B. 3-hour 100-g oral glucose tolerance test
explanationHtml: ACOG's two-step approach screens at 24–28 weeks with a nonfasting 50-g glucose challenge. A positive result (≥130, 135, or 140 mg/dL depending on the practice, but <200 mg/dL) is followed by a diagnostic fasting 3-hour 100-g OGTT. Gestational diabetes is diagnosed when ≥2 values are abnormal (Carpenter-Coustan: fasting ≥95, 1 h ≥180, 2 h ≥155, 3 h ≥140 mg/dL). The one-step 75-g 2-hour OGTT (IADPSG) is an alternative.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and E, treatment needs a diagnosis first. When GDM is diagnosed, medical nutrition therapy is first-line and insulin is the preferred drug if targets are not met. C, repeating the screen delays diagnosis. D, HbA<sub>1c</sub> is insensitive for GDM. It is used early in pregnancy to detect pre-existing diabetes, not to diagnose GDM.

stemHtml:
A 35-year-old man comes for a routine examination. He has no symptoms and no history of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or hypertension. He does not smoke. His father had a myocardial infarction at age 48. BMI is 25 kg/m2, and blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg. Examination shows thickening of the Achilles tendons. Fasting lipid panel:
TestResult
Total cholesterol292 mg/dL
LDL cholesterol212 mg/dL (repeat 205 mg/dL)
HDL cholesterol48 mg/dL
Triglycerides160 mg/dL
TSH, fasting glucose, liver enzymes, and urinalysis are normal. In addition to lifestyle counseling, which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: High-intensity statin therapy, such as atorvastatin 40–80 mg daily

options.label: B
options.html: Lifestyle modification alone and recheck lipids in 6 months

options.label: C
options.html: Low-intensity statin therapy, such as pravastatin 10 mg daily

options.label: E
options.html: Calculate the 10-year ASCVD risk and start a statin only if risk is ≥7.5%

answerHtml: Answer: A. High-intensity statin therapy, such as atorvastatin 40–80 mg daily
explanationHtml: The 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline names primary severe hypercholesterolemia (LDL-C ≥190 mg/dL, ages 20–75) as a statin benefit group. These patients get a high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 40–80 or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg) without calculating 10-year risk. The goal is at least a 50% LDL reduction. His tendon xanthomas and premature family history suggest heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, so cascade screening of first-degree relatives is warranted. If LDL stays ≥100 mg/dL on maximal statin, add ezetimibe and then a PCSK9 inhibitor.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B and C, lifestyle alone or low-intensity therapy undertreats his very high lifetime risk. D, ezetimibe is an add-on, not first-line. E, the pooled cohort equations are not used, and would underestimate risk, when LDL is ≥190.

stemHtml: A 47-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his sister after she found a goodbye letter he wrote to his children. He was laid off 2 months ago, is going through a divorce, and has had depressed mood, insomnia, and weight loss for 6 weeks. He drinks 6–8 beers daily. He says that he has a loaded handgun at home and plans to shoot himself this weekend "when the kids are with their mother." He refuses admission and says he wants to go home. He is not intoxicated (blood alcohol undetectable), and his medical evaluation shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Have him sign a no-suicide contract and schedule outpatient follow-up in 1 week

options.label: B
options.html: Prescribe sertraline and discharge him with a crisis hotline number

options.label: C
options.html: Discharge him to his sister's care after she agrees to remove the firearm

options.label: D
options.html: Admit him to an inpatient psychiatric unit, involuntarily if necessary

options.label: E
options.html: Respect his autonomy and discharge him because he has decision-making capacity

answerHtml: Answer: D. Admit him to an inpatient psychiatric unit, involuntarily if necessary
explanationHtml: He is at imminent, very high suicide risk. He has a specific plan, a lethal means available, a timeline, preparatory behavior (a goodbye letter), and several risk factors: male sex, middle age, alcohol use, depression, and recent losses (job and divorce). A patient who is an imminent danger to himself because of a mental illness can be held involuntarily for emergency evaluation and treatment under state law. Inpatient admission is the only way to keep him safe. This is one of the recognized limits on autonomy in US law, along with danger to others and grave disability.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, no-suicide contracts are not protective and are not recommended. B, an SSRI takes weeks to work, and outpatient care is unsafe with imminent intent. C, means restriction is important but not sufficient with a specific plan and intent. E, the danger-to-self exception overrides a refusal in this setting; his acute suicidality from depression also undermines the reliability of his decision.

stemHtml:
A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of 2 days of headache, confusion, and petechiae on her legs. Temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F), pulse is 106/min, and blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg. She is disoriented, with intermittent word-finding difficulty. Laboratory studies show:
TestResult
Hemoglobin7.9 g/dL
Platelet count14,000/mm3
Reticulocyte count8%
Peripheral smearNumerous schistocytes
LDH1,450 U/L
HaptoglobinUndetectable
PT/INR and aPTTNormal
FibrinogenNormal
Creatinine1.3 mg/dL
Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) testNegative
Blood is sent for ADAMTS13 activity. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
answerHtml: Answer: B. Therapeutic plasma exchange
explanationHtml: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes, high LDH, low haptoglobin, negative DAT), severe thrombocytopenia, neurologic symptoms, fever, and mild renal involvement with normal coagulation studies is thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. It is usually caused by autoantibodies against ADAMTS13 (activity <10%), and a high PLASMIC score supports the diagnosis. Untreated mortality is about 90%, so plasma exchange should start urgently, without waiting for the ADAMTS13 result. It removes the antibodies and replaces the enzyme. ISTH guidance adds glucocorticoids, caplacizumab (anti-vWF), and often rituximab.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, platelet transfusion is relatively contraindicated ("fuel on the fire," microthrombi) unless there is life-threatening bleeding or a procedure is needed. C, IVIG is used for ITP, which does not cause MAHA. D, splenectomy is reserved for refractory or relapsing cases. E, there is no indication for anticoagulation, and it would raise bleeding risk with platelets of 14,000.

stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation, not on anticoagulation, is brought to the emergency department because of the sudden onset of severe, diffuse abdominal pain 4 hours ago, followed by one episode of vomiting and a loose bowel movement. She is writhing in pain. Pulse is 116/min and irregularly irregular, and blood pressure is 142/86 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft and only mildly tender, with no guarding or rebound. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 19,000/mm<sup>3</sup>, serum lactate of 3.8 mmol/L, and normal lipase. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.html: Supine and upright abdominal x-rays alone

options.label: D
options.html: CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis

answerHtml: Answer: D. CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis
explanationHtml: Sudden severe abdominal pain out of proportion to the exam, gut emptying (vomiting, diarrhea), leukocytosis, and a raised lactate in a patient with AF off anticoagulation suggest acute mesenteric ischemia from a superior mesenteric artery embolus. The diagnostic test of choice is CT angiography (multidetector CTA), which should be done promptly, without waiting on creatinine concerns. Start IV heparin, fluids, and broad-spectrum antibiotics at the same time, and arrange urgent revascularization (embolectomy or endovascular). Laparotomy is needed if there are peritoneal signs, to resect nonviable bowel.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, colonoscopy can show ischemic colitis but does not image the SMA, and insufflation can be harmful. B, plain films are usually normal early ("thumbprinting" and pneumatosis appear late) and delay diagnosis. C, upper endoscopy is not indicated. E, HIDA is used for acute cholecystitis.

stemHtml: A new blood biomarker screening program for pancreatic cancer is evaluated in an observational study. Among patients whose cancer was detected by screening, median survival from the date of diagnosis was 3.1 years, compared with 1.2 years among patients whose cancer was diagnosed after symptoms developed. However, the cancers were of the same stage distribution and histology, treatments were identical, and in both groups the average age at death from pancreatic cancer was 71 years. Pancreatic cancer mortality in the screened population was unchanged. Which of the following best explains the apparent survival benefit?
answerHtml: Answer: E. Lead-time bias
explanationHtml: Lead-time bias happens when screening moves the date of diagnosis earlier without changing when the patient dies. Survival measured from diagnosis looks longer even though the disease course is unchanged. The giveaways are an identical age at death and unchanged disease-specific mortality. Screening benefit should therefore be judged by mortality in randomized trials, not by survival from diagnosis.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, length-time bias happens when screening preferentially detects slower-growing, less aggressive tumors with a better prognosis. Here stage and histology were the same and the timing of death did not change. B, observer bias comes from investigators' knowledge of exposure affecting how outcomes are assessed. C, recall bias affects retrospective self-report (case-control studies). D, the Hawthorne effect is a change in subjects' behavior because they know they are being studied.

stemHtml: A 42-year-old woman comes for follow-up of hypertension diagnosed 2 years ago. Her blood pressure remains elevated despite adherence to amlodipine 10 mg, lisinopril 40 mg, and chlorthalidone 25 mg daily. Home readings average 154/96 mm Hg. She reports muscle cramps and fatigue. She does not take NSAIDs, decongestants, or oral contraceptives, and has no symptoms of sleep apnea. BMI is 24 kg/m<sup>2</sup>. Examination shows no abdominal bruit, cushingoid features, or edema. Laboratory studies show a serum potassium of 3.0 mEq/L, sodium of 143 mEq/L, bicarbonate of 31 mEq/L, and creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: C
options.html: Plasma aldosterone concentration and plasma renin activity

options.label: D
options.html: CT scan of the adrenal glands

answerHtml: Answer: C. Plasma aldosterone concentration and plasma renin activity
explanationHtml: Resistant hypertension (uncontrolled on three agents including a diuretic) with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis strongly suggests primary hyperaldosteronism, the most common cause of secondary hypertension. Endocrine Society guidance recommends screening patients with resistant hypertension or hypertension with hypokalemia (the 2025 update broadens this to all adults with hypertension). Screening uses the aldosterone-to-renin ratio, ideally on a morning sample after correcting hypokalemia. Most antihypertensives can be continued for the first screen. A positive screen (high aldosterone, suppressed renin) is followed by confirmatory testing (e.g., saline suppression), then adrenal CT and adrenal venous sampling for lateralization before surgery.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, renovascular disease (fibromuscular dysplasia in a young woman) is possible, but an abdominal bruit, flash pulmonary edema, or a creatinine rise on ACE inhibitor would be expected, and hypokalemia with alkalosis points first to aldosterone. B and E, pheochromocytoma and Cushing syndrome are less likely without paroxysms or cushingoid features. D, imaging before biochemical confirmation is wrong: adrenal incidentalomas are common and can mislead.

stemHtml: A 40-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, comes to the clinic to discuss the results of genetic testing performed after her sister was diagnosed with ovarian cancer at age 46. She carries a pathogenic BRCA1 variant. She has completed childbearing. She has annual breast MRI and mammography, both normal most recently 4 months ago. Pelvic examination shows no abnormalities. She asks how to reduce her ovarian cancer risk. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.label: B
options.html: Annual transvaginal ultrasonography and CA-125 measurement instead of surgery

answerHtml: Answer: A. Risk-reducing bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
explanationHtml: BRCA1 carriers have a lifetime ovarian (tubal) cancer risk of about 40–45%, and there is no effective screening. NCCN and ACOG recommend risk-reducing BSO at age 35–40 for BRCA1 carriers once childbearing is complete (40–45 for BRCA2). It reduces ovarian, tubal, and peritoneal cancer risk by about 80% and lowers all-cause mortality. Many serous "ovarian" cancers start in the fallopian tube, so the tubes must be removed completely. Discuss surgical menopause, and offer short-term hormone therapy, which is generally considered acceptable in carriers without breast cancer.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, TVUS and CA-125 have not reduced mortality and are only a short-term option for women who decline or delay surgery. C, removing the uterus while keeping the ovaries and tubes does not address the risk. D, waiting misses the window when risk climbs sharply (BRCA1 ovarian cancers often occur in the 40s). E, tamoxifen reduces breast cancer risk but not ovarian cancer risk. Oral contraceptives do reduce ovarian cancer risk but are much less effective than surgery.

stemHtml: A 14-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of episodes of inconsolable crying in which he draws his knees up to his chest, every 15–20 minutes for the past 8 hours. Between episodes he is lethargic. He vomited twice and passed a stool mixed with dark red mucus. Temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 140/min, and blood pressure is 92/58 mm Hg. A sausage-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant. There is no abdominal distention, guarding, or rebound. IV fluids are started, and he remains hemodynamically stable. Ultrasonography shows a "target" sign in the right upper quadrant. There is no free air on x-ray. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: CT scan of the abdomen with contrast

options.label: E
options.html: Air or hydrostatic contrast enema reduction

answerHtml: Answer: E. Air or hydrostatic contrast enema reduction
explanationHtml: Intermittent colicky pain, lethargy, "currant jelly" stool, a sausage-shaped mass, and a target sign on ultrasound are diagnostic of ileocolic intussusception, the most common cause of bowel obstruction from 6 months to 3 years. In a stable child without peritonitis or perforation, a pneumatic (air) or hydrostatic enema under fluoroscopic or ultrasound guidance both confirms and treats it, with success rates of about 80–90%. A pediatric surgeon should be available in case of perforation. Watch for recurrence over the next 24 hours.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, surgery is for peritonitis, perforation, shock, or a failed enema. B, CT adds radiation and delay; ultrasound has already made the diagnosis. C, a barium follow-through is not used. D, delay risks bowel ischemia, necrosis, and perforation.

stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of a new right-sided headache for 3 weeks, pain in the jaw when chewing, and scalp tenderness when brushing her hair. Yesterday she had an episode of blurred vision in the right eye that lasted 5 minutes. She also has aching and stiffness in her shoulders in the morning. Temperature is 37.8°C (100.0°F). The right temporal artery is tender and nodular, with a reduced pulse. Visual acuity and funduscopic examination are currently normal. ESR is 92 mm/h and C-reactive protein is 6.4 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Temporal artery biopsy, and start corticosteroids only if biopsy confirms the diagnosis

answerHtml: Answer: C. Start high-dose glucocorticoids immediately
explanationHtml: A new headache in a patient over 50, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, an abnormal temporal artery, polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms, a high ESR/CRP, and transient monocular visual loss (amaurosis fugax) is giant cell arteritis with ischemic visual symptoms. To prevent permanent blindness, glucocorticoids are started immediately: prednisone 40–60 mg/day, or IV methylprednisolone pulse when there is visual loss, per ACR 2021. Temporal artery biopsy (or vascular ultrasound) is then done within about 1–2 weeks, and histology stays positive during that time. Tocilizumab is added as a steroid-sparing agent.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, withholding steroids until biopsy risks irreversible vision loss. B, MRI does not change immediate management. D, NSAIDs do not treat vasculitis. E, 15 mg is the polymyalgia rheumatica dose and is inadequate for GCA.

stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman who recently emigrated from India is starting work as a nurse in a US hospital. Pre-employment interferon-γ release assay (IGRA) is positive. She received BCG vaccine as an infant. She has no cough, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. She is not pregnant, does not have HIV infection, and takes no medications. Chest x-ray shows no abnormalities. Liver enzymes are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: No treatment, because the positive result is caused by BCG vaccination

options.label: D
options.html: Sputum acid-fast bacilli smear and culture on 3 specimens before any decision

answerHtml: Answer: B. Daily rifampin for 4 months
explanationHtml: A positive IGRA with no symptoms and a normal chest x-ray is latent TB infection. IGRAs use antigens (ESAT-6, CFP-10) that are absent from BCG and most nontuberculous mycobacteria, so a positive result is not explained by BCG. This is a key NEET PG → USMLE difference, and one reason IGRA is preferred in BCG-vaccinated people. CDC/NTCA preferred regimens are short rifamycin-based courses: 4 months of daily rifampin (4R), 3 months of weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine (3HP), or 3 months of daily isoniazid plus rifampin (3HR). They have better completion rates and less hepatotoxicity than 6–9 months of isoniazid.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A, four-drug therapy is for active TB. C, IGRA is not affected by BCG, and she has a risk factor (birth in a high-burden country). D, sputum testing is for patients with symptoms or an abnormal CXR. E, repeating the test delays treatment of a confirmed infection.

stemHtml: A 78-year-old man is intubated in the ICU after a massive left hemispheric hemorrhagic stroke. Neurology estimates that he has almost no chance of regaining independent function. He has no advance directive and did not designate a health care power of attorney. His wife of 50 years says that he told her many times he would "never want to be kept alive on machines," and she asks for a transition to comfort care. His adult son, who lives in another state, insists that "everything be done." His adult daughter agrees with her mother. In accordance with standard surrogate hierarchy, which of the following is the most appropriate way to proceed?

options.label: A
options.html: Follow the wife's decision, based on the patient's previously expressed wishes

options.label: B
options.html: Follow the majority decision of the adult children

options.label: C
options.html: The physician should decide based on the patient's best interest

options.label: D
options.html: Obtain a court-appointed guardian before any change in care

options.label: E
options.html: Continue full treatment indefinitely until all family members agree

answerHtml: Answer: A. Follow the wife's decision, based on the patient's previously expressed wishes
explanationHtml: When a patient without capacity has no advance directive or appointed agent, decisions pass to surrogates in a hierarchy that is typical across most US states: legal guardian, then spouse, then adult children, then parents, then adult siblings, then other relatives or close friends. The surrogate uses substituted judgment, meaning what the patient would have wanted, which here is clear from his repeated statements. The team should still hold a family meeting, explain the prognosis, and offer palliative care and ethics consultation to support the son. But the son's objection does not override the legally recognized surrogate.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: B, the children rank below the spouse, and the decision is not a vote. C, the physician defers to the surrogate. "Best interest" is the standard only when the patient's wishes are unknown. D, courts are a last resort for intractable conflict or when no surrogate is available. E, insisting on consensus can prolong treatment the patient did not want.

stemHtml: A screening test for colorectal neoplasia uses a fecal biomarker concentration, with values at or above 100 ng/mL considered positive. Investigators propose lowering the positivity cutoff to 50 ng/mL. Assuming disease prevalence in the screened population stays the same, which of the following changes in test characteristics is most likely to result from lowering the cutoff?

options.label: B
options.html: Sensitivity increases and positive predictive value increases

options.label: C
options.html: Specificity increases and negative predictive value decreases

options.label: D
options.html: Sensitivity increases and negative predictive value increases

answerHtml: Answer: D. Sensitivity increases and negative predictive value increases
explanationHtml: If higher values indicate disease, lowering the cutoff classifies more people as positive. More true cases are caught, so false negatives fall and sensitivity rises. More healthy people test positive, so false positives rise and specificity falls. With fewer false negatives, a negative result is more reassuring and NPV rises. With more false positives, PPV falls. This is how the trade-off along an ROC curve works.
whyNotHtml: Why the others are wrong: A and C describe raising the cutoff. B, PPV falls because of the extra false positives. E, a single cutoff change cannot raise both sensitivity and specificity; that would need a better test (a larger area under the ROC curve).
